text: Corollary 16.43.2 . BD99C3A4D1ED There are positive smooth strictly PSH functions $u,v$ on $\mathbb C^2$ with $u-v\to 0$ at infinity and finite total Monge–Ampère masses, such that $\int (dd^ cu)^2>\int (dd^ cv)^2$. e \mathbb C^ n$ be an unbounded domain, and define $W_ D$ by the same jointly SH, nonpositive, separately PSH family and distance constraint as in proposition 7.19.3 , now with the extended slice convention. Then $W_ D$ is jointly USC and SH or identically $-\infty $, is separately PSH, is symmetric, and satisfies $W_ D\leq g_ D$. Moreover $W_ D=g_ D$ if and only if $g_ D$ is symmetric. No isolated-pole, local boundedness or total-mass assertion is included. For $D=\mathbb C^ n$ put $W_ D=g_ D=-\infty $. Proof. If the defining family is empty there is nothing to regularize. Otherwise its joint upper envelope regularization $F$ is SH by the canonical envelope theorem; the uniform upper bound is zero. The continuous distance constraint off the diagonal persists, and its local logarithmic upper bound forces value $-\infty $ on the diagonal. For fixed $w_0$, the upper regularizations in $z$ of \[  \sup _{|w-w_0|<\epsilon }W_ D(z,w)  \] are PSH or identically $-\infty $. They decrease to $F(z,w_0)$, since iterated upper limits over shrinking rectangles give precisely the joint upper limit. The canonical decreasing-limit theorem proves the slice property, including a collapsed slice. The other group is the same. Thus $F$ is admissible, so the raw envelope equals $F$. The defining family is unchanged by swapping variables. Negativity and the local logarithmic pole bound give $W_ D\leq g_ D$. If $g_ D$ is symmetric, it is separately PSH and jointly USC by the preceding proposition. We justify joint SH without assuming joint PSH. On a product of two small balls, separate submean inequalities and Tonelli applied to $-g_ D\geq 0$ show that its integral is finite whenever its value at the center is finite. Local integrability propagates across chains of overlapping product balls: choose a finite-valued point in the overlap and repeat on balls centered there. The converse follows from symmetry of $W_ D$. The complex Hessian of $q$ has upper-left entry $|w|^2$ and determinant $|w|^2$. Since $w
e 0$ on the boundary, it is positive definite on a boundary neighborhood. Thus the boundary is strongly pseudoconvex. The function $-\log (1-q)+|z|^2+|w|^2$ is a PSH exhaustion, so the domain also satisfies the global pseudoconvexity condition. title: 9.23 Smooth positive matrix factorization on the circle
search_title: Smooth positive matrix factorization on the circle
section: 9.23 Smooth positive matrix factorization on the circle
text: Theorem 9.23.1 . 35AF621E1787 Let $m\geq 2$ and let $W:S^1\to \operatorname {Herm}_ m$ be smooth and positive definite at every point. There is a matrix function $H$, holomorphic on the unit disc and smooth on its closure, such that $H$ is invertible everywhere on the closed disc and \[  W=H^*H\quad \hbox{on }S^1.  \] Any two such factors differ by multiplication on the left by a constant unitary matrix. This assertion is about smooth data; no density assertion in a full Hölder norm is needed. Proof. Use normalized angular measure and the Fourier boundary calculus of Proposition 9.20.1 . Let $\mathcal H$ be the closed subspace of $L^2(S^1,\mathbb C^ m)$ whose negative Fourier coefficients vanish. Parseval's identity makes the projection $P$ onto the nonnegative coefficients an orthogonal projection of norm one. The Fourier series identifies each element of $\mathcal H$ with a holomorphic function on the disc: on $|\zeta |\leq r<1$ its power series converges uniformly by Cauchy–Schwarz and $\sum r^{2j}<\infty $. Its value at zero is its constant coefficient, a continuous map on $\mathcal H$. Compactness and positivity give $0<cI\leq W\leq CI$. Define the bounded self-adjoint operator $T f=P(Wf)$ on $\mathcal H$. It obeys \[  \langle Tf,f\rangle =\int f^*Wf\geq c\| f\| _2^2, \qquad \| Tf\| _2\geq c\| f\| _2.  \] The second inequality makes its range closed: a Cauchy sequence of images has a Cauchy sequence of preimages. The orthogonal complement of its range is the kernel of its adjoint, which is zero by the first inequality. Consequently $T$ is onto and $\| T^{-1}\| \leq c^{-1}$. For each $v\in \mathbb C^ m$, minimize $\int f^*Wf$ over $f\in \mathcal H$ with $f(0)=v$. This is a nonempty closed affine subspace in the equivalent weighted Hilbert norm. The Hilbert projection theorem gives its unique minimizer; variation gives orthogonality to the subspace with zero constant coefficient. The minimizer depends linearly on $v$, since these orthogonality equations and the value at zero are linear and uniquely determine it. Let $F$ be the matrix of minimizers for the standard basis vectors. Then $F(0)=I$, and variation by every $h\in \mathcal H$ with $h(0)=0$ gives \[  P(WF)=M  \] for some constant matrix $M$. Indeed these $h$ span exactly the positive Fourier modes. All equations apply column by column. We next prove that $F$ is smooth, rather than assume a boundary regularity theorem. Write $\tau _ h f(\theta )=f(\theta +h)$ and $\delta _ h=(\tau _ h-I)/h$. Translation preserves $\mathcal H$ and commutes with $P$. Translating the last equation and subtracting it gives \[  T(\delta _ h F)=-P((\delta _ h W)\tau _ h F).  \] The right hand side is uniformly bounded in $L^2$, since $W$ is $C^1$ and translations preserve the $L^2$ norm. The inverse estimate for $T$ bounds $\delta _ hF$ in $L^2$. If $a_ j$ are its Fourier coefficients, Parseval and Fatou give $\sum j^2|a_ j|^2<\infty $ by letting $h\to 0$ in $\sum |(e^{ijh}-1)/h|^2|a_ j|^2$. This is precisely the first weak angular derivative in $L^2$; the difference quotients converge to it by dominated convergence using $|e^{ijh}-1|\leq |jh|$. Inductively suppose the first $k$ weak derivatives are in $L^2$. Differentiation of $P(WF)=M$ in distributions is legitimate, since $P$ commutes with the angular derivative and $W$ is smooth. For $k\geq 1$ it yields \[  T F^{(k)}=-\sum _{\ell =1}^ k\binom {k}{\ell } P(W^{(\ell )}F^{(k-\ell )}).  \] This right hand side has one $L^2$ derivative under the induction hypothesis. Difference quotients of this equation therefore give \[  T\delta _ h F^{(k)} =\delta _ h\! \left(-\sum _{\ell =1}^ k\binom {k}{\ell } P(W^{(\ell )}F^{(k-\ell )})\right) -P((\delta _ h W)\tau _ h F^{(k)}),  \] whose right hand side is uniformly bounded in $L^2$. The same Fourier argument proves the next derivative. Thus $F$ has angular derivatives of every order in $L^2$. For every integer $r\geq 0$, Cauchy–Schwarz with a Fourier weight of order greater than $r+1/2$ gives $\sum _ j(1+j)^ r|a_ j|<\infty $. Its holomorphic power series and all derivatives consequently converge uniformly on the closed disc. This proves the asserted smoothness. The Fourier coefficients of $WF$ have indices at most zero. Those of $F^*$ do also; the latter are absolutely summable to every order. Hence $F^*WF$ has only nonpositive Fourier modes. It is Hermitian on the circle, so the coefficient of index $-j$ is the adjoint of the coefficient of index $j$. Every nonconstant coefficient vanishes. Write $F^*WF=A$, a constant Hermitian matrix. For $v\in \mathbb C^ m$, \[  v^*Av=\int (Fv)^*W(Fv)\geq c\| Fv\| _2^2 \geq c|F(0)v|^2=c|v|^2.  \] Thus $A$ is positive definite and $F$ is invertible on the circle. It is invertible in the interior too. If $F(a)v=0$ with $v\ne 0$, then $a\ne 0$, and $f=Fv$ is the unique minimizer with $f(0)=v$. For $b_ a(\zeta )=(\zeta -a)/(1-\overline a\zeta )$, the function $\widetilde f=b_ a(0)f/b_ a$ is holomorphic, smooth on the closed disc and has value $v$ at zero. The removable zero at $a$ is used componentwise. Since $|b_ a|=1$ on the circle, its weighted squared norm is $|a|^2$ times that of $f$, strictly smaller. This contradicts minimality. Therefore $\det F$ never vanishes on the closed disc. Its inverse is holomorphic inside and smooth up to the boundary by the adjugate formula. Set $H=A^{1/2}F^{-1}$, using the positive square root of the finite positive Hermitian matrix $A$. The identity $F^*WF=A$ proves $W=H^*H$. For uniqueness let $H_1,H_2$ be two factors and put $G=H_2H_1^{-1}$. It and its inverse are holomorphic and smooth on the closed disc, and $G^*G=I$ on the circle. The scalar maximum principle applied to $u^*Gv$, for fixed unit vectors $u,v$, gives $\| G(\zeta )\| \leq 1$; applied to its inverse it gives $\| G(\zeta )^{-1}\| \leq 1$. Thus all singular values are one at every interior point. Each column has constant squared norm one; applying the planar Laplacian shows that the sum of the squared absolute values of its holomorphic derivatives is zero. Every entry is constant. The constant matrix is unitary, as required. $\square$

section: 9.24 Smooth Green functions on strongly convex domains
text:
We use the complex bilinear pairing $g\cdot v=\sum g_ jv_ j$ for covectors, and write $r_ z$ for the complex differential of a real defining function. The positive stationary multiplier is normalized by $|g(0)|=1$ when parameters are needed. Sobolev norms below are angular norms on the unit circle. Write $\mathcal H$ for the Hardy subspace of $L^2$ with nonnegative Fourier coefficients, and $H^ s$ for angular Sobolev spaces. Smooth means $C^\infty $. Strong real convexity includes convexity of the domain and positivity of $D^2r$ on the real boundary tangent spaces for $r<0$ inside. Lemma 9.24.1 . EEFBD40AC261 Let $M$ be a smooth totally real submanifold of maximal real dimension in a complex manifold. A holomorphic map on a half-disc, which is $C^{1/2}$ up to its straight boundary interval and maps that interval into $M$, is smooth locally up to that interval. Proof. Work in a complex coordinate chart and parametrize $M$ near a point by a smooth map $\varphi :V\subset \mathbb R^ d	o \mathbb C^ d$. Total reality says that its derivative has an invertible complex linear extension. For an integer $N$ define, locally, \[  \Phi _ N(x+iy)=\sum _{| eta |\leq N}  rac{(iy)^ eta }{ eta !}\partial _ x^ eta \varphi (x).  \] Terms of degrees below $N$ cancel in $ ar\partial \Phi _ N$. On compact coordinate patches, $D^ j ar\partial \Phi _ N=O(|y|^{N-j})$ for $j\leq N$. Along $y=0$ its real derivative is the invertible complexification of $D\varphi $, so it has a smooth real inverse $\Psi _ N$ near the chosen point. Differentiating $\Phi _ N\circ \Psi _ N=I$ gives \[  (\Psi _ N)_{ ar w} =-((\Phi _ N)_ z\circ \Psi _ N)^{-1} ((\Phi _ N)_{ ar z}\circ \Psi _ N) \overline{(\Psi _ N)_ w}.  \] The inverse and its derivatives are bounded on smaller patches; distances to $M$ and to $\mathbb R^ d$ are comparable there. It follows, also after differentiating, that \[  D^ j(\Psi _ N)_{ ar w}(w) =O(\operatorname {dist}(w,M)^{N-j}),\qquad j\leq N.  \] Let $f$ be the given map, $z=x+iy$ with $y>0$. Its boundary Hölder estimate gives $\operatorname {dist}(f(z),M)\leq Cy^{1/2}$. Cauchy's formula on the disc of radius $y/2$, after subtracting $f(x)$, gives $|D^ j f(z)|\leq C_ j y^{1/2-j}$ for $j\geq 1$. Put $h=\Psi _ N\circ f$. It is real on the boundary interval and \[   ar\partial h=((\Psi _ N)_{ ar w}\circ f)\overline{f'}.  \] In a derivative of order $j$, a term with $\ell $ derivatives of $(\Psi _ N)_{ ar w}$ has $\ell +1$ factors from derivatives of $f$, with total derivative order $j+1$. The preceding estimates give \[  D^ j ar\partial h=O(y^{(N-1)/2-j}).  \] For any specified integer $k$, choose $N>2k+3$. Reflect $h$ by $h(z)=\overline{h( ar z)}$ into the lower half-disc. Its reflected $ ar\partial $ has a $C^ k$ extension, with all derivatives through order $k$ equal to zero on the real interval. This follows directly from the displayed vanishing bounds on both sides, successively integrating the normal derivatives. The reflected $h$ is continuous. Integration by parts above and below height $\epsilon $, followed by $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, shows that its distributional $ ar\partial $ is this extended function: the two boundary terms cancel by continuity. text: Lemma 9.24.1 . EEFBD40AC261 Let $M$ be a smooth totally real submanifold of maximal real dimension in a complex manifold. Work in a complex coordinate chart and parametrize $M$ near a point by a smooth map $\varphi :V\subset \mathbb R^ d\to \mathbb C^ d$. Total reality says that its derivative has an invertible complex linear extension. For an integer $N$ define, locally, \[  \Phi _ N(x+iy)=\sum _{|\beta |\leq N} \frac{(iy)^\beta }{\beta !}\partial _ x^\beta \varphi (x).  \] Terms of degrees below $N$ cancel in $\bar\partial \Phi _ N$. On compact coordinate patches, $D^ j\bar\partial \Phi _ N=O(|y|^{N-j})$ for $j\leq N$. Along $y=0$ its real derivative is the invertible complexification of $D\varphi $, so it has a smooth real inverse $\Psi _ N$ near the chosen point. Differentiating $\Phi _ N\circ \Psi _ N=I$ gives \[  (\Psi _ N)_{\bar w} =-((\Phi _ N)_ z\circ \Psi _ N)^{-1} ((\Phi _ N)_{\bar z}\circ \Psi _ N) \overline{(\Psi _ N)_ w}.  \] The inverse and its derivatives are bounded on smaller patches; distances to $M$ and to $\mathbb R^ d$ are comparable there. It follows, also after differentiating, that \[  D^ j(\Psi _ N)_{\bar w}(w) =O(\operatorname {dist}(w,M)^{N-j}),\qquad j\leq N.  \] Let $f$ be the given map, $z=x+iy$ with $y>0$. Its boundary Hölder estimate gives $\operatorname {dist}(f(z),M)\leq Cy^{1/2}$. Cauchy's formula on the disc of radius $y/2$, after subtracting $f(x)$, gives $|D^ j f(z)|\leq C_ j y^{1/2-j}$ for $j\geq 1$. Put $h=\Psi _ N\circ f$. It is real on the boundary interval and \[  \bar\partial h=((\Psi _ N)_{\bar w}\circ f)\overline{f'}.  \] In a derivative of order $j$, a term with $\ell $ derivatives of $(\Psi _ N)_{\bar w}$ has $\ell +1$ factors from derivatives of $f$, with total derivative order $j+1$. The preceding estimates give \[  D^ j\bar\partial h=O(y^{(N-1)/2-j}).  \] For any specified integer $k$, choose $N>2k+3$. Reflect $h$ by $h(z)=\overline{h(\bar z)}$ into the lower half-disc. Its reflected $\bar\partial $ has a $C^ k$ extension, with all derivatives through order $k$ equal to zero on the real interval. This follows directly from the displayed vanishing bounds on both sides, successively integrating the normal derivatives. The reflected $h$ is continuous. Integration by parts above and below height $\epsilon $, followed by $\epsilon \downarrow 0$, shows that its distributional $\bar\partial $ is this extended function: the two boundary terms cancel by continuity. The derivatives of $h$ are locally integrable by the same estimates and the chain rule. Multiply the extended right hand side by a compactly supported smooth cutoff equal to one near the point. Its Cauchy transform solves the $\bar\partial $ equation and is $C^ k$: transfer each of the first $k$ derivatives to the compactly supported $C^ k$ datum in the convolution with the locally integrable kernel $1/(\pi z)$. Continuity follows from translation continuity of that kernel on bounded sets. The difference from the reflected $h$ is distributionally holomorphic, hence holomorphic: convolution with small smooth kernels gives holomorphic functions converging locally uniformly to this continuous difference. Thus $h$, and then $f=\Phi _ N\circ h$, is $C^ k$. Since $k$ was arbitrary, $f$ is smooth. A separate finite Taylor extension is enough for each $k$; no infinite almost-analytic extension theorem is assumed. $\square$

Consequently the unique parametrization of $K$ is \[  v=\zeta (icf'/\alpha +Nk), \qquad c\in \mathbb R,\quad k\in \mathcal H^{n-1}.  \] It is an isomorphism for $L^2$ and each angular $H^ s$ norm. The form $B$ becomes a pointwise smooth uniformly positive real matrix form on the values of $(c,k)$, compressed to the fixed translation-invariant subspace consisting of a real constant component and complex Hardy components. The preceding projected form lemma gives its inverse bounded on every integer $H^ s$. The forcing vector of its Hilbert equation is obtained by smooth multiplications, Fourier projections and the finite functional $w'(0)$; it is in $H^ s$ whenever the data are. Thus $v\in H^ s$. The representing function of $L\circ R$ has the same regularity, since the adjoints of the displayed smooth multiplications and Fourier projections also preserve $H^ s$. This gives $\lambda \in H^ s$, and then $h\in H^ s$ by its formula. In particular the full linearized operator is a bounded isomorphism on the asserted Sobolev spaces. For completeness the nonlinear local step requires no additional existence theorem. Angular $H^ s$, $s\geq 2$, is a Banach algebra: Fourier convolution, the inequality $(1+|j+k|)^ s\leq C_ s((1+|j|)^ s+(1+|k|)^ s)$ and Cauchy–Schwarz imply the product estimate, because $\sum (1+|j|)^{-2s}<\infty $. The same Fourier estimate gives the continuous embedding in continuous functions. Smooth composition is smooth on these spaces. One checks this first in $H^1$ by the ordinary chain rule and the product estimate, and then inducts using $(F\circ u)'=(DF\circ u)u'$; Taylor's integral remainder and the product bound give the Fréchet derivatives $(D^ jF\circ u)\prod h_ i$ at every order. Smooth approximation proves the same identities for Sobolev functions. Apply these facts to the boundary map \[  (f,g,\rho )\longmapsto (r(f),\  g/\zeta -\rho r_ z(f),\  f(0),\  g(0)).  \] It is a smooth map between the indicated real Banach spaces and its derivative is the isomorphism just proved. Multiply by its inverse at the base point. In a small ball the equation is equivalent to a fixed-point map with derivative norm less than $1/2$. For parameters near the base it maps that ball into itself, so successive iterates converge to its unique solution. Differentiating the fixed-point equation and using the convergent Neumann series for its derivative gives smooth parameter dependence, inductively at every order. Positivity of $\rho $ persists by the continuous embedding. The boundary values of $f$ remain on $\partial D$, and the holomorphic maximum principle for real supporting linear functionals puts $f(\Delta )$ in $D$ when $f(0)\in D$. Thus these are genuine stationary discs. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.24.5
section: 9.24 Smooth Green functions on strongly convex domains
text: Theorem 9.24.5 . A2E9734AB1F5 Let $n\geq 2$ and let $D\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded convex domain, with smooth boundary and strictly positive real second fundamental form. Then its isolated pole Green function is smooth on $(D\times D)\setminus \{ (a,a):a\in D\} $. For fixed $a$ it is the unique negative PSH function that is locally bounded and maximal off $a$, has zero boundary limits, and has singularity $\log |z-a|+O(1)$; off $a$ it solves the classical homogeneous complex Monge–Ampère equation. Proof. By Theorem 9.20.5 , each $a\ne z$ lies on a stationary disc $f$ with $f(0)=a$ and $f(t)=z$, $0<t<1$. Normalize its lift by $|g(0)|=1$. The previous lemmas make it smooth and give local smooth dependence on $(a,b)$, $b=g(0)$. Consider the finite-dimensional map \[  (a,b,t)\longmapsto (a,f_{a,b}(t)),\qquad |b|=1.  \] Both domain and target have real dimension $4n$. We show that its differential is injective. A kernel variation has $\dot a=0$ and $v(t)+f'(t)\dot t=0$. Tangency gives $g\cdot v/\zeta =ic$ for a real constant $c$. Pairing the last equation with $g(t)$ yields \[  ict+\alpha \dot t=0.  \] Thus $c=\dot t=0$ and $v(t)=0$. The holomorphic function $h\cdot v/\zeta $ is smooth on the closed disc, since $v(0)=0$. Integrate its real part against the positive Poisson kernel based at $t$. Its integral is its real value at $t$, which is zero. In the linearized stationary equation the real multiplier term vanishes by tangency, so this same integral is the positive weighted integral of $\rho D^2r(f)[v,v]/2$. Strong convexity forces $v=0$ on the circle and hence everywhere. Now $h=(\lambda /\rho )g$ on the circle. The holomorphic wedge $h\wedge g$ vanishes there and hence inside. Since $g$ is nowhere zero, the ratios glue to a holomorphic scalar with real boundary values; it is a real constant $s$. Hence $h=sg$ and $\dot b=sb$. The normalization $|b|=1$ gives $0=\operatorname {Re}(\bar b\cdot \dot b)=s$, so the entire kernel variation is zero. The finite-dimensional inverse function theorem, or the same contraction proof, gives a smooth local inverse $(a,z)\mapsto (b,t)$. The local discs are convex complex geodesics by their stationary left inverses. Therefore the Green identity in Theorem 9.20.5 gives $g_ D(f_{a,b}(t),a)=\log t$. Evaluation at interior $t$ is smooth for these Sobolev-valued families: its derivatives follow from the uniformly convergent holomorphic series on compact subdiscs. Hence $g_ D(z,a)$ is smooth near every off-diagonal pair. No smoothness at the pole is asserted. A smooth strongly convex domain is hyperconvex: a negative convex defining function near its boundary, patched to a negative constant inside by a maximum, gives a negative PSH exhaustion. Propositions 7.17.4 and 7.17.7 therefore give zero boundary limits and uniqueness. The two ball comparisons in Proposition 7.17.1 give its logarithmic singularity. Maximality and the bounded Bedford–Taylor criterion away from the pole give zero Monge–Ampère measure there. Since the function is now smooth, the canonical smooth determinant formula makes this the classical homogeneous equation. $\square$

title: 5.53 Currents on real manifolds and fiber signs

section: 5.53 Currents on real manifolds and fiber signs
text: A current of degree $q$ on an oriented real $m$-manifold acts on compactly supported smooth $(m-q)$-forms. We use $\langle \mathrm dT,\phi \rangle =(-1)^{q+1}\langle T,\mathrm d\phi \rangle $ and $\langle T\wedge \alpha ,\phi \rangle =\langle T,\alpha \wedge \phi \rangle $. Thus a locally integrable form represents the current obtained by putting that form before the test form in the integral. The usual local coefficient-distribution definition applies in real charts as well. Theorem 5.53.1 . CCE8A237C582 Let $F\colon M_1\to M_2$ be smooth between oriented manifolds of dimensions $m_1,m_2$, and suppose $F$ is proper on $\operatorname {Supp}T$. The direct image defined by \[  \langle F_*T,\phi \rangle =\langle T,F^*\phi \rangle  \] has the same dimension as $T$, satisfies the projection formula and $\operatorname {Supp}F_*T\subset F(\operatorname {Supp}T)$, and obeys \[  \mathrm d(F_*T)=(-1)^{m_1-m_2}F_*(\mathrm dT).  \] Direct images compose whenever the composite is proper on the current's support. If $H\colon [0,1]\times M_1\to M_2$ is a smooth homotopy proper on $[0,1]\times \operatorname {Supp}T$, with endpoint maps $F,G$, then \[  F_*T-G_*T=(-1)^{m_1+1-m_2}\mathrm d H_*([0,1]\otimes T)-H_*([0,1]\otimes \mathrm dT).  \] In particular closed currents have cohomologous endpoint images. Proof. For a test form supported in a fixed compact set $K\subset M_2$, insert a smooth cutoff equal to one near $F^{-1}(K)\cap \operatorname {Supp}T$. Properness makes this set compact. The result is independent of the cutoff, and the chain rule bounds each seminorm of its pullback by finitely many seminorms of the original form. This proves continuity and defines a current. Tests disjoint from $F(\operatorname {Supp}T)$ give zero. Pullback preserves degree, so the current dimension is preserved. The projection formula follows by pulling back $\alpha \wedge \phi $. If $T$ has dimension $p$, the signs in the definitions of the two derivatives are $(-1)^{m_2-p+1}$ and $(-1)^{m_1-p+1}$. Since $F^*\mathrm d\phi =\mathrm dF^*\phi $, their ratio is $(-1)^{m_1-m_2}$. Cutoff derivatives have support away from the relevant current support and contribute zero. This proves the derivative formula. For composition, properness of $GF$ on the support implies properness of $F$ there: the preimage of a compact $K\subset M_2$ is a closed subset of the compact preimage of $G(K)$. It also implies properness of $G$ on $F(\operatorname {Supp}T)$, since its inverse image of a compact set is the $F$-image of a compact set. Now $(GF)^*=F^*G^*$ proves composition. Here is an explicit convention for the tensor in the homotopy formula. For $T$ of degree $q$ and a test form $\eta =a(t,x)+\mathrm dt\wedge b(t,x)$ on $\mathbb R\times M_1$, put \[  \langle [0,1]\otimes T,\eta \rangle =(-1)^ q\int _0^1\langle T,b(t,\cdot )\rangle \, \mathrm dt.  \] It is a current by the compact-parameter seminorm bounds. Differentiating this formula and integrating in $t$ gives \[  \mathrm d([0,1]\otimes T) =(\delta _0-\delta _1)\otimes T+[0,1]\otimes \mathrm dT.  \] The endpoint terms act on the restriction of $a$ to that endpoint, and push forward to $F_*T$ and $G_*T$. Apply the derivative formula to $H$, whose source dimension is $m_1+1$, and rearrange. A closed current removes the last term, giving the final assertion. Here smoothness of the homotopy at its endpoints is understood in the usual sense of a smooth extension to a neighborhood of the cylinder. The tensor is supported in that cylinder, so any such extension gives the same direct image; no properness outside its support is needed. $\square$ Theorem 5.53.2 . 01AAD02BF915 Let $F\colon M_1\to M_2$ be a submersion of relative dimension $r=m_1-m_2$. Orient its fibers by placing the fiber orientation before the base orientation. For a current $T$ of degree $q$ on $M_2$, its form-compatible pullback is \[  \langle F^*T,\phi \rangle =(-1)^{rq}\langle T,F_*\phi \rangle , \qquad \deg \phi =m_1-q,  \] where $F_*\phi $ is integration of a compactly supported test form along the fibers. This pullback agrees with ordinary pullback of smooth forms, preserves degree and satisfies \[  \mathrm dF^*T=F^*\mathrm dT,\qquad F^*(T\wedge \alpha )=F^*T\wedge F^*\alpha .  \] For submersions between complex manifolds the defining parity factor is one. Proof. A partition of unity reduces fiber integration to the projection $(x,y)\mapsto y$. If the fiber dimension is $r$, only coefficients containing $\mathrm dx_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dx_ r$ contribute; integrate their coefficients in $x$. Differentiation under the integral shows that the result is smooth with compact support in the image of the test support, and gives continuous maps between test spaces on every fixed compact support. The compactly supported fiber-coordinate derivatives integrate to zero, while a base differential crosses $r$ fiber differentials. Hence \[  F_*(\mathrm d\phi )=(-1)^ r\mathrm dF_*\phi , \qquad F_*(F^*\alpha \wedge \phi ) =(-1)^{r\deg \alpha }\alpha \wedge F_*\phi .  \] These identities are intrinsic and so persist after the partition of unity. For a smooth $q$-form $t$, Fubini and the second sign give \[  \int _{M_1}F^*t\wedge \phi =(-1)^{rq}\int _{M_2}t\wedge F_*\phi ,  \] so the definition agrees with forms. The derivative identity follows by comparing signs $(-1)^{q+1+rq+r}$ and $(-1)^{r(q+1)+q+1}$ in its two pairings. For the product identity, the additional sign $(-1)^{r\deg \alpha }$ in fiber integration is exactly the change from $rq$ to $r(q+\deg \alpha )$ in the definition. This proves both identities. Continuity of the test-space map proves the current's continuity without a properness assumption on the entire submersion. Finally complex source and target dimensions give even real $r$ and even $m_1-m_2$. $\square$

title: 5.20.19 Convex fibers in the minimum principle
search_title: Convex fibers in the minimum principle
section: 5.20 Plurisubharmonic metrics on line bundles
text: Example 5.20.20 (The role of convex fibers) . A5E29B2DEA26 There is a connected pseudoconvex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^2$, invariant under imaginary translations in the last two variables, and an invariant pluriharmonic function whose fiberwise infimum is finite but not subharmonic. Thus the convex-fiber hypothesis in the Kiselman minimum principle cannot simply be omitted. Proof. Fix $0<\delta <1$, put \[  A=\{ s\in \mathbb C:1<|s|<2\} ,\qquad T=\{ \eta \in \mathbb C^2:|\operatorname {Re}\eta |<\delta \} ,  \] and consider $F:A\times T\longrightarrow \mathbb C\times \mathbb C^2$ given by \[  F(s,\eta )=\bigl (s^2,(s,-\mathrm i s)+\eta \bigr ).  \] Its derivative is invertible since $2s\ne 0$. If two points have the same image, their first coordinates are $s$ and either $s$ or $-s$. In the latter case the real parts of their last coordinates belong to balls of radius $\delta $ centered at $(\operatorname {Re}s,\operatorname {Im}s)$ and its negative. These balls are disjoint since their centers have distance $2|s|>2\delta $. Therefore $F$ is injective, and the holomorphic inverse function theorem makes it a biholomorphism onto a connected open image $\Omega $. For completeness, $A\times T$ has the smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion \[  \rho (s,\eta )=-\log (|s|^2-1)-\log (4-|s|^2) -\log \bigl (\delta ^2-|\operatorname {Re}\eta |^2\bigr ) +|\operatorname {Im}\eta |^2.  \] Indeed, the two radial terms in $s$ have complex second derivatives $1/(|s|^2-1)^2$ and $4/(4-|s|^2)^2$, respectively. The last two terms are convex functions of the real coordinates of $\eta $, hence are plurisubharmonic. Each summand is bounded below on its domain, and their sum tends to $+\infty $ at every boundary approach or unbounded imaginary direction. Its sublevels are consequently compact. Pulling this exhaustion through $F^{-1}$ proves that $\Omega $ is pseudoconvex. Translation of $\eta $ by any vector in $\mathrm i\mathbb R^2$ preserves $T$, so $\Omega $ has the required invariance. Its projection is $1<|z|<4$. For either square root $s$ of $z$, the real fiber is the union of the balls of radius $\delta $ centered at $\pm (\operatorname {Re}s,\operatorname {Im}s)$. Take $\varphi (z,w)=\operatorname {Re}w_1$. Its fiberwise infimum is \[  v(z)=-|\operatorname {Re}\sqrt z|-\delta ,  \] independently of the choice of square root. Fix $z_0=-a$ with $1<a<4$. On a disc about $z_0$ choose a holomorphic square root $h$ satisfying $h(z_0)=\mathrm i\sqrt a$. The harmonic function $\operatorname {Re}h$ vanishes at $z_0$ and has nonzero differential there. On every sufficiently small centered circle its absolute value has strictly positive average. Thus the average of $v$ is strictly less than $-\delta =v(z_0)$, contradicting the submean inequality. $\square$

title: 5.54 Global smoothing and the Poincaré lemma for currents
search_title: Global smoothing and the Poincaré lemma for currents
section: 5.54 Global smoothing and the Poincaré lemma for currents
text:
Currents on an oriented real $m$-manifold have the degree and derivative conventions of section 5.53 . An operator taking degree $q$ to degree $q-1$ is zero when $q=0$. Weak convergence is convergence on every compactly supported smooth test form. Lemma 5.54.1 . A748F8312A04 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$ be open. There is a smooth function $\psi $ on $\mathbb R^ m$, positive exactly on $\Omega $, such that $0\leq \psi \leq 1/4$ and $|
abla \psi |\leq 1/4$. For $|v|\leq 1$ the maps \[  F_ v(x)=x+\psi (x)v  \] are smooth diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb R^ m$ preserving $\Omega $. For every compact $K\subset \Omega $, the set \[  \{ (t,v,x):0\leq t\leq 1,\  |v|\leq 1,\  F_{tv}(x)\in K\}   \] is a compact subset of $[0,1]	imes \overline B(0,1)	imes \Omega $. Proof. The empty set is immediate, with $\psi =0$. Otherwise choose nonnegative smooth compactly supported functions $b_ j$ on $\Omega $ such that at least one is positive at each point. Explicitly, cover $\Omega $ by countably many balls $B(a_ j,r_ j)\Subset \Omega $, and take $b_ j(x)=\exp (-1/(r_ j^2-|x-a_ j|^2))$ inside the ball and zero outside. This is the same dimension-free cutoff construction . Choose $c_ j>0$ with \[  c_ j\left(1+\sum _{|\alpha |\leq j+1} \| \partial ^\alpha b_ j\| _\infty ight)\leq 2^{-j-2} \quad (j\geq 1), \qquad \psi =\sum _{j\geq 1}c_ jb_ j.  \] Every differentiated tail converges uniformly: for a derivative of order $k$, use this bound for $j\geq k$. Thus the sum is globally smooth. It vanishes off $\Omega $ and is positive on $\Omega $. The bounds for the zeroth and first derivatives, using the sum of the absolute first partial derivatives to bound the Euclidean gradient, give the asserted constants. For fixed $y,v$, the map $x\mapsto y-\psi (x)v$ is a contraction of $\mathbb R^ m$ with constant at most $1/4$. Iteration is Cauchy by the geometric-series estimate, so it gives the unique solution of $F_ v(x)=y$. Moreover $D F_ v=I+v\otimes 
abla \psi $ is invertible, since its perturbation of $I$ has norm at most $1/4$. The inverse function theorem therefore makes the inverse smooth. The map fixes the complement of $\Omega $ pointwise; injectivity and surjectivity imply $F_ v(\Omega )=\Omega $. The set in the statement is closed in the full Euclidean product and bounded, because $|x|\leq \max _ K|y|+1/4$. It is therefore compact. None of its points has $x
otin \Omega $, since such an $x$ is fixed by $F_{tv}$ and cannot be mapped into $K$. This proves the claimed compact containment, uniformly in both parameters. $\square$ Theorem 5.54.2 . 7D93F6AD9C80 On every open $\Omega \subset \mathbb R^ m$ there are linear operators $R_\varepsilon $ and $K_\varepsilon $, $0<\varepsilon <1$, on currents, of respective degree $0$ and $-1$, such that $R_\varepsilon T$ is smooth and \[  R_\varepsilon T-T=\mathrm dK_\varepsilon T +K_\varepsilon \mathrm dT, \qquad \mathrm dR_\varepsilon T=R_\varepsilon \mathrm dT.  \] As $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, $R_\varepsilon T	o T$ and $K_\varepsilon T	o 0$ weakly. If $T$ has order at most the nonnegative integer $s$, then $K_\varepsilon T$ has order at most $s$. In particular every closed current is cohomologous to a smooth closed form. Proof. Choose $\psi ,F_ v$ as in the lemma and a nonnegative smooth probability kernel $ho _\varepsilon $ supported in $B(0,\varepsilon )$. Put $H_ v(t,x)=F_{tv}(x)$ and define \[  R_\varepsilon T=\int ho _\varepsilon (v)(F_ v)_*T\, \mathrm dv, \qquad K_\varepsilon T= \int ho _\varepsilon (v)(H_ v)_*([0,1]\otimes T)\, \mathrm dv.  \] These are weak integrals, defined by pairing with a test form. For tests supported in a fixed compact $K$, the lemma gives one compact subset of $\Omega $ containing every relevant inverse image. Pullback and its coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on this compact set for $t\in [0,1]$ and $v$ in the kernel support. Thus current continuity defines both integrals. More precisely, when $T$ has order at most $s$, the resulting bound uses only test derivatives of order at most $s$; integrating the parameters does not raise that order. This proves the order assertion for $K_\varepsilon T$. The real dimensions of the source and target of $F_ v$ are equal, so its pushforward commutes with $\mathrm d$. The sign-corrected homotopy in theorem 5.53.1 , with endpoints the identity and $F_ v$, gives \[  (F_ v)_*T-T=\mathrm d(H_ v)_*([0,1]\otimes T) +(H_ v)_*([0,1]\otimes \mathrm dT).  \] Averaging proves both displayed identities. This argument uses properness only on the tensor support; the lemma supplies it uniformly. We verify smoothness, including the test-space assertion needed for distribution coefficients. Write a test form of degree $m-q$ as $\phi =\sum _ I\phi _ I(y)\, \mathrm dy_ I$. abla \psi |\leq 1/4$. For $|v|\leq 1$ the maps \[  F_ v(x)=x+\psi (x)v  \] are smooth diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb R^ m$ preserving $\Omega $. For every compact $K\subset \Omega $, the set \[  \{ (t,v,x):0\leq t\leq 1,\  |v|\leq 1,\  F_{tv}(x)\in K\}   \] is a compact subset of $[0,1]	imes \overline B(0,1)	imes \Omega $. Proof. title: 9.26 Local holomorphic separation and strict exhaustion
search_title: Local holomorphic separation and strict exhaustion
section: 9.26 Local holomorphic separation and strict exhaustion
text: Throughout this section complex manifolds are Hausdorff and second countable. A possibly extended real function $\psi :X\to [-\infty ,\infty )$ is an exhaustion if $\{ \psi <c\} $ is relatively compact for every real $c$. Equivalently, for each $c$ there is a compact $K$ such that $\psi \geq c$ on $X\setminus K$: take the closure of the strict sublevel in one direction, and use closedness of compact sets in the other. For a finite continuous function this is equivalent to compactness of every closed sublevel, by comparing levels $c$ and $c+1$. We say that global holomorphic functions locally separate points if for each $x\in X$ there is a neighborhood $V$ such that each $y\in V\setminus \{ x\} $ is distinguished from $x$ by some function in $\mathcal O(X)$. This assumption does not specify independent differentials or separation of every pair of points in $X$. Theorem 9.26.1 . C1041DBBD4EC If global holomorphic functions locally separate points on $X$, then $X$ has a nonnegative smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function. If $X$ is also holomorphically convex, that function can be chosen to be an exhaustion. Proof. Fix a point $x$ in a positive-dimensional component. Choose coordinates centered at $x$ such that the closed unit ball is contained in the neighborhood $V$ from local separation and in the coordinate chart. For each $y$ on the unit sphere choose $f\in \mathcal O(X)$, subtract $f(x)$ and multiply by a constant so that $f(x)=0$ and $|f(y)|^2>2$. Finitely many such functions cover the sphere by the open sets where the corresponding squared modulus is greater than $2$. Their sum $v=\sum _{j=1}^ N|f_ j|^2$ is smooth, nonnegative and plurisubharmonic on all of $X$, is zero at $x$, and exceeds $2$ on the sphere. On the coordinate ball put $q=(1+|z|^2)/3$. Use the normalized regularized maximum in Euclidean Richberg smoothing , with both fixed parameters equal to some $\eta \in (0,1/24)$. On a neighborhood of $x$ we have $q-v>2\eta $, and on a collar of the unit sphere we have $v-q>2\eta $. The branch deletion property therefore makes $M_\eta (v,q)$ equal to $q$ near $x$ and equal to $v$ on that collar. Define $u_ x=M_\eta (v,q)$ inside the ball and $u_ x=v$ elsewhere. The formulas agree on the collar, so $u_ x$ is globally smooth. The positivity and convexity properties of the same maximum make it nonnegative and plurisubharmonic. Near $x$ its Hessian is the positive definite Hessian of $q$. Choose countably many such strict neighborhoods $W_ j$ covering the positive-dimensional components and write $u_ j$ for their functions. Take a countable exhaustion by compact coordinate pieces, and let $p_ r$ be the maximum of the absolute values of coordinate derivatives of order at most $r$ on the first $r$ such pieces. These seminorms are finite on each smooth $u_ j$. Choose $a_ j>0$ so that \[  a_ j\bigl (1+\max _{r\leq j}p_ r(u_ j)\bigr )\leq 2^{-j}.  \] For fixed $r$ this bounds the tail of every derivative of order at most $r$ by a summable geometric series. Consequently $u=\sum _ j a_ j u_ j$ is smooth, with termwise differentiated series on every compact coordinate piece. Each summand is nonnegative and has nonnegative complex Hessian. At a point of $W_ j$ its $j$th Hessian is positive definite, so $H_ u$ is positive definite there. On zero-dimensional components set $u=0$; strictness there is vacuous. This proves the first assertion. Under holomorphic convexity, plurisubharmonic exhaustions from holomorphic convexity supplies a smooth nonnegative plurisubharmonic exhaustion $\rho $ on $X$. Then $\rho +u$ is smooth and strictly plurisubharmonic. Its closed sublevels are closed subsets of the compact sublevels of $\rho $, proving the assertion. This argument uses only the stated local separation property. $\square$ For clarity, call a manifold weakly pseudoconvex here if it admits a smooth plurisubharmonic exhaustion, and strongly pseudoconvex if it admits a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion. The theorem proves the latter property from holomorphic convexity and local separation. It does not use the converse Levi problem or the later conclusion of global point or jet separation. Proposition 9.26.2 . A1FE9ED85940 Each of the following four properties is preserved by finite products and closed complex submanifolds: holomorphic convexity; holomorphic convexity together with local separation by global holomorphic functions; weak pseudoconvexity; strong pseudoconvexity. They are also preserved by finite intersections of complex submanifolds having the property, and by $S\cap F^{-1}(S')$, where $F:X\to Y$ is holomorphic and $S\subset X$, $S'\subset Y$ have the property, provided the indicated intersection is a complex submanifold with its induced structure. The individual submanifolds need not be closed in $X$ or $Y$. If $X$ is weakly or strongly pseudoconvex and $v$ is smooth plurisubharmonic on $X$, then $\{ v<c\} $ has the same respective property for every real $c$. Proof. For a compact subset $K\subset X_1\times X_2$, the hull inequalities for functions pulled back from the factors give \[  \widehat K_{X_1\times X_2} \subset \widehat{\operatorname {pr}_1K}_{X_1} \times \widehat{\operatorname {pr}_2K}_{X_2}.  \] If both factors are holomorphically convex, the right side is compact and the left side is closed, so the product is holomorphically convex. For a compact $K\subset S\subset X$ with $S$ closed, restriction of holomorphic test functions gives $\widehat K_ S\subset \widehat K_ X\cap S$. The right side is compact; closedness of the hull in $S$ proves holomorphic convexity of $S$. Local separation is preserved by products, using a distinguishing function in a factor where two nearby points differ. It is preserved by submanifolds, by restricting the distinguishing functions and the corresponding neighborhoods. A finite continuous exhaustion is bounded below: otherwise a sequence of values tending to $-\infty $ would lie in one compact closed sublevel, contradicting continuity there. Thus smooth exhaustions can be shifted to be nonnegative. The sum of two such exhaustions on a product is plurisubharmonic and proper, since each closed sublevel lies in the product of two compact sublevels. If both are strict, the Hessian of their sum is positive on every nonzero product tangent vector. Restriction to a closed complex submanifold preserves properness and positivity; strictness is preserved on its nonzero tangent vectors. This proves the first assertion for all four properties. For finitely many submanifolds $S_ j\subset X$, their intersection maps diagonally into $\prod _ j S_ j$. Its image is closed there, because the diagonal of the Hausdorff manifold $X$ is closed. Under the stated submanifold assumption this is a holomorphic embedding. Likewise $x\mapsto (x,F(x))$ embeds $S\cap F^{-1}(S')$ as a closed complex submanifold of $S\times S'$: its image is the intersection with the closed graph of $F$ in $X\times Y$. The product and closed-submanifold cases just proved give both assertions without assuming $S$ or $S'$ closed in their ambient manifolds. Finally, let $\rho \geq 0$ be an exhaustion with the required plurisubharmonicity on $X$. On $G=\{ v<c\} $ put \[  \sigma =\rho +\frac1{c-v}.  \] The second summand has nonnegative complex Hessian, by the chain rule for the increasing convex function $t\mapsto 1/(c-t)$. Thus $\sigma $ is plurisubharmonic and is strict when $\rho $ is. For $A>0$, its closed $A$-sublevel is a closed subset of $\{ \rho \leq A,\  v\leq c-1/A\} $, a compact subset of $G$. For $A\leq 0$ it is empty. Hence $\sigma $ is an exhaustion. $\square$

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ have $C^2$ boundary, and let $ho $ be a local $C^2$ defining function, negative on $\Omega $. Identify a real vector with its complex coordinate coefficients. These are boundary conditions, as distinct from existence of a strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion on a manifold. Proposition 9.34.1 . 07D51E96DD30 If $\xi ,\eta $ are $C^1$ real sections of $D$ and $

Now $\mathrm d eta =2\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial ho $, and direct evaluation gives \[  \mathrm d eta (\xi ,\eta ) =2\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}ho _{z_ j ar z_ k} (\xi _ j ar\eta _ k-\eta _ j ar\xi _ k) =-4\operatorname {Im}\sum _{j,k}ho _{z_ j ar z_ k}\xi _ j ar\eta _ k.  \] The left side depends only on the oriented hypersurface. The distribution $D$ has real rank $2n-2$ and is $C^{k-1}$. Apply the Frobenius theorem for constant-rank real distributions to obtain local integral plaques and $C^{k-1}$ foliation charts. Each plaque has complex tangent spaces, so holomorphic regularity of complex tangent submanifolds makes it a complex hypersurface. u ,\mathrm d

text: A bounded negative exhaustion below means a continuous function $u<0$ whose closed sublevels $\{ u\leq c\} $ are compact for every $c<0$, with upper endpoint zero at the boundary. The function $-\log (-u)$ is then an exhaustion in the unbounded convention. Theorem 9.35.1 . AC8A460928B4 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ be a bounded pseudoconvex open set with $C^2$ boundary, and let $\delta $ be its interior Euclidean boundary distance. There are $\eta \in (0,1)$ and a strictly plurisubharmonic $u\in C^2(\Omega )\cap C(\overline\Omega )$ such that $-1\leq u<0$ in $\Omega $, $u=0$ on the boundary, and \[  c\delta (z)^\eta \leq -u(z)\leq C\delta (z)^\eta  \] near the boundary, for positive constants $c,C$. In particular $u$ is a bounded negative exhaustion and $\Omega $ is hyperconvex. One may write $u=-(-\rho )^\eta $ with a $C^2$ regular defining function $\rho $ on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $. The same $\rho $ works for every smaller positive exponent. With $C^ r$ boundary, $2\leq r\leq \infty $, the defining function and the interior exhaustion may be chosen $C^ r$. Proof. The empty case is vacuous. Otherwise the compact boundary is nonempty. The signed-distance construction in theorem 9.34.2 gives a uniform boundary collar on which $q=-\delta $ is $C^2$, with $|\nabla q|=1$ and bounded complex Hessian. Compactness of the boundary makes the collar width and Hessian bound uniform. By Oka's boundary-distance criterion , $-\log \delta $ is plurisubharmonic. Thus $H_ q$ is nonnegative on $\ker \partial q$ at every point of the inner collar. Write $\xi =\xi _ T+\xi _ N$ for the orthogonal decomposition into $\ker \partial q$ and its complex normal. Since $|\partial q|=1/2$, we have $|\xi _ N|=2|\partial q(\xi )|$. If $M$ bounds the operator norm of $H_ q$, its tangential nonnegativity gives \[  H_ q(\xi )\geq -2M|\xi _ T||\xi _ N|-M|\xi _ N|^2 \geq -6M|\xi |\, |\partial q(\xi )|.  \] Put $A=6M$. Dividing by $\delta $ and applying $ab\leq \varepsilon b^2+a^2/(4\varepsilon )$ yields, for every $\varepsilon >0$, \[  -\frac{H_\delta (\xi )}{\delta } +\varepsilon \frac{|\partial \delta (\xi )|^2}{\delta ^2} +C_\varepsilon |\xi |^2\geq 0, \qquad C_\varepsilon =\frac{A^2}{4\varepsilon }.  \] This estimate uses only $C^2$ boundary regularity. Choose $R\geq 1$ bounding $|z|$ on $\overline\Omega $, put $K=C_{1/2}+1$ and set $\psi =-\log \delta +K|z|^2$ in the collar. Write $a=|\partial \delta (\xi )|/\delta $. title: 9.36 Holomorphic extension of tangential CR data

section: 9.36 Holomorphic extension of tangential CR data
text: Theorem 9.36.1 . E17A6BD70890 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 2$, be bounded with $C^2$ connected boundary. Every $f\in C^1(\partial \Omega )$ annihilated by the tangential $(0,1)$ vector fields is the boundary value of some $F\in \mathcal O(\Omega )\cap C(\overline\Omega )$. Proof. The normal-coordinate construction in theorem 9.34.2 gives a $C^1$ nearest-point projection to $\partial \Omega $ on a uniform collar. Compose $f$ with that projection and multiply by a smooth function of signed distance which is one near zero and vanishes before the edge of the collar. Extension by zero gives a compactly supported $C^1$ function $f_0$ on $\mathbb C^ n$ agreeing with $f$ on the boundary. Put \[  v=\mathbf1_\Omega \bar\partial f_0.  \] This is a compactly supported $(0,1)$-current with bounded measurable coefficients. We check that it is closed. For a regular defining function $\rho $, the tangential CR condition is equivalent to \[  \bar\partial f_0\wedge \bar\partial \rho =0 \quad \text{on }\partial \Omega .  \] Indeed, the $(0,1)$ tangent hyperplane is the kernel of $\bar\partial \rho $; a covector vanishing on that hyperplane is a multiple of $\bar\partial \rho $. This condition is independent of the chosen extension, since the differential of a function vanishing on the boundary is normal there. The boundary-graph calculation in the coefficient Koppelman formula (Fubini and one-variable integration by parts) gives the coefficient-distribution identity \[  \bar\partial \mathbf1_\Omega =-\frac{\bar\partial \rho }{|\nabla \rho |}\, \mathrm d\sigma ,  \] where $\mathrm d\sigma $ is surface measure, viewed as a scalar distribution in the ambient space. For smooth $f_0$ this proves $\bar\partial v=0$. For the given $C^1$ extension, mollify $f_0$ in the ambient space. The approximations converge in $C^1$ on a fixed compact set, so the interior forms and their boundary measure terms converge in distributions. Their limiting boundary wedge is zero by the displayed CR condition, again giving $\bar\partial v=0$. Use the normalized global current homotopy operator from the compact-support Dolbeault homotopy operator . For this degree-one input, its scalar coefficient kernels $k_ j$ are smooth away from zero and satisfy \[  |k_ j(x)|\leq C_ n|x|^{1-2n}.  \] The current homotopy identity gives a distributional solution $u=Kv$, $\bar\partial u=v$. Since $v$ has bounded compactly supported coefficients, this is an ordinary convolution integral and $u$ is continuous. To see this directly, the integral over a ball of radius $r$ around a possible kernel singularity is at most $C\| v\| _\infty r$, uniformly in its center. For two nearby centers remove both such balls; on the remaining bounded difference set the kernels are uniformly continuous. First choosing $r$ small and then taking the centers close proves continuity, even across the jump of $v$ on the boundary. The same kernel bound gives $u(z)\to 0$ at infinity. Outside a closed ball containing the support of $v$, the equation makes $u$ holomorphic by scalar distributional CR regularity. Fix the first $n-1$ coordinates sufficiently far from that ball. The remaining-variable function is entire and tends to zero at infinity, hence vanishes by Liouville. This gives a nonempty open zero set in the connected exterior of the ball; identity makes $u$ vanish on that entire exterior. Thus $u$ has compact support. This is where $n\geq 2$ is used. Finally $E=\mathbb C^ n\setminus \overline\Omega $ is connected. Here is the required topological argument. Each boundary point has a connected outer half-neighborhood, hence is adjacent to just one component of $E$. That component is locally constant as a function of the boundary point, so connectedness of the boundary makes it the same component everywhere. The unbounded component of $E$ has a nonempty boundary contained in $\partial \Omega $, so it is this component. Any other component would also have a nonempty boundary there and the same outer half-neighborhood, a contradiction. The function $u$ is holomorphic on $E$ and vanishes near infinity. Identity therefore gives $u=0$ on $E$, and continuity gives $u=0$ on $\partial \Omega $. Consequently $F=f_0-u$ is continuous on $\overline\Omega $, has boundary values $f$, and satisfies $\bar\partial F=0$ inside $\Omega $. Scalar CR regularity makes it holomorphic, as required. $\square$

title: 2.10.1 Topologies on test forms and weak compactness of currents

section: 2.10 Test-form topology and compactness of currents
text:
Let $M$ be a smooth Hausdorff real manifold of dimension $m$ with a countable basis, and let $0\leq p\leq m$. Write $\mathcal E^ p_ s(M)=C^ s(M,\Lambda ^ pT^*M\otimes \mathbb C)$ for $s\in \mathbb N\cup \{ \infty \} $, with the topology of uniform convergence on compact coordinate sets of all coefficient derivatives of order at most $s$. For a compact set $K\subset M$, let $\mathcal D^ p_{K,s}$ be the closed-support subspace of forms supported in $K$. Put $\mathcal D^ p(M)= igcup _ K\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$. The notation $\mathcal D'_ p(M)$ means the complex-linear functionals whose restriction to every $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is continuous. Neither the topology of forms nor these functionals require an orientation. Pairings with differential-form coefficients use an orientation when appropriate. Proposition 2.10.2 . BC76137F21A7 Every $\mathcal E^ p_ s(M)$ is a Fréchet space. Each $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is Fréchet, whereas $\mathcal D^ p_{K,s}$ is Banach for finite $s$, with a norm obtained from finitely many compact coordinate sets covering $K$ and all coefficient derivatives of order at most $s$. Proof. Choose countably many charts covering $M$, and in each chart choose countably many compact coordinate cubes whose interiors cover the chart. The coefficient seminorms on these cubes, with the permitted derivative orders, form a countable family. They generate the stated topology: given any other compact coordinate set, finitely many interiors of the chosen cubes cover it, and the chain rule on their compact intersections bounds its coefficient derivatives by finitely many of the chosen seminorms. After replacing a countable family $(q_ j)$ by its successive maxima, a compatible translation-invariant metric is \[  d(u,v)=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\min \{ 1,q_ j(u-v)\} .  \] The seminorms separate forms, so this is a metric. A Cauchy sequence has uniform limits for each coefficient and each permitted derivative on every compact cube. The limits are consistent on overlaps, by the coordinate-change formula and its derivatives. On a smaller coordinate rectangle the identity \[  f_
u (x+te_ a)-f_
u (x) =\int _0^ t\partial _ a f_
u (x+re_ a)\, \mathrm dr  \] passes to the limit whenever the first derivatives are among the permitted ones. Thus the coefficient limit is differentiable with the prescribed first derivatives. Applying the same argument to successive derivatives proves $C^ s$ regularity, or smoothness if $s=\infty $. For $s=0$ only uniform convergence and continuity are needed. This proves completeness for the metric above and hence the Fréchet assertion. The support condition is closed, since convergence of values outside $K$ preserves their vanishing. Thus $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is a closed Fréchet subspace. For finite $s$, choose compact coordinate sets $L_1,\ldots ,L_ N$ whose interiors cover $K$, and set \[  P_{K,s}(u)=\max _{1\leq j\leq N}\  \max _{|I|=p,\, |\alpha |\leq s} \sup _{L_ j}|\partial ^\alpha u_{j,I}|.  \] This is a norm on $\mathcal D^ p_{K,s}$. Outside $K$ every coefficient and permitted derivative vanishes. Inside $K$, coordinate changes on the compact intersections with the $L_ j$ show that every defining seminorm is bounded by a constant times $P_{K,s}$. Consequently the norm induces the subspace topology. A norm-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in $\mathcal E^ p_ s(M)$, its limit remains supported in $K$, and convergence on the finitely many $L_ j$ gives convergence in the norm. This proves the Banach assertion. Empty spaces and $K=\varnothing $ give the zero space, with its unique topology. $\square$ Give $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ the locally convex topology generated by all seminorms whose restriction to every $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is continuous. This extends the scalar test-function topology of the topology of test functions and distributions , rather than changing it. It is the finest locally convex topology making all these inclusions continuous. Indeed, the continuous seminorms of any such topology belong to the displayed family. A linear functional on $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ is continuous exactly when all its fixed-support restrictions are continuous: in the reverse direction its absolute value is itself an allowed seminorm. Thus its continuous dual is precisely $\mathcal D'_ p(M)$. Proposition 2.10.3 . 257A408A0F68 The topology just defined induces the usual smooth topology on every $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$. A family of test forms is bounded for this topology if and only if its supports are contained in one compact set and all coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on compact coordinate sets. A sequence converges in this topology if and only if its terms and limit have support in one compact set and converge there in every smooth coefficient seminorm. If $M$ is noncompact, $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ is dense and proper in $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ and is incomplete for the topology induced from that space. Its locally convex test-form topology is strictly finer and is not Fréchet. If $M$ is compact, the two spaces and their topologies coincide and are Fréchet. Proof. Every smooth coefficient seminorm restricts continuously to every fixed-support space, so the inclusion $\mathcal D^ p(M)\longrightarrow \mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ is continuous. Conversely, each allowed seminorm is continuous on a fixed-support space by definition. These two observations prove the first assertion. Choose compact sets $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ whose interiors exhaust $M$. Such an exhaustion follows from a countable cover by relatively compact coordinate balls: at each step include the first $j$ closed balls and finitely many more whose interiors cover the preceding compact set. Suppose a bounded family $B$ of test forms has no common compact support. For every $j$ choose $u_ j\in B$ and $x_ j
otin K_ j$ with $u_ j(x_ j)
eq 0$. The points $x_ j$ leave every compact set. Choose a complex-linear functional $\ell _ j$ on the finite-dimensional fiber at $x_ j$ with $\ell _ j(u_ j(x_ j))
eq 0$, and choose $c_ j>0$ so that $c_ j|\ell _ j(u_ j(x_ j))|\geq j$. Then \[  q(u)=\sup _ j c_ j|\ell _ j(u(x_ j))|  \] is finite for every compactly supported $u$. On every fixed-support space only finitely many terms can be nonzero; they are continuous point-evaluation seminorms. Hence $q$ is an allowed continuous seminorm, whereas $\sup _{u\in B}q(u)=\infty $, a contradiction. This proves the common-support assertion. The remaining boundedness characterization follows from the first assertion: on a fixed-support space a continuous seminorm is bounded by a constant times finitely many coefficient seminorms. Here boundedness in a locally convex space is equivalently boundedness for every continuous seminorm. A convergent sequence together with its limit is bounded, because each of its continuous seminorms is bounded. It therefore has common compact support, and convergence is smooth by the continuous inclusion into $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$. Conversely, convergence in a fixed-support space implies convergence in $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ by continuity of its inclusion. This proves the sequence assertion; no corresponding common-support assertion for arbitrary convergent nets is made. Smooth compact cutoffs $\chi _ j=1$ near $K_ j$ give $\chi _ j u\longrightarrow u$ in $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ for every smooth form $u$, proving density. The real-coordinate cutoff construction preceding Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners supplies these cutoffs. If $M$ is noncompact, choose points escaping every compact set and pairwise disjoint, locally finite, relatively compact coordinate neighborhoods of them. They can be chosen recursively outside an exhaustion enlarged to contain the previously chosen closures. Nonzero smooth $p$-forms supported in these neighborhoods have a locally finite sum with noncompact support. Call this form $u$. The sequence $\chi _ j u$ is Cauchy in the induced smooth topology and has no limit there in $\mathcal D^ p(M)$, since its unique smooth limit is $u$. This proves properness and incompleteness. Choose instead one nonzero test form $v_ j$ supported outside $K_ j$ and normalize it to have value $1$ under a fiber functional at a point outside $K_ j$. Then $v_ j	o 0$ in the induced smooth topology, whereas the seminorm constructed above with weights $c_ j=j$ prevents convergence in the test-form topology. Thus that topology is strictly finer. Each $\mathcal D^ p_{K_ j,\infty }$ is a closed proper linear subspace of $\mathcal D^ p(M)$: it is the common kernel of the point evaluations outside $K_ j$, and a nonzero bump form outside $K_ j$ proves properness. A proper linear subspace has empty interior, since a neighborhood of zero absorbs every vector. These spaces cover $\mathcal D^ p(M)$. It therefore cannot be Fréchet, by the Baire property of a complete metric space. For completeness, if a complete metric space were a countable union of closed sets with empty interior, one could choose nested closed balls of positive radii at most $2^{-j}$, each contained in the interior of its predecessor and disjoint from the $j$th closed set. Their centers are Cauchy and their common limit belongs to none of the sets, a contradiction. Finally, if $M$ is compact then $\mathcal D^ p(M)=\mathcal D^ p_{M,\infty }=\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$; the fixed-support assertion proves equality of topologies. $\square$ Proposition 2.10.4 . 5481DD68A367 Restriction identifies the continuous dual of $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ with the currents in $\mathcal D'_ p(M)$ having compact support. A compactly supported current acts on an arbitrary smooth form by inserting any compact cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of its support. Proof. Continuity of a linear functional $L$ on $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ gives a bound by a constant times finitely many compact coordinate seminorms. If $C$ is the union of those compact sets, this bound shows that the current obtained by restriction vanishes on tests supported in $M\setminus C$. Thus its support is contained in $C$. Conversely let $T$ have compact support $C$, and choose a compactly supported smooth $\chi $ equal to one near $C$. Set \[  L(u)=T(\chi u),\qquad u\in \mathcal E^ p_\infty (M).  \] If $\chi '$ is another such cutoff, $(\chi -\chi ')u$ has compact support and vanishes near $C$, so $T((\chi -\chi ')u)=0$. Indeed, the support definition and a finite partition of unity show that $T$ annihilates every test form supported outside $C$. This proves independence and also shows that $L$ restricts to $T$. On the fixed-support space with support $\operatorname {Supp}\chi $, continuity of $T$ bounds it by finitely many coefficient seminorms of some finite order. The Leibniz rule bounds those seminorms of $\chi u$ by a constant times finitely many compact coefficient seminorms of $u$. Hence $L$ is continuous on $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$. Finally, two continuous extensions agree on the dense test-form subspace, so they agree everywhere. This proves the identification. $\square$ Theorem 2.10.5 . 423C948D346B Let $A\subset \mathcal D'_ p(M)$ satisfy \[  \sup _{T\in A}|T(u)|<\infty \quad 	ext{for every }u\in \mathcal D^ p(M).  \] Then its closure for pointwise convergence on test forms is compact and consists of currents. In particular, every weakly closed, pointwise bounded family of currents is weakly compact. Proof. The empty family needs no argument. Fix a compact set $K$, put $E_ K=\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$, and consider the closed sets \[  F_ n=\{ u\in E_ K: |T(u)|\leq n	ext{ for every }T\in A\} , \qquad n\geq 1.  \] Pointwise boundedness gives $E_ K= igcup _ n F_ n$. For $v\in U$, \[  |T(v)|\leq |T(u_0+v)|+|T(u_0)|\leq 2n \quad (T\in A).  \] There are $r\in \mathbb N$ and $\varepsilon >0$ such that $\{ P_{K,r}<\varepsilon \} \subset U$, using the finite-coordinate norms from proposition 2.10.2 . title: Proposition 2.10.2
section: 2.10 Test-form topology and compactness of currents
text:
Proposition 2.10.2 . BC76137F21A7 Every $\mathcal E^ p_ s(M)$ is a Fréchet space. Each $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is Fréchet, whereas $\mathcal D^ p_{K,s}$ is Banach for finite $s$, with a norm obtained from finitely many compact coordinate sets covering $K$ and all coefficient derivatives of order at most $s$. Proof. Choose countably many charts covering $M$, and in each chart choose countably many compact coordinate cubes whose interiors cover the chart. The coefficient seminorms on these cubes, with the permitted derivative orders, form a countable family. They generate the stated topology: given any other compact coordinate set, finitely many interiors of the chosen cubes cover it, and the chain rule on their compact intersections bounds its coefficient derivatives by finitely many of the chosen seminorms. After replacing a countable family $(q_ j)$ by its successive maxima, a compatible translation-invariant metric is \[  d(u,v)=\sum _{j\geq 1}2^{-j}\min \{ 1,q_ j(u-v)\} .  \] The seminorms separate forms, so this is a metric. A Cauchy sequence has uniform limits for each coefficient and each permitted derivative on every compact cube. The limits are consistent on overlaps, by the coordinate-change formula and its derivatives. On a smaller coordinate rectangle the identity \[  f_
u (x+te_ a)-f_
u (x) =\int _0^ t\partial _ a f_
u (x+re_ a)\, \mathrm dr  \] passes to the limit whenever the first derivatives are among the permitted ones. Thus the coefficient limit is differentiable with the prescribed first derivatives. Applying the same argument to successive derivatives proves $C^ s$ regularity, or smoothness if $s=\infty $. For $s=0$ only uniform convergence and continuity are needed. This proves completeness for the metric above and hence the Fréchet assertion. The support condition is closed, since convergence of values outside $K$ preserves their vanishing. Thus $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$ is a closed Fréchet subspace. For finite $s$, choose compact coordinate sets $L_1,\ldots ,L_ N$ whose interiors cover $K$, and set \[  P_{K,s}(u)=\max _{1\leq j\leq N}\  \max _{|I|=p,\, |\alpha |\leq s} \sup _{L_ j}|\partial ^\alpha u_{j,I}|.  \] This is a norm on $\mathcal D^ p_{K,s}$. Outside $K$ every coefficient and permitted derivative vanishes. Inside $K$, coordinate changes on the compact intersections with the $L_ j$ show that every defining seminorm is bounded by a constant times $P_{K,s}$. Consequently the norm induces the subspace topology. A norm-Cauchy sequence is Cauchy in $\mathcal E^ p_ s(M)$, its limit remains supported in $K$, and convergence on the finitely many $L_ j$ gives convergence in the norm. This proves the Banach assertion. Empty spaces and $K=\varnothing $ give the zero space, with its unique topology. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.10.3
section: 2.10 Test-form topology and compactness of currents
text:
Proposition 2.10.3 . 257A408A0F68 The topology just defined induces the usual smooth topology on every $\mathcal D^ p_{K,\infty }$. A family of test forms is bounded for this topology if and only if its supports are contained in one compact set and all coefficient derivatives are uniformly bounded on compact coordinate sets. A sequence converges in this topology if and only if its terms and limit have support in one compact set and converge there in every smooth coefficient seminorm. If $M$ is noncompact, $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ is dense and proper in $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ and is incomplete for the topology induced from that space. Its locally convex test-form topology is strictly finer and is not Fréchet. If $M$ is compact, the two spaces and their topologies coincide and are Fréchet. Proof. Every smooth coefficient seminorm restricts continuously to every fixed-support space, so the inclusion $\mathcal D^ p(M)\longrightarrow \mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ is continuous. Conversely, each allowed seminorm is continuous on a fixed-support space by definition. These two observations prove the first assertion. Choose compact sets $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ whose interiors exhaust $M$. Such an exhaustion follows from a countable cover by relatively compact coordinate balls: at each step include the first $j$ closed balls and finitely many more whose interiors cover the preceding compact set. Suppose a bounded family $B$ of test forms has no common compact support. For every $j$ choose $u_ j\in B$ and $x_ j
otin K_ j$ with $u_ j(x_ j)
eq 0$. The points $x_ j$ leave every compact set. Choose a complex-linear functional $\ell _ j$ on the finite-dimensional fiber at $x_ j$ with $\ell _ j(u_ j(x_ j))
eq 0$, and choose $c_ j>0$ so that $c_ j|\ell _ j(u_ j(x_ j))|\geq j$. Then \[  q(u)=\sup _ j c_ j|\ell _ j(u(x_ j))|  \] is finite for every compactly supported $u$. On every fixed-support space only finitely many terms can be nonzero; they are continuous point-evaluation seminorms. Hence $q$ is an allowed continuous seminorm, whereas $\sup _{u\in B}q(u)=\infty $, a contradiction. This proves the common-support assertion. The remaining boundedness characterization follows from the first assertion: on a fixed-support space a continuous seminorm is bounded by a constant times finitely many coefficient seminorms. Here boundedness in a locally convex space is equivalently boundedness for every continuous seminorm. A convergent sequence together with its limit is bounded, because each of its continuous seminorms is bounded. It therefore has common compact support, and convergence is smooth by the continuous inclusion into $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$. Conversely, convergence in a fixed-support space implies convergence in $\mathcal D^ p(M)$ by continuity of its inclusion. This proves the sequence assertion; no corresponding common-support assertion for arbitrary convergent nets is made. Smooth compact cutoffs $\chi _ j=1$ near $K_ j$ give $\chi _ j u\longrightarrow u$ in $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ for every smooth form $u$, proving density. The real-coordinate cutoff construction preceding Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners supplies these cutoffs. If $M$ is noncompact, choose points escaping every compact set and pairwise disjoint, locally finite, relatively compact coordinate neighborhoods of them. They can be chosen recursively outside an exhaustion enlarged to contain the previously chosen closures. Nonzero smooth $p$-forms supported in these neighborhoods have a locally finite sum with noncompact support. Call this form $u$. The sequence $\chi _ j u$ is Cauchy in the induced smooth topology and has no limit there in $\mathcal D^ p(M)$, since its unique smooth limit is $u$. This proves properness and incompleteness. Choose instead one nonzero test form $v_ j$ supported outside $K_ j$ and normalize it to have value $1$ under a fiber functional at a point outside $K_ j$. Then $v_ j	o 0$ in the induced smooth topology, whereas the seminorm constructed above with weights $c_ j=j$ prevents convergence in the test-form topology. Thus that topology is strictly finer. Each $\mathcal D^ p_{K_ j,\infty }$ is a closed proper linear subspace of $\mathcal D^ p(M)$: it is the common kernel of the point evaluations outside $K_ j$, and a nonzero bump form outside $K_ j$ proves properness. A proper linear subspace has empty interior, since a neighborhood of zero absorbs every vector. These spaces cover $\mathcal D^ p(M)$. It therefore cannot be Fréchet, by the Baire property of a complete metric space. For completeness, if a complete metric space were a countable union of closed sets with empty interior, one could choose nested closed balls of positive radii at most $2^{-j}$, each contained in the interior of its predecessor and disjoint from the $j$th closed set. Their centers are Cauchy and their common limit belongs to none of the sets, a contradiction. Finally, if $M$ is compact then $\mathcal D^ p(M)=\mathcal D^ p_{M,\infty }=\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$; the fixed-support assertion proves equality of topologies. $\square$

title: Proposition 2.10.4
section: 2.10 Test-form topology and compactness of currents
text: Proposition 2.10.4 . 5481DD68A367 Restriction identifies the continuous dual of $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ with the currents in $\mathcal D'_ p(M)$ having compact support. A compactly supported current acts on an arbitrary smooth form by inserting any compact cutoff equal to one on a neighborhood of its support. Proof. Continuity of a linear functional $L$ on $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$ gives a bound by a constant times finitely many compact coordinate seminorms. If $C$ is the union of those compact sets, this bound shows that the current obtained by restriction vanishes on tests supported in $M\setminus C$. Thus its support is contained in $C$. Conversely let $T$ have compact support $C$, and choose a compactly supported smooth $\chi $ equal to one near $C$. Set \[  L(u)=T(\chi u),\qquad u\in \mathcal E^ p_\infty (M).  \] If $\chi '$ is another such cutoff, $(\chi -\chi ')u$ has compact support and vanishes near $C$, so $T((\chi -\chi ')u)=0$. Indeed, the support definition and a finite partition of unity show that $T$ annihilates every test form supported outside $C$. This proves independence and also shows that $L$ restricts to $T$. On the fixed-support space with support $\operatorname {Supp}\chi $, continuity of $T$ bounds it by finitely many coefficient seminorms of some finite order. The Leibniz rule bounds those seminorms of $\chi u$ by a constant times finitely many compact coefficient seminorms of $u$. Hence $L$ is continuous on $\mathcal E^ p_\infty (M)$. Finally, two continuous extensions agree on the dense test-form subspace, so they agree everywhere. This proves the identification. $\square$

title: 5.55 Integration over real submanifolds
section: 5.55 Integration over real submanifolds
text: Proposition 5.55.1 . E09F702EB680 Let $M$ be an oriented smooth real manifold of dimension $m$, and let $Z\subset M$ be a closed oriented embedded submanifold of class $C^1$ and dimension $p$, possibly with boundary. Integration defines an order-zero current $[Z]$ of degree $m-p$, with support $Z$. With the outward-normal-first boundary orientation and the convention $\langle \mathrm dT,\alpha \rangle =(-1)^{\deg T+1} \langle T,\mathrm d\alpha \rangle $, one has \[  \mathrm d[Z]=(-1)^{m-p+1}[\partial Z].  \] In particular $[Z]$ is normal, and it is closed if $\partial Z$ is empty. Proof. In a $C^1$ parameterization $F$ of $Z$, pullback of a continuous $p$-form involves only the coefficients of the form and the first derivatives of $F$. A compact subset of $M$ meets $Z$ in a compact set, covered by finitely many relatively compact parameter patches. The continuous Jacobians are bounded on those patches. A partition of unity therefore gives, for every compact $K\subset M$, \[  \left|\int _ Z\alpha \right|\leq C_ K\| \alpha \| _{C^0(K)} \qquad (\operatorname {Supp}\alpha \subset K).  \] Here use finitely many fixed ambient coordinates for the coefficient norm. Change of variables for $C^1$ parameterizations makes the integral independent of the charts. This proves the order-zero assertion. Its support is contained in $Z$ by closedness. Near every interior point one can choose a smooth ambient $p$-form whose pullback is positive on a small oriented parameter patch. Thus the current is nonzero there. Boundary points are limits of interior points, giving equality of the support with $Z$. We supply the required $C^1$ Stokes argument, since the pullback of a smooth form by a merely $C^1$ parameterization need not be $C^1$. Localize a smooth compactly supported $(p-1)$-form $\alpha $ by an ambient smooth partition of unity near $Z\cap \operatorname {Supp}\alpha $. It suffices to treat one parameter patch, with fixed parameter domain an open box or a half-box $\{ s_ p\geq 0\} $. The pullback has compact support away from all artificial sides. Work in one ambient coordinate chart. The coordinate map $F$ has a $C^1$ extension across the flat boundary: for negative $t=s_ p$ put \[  F(s',t)=3F(s',-t)-2F(s',-2t)  \] on a smaller box. The value and all first derivatives match at $t=0$, including the normal derivative $-3+4=1$. Mollification yields smooth maps $F_ j\to F$ in $C^1$ on the compact parameter region in question, with values in the same ambient chart. They need not be embeddings. For all sufficiently large $j$, the pullbacks of the localized form have support in one fixed compact parameter region away from the artificial sides. Indeed, choose the ambient support compactly inside the original patch and a larger compact parameter neighborhood; on its boundary the image of $F$ is separated from that support, and uniform convergence preserves the separation. Smooth pullback commutes with $\mathrm d$. The smooth half-box Stokes formula, already proved by coordinate Fubini in Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners , gives \[  \int F_ j^*(\mathrm d\alpha ) =\int _{s_ p=0}F_ j^*\alpha  \] with the induced orientation; in an interior patch the right side is zero. Uniform $C^1$ convergence gives uniform convergence of both pullbacks on these fixed compact sets. Passing to the limit proves the same equality for $F$. Summing the ambient partition cancels its differentiated coefficients and proves $\int _ Z\mathrm d\alpha =\int _{\partial Z}\alpha $. The displayed current sign now follows from the stated differential convention. Since $\partial Z$ is a closed $C^1$ submanifold of dimension $p-1$, its integration current is of order zero by the same chart estimate. Thus $[Z]$ and its derivative both have order zero. If $p=0$, compact sets meet the closed discrete submanifold in finitely many points; the current is the oriented point sum, and its derivative and boundary both vanish. $\square$
