title: 9.28 Strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions on coverings
section: 9.28 Strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions on coverings
text:
The manifolds below are Hausdorff and have a countable basis. A finite continuous exhaustion has compact closed sublevels. Strong pseudoconvexity means the existence of a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion, as in section 9.26 . A holomorphic unramified covering is a covering map whose restrictions to its local sheets are biholomorphisms. We first supply the metric compactness needed in the construction. For a Riemannian metric $g$, the length distance $d_ g$ is the infimum of the lengths of piecewise smooth connecting paths. On a connected manifold these distances are finite: the points accessible from one point by finitely many coordinate segments form an open and closed set. The distance induces the manifold topology. Indeed, on a compact coordinate ball the metric has fixed positive lower and upper Euclidean bounds; a path leaving a smaller concentric ball has a fixed positive length before its first exit, whereas a coordinate segment gives the local upper distance bound. Lemma 9.28.1 . 9DBBB1BAE0CF In a complete, locally compact length metric space, every closed bounded ball is compact. In particular, this holds for the length distance of a complete Riemannian metric. Proof. Fix a center $o$. Local compactness gives a small closed ball about $o$ contained in a compact neighborhood, hence compact. Let $R$ be the supremum of the radii of compact closed balls about $o$. All closed balls of radius $r<R$ are compact, since each is a closed subset of a compact ball of a larger radius. Suppose $R<\infty $. The closed ball of radius $R$ is totally bounded. For an arbitrary $\varepsilon >0$, choose $r<R$ with $R-r<\varepsilon /4$. A point $y$ of that ball can be joined to $o$ by a path of length less than $d(o,y)+\varepsilon /4$. If its length exceeds $r$, cut it after length $r$; the cut point lies in the compact ball of radius $r$ and its distance to $y$ is less than $\varepsilon /2$. If its length does not exceed $r$, then $y$ already lies in that ball. A finite $\varepsilon /2$-net of the smaller ball is thus a finite $\varepsilon $-net of the ball of radius $R$. The latter ball is complete, being closed in a complete space, and therefore compact. Here completeness and total boundedness imply compactness by the finite-net and Cauchy-subsequence argument used in the Arzelà–Ascoli compactness theorem . For each point of this compact ball choose $a_ p>0$ such that the closed metric ball $\overline B(p,3a_ p)$ is compact. Finitely many $B(p_ i,a_ i)$ cover it. Put $a=\min _ i a_ i>0$. Any point $y$ with $d(o,y)\leq R+a/2$ has a connecting path of length less than $R+3a/4$. If that length exceeds $R$, its cut point after length $R$ belongs to $B(p_ i,a_ i)$ for some $i$, and then $d(y,p_ i)<a_ i+3a/4<2a_ i$. If its length is at most $R$, then $y$ itself lies in one of the $B(p_ i,a_ i)$. Thus the closed ball of radius $R+a/2$ is contained in the finite union of the compact closed balls $\overline B(p_ i,3a_ i)$. Being closed, it is compact, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R=\infty $. $\square$ Proposition 9.28.2 . E200BE9CFD9E Let $\pi :\widetilde X	o X$ be an unramified covering of connected complex manifolds. If $g$ is a Riemannian metric on $X$ complete for its length distance, then $\widetilde g=\pi ^*g$ is complete. For every $y_0\in \widetilde X$, \[  \delta _0(y)=d_{\widetilde g}(y,y_0)  \] is a nonnegative continuous exhaustion and is $1$-Lipschitz. Proof. Projection preserves the length of every piecewise smooth path, so $d_ g(\pi y,\pi z)\leq d_{\widetilde g}(y,z)$. Let $(y_ j)$ be Cauchy upstairs. Its projections converge to some $x\in X$. Choose an evenly covered neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and $a>0$ so that $B_ g(x,4a)\subset V$. For all sufficiently large indices, $\pi y_ j\in B_ g(x,a)$ and $d_{\widetilde g}(y_ j,y_ k)<a/2$. A path joining $y_ j$ to $y_ k$ with length less than $a$ projects entirely into $B_ g(x,2a)\subset V$. The path upstairs therefore lies in one sheet of $\pi ^{-1}(V)$. Fixing one sufficiently large $j$ shows that the whole tail belongs to that same sheet. On it the inverse of $\pi $ is continuous, so $y_ k$ converges to the inverse image of $x$ in the sheet. The length distance induces the manifold topology, proving completeness. The metric is locally compact because the manifold is locally Euclidean. The preceding lemma makes its closed balls compact. These balls are precisely the nonnegative closed sublevels of $\delta _0$. The triangle inequality proves its continuity and $1$-Lipschitz bound. $\square$ Proposition 9.28.3 . 7808CCD76C79 Under the same hypotheses there is a smooth real exhaustion $\delta $ on $\widetilde X$ with $|\delta -\delta _0|\leq 1$. For each compact subset of a coordinate open set in $X$ and each positive derivative order, the coordinate derivatives of $\delta $ are bounded there uniformly over all sheets of the covering. title: Lemma 9.28.1
section: 9.28 Strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions on coverings
text: Lemma 9.28.1 . 9DBBB1BAE0CF In a complete, locally compact length metric space, every closed bounded ball is compact. In particular, this holds for the length distance of a complete Riemannian metric. Proof. Fix a center $o$. Local compactness gives a small closed ball about $o$ contained in a compact neighborhood, hence compact. Let $R$ be the supremum of the radii of compact closed balls about $o$. All closed balls of radius $r<R$ are compact, since each is a closed subset of a compact ball of a larger radius. Suppose $R<\infty $. The closed ball of radius $R$ is totally bounded. For an arbitrary $\varepsilon >0$, choose $r<R$ with $R-r<\varepsilon /4$. A point $y$ of that ball can be joined to $o$ by a path of length less than $d(o,y)+\varepsilon /4$. If its length exceeds $r$, cut it after length $r$; the cut point lies in the compact ball of radius $r$ and its distance to $y$ is less than $\varepsilon /2$. If its length does not exceed $r$, then $y$ already lies in that ball. A finite $\varepsilon /2$-net of the smaller ball is thus a finite $\varepsilon $-net of the ball of radius $R$. The latter ball is complete, being closed in a complete space, and therefore compact. Here completeness and total boundedness imply compactness by the finite-net and Cauchy-subsequence argument used in the Arzelà–Ascoli compactness theorem . For each point of this compact ball choose $a_ p>0$ such that the closed metric ball $\overline B(p,3a_ p)$ is compact. Finitely many $B(p_ i,a_ i)$ cover it. Put $a=\min _ i a_ i>0$. Any point $y$ with $d(o,y)\leq R+a/2$ has a connecting path of length less than $R+3a/4$. If that length exceeds $R$, its cut point after length $R$ belongs to $B(p_ i,a_ i)$ for some $i$, and then $d(y,p_ i)<a_ i+3a/4<2a_ i$. If its length is at most $R$, then $y$ itself lies in one of the $B(p_ i,a_ i)$. Thus the closed ball of radius $R+a/2$ is contained in the finite union of the compact closed balls $\overline B(p_ i,3a_ i)$. Being closed, it is compact, contradicting the definition of $R$. Hence $R=\infty $. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.28.2
section: 9.28 Strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustions on coverings
text: Proposition 9.28.2 . E200BE9CFD9E Let $\pi :\widetilde X\to X$ be an unramified covering of connected complex manifolds. If $g$ is a Riemannian metric on $X$ complete for its length distance, then $\widetilde g=\pi ^*g$ is complete. For every $y_0\in \widetilde X$, \[  \delta _0(y)=d_{\widetilde g}(y,y_0)  \] is a nonnegative continuous exhaustion and is $1$-Lipschitz. Proof. Projection preserves the length of every piecewise smooth path, so $d_ g(\pi y,\pi z)\leq d_{\widetilde g}(y,z)$. Let $(y_ j)$ be Cauchy upstairs. Its projections converge to some $x\in X$. Choose an evenly covered neighborhood $V$ of $x$ and $a>0$ so that $B_ g(x,4a)\subset V$. For all sufficiently large indices, $\pi y_ j\in B_ g(x,a)$ and $d_{\widetilde g}(y_ j,y_ k)<a/2$. A path joining $y_ j$ to $y_ k$ with length less than $a$ projects entirely into $B_ g(x,2a)\subset V$. The path upstairs therefore lies in one sheet of $\pi ^{-1}(V)$. Fixing one sufficiently large $j$ shows that the whole tail belongs to that same sheet. On it the inverse of $\pi $ is continuous, so $y_ k$ converges to the inverse image of $x$ in the sheet. The length distance induces the manifold topology, proving completeness. The metric is locally compact because the manifold is locally Euclidean. The preceding lemma makes its closed balls compact. These balls are precisely the nonnegative closed sublevels of $\delta _0$. The triangle inequality proves its continuity and $1$-Lipschitz bound. $\square$

section: 10.33 Vector-bundle curvature and compact Dolbeault estimates
text: Let $(X,\omega )$ be a Kähler manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $(E,h)$ be a holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric. Inner products are linear in the first variable. We use $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$, and the unscaled Chern curvature is denoted by $\Theta (E)$. Thus for a line bundle with squared frame norm $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$, $\mathrm i\Theta (E)=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \phi =2\pi c_1(E,h)$. The pointwise metric on forms is induced by $g(v,w)=\omega (v,Jw)$, and $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$. In a holomorphic frame write $h(v,w)=w^*Hv$. Its Chern connection is \[  D'=\partial +A\wedge ,\qquad D''=\bar\partial , \qquad A=H^{-1}\partial H.  \] If the frame changes by a holomorphic invertible matrix $G$, then $H$ changes to $G^*HG$ and $A$ to $G^{-1}AG+G^{-1}\partial G$, so these operators are intrinsic. The identities $HA=\partial H$ and $A^*H=\bar\partial H$ verify metric compatibility by differentiating $w^*Hv$. Differentiating $H^{-1}H=1$ gives $\partial A+A\wedge A=0$, whence 0BB4122DCA2A 10.33.1 \begin{equation}  (D')^2=(D'')^2=0,\qquad D'D''+D''D'=\Theta (E)\wedge ,\qquad \Theta (E)=\bar\partial (H^{-1}\partial H). \end{equation} Here matrix-valued forms act by exterior multiplication on the left, with the usual graded product rule. Let $\delta ',\delta ''$ be the formal adjoints of $D',D''$, and put $\Delta '=D'\delta '+\delta 'D'$ and $\Delta ''=D''\delta ''+\delta ''D''$. The Lefschetz operators are $L=\omega \wedge $ and $\Lambda =L^*$. For operators of total degrees $a,b$ use $[P,Q]=PQ-(-1)^{ab}QP$. Theorem 10.33.2 . 836B94BFF74C On all smooth $E$-valued forms, 8552D5DC8CAA 10.33.3 \begin{equation}  [\Lambda ,D']=\mathrm i\delta '',\qquad [\Lambda ,D'']=-\mathrm i\delta ',\qquad [D',\delta '']=[D'',\delta ']=0, \end{equation} and FC33C3E2A980 10.33.4 \begin{equation}  \Delta ''=\Delta '+B,\qquad B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda ]. \end{equation} Consequently, for every compactly supported smooth $E$-valued $(p,q)$-form $v$, 77EDE4CBDD16 10.33.5 \begin{equation}  \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2 =\| D'v\| ^2+\| \delta 'v\| ^2+\int _ X\langle Bv,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Proof. The scalar Kähler calculation in the line-bundle Bochner–Kodaira identity applies componentwise in a Chern-normal frame. Here are the frame reduction and the operator signs. Choose Kähler normal coordinates at a point by Kähler normal coordinates , rescaled so that $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$ at the point. A constant frame change makes $H=1$ there. The holomorphic frame change $G(z)=1-\sum _ j(\partial _ jH)(0)z_ j$, on a sufficiently small neighborhood, then makes every first derivative of $H$ vanish at the point. Thus $A=0$ there. The coefficients of the pointwise form metric and volume also have vanishing first derivatives there. Write $\epsilon _ j,\bar\epsilon _ j$ for exterior multiplication by $\mathrm dz_ j,\mathrm d\bar z_ j$ and $\iota _ j,\bar\iota _ j$ for their pointwise adjoints. At the point, \[  \Lambda =-\mathrm i\sum _ j\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j,\quad D'=\sum _ j\epsilon _ j\partial _ j,\quad D''=\sum _ j\bar\epsilon _ j\partial _{\bar j},\quad \delta '=-\sum _ j\iota _ j\partial _{\bar j},\quad \delta ''=-\sum _ j\bar\iota _ j\partial _ j.  \] The adjoint formulas follow by one integration by parts; the extra zeroth-order coefficients involve only first derivatives of the metric and vanish at this point. The exterior and contraction operators satisfy $\iota _ j\epsilon _ k+\epsilon _ k\iota _ j=\delta _{jk}$ and the analogous barred relation, while all mixed anticommutators vanish. These relations give the first two identities in ( 10.33.3 ). They are identities of first-order operators: their commutators involve only first derivatives of the coefficients of $\Lambda $, which also vanish at the point. Since the point is arbitrary, the identities hold globally. For completeness the graded Jacobi identity gives \[  [D'',[\Lambda ,D']] =[[D'',\Lambda ],D']+[\Lambda ,[D'',D']] =\mathrm i\Delta '+[\Lambda ,\Theta (E)].  \] Multiply by $-\mathrm i$ and use $\delta ''=-\mathrm i[\Lambda ,D']$ to obtain ( 10.33.4 ). Also $[D',[\Lambda ,D']]=0$ follows by expanding and using $(D')^2=0$; the same expansion for $D''$ proves the last two commutators in ( 10.33.3 ). Integrating the operator identity and applying the defining identities of the formal adjoints proves ( 10.33.5 ). $\square$ At a point choose an $\omega $-unitary $(1,0)$-coframe $\theta _1,\ldots ,\theta _ n$ and an $h$-unitary frame of $E$, and write \[  \mathrm i\Theta (E)=\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}R_{j\bar k} \theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ k.  \] The endomorphisms satisfy $R_{j\bar k}^*=R_{k\bar j}$: in the normal holomorphic frame above $R_{j\bar k}=-\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k}H$, and $H=H^*$. The curvature form on $T^{1,0}X\otimes E$ is \[  \mathcal R(\xi ,\xi )=\sum _{j,k} \langle R_{j\bar k}\xi _ j,\xi _ k\rangle , \qquad \xi =(\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ n).  \] A metric is Nakano-positive when this form is positive on every nonzero tensor. It is $m$-positive when the same holds on every nonzero tensor of rank at most $m$, the rank being the rank of $T^{1,0*}X\longrightarrow E$ determined by that tensor. Thus Nakano positivity is $m$-positivity for $m\geq \min (n,r)$. Proposition 10.33.6 . DAA549FD5760 In the unitary frames, exterior and contraction operators being denoted as before, the curvature operator on $(p,q)$-forms is 794C2246496E 10.33.7 \begin{equation}  B=\sum _{j,k}R_{j\bar k} \bigl (\epsilon _ j\iota _ k+\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j -\delta _{jk}\bigr ). \end{equation} For $1\leq q\leq n$ and an $(n,q)$-form $v=\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \theta _ n\wedge \sum _{|J|=q}v_ J\bar\theta _ J$, with increasing $J$, this gives 64227AA6EECF 10.33.8 \begin{equation}  \langle Bv,v\rangle =\sum _{|S|=q-1}\sum _{j,k} \langle R_{j\bar k}v_{jS},v_{kS}\rangle . \end{equation} The coefficient $v_{jS}$ is alternating in $jS$ and is zero for $j\in S$. If $\mathcal R(\xi ,\xi )\geq \varepsilon |\xi |^2$ on tensors of rank at most $m$, and $m\geq \min (n-q+1,r)$, then 7D37E558834B 10.33.9 \begin{equation}  \langle Bv,v\rangle \geq q\varepsilon |v|^2. \end{equation} Proof. For each $j,k,l$, the anticommutation rules give \[  [\epsilon _ j\bar\epsilon _ k,\bar\iota _ l\iota _ l] =\delta _{kl}\epsilon _ j\iota _ l +\delta _{jl}\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ l -\delta _{jl}\delta _{kl}.  \] Indeed, moving $\bar\epsilon _ k$ past $\bar\iota _ l$ in the first product and $\iota _ l$ past $\epsilon _ j$ in the second cancels the remaining four-operator products; use $\bar\iota _ l\bar\epsilon _ k=\delta _{lk}-\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ l$ for the final two terms. Multiplication by the factors $\mathrm i$ and $-\mathrm i$ in $\mathrm i\Theta (E)$ and $\Lambda $, and summation in $l$, proves ( 10.33.7 ). On holomorphic top degree $\epsilon _ j\iota _ k=\delta _{jk}$, leaving $B=\sum _{j,k}R_{j\bar k}\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j$. Taking its quadratic form gives $\sum _{j,k}\langle R_{j\bar k}\bar\iota _ jv,\bar\iota _ kv\rangle $. The common sign $(-1)^ n$ from passing the barred contraction through the holomorphic top form cancels in this pairing. Expanding in the orthonormal $\bar\theta _ S$ proves ( 10.33.8 ). For fixed $S$, the tensor $(v_{jS})_ j$ has zero rows for $j\in S$, so its rank is at most $\min (n-q+1,r)$. Apply the assumed lower bound to each such tensor and use $\sum _ S\sum _ j|v_{jS}|^2=q\sum _ J|v_ J|^2$; each increasing $J$ is counted once for each of its $q$ indices. This proves ( 10.33.9 ). $\square$ We use explicit analytic Dolbeault cohomology: \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)= \frac{\ker (D'':C^\infty _{p,q}(X,E)\to C^\infty _{p,q+1}(X,E))}{D''C^\infty _{p,q-1}(X,E)},  \] with denominator zero when $q=0$. Formula ( 10.33.7 ) and $R_{j\bar k}^*=R_{k\bar j}$ show that $B$ is pointwise Hermitian. These groups use smooth forms; the following argument includes the regularity needed for smooth primitives. Theorem 10.33.10 . 9B323DF3F730 Assume now that $X$ is compact. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$ and $1\leq q\leq n$. If $B\geq \lambda \operatorname {Id}$ on $\Lambda ^{p,q}T^*X\otimes E$ for a constant $\lambda >0$, then D5878EE600F1 10.33.11 \begin{equation}  \lambda \| v\| ^2\leq \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2 \qquad (v\in C^\infty _{p,q}(X,E)). \end{equation} Every distributionally $D''$-closed $f\in L^2_{p,q}(X,E)$ has a solution $u\in L^2_{p,q-1}(X,E)$ with 0E5CF028319E 10.33.12 \begin{equation}  D''u=f,\qquad \| u\| ^2\leq \lambda ^{-1}\| f\| ^2. \end{equation} There is a unique solution of smallest $L^2$ norm. When $f$ is smooth this solution is smooth, belongs to the image of $\delta ''$, and satisfies $\delta ''u=0$. In particular $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0$. If $q=0$ and $B\geq \lambda \operatorname {Id}$ in that bidegree, then $H^{p,0}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0$ as well. Proof. The energy identity proves ( 10.33.11 ). section: 10.39 Compact jet interpolation and positive line bundles
text: For a holomorphic line bundle $L$ and $x\in X$, write \[  J_ x^ m L=\mathcal O(L)_ x/\mathfrak m_ x^{m+1}\mathcal O(L)_ x, \qquad m\geq 0,  \] where $\mathfrak m_ x$ is the maximal ideal of holomorphic function germs vanishing at $x$. Thus $J_ x^0L=L_ x$. A smooth quadratic metric $h$ is positive if its normalized curvature $c_1(L,h)=\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)/(2\pi )$ is positive definite. Throughout, $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$. Theorem 10.39.1 . 1EAA4FEF8A05 Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $L\to X$ carry a smooth positive metric. Fix distinct points $x_1,\ldots ,x_ N$, with $N\geq 1$. There is a constant $C>0$ such that \[  H^0(X,L^{\otimes k})\longrightarrow \bigoplus _{j=1}^ N J_{x_ j}^ m L^{\otimes k}  \] is surjective for all integers $m\geq 0$ and $k\geq C(m+1)$. Proof. Fix a positive metric $h$ on $L$ and put $\omega =c_1(L,h)$; this is a Kähler form. Give $K_ X^{-1}$ the metric dual to that induced by $\omega $ on $K_ X=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*X$. Compactness gives $b\geq 0$ with FB388D7D27DE 10.39.2 \begin{equation}  c_1(K_ X^{-1},h_{K^{-1},\omega })\geq -b\omega . \end{equation} Choose disjoint relatively compact coordinate balls centered at the $x_ j$. In each choose a nonpositive cutoff logarithm $\psi _ j$, equal to $\log |z-z(x_ j)|^2$ plus a constant near $x_ j$ and zero near and outside the boundary of its ball. The cutoff construction in weighted point extension on compact Kähler manifolds , Step 1, gives these functions; each is quasi-plurisubharmonic, smooth away from $x_ j$. Its Hessian is nonnegative in the inner ball and has a finite lower bound on the cutoff annulus. Hence there is $B\geq 0$, independent of $m$ and $k$, such that \[  dd^ c\sum _ j\psi _ j\geq -B\omega .  \] Put $\Psi =(n+m)\sum _ j\psi _ j$. On $M=X\setminus \{ x_1,\ldots ,x_ N\} $ the line bundle and smooth metric \[  F=L^{\otimes k}\otimes K_ X^{-1},\qquad h_ F=(h^ k\otimes h_{K^{-1},\omega })\mathrm e^{-\Psi }  \] therefore satisfy E2EBA8B81545 10.39.3 \begin{equation}  c_1(F,h_ F)\geq \bigl (k-b-(n+m)B\bigr )\omega \geq \omega \quad \hbox{if } k\geq b+(n+m)B+1. \end{equation} The constant $C=b+1+nB$ has the property that $k\geq C(m+1)$ implies this last inequality. Represent the prescribed jets in local holomorphic frames by polynomials of degree at most $m$. Smooth cutoffs supported in the chosen balls, equal to one near their centers, give a global smooth section $G$ of $L^{\otimes k}$ with exactly those holomorphic germs near the $x_ j$. Thus $g=\bar\partial G$ is closed and vanishes near every $x_ j$. To apply the estimate to $F$-valued forms, use the canonical identification \[  \mathcal I_ q(\alpha \otimes e) =(\alpha \wedge \tau )\otimes (e\otimes \tau ^{-1}),  \] where $e$ is a local frame of $L^{\otimes k}$, $\alpha $ has type $(0,q)$ and $\tau $ is a local nowhere zero holomorphic $n$-form. The weighted norm of $\mathcal I_1g$ is finite, since its support is a compact subset of $M$. By complete metrics and cutoffs away from analytic poles , applied to $\Psi $, $M$ has the auxiliary Kähler form and cutoffs required in the complete-metric line-bundle $L^2$ estimate . F55376F6016B Let $X$ be a connected compact complex manifold of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $L\to X$ be a holomorphic line bundle. For each fixed pair, $G$ can be formed in disjoint smaller neighborhoods, and its weighted error norm is finite. A uniform bound for that norm is not needed for surjectivity. Thus the same $k_0$ works even for pairs arbitrarily close to the diagonal. Fix $k\geq k_0$. The space $V_ k=H^0(X,L^{\otimes k})$ is finite dimensional by compactness of bounded holomorphic sections . Surjectivity of first jets includes evaluation at each point, so any basis of $V_ k$ defines a holomorphic map \[  \Phi _ k:X\longrightarrow \mathbb P(V_ k^*).  \] It is injective: for $x\ne y$ there is a section vanishing at $x$ and nonzero at $y$, whereas equality of the projective evaluation points would make their evaluation kernels equal. They therefore detect every nonzero tangent vector. Selecting $n$ of them with independent differentials and using the holomorphic inverse and submersion theorems shows that $\Phi _ k$ is a holomorphic embedding locally. Globally it is a homeomorphism onto its image, since $X$ is compact and projective space is Hausdorff. title: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
section: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
text:
All complex spaces in this section are reduced, Hausdorff and have a countable basis. Normality is understood stalkwise; in particular, every normal point has an irreducible germ. A meromorphic function is a section of the sheaf of total rings of fractions of the structure sheaf, so its local denominators are nonzerodivisors. On a normal space the local rings are domains. These are the conventions of reduced spaces and normalization . Corollary 9.38.1 . 512196636E86 Let $X$ be a normal complex space, and let $A\subset X$ be an analytic subset such that \[  \dim (A,x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2\qquad (x\in A).  \] Every holomorphic function on $X\setminus A$ has a unique holomorphic extension to $X$. Proof. The assertion is local at points of $A$. Near such a point, $X$ is an irreducible pure-dimensional normal space. The codimension hypothesis therefore holds on each local branch. If $f$ is holomorphic off $A$, the function $|f|^2$ there is locally the restriction of the squared modulus of an ambient holomorphic function, hence is locally plurisubharmonic. By upper bounds near analytic subsets of codimension at least two it is locally bounded above near $A$. Thus $f$ is locally bounded, and the bounded extension on normal spaces in the normal locus and bounded holomorphic continuation extends it holomorphically. The complement of $A$ is dense; uniqueness follows from continuity, so the local extensions glue. In local dimensions zero and one the hypothesis forces $A$ to be empty. $\square$ For a meromorphic function $f$, its pole set is $P_ f=\{ x:f_ x
otin \mathcal O_{X,x}\} $. This is a failure to be a holomorphic germ, not merely the zero set of a chosen denominator. Lemma 9.38.2 . DA978F0F96EA On a normal complex space $X$, the pole set of a meromorphic function is a nowhere dense analytic subset. Near a point where $X$ has dimension $n$, this pole set is either empty or pure of dimension $n-1$. Proof. Work on a small irreducible normal neighborhood on which $f=g/h$, with $g,h$ holomorphic and $h$ a nonzerodivisor. Define the ideal sheaf \[  \mathcal J=\{ u\in \mathcal O_ X:uf\in \mathcal O_ X\} .  \] It is the first-coordinate image of the kernel of $(g,-h):\mathcal O_ X^2	o \mathcal O_ X$, since $ug=vh$ is equivalent to $uf=v$. Consequently it is coherent by kernels and exact sequences of coherent modules . Its definition is independent of the representation of $f$, and \[  P_ f=\{ x:\mathcal J_ x
e \mathcal O_{X,x}\}  =\operatorname {Supp}(\mathcal O_ X/\mathcal J).  \] The coherent-support criterion proved in the normal locus and bounded holomorphic continuation makes this set analytic. It is contained in $\{ h=0\} $, which is nowhere dense because $h$ is a nonzerodivisor. Suppose that a local branch $D$ of $P_ f$ has dimension at most $n-2$. Choose a regular point of a small representative of $D$ outside its other pole branches. After shrinking there, the whole pole set has dimension at most $n-2$. On its complement $f$ is holomorphic, so corollary 9.38.1 gives a holomorphic extension across it. This extension agrees with $f$ as a meromorphic function: after multiplying a local difference by a nonzero denominator, its holomorphic numerator vanishes on a dense set and hence everywhere. The chosen point is therefore not a pole, a contradiction. No branch has dimension $n$, since $P_ f$ is nowhere dense. Thus all nonempty pole branches have dimension $n-1$. This also includes isolated poles when $n=1$; for $n=0$ the local ring is $\mathbb C$ and there are no poles. $\square$ Theorem 9.38.3 . 3F94BF9B4F4B For a normal complex space $X$, the singular locus satisfies \[  \dim (X_{\mathrm{sing}},x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2 \qquad (x\in X_{\mathrm{sing}}).  \] Proof. A zero-dimensional reduced germ is a point, and a normal one-dimensional space is regular by parametrization of irreducible analytic curves . We may therefore work on an irreducible pure $n$-dimensional normal neighborhood, $n\geq 2$. The singular locus is analytic of smaller dimension by analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Suppose that it has a branch of dimension $n-1$. Choose a regular point of that branch outside the others and shrink once more. We obtain a neighborhood $U$ for which $D=U_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a nonempty connected complex manifold of dimension $n-1$, closed and analytic in $U$. Take the proper bimeromorphic resolution $\pi :M	o U$ of the stated resolution-of-singularities input . Its image is closed and contains the dense regular locus, so it is surjective. Every component of the manifold $M$ meets the dense isomorphism locus and therefore has dimension $n$. The analytic set $E=\pi ^{-1}(D)$ is nowhere dense by nowhere-dense inverse images under bimeromorphic maps , so all its branches have dimension at most $n-1$. Fix a compact neighborhood $K$ of a point in the manifold $D$, with nonempty relative interior. By local finiteness of irreducible components and compactness of $\pi ^{-1}(K)$, only finitely many irreducible components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ s$ of $E$ meet this inverse image. Each $E_ j$ is closed in $M$, so its restriction of $\pi $ is proper; hence $\pi (E_ j)$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem . If this image is not all of $D$, it has dimension at most $n-2$. Call $E_ j$ dominating if $\pi (E_ j)=D$. Such a component has dimension $n-1$, since the dimension of an analytic image is at most that of its source by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . We describe an analytic exceptional subset $Q_ j$ of each dominating $E_ j$, including its singular locus and the critical points of $\pi |_{(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}}$, by local determinants. Since $E_ j$ is a hypersurface in the smooth $n$-fold $M$, a local generator $e$ of its reduced ideal exists by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces . The same lemma gives $\mathrm de
e 0$ exactly on the regular part of $E_ j$: there it is a unit times a transverse coordinate, and a nonzero differential conversely gives a submanifold by the implicit function theorem. Near $\pi (y)\in D$, choose ambient holomorphic functions $t_1,\ldots ,t_{n-1}$ whose restrictions are coordinates on $D$. Define $Q_ j$ locally on $E_ j$ by 22FF23DD18BA 9.38.4  egin{equation}  \mathrm de\wedge \mathrm d(t_1\circ \pi )\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d(t_{n-1}\circ \pi )=0. \end{equation} In a chart of $M$ this is the vanishing of one holomorphic determinant, together with $e=0$. At a singular point of $E_ j$, $\mathrm de=0$. At a regular point, the determinant vanishes precisely when the restriction of $\mathrm d\pi $ to $T E_ j$ has rank less than $n-1$. Thus its zero set is intrinsic on the regular part and contains the whole singular locus, independently of these choices. The local analytic sets agree on overlaps and define a closed analytic subset $Q_ j$ of $E_ j$. This subset is proper. Otherwise the differential of $\pi $ on $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ would have rank at most $n-2$ everywhere. Its image would be $\mathcal H^{2n-2}$-null by dimension bounds for holomorphic images ; the image of the singular locus is also null, by its smaller dimension and the analytic stratification of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Countably many charts suffice for these conclusions. The union could not equal the manifold $D$, contradicting dominance. Consequently $\dim Q_ j\leq n-2$, by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . Its proper image $\pi (Q_ j)$ is analytic of dimension at most $n-2$ by the same image theorems. Choose $a$ in the relative interior of $K$ outside the finite union of the sets $\pi (E_ j)$ for nondominating $E_ j$ and $\pi (Q_ j)$ for dominating ones. All these sets have smaller dimension than $D$, so such $a$ exists. Every point $y\in \pi ^{-1}(a)$ lies on one of the listed components, and every listed component through $y$ is dominating, with $y
otin Q_ j$. Near $y$ its map to $D$ is therefore a local biholomorphism, by the holomorphic inverse function theorem. Local finiteness allows a neighborhood of $y$ that meets only the finitely many components through $y$; their fibers over $a$ are isolated there. Thus the whole compact fiber $\pi ^{-1}(a)$ is discrete and hence finite. Take pairwise disjoint coordinate balls $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ around its points. Properness gives a neighborhood $V$ of $a$ with $\pi ^{-1}(V)\subset  igcup _ i B_ i$: use $V=U\setminus \pi (M\setminus  igcup _ i B_ i)$ and shrink if necessary. Each fiber over $V$ is compact, and its part in any $B_ i$ is compact as well, since the balls are disjoint and cover that fiber. It is a compact analytic subset of a coordinate ball, hence finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . Therefore $\pi :\pi ^{-1}(V)	o V$ is finite and bimeromorphic. The target is normal, so finite bimeromorphic maps to normal spaces makes it an isomorphism. Since its source is smooth, $a$ is regular in $U$, contradicting $a\in D$. No singular branch of codimension one can occur. $\square$ Theorem 9.38.5 . F35BA7139EC4 Let $X$ be a normal complex space, and let $A\subset X$ be analytic with $\dim (A,x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2$ for every $x\in A$. Every meromorphic function on $X\setminus A$ extends uniquely to a meromorphic function on $X$. Proof. Uniqueness is local. The difference of two extensions has, near any point, a nonzero holomorphic denominator and a holomorphic numerator that vanishes on a dense subset of $X\setminus A$. The numerator vanishes everywhere by continuity. Thus it suffices to construct an extension near each $x\in A$. Work on an irreducible pure $n$-dimensional normal neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Here $n\geq 2$, since $A$ is empty in the lower dimensions, and shrink so that $\dim (A\cap U)\leq n-2$. Let $f$ be the given meromorphic function. By lemma 9.38.2 , its pole set $P\subset U\setminus A$ is either empty or pure of dimension $n-1$. The Remmert–Stein theorem the Remmert–Stein extension theorem makes its closure $D$ in $U$ analytic. Every local branch of $D$ has dimension $n-1$ and is not contained in $A$. Indeed, branches contained in $A$ could be discarded without changing the dense subset $P$, contradicting irredundancy of the branch decomposition; every remaining branch has regular points outside $A$ and the other branches, where $D$ coincides with $P$, and purity fixes its dimension. Shrink $U$ so that $D$ has only finitely many irreducible components $D_1,\ldots ,D_ r$, all meeting $x$. Such a shrinking follows from local finiteness of global components. If $D$ is empty, $f$ is holomorphic on $U\setminus A$ and corollary 9.38.1 already gives the required extension. Since $(D,x)$ is a proper analytic subgerm of $(U,x)$, some local holomorphic defining function has a nonzero germ in $\mathcal O_{U,x}$. Choose a representative $h$ and shrink so that $h$ vanishes on all of $D$. The function $h$ is not identically zero on any nonempty open subset of the irreducible space $U$, by the identity theorem on its connected regular locus and density. Its germ is therefore a nonzerodivisor at every point of $U$. Each $D_ j\setminus A$ is irreducible. To see this, its regular locus contains $(D_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus A$, which is connected by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , since $(D_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected and $A$ meets it in a proper analytic subset. This set is dense in $D_ j\setminus A$. A decomposition into two proper closed analytic subsets would restrict to a decomposition of that connected manifold into two proper analytic subsets, which is impossible; if one contained the whole manifold, density would make it all of $D_ j\setminus A$. By theorem 9.38.3 , each $D_ j$ has regular points of $U$ outside $A$ and the other components. Choose such a point on its own regular locus. In a manifold coordinate neighborhood there, write $D_ j=\{ 	au =0\} $ and $f=a/b$ with $a,b$ holomorphic and $b
e 0$. Expanding in $	au $ gives $b=	au ^{m_ j}b_0$ with $m_ j\geq 0$ finite and $b_0|_{\{ 	au =0\} }$ not identically zero. Move the chosen point slightly within $D_ j$, keeping it away from $A$, the other components and $U_{\mathrm{sing}}$, so that $b_0$ is nonzero. Call the resulting point $q_ j$. Then $	au ^{m_ j}f$ is holomorphic near $q_ j$. Since $h$ vanishes on $D_ j$, the coordinate ideal formula gives $h=	au h_1$ there, and $h^{m_ j}f$ is holomorphic near $q_ j$ as well. This construction uses only one local quotient at each of the finitely many components; no global numerator or denominator for $f$ on $U\setminus A$ is assumed. Put $m=\max (1,m_1,\ldots ,m_ r)$ and $g=h^ m f$ on $U\setminus A$. Its pole set is contained in $P$, is pure of dimension $n-1$ when nonempty, and avoids each $q_ j$. Every irreducible component of this pole set is contained in some $D_ j\setminus A$, by the finite-union property for irreducible analytic sets. Both have dimension $n-1$; by irreducibility of $D_ j\setminus A$ and strict dimension drop, that component must be all of $D_ j\setminus A$. This contradicts holomorphy near $q_ j$. Thus $g$ has no poles and is holomorphic on $U\setminus A$. Extend $g$ holomorphically to $G$ on $U$ by corollary 9.38.1 . The quotient $G/h^ m$ is meromorphic on $U$, since every germ of $h$ is a nonzerodivisor, and it agrees with $f$ as a meromorphic function on $U\setminus A$. The local extensions glue by uniqueness. $\square$

title: Corollary 9.38.1
section: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
text: Corollary 9.38.1 . 512196636E86 Let $X$ be a normal complex space, and let $A\subset X$ be an analytic subset such that \[  \dim (A,x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2\qquad (x\in A).  \] Every holomorphic function on $X\setminus A$ has a unique holomorphic extension to $X$. Proof. The assertion is local at points of $A$. Near such a point, $X$ is an irreducible pure-dimensional normal space. The codimension hypothesis therefore holds on each local branch. If $f$ is holomorphic off $A$, the function $|f|^2$ there is locally the restriction of the squared modulus of an ambient holomorphic function, hence is locally plurisubharmonic. By upper bounds near analytic subsets of codimension at least two it is locally bounded above near $A$. Thus $f$ is locally bounded, and the bounded extension on normal spaces in the normal locus and bounded holomorphic continuation extends it holomorphically. The complement of $A$ is dense; uniqueness follows from continuity, so the local extensions glue. In local dimensions zero and one the hypothesis forces $A$ to be empty. $\square$

title: Lemma 9.38.2
section: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
text: Lemma 9.38.2 . DA978F0F96EA On a normal complex space $X$, the pole set of a meromorphic function is a nowhere dense analytic subset. Near a point where $X$ has dimension $n$, this pole set is either empty or pure of dimension $n-1$. Proof. Work on a small irreducible normal neighborhood on which $f=g/h$, with $g,h$ holomorphic and $h$ a nonzerodivisor. Define the ideal sheaf \[  \mathcal J=\{ u\in \mathcal O_ X:uf\in \mathcal O_ X\} .  \] It is the first-coordinate image of the kernel of $(g,-h):\mathcal O_ X^2\to \mathcal O_ X$, since $ug=vh$ is equivalent to $uf=v$. Consequently it is coherent by kernels and exact sequences of coherent modules . Its definition is independent of the representation of $f$, and \[  P_ f=\{ x:\mathcal J_ x\ne \mathcal O_{X,x}\}  =\operatorname {Supp}(\mathcal O_ X/\mathcal J).  \] The coherent-support criterion proved in the normal locus and bounded holomorphic continuation makes this set analytic. It is contained in $\{ h=0\} $, which is nowhere dense because $h$ is a nonzerodivisor. Suppose that a local branch $D$ of $P_ f$ has dimension at most $n-2$. Choose a regular point of a small representative of $D$ outside its other pole branches. After shrinking there, the whole pole set has dimension at most $n-2$. On its complement $f$ is holomorphic, so corollary 9.38.1 gives a holomorphic extension across it. This extension agrees with $f$ as a meromorphic function: after multiplying a local difference by a nonzero denominator, its holomorphic numerator vanishes on a dense set and hence everywhere. The chosen point is therefore not a pole, a contradiction. No branch has dimension $n$, since $P_ f$ is nowhere dense. Thus all nonempty pole branches have dimension $n-1$. This also includes isolated poles when $n=1$; for $n=0$ the local ring is $\mathbb C$ and there are no poles. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.38.3
section: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
text: Theorem 9.38.3 . 3F94BF9B4F4B For a normal complex space $X$, the singular locus satisfies \[  \dim (X_{\mathrm{sing}},x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2 \qquad (x\in X_{\mathrm{sing}}).  \] Proof. A zero-dimensional reduced germ is a point, and a normal one-dimensional space is regular by parametrization of irreducible analytic curves . We may therefore work on an irreducible pure $n$-dimensional normal neighborhood, $n\geq 2$. The singular locus is analytic of smaller dimension by analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Suppose that it has a branch of dimension $n-1$. Choose a regular point of that branch outside the others and shrink once more. We obtain a neighborhood $U$ for which $D=U_{\mathrm{sing}}$ is a nonempty connected complex manifold of dimension $n-1$, closed and analytic in $U$. Take the proper bimeromorphic resolution $\pi :M\to U$ of the stated resolution-of-singularities input . Its image is closed and contains the dense regular locus, so it is surjective. Every component of the manifold $M$ meets the dense isomorphism locus and therefore has dimension $n$. The analytic set $E=\pi ^{-1}(D)$ is nowhere dense by nowhere-dense inverse images under bimeromorphic maps , so all its branches have dimension at most $n-1$. Fix a compact neighborhood $K$ of a point in the manifold $D$, with nonempty relative interior. By local finiteness of irreducible components and compactness of $\pi ^{-1}(K)$, only finitely many irreducible components $E_1,\ldots ,E_ s$ of $E$ meet this inverse image. Each $E_ j$ is closed in $M$, so its restriction of $\pi $ is proper; hence $\pi (E_ j)$ is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem . If this image is not all of $D$, it has dimension at most $n-2$. Call $E_ j$ dominating if $\pi (E_ j)=D$. Such a component has dimension $n-1$, since the dimension of an analytic image is at most that of its source by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . We describe an analytic exceptional subset $Q_ j$ of each dominating $E_ j$, including its singular locus and the critical points of $\pi |_{(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}}$, by local determinants. Since $E_ j$ is a hypersurface in the smooth $n$-fold $M$, a local generator $e$ of its reduced ideal exists by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces . The same lemma gives $\mathrm de\ne 0$ exactly on the regular part of $E_ j$: there it is a unit times a transverse coordinate, and a nonzero differential conversely gives a submanifold by the implicit function theorem. Near $\pi (y)\in D$, choose ambient holomorphic functions $t_1,\ldots ,t_{n-1}$ whose restrictions are coordinates on $D$. Define $Q_ j$ locally on $E_ j$ by 22FF23DD18BA 9.38.4 \begin{equation}  \mathrm de\wedge \mathrm d(t_1\circ \pi )\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm d(t_{n-1}\circ \pi )=0. \end{equation} In a chart of $M$ this is the vanishing of one holomorphic determinant, together with $e=0$. At a singular point of $E_ j$, $\mathrm de=0$. At a regular point, the determinant vanishes precisely when the restriction of $\mathrm d\pi $ to $T E_ j$ has rank less than $n-1$. Thus its zero set is intrinsic on the regular part and contains the whole singular locus, independently of these choices. The local analytic sets agree on overlaps and define a closed analytic subset $Q_ j$ of $E_ j$. This subset is proper. Otherwise the differential of $\pi $ on $(E_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ would have rank at most $n-2$ everywhere. Its image would be $\mathcal H^{2n-2}$-null by dimension bounds for holomorphic images ; the image of the singular locus is also null, by its smaller dimension and the analytic stratification of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Countably many charts suffice for these conclusions. The union could not equal the manifold $D$, contradicting dominance. Consequently $\dim Q_ j\leq n-2$, by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . Its proper image $\pi (Q_ j)$ is analytic of dimension at most $n-2$ by the same image theorems. Choose $a$ in the relative interior of $K$ outside the finite union of the sets $\pi (E_ j)$ for nondominating $E_ j$ and $\pi (Q_ j)$ for dominating ones. All these sets have smaller dimension than $D$, so such $a$ exists. Every point $y\in \pi ^{-1}(a)$ lies on one of the listed components, and every listed component through $y$ is dominating, with $y\notin Q_ j$. Near $y$ its map to $D$ is therefore a local biholomorphism, by the holomorphic inverse function theorem. Local finiteness allows a neighborhood of $y$ that meets only the finitely many components through $y$; their fibers over $a$ are isolated there. Thus the whole compact fiber $\pi ^{-1}(a)$ is discrete and hence finite. Take pairwise disjoint coordinate balls $B_1,\ldots ,B_ l$ around its points. Properness gives a neighborhood $V$ of $a$ with $\pi ^{-1}(V)\subset \bigcup _ i B_ i$: use $V=U\setminus \pi (M\setminus \bigcup _ i B_ i)$ and shrink if necessary. Each fiber over $V$ is compact, and its part in any $B_ i$ is compact as well, since the balls are disjoint and cover that fiber. It is a compact analytic subset of a coordinate ball, hence finite by the maximum principle on analytic branches . Therefore $\pi :\pi ^{-1}(V)\to V$ is finite and bimeromorphic. The target is normal, so finite bimeromorphic maps to normal spaces makes it an isomorphism. Since its source is smooth, $a$ is regular in $U$, contradicting $a\in D$. No singular branch of codimension one can occur. $\square$

title: Theorem 9.38.5
section: 9.38 Continuation on normal complex spaces
text: Theorem 9.38.5 . F35BA7139EC4 Let $X$ be a normal complex space, and let $A\subset X$ be analytic with $\dim (A,x)\leq \dim (X,x)-2$ for every $x\in A$. Every meromorphic function on $X\setminus A$ extends uniquely to a meromorphic function on $X$. Proof. Uniqueness is local. The difference of two extensions has, near any point, a nonzero holomorphic denominator and a holomorphic numerator that vanishes on a dense subset of $X\setminus A$. The numerator vanishes everywhere by continuity. Thus it suffices to construct an extension near each $x\in A$. Work on an irreducible pure $n$-dimensional normal neighborhood $U$ of $x$. Here $n\geq 2$, since $A$ is empty in the lower dimensions, and shrink so that $\dim (A\cap U)\leq n-2$. Let $f$ be the given meromorphic function. By lemma 9.38.2 , its pole set $P\subset U\setminus A$ is either empty or pure of dimension $n-1$. The Remmert–Stein theorem the Remmert–Stein extension theorem makes its closure $D$ in $U$ analytic. Every local branch of $D$ has dimension $n-1$ and is not contained in $A$. Indeed, branches contained in $A$ could be discarded without changing the dense subset $P$, contradicting irredundancy of the branch decomposition; every remaining branch has regular points outside $A$ and the other branches, where $D$ coincides with $P$, and purity fixes its dimension. Shrink $U$ so that $D$ has only finitely many irreducible components $D_1,\ldots ,D_ r$, all meeting $x$. Such a shrinking follows from local finiteness of global components. If $D$ is empty, $f$ is holomorphic on $U\setminus A$ and corollary 9.38.1 already gives the required extension. Since $(D,x)$ is a proper analytic subgerm of $(U,x)$, some local holomorphic defining function has a nonzero germ in $\mathcal O_{U,x}$. Choose a representative $h$ and shrink so that $h$ vanishes on all of $D$. The function $h$ is not identically zero on any nonempty open subset of the irreducible space $U$, by the identity theorem on its connected regular locus and density. Its germ is therefore a nonzerodivisor at every point of $U$. Each $D_ j\setminus A$ is irreducible. To see this, its regular locus contains $(D_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}\setminus A$, which is connected by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements , since $(D_ j)_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected and $A$ meets it in a proper analytic subset. This set is dense in $D_ j\setminus A$. A decomposition into two proper closed analytic subsets would restrict to a decomposition of that connected manifold into two proper analytic subsets, which is impossible; if one contained the whole manifold, density would make it all of $D_ j\setminus A$. By theorem 9.38.3 , each $D_ j$ has regular points of $U$ outside $A$ and the other components. Choose such a point on its own regular locus. In a manifold coordinate neighborhood there, write $D_ j=\{ \tau =0\} $ and $f=a/b$ with $a,b$ holomorphic and $b\ne 0$. Expanding in $\tau $ gives $b=\tau ^{m_ j}b_0$ with $m_ j\geq 0$ finite and $b_0|_{\{ \tau =0\} }$ not identically zero. Move the chosen point slightly within $D_ j$, keeping it away from $A$, the other components and $U_{\mathrm{sing}}$, so that $b_0$ is nonzero. Call the resulting point $q_ j$. Then $\tau ^{m_ j}f$ is holomorphic near $q_ j$. Since $h$ vanishes on $D_ j$, the coordinate ideal formula gives $h=\tau h_1$ there, and $h^{m_ j}f$ is holomorphic near $q_ j$ as well. This construction uses only one local quotient at each of the finitely many components; no global numerator or denominator for $f$ on $U\setminus A$ is assumed. Put $m=\max (1,m_1,\ldots ,m_ r)$ and $g=h^ m f$ on $U\setminus A$. Its pole set is contained in $P$, is pure of dimension $n-1$ when nonempty, and avoids each $q_ j$. Every irreducible component of this pole set is contained in some $D_ j\setminus A$, by the finite-union property for irreducible analytic sets. Both have dimension $n-1$; by irreducibility of $D_ j\setminus A$ and strict dimension drop, that component must be all of $D_ j\setminus A$. This contradicts holomorphy near $q_ j$. Thus $g$ has no poles and is holomorphic on $U\setminus A$. Extend $g$ holomorphically to $G$ on $U$ by corollary 9.38.1 . The quotient $G/h^ m$ is meromorphic on $U$, since every germ of $h$ is a nonzerodivisor, and it agrees with $f$ as a meromorphic function on $U\setminus A$. The local extensions glue by uniqueness. $\square$

title: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: All spaces in this section are topological spaces; no separation hypothesis is imposed unless stated. Sheaves and complexes are sheaves of abelian groups. The same constructions apply to modules over a fixed commutative ring, with linear morphisms. An additional module structure over a sheaf of rings will be used only where explicitly specified. We work with the usual axiom of choice. Empty products of groups and sections over the empty set are zero. A presheaf $P$ assigns a group $P(U)$ to each open set, with identity and composable restriction maps. It is a sheaf if compatible sections on an open cover glue uniquely. Its stalk at $x$ is \[  P_ x=\underset {U\ni x}{\mathop{\rm colim}}P(U): \quad s_ x=t_ x\  \Longleftrightarrow  s|_ W=t|_ W\text{ for some open }W\ni x.  \] These are the sheaf and stalk conventions used in the existing analytic sheaf algebra; no second coherence theorem is needed. Proposition 10.43.1 . C3C8B03F46AB Every presheaf $P$ has a sheafification $P^\# $ with the same stalks, characterized by \[  \operatorname {Hom}(P^\# ,F)=\operatorname {Hom}(P,F) \quad \text{for every sheaf }F.  \] A morphism of sheaves is injective, surjective or an isomorphism exactly when the respective condition holds on every stalk. Kernels are computed on sections. Images and cokernels are the sheafifications of their presheaf versions, and are computed on stalks. Consequently exactness is stalkwise, sheafification preserves short exact sequences of presheaves, and the section functor $\Gamma (U,-)$ is left exact. The sheafification of the constant presheaf $M$ is the sheaf $\underline M$ of locally constant functions with values in the discrete group $M$. Proof. Form the disjoint union $E=\coprod _ xP_ x$. A section $s\in P(U)$ gives $[s,U]=\{ s_ x:x\in U\} \subset E$. These sets form a basis: their intersection is $[s,W]$, where $W\subset U\cap V$ is the open set on which $s_ x=t_ x$. The projection $E\to X$ maps each basic set homeomorphically to its domain. Let $P^\# (U)$ be its continuous sections. They glue by the elementary pasting property for continuous maps. Every such section is locally of the form $x\mapsto s_ x$, so evaluation at $x$ identifies $(P^\# )_ x$ with $P_ x$. Group operations are defined locally on representatives and are independent of choices. The map $P\to P^\# $ sends $s$ to its germs. Given $P\to F$, send every local representative $s$ to its image in $F$ and glue; equality of germs makes the local images agree. This proves existence and uniqueness in the displayed property. If $P$ is already a sheaf, local representatives glue uniquely and this map is an isomorphism. Conversely, continuous sections of any local homeomorphism to $X$ recover its fibers as stalks, so the description also identifies sheaves with their spaces of germs. A sheaf section is zero if and only if all its germs are zero: local vanishing and uniqueness of gluing prove this. Thus stalkwise injection implies injection on sections. If a sheaf map is stalkwise surjective, every section of its target has local lifts. For a stalkwise isomorphism these lifts are unique on overlaps and glue, proving the isomorphism assertion. The kernel presheaf is a sheaf by gluing. A germ in its kernel is represented by a section whose image vanishes after a restriction, which proves the kernel formula on stalks. The same representative argument gives the stalk image and cokernel after sheafification. For example, a section in the sheaf image has local lifts, which may fail to glue globally. These facts prove the exactness assertions: whenever a germ maps to zero, shrink a representative to make its image zero and then lift it at the stalk. For an objectwise exact sequence of presheaves, this is the same elementary argument for a filtered colimit of groups. Finally, a target section in the kernel of the second map of a sheaf sequence has unique local lifts through its first map, and they glue. This proves left exactness of sections. Local representatives of the constant presheaf are exactly locally constant maps, proving the last assertion. $\square$ For example, local functions of a prescribed local regularity, continuous sections of a bundle, and arbitrary maps $U\to M$ with pointwise group operations are sheaves, by pasting. The germ-space construction and its universal property apply also to presheaves of sets: the same proof omits only the group operations. If the stalks are nonempty, the germ projection is onto. The constant presheaf need not be a sheaf: different constants on two disjoint nonempty open sets need not glue to a constant. Nor need the quotient presheaf of two sheaves be a sheaf. On the circle the map $C(U,\mathbb R)\to C(U,S^1)$, $a\mapsto e^{2\pi i a}$, has kernel $C(U,\mathbb Z)$ and local lifts. Its quotient sheaf is $C(-,S^1)$. The identity of $S^1$ has no global lift: a lift along $e^{2\pi it}$ would differ from $t$ by a continuous integer, hence a constant, in contradiction with equal values at $t=0,1$. Local lifts on arcs therefore give a compatible family in the quotient presheaf with no global lift. Proposition 10.43.2 . 64E16AF43980 For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$, the direct image $(f_*F)(V)=F(f^{-1}V)$ is a sheaf and is left exact. There is an exact inverse-image functor $f^{-1}$, with \[  (f^{-1}B)_ x=B_{f(x)},\qquad \operatorname {Hom}_ X(f^{-1}B,F)=\operatorname {Hom}_ Y(B,f_*F).  \] Its unit $B\to f_*f^{-1}B$ pulls sections back along $f$ and its counit $f^{-1}f_*F\to F$ sends a germ of a section near a whole inverse image to its germ at $x$. These maps need not be isomorphisms. For a finite $q$-sheet covering, $f_*\underline M$ is locally $\underline M^ q$, with transition maps permuting the sheets; it need not be a constant sheaf. Proof. The direct-image assertion follows by gluing on inverse images and left exactness of sections. Define $f^{-1}B$ by sheafifying \[  U\longmapsto \underset {V\supset f(U)}{\mathop{\rm colim}}B(V), \qquad V\subset Y\text{ open}.  \] A representative has a germ at $f(x)$. Every such germ is obtained by restricting to $U\subset f^{-1}V$. If two representatives have the same germ at $f(x)$, they agree on a smaller neighborhood $W$ of $f(x)$; restrict $U$ further to $U\cap f^{-1}W$. This proves the stalk formula and, by proposition 10.43.1 , exactness. For a map $B\to f_*F$, a section $b\in B(V)$ gives a section of $F$ on $f^{-1}V$; restrict these sections and use the sheafification property to obtain $f^{-1}B\to F$. Conversely pull $b$ back to $f^{-1}B$ and apply a map to $F$. The two constructions undo each other on local representatives, proving the adjunction and its stated maps. Equivalently, the space of germs of $f^{-1}B$ is the pullback of the space of germs of $B$; the same basic neighborhoods verify this directly. Over an evenly covered open $V$, sections on $f^{-1}V=\coprod _{j=1}^ qV_ j$ are $q$ independently locally constant functions on $V$. A change of sheet labels permutes these functions, locally constantly on each overlap. In the connected double cover of the circle, global sections of $f_*\underline{\mathbb Z}$ form $\mathbb Z$, whereas global sections of the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb Z}^2$ form $\mathbb Z^2$. These abelian groups are not isomorphic: their quotients by twice the group have respectively two and four elements. Thus the local description cannot in general be promoted to a global constant-sheaf isomorphism. $\square$ Lemma 10.43.3 . FE20ED71F10C A degreewise short exact sequence of complexes $0\to A^\bullet \xrightarrow {i}B^\bullet \xrightarrow {p}C^\bullet \to 0$ of abelian groups gives a natural long exact sequence \[  \cdots \to H^ r(A)\to H^ r(B)\to H^ r(C) \xrightarrow {\partial }H^{r+1}(A)\to \cdots .  \] In a commutative diagram of exact five-term sequences, the middle vertical map is injective if the second and fourth maps are injective and the first is surjective; it is surjective if the second and fourth are surjective and the fifth is injective. Proof. For a cocycle $c\in C^ r$, choose $b\in B^ r$ with $pb=c$. There is a unique $a\in A^{r+1}$ with $ia=db$, and $da=0$ because $i(da)=d^2b=0$. Put $\partial [c]=[a]$. Changing $b$ by $ik$ changes $a$ by $dk$; changing $c$ by $dc_0$ and a lift by $db_0$ changes nothing else. This proves well-definedness and additivity. At $H^ r(B)$, a closed $b$ whose image is $dc_0$ can be replaced by $b-db_0$ for a lift $b_0$ of $c_0$, after which it is $ia$ with $a$ closed. At $H^ r(C)$, if $db=ia$ and $a=dk$, then $b-ik$ is a closed lift; conversely a closed lift gives zero connecting class. At $H^{r+1}(A)$, if $ia=db$, then $pb$ is closed and its connecting class is $[a]$; conversely every connecting class maps to zero in $H^{r+1}(B)$. These checks prove exactness at every position. Applying a morphism to these lifts proves naturality. The same lift calculation applies to an ungraded differential group by repeating it in every integer degree; its long exact sequence is the corresponding cyclic exact sequence. For the injective five-lemma assertion, let $a_3$ map to zero below. Its image in the fourth group is zero by fourth-map injectivity, so $a_3$ comes from $a_2$. The image of $a_2$ below comes from $b_1$; lift $b_1$ to $a_1$, subtract its image from $a_2$, and use second-map injectivity. The resulting $a_3$ is zero. For surjectivity, start with $b_3$ and lift its image in the fourth group to $a_4$. Its image in the fifth group is zero by fifth-map injectivity; lift $a_4$ to $a_3$. The difference $b_3-\varphi _3a_3$ comes from $b_2$; lift $b_2$ using second-map surjectivity and add its image to $a_3$. This gives the desired preimage. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.43.2
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Proposition 10.43.2 . 64E16AF43980 For a continuous map $f:X\to Y$, the direct image $(f_*F)(V)=F(f^{-1}V)$ is a sheaf and is left exact. There is an exact inverse-image functor $f^{-1}$, with \[  (f^{-1}B)_ x=B_{f(x)},\qquad \operatorname {Hom}_ X(f^{-1}B,F)=\operatorname {Hom}_ Y(B,f_*F).  \] Its unit $B\to f_*f^{-1}B$ pulls sections back along $f$ and its counit $f^{-1}f_*F\to F$ sends a germ of a section near a whole inverse image to its germ at $x$. These maps need not be isomorphisms. For a finite $q$-sheet covering, $f_*\underline M$ is locally $\underline M^ q$, with transition maps permuting the sheets; it need not be a constant sheaf. Proof. The direct-image assertion follows by gluing on inverse images and left exactness of sections. Define $f^{-1}B$ by sheafifying \[  U\longmapsto \underset {V\supset f(U)}{\mathop{\rm colim}}B(V), \qquad V\subset Y\text{ open}.  \] A representative has a germ at $f(x)$. Every such germ is obtained by restricting to $U\subset f^{-1}V$. If two representatives have the same germ at $f(x)$, they agree on a smaller neighborhood $W$ of $f(x)$; restrict $U$ further to $U\cap f^{-1}W$. This proves the stalk formula and, by proposition 10.43.1 , exactness. For a map $B\to f_*F$, a section $b\in B(V)$ gives a section of $F$ on $f^{-1}V$; restrict these sections and use the sheafification property to obtain $f^{-1}B\to F$. Conversely pull $b$ back to $f^{-1}B$ and apply a map to $F$. The two constructions undo each other on local representatives, proving the adjunction and its stated maps. Equivalently, the space of germs of $f^{-1}B$ is the pullback of the space of germs of $B$; the same basic neighborhoods verify this directly. Over an evenly covered open $V$, sections on $f^{-1}V=\coprod _{j=1}^ qV_ j$ are $q$ independently locally constant functions on $V$. A change of sheet labels permutes these functions, locally constantly on each overlap. In the connected double cover of the circle, global sections of $f_*\underline{\mathbb Z}$ form $\mathbb Z$, whereas global sections of the constant sheaf $\underline{\mathbb Z}^2$ form $\mathbb Z^2$. These abelian groups are not isomorphic: their quotients by twice the group have respectively two and four elements. Thus the local description cannot in general be promoted to a global constant-sheaf isomorphism. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.43.3
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Lemma 10.43.3 . FE20ED71F10C A degreewise short exact sequence of complexes $0\to A^\bullet \xrightarrow {i}B^\bullet \xrightarrow {p}C^\bullet \to 0$ of abelian groups gives a natural long exact sequence \[  \cdots \to H^ r(A)\to H^ r(B)\to H^ r(C) \xrightarrow {\partial }H^{r+1}(A)\to \cdots .  \] In a commutative diagram of exact five-term sequences, the middle vertical map is injective if the second and fourth maps are injective and the first is surjective; it is surjective if the second and fourth are surjective and the fifth is injective. Proof. For a cocycle $c\in C^ r$, choose $b\in B^ r$ with $pb=c$. There is a unique $a\in A^{r+1}$ with $ia=db$, and $da=0$ because $i(da)=d^2b=0$. Put $\partial [c]=[a]$. Changing $b$ by $ik$ changes $a$ by $dk$; changing $c$ by $dc_0$ and a lift by $db_0$ changes nothing else. This proves well-definedness and additivity. At $H^ r(B)$, a closed $b$ whose image is $dc_0$ can be replaced by $b-db_0$ for a lift $b_0$ of $c_0$, after which it is $ia$ with $a$ closed. At $H^ r(C)$, if $db=ia$ and $a=dk$, then $b-ik$ is a closed lift; conversely a closed lift gives zero connecting class. At $H^{r+1}(A)$, if $ia=db$, then $pb$ is closed and its connecting class is $[a]$; conversely every connecting class maps to zero in $H^{r+1}(B)$. These checks prove exactness at every position. Applying a morphism to these lifts proves naturality. The same lift calculation applies to an ungraded differential group by repeating it in every integer degree; its long exact sequence is the corresponding cyclic exact sequence. For the injective five-lemma assertion, let $a_3$ map to zero below. Its image in the fourth group is zero by fourth-map injectivity, so $a_3$ comes from $a_2$. The image of $a_2$ below comes from $b_1$; lift $b_1$ to $a_1$, subtract its image from $a_2$, and use second-map injectivity. The resulting $a_3$ is zero. For surjectivity, start with $b_3$ and lift its image in the fourth group to $a_4$. Its image in the fifth group is zero by fifth-map injectivity; lift $a_4$ to $a_3$. The difference $b_3-\varphi _3a_3$ comes from $b_2$; lift $b_2$ using second-map surjectivity and add its image to $a_3$. This gives the desired preimage. $\square$

title: 10.43.4 An explicit flabby resolution
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: A resolution of $F$ is an augmented complex $0\to F\to L^0\to L^1\to \cdots $ that is exact on stalks; its terms in negative complex degrees are zero. Acyclicity of its terms is a separate additional condition. A sheaf $F$ is flabby if $F(V)\to F(U)$ is onto for every inclusion of open sets $U\subset V$. It is equivalent to require extensions to $X$, since an extension to $X$ can be restricted to $V$. Flabbiness is local on the base. More precisely, it is enough that every section on an open $U$ extend across each point $x$: there is an open $W\ni x$ with an extension on $W$ agreeing on $U\cap W$. To see this, order its open-domain extensions by extension and apply gluing to chains. A maximal domain must be $X$, since otherwise the stated local extension enlarges it. Conversely a flabby sheaf has this property. If the sheaf is flabby on each member of an open cover, extend the restriction of a section to such a member near $x$ to obtain this same property. Define the functor \[  (GF)(U)=\prod _{x\in U}F_ x, \qquad \eta _ F:F\longrightarrow GF,\quad s\longmapsto (s_ x)_ x.  \] Restriction in $GF$ forgets factors. Thus $GF$ is a flabby sheaf, and $\eta _ F$ is injective. Both $G$ and $\Gamma (X,G-)$ are exact: a short exact sequence gives exact stalk sequences, and their products are exact, since each coordinate can be lifted separately. The same statements hold on every open subset. Theorem 10.43.5 . E24E008710DC Put $C^{-1}F=F$, $C^ qF=G^{q+1}F$ for $q\ge 0$, and \[  d^{-1}=\eta _ F,\qquad d^ q=\sum _{i=0}^{q+1}(-1)^ i\delta _ i^ q, \quad \delta _ i^ q=G^ i\eta _{G^{q+1-i}F}\quad (q\ge 0).  \] Then $0\to F\to C^0F\to C^1F\to \cdots $ is a functorial resolution by flabby sheaves. Each functor $\Gamma (U,C^ q-)$ is exact. Restriction of this resolution to an open set $U$ is the same construction on $U$. Proof. For every sheaf map $a:B\to B'$, its action on germs gives $G(a)\eta _ B=\eta _{B'}a$. Applied successively inside iterates of $G$, this identity gives, for $i<j$, \[  \delta _ j^{q+1}\delta _ i^ q=\delta _ i^{q+1}\delta _{j-1}^ q.  \] Indeed, after removing the common outer $G^ i$, this is precisely naturality of $\eta $ for the map obtained by inserting $\eta $ in the $(j-i)$th position. In the expansion of $d^{q+1}d^ q$ these two composites have opposite signs; every term occurs in exactly one such pair. Thus $d^2=0$, including $d^0\eta _ F=0$. Fix $x$. Evaluation at $x$ gives a well-defined map $e_ x^ B:(GB)_ x\to B_ x$: represent a germ by an arbitrary assignment $(b_ y)$ near $x$ and take $b_ x$. It satisfies $e_ x^ B\eta _{B,x}=\mathrm{id}$ and $e_ x^{B'}G(a)_ x=a_ xe_ x^ B$. Set $h^ q=e_ x^{G^ qF}:(C^ qF)_ x\to (C^{q-1}F)_ x$ for $q\ge 0$. Then $h^{q+1}\delta _0^ q=\mathrm{id}$ and, for $i\ge 1$, $h^{q+1}\delta _ i^ q=\delta _{i-1}^{q-1}h^ q$. Hence \[  h^{q+1}d^ q+d^{q-1}h^ q=\mathrm{id},\qquad h^0\eta _{F,x}=\mathrm{id}.  \] This proves exactness on every stalk, hence sheaf exactness. Each $C^ qF$ is flabby by its outer $G$. Exactness of $G$ inductively and of $\Gamma (U,G-)$ proves the assertion about sections. The constructions commute with sheaf maps by their definitions. On $V\subset U$, $(G_ XF)(V)=\prod _{x\in V}F_ x=(G_ U(F|_ U))(V)$; iteration proves the restriction assertion. $\square$ Definition 10.43.6 . 8B7E0E3149DB Here $C^\bullet F$ means the unaugmented complex with terms $C^ qF$ for $q\ge 0$ and zero terms for $q<0$. The symbol $C^{-1}F=F$ above was used only to describe the augmentation and its stalk homotopy. Define \[  H^ q(U,F)=H^ q\bigl (\Gamma (U,C^\bullet F),d\bigr ) \quad (q\ge 0),\qquad H^ q(U,F)=0\quad (q<0).  \] A sheaf is acyclic on $U$ if these groups vanish for $q>0$. Theorem 10.43.7 . 847001406E77 One has $H^0(U,F)=F(U)$. Every short exact sheaf sequence $0\to F\to B\to Q\to 0$ gives a natural long exact sequence \[  0\to F(U)\to B(U)\to Q(U)\to H^1(U,F)\to \cdots .  \] In particular $B(U)\to Q(U)$ is onto if $H^1(U,F)=0$. Every flabby sheaf is acyclic on every open subset. If $X=U\cup V$, there is a natural Mayer–Vietoris sequence \[  \cdots \to H^ r(X,F)\to H^ r(U,F)\oplus H^ r(V,F) \to H^ r(U\cap V,F)\to H^{r+1}(X,F)\to \cdots ,  \] where the middle restriction difference is $b|_{U\cap V}-a|_{U\cap V}$. Proof. Left exactness of sections identifies the kernel in degree zero with $F(U)$. By theorem 10.43.5 , applying $\Gamma (U,C^\bullet -)$ to a short exact sequence gives a degreewise short exact sequence of complexes; apply lemma 10.43.3 . We first prove an extension fact without using cohomology. If $0\to A\to B\xrightarrow {p}Q\to 0$ is exact and $A$ flabby, then $B(U)\to Q(U)$ is onto. Given $t\in Q(U)$, order all its partial lifts $b\in B(W)$, $W\subset U$ open, by extension. Chains have upper bounds by gluing, so take a maximal lift. If $x\in U\setminus W$, choose a local lift $b_0$ on $W_0\ni x$. On $W\cap W_0$, the difference $b-b_0$ is the image of a section of $A$, by left exactness of sections. Extend this section to $W_0$ using flabbiness, add it to $b_0$, and glue with $b$. This contradicts maximality. Thus $W=U$. If also $B$ is flabby, lifting a section of $Q(U)$ to $B(U)$ and extending to $X$ shows that $Q$ is flabby. Now suppose $F$ is flabby. Set $Z^0=F$ and $Z^{q+1}=\ker (d^{q+1}:C^{q+1}F\to C^{q+2}F)$. Exactness of the resolution gives $0\to Z^ q\to C^ qF\to Z^{q+1}\to 0$. The extension fact shows inductively that every $Z^ q$ is flabby and that these sequences are exact on sections over every open set. Hence the complex defining $H^ q(U,F)$ is exact for $q>0$. Finally each $C^ qF$ is a sheaf and flabby, so \[  0\to C^ qF(X)\to C^ qF(U)\oplus C^ qF(V) \to C^ qF(U\cap V)\to 0  \] is exact: the kernel is the sheaf gluing condition and surjectivity follows by extending the desired section from $U\cap V$ to $V$. Apply the cochain long exact sequence and the restriction assertion of theorem 10.43.5 . $\square$ Theorem 10.43.8 . 9C38CEDEED0B Let $0\to F\to L^0\xrightarrow {d}L^1\to \cdots $ be a resolution of sheaves of abelian groups. If every $L^ j$ is acyclic on $X$, then there are natural isomorphisms \[  H^ q\bigl (L^\bullet (X)\bigr )\simeq H^ q(X,F),\qquad q\ge 0.  \] They commute with morphisms of augmented resolutions. Thus a morphism between two acyclic resolutions inducing the identity on $F$ induces an isomorphism on section cohomology. Exactness of a resolution alone, without its acyclicity hypothesis, is not asserted to have this property. Proof. Put $Z^0=F$ and $Z^ j=\ker (L^ j\to L^{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$. For $j\ge 1$ there is a short exact sequence $0\to Z^{j-1}\to L^{j-1}\to Z^ j\to 0$. Its long exact sequence identifies \[  Z^ j(X)/dL^{j-1}(X)\simeq H^1(X,Z^{j-1})  \] and gives connecting isomorphisms $H^ s(X,Z^ j)\simeq H^{s+1}(X,Z^{j-1})$ for $s\ge 1$. For fixed $q\ge 1$, the first quotient with $j=q$ is exactly $H^ q(L^\bullet (X))$. Follow it by the $q-1$ connecting isomorphisms ending at $H^ q(X,Z^0)=H^ q(X,F)$. No shift past $Z^0$ is made. For $q=0$, left exactness gives $\ker d=F(X)$ directly. Naturality of every connecting map, proved in lemma 10.43.3 , proves the naturality assertions. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.43.8
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Theorem 10.43.8 . 9C38CEDEED0B Let $0\to F\to L^0\xrightarrow {d}L^1\to \cdots $ be a resolution of sheaves of abelian groups. If every $L^ j$ is acyclic on $X$, then there are natural isomorphisms \[  H^ q\bigl (L^\bullet (X)\bigr )\simeq H^ q(X,F),\qquad q\ge 0.  \] They commute with morphisms of augmented resolutions. Thus a morphism between two acyclic resolutions inducing the identity on $F$ induces an isomorphism on section cohomology. Exactness of a resolution alone, without its acyclicity hypothesis, is not asserted to have this property. Proof. Put $Z^0=F$ and $Z^ j=\ker (L^ j\to L^{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$. For $j\ge 1$ there is a short exact sequence $0\to Z^{j-1}\to L^{j-1}\to Z^ j\to 0$. Its long exact sequence identifies \[  Z^ j(X)/dL^{j-1}(X)\simeq H^1(X,Z^{j-1})  \] and gives connecting isomorphisms $H^ s(X,Z^ j)\simeq H^{s+1}(X,Z^{j-1})$ for $s\ge 1$.
