title: 10.43.9 Partitions and differential resolutions
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Proposition 10.43.10 . 0C328241C3B1 Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of unital rings on $X$ such that every open cover $(U_ i)$ admits sections $\phi _ i\in \mathcal A(X)$ with locally finite supports, $\operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i\subset U_ i$ and $\sum _ i\phi _ i=1$. Every sheaf $F$ of $\mathcal A$-modules is acyclic on $X$. In particular, on a Hausdorff smooth manifold with a countable basis, all sheaves of $C^\infty $-modules are acyclic. Proof. The support of a section means its closed germ support: a zero germ is zero in a neighborhood. Give $GF$ the $\mathcal A$-action $(a s)_ x=a_ xs_ x$. The maps $\eta $, their iterates and all coface maps are $\mathcal A$-linear, so the Godement differential is linear over $\mathcal A$. Let $z\in C^ qF(X)$ be closed, $q>0$. Exactness on stalks gives local sections $b_ i\in C^{q-1}F(U_ i)$ with $db_ i=z$. Multiply by a subordinate $\phi _ i$. The section $\phi _ i b_ i$ extends by zero: it is zero on $U_ i\setminus \operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i$, and $U_ i$ together with $X\setminus \operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i$ covers $X$. The locally finite sum $b=\sum _ i\phi _ i b_ i$ is a sheaf section and $db=\sum _ i\phi _ i z=z$. This proves acyclicity. For the final assertion use the existing smooth partition construction: exhaust each connected component by compact unions of chart balls, choose finitely many compactly supported bumps on each compact annular layer subordinate to the given cover, and divide by their positive locally finite sum. Its proof uses only real coordinates, as in manifold cutoffs, partitions and compact-support Stokes , Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners , and applies in every real dimension. The partition supports are contained in their open chart domains. $\square$ Corollary 10.43.11 . EE08E1840318 For a Hausdorff smooth manifold $M$ with a countable basis, the smooth de Rham complex computes $H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb R})$. If $M$ is oriented, inclusion of smooth forms in real currents induces an isomorphism of their de Rham cohomology groups. On a complex manifold, for every $p$, inclusion of smooth $(p,\bullet )$-forms in $(p,\bullet )$-currents induces isomorphisms \[  H^ q(\mathcal E^{p,\bullet }(X),\bar\partial ) \simeq H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D'^{p,\bullet }(X),\bar\partial ).  \] Here $\Omega _ X^ p$ is the sheaf of holomorphic p-forms. These groups are ordinary section cohomology; no compact-support or singular-cohomology comparison is asserted. More generally, if $E$ is a holomorphic vector bundle and $\mathcal O(E)$ its sheaf of holomorphic sections, then \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E) :=H^ q(\mathcal E^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E) \simeq H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O(E)) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D'^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E),  \] compatibly with the inclusion of smooth $E$-valued forms in currents. Proof. In dimension zero the assertions are immediate on the discrete coordinate balls. In positive dimension the real homotopy formula the de Rham homotopy formula on a coordinate ball gives exactness of the smooth de Rham sheaf complex in positive degrees, and its degree zero kernel is the locally constant sheaf. The same local exactness for currents follows from theorem 5.54.2 : a closed current is a smooth closed form plus an exact current, and the smooth form has a local primitive. Closed scalar distributions are locally constant by distributions with zero gradient . On an oriented $M$, integration defines the inclusion of smooth forms in currents and it induces the identity on this degree-zero kernel. Each sheaf of forms or currents is a $C^\infty $-module, hence acyclic by proposition 10.43.10 . Apply theorem 10.43.8 to the two resolutions. For $\bar\partial $, local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents for forms and currents supplies positive-degree exactness. In degree zero, holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions applied to the coefficients says precisely that the kernel consists of holomorphic p-forms. Complex manifolds have their canonical orientation. These sheaves are again $C^\infty $-modules. The same comparison theorem proves all three isomorphisms. Their differentials need only be additive; they are not claimed to be $C^\infty $-linear. It is the Godement differential used to prove acyclicity of each individual sheaf that is module-linear. For the bundle assertion, define $\bar\partial _ E$ coefficientwise in a local holomorphic frame. Changes of frame are holomorphic matrices, whose $\bar\partial $ is zero, so the local operators agree, for smooth forms and for distribution coefficients. The same local frames reduce positive-degree exactness to the scalar local exactness already used, and identify the degree-zero kernel with $\Omega _ X^ p\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O(E)$ by the scalar holomorphy lemma. Each smooth or current term is still a sheaf of $C^\infty $-modules and hence is acyclic. The inclusion commutes with $\bar\partial _ E$ and is the identity on this kernel. Applying theorem 10.43.8 proves both isomorphisms and their compatibility, with no global trivialization of $E$ required. $\square$ On an unoriented real manifold, ordinary currents defined as duals of compactly supported ordinary forms instead resolve the real orientation local system. Indeed, choose an orientation in each coordinate ball. The closed degree-zero generator is integration against $1$ in that orientation, and changing the chosen orientation changes this generator by its sign. These signs are exactly the transition maps of the orientation local system. Tensoring this current complex with that local system cancels the signs and gives a resolution of $\underline{\mathbb R}$; locally the system has constant signs, so the differential and all local exactness statements persist. This is the orientation-twisted version of the real-current comparison. Corollary 10.43.12 . B5B64990368D Every real closed $(1,1)$-current $T$ has locally a real distribution $u$ with $T=i\partial \bar\partial u$. If $T$ is smooth, $u$ can be chosen smooth. Proof. Local real current exactness, used in corollary 10.43.11 , gives $T=dS$; replace $S$ by its real part. Write $S=S^{1,0}+S^{0,1}$, so $S^{1,0}=\overline{S^{0,1}}$. Since $T^{0,2}=0$, one has $\bar\partial S^{0,1}=0$. By local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents , on a smaller neighborhood $S^{0,1}=\bar\partial v$. Therefore \[  T=\partial \bar\partial v+\bar\partial \partial \bar v =\partial \bar\partial (v-\bar v) =i\partial \bar\partial (2\operatorname {Im}v).  \] Take $u=2\operatorname {Im}v$. For smooth $T$, first use the smooth real homotopy to choose smooth $S$, and then the smooth clause of the same local complex exactness theorem to choose smooth $v$. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.43.10
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Proposition 10.43.10 . 0C328241C3B1 Let $\mathcal A$ be a sheaf of unital rings on $X$ such that every open cover $(U_ i)$ admits sections $\phi _ i\in \mathcal A(X)$ with locally finite supports, $\operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i\subset U_ i$ and $\sum _ i\phi _ i=1$. Every sheaf $F$ of $\mathcal A$-modules is acyclic on $X$. In particular, on a Hausdorff smooth manifold with a countable basis, all sheaves of $C^\infty $-modules are acyclic. Proof. The support of a section means its closed germ support: a zero germ is zero in a neighborhood. Give $GF$ the $\mathcal A$-action $(a s)_ x=a_ xs_ x$. The maps $\eta $, their iterates and all coface maps are $\mathcal A$-linear, so the Godement differential is linear over $\mathcal A$. Let $z\in C^ qF(X)$ be closed, $q>0$. Exactness on stalks gives local sections $b_ i\in C^{q-1}F(U_ i)$ with $db_ i=z$. Multiply by a subordinate $\phi _ i$. The section $\phi _ i b_ i$ extends by zero: it is zero on $U_ i\setminus \operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i$, and $U_ i$ together with $X\setminus \operatorname {Supp}\phi _ i$ covers $X$. The locally finite sum $b=\sum _ i\phi _ i b_ i$ is a sheaf section and $db=\sum _ i\phi _ i z=z$. This proves acyclicity. For the final assertion use the existing smooth partition construction: exhaust each connected component by compact unions of chart balls, choose finitely many compactly supported bumps on each compact annular layer subordinate to the given cover, and divide by their positive locally finite sum. Its proof uses only real coordinates, as in manifold cutoffs, partitions and compact-support Stokes , Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners , and applies in every real dimension. The partition supports are contained in their open chart domains. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.43.11
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Corollary 10.43.11 . EE08E1840318 For a Hausdorff smooth manifold $M$ with a countable basis, the smooth de Rham complex computes $H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb R})$. If $M$ is oriented, inclusion of smooth forms in real currents induces an isomorphism of their de Rham cohomology groups. On a complex manifold, for every $p$, inclusion of smooth $(p,\bullet )$-forms in $(p,\bullet )$-currents induces isomorphisms \[  H^ q(\mathcal E^{p,\bullet }(X),\bar\partial ) \simeq H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D'^{p,\bullet }(X),\bar\partial ).  \] Here $\Omega _ X^ p$ is the sheaf of holomorphic p-forms. These groups are ordinary section cohomology; no compact-support or singular-cohomology comparison is asserted. More generally, if $E$ is a holomorphic vector bundle and $\mathcal O(E)$ its sheaf of holomorphic sections, then \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E) :=H^ q(\mathcal E^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E) \simeq H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O(E)) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D'^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E),  \] compatibly with the inclusion of smooth $E$-valued forms in currents. Proof. In dimension zero the assertions are immediate on the discrete coordinate balls. In positive dimension the real homotopy formula the de Rham homotopy formula on a coordinate ball gives exactness of the smooth de Rham sheaf complex in positive degrees, and its degree zero kernel is the locally constant sheaf. The same local exactness for currents follows from theorem 5.54.2 : a closed current is a smooth closed form plus an exact current, and the smooth form has a local primitive. Closed scalar distributions are locally constant by distributions with zero gradient . On an oriented $M$, integration defines the inclusion of smooth forms in currents and it induces the identity on this degree-zero kernel. Each sheaf of forms or currents is a $C^\infty $-module, hence acyclic by proposition 10.43.10 . Apply theorem 10.43.8 to the two resolutions. For $\bar\partial $, local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents for forms and currents supplies positive-degree exactness. In degree zero, holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions applied to the coefficients says precisely that the kernel consists of holomorphic p-forms. Complex manifolds have their canonical orientation. These sheaves are again $C^\infty $-modules. The same comparison theorem proves all three isomorphisms. Their differentials need only be additive; they are not claimed to be $C^\infty $-linear. It is the Godement differential used to prove acyclicity of each individual sheaf that is module-linear. For the bundle assertion, define $\bar\partial _ E$ coefficientwise in a local holomorphic frame. Changes of frame are holomorphic matrices, whose $\bar\partial $ is zero, so the local operators agree, for smooth forms and for distribution coefficients. The same local frames reduce positive-degree exactness to the scalar local exactness already used, and identify the degree-zero kernel with $\Omega _ X^ p\otimes _{\mathcal O_ X}\mathcal O(E)$ by the scalar holomorphy lemma. Each smooth or current term is still a sheaf of $C^\infty $-modules and hence is acyclic. The inclusion commutes with $\bar\partial _ E$ and is the identity on this kernel. Applying theorem 10.43.8 proves both isomorphisms and their compatibility, with no global trivialization of $E$ required. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.43.12
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: Corollary 10.43.12 . B5B64990368D Every real closed $(1,1)$-current $T$ has locally a real distribution $u$ with $T=i\partial \bar\partial u$. If $T$ is smooth, $u$ can be chosen smooth. Proof. Local real current exactness, used in corollary 10.43.11 , gives $T=dS$; replace $S$ by its real part. Write $S=S^{1,0}+S^{0,1}$, so $S^{1,0}=\overline{S^{0,1}}$. Since $T^{0,2}=0$, one has $\bar\partial S^{0,1}=0$. By local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents , on a smaller neighborhood $S^{0,1}=\bar\partial v$. Therefore \[  T=\partial \bar\partial v+\bar\partial \partial \bar v =\partial \bar\partial (v-\bar v) =i\partial \bar\partial (2\operatorname {Im}v).  \] Take $u=2\operatorname {Im}v$. For smooth $T$, first use the smooth real homotopy to choose smooth $S$, and then the smooth clause of the same local complex exactness theorem to choose smooth $v$. $\square$

title: 10.43.13 Čech complexes and acyclic covers
section: 10.43 Sheaves, resolutions and cohomology
text: For an open cover $\mathcal U=(U_ i)$ use all ordered index tuples, including repetitions, without an alternating restriction, and put \[  \check C^ r(\mathcal U,F)=\prod _{i_0,\ldots ,i_ r} F(U_{i_0}\cap \cdots \cap U_{i_ r}),\quad (\delta c)_{i_0\ldots i_{r+1}} =\sum _{j=0}^{r+1}(-1)^ jc_{i_0\ldots \widehat i_ j\ldots i_{r+1}}.  \] Restrictions to the common intersection are understood. Equal omissions cancel in pairs, so $\delta ^2=0$. Write $\check H^ r(\mathcal U,F)$ for its cohomology; the gluing axiom gives $\check H^0(\mathcal U,F)=F(X)$. Lemma 10.43.14 . E9E0A2A2589C For every cover, $\check H^ r(\mathcal U,F)=0$ for $r>0$ if $F$ is flabby. The same holds for a module over a sheaf of rings with a partition of unity subordinate to this cover. Proof. For a partition $(\phi _ i)$, extend $\phi _ jc_{j i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$ by zero and put $(hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}=\sum _ j\phi _ jc_{j i_0\ldots i_{r-1}}$. The sum is locally finite. Expanding the finite omission sums gives \[  (\delta hc)_{i_0\ldots i_ r} =\sum _ j\phi _ j\bigl (c_{i_0\ldots i_ r}-(\delta c)_{j i_0\ldots i_ r}\bigr ), \qquad \delta h+h\delta =\mathrm{id}\quad (r>0).  \] For $F=GB$, choose for each point one index of a set containing it. The characteristic functions of this partition of the underlying set act on $GB(U)=\prod _{x\in U}B_ x$. The same formula is defined pointwise, with exactly one summand at each point; no local finiteness or continuity of these characteristic functions is needed. Thus $GB$ is Čech-acyclic. For flabby $F$, in $0\to F\to GF\to Q\to 0$ the quotient $Q$ is flabby, and sections are onto on every intersection, by the extension fact in theorem 10.43.7 . Taking products gives a short exact sequence of Čech complexes. Its long exact sequence, $\check H^0=\Gamma $, and surjectivity $GF(X)\to Q(X)$ give $\check H^1(\mathcal U,F)=0$. For $r>1$, they give $\check H^ r(\mathcal U,F)\simeq \check H^{r-1}(\mathcal U,Q)$. Induction, simultaneously over all flabby sheaves, proves the result. $\square$ Lemma 10.43.15 . 9D23E3CA1553 Let $D^{a,b}$, $a,b\ge 0$, be a double complex whose horizontal and vertical differentials $\delta ,d$ commute. Give its total complex the differential $\delta +(-1)^ a d$; its square is zero because the two cross terms have opposite signs and $\delta d=d\delta $. If each augmented horizontal row $0\to A^ b\to D^{0,b}\to D^{1,b}\to \cdots $ is exact and its augmentation commutes with the vertical differential, then $A^\bullet \to \operatorname {Tot}D$ induces an isomorphism on cohomology. The analogous assertion holds for exact augmented vertical columns. Proof. A total degree n has only $n+1$ components, so all the following eliminations are finite. For a total cocycle, its component at $(n,0)$ is horizontally closed, by the cocycle equation at $(n+1,0)$. If $n>0$, subtract the total differential of a horizontal preimage in $(n-1,0)$. This kills that component and changes only the component at $(n-1,1)$. The next cocycle equation makes this component horizontally closed. Repeat until only the component at $(0,n)$ remains. It is in the kernel of $\delta $, hence comes from a unique $a\in A^ n$; the vertical cocycle equation gives $da=0$. This proves surjectivity, also for $n=0$ without an elimination. If the image of $a\in A^ n$ is the total differential of $b$ of degree $n-1$, its components with positive horizontal degree vanish. Start with the highest horizontal component of $b$. Its horizontal differential is zero; if that degree is positive, subtract the total differential of a horizontal preimage. This preserves the differential of $b$ and kills that component. Continue until $b$ lies in $(0,n-1)$; it is horizontally closed, hence comes from $a'\in A^{n-1}$, and $da'=a$ by injectivity of the augmentation. For $n=0$ there is no incoming boundary. This proves injectivity. Transposing the indices and multiplying the $(a,b)$-component by $(-1)^{ab}$ identifies the total differential with $d+(-1)^ b\delta $, proving the vertical assertion with its signs. All augmentations and conclusions commute with double-complex maps. $\square$ Theorem 10.43.16 . 678E4157C53F For every open cover there is a natural map $\check H^ r(\mathcal U,F)\to H^ r(X,F)$, injective in degree one. Consequently all refinement maps in degree one are injective. If every nonempty finite intersection of members of $\mathcal U$ is acyclic for $F$, this map is an isomorphism in every degree. Refinement maps on Čech cohomology are independent of the chosen refinement function. Consequently the direct limit $\check H^ r(X,F)$ over covers is defined and has a natural map to $H^ r(X,F)$. No equality of these two global theories for an arbitrary space is asserted here. Proof. Use $D^{a,b}=\check C^ a(\mathcal U,C^ bF)$. Restriction commutes with the Godement differential. Its horizontal rows are exact after augmentation by $C^ bF(X)$, by the preceding Čech lemma. Thus lemma 10.43.15 gives $H^*(\operatorname {Tot}D)\simeq H^*(X,F)$. The inclusion of $\check C^ a(\mathcal U,F)$ in $D^{a,0}$ gives the natural map. If a degree-one Čech cocycle becomes a total boundary, it is the total differential of $b\in D^{0,0}$. Its $(0,1)$-component is zero, so $db=0$ and each component of $b$ is already a section of $F$. The original cocycle is therefore the Čech boundary $\delta b$. This proves degree-one injectivity; compatibility with refinement then proves injectivity of refinement maps in that degree. If the cover is acyclic, the vertical columns are exact after this augmentation: they are products of the complexes defining the cohomology on the intersections. Cohomology commutes with these products, because kernels are coordinatewise and a family of boundaries has a family of preimages by choice. The vertical comparison lemma proves the desired isomorphism. If $V_ j\subset U_{\rho (j)}$, restriction defines a cochain map $\rho ^*$. For two choices $\rho ,\sigma $, set, in positive degree, \[  (hc)_{j_0\ldots j_{r-1}} =\sum _{k=0}^{r-1}(-1)^ k c_{\rho (j_0)\ldots \rho (j_ k)\sigma (j_ k)\ldots \sigma (j_{r-1})},  \] restricted to $V_{j_0}\cap \cdots \cap V_{j_{r-1}}$, and set $h=0$ in degree zero. In $\delta h+h\delta $, omission of an index strictly before or after the change from $\rho $ to $\sigma $ occurs twice with opposite signs. The remaining internal adjacent-change terms cancel between consecutive k; the two endpoints are $\sigma ^*c-\rho ^*c$. Thus the maps induce the same map on cohomology. The double-complex construction commutes with refinement and with coefficient maps, so its map to $H^ r(X,F)$ also does. Covers, taken as sets of open subsets, form a set directed by common intersection refinement. The usual filtered colimit of these groups and maps is therefore defined; the compatible comparison maps descend to it. $\square$

On an open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ we write $u=\sum _{|J|=r}u_ J\, \mathrm d ar z_ J$, with increasing multi-indices, and put $|u|^2=\sum _ J|u_ J|^2$ and $\| u\| _\Phi ^2=\int _\Omega |u|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi }\, \mathrm dV$, where $\mathrm dV$ is Lebesgue measure. The coefficient $u_{jK}$ is alternating in $jK$, and is zero when $j\in K$. Let $e_ j$ be exterior multiplication by $\mathrm d ar z_ j$ and $i_ j=e_ j^*$ its contraction. On disconnected open sets, plurisubharmonic weights are understood componentwise, with the usual nontrivial, locally integrable convention. For a Hermitian matrix $A=(a_{j ar k})$ define \[  C_ r(A)=\sum _{j,k}a_{j ar k}e_ ki_ j \quad \hbox{on }\Lambda ^{0,r},\qquad C_0(A)=0.  \] For $1\leq r\leq n$, proposition 10.33.6 gives 429FD29B9B0E 6.25.1  egin{equation}  \langle C_ r(A)u,uangle =\sum _{|K|=r-1}\sum _{j,k}a_{j ar k}u_{jK}\overline{u_{kK}}, \qquad \sum _{K,j}|u_{jK}|^2=r|u|^2. \end{equation} In a unitary coframe diagonalizing $A$, the eigenvalue on $\mathrm d ar z_ J$ is $\sum _{j\in J}\lambda _ j$. Thus, if $0\leq \lambda _1\leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ n$ are the eigenvalues of $A$, 3536F4E27C58 6.25.2  egin{equation}  C_ r(A)\geq (\lambda _1+\cdots +\lambda _ r)\operatorname {Id} \geq r\lambda _1\operatorname {Id}\qquad (r\geq 1). \end{equation} In particular $C_ r$ preserves the order of Hermitian matrices. For a positive semidefinite Hermitian operator $B$ on this finite coefficient space use the dual energy \[  |g|_{B^{-1}}^2 =\sup _{v
e 0} rac{|\langle g,vangle |^2}{\langle Bv,vangle },  \] where $0/0=0$ and a positive numerator divided by zero is $+\infty $. The finite-dimensional dual-energy argument preceding Hörmander's smooth-weight $L^2$ estimate applies in this space without change: this function is measurable for measurable $g$ and continuous $B$, it decreases when $B$ increases, and $|g|^2\leq (1+\| B\| )|g|_{B^{-1}}^2$. For $\Phi \in C^\infty (\Omega ,\mathbb R)$ set \[  \delta _\Phi =\sum _ j i_ j(-\partial _{z_ j}+\partial _{z_ j}\Phi ), \qquad B_ r(\Phi )=C_ r(H_\Phi ),\quad H_\Phi =(\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{ ar z_ k}\Phi ).  \] Here $\delta _\Phi $ is the formal adjoint of $ ar\partial $ for the single weight $\Phi $; it is zero on functions. Lemma 6.25.3 . FBCE435FE2B2 For $0\leq r\leq n$ and every smooth compactly supported $(0,r)$-form, F84EB59431A3 6.25.4  egin{equation}  \| \delta _\Phi v\| _\Phi ^2+\|  ar\partial v\| _\Phi ^2 =\sum _{J,k}\| \partial _{ ar z_ k}v_ J\| _\Phi ^2 +\int _\Omega \langle B_ r(\Phi )v,vangle \mathrm e^{-\Phi }\, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} The operators to a nonexistent degree are zero. Proof. Apply theorem 10.33.2 to the trivial line bundle with squared norm $\mathrm e^{-\Phi }$, the flat form $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d ar z_ j$, and $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n\wedge v$. AD693145F35D Fix $1\leq q\leq n$, and let $\Phi ,\psi $ be smooth real functions on $\Omega $. u $ preserves both domains. Since $\Phi _1-2\Phi _2=-\Phi _3$ and $\Phi _3-\Phi _2=\psi $, the squared norms of both error terms are at most \[  \int _\Omega |v|^2| ar\partial \chi _
u |^2 \mathrm e^{-\Phi _3}\, \mathrm dV \leq \| v\| _{\Phi _2}^2.  \] Their integrands tend to zero pointwise and are dominated by $|v|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi _2}$. Dominated convergence, also for $\chi _
u v$, $\chi _

Since $B_ q(\varphi _ j+\tau )\geq B_ q(\tau )$ and $\varphi _ j\geq \varphi $, the preceding theorem gives solutions $u_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with \[  \bar\partial u_ j=g,\qquad \int _{\Omega _ j}|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ j-\tau }\,  \mathrm dV\leq M.  \] For compact $K\subset \Omega _ k$ and $j\geq k$ this also bounds $\int _ K|u_ j|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi _ k-\tau }$ by $M$, and hence gives a local unweighted $L^2$ bound. text: Lemma 6.25.12 . FA7DAEDEEAF0 Let $1\leq q\leq n$ and $\Phi \in C^\infty (\Omega ,\mathbb R)$. If $g$ is smooth and the equation $\bar\partial u=g$ has a solution in $L^2_{0,q-1}(\Omega ,\mathrm e^{-\Phi })$, its solution of smallest norm is smooth in $\Omega $ and satisfies $\delta _\Phi u=0$. Proof. The maximal operator $T=\bar\partial $ from degrees $q-1$ to $q$ is closed, and its kernel is a closed subspace of the weighted Hilbert space. Even if $g$ is not globally in the weighted $L^2$ space, all weighted $L^2$ solutions of the distributional equation form the affine subspace $u_0+\ker T$. Orthogonal projection therefore gives a unique smallest-norm solution $u\perp \ker T$. If $q\geq 2$, the maximal operator $P=\bar\partial $ from degree $q-2$ has range in $\ker T$. Hence $u\perp \operatorname {Ran}P$, which by the defining adjoint identity means $u\in \operatorname {Dom}P^*$ and $P^*u=0$. Testing on compact supports gives $\delta _\Phi u=0$ distributionally. For $q=1$ the same equation is automatic for degree reasons. Thus $\bar\partial u=g$ and $\delta _0u=-\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\Phi )i_ ju$ are locally $L^2$. Let $\chi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$. Then $w=\chi u$ and both constant-coefficient derivatives $\bar\partial w,\delta _0w$ are $L^2$. Mollify $w$ inside a fixed compact neighborhood of its support. The unweighted identity ( 6.25.4 ), followed by integration by parts in each real coordinate, gives \[  \tfrac 14\| \nabla w_\eta \| _{L^2}^2 =\sum _{J,k}\| \partial _{\bar z_ k}(w_\eta )_ J\| _{L^2}^2 =\| \bar\partial w_\eta \| _{L^2}^2+ \| \delta _0w_\eta \| _{L^2}^2.  \] The right side is bounded uniformly in $\eta $, since convolution commutes with both operators. Weak compactness of the derivatives and convergence $w_\eta \to w$ in $L^2$ identify the weak limits as the distributional derivatives of $w$. Therefore $u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. On coefficient forms the weighted Laplacian is \[  \Delta _\Phi =\bar\partial \delta _\Phi +\delta _\Phi \bar\partial =-\sum _ j\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ j} +\sum _ j(\partial _{z_ j}\Phi )\partial _{\bar z_ j} +\sum _{j,k}(\partial _{z_ j}\partial _{\bar z_ k}\Phi )e_ ki_ j.  \] This follows by $i_ je_ k+e_ ki_ j=\delta _{jk}$; its principal real part is $-\tfrac 14\Delta $ on each coefficient. On any relatively compact coordinate ball its divergence-form principal coefficients are $\tfrac 14\delta _{ij}\delta _{IJ}$, and its remaining coefficients are smooth first- and zeroth-order matrices. The hypotheses of interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form apply to the $H^1$ solution. E01D1C3D97E4 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, be pseudoconvex, let $\varphi \in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$, and fix $0\leq p\leq n$, $1\leq q\leq n$ and $0<\varepsilon \leq 1$. For a distributionally $\bar\partial $-closed $(p,q)$-form $g\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ such that \[  I=\int _\Omega (1+|z|^2)|g|^2\mathrm e^{-\varphi }\,  \mathrm dV<\infty ,  \] there is a $(p,q-1)$-form $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with 114551AF385D 6.25.14 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial u=g,\qquad \int _\Omega (1+|z|^2)^{-\varepsilon }|u|^2 \mathrm e^{-\varphi }\, \mathrm dV \leq \frac4{q\varepsilon ^2}I. \end{equation} If $g$ and $\varphi $ are smooth, $u$ can be chosen smooth. Proof. Put $s=1+|z|^2$ and $\tau =\log (1+s^\varepsilon )$. Direct differentiation gives \[  h'+(s-1)h'' =\frac{\varepsilon s^{\varepsilon -2} (1+\varepsilon (s-1)+s^\varepsilon )}{(1+s^\varepsilon )^2} \geq \frac{\varepsilon ^2}{2s(1+s^\varepsilon )}=:\lambda (s)>0.  \] Indeed the numerator in parentheses is at least $\varepsilon s$, and $s^\varepsilon /(1+s^\varepsilon )\geq 1/2$. Apply theorem 6.25.10 for $q\geq 2$, and the existing the singular-weight $L^2$ estimate with a smooth curvature lower bound for $q=1$, to each holomorphic coefficient family. Since \[  \frac{\mathrm e^{-\tau }}{q\lambda (s)} \leq \frac{2s}{q\varepsilon ^2}, \qquad s^{-\varepsilon }\leq \frac2{1+s^\varepsilon },  \] the solution satisfies ( 6.25.14 ). If both data and weight are smooth, choose instead the solution of smallest norm for the smooth weight $\Phi =\varphi +\tau $; its norm still satisfies the intermediate bound, and lemma 6.25.12 makes it smooth. text: All manifolds are Hausdorff and have a countable basis. For a current of dimension $p$ use the dimensional boundary \[  (\partial T)(\eta )=T(\mathrm d\eta ),\qquad \partial T=0\quad (p=0).  \] On an oriented ambient manifold of dimension $m$, this is $\partial T=(-1)^{m-p+1}\mathrm dT$, with the derivative convention of section 5.53 . Normality means that $T$ and $\partial T$ both have measure coefficients. Order-zero currents act on continuous compactly supported forms by their coefficient measures, as in the conventions for currents and positivity . In Euclidean coordinates we may equivalently write this action as \[  T(\alpha )=\sum _{|I|=p}\int \alpha _ I\, \mathrm d\mu _ I, \qquad \alpha =\sum _{|I|=p}\alpha _ I\, \mathrm dx_ I.  \] This representation uses dimension rather than complementary form degree; the signs converting the two coefficient descriptions are the existing complementary-index signs. Lemma 5.56.1 . A6C399681838 If $T$ is normal on a smooth manifold and $h$ is a $C^1$ function, then $hT$ is normal and 05D16BBEFEE0 5.56.2 \begin{equation}  \partial (hT)(\eta ) =(\partial T)(h\eta )-T(\mathrm dh\wedge \eta ). \end{equation} If $F$ is a $C^1$ map between smooth manifolds and is proper on $\operatorname {Supp}T$, the formula \[  (F_*T)(\alpha )=T(F^*\alpha )  \] defines a normal current, preserves dimension, and satisfies $\partial (F_*T)=F_*(\partial T)$. Pullback in this formula is a continuous form, evaluated by the order-zero extension. The usual support inclusion and composition rule hold for these pushforwards. Proof. Everything is local on compact sets. A continuous form supported in a fixed compact coordinate set has its pairing bounded by the sum of the total variations of the coefficient measures there, times its coefficient sup norm. Smooth forms are dense among continuous forms with compact support, after slightly enlarging the support, by the existing mollifier construction. Approximate $h$ in $C^1$ on the compact set in question by smooth functions $h_ j$. The smooth product identity follows by expanding $\mathrm d(h_ j\eta )$. Its three pairings converge to those in ( 5.56.2 ), since $T$ and $\partial T$ have order zero and $h_ j$, $\mathrm dh_ j$ converge uniformly. The right side is order zero as a functional of $\eta $; thus $hT$ is normal. A partition of unity gives the statement in all charts. For the map assertion, first suppose the source is a Euclidean open set, $T$ has compact support $L$, and $F$ takes a neighborhood of $L$ into one target chart. Mollifying the coordinate functions gives smooth $F_ j\to F$ in $C^1$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $L$, with values in that chart. The approximants need not be injective. For every smooth target test form $\alpha $, both $F_ j^*\alpha \to F^*\alpha $ and $F_ j^*(\mathrm d\alpha )\to F^*(\mathrm d\alpha )$ uniformly on $L$: pullback uses only first derivatives of the maps. Insert one fixed source cutoff equal to one near $L$ in all pairings. The already proved smooth pushforward calculus gives \[  (F_{j*}T)(\mathrm d\eta ) =(F_{j*}\partial T)(\eta ).  \] Order-zero continuity on both sides passes this equality to the limit. This proves boundary commutation without differentiating the generally nonsmooth form $F^*\eta $. The resulting functionals have measure coefficients: in the displayed dimensional coefficient representation, their measures are finite sums of the pushforwards of $\mu _ I$ multiplied by the continuous minors of $DF$. Compactness of $L$ gives locally finite total variation. The same argument applies to $\partial T$. Thus $F_*T$ is normal, not merely a distributional limit. For a general $T$ and $F$, fix the compact support $K$ of the target test. Properness on $\operatorname {Supp}T$ makes $\operatorname {Supp}T\cap F^{-1}(K)$ compact. Use a source cutoff equal to one near this compact set and compactly supported in a neighborhood covered by finitely many source charts mapping to target charts. The preceding compact argument applies to the finitely many localized currents. In their boundary formula the cutoff derivatives either sum to zero near that set or are supported away from the pullback test. They therefore contribute zero. This proves both independence of the cutoffs and the boundary identity globally. Here $\operatorname {Supp}\partial T\subset \operatorname {Supp}T$, directly from the distributional definition, so the same properness suffices for the boundary. Smooth chart partitions or additional target localization provide the stated finite reductions. Tests supported outside $F(\operatorname {Supp}T)$ vanish; properness on the closed support makes its image closed. Finally the first-derivative chain rule gives $(G\circ F)^*\alpha =F^*G^*\alpha $ for continuous forms. The order-zero extensions and cutoffs then give composition whenever the relevant pushforwards are defined. $\square$ We specify what a normal current on a merely $C^1$ manifold means. A continuous differential form is intrinsic there: its chart transition rule uses only the continuous first derivatives. An order-zero dimensional current is a linear functional on continuous compactly supported forms, locally represented by finite families of complex Radon measures in these coordinates. Call it normal if the coordinate current in each chart has order-zero distributional boundary, computed against smooth Euclidean tests. It is enough to check one $C^1$ atlas. Indeed, on an overlap the coordinate change is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism, so lemma 5.56.1 transports both the current and its boundary by the same rule. The local boundaries agree as order-zero functionals on overlaps and hence glue. This defines an intrinsic boundary $\partial T$ and proves independence of the chosen atlas. No higher derivatives of a chart are used. The lemma consequently holds for $C^1$ manifolds and maps as well. To see the global step explicitly, work in coordinate patches and localize by a finite $C^1$ partition near each relevant compact set. Such partitions are obtained by pulling back ordinary smooth coordinate bumps, summing them, and dividing by their positive sum. Formula ( 5.56.2 ) is coordinate invariant by the first-derivative chain rule; its extra terms cancel when the partition sums to one. The Euclidean proof then gives the asserted boundary commutation in every target chart. Gluing order-zero functionals uses a finite partition on the support of each test, just as in gluing of currents . If a manifold has a smooth structure this definition agrees exactly with its ordinary normal currents. In particular, if the oriented source and target dimensions are $a$ and $b$, respectively, the dimensional boundary identity reads \[  \mathrm d(F_*T)=(-1)^{a-b}F_*(\mathrm dT).  \] This retains the real pushforward parity rather than imposing complex even-dimensional conventions on the submanifold. A dimensional normal current on $Y$ itself requires no orientation of $Y$. Theorem 5.56.3 . D47CED9844B5 Let $M$ be a smooth real manifold, and let $Y\subset M$ be an embedded $C^1$ submanifold without boundary, of dimension $d$. Let $T$ be a normal current of dimension $p$ on $M$ with $\operatorname {Supp}T\subset Y$. There is a unique normal current $\Theta $ of dimension $p$ on $Y$ such that \[  T=j_*\Theta ,\qquad j:Y\hookrightarrow M.  \] Its support is $j^{-1}(\operatorname {Supp}T)$, and $j$ is proper on this support even when $Y$ is not closed in $M$. If $p>d$, then $T=0$. Proof. First note why the defining-function argument is legitimate at class $C^1$. If $h$ is $C^1$ and zero on $Y$, then $hT=0$ and $h\partial T=0$, since both sets of coefficient measures are supported in $Y$. The product formula gives CF698A54DF16 5.56.4 \begin{equation}  T(\mathrm dh\wedge \eta )=0. \end{equation} It holds also for continuous compactly supported $\eta $, by order-zero continuity and smooth approximation. Thus these conormal equations do not assert that a $C^1$ defining function is a smooth test coefficient. Work locally in smooth ambient coordinates $(s,t)$ in which $Y$ is the graph $t=f(s)$ of a $C^1$ map, with $s\in A\subset \mathbb R^ d$ and $t\in \mathbb R^ q$, $q=m-d$. After shrinking, the map \[  F:A\times B\longrightarrow W,\qquad F(s,u)=(s,f(s)+u),  \] is a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto an open neighborhood $W\subset M$ of this graph piece, and $Y\cap W=F(A\times \{ 0\} )$. The previous calculus makes $S=(F^{-1})_*(T|_ W)$ normal, with support in $A\times \{ 0\} $. Applying the conormal identity to the smooth coordinates $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ gives $S(\mathrm du_ j\wedge \eta )=0$ for every $j$. Write the dimensional coefficient measures of $S$ in the coordinates $(s,u)$. If an increasing $p$-index contains any normal coordinate, its coefficient is zero: test its coefficient form, up to a sign, as $\mathrm du_ j\wedge \eta $. Hence only indices consisting of $s$-coordinates survive. All their measures are supported on $A\times \{ 0\} $. If $p>d$ there are no such indices, so $S=0$. For $p\leq d$, transport these measures to $A$ under the projection $P(s,u)=s$ and let $Q$ be the resulting current on $A$. In fact $Q=P_*S$, because pullback by $P$ selects precisely these tangential coefficients. This pushforward is defined: for compact $C\subset A$, its intersection with $\operatorname {Supp}S$ lies in the compact set $C\times \{ 0\} $ and is closed there. Thus $P$ is proper on $\operatorname {Supp}S$, and $Q$ is normal by the lemma. For the inclusion $i:A\to A\times B$, $i(s)=(s,0)$, coefficient evaluation gives $S=i_*Q$. It also proves uniqueness, or one can apply $P_*$ and use $P\circ i=\mathrm{Id}$. In complementary form-degree notation the same calculation says that every coefficient term contains the full normal conormal wedge $\mathrm du_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm du_ q$, as in the hint. Transport $Q$ to $Y\cap W$ by the $C^1$ graph chart. The intrinsic definition makes it a normal current there, and composition gives its inclusion pushforward into $W$ equal to $T|_ W$. The local currents on $Y$ agree on overlaps. For uniqueness there, flatten either graph chart and apply the injectivity just proved; equivalently, continuous tangent forms in that chart extend to continuous ambient forms by the projection and a normal cutoff. Equality on ambient smooth tests gives equality on continuous tests by order-zero density. The local currents and their boundaries therefore glue to a normal current $\Theta $ on $Y$. This gluing is valid without orienting $Y$. The same local injection shows $\operatorname {Supp}\Theta =j^{-1}(\operatorname {Supp}T)$. The support of $T$ is closed in $M$. For any compact $K\subset M$, the set $K\cap \operatorname {Supp}T$ is compact and lies in $Y$; its inverse image under the subspace homeomorphism is compact in $Y$. This proves properness on the support, so $j_*\Theta $ is globally defined. The local identities give the global identity and uniqueness. If $p>d$ all the local currents vanish, proving the dimension assertion. $\square$ The normality assumption cannot be dropped, even on smooth submanifolds. The following examples also distinguish its two order-zero requirements. Work on $\mathbb R^2$ with coordinates $(x,y)$, and choose a fixed smooth compactly supported $\zeta $ equal to one near the origin. First, the dimension-zero current $A(f)=\partial _ y f(0)$ is supported at the origin and has boundary zero. It is not order zero, since the uniformly bounded tests $f_ k=\zeta \sin (ky)$ give $A(f_ k)=k$. For the submanifold $Y=\{ y=0\} $ it cannot be an inclusion pushforward of any current on $Y$, even one of higher order: the test $y\zeta $ restricts to zero on $Y$, while $A(y\zeta )=1$. Second, the dimension-one current $B(a\, \mathrm dx+b\, \mathrm dy)=b(0)$ has order zero and support at the origin, but $\partial B(f)=\partial _ y f(0)$ has order one. It also cannot come from $\{ y=0\} $, since that inclusion kills $\zeta \, \mathrm dy$ whereas $B$ evaluates it to one. Thus order zero of $T$ alone does not imply the support theorem. Finally let the dimension-two point current be $R(c\, \mathrm dx\wedge \mathrm dy)=c(0)$ and put $C=\partial R$. Then \[  C(a\, \mathrm dx+b\, \mathrm dy) =\partial _ xb(0)-\partial _ ya(0),\qquad \partial C=0.  \] This current is nonzero, supported on the zero-dimensional submanifold $\{ 0\} $, and has dimension one. It is not order zero: the uniformly bounded forms $\zeta \sin (kx)\, \mathrm dy$ have $C$-values $k$. Thus the dimension conclusion also fails without normality, even for a closed current. These evaluations use the same measure-versus-point-derivative distinction as the Dirac derivative as a distribution of positive order .

text: A tube in $\mathbb C^ n$ has the form $T_\omega =\omega +\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$, where $\omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ is open. Convex hulls here are taken with real convex combinations, also when the ambient space is $\mathbb C^ n=\mathbb R^{2n}$. We prove the extension assertion directly with Cauchy integrals. The Cauchy formula and identity theorem used below are those accompanying holomorphic power series and Cauchy bounds . Write $\mathbb D=\{ |\zeta |<1\} $ and $P_\rho =\{ w\in \mathbb C^ n:\max _ j|w_ j|<\rho \} $. For a smooth real vector-valued function $\gamma $ on the unit circle put 483A1D288F9C 9.39.1 \begin{equation}  A_\gamma (\zeta )=\frac1{2\pi } \int _0^{2\pi }\frac{\mathrm e^{\mathrm it}+\zeta }{\mathrm e^{\mathrm it}-\zeta }\gamma (t)\, \mathrm dt. \end{equation} This is a holomorphic vector-valued map on $\mathbb D$, smooth up to its boundary, with \[  \operatorname {Re}A_\gamma (\mathrm e^{\mathrm it})=\gamma (t),\qquad A_\gamma (0)=\frac1{2\pi }\int _0^{2\pi }\gamma (t)\, \mathrm dt\in \mathbb R^ n.  \] Indeed, the real part of its kernel is the Poisson kernel, a positive kernel of integral one whose mass outside any fixed neighborhood of zero tends to zero at the boundary. Lemma 9.39.2 . 7D65E928B1FB Let $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be open, $f\in \mathcal O(U)$, and let $A_ s:\overline{\mathbb D}\to \mathbb C^ n$, $0\leq s\leq 1$, be a family of holomorphic discs smooth up to the boundary, continuous in that smooth topology, such that $A_ s(\partial \mathbb D)\subset U$. Assume $A_0$ is constant. Then for every $s$ the boundary function $f(A_ s(\tau )+w)$ has a holomorphic extension in $\tau $ to $\mathbb D$ for all sufficiently small translations $w$. Its value at $\zeta =0$ is BA7B66342790 9.39.3 \begin{equation}  g_{A_ s}(w)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i} \int _{|\tau |=1}f(A_ s(\tau )+w)\frac{\mathrm d\tau }{\tau }. \end{equation} Whenever two such discs $A,B$ are sufficiently close, their center germs satisfy 6921BEE69455 9.39.4 \begin{equation}  g_ B(w)=g_ A\bigl (w+B(0)-A(0)\bigr ) \end{equation} for small $w$. Proof. The union of all boundary images is compact in $U$. Choose $\rho >0$ such that all its translates by $\overline{P_\rho }$ lie in $U$. For $k\geq 0$ consider the holomorphic functions of $w\in P_\rho $ \[  M_{s,k}(w)=\frac1{2\pi \mathrm i}\int _{|\tau |=1} f(A_ s(\tau )+w)\tau ^ k\, \mathrm d\tau .  \] All these moments vanish exactly when the smooth boundary function has no negative Fourier coefficients, equivalently when it is the boundary value of its holomorphic Cauchy integral on the disc. The equivalence follows by its rapidly convergent Fourier series; alternatively the Poisson kernels above recover the boundary values uniformly. The set of $s$ for which all the moments vanish identically on $P_\rho $ is closed, and contains zero. It is open as well. At such a parameter $s_0$ the Cauchy integral $H(\zeta ,w)$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb D\times P_\rho $, continuous up to the circle, and equals $f(A_{s_0}(\tau )+w)$ there. For $s$ close to $s_0$ we have $\sup _{\overline{\mathbb D}}|A_ s-A_{s_0}|_\infty <\rho /4$. A02A83950E4E Let $a\in \mathbb R^ n$, let $h\in C^\infty _ c(\mathbb R,\mathbb R^ n)$ be supported in $[0,L]$, with $L>0$, and put, periodically on the circle, \[  \gamma _\eta (t)=a+h(t/\eta ),\qquad 0<\eta L<\pi /4,  \] where the added term is zero off $[0,\eta L]$. E5EB0154B387 Let $\omega \subset \mathbb R^ n$ be nonempty, open and connected. Every $f\in \mathcal O(T_\omega )$ has a unique holomorphic extension to \[  T_{\operatorname {conv}\omega } =\operatorname {conv}(T_\omega ).  \] Proof. Fix $a\in \omega $. The loops depend smoothly on $p\in P$: interval endpoints depend affinely on the times, and every parameter derivative matches at the flat joins. On compact subsets of $P$ the durations stay positive, so this assertion holds in every smooth norm on the circle. There is a fixed travel mean $c\in \operatorname {conv}\omega $ such that F09A8AEAD47E 9.39.8 \begin{equation}  A_{\gamma _ p}(0)=\delta c+\sum _{j=0}^ N\mu _ j b_ j=:m(p). \end{equation} To see $c\in \operatorname {conv}\omega $ without a closure assumption, partition the finitely many paths into sufficiently short intervals on which their images lie in balls contained in $\omega $. Each interval's mean lies in its ball; their finite convex combination is $c$. For every $p$, this loop contracts smoothly to $a$ through loops in $\omega $: replace each outward path $\beta _ j(\chi (u))$ by $\beta _ j(s\chi (u))$, use its reverse on the return trip, and dwell at $\beta _ j(s)$, for $0\leq s\leq 1$. The time intervals remain unchanged. The Schwarz discs of these loops, also after any fixed imaginary translation $\mathrm iy$, have their boundary in $T_\omega $ and start at the constant disc $a+\mathrm iy$. The boundary images of each such compact parameter family are compact in $T_\omega $; smoothness bounds their imaginary parts and their real parts lie in the fixed compact union of the paths. With $z=x+\mathrm iy$ the conic equations become \[  \frac\varepsilon 2|y|^2 =1-x_1-x_2+\frac\varepsilon 2|x|^2,\qquad (1-\varepsilon x_1)y_1+(1-\varepsilon x_2)y_2=0.  \] On the closed triangle $(1+\varepsilon )T$ the first equality bounds $|y|^2$ by $2/\varepsilon +(1+\varepsilon )^2$, so $M_\varepsilon $ is closed and bounded. It cannot meet the hypotenuse $x_1+x_2=1+\varepsilon $: there the right side is at most $-\varepsilon +\varepsilon (1+\varepsilon )^2/2<0$. Thus its relative boundary in the conic lies above $x_1=0$ or $x_2=0$. The conic is nonsingular because its only possible critical point is $(1/\varepsilon ,1/\varepsilon )$, whose defining left side is $1/\varepsilon \neq 1$. Equivalently, its translated equation is $u v=2(1-\varepsilon )/\varepsilon ^2$ for $u=(z_1-1/\varepsilon )+\mathrm i(z_2-1/\varepsilon )$ and its counterpart $v$ with the minus sign. With $c_\varepsilon =2(1-\varepsilon )/\varepsilon ^2$, its parametrization is \[  z_1=\varepsilon ^{-1}+\tfrac 12(u+c_\varepsilon /u),\qquad z_2=\varepsilon ^{-1}+\tfrac 1{2\mathrm i}(u-c_\varepsilon /u), \qquad u\in \mathbb C^*.  \] For any $x\in T$ the right side of the first displayed equation is nonnegative. This proves the projection claim. The boundary projection consists of axis points of lengths at most $1+\varepsilon $; their scalings stay on these same axis segments. Finally $0\in \omega $ and the real parts of $M_\varepsilon $ are bounded, so all small positive scalings of its entire real projection lie in a fixed ball about zero contained in $\omega $. These prove the remaining scaling assertions. $\square$

For every $p$, this loop contracts smoothly to $a$ through loops in $\omega $: replace each outward path $\beta _ j(\chi (u))$ by $\beta _ j(s\chi (u))$, use its reverse on the return trip, and dwell at $\beta _ j(s)$, for $0\leq s\leq 1$. The time intervals remain unchanged. The Schwarz discs of these loops, also after any fixed imaginary translation $\mathrm iy$, have their boundary in $T_\omega $ and start at the constant disc $a+\mathrm iy$. The boundary images of each such compact parameter family are compact in $T_\omega $; smoothness bounds their imaginary parts and their real parts lie in the fixed compact union of the paths. By lemma 9.39.2 each $A_{\gamma _ p}+\mathrm iy$ therefore defines a holomorphic center germ at $m(p)+\mathrm iy$ by ( 9.39.3 ). Put $D=m(P)$. It is convex, and it is open in $\mathbb R^ n$: the vectors $b_ j-b_0$ span $\mathbb R^ n$, so variations of the $\mu _ j$ with zero sum give a surjective linear mean map while $\delta $ is held fixed. A linear right inverse gives a local affine section at every parameter, remaining in $P$ for small variations. Also 00458B646C9D 9.39.9 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {int}C\subset D\subset \operatorname {conv}\omega . \end{equation} For the first inclusion, positive convex coefficients on all $b_ j$ map onto $\operatorname {int}C$. One direction follows from the same local surjectivity. Conversely the average $\bar b$ of all the $b_ j$ is an interior point; for $x\in \operatorname {int}C$ and small $e>0$ the point $(x-e\bar b)/(1-e)$ lies in $C$. Its nonnegative coefficients, mixed with the positive equal coefficients of $e\bar b$, give positive coefficients for $x$. For sufficiently small $\delta >0$ apply this to $(x-\delta c)/(1-\delta )$ and set $\mu _ j=(1-\delta )\lambda _ j$. The second inclusion in ( 9.39.9 ) follows from ( 9.39.8 ). We now check that the germs define one holomorphic function $F_ D$ on $D+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$. If $m(p)=m(p')$, the fiber $P\cap m^{-1}(m(p))$ is convex. Along its line segment the boundary discs vary continuously in every smooth norm and their centers are fixed. Local consistency ( 9.39.4 ) therefore makes their center germs equal; a finite chain of overlapping parameter neighborhoods along the segment gives equality of the endpoint germs. Thus the germ does not depend on the representative of its center. This is the single-valuedness step. To check holomorphy rather than only well-defined values, fix $z_0=m(p_0)+\mathrm iy_0$ and choose the local affine section of $m$ above. For $z=x+\mathrm iy$ close to $z_0$, the corresponding discs are close to $A_{\gamma _{p_0}}+\mathrm iy_0$. Formula ( 9.39.4 ) says that their center values equal the fixed holomorphic germ at $z_0$ evaluated at $z-z_0$. Hence these values form a holomorphic function $F_ D$, and its germ at each center is exactly the Cauchy germ constructed there. It remains to identify that germ with the original function. For small $\delta >0$ choose $\mu _ j=\delta $ for $1\leq j\leq N$ and $\mu _0=1-(N+1)\delta $. The entire nonconstant part of $\gamma _ p$ is then compressed into an arc of length $O(\delta )$, with a fixed smooth profile based at $a$; the remaining arc is constant $a$. In the angular variable it has the form in lemma 9.39.5 , after absorbing a fixed factor into its profile and scale. The center $m(p)$ tends to $a$. Because $a\in \operatorname {int}C\subset D$, a fixed complex polydisc about $a+\mathrm iy$ lies in $D+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$. On a sufficiently small fixed translation polydisc the boundary Cauchy integrals tend locally uniformly to $f(a+\mathrm iy+w)$ by ( 9.39.6 ). They equal $F_ D(m(p)+\mathrm iy+w)$ there: equality first holds as germs, and then on this fixed polydisc by the identity theorem, after making it small enough that all its centers and translates remain in $D$ and its boundary translates remain in $T_\omega $. Continuity of $F_ D$ now gives $F_ D(a+\mathrm iy+w)=f(a+\mathrm iy+w)$ near zero. In particular $F_ D=f$ on a neighborhood of $a$. The domains $D$ obtained from finite choices above cover $\operatorname {conv}\omega $. Indeed, for any $x$ in that open convex set, choose a small real coordinate cross about $x$ still in it. Each of its finitely many vertices is a finite convex combination of points of $\omega $. Collect those points together with $a$ and a small coordinate cross in $\omega $ about $a$. Their convex hull contains both $x$ and $a$ in its interior, so ( 9.39.9 ) places $x$ in the corresponding $D$. The convex hull of an open set is open: in any finite convex representation, varying a point with positive coefficient supplies a ball about the represented point. Any two resulting convex sets $D,D'$ contain $a$ in their interiors. Their tube intersection $(D\cap D')+\mathrm i\mathbb R^ n$ is connected, and $F_ D,F_{D'}$ agree near $a$ with $f$. The identity theorem makes them agree throughout that intersection. They consequently glue to a single holomorphic function on $T_{\operatorname {conv}\omega }$. It agrees with $f$ near $a$ and hence on all of the connected original tube. The same identity theorem proves uniqueness. Finally the real part of any convex combination from $T_\omega $ lies in $\operatorname {conv}\omega $. Conversely, for $x=\sum t_ jx_ j$ and any $y\in \mathbb R^ n$, the equality $x+\mathrm iy=\sum t_ j(x_ j+\mathrm iy)$ proves the asserted equality of convex hulls. $\square$

title: Proposition 9.39.10
section: 9.39 Holomorphic extension from a connected tube
text: Proposition 9.39.10 . 08FF9CEC303A Let $\omega \subset \mathbb R^2$ be open and connected, let $T=\{ x_1,x_2\geq 0,\  x_1+x_2\leq 1\} $, and suppose $[0,1]\times \{ 0\} $ and $\{ 0\} \times [0,1]$ lie in $\omega $. Every function in $\mathcal O(T_\omega )$ extends to a neighborhood of $T+\mathrm i\mathbb R^2$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon >0$, the affine conic \[  Q_\varepsilon =\{ z_1+z_2-\tfrac \varepsilon 2(z_1^2+z_2^2)=1\}   \] is nonsingular, and $M_\varepsilon =Q_\varepsilon \cap \pi ^{-1}((1+\varepsilon )T)$, $\pi (z)=\operatorname {Re}z$, is compact. Its relative boundary lies above the two axis edges, and $\pi (M_\varepsilon )\supset T$; in particular $\pi ([0,1]M_\varepsilon )\supset T$. For $0\leq t\leq 1$, $t\partial M_\varepsilon \subset T_\omega $, and $tM_\varepsilon \subset T_\omega $ for all sufficiently small $t$. Proof. The triangle is the convex hull of three points of $\omega $ and so lies in the open set $\operatorname {conv}\omega $. Its compactness gives a real neighborhood still in that set. The preceding theorem supplies the claimed extension, with its already proved uniqueness and consistency. Take $0<\varepsilon <1/4$, also small enough that both axis segments of length $1+\varepsilon $ lie in $\omega $, which is possible by openness and compactness of the original two edges. With $z=x+\mathrm iy$ the conic equations become \[  \frac\varepsilon 2|y|^2 =1-x_1-x_2+\frac\varepsilon 2|x|^2,\qquad (1-\varepsilon x_1)y_1+(1-\varepsilon x_2)y_2=0.  \] On the closed triangle $(1+\varepsilon )T$ the first equality bounds $|y|^2$ by $2/\varepsilon +(1+\varepsilon )^2$, so $M_\varepsilon $ is closed and bounded. It cannot meet the hypotenuse $x_1+x_2=1+\varepsilon $: there the right side is at most $-\varepsilon +\varepsilon (1+\varepsilon )^2/2<0$. Thus its relative boundary in the conic lies above $x_1=0$ or $x_2=0$. The conic is nonsingular because its only possible critical point is $(1/\varepsilon ,1/\varepsilon )$, whose defining left side is $1/\varepsilon \neq 1$. Equivalently, its translated equation is $u v=2(1-\varepsilon )/\varepsilon ^2$ for $u=(z_1-1/\varepsilon )+\mathrm i(z_2-1/\varepsilon )$ and its counterpart $v$ with the minus sign. With $c_\varepsilon =2(1-\varepsilon )/\varepsilon ^2$, its parametrization is \[  z_1=\varepsilon ^{-1}+\tfrac 12(u+c_\varepsilon /u),\qquad z_2=\varepsilon ^{-1}+\tfrac 1{2\mathrm i}(u-c_\varepsilon /u), \qquad u\in \mathbb C^*.  \] For any $x\in T$ the right side of the first displayed equation is nonnegative. The real vector $(1-\varepsilon x_1,1-\varepsilon x_2)$ is nonzero. Choose a real vector $y$ perpendicular to it with the prescribed nonnegative squared norm; then $x+\mathrm iy\in M_\varepsilon $. This proves the projection claim. The boundary projection consists of axis points of lengths at most $1+\varepsilon $; their scalings stay on these same axis segments. Finally $0\in \omega $ and the real parts of $M_\varepsilon $ are bounded, so all small positive scalings of its entire real projection lie in a fixed ball about zero contained in $\omega $. These prove the remaining scaling assertions. $\square$

title: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
