section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: All manifolds below have no boundary. Hermitian inner products are linear in the first entry. A formal adjoint is taken for the indicated bundle metrics and positive volume density. Differential operators act on distributional sections by their formal adjoints. Lemma 10.46.1 . 2EE58CB34CD0 Let $M$ be a compact real manifold of dimension $d\geq 1$, let $V$ be a smooth Hermitian vector bundle, and let \[  P=A^*A+BB^*  \] on $C^\infty (M,V)$, where $A$ and $B$ are first-order differential operators between smooth Hermitian bundles. Suppose that in every coordinate chart the second-order part of $P$ is $-\sum a^{ij}(x)\partial _ i\partial _ j$ on every coefficient, with $(a^{ij})$ real symmetric positive definite. Then: $(P+1)^{-1}=T$ exists on distributional sections. For every integer $s$, it is bounded from $H^ s$ to $H^{s+2}$. On $L^2$, $T$ is compact, self-adjoint and positive. The space $\mathcal H=\ker P$ consists of smooth sections and is finite dimensional. Let $\Pi $ be its orthogonal projection. There is a bounded self-adjoint operator $G$ on $L^2$, zero on $\mathcal H$, with \[  PGf=f-\Pi f,\qquad GPu=u-\Pi u\quad (u\in C^\infty ).  \] For every integer $s\geq 0$, $G:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ is bounded. In particular $G$ preserves smooth sections and is continuous for their smooth topology. Proof. Sobolev spaces and local regularity. Use a finite coordinate cover, bundle frames and smooth cutoffs to define the integer Sobolev norms by sums of coefficient derivative norms; $H^0=L^2$, and negative spaces are Hilbert duals for this pairing. The coordinate-change, convolution and duality proofs of Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding apply to these coefficient vectors: the changes of frame are smooth invertible matrices, and their derivatives and coordinate Jacobians are bounded on the compact supports. Thus the norms are independent of those choices up to equivalence, smooth sections are dense, every distribution belongs to some $H^{-r}$, and membership in every $H^ r$ implies smoothness. For the last assertions the local Fourier estimate uses \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ d}(1+|\xi |^2)^{\ell -s}\, \mathrm d\xi <\infty \quad \text{when }s>\ell +d/2.  \] This is the same coefficient argument in real dimension $d$; it does not use a complex structure or closedness of a metric form. We need only the compact inclusion $H^1\hookrightarrow L^2$. For a bounded $H^1$ sequence supported in a fixed coordinate compact set, its Fourier part on $|\xi |>R$ has $L^2$ norm at most $C/R$. The inverse transforms of the parts on $|\xi |\leq R$ have uniformly bounded values and first derivatives, hence have uniformly convergent subsequences on that compact set. A diagonal subsequence over integer $R$ is Cauchy in $L^2$. Apply this in the finitely many frames and sum the cutoffs to obtain the asserted compact inclusion. The arbitrary-vector divergence-form estimate in interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form applies to $P+1$: after integration by parts its principal coefficient matrix is $a^{ij}H\rho $, where $H$ is the positive bundle metric matrix and $\rho $ the positive volume density. This is uniformly positive on coefficient derivative arrays on compact subcharts. If $d$ is odd, one may reduce literally to that even-dimensional local estimate by adding a variable $t$: extend the coefficients, the weak solution and the right-hand side independently of $t$ and replace $P+1$ by $P+1-\partial _ t^2$ on a product subchart. Its principal form is again uniformly positive. Interior regularity there, followed by integration in $t$ on a smaller interval, gives the same bounds for the original coefficient derivatives. Consequently a weak $H^1$ solution of $(P+1)v=f\in H^ s$, $s\geq 0$, lies in $H^{s+2}$, with 4829F3D4B3BB 10.46.2 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq C_ s (\| f\| _{H^ s}+\| v\| _{H^1}). \end{equation} Use smaller subcharts and a finite partition for this global bound. The shifted inverse. Put $Q(v,w)=\langle Av,Aw\rangle +\langle B^*v,B^*w\rangle $. The scalar positive principal part gives Gårding's estimate BFB042AF3883 10.46.3 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{H^1}^2\leq C\bigl (Q(v,v)+\| v\| _{L^2}^2\bigr ). \end{equation} Here is the required form of the argument. For a section supported in one chart, one integration by parts in $\langle Pv,v\rangle $ gives the positive principal form $\int a^{ij}\langle \partial _ jv,\partial _ iv\rangle \rho $ and an error bounded by $C\| v\| _{L^2}\| v\| _{H^1}$. Its positive lower bound controls all first derivatives. Absorb the error by Young's inequality. Apply this to the finitely many cutoff sections; $A(\chi v)-\chi Av$ and $B^*(\chi v)-\chi B^*v$ are bounded zero-order terms, so summation gives ( 10.46.3 ). This is the scalar-principal-part Gårding mechanism, rather than a claim for arbitrary elliptic order. The form $Q_1=Q+\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle $ is a Hilbert inner product equivalent to the $H^1$ norm. By Hilbert projection and Riesz representation , for every $f\in H^{-1}$ there is a unique $v=Tf\in H^1$ satisfying \[  Q_1(v,w)=\langle f,w\rangle \quad (w\in H^1),\qquad \| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\| f\| _{H^{-1}}.  \] This is the distributional equation $(P+1)v=f$. By ( 10.46.2 ), $T:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ is bounded for $s\geq 0$. In particular $T$ preserves smooth sections, and $T(P+1)u=u$ for smooth $u$ by uniqueness of the weak solution. On $L^2$, \[  \langle Tf,g\rangle =Q_1(Tf,Tg)=\langle f,Tg\rangle , \qquad \langle Tf,f\rangle =Q_1(Tf,Tf)\geq 0.  \] It is therefore self-adjoint and positive, and is compact because it maps bounded $L^2$ sets to bounded $H^1$ sets. Extend $T$ to distributions by transposition. Its positive-order Sobolev bounds give $T:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ for $s\leq -2$ by duality; for $s=-1$ this extension agrees with the weak construction above. Transposing the two identities on smooth sections gives $(P+1)T=T(P+1)=I$ on distributions. If $Pu=0$ distributionally, then $u=Tu$; iteration raises its Sobolev order indefinitely, so $u$ is smooth. In particular $\mathcal H=\ker (I-T)$ on $L^2$. Its closed unit ball is compact, since $T$ is compact and is the identity there. An infinite orthonormal sequence would contradict compactness, so $\dim \mathcal H<\infty $. The needed Fredholm alternative. Set $S=I-T$. It preserves $\mathcal H^\perp $. There is $c>0$ with \[  \| Sv\| _{L^2}\geq c\| v\| _{L^2}\quad (v\in \mathcal H^\perp ).  \] Otherwise take $\| v_ j\| =1$, $v_ j\perp \mathcal H$ and $Sv_ j\to 0$. A subsequence of $Tv_ j$ converges, so $v_ j=Sv_ j+Tv_ j$ converges to a unit vector in both $\ker S=\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal H^\perp $, a contradiction. The inequality makes the range of $S$ on $\mathcal H^\perp $ closed. Since $S$ is self-adjoint, $(\operatorname {ran}S)^\perp =\ker S=\mathcal H$; hence that range is also dense in $\mathcal H^\perp $ and equals it. For $f\in L^2$ define \[  Gf=(S|_{\mathcal H^\perp })^{-1}T(I-\Pi )f.  \] This is well defined since self-adjointness of $T$ and $Th=h$ show that $T$ preserves $\mathcal H^\perp $. The equation for $w=Gf$ is $w=T(w+(I-\Pi )f)$. Thus $w\in H^2$ and $Pw=(I-\Pi )f$, with a bound from $L^2$ to $H^2$. Bootstrapping this equation using the bounds for $T$ gives $\| Gf\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq C_ s\| f\| _{H^ s}$ for $s\geq 0$; $\Pi $ is bounded on every such space, being a finite projection onto smooth sections. If $u$ is smooth, $u-\Pi u$ is the unique solution orthogonal to $\mathcal H$ of $Pw=Pu$, proving the other Green identity. Finally, integration by parts for the $H^2$ sections $Gf,Gg$ gives \[  \langle Gf,g\rangle =\langle Gf,PGg\rangle =\langle PGf,Gg\rangle =\langle f,Gg\rangle ,  \] after deleting their harmonic components. Thus $G$ is self-adjoint. No spectral decomposition theorem is needed. $\square$ Theorem 10.46.4 . BD1EEDFB2146 Let $D_ q:C^\infty (M,V_ q)\to C^\infty (M,V_{q+1})$ be a finite complex of first-order differential operators on a compact manifold, so $D_{q+1}D_ q=0$. Suppose that every \[  P_ q=D_{q-1}D_{q-1}^*+D_ q^*D_ q  \] has positive scalar principal part as in lemma 10.46.1 . Then its harmonic space $\mathcal H_ q$ is finite dimensional and smooth, and there is the orthogonal decomposition EC545E917BCF 10.46.5 \begin{equation}  C^\infty (M,V_ q)=\mathcal H_ q\  \oplus  D_{q-1}C^\infty (M,V_{q-1})\  \oplus  D_ q^*C^\infty (M,V_{q+1}). \end{equation} Both images are closed in the smooth topology. Every class in the smooth cohomology of $D$ has a unique harmonic representative. Proof. Apply the preceding lemma with $A=D_ q$ and $B=D_{q-1}$. The energy identity shows that $h$ is harmonic precisely when $D_ qh=D_{q-1}^*h=0$. The Green identity gives the decomposition \[  f=\Pi _ qf+D_{q-1}D_{q-1}^*G_ qf+D_ q^*D_ qG_ qf.  \] All terms are smooth. Harmonic sections are orthogonal to both images, and the latter are orthogonal because $\langle D_{q-1}a,D_ q^*b\rangle =\langle D_ qD_{q-1}a,b\rangle =0$. Thus the three summands form a direct orthogonal sum. Each component operator is continuous for the smooth topology by the Sobolev bounds on $G_ q$. It is a projection onto its displayed image by uniqueness of the decomposition, so that image is closed. For completeness, $P_{q+1}D_ q=D_ qP_ q$ on smooth sections, by $D_{q+1}D_ q=D_ qD_{q-1}=0$. The section $D_ qG_ qf$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal H_{q+1}$ and solves $P_{q+1}D_ qG_ qf=D_ qf$, since $D_ q\Pi _ qf=0$. Uniqueness of the orthogonal solution gives $D_ qG_ qf=G_{q+1}D_ qf$. If $D_ qf=0$, the last term of the decomposition vanishes and \[  f=\Pi _ qf+D_{q-1}(D_{q-1}^*G_ qf).  \] An exact harmonic section is orthogonal to itself and hence zero. This proves existence and uniqueness of the harmonic representative. $\square$ For a holomorphic bundle $E$ on a complex manifold, let $\mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)$ be its smooth forms, and set \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E) =\ker (\bar\partial _ E:\mathcal A^{p,q}\to \mathcal A^{p,q+1}) /\bar\partial _ E\mathcal A^{p,q-1}.  \] The canonical Dolbeault operator acts in holomorphic frames and has $\bar\partial _ E^2=0$. Negative or out-of-range bidegrees are zero. Theorem 10.46.6 . AEB699DDD0FF Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $n\geq 1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric, and let $E$ be a holomorphic Hermitian vector bundle. In every bidegree there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition \[  \mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H^{p,q}(X,E) \oplus \bar\partial _ E\mathcal A^{p,q-1}(X,E) \oplus \bar\partial _ E^*\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E),  \] where $\mathcal H^{p,q}$ is the kernel of $\square _ E=\bar\partial _ E\bar\partial _ E^* +\bar\partial _ E^*\bar\partial _ E$. These harmonic spaces are finite dimensional and represent the analytic Dolbeault cohomology uniquely. The images are closed in the smooth topology, and the Green operator has the nonnegative-integer Sobolev estimates above. Proof. Only the principal part needs checking. Let $g$ be the underlying Riemannian metric and freeze a holomorphic coordinate frame and the bundle metric at a point. For a real covector $\xi $, write $\epsilon _\xi $ for exterior multiplication by $\xi ^{0,1}$. With the Fourier convention $\partial _ j\mapsto \mathrm i\xi _ j$, the frozen symbols of $\bar\partial _ E$ and its formal adjoint are $\mathrm i\epsilon _\xi $ and $-\mathrm i\epsilon _\xi ^*$. The resulting anticommutator on exterior forms is $|\xi ^{0,1}|^2 I=\tfrac 12|\xi |_ g^2 I$. Indeed, in an orthonormal exterior basis, wedge followed by contraction and contraction followed by wedge add to the identity in a given unit direction; polarization gives the stated formula. Derivatives of the metric, frames and volume density contribute only lower-order terms. Thus the principal differential part of $\square _ E$ is $-\tfrac 12\sum g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$. Apply theorem 10.46.4 for fixed $p$. No Kähler condition or curvature sign is used. $\square$ Theorem 10.46.7 (Analytic Serre duality) . ECC57883D8C5 Under the preceding hypotheses, evaluation of $E\otimes E^*$ and integration give a perfect complex bilinear pairing \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)\times H^{n-p,n-q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb C, \qquad ([u],[v])\longmapsto \int _ Xu\wedge v.  \] Here $E^*$ is the holomorphic dual with its dual metric. Proof. Use the complex orientation, Riemannian volume and complex-linear extension of the real Hodge star, normalized by $\alpha \wedge *\overline\beta =\langle \alpha ,\beta \rangle \, \mathrm dV$. In a local smooth unitary frame $(e_\lambda )$ of $E$, define the conjugate-linear operator \[  \# _ E\Bigl (\sum _\lambda \alpha _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda \Bigr ) =\sum _\lambda *\overline{\alpha _\lambda }\otimes e_\lambda ^*.  \] It is independent of the unitary frame, and is characterized by $u\wedge \# _ Ev=\langle u,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$ for forms of equal bidegree. The orthogonal exterior basis of a Hermitian vector space shows that it maps $(p,q)$ to $(n-p,n-q)$, is an isometry, and satisfies 43FE5EF9F504 10.46.8 \begin{equation}  \# _{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k(2n-k)}u=(-1)^ ku, \qquad k=p+q. \end{equation} The double dual is identified naturally with $E$. The dual Dolbeault operator has the evaluation Leibniz rule \[  \bar\partial (u\wedge v)=\bar\partial _ Eu\wedge v +(-1)^ k u\wedge \bar\partial _{E^*}v.  \] For $a\in \mathcal A^{p,q-1}(X,E)$, Stokes applied to $a\wedge \# _ Eu$, of type $(n,n-1)$, gives \[  0=\int _ X\bar\partial _ Ea\wedge \# _ Eu +(-1)^{k-1}\int _ Xa\wedge \bar\partial _{E^*}\# _ Eu.  \] The first integral equals $\langle \bar\partial _ Ea,u\rangle =\langle a,\bar\partial _ E^*u\rangle $. Testing against all $a$ therefore proves 99D5D2E0FF70 10.46.9 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial _{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^ k\# _ E\bar\partial _ E^*u, \qquad \bar\partial _{E^*}^*\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k+1}\# _ E\bar\partial _ Eu. \end{equation} The second identity follows by applying the first to $E^*$ and $\# _ Eu$ and using ( 10.46.8 ); it contains $\bar\partial _ Eu$, without an adjoint on this right-hand side. The two identities have respective bidegrees $(n-p,n-q+1)$ and $(n-p,n-q-1)$. At endpoint bidegrees the zero-form conventions give the same identities. Applying the two identities successively yields \[  \square _{E^*}\# _ Eu=\# _ E\square _ Eu.  \] Thus $\# $ is a conjugate-linear bijection of the complementary harmonic spaces. The integral pairing descends to cohomology: if one closed factor is changed by a Dolbeault boundary, its integral against the other is zero by the Leibniz rule and Stokes. For any nonzero harmonic $u$, its complementary harmonic form $\# _ Eu$ satisfies \[  \int _ Xu\wedge \# _ Eu=\| u\| _{L^2}^2>0.  \] This proves nondegeneracy on the left. Apply the same argument to $E^*$ and exchange the factors, whose graded sign is nonzero, to obtain nondegeneracy on the right. Both groups are finite dimensional by theorem 10.46.6 , so the pairing is perfect. No sheaf-cohomology comparison is needed for this analytic statement. $\square$ Corollary 10.46.10 . 385FAE3FDC0C Let $M$ be a compact oriented Riemannian manifold, and let $E$ have a flat Hermitian connection $D_ E$. The smooth complex of $E$-valued forms has the orthogonal Hodge decomposition, finite-dimensional cohomology with unique harmonic representatives, and a perfect pairing \[  H^ k_{D_ E}(M,E)\times H^{d-k}_{D_{E^*}}(M,E^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb C, \qquad ([u],[v])\longmapsto \int _ Mu\wedge v, \quad d=\dim _{\mathbb R}M.  \] Proof. Flatness is the condition $D_ E^2=0$. Exterior multiplication by a real covector and its contraction have anticommutator $|\xi |_ g^2I$; the connection changes only the lower-order terms of the differential. Consequently $D_ ED_ E^*+D_ E^*D_ E$ has principal part $-\sum g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$, and theorem 10.46.4 applies. The dual connection is defined by the evaluation Leibniz rule; its curvature is the negative transpose of that of $D_ E$, so it is flat as well. Define $\# _ E$ by the same unitary-frame formula using the real $d$-dimensional Hodge star. Now $\# _{E^*}\# _ E=(-1)^{k(d-k)}$ on degree $k$. The evaluation rule for the dual connection and Stokes in degree $d-1$ give \[  D_{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^ k\# _ ED_ E^*u, \qquad D_{E^*}^*\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k+1}\# _ ED_ Eu.  \] For the second formula, applying the first to the dual and then squaring $\# $ gives exponent $k(d-k)+(d-k)+(d-k-1)(k+1)\equiv k+1\pmod2$. The Laplacians therefore intertwine, and the harmonic pairing is perfect by the same positive integral argument. $\square$ Remark 10.46.11 . 6FB01A5707A6 Disconnected compact manifolds cause no change: there are finitely many components and the statements apply to their finite direct sums. In dimension zero all spaces are finite-dimensional fiber sums, the differentials and Green operators are zero, and the pairings are ordinary fiber evaluation summed over the points, with orientation signs in the real case. Exterior differentiation on a metric bundle is used only with its specified connection; a Chern connection with nonzero curvature is not asserted to define a de Rham complex. The Dolbeault theorem uses only the canonical square-zero holomorphic-bundle operator.

title: Lemma 10.46.1
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Lemma 10.46.1 . 2EE58CB34CD0 Let $M$ be a compact real manifold of dimension $d\geq 1$, let $V$ be a smooth Hermitian vector bundle, and let \[  P=A^*A+BB^*  \] on $C^\infty (M,V)$, where $A$ and $B$ are first-order differential operators between smooth Hermitian bundles. Suppose that in every coordinate chart the second-order part of $P$ is $-\sum a^{ij}(x)\partial _ i\partial _ j$ on every coefficient, with $(a^{ij})$ real symmetric positive definite. Then: $(P+1)^{-1}=T$ exists on distributional sections. For every integer $s$, it is bounded from $H^ s$ to $H^{s+2}$. On $L^2$, $T$ is compact, self-adjoint and positive. The space $\mathcal H=\ker P$ consists of smooth sections and is finite dimensional. Let $\Pi $ be its orthogonal projection. There is a bounded self-adjoint operator $G$ on $L^2$, zero on $\mathcal H$, with \[  PGf=f-\Pi f,\qquad GPu=u-\Pi u\quad (u\in C^\infty ).  \] For every integer $s\geq 0$, $G:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ is bounded. In particular $G$ preserves smooth sections and is continuous for their smooth topology. Proof. Sobolev spaces and local regularity. Use a finite coordinate cover, bundle frames and smooth cutoffs to define the integer Sobolev norms by sums of coefficient derivative norms; $H^0=L^2$, and negative spaces are Hilbert duals for this pairing. The coordinate-change, convolution and duality proofs of Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding apply to these coefficient vectors: the changes of frame are smooth invertible matrices, and their derivatives and coordinate Jacobians are bounded on the compact supports. Thus the norms are independent of those choices up to equivalence, smooth sections are dense, every distribution belongs to some $H^{-r}$, and membership in every $H^ r$ implies smoothness. For the last assertions the local Fourier estimate uses \[  \int _{\mathbb R^ d}(1+|\xi |^2)^{\ell -s}\, \mathrm d\xi <\infty \quad \text{when }s>\ell +d/2.  \] This is the same coefficient argument in real dimension $d$; it does not use a complex structure or closedness of a metric form. We need only the compact inclusion $H^1\hookrightarrow L^2$. For a bounded $H^1$ sequence supported in a fixed coordinate compact set, its Fourier part on $|\xi |>R$ has $L^2$ norm at most $C/R$. The inverse transforms of the parts on $|\xi |\leq R$ have uniformly bounded values and first derivatives, hence have uniformly convergent subsequences on that compact set. A diagonal subsequence over integer $R$ is Cauchy in $L^2$. Apply this in the finitely many frames and sum the cutoffs to obtain the asserted compact inclusion. The arbitrary-vector divergence-form estimate in interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form applies to $P+1$: after integration by parts its principal coefficient matrix is $a^{ij}H\rho $, where $H$ is the positive bundle metric matrix and $\rho $ the positive volume density. This is uniformly positive on coefficient derivative arrays on compact subcharts. If $d$ is odd, one may reduce literally to that even-dimensional local estimate by adding a variable $t$: extend the coefficients, the weak solution and the right-hand side independently of $t$ and replace $P+1$ by $P+1-\partial _ t^2$ on a product subchart. Its principal form is again uniformly positive. Interior regularity there, followed by integration in $t$ on a smaller interval, gives the same bounds for the original coefficient derivatives. Consequently a weak $H^1$ solution of $(P+1)v=f\in H^ s$, $s\geq 0$, lies in $H^{s+2}$, with 4829F3D4B3BB 10.46.2 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq C_ s (\| f\| _{H^ s}+\| v\| _{H^1}). \end{equation} Use smaller subcharts and a finite partition for this global bound. The shifted inverse. Put $Q(v,w)=\langle Av,Aw\rangle +\langle B^*v,B^*w\rangle $. The scalar positive principal part gives Gårding's estimate BFB042AF3883 10.46.3 \begin{equation}  \| v\| _{H^1}^2\leq C\bigl (Q(v,v)+\| v\| _{L^2}^2\bigr ). \end{equation} Here is the required form of the argument. For a section supported in one chart, one integration by parts in $\langle Pv,v\rangle $ gives the positive principal form $\int a^{ij}\langle \partial _ jv,\partial _ iv\rangle \rho $ and an error bounded by $C\| v\| _{L^2}\| v\| _{H^1}$. Its positive lower bound controls all first derivatives. Absorb the error by Young's inequality. Apply this to the finitely many cutoff sections; $A(\chi v)-\chi Av$ and $B^*(\chi v)-\chi B^*v$ are bounded zero-order terms, so summation gives ( 10.46.3 ). This is the scalar-principal-part Gårding mechanism, rather than a claim for arbitrary elliptic order. The form $Q_1=Q+\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle $ is a Hilbert inner product equivalent to the $H^1$ norm. By Hilbert projection and Riesz representation , for every $f\in H^{-1}$ there is a unique $v=Tf\in H^1$ satisfying \[  Q_1(v,w)=\langle f,w\rangle \quad (w\in H^1),\qquad \| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\| f\| _{H^{-1}}.  \] This is the distributional equation $(P+1)v=f$. By ( 10.46.2 ), $T:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ is bounded for $s\geq 0$. In particular $T$ preserves smooth sections, and $T(P+1)u=u$ for smooth $u$ by uniqueness of the weak solution. On $L^2$, \[  \langle Tf,g\rangle =Q_1(Tf,Tg)=\langle f,Tg\rangle , \qquad \langle Tf,f\rangle =Q_1(Tf,Tf)\geq 0.  \] It is therefore self-adjoint and positive, and is compact because it maps bounded $L^2$ sets to bounded $H^1$ sets. Extend $T$ to distributions by transposition. Its positive-order Sobolev bounds give $T:H^ s\to H^{s+2}$ for $s\leq -2$ by duality; for $s=-1$ this extension agrees with the weak construction above. Transposing the two identities on smooth sections gives $(P+1)T=T(P+1)=I$ on distributions. If $Pu=0$ distributionally, then $u=Tu$; iteration raises its Sobolev order indefinitely, so $u$ is smooth. In particular $\mathcal H=\ker (I-T)$ on $L^2$. Its closed unit ball is compact, since $T$ is compact and is the identity there. An infinite orthonormal sequence would contradict compactness, so $\dim \mathcal H<\infty $. The needed Fredholm alternative. Set $S=I-T$. It preserves $\mathcal H^\perp $. There is $c>0$ with \[  \| Sv\| _{L^2}\geq c\| v\| _{L^2}\quad (v\in \mathcal H^\perp ).  \] Otherwise take $\| v_ j\| =1$, $v_ j\perp \mathcal H$ and $Sv_ j\to 0$. A subsequence of $Tv_ j$ converges, so $v_ j=Sv_ j+Tv_ j$ converges to a unit vector in both $\ker S=\mathcal H$ and $\mathcal H^\perp $, a contradiction. The inequality makes the range of $S$ on $\mathcal H^\perp $ closed. Since $S$ is self-adjoint, $(\operatorname {ran}S)^\perp =\ker S=\mathcal H$; hence that range is also dense in $\mathcal H^\perp $ and equals it. For $f\in L^2$ define \[  Gf=(S|_{\mathcal H^\perp })^{-1}T(I-\Pi )f.  \] This is well defined since self-adjointness of $T$ and $Th=h$ show that $T$ preserves $\mathcal H^\perp $. The equation for $w=Gf$ is $w=T(w+(I-\Pi )f)$. Thus $w\in H^2$ and $Pw=(I-\Pi )f$, with a bound from $L^2$ to $H^2$. Bootstrapping this equation using the bounds for $T$ gives $\| Gf\| _{H^{s+2}}\leq C_ s\| f\| _{H^ s}$ for $s\geq 0$; $\Pi $ is bounded on every such space, being a finite projection onto smooth sections. If $u$ is smooth, $u-\Pi u$ is the unique solution orthogonal to $\mathcal H$ of $Pw=Pu$, proving the other Green identity. Finally, integration by parts for the $H^2$ sections $Gf,Gg$ gives \[  \langle Gf,g\rangle =\langle Gf,PGg\rangle =\langle PGf,Gg\rangle =\langle f,Gg\rangle ,  \] after deleting their harmonic components. Thus $G$ is self-adjoint. No spectral decomposition theorem is needed. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.46.4
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Theorem 10.46.4 . BD1EEDFB2146 Let $D_ q:C^\infty (M,V_ q)\to C^\infty (M,V_{q+1})$ be a finite complex of first-order differential operators on a compact manifold, so $D_{q+1}D_ q=0$. Suppose that every \[  P_ q=D_{q-1}D_{q-1}^*+D_ q^*D_ q  \] has positive scalar principal part as in lemma 10.46.1 . Then its harmonic space $\mathcal H_ q$ is finite dimensional and smooth, and there is the orthogonal decomposition EC545E917BCF 10.46.5 \begin{equation}  C^\infty (M,V_ q)=\mathcal H_ q\  \oplus  D_{q-1}C^\infty (M,V_{q-1})\  \oplus  D_ q^*C^\infty (M,V_{q+1}). \end{equation} Both images are closed in the smooth topology. Every class in the smooth cohomology of $D$ has a unique harmonic representative. Proof. Apply the preceding lemma with $A=D_ q$ and $B=D_{q-1}$. The energy identity shows that $h$ is harmonic precisely when $D_ qh=D_{q-1}^*h=0$. The Green identity gives the decomposition \[  f=\Pi _ qf+D_{q-1}D_{q-1}^*G_ qf+D_ q^*D_ qG_ qf.  \] All terms are smooth. Harmonic sections are orthogonal to both images, and the latter are orthogonal because $\langle D_{q-1}a,D_ q^*b\rangle =\langle D_ qD_{q-1}a,b\rangle =0$. Thus the three summands form a direct orthogonal sum. Each component operator is continuous for the smooth topology by the Sobolev bounds on $G_ q$. It is a projection onto its displayed image by uniqueness of the decomposition, so that image is closed. For completeness, $P_{q+1}D_ q=D_ qP_ q$ on smooth sections, by $D_{q+1}D_ q=D_ qD_{q-1}=0$. The section $D_ qG_ qf$ is orthogonal to $\mathcal H_{q+1}$ and solves $P_{q+1}D_ qG_ qf=D_ qf$, since $D_ q\Pi _ qf=0$. Uniqueness of the orthogonal solution gives $D_ qG_ qf=G_{q+1}D_ qf$. If $D_ qf=0$, the last term of the decomposition vanishes and \[  f=\Pi _ qf+D_{q-1}(D_{q-1}^*G_ qf).  \] An exact harmonic section is orthogonal to itself and hence zero. This proves existence and uniqueness of the harmonic representative. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.46.6
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Theorem 10.46.6 . AEB699DDD0FF Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $n\geq 1$ with a smooth Hermitian metric, and let $E$ be a holomorphic Hermitian vector bundle. In every bidegree there is an orthogonal smooth decomposition \[  \mathcal A^{p,q}(X,E)=\mathcal H^{p,q}(X,E) \oplus \bar\partial _ E\mathcal A^{p,q-1}(X,E) \oplus \bar\partial _ E^*\mathcal A^{p,q+1}(X,E),  \] where $\mathcal H^{p,q}$ is the kernel of $\square _ E=\bar\partial _ E\bar\partial _ E^* +\bar\partial _ E^*\bar\partial _ E$. These harmonic spaces are finite dimensional and represent the analytic Dolbeault cohomology uniquely. The images are closed in the smooth topology, and the Green operator has the nonnegative-integer Sobolev estimates above. Proof. Only the principal part needs checking. Let $g$ be the underlying Riemannian metric and freeze a holomorphic coordinate frame and the bundle metric at a point. For a real covector $\xi $, write $\epsilon _\xi $ for exterior multiplication by $\xi ^{0,1}$. With the Fourier convention $\partial _ j\mapsto \mathrm i\xi _ j$, the frozen symbols of $\bar\partial _ E$ and its formal adjoint are $\mathrm i\epsilon _\xi $ and $-\mathrm i\epsilon _\xi ^*$. The resulting anticommutator on exterior forms is $|\xi ^{0,1}|^2 I=\tfrac 12|\xi |_ g^2 I$. Indeed, in an orthonormal exterior basis, wedge followed by contraction and contraction followed by wedge add to the identity in a given unit direction; polarization gives the stated formula. Derivatives of the metric, frames and volume density contribute only lower-order terms. Thus the principal differential part of $\square _ E$ is $-\tfrac 12\sum g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$. Apply theorem 10.46.4 for fixed $p$. No Kähler condition or curvature sign is used. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.46.7 (Analytic Serre duality)
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Theorem 10.46.7 (Analytic Serre duality) . ECC57883D8C5 Under the preceding hypotheses, evaluation of $E\otimes E^*$ and integration give a perfect complex bilinear pairing \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)\times H^{n-p,n-q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb C, \qquad ([u],[v])\longmapsto \int _ Xu\wedge v.  \] Here $E^*$ is the holomorphic dual with its dual metric. Proof. Use the complex orientation, Riemannian volume and complex-linear extension of the real Hodge star, normalized by $\alpha \wedge *\overline\beta =\langle \alpha ,\beta \rangle \, \mathrm dV$. In a local smooth unitary frame $(e_\lambda )$ of $E$, define the conjugate-linear operator \[  \# _ E\Bigl (\sum _\lambda \alpha _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda \Bigr ) =\sum _\lambda *\overline{\alpha _\lambda }\otimes e_\lambda ^*.  \] It is independent of the unitary frame, and is characterized by $u\wedge \# _ Ev=\langle u,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV$ for forms of equal bidegree. The orthogonal exterior basis of a Hermitian vector space shows that it maps $(p,q)$ to $(n-p,n-q)$, is an isometry, and satisfies 43FE5EF9F504 10.46.8 \begin{equation}  \# _{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k(2n-k)}u=(-1)^ ku, \qquad k=p+q. \end{equation} The double dual is identified naturally with $E$. The dual Dolbeault operator has the evaluation Leibniz rule \[  \bar\partial (u\wedge v)=\bar\partial _ Eu\wedge v +(-1)^ k u\wedge \bar\partial _{E^*}v.  \] For $a\in \mathcal A^{p,q-1}(X,E)$, Stokes applied to $a\wedge \# _ Eu$, of type $(n,n-1)$, gives \[  0=\int _ X\bar\partial _ Ea\wedge \# _ Eu +(-1)^{k-1}\int _ Xa\wedge \bar\partial _{E^*}\# _ Eu.  \] The first integral equals $\langle \bar\partial _ Ea,u\rangle =\langle a,\bar\partial _ E^*u\rangle $. Testing against all $a$ therefore proves 99D5D2E0FF70 10.46.9 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial _{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^ k\# _ E\bar\partial _ E^*u, \qquad \bar\partial _{E^*}^*\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k+1}\# _ E\bar\partial _ Eu. \end{equation} The second identity follows by applying the first to $E^*$ and $\# _ Eu$ and using ( 10.46.8 ); it contains $\bar\partial _ Eu$, without an adjoint on this right-hand side. The two identities have respective bidegrees $(n-p,n-q+1)$ and $(n-p,n-q-1)$. At endpoint bidegrees the zero-form conventions give the same identities. Applying the two identities successively yields \[  \square _{E^*}\# _ Eu=\# _ E\square _ Eu.  \] Thus $\# $ is a conjugate-linear bijection of the complementary harmonic spaces. The integral pairing descends to cohomology: if one closed factor is changed by a Dolbeault boundary, its integral against the other is zero by the Leibniz rule and Stokes. For any nonzero harmonic $u$, its complementary harmonic form $\# _ Eu$ satisfies \[  \int _ Xu\wedge \# _ Eu=\| u\| _{L^2}^2>0.  \] This proves nondegeneracy on the left. Apply the same argument to $E^*$ and exchange the factors, whose graded sign is nonzero, to obtain nondegeneracy on the right. Both groups are finite dimensional by theorem 10.46.6 , so the pairing is perfect. No sheaf-cohomology comparison is needed for this analytic statement. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.46.10
search_title: Compact flat bundle de rham hodge
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Corollary 10.46.10 . 385FAE3FDC0C Let $M$ be a compact oriented Riemannian manifold, and let $E$ have a flat Hermitian connection $D_ E$. The smooth complex of $E$-valued forms has the orthogonal Hodge decomposition, finite-dimensional cohomology with unique harmonic representatives, and a perfect pairing \[  H^ k_{D_ E}(M,E)\times H^{d-k}_{D_{E^*}}(M,E^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb C, \qquad ([u],[v])\longmapsto \int _ Mu\wedge v, \quad d=\dim _{\mathbb R}M.  \] Proof. Flatness is the condition $D_ E^2=0$. Exterior multiplication by a real covector and its contraction have anticommutator $|\xi |_ g^2I$; the connection changes only the lower-order terms of the differential. Consequently $D_ ED_ E^*+D_ E^*D_ E$ has principal part $-\sum g^{ij}\partial _ i\partial _ j I$, and theorem 10.46.4 applies. The dual connection is defined by the evaluation Leibniz rule; its curvature is the negative transpose of that of $D_ E$, so it is flat as well. Define $\# _ E$ by the same unitary-frame formula using the real $d$-dimensional Hodge star. Now $\# _{E^*}\# _ E=(-1)^{k(d-k)}$ on degree $k$. The evaluation rule for the dual connection and Stokes in degree $d-1$ give \[  D_{E^*}\# _ Eu=(-1)^ k\# _ ED_ E^*u, \qquad D_{E^*}^*\# _ Eu=(-1)^{k+1}\# _ ED_ Eu.  \] For the second formula, applying the first to the dual and then squaring $\# $ gives exponent $k(d-k)+(d-k)+(d-k-1)(k+1)\equiv k+1\pmod2$. The Laplacians therefore intertwine, and the harmonic pairing is perfect by the same positive integral argument. $\square$

title: Remark 10.46.11
section: 10.46 Compact Hodge theory and analytic duality
text: Remark 10.46.11 . 6FB01A5707A6 Disconnected compact manifolds cause no change: there are finitely many components and the statements apply to their finite direct sums. In dimension zero all spaces are finite-dimensional fiber sums, the differentials and Green operators are zero, and the pairings are ordinary fiber evaluation summed over the points, with orientation signs in the real case. Exterior differentiation on a metric bundle is used only with its specified connection; a Chern connection with nonzero curvature is not asserted to define a de Rham complex. The Dolbeault theorem uses only the canonical square-zero holomorphic-bundle operator.

title: 5.60 Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
search_title: Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
section: 5.60 Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
text: We use $d^ c=\frac{i}{4\pi }(\bar\partial -\partial )$, so that $dd^ c=\frac{i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial $, and in coordinates write $\beta =\frac{i}{2}\sum _ j dz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j$. A current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on an $n$-dimensional manifold has bidegree $(n-p,n-p)$ and acts on forms of bidegree $(p,p)$. Its local trace measure is $T\wedge \beta ^ p$. By coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents , this measure controls all coefficient variations on compact coordinate sets. Definition 5.60.1 . 319D3EF2599F A subset $E$ of a complex manifold $X$ is locally complete pluripolar if every point has a neighborhood $U$ and a locally integrable plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $U$ such that $E\cap U=\{ u=-\infty \} $. In the following extension statements $E$ is also required to be closed. In particular, such a set contains no component of a coordinate neighborhood. A proper analytic subset with no component of $X$ is locally complete pluripolar: use local holomorphic equations and plurisubharmonicity of logarithmic holomorphic norms . Merely being contained in a pole set is not the hypothesis in this definition. Lemma 5.60.2 . 899DA22762FD Let $E$ be closed and locally complete pluripolar in $X$. Every point has a coordinate neighborhood $\Omega $ on which there are a function $v\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$, smooth and finite on $\Omega \setminus E$, with $v=-\infty $ exactly on $E\cap \Omega $; smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ k$ on $\Omega $ with $0\leq v_ k\leq 1$, increasing to $1$ locally uniformly on $\Omega \setminus E$, each identically zero on a neighborhood of $E\cap \Omega $. Proof. The assertion is immediate if $E$ is empty near the point: take $v=0$ and $v_ k=1$. Otherwise work in nested bounded coordinate balls $\Omega \Subset \Omega _0\Subset \Omega _1$ with $E\cap \Omega _1=\{ u=-\infty \} $, where $u$ is plurisubharmonic. Shrinking the balls and subtracting a constant gives $u\leq 0$ on $\Omega _1$. Choose a smooth convex nondecreasing function $\chi $ on $[0,1]$, zero on $[0,1/2]$, with $\chi (1)=1$. Put \[  a_ k=\chi (e^{u/k}),\qquad e^{-\infty }=0.  \] These are plurisubharmonic, $0\leq a_ k\leq 1$, and increase to $1$ off $E$. For completeness, convex nondecreasing composition preserves plurisubharmonicity here: apply the smooth Hessian criterion to a decreasing local smooth regularization of $u$, and then the decreasing limit theorem. The function $t\mapsto \chi (e^{t/k})$ is convex and nondecreasing; on the bounded ranges needed for regularization it can be extended with these properties. The limit is finite everywhere after composition and hence is not identically $-\infty $. Moreover $a_ k=0$ on the open neighborhood $\omega _ k=\{ u<-k\log 2\} $ of $E\cap \Omega _1$. Choose a positive convolution radius $\varepsilon _ k$ so small that $b_ k=a_ k*\rho _{\varepsilon _ k}$ is defined on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ and is zero near $E\cap \overline\Omega $. This is possible because $E\cap \overline\Omega $ is compact and contained in the open set $\omega _ k\cap \Omega _0$; when this compact set is empty there is no vanishing constraint. Radial regularization gives smooth plurisubharmonic functions with $a_ k\leq b_ k\leq 1$ by the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . Consequently \[  w_ k=\max _{1\leq j\leq k}b_ j  \] is continuous plurisubharmonic, increases to $1$ off $E$, and is zero near $E\cap \Omega $. Dini's theorem gives uniform convergence on each compact subset of $\Omega \setminus E$. Take an increasing compact exhaustion $K_ s$ of $\Omega \setminus E$ whose interiors cover it. Select strictly increasing indices $k_ s$ such that $0\leq 1-w_{k_ s}\leq 2^{-s}$ on $K_ s$. The series \[  w=|z|^2+\sum _{s=1}^{\infty }(w_{k_ s}-1)  \] converges locally uniformly off $E$, and is $-\infty $ on $E$. Its partial sums decrease and are plurisubharmonic; their limit is finite off $E$, so decreasing nets of plurisubharmonic functions shows that $w$ is plurisubharmonic. Applying the same theorem after subtracting $|z|^2$ shows that its complex Hessian is bounded below by the identity. It is continuous off $E$ and bounded above by $\sup _\Omega |z|^2$. It also tends to $-\infty $ at $E$: for any $N$, the first $N$ terms $w_{k_ s}$ vanish on a common neighborhood of $E\cap \Omega $, so there $w\leq \sup _\Omega |z|^2-N$. Apply relative Richberg smoothing on the manifold $\Omega \setminus E$, with error function $1$. It gives a smooth plurisubharmonic $v$ there with $w\leq v\leq w+1$. Extend $v$ by $-\infty $ on $E$. This extension is plurisubharmonic without an additional removability premise: for each positive integer $N$, the function equal to $\max \{ v,-N\} $ off $E$ and to $-N$ on $E$ is locally constant near $E$ and is plurisubharmonic elsewhere by maximum and boundary gluing of plurisubharmonic functions . These functions decrease to the extended $v$, which is finite off $E$; apply the decreasing limit theorem. Subtract a constant so that $v\leq 0$. Then \[  v_ k=\chi (e^{v/k})  \] has all the stated properties. It is smooth across $E$ because it is identically zero near $E$; it is plurisubharmonic by the same composition argument, increases pointwise to $1$ off $E$, and Dini's theorem gives the stated compact uniform convergence. In dimension zero local integrability makes the local pole set empty, so the initial empty-set case applies. $\square$ Theorem 5.60.3 (Skoda–El Mir extension) . BB0A0DD22A5E Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $E\subset X$ be closed and locally complete pluripolar, and let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $X\setminus E$, $0\leq p\leq n$. Suppose its mass is locally finite near $E$. Then extending every coefficient measure by zero on $E$ defines a closed positive current $\widetilde T$ on $X$. Its coefficient measures give $E$ zero mass. Proof. The mass hypothesis and compactness give $\int _{K\setminus E}T\wedge \beta ^ p<\infty $ on every compact coordinate set $K$. Trace domination therefore makes the coefficient extensions locally finite. Smooth changes of coordinates commute with restriction of coefficient measures to $X\setminus E$, so the local extensions glue. Positivity follows either from the coefficient description or by integrating nonnegative strongly positive test forms off $E$. It remains to prove closedness locally. If $p=0$, the current has real degree $2n$, so its exterior derivative vanishes by degree. First let $p=1$ and denote the current by $\Theta $. On a neighborhood $\Omega $ supplied by lemma 5.60.2 , write $\mu =\widetilde\Theta \wedge \beta $ and use its functions $v_ k$. For a smooth compactly supported real one-form $\eta $, put $K=\operatorname {supp}\eta $ and choose a nonnegative $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ equal to $1$ near $K$; write $L=\operatorname {supp}\psi $. On $\Omega \setminus E$ the measure $dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta $ is positive. Since $0\leq v_ k\leq 1$ and $dd^ cv_ k\geq 0$, 45 \begin{align}  2\int \psi \, dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta & \leq \int \psi \, dd^ c(v_ k^2)\wedge \Theta \notag \\ & =\int v_ k^2\, dd^ c\psi \wedge \Theta \leq C_\psi \mu (L). \tag{5.60.4} \end{align} All integrals are over $\Omega \setminus E$. The integration by parts uses only the closedness of $\Theta $ there: for each fixed $k$, $\psi v_ k^2$ and its derivatives have compact support away from $E$. One may insert a compact cutoff in $\Omega \setminus E$ equal to one near that support; its derivative terms vanish because $v_ k$ is zero near $E$. The last inequality is coefficient domination, and its constant depends on $\psi $, not on $k$. Choose smooth $\theta :[0,1]\to [0,1]$ equal to zero on $[0,1/3]$ and to one on $[2/3,1]$. The smooth-case Cauchy–Schwarz calculation underlying the bounded-potential current chain rule gives FE0A285FF079 5.60.5 \begin{equation}  \left|\int \theta '(v_ k)\eta \wedge dv_ k\wedge \Theta \right|^2 \leq C_\eta \left(\int \psi \, dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta \right) \left(\int _ K|\theta '(v_ k)|^2\, d\mu \right). \end{equation} Here the calculation is used on $\Omega \setminus E$ and does not assume that $\widetilde\Theta $ is closed. More explicitly, the coefficient matrix $H$ with $\frac{i}{2\pi }dz_ k\wedge d\bar z_ j\wedge \Theta =h_{jk}\mu $ is positive semidefinite with trace $1/\pi $. If $e$ is the vector of coefficients of the $(1,0)$ part of $\eta $, the two densities in the canonical calculation are $|H^{1/2}\partial v_ k|^2$ and $4\pi \operatorname {Im}\langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial v_ k\rangle $. The scalar Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $|H^{1/2}e|^2\leq |e|^2/\pi $ prove ( 5.60.5 ). Thus no cutoff depending on $k$ enters its constant. The first factor in ( 5.60.5 ) is uniformly bounded by ( 5.60.4 ). The second tends to zero by dominated convergence: $v_ k\to 1$ off $E$, $\theta '(1)=0$, $\mu (K)<\infty $, and $\mu (E)=0$. Now $S_ k=\theta (v_ k)\widetilde\Theta $ is zero near $E$, so \[  dS_ k=\theta '(v_ k)\, dv_ k\wedge \Theta  \] extended by zero. The estimate shows that $dS_ k\to 0$ on real one-form tests, hence on all one-form tests by complex linearity. Dominated convergence against every coefficient variation gives $S_ k\to \widetilde\Theta $. Weak continuity of differentiation proves $d\widetilde\Theta =0$. For $p\geq 1$, choose a real basis $\gamma _ s$ of constant $(p-1,p-1)$-forms consisting of decomposable strongly positive forms; such a basis exists by strong and weak positivity of differential forms . The currents $T\wedge \gamma _ s$ are closed positive of bidimension $(1,1)$ and have locally finite mass by coefficient domination. Zero extension commutes with multiplication by $\gamma _ s$, so the case just proved gives $d\widetilde T\wedge \gamma _ s=0$ for every $s$. Every constant form of bidegree $(p-1,p)$ is a sum of a constant $(p-1,p-1)$-form wedged with a $(0,1)$-form; the analogous statement holds for $(p,p-1)$. Expand these forms in the basis $\gamma _ s$ and allow arbitrary smooth compactly supported coefficients. All tests of $\partial \widetilde T$ and $\bar\partial \widetilde T$ therefore vanish. This includes $p=n$ and proves the theorem. $\square$ Corollary 5.60.6 . 53F93547F96E If $T$ is a closed positive current on $X$ and $E$ is closed and locally complete pluripolar, both coefficient restrictions $\mathbf1_ E T$ and $\mathbf1_{X\setminus E}T$ are closed positive currents. Proof. The restriction of $T$ to $X\setminus E$ has locally finite mass near $E$. Its zero extension is $\mathbf1_{X\setminus E}T$, closed by theorem 5.60.3 . title: Definition 5.60.1
section: 5.60 Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
text: Definition 5.60.1 . 319D3EF2599F A subset $E$ of a complex manifold $X$ is locally complete pluripolar if every point has a neighborhood $U$ and a locally integrable plurisubharmonic function $u$ on $U$ such that $E\cap U=\{ u=-\infty \} $. In the following extension statements $E$ is also required to be closed.

title: Lemma 5.60.2
section: 5.60 Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
text: Lemma 5.60.2 . 899DA22762FD Let $E$ be closed and locally complete pluripolar in $X$. Every point has a coordinate neighborhood $\Omega $ on which there are a function $v\in \operatorname {PSH}(\Omega )$, smooth and finite on $\Omega \setminus E$, with $v=-\infty $ exactly on $E\cap \Omega $; smooth plurisubharmonic functions $v_ k$ on $\Omega $ with $0\leq v_ k\leq 1$, increasing to $1$ locally uniformly on $\Omega \setminus E$, each identically zero on a neighborhood of $E\cap \Omega $. Proof. The assertion is immediate if $E$ is empty near the point: take $v=0$ and $v_ k=1$. Otherwise work in nested bounded coordinate balls $\Omega \Subset \Omega _0\Subset \Omega _1$ with $E\cap \Omega _1=\{ u=-\infty \} $, where $u$ is plurisubharmonic. Shrinking the balls and subtracting a constant gives $u\leq 0$ on $\Omega _1$. Choose a smooth convex nondecreasing function $\chi $ on $[0,1]$, zero on $[0,1/2]$, with $\chi (1)=1$. Put \[  a_ k=\chi (e^{u/k}),\qquad e^{-\infty }=0.  \] These are plurisubharmonic, $0\leq a_ k\leq 1$, and increase to $1$ off $E$. For completeness, convex nondecreasing composition preserves plurisubharmonicity here: apply the smooth Hessian criterion to a decreasing local smooth regularization of $u$, and then the decreasing limit theorem. The function $t\mapsto \chi (e^{t/k})$ is convex and nondecreasing; on the bounded ranges needed for regularization it can be extended with these properties. The limit is finite everywhere after composition and hence is not identically $-\infty $. Moreover $a_ k=0$ on the open neighborhood $\omega _ k=\{ u<-k\log 2\} $ of $E\cap \Omega _1$. Choose a positive convolution radius $\varepsilon _ k$ so small that $b_ k=a_ k*\rho _{\varepsilon _ k}$ is defined on a neighborhood of $\overline\Omega $ and is zero near $E\cap \overline\Omega $. This is possible because $E\cap \overline\Omega $ is compact and contained in the open set $\omega _ k\cap \Omega _0$; when this compact set is empty there is no vanishing constraint. Radial regularization gives smooth plurisubharmonic functions with $a_ k\leq b_ k\leq 1$ by the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . Consequently \[  w_ k=\max _{1\leq j\leq k}b_ j  \] is continuous plurisubharmonic, increases to $1$ off $E$, and is zero near $E\cap \Omega $. Dini's theorem gives uniform convergence on each compact subset of $\Omega \setminus E$. Take an increasing compact exhaustion $K_ s$ of $\Omega \setminus E$ whose interiors cover it. Select strictly increasing indices $k_ s$ such that $0\leq 1-w_{k_ s}\leq 2^{-s}$ on $K_ s$. The series \[  w=|z|^2+\sum _{s=1}^{\infty }(w_{k_ s}-1)  \] converges locally uniformly off $E$, and is $-\infty $ on $E$. Its partial sums decrease and are plurisubharmonic; their limit is finite off $E$, so decreasing nets of plurisubharmonic functions shows that $w$ is plurisubharmonic. Applying the same theorem after subtracting $|z|^2$ shows that its complex Hessian is bounded below by the identity. It is continuous off $E$ and bounded above by $\sup _\Omega |z|^2$. It also tends to $-\infty $ at $E$: for any $N$, the first $N$ terms $w_{k_ s}$ vanish on a common neighborhood of $E\cap \Omega $, so there $w\leq \sup _\Omega |z|^2-N$. Apply relative Richberg smoothing on the manifold $\Omega \setminus E$, with error function $1$. It gives a smooth plurisubharmonic $v$ there with $w\leq v\leq w+1$. Extend $v$ by $-\infty $ on $E$. This extension is plurisubharmonic without an additional removability premise: for each positive integer $N$, the function equal to $\max \{ v,-N\} $ off $E$ and to $-N$ on $E$ is locally constant near $E$ and is plurisubharmonic elsewhere by maximum and boundary gluing of plurisubharmonic functions . These functions decrease to the extended $v$, which is finite off $E$; apply the decreasing limit theorem. Subtract a constant so that $v\leq 0$. Then \[  v_ k=\chi (e^{v/k})  \] has all the stated properties. It is smooth across $E$ because it is identically zero near $E$; it is plurisubharmonic by the same composition argument, increases pointwise to $1$ off $E$, and Dini's theorem gives the stated compact uniform convergence. In dimension zero local integrability makes the local pole set empty, so the initial empty-set case applies. $\square$

title: Theorem 5.60.3 (Skoda–El Mir extension)
section: 5.60 Extension of positive currents across complete pluripolar sets
text: Theorem 5.60.3 (Skoda–El Mir extension) . BB0A0DD22A5E Let $X$ be a complex manifold of dimension $n$, let $E\subset X$ be closed and locally complete pluripolar, and let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $X\setminus E$, $0\leq p\leq n$. Suppose its mass is locally finite near $E$. Then extending every coefficient measure by zero on $E$ defines a closed positive current $\widetilde T$ on $X$. Its coefficient measures give $E$ zero mass. Proof. The mass hypothesis and compactness give $\int _{K\setminus E}T\wedge \beta ^ p<\infty $ on every compact coordinate set $K$. Trace domination therefore makes the coefficient extensions locally finite. Smooth changes of coordinates commute with restriction of coefficient measures to $X\setminus E$, so the local extensions glue. Positivity follows either from the coefficient description or by integrating nonnegative strongly positive test forms off $E$. It remains to prove closedness locally. If $p=0$, the current has real degree $2n$, so its exterior derivative vanishes by degree. First let $p=1$ and denote the current by $\Theta $. On a neighborhood $\Omega $ supplied by lemma 5.60.2 , write $\mu =\widetilde\Theta \wedge \beta $ and use its functions $v_ k$. For a smooth compactly supported real one-form $\eta $, put $K=\operatorname {supp}\eta $ and choose a nonnegative $\psi \in C_ c^\infty (\Omega )$ equal to $1$ near $K$; write $L=\operatorname {supp}\psi $. On $\Omega \setminus E$ the measure $dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta $ is positive. Since $0\leq v_ k\leq 1$ and $dd^ cv_ k\geq 0$, 45 \begin{align}  2\int \psi \, dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta & \leq \int \psi \, dd^ c(v_ k^2)\wedge \Theta \notag \\ & =\int v_ k^2\, dd^ c\psi \wedge \Theta \leq C_\psi \mu (L). \tag{5.60.4} \end{align} All integrals are over $\Omega \setminus E$. The integration by parts uses only the closedness of $\Theta $ there: for each fixed $k$, $\psi v_ k^2$ and its derivatives have compact support away from $E$. One may insert a compact cutoff in $\Omega \setminus E$ equal to one near that support; its derivative terms vanish because $v_ k$ is zero near $E$. The last inequality is coefficient domination, and its constant depends on $\psi $, not on $k$. Choose smooth $\theta :[0,1]\to [0,1]$ equal to zero on $[0,1/3]$ and to one on $[2/3,1]$. The smooth-case Cauchy–Schwarz calculation underlying the bounded-potential current chain rule gives FE0A285FF079 5.60.5 \begin{equation}  \left|\int \theta '(v_ k)\eta \wedge dv_ k\wedge \Theta \right|^2 \leq C_\eta \left(\int \psi \, dv_ k\wedge d^ cv_ k\wedge \Theta \right) \left(\int _ K|\theta '(v_ k)|^2\, d\mu \right). \end{equation} Here the calculation is used on $\Omega \setminus E$ and does not assume that $\widetilde\Theta $ is closed. More explicitly, the coefficient matrix $H$ with $\frac{i}{2\pi }dz_ k\wedge d\bar z_ j\wedge \Theta =h_{jk}\mu $ is positive semidefinite with trace $1/\pi $. If $e$ is the vector of coefficients of the $(1,0)$ part of $\eta $, the two densities in the canonical calculation are $|H^{1/2}\partial v_ k|^2$ and $4\pi \operatorname {Im}\langle H^{1/2}e,H^{1/2}\partial v_ k\rangle $. The scalar Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and $|H^{1/2}e|^2\leq |e|^2/\pi $ prove ( 5.60.5 ). Thus no cutoff depending on $k$ enters its constant. The first factor in ( 5.60.5 ) is uniformly bounded by ( 5.60.4 ). The second tends to zero by dominated convergence: $v_ k\to 1$ off $E$, $\theta '(1)=0$, $\mu (K)<\infty $, and $\mu (E)=0$. Now $S_ k=\theta (v_ k)\widetilde\Theta $ is zero near $E$, so \[  dS_ k=\theta '(v_ k)\, dv_ k\wedge \Theta  \] extended by zero. The estimate shows that $dS_ k\to 0$ on real one-form tests, hence on all one-form tests by complex linearity. Dominated convergence against every coefficient variation gives $S_ k\to \widetilde\Theta $. Weak continuity of differentiation proves $d\widetilde\Theta =0$. For $p\geq 1$, choose a real basis $\gamma _ s$ of constant $(p-1,p-1)$-forms consisting of decomposable strongly positive forms; such a basis exists by strong and weak positivity of differential forms . The currents $T\wedge \gamma _ s$ are closed positive of bidimension $(1,1)$ and have locally finite mass by coefficient domination. Zero extension commutes with multiplication by $\gamma _ s$, so the case just proved gives $d\widetilde T\wedge \gamma _ s=0$ for every $s$. Every constant form of bidegree $(p-1,p)$ is a sum of a constant $(p-1,p-1)$-form wedged with a $(0,1)$-form; the analogous statement holds for $(p,p-1)$. Expand these forms in the basis $\gamma _ s$ and allow arbitrary smooth compactly supported coefficients. All tests of $\partial \widetilde T$ and $\bar\partial \widetilde T$ therefore vanish. This includes $p=n$ and proves the theorem. $\square$

title: 5.61 Integration over analytic sets
section: 5.61 Integration over analytic sets
text: Lemma 5.61.1 . 8C07385777E6 Let $A$ be a closed pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset of a complex manifold $X$. Integration over its regular locus, with the complex orientation, has locally finite mass near its singular locus. Proof. If $p=0$, the analytic set is locally a finite set of points, and the assertion is immediate. Let $p\geq 1$ and work near $x\in A$ in coordinates in $\mathbb C^ n$. There are finitely many local branches, all of dimension $p$. It suffices to bound the volume on each branch: the regular locus of their union is contained in the union of their regular loci, so its positive trace mass is bounded by their sum. Shrink to representatives of these finitely many branches. For one branch choose a real basis of constant $(p,p)$-forms made of decomposable strongly positive forms, using strong and weak positivity of differential forms : \[  \gamma _ s=i\ell _{s,1}\wedge \overline{\ell _{s,1}}\wedge \cdots \wedge i\ell _{s,p}\wedge \overline{\ell _{s,p}},  \] where the $\ell _{s,j}$ are linearly independent complex linear one-forms. Complete their linear coordinate functions to a coordinate system. By finite local parametrization of analytic germs , after arbitrarily small perturbations of these coordinates the first $p$ coordinate functions $w_1,\ldots ,w_ p$ define a proper finite projection of the branch in a polydisc $P_ s=\Delta '_ s\times \Delta ''_ s$ onto $\Delta '_ s$. The perturbations can be so small that the resulting forms $\gamma _ s$ remain a basis. The polydiscs for different $s$ need not agree; there is a common neighborhood $V$ of $x$ contained in all of them. Off the analytic discriminant $S_ s=\{ \delta _ s=0\} $ the projection is a $q_ s$-sheeted holomorphic covering, whose total space is dense in the branch. The remaining part of its regular locus is a proper analytic subset of that manifold. It has zero smooth volume by measure-zero holomorphic zero sets ; this assertion is local on the regular locus, and no component can be contained in the discriminant because the covering locus is dense. Change of variables on the covering sheets, or a partition of unity in the base, gives \[  \int _{A_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap P_ s}\gamma _ s =q_ s\int _{\Delta '_ s\setminus S_ s} i\, dw_1\wedge d\bar w_1\wedge \cdots \wedge i\, dw_ p\wedge d\bar w_ p<\infty .  \] Here $A$ in this calculation denotes the chosen branch. Express the fixed trace form as $\beta ^ p=\sum _ s c_ s\gamma _ s$. On the regular locus every $\gamma _ s$ is nonnegative, whence \[  \int _{A_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap V}\beta ^ p \leq \sum _ s|c_ s|\int _{A_{\mathrm{reg}}\cap P_ s}\gamma _ s<\infty .  \] Adding the finitely many branch bounds proves local trace finiteness. Coefficient domination proves local finiteness of the full current mass. The argument works for $p=n$, when a full-dimensional branch has projection degree one. $\square$ Theorem 5.61.2 . B7EB7069B315 For every closed pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset $A$ of a complex manifold $X$, the formula \[  \langle [A],\alpha \rangle =\int _{A_{\mathrm{reg}}}\alpha , \qquad \alpha \in C_ c^\infty (X,\Lambda ^{p,p}),  \] defines a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$. Its coefficient measures give $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$ zero mass. Proof. The singular locus is closed analytic and has dimension at most $p-1$ by analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Thus $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is a closed complex submanifold of $X\setminus A_{\mathrm{sing}}$; its integration current there is closed and positive by the integration current of a closed complex submanifold . The preceding lemma gives locally finite mass near the singular locus. Locally that locus is the exact pole set of $\log \sum _ j|g_ j|^2$ for holomorphic equations $g_ j$, by plurisubharmonicity of logarithmic holomorphic norms ; it is a proper analytic subset, so the potential is locally integrable. Apply theorem 5.60.3 with $E=A_{\mathrm{sing}}$. The zero extension is precisely the displayed integral and has the asserted zero mass. When $p=0$, $A$ is locally finite and regular, and the resulting top-degree counting current is closed by degree. The empty analytic set gives the zero current. $\square$

title: 2.12 Open maps, compact perturbations and finite cohomology
search_title: Open maps, compact perturbations and finite cohomology
section: 2.12 Open maps, compact perturbations and finite cohomology
text: All locally convex spaces here are Hausdorff, over $\mathbb C$. A Fréchet space is complete and metrizable. A continuous linear map $h:E\to F$ is compact if $\overline{h(U)}$ is compact for some neighborhood $U$ of zero. This is compactness on one neighborhood, not merely compactness on bounded sets. We use the dominated-linear-extension argument already proved in the proof of Lamari's positivity criterion . It extends a real linear functional dominated by a finite sublinear function on any real vector space; no geometric hypothesis enters that extension argument. Applied to continuous seminorms it implies that continuous linear functionals separate points of a Hausdorff locally convex space. For complex functionals, extend the real part and use $\ell (x)=a(x)-i a(ix)$. A finite-dimensional subspace $L$ is closed and has a continuous linear projection: on its Euclidean unit sphere finitely many continuous seminorms have a maximum bounded below by a positive number. This maximum controls every coordinate functional of $L$; dominated extension gives continuous coordinate functionals on the whole space and hence the projection. The same seminorm bound shows that $L$ has its usual finite-dimensional topology and is closed. These facts also show that a closed finite-codimensional subspace has a finite-dimensional continuous complement, by passing to its Hausdorff finite-dimensional quotient. Proposition 2.12.1 . 71B16A3EF23E A quotient of a Fréchet space by a closed linear subspace is Fréchet. Every continuous surjective linear map between Fréchet spaces is open. A linear map between Fréchet spaces whose graph is closed is continuous. Proof. Let $(p_ j)$ be increasing defining seminorms on $E$ and let $N\subset E$ be closed. The seminorms $\bar p_ j([x])=\inf _{n\in N}p_ j(x+n)$ define its Hausdorff quotient topology. Indeed their open balls are exactly the images of the corresponding open seminorm balls, and $\bar p_ j([x])=0$ for all $j$ implies $x\in \overline N=N$. For a Cauchy sequence in the quotient choose a subsequence whose successive differences have representatives $v_ j$ satisfying $p_ j(v_ j)<2^{-j}$. Starting from one representative and adding these $v_ j$ gives a Cauchy sequence in $E$, because for every fixed $r$ its tail has $p_ r$-size at most a geometric series. Completeness gives a quotient limit for the subsequence and then for the original Cauchy sequence. This proves the assertion. Let $A:E\to F$ be continuous and surjective, and let $U$ be a zero neighborhood in $E$. Choose a closed convex balanced neighborhood $B\subset U$. Choose convex balanced neighborhoods $V_ j\subset 2^{-j-1}B$, $j\geq 0$, so small that $d_ E(v,0)<2^{-j}$ for $v\in V_ j$, using a complete translation-invariant defining metric. Since $F=\bigcup _{n\geq 1}A(nV_ j)$, the Baire property makes $\overline{A(V_ j)}$ a neighborhood of zero. Here Baire is the complete-metric nested-ball argument already supplied in proposition 2.10.3 ; convexity and balance move a nonempty interior to zero. Choose open neighborhoods $W_ j\subset \overline{A(V_ j)}$ with $d_ F(w,0)<2^{-j}$ for $w\in W_ j$. For $y_0\in W_0$, successively choose $x_ j\in V_ j$ so that $y_{j+1}=y_ j-Ax_ j\in W_{j+1}$. Density in the indicated closure permits each choice. The series $\sum _ jx_ j$ is Cauchy for the complete metric, and every partial sum belongs to $B$ by convexity and the sum of the coefficients $2^{-j-1}$. Its limit $x$ belongs to $B\subset U$. The residuals tend to zero, so $Ax=y_0$. Thus $W_0\subset A(U)$, proving openness. Finally, a closed graph is a closed Fréchet subspace of $E\times F$; its projection to $E$ is a continuous linear bijection, whose inverse is continuous by openness. Compose with the other projection. $\square$ For a continuous linear $g:E\to F$, call $g$ a closed embedding if it is a topological isomorphism onto a closed subspace. Call it a quasi-monomorphism if $\ker g$ is finite dimensional and the induced map $E/\ker g\to F$ is a closed embedding. Call it a quasi-epimorphism if it is open onto a closed finite-codimensional image. A quasi-isomorphism has both properties. Corollary 2.12.2 . 181D2DF97074 For continuous linear maps between Fréchet spaces, a closed embedding is the same as an injection with closed image, and a quasi-monomorphism is the same as a map with finite-dimensional kernel and closed image. A finite-codimensional image is automatically closed, and the map onto it is open. Thus quasi-epimorphism is equivalent to finite codimension of the image. Proof. For closed image, apply the preceding proposition to $E/\ker g\to g(E)$. If the image is only known to have finite algebraic codimension, choose a finite-dimensional algebraic complement $S\subset F$. The map \[  (E/\ker g)\oplus S\longrightarrow F,\qquad ([x],s)\longmapsto gx+s  \] is a continuous linear bijection of Fréchet spaces. It is a homeomorphism by the proposition; hence its image of the closed subspace $(E/\ker g)\oplus \{ 0\} $ is closed. Openness onto this image follows in the same way. This assertion concerns images of continuous Fréchet maps, not arbitrary algebraic subspaces of finite codimension. $\square$ Theorem 2.12.3 . E27FE1F7DE85 Let $g,h:E\to F$ be continuous linear maps, with $h$ compact. If $g$ is a quasi-monomorphism, then $g+h$ is a quasi-monomorphism. This assertion holds for Hausdorff locally convex spaces. If $E,F$ are Fréchet and $g$ is a quasi-epimorphism, then $g+h$ is a quasi-epimorphism. Consequently compact perturbations preserve quasi-isomorphisms between Fréchet spaces. Proof. For the first assertion remove $\ker g$ by its continuous finite-dimensional complement. On that complement identify $E$ with the closed subspace $g(E)\subset F$, so $g(x)=x$. Choose a convex balanced open $U\subset E$ with $K=\overline{h(U)}$ compact, and a convex balanced open $V\subset F$ such that $V\cap E\subset U$. Continuous functionals separate every nonzero point. A finite subcover of the compact set $K\setminus \tfrac 14V$ by sets where one such functional is nonzero produces a closed finite-codimensional $F_0\subset F$ with $K\cap F_0\subset \tfrac 14V$. Replace $E$ by the closed finite-codimensional subspace $E_0=h^{-1}(F_0)$ and $U$ by $U_0=U\cap E_0$. Then $K_0=\overline{h(U_0)}$ is compact and $K_0\subset \tfrac 14V$, while $V\cap E_0\subset U_0$. Let $q$ be the Minkowski seminorm of $V$, and put $f=g+h$. For $x\in E_0$ and $t>q(x)$ we have $x\in tU_0$, so $h(x)\in tK_0$ and $q(hx)\leq t/4$. Letting $t\downarrow q(x)$ gives A0294A1D9E73 2.12.4 \begin{equation}  q(hx)\leq \tfrac 14q(x),\qquad q(x)\leq \tfrac 43q(fx). \end{equation} For any prescribed neighborhood $\Omega $ in $E_0$, choose a balanced neighborhood $W$ in $F$ with $(W+W)\cap E_0\subset \Omega $. Compactness makes $K_0$ bounded, so choose $t>0$ with $tK_0\subset W$. If $fx\in W$ and $q(fx)<3t/4$, then $x\in tU_0$ and $hx\in W$; thus $x=fx-hx\in \Omega $. This proves inverse continuity at zero and also injectivity, by intersecting all $\Omega $. We must also prove closedness of the image. Along it, $x_ i=fx_ i-hx_ i\to y-z$. Since $E_0$ is closed in $F$, $x=y-z$ belongs to $E_0$. Its induced topology and continuity of $h$ imply $hx=z$, hence $fx=y$. A finite-dimensional extension of a closed subspace is closed, as seen in the Hausdorff quotient. The kernel of $f$ injects into the finite-dimensional quotient by the closed subspace on which $f$ is injective, so it is finite dimensional. To check the quotient topology as well, choose vectors mapping to a basis of $f(E)/f(E_0)$. The resulting finite-dimensional complement to $f(E_0)$ is continuous, and its basis lifts, together with the continuous inverse on $f(E_0)$, give a continuous map into $E/\ker f$ inverse to the induced map. This proves the full quasi-monomorphism assertion. For the second assertion first quotient $F$ by a finite-dimensional complement to $g(E)$. The compact image of $K$ is the closure of the image of $h(U)$ and is contained in $\tfrac 14$ of the image of $V$. Finite-dimensional quotients remain Fréchet. Renaming the induced data, we have \[  g(E)=F,\qquad K\subset \tfrac 12V.  \] Let $y_0\in V$. If $y_ n$ is a residual, choose $x_ n$ with $gx_ n=y_ n$, and put $y_{n+1}=y_ n-fx_ n=-hx_ n$. The partial sums are thus Cauchy in every defining neighborhood, and completeness gives $x=\sum _ nx_ n\in E$. The residuals tend to zero, since they lie in scalar multiples of the bounded compact set $K$. Hence $fx=y_0$. The image contains $V$ and is all of $F$ by linearity. D8E2BCEBC75D Let $(E^\bullet ,d)$ and $(F^\bullet ,\delta )$ be complexes of Fréchet spaces with continuous differentials, and let $\rho ^\bullet :E^\bullet \to F^\bullet $ be a continuous chain map. Cycle spaces are closed Fréchet subspaces. text: Proposition 2.12.1 . 71B16A3EF23E A quotient of a Fréchet space by a closed linear subspace is Fréchet. Every continuous surjective linear map between Fréchet spaces is open. A linear map between Fréchet spaces whose graph is closed is continuous. Proof. Let $(p_ j)$ be increasing defining seminorms on $E$ and let $N\subset E$ be closed. The seminorms $\bar p_ j([x])=\inf _{n\in N}p_ j(x+n)$ define its Hausdorff quotient topology. Indeed their open balls are exactly the images of the corresponding open seminorm balls, and $\bar p_ j([x])=0$ for all $j$ implies $x\in \overline N=N$. For a Cauchy sequence in the quotient choose a subsequence whose successive differences have representatives $v_ j$ satisfying $p_ j(v_ j)<2^{-j}$. Starting from one representative and adding these $v_ j$ gives a Cauchy sequence in $E$, because for every fixed $r$ its tail has $p_ r$-size at most a geometric series. Completeness gives a quotient limit for the subsequence and then for the original Cauchy sequence. This proves the assertion. Let $A:E\to F$ be continuous and surjective, and let $U$ be a zero neighborhood in $E$. Choose a closed convex balanced neighborhood $B\subset U$. Choose convex balanced neighborhoods $V_ j\subset 2^{-j-1}B$, $j\geq 0$, so small that $d_ E(v,0)<2^{-j}$ for $v\in V_ j$, using a complete translation-invariant defining metric. Since $F=\bigcup _{n\geq 1}A(nV_ j)$, the Baire property makes $\overline{A(V_ j)}$ a neighborhood of zero. Here Baire is the complete-metric nested-ball argument already supplied in proposition 2.10.3 ; convexity and balance move a nonempty interior to zero. Choose open neighborhoods $W_ j\subset \overline{A(V_ j)}$ with $d_ F(w,0)<2^{-j}$ for $w\in W_ j$. For $y_0\in W_0$, successively choose $x_ j\in V_ j$ so that $y_{j+1}=y_ j-Ax_ j\in W_{j+1}$. Density in the indicated closure permits each choice. The series $\sum _ jx_ j$ is Cauchy for the complete metric, and every partial sum belongs to $B$ by convexity and the sum of the coefficients $2^{-j-1}$. Its limit $x$ belongs to $B\subset U$. The residuals tend to zero, so $Ax=y_0$. Thus $W_0\subset A(U)$, proving openness. Finally, a closed graph is a closed Fréchet subspace of $E\times F$; its projection to $E$ is a continuous linear bijection, whose inverse is continuous by openness. Compose with the other projection. $\square$

text: Corollary 2.12.2 . 181D2DF97074 For continuous linear maps between Fréchet spaces, a closed embedding is the same as an injection with closed image, and a quasi-monomorphism is the same as a map with finite-dimensional kernel and closed image. A finite-codimensional image is automatically closed, and the map onto it is open. Thus quasi-epimorphism is equivalent to finite codimension of the image. Proof. For closed image, apply the preceding proposition to $E/\ker g\to g(E)$. If the image is only known to have finite algebraic codimension, choose a finite-dimensional algebraic complement $S\subset F$. The map \[  (E/\ker g)\oplus S\longrightarrow F,\qquad ([x],s)\longmapsto gx+s  \] is a continuous linear bijection of Fréchet spaces. It is a homeomorphism by the proposition; hence its image of the closed subspace $(E/\ker g)\oplus \{ 0\} $ is closed. Openness onto this image follows in the same way. This assertion concerns images of continuous Fréchet maps, not arbitrary algebraic subspaces of finite codimension. $\square$

Manifolds in this section are Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. Completeness of a Riemannian metric means completeness of its length distance on each connected component. We use the metrics, unscaled curvature and formal adjoints of section 10.33 ; in particular $\mathrm dV_\omega =\omega ^ n/n!$ and $\mathrm i\Theta (L)=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial \phi $ for a line frame of squared norm $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$. Write $\mathcal H(f)=\mathrm i\partial  ar\partial f$. Lemma 6.26.1 . 87F36288392E A complete smooth Riemannian manifold admits smooth compactly supported functions $0\leq \chi _ R\leq 1$, $R\geq 1$, eventually equal to one near every compact set, with 917B532008FD 6.26.2  egin{equation}  |\mathrm d\chi _ R|_ g\leq C/R \end{equation} for one constant $C$ independent of $R$. Proof. On a connected component let $r_0$ be distance from a fixed point. It is $1$-Lipschitz, and its closed sublevels are compact by lemma 9.28.1 . In the disconnected case enumerate the components and add their indices to the respective distance functions. There are at most countably many components, and the resulting $r_0\geq 0$ is still proper and is $1$-Lipschitz within each component. Choose a countable locally finite cover by nested coordinate balls $U_ i\Subset W_ i$ and a smooth nonnegative partition of unity $	heta _ i$ with compact support in $U_ i$, as in manifold cutoffs, partitions and compact-support Stokes . Make the balls small enough that the matrix of $g$ on $W_ i$ lies between half and twice one fixed positive matrix $g_ i$. Take $W_ i$ to be a coordinate Euclidean ball. Straight segments show that $r_0$ in these coordinates is Lipschitz with constant $\sqrt2$ for the norm $g_ i$. Let $A_ i=\sup |\mathrm d	heta _ i|_ g<\infty $ and choose $0<e_ i\leq \min \{ 1,2^{-i}/(1+A_ i)\} $. Convolve $r_0$ on $W_ i$ with a nonnegative smooth kernel of sufficiently small radius to obtain a smooth $r_ i$ near $\overline U_ i$ such that \[  |r_ i-r_0|\leq e_ i,\qquad |\mathrm dr_ i|_ g\leq 2.  \] For clarity, the gradient estimate does not require differentiating the distance function: the difference of two convolution values along a coordinate vector $v$ is bounded by $\sqrt2|v|_{g_ i}$ times the increment. Taking its derivative and comparing the dual norms of $g_ i$ and $g$ gives the factor2. The approximation error follows from the same Lipschitz estimate times the convolution radius. Set $r=\sum _ i	heta _ i r_ i$. This is smooth and $|r-r_0|\leq 1$. At each point its differential satisfies \[  \mathrm dr=\sum _ i	heta _ i\mathrm dr_ i+ \sum _ i(r_ i-r_0)\mathrm d	heta _ i, \qquad |\mathrm dr|_ g\leq 2+\sum _ i e_ iA_ i\leq 3.  \] Here $\sum _ i\mathrm d	heta _ i=0$ cancels the unbounded value $r_0$ after differentiating the smooth summands; $r_0$ itself has not been differentiated. The function $r$ is proper and $r\geq -1$. Choose a smooth $\eta :\mathbb R	o [0,1]$ equal to one on $(-\infty ,1]$ and zero on $[2,\infty )$, and put $\chi _ R=\eta ((r+2)/R)$. These functions have the stated support and eventual equality properties, and $|\mathrm d\chi _ R|_ g\leq 3\| \eta '\| _\infty /R$. $\square$ Corollary 6.26.3 . Compactly supported smooth forms are dense in each of their graph domains and in their joint graph domain. Proof. Convergence in the global $L^2$ norms implies local distributional convergence, proving closedness. On that support use a finite frame cover and partition of unity. The complete smooth-matrix first-order commutator proof in graph-norm density by cutoffs and mollification applies to the joint vector of operators $(D'',\delta '')$ in any bidegree and rank. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$, $1\leq q\leq n$, and suppose $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]\geq 0$ in bidegree $(p,q)$. If $g\in L^2_{p,q}(X,E)$ satisfies $D''g=0$ distributionally and \[  M=\int _ X|g|_{B^{-1}}^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty ,  \] there is $u\in L^2_{p,q-1}(X,E)$ with FDA2D94CB453 6.26.6  egin{equation}  D''u=g,\qquad \| u\| ^2\leq M. \end{equation} Its unique solution of smallest norm satisfies $\delta ''u=0$ distributionally and is smooth in $X$ when $g$ is smooth. Proof. For compactly supported smooth $v$, the Kähler identity theorem 10.33.2 gives \[  \int _ X\langle Bv,vangle \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2.  \] Set $T=D''$ from degree $(p,q-1)$ to $(p,q)$ and $S=D''$ to degree $(p,q+1)$ with maximal domains. For $q=n$ the latter space is zero and $S=0$. The preceding lemma supplies closedness, dense domains, $T^*=\delta ''$ and joint graph density; $ST=0$ follows from $(D'')^2=0$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[  |\langle g,vangle |^2 \leq M igl (\| T^*v\| ^2+\| Sv\| ^2 igr ).  \] Since $g$ is globally $L^2$, both sides are continuous in the joint graph norm, so this holds on the full domains. Apply Hilbert-complex solvability from the dual energy estimate to obtain ( 6.26.6 ). Its minimum-norm solution is orthogonal to the closed kernel of $T$. The preceding maximal $D''$ operator has range in that kernel; the adjoint definition gives $\delta ''u=0$. When $q=1$ this equation is automatic. We justify the claimed local regularity. In local coordinates and smooth frames the principal symbol of $\Delta ''$ is $|\xi |_\omega ^2\operatorname {Id}/2$, as explicitly computed in equation 10.33.13 . For a smooth compactly supported coefficient vector $w$ in a fixed relatively compact coordinate ball, the same integration-by-parts calculation gives 8AF50F0EE8AA 6.26.7  egin{equation}  \| w\| _{H^1}^2\leq C igl ( \| D''w\| ^2+\| \delta ''w\| ^2+\| w\| ^2 igr ). \end{equation} Indeed its principal form is $	frac 12\int g^{ij}G_{AB}\partial _ jw_ A \overline{\partial _ iw_ B}ho $, where $G$ is the positive coefficient metric and $ho $ the volume density. It is uniformly positive on the entire matrix of first derivatives on this compact set. The remaining terms have absolute value at most $C\| w\| \| w\| _{H^1}$ and are absorbed by Young's inequality. This is a local use of the proved calculation; compactness of $X$ is not assumed. Now $D''u=g$ and $\delta ''u=0$ are locally $L^2$. Localize by a compactly supported chart cutoff and use the same matrix commutator approximation as above. The smooth approximants are bounded in $H^1$ by ( 6.26.7 ). Weak compactness of their derivatives identifies the weak limit as the distributional derivatives of the localized $u$, so $u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The equation $\Delta ''u=\delta ''g$ has smooth right-hand side. Its divergence-form principal coefficients are $	frac 12g^{ij}G_{AB}ho $ and its remaining coefficients are smooth first- and zeroth-order matrices.
