No global Laplacian self-adjointness or harmonic decomposition is used. $\square$ In degree $(n,q)$, proposition 10.33.6 describes $B$ by the Nakano form on the tensors $(v_{jS})_ j$. Thus a lower curvature bound $\varepsilon (x)$ on tensors of rank at most $\min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$ gives $B\geq q\varepsilon (x)$. For a line bundle with semipositive curvature eigenvalues $\lambda _1\leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ n$, the inverse energy is bounded by $|g|^2/(\lambda _1+\cdots +\lambda _ q)$. These statements retain the global $L^2$ hypothesis of the theorem; no noncomplete-metric estimate has been inferred from them. Lemma 6.26.8 . 4BD00ED77586 If a Kähler manifold $(X,\omega _0)$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion $ho \geq 0$, then $\omega _0+\mathcal H(\mathrm e^ho )$ is complete Kähler. If $ho $ is strictly PSH, then $\omega =\mathcal H(\mathrm e^ho )$ itself is complete Kähler, without a prior Kähler metric. Proof. The chain rule gives \[  \mathcal H(\mathrm e^ho )=\mathrm e^ho (\mathcal H(ho )+\mathrm i\partial ho \wedge  ar\partial ho ).  \] Each stated form is closed and positive definite. In its induced real metric, $|\mathrm dho |^2\leq 2\mathrm e^{-ho }\leq 2$, by the displayed rank-one lower bound and the relation $|\mathrm dho |^2=2|\partial ho |^2$. Consequently a Cauchy sequence for the length distance has bounded $ho $-values and lies in one compact sublevel. It has a convergent subsequence in the manifold topology, which is the length topology by the local metric comparison proved before lemma 9.28.1 . Cauchyness makes the whole sequence converge. This proves completeness on each component. $\square$ We will use a simple fast-weight construction on a manifold with a smooth nonnegative strict-PSH exhaustion $ho $. Put $ eta =\mathcal H(ho )>0$. If $A$ is any continuous positive $(1,1)$-form, $C\geq 0$ is continuous, and $F\geq 0$ is locally integrable, then there is a smooth convex increasing $\chi $ such that B9439CD62E8F 6.26.9  egin{equation}  \mathcal H(\chi \circ ho )\geq C eta +A, \qquad \int _ X F\mathrm e^{-\chi (ho )}\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty . \end{equation} Here $\omega $ may be any fixed smooth Hermitian form. To check the construction explicitly, bound $C eta +A$ relative to $ eta $ on each compact sublevel and let $a_ k=\int _{\{ k\leq ho \leq k+1\} }F\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty $. Choose nondecreasing $M_ k\geq 1$ larger than the relative-form bound on $\{ ho \leq k+2\} $ and than $\log (2^{k+1}(1+a_{k+1}))$. For a smooth nondecreasing step $\zeta $ equal to zero on $(-\infty ,0]$ and one on $[1,\infty )$ set \[  b(t)=M_0+\sum _{k\geq 0}(M_{k+1}-M_ k)\zeta (t-k), \qquad \chi (t)=\int _0^ t b(s)\, \mathrm ds.  \] These sums are locally finite. On $[k,k+1]$, $\chi '\geq M_ k$; the chain rule proves the form bound. For $k\geq 1$, $\chi (k)\geq M_{k-1}\geq \log (2^ k(1+a_ k))$, so the integral on that band is at most $2^{-k}$. The initial compact band has finite integral. This proves ( 6.26.9 ). Corollary 6.26.10 . E5505B695336 Let $X$ have a smooth PSH exhaustion, and let $(E,h)$ be an $m$-positive holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r$, with $m\geq 1$. For $1\leq q\leq n$ and $m\geq \min (n-q+1,r)$, every distributionally closed locally $L^2$ $E$-valued $(n,q)$-form has a locally $L^2$ primitive. For smooth data a smooth primitive exists; in particular the smooth analytic Dolbeault group $H^{n,q}_{ ar\partial }(X,E)$ is zero. Proof. Positivity on rank-one tensors implies $\omega _0=\mathrm i\operatorname {Tr}\Theta (E)>0$: evaluate on a nonzero base vector and sum its strictly positive pairings over an orthonormal fiber basis. This is a closed form, since the Chern matrix formula gives $\operatorname {Tr}\Theta (E)= ar\partial \partial \log \det H$ in a holomorphic frame. Thus $X$ is Kähler. Shift its PSH exhaustion $ho $ to be nonnegative and use lemma 6.26.8 to make a complete Kähler form $\widehat\omega $. By proposition 10.33.6 , the curvature operator $B$ on $(n,q)$ is positive definite. Its least eigenvalue $\lambda (x)>0$ is continuous. The bandwise step construction just used for ( 6.26.9 ), without its strict-Hessian domination requirement, chooses a smooth convex increasing $\chi $ such that \[  \int _ X(1+\lambda ^{-1})|g|^2 \mathrm e^{-\chi (ho )}\, \mathrm dV_{\widehat\omega } <\infty .  \] Only the finite integrals on compact exhaustion bands are needed. For $h_\chi =h\mathrm e^{-\chi (ho )}$ the curvature increases by the semipositive scalar form $\mathcal H(\chi (ho ))$; in holomorphic top degree its operator therefore increases as well. The displayed integral bounds both the ordinary $L^2$ norm and inverse-curvature energy for $(E,h_\chi ,\widehat\omega )$. Apply theorem 6.26.5 . Its solution is locally $L^2$, and is smooth for smooth data by the proved minimum-norm regularity. This establishes the analytic quotient conclusion without a sheaf-cohomology identification. $\square$

text: Lemma 6.26.1 . 87F36288392E A complete smooth Riemannian manifold admits smooth compactly supported functions $0\leq \chi _ R\leq 1$, $R\geq 1$, eventually equal to one near every compact set, with 917B532008FD 6.26.2 \begin{equation}  |\mathrm d\chi _ R|_ g\leq C/R \end{equation} for one constant $C$ independent of $R$. Proof. On a connected component let $r_0$ be distance from a fixed point. It is $1$-Lipschitz, and its closed sublevels are compact by lemma 9.28.1 . In the disconnected case enumerate the components and add their indices to the respective distance functions. There are at most countably many components, and the resulting $r_0\geq 0$ is still proper and is $1$-Lipschitz within each component. Choose a countable locally finite cover by nested coordinate balls $U_ i\Subset W_ i$ and a smooth nonnegative partition of unity $\theta _ i$ with compact support in $U_ i$, as in manifold cutoffs, partitions and compact-support Stokes . Make the balls small enough that the matrix of $g$ on $W_ i$ lies between half and twice one fixed positive matrix $g_ i$. Take $W_ i$ to be a coordinate Euclidean ball. Straight segments show that $r_0$ in these coordinates is Lipschitz with constant $\sqrt2$ for the norm $g_ i$. Let $A_ i=\sup |\mathrm d\theta _ i|_ g<\infty $ and choose $0<e_ i\leq \min \{ 1,2^{-i}/(1+A_ i)\} $. Convolve $r_0$ on $W_ i$ with a nonnegative smooth kernel of sufficiently small radius to obtain a smooth $r_ i$ near $\overline U_ i$ such that \[  |r_ i-r_0|\leq e_ i,\qquad |\mathrm dr_ i|_ g\leq 2.  \] For clarity, the gradient estimate does not require differentiating the distance function: the difference of two convolution values along a coordinate vector $v$ is bounded by $\sqrt2|v|_{g_ i}$ times the increment. Taking its derivative and comparing the dual norms of $g_ i$ and $g$ gives the factor2. The approximation error follows from the same Lipschitz estimate times the convolution radius. Set $r=\sum _ i\theta _ i r_ i$. This is smooth and $|r-r_0|\leq 1$. At each point its differential satisfies \[  \mathrm dr=\sum _ i\theta _ i\mathrm dr_ i+ \sum _ i(r_ i-r_0)\mathrm d\theta _ i, \qquad |\mathrm dr|_ g\leq 2+\sum _ i e_ iA_ i\leq 3.  \] Here $\sum _ i\mathrm d\theta _ i=0$ cancels the unbounded value $r_0$ after differentiating the smooth summands; $r_0$ itself has not been differentiated. The function $r$ is proper and $r\geq -1$. Choose a smooth $\eta :\mathbb R\to [0,1]$ equal to one on $(-\infty ,1]$ and zero on $[2,\infty )$, and put $\chi _ R=\eta ((r+2)/R)$. These functions have the stated support and eventual equality properties, and $|\mathrm d\chi _ R|_ g\leq 3\| \eta '\| _\infty /R$. $\square$

text: Lemma 6.26.4 . 3A311E8B52D5 Let $(X,\omega )$ be complete Hermitian and $(E,h)$ a smooth Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. In every bidegree the maximal distributional operator $D''$ is closed and densely defined. Its Hilbert adjoint is exactly the maximal distributional formal adjoint $\delta ''$. Compactly supported smooth forms are dense in each of their graph domains and in their joint graph domain. Proof. Convergence in the global $L^2$ norms implies local distributional convergence, proving closedness. Chart cutoffs and coefficient mollification give density of compactly supported smooth forms in $L^2$, hence dense operator domains. Use lemma 6.26.1 . The product rules are \[  D''(\chi _ Rv)=\chi _ RD''v+\bar\partial \chi _ R\wedge v, \qquad \delta ''(\chi _ Rv)=\chi _ R\delta ''v- (\bar\partial \chi _ R\wedge )^*v.  \] Wedge and contraction by a covector have operator norm at most its norm, in every degree and bundle rank, by a unitary-coframe calculation. Thus each error is bounded in $L^2$ by $C\| v\| /R$. Dominated convergence reduces each maximal graph approximation, simultaneously when required, to compact support. On that support use a finite frame cover and partition of unity. The complete smooth-matrix first-order commutator proof in graph-norm density by cutoffs and mollification applies to the joint vector of operators $(D'',\delta '')$ in any bidegree and rank. It gives compactly supported smooth approximation in the joint graph norm; using either operator alone gives its individual assertion. If $v$ is in the Hilbert adjoint domain, testing on compact supports identifies its adjoint distribution as $\delta ''v$. Conversely, if $v,\delta ''v$ are $L^2$, approximate any $u$ in the maximal $D''$ domain in its graph norm by compactly supported smooth forms. The distributional identity $\langle D''u_ j,v\rangle = \langle u_ j,\delta ''v\rangle $ passes to the limit. This is precisely the defining Hilbert adjoint identity. This proves domain equality by graph approximation. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.26.5
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.26 Complete Kähler estimates and discrete interpolation
text: Theorem 6.26.5 . 84AFC5445E6E Let $(X,\omega )$ be complete Kähler, of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $(E,h)$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$, $1\leq q\leq n$, and suppose $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]\geq 0$ in bidegree $(p,q)$. If $g\in L^2_{p,q}(X,E)$ satisfies $D''g=0$ distributionally and \[  M=\int _ X|g|_{B^{-1}}^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty ,  \] there is $u\in L^2_{p,q-1}(X,E)$ with FDA2D94CB453 6.26.6 \begin{equation}  D''u=g,\qquad \| u\| ^2\leq M. \end{equation} Its unique solution of smallest norm satisfies $\delta ''u=0$ distributionally and is smooth in $X$ when $g$ is smooth. Proof. For compactly supported smooth $v$, the Kähler identity theorem 10.33.2 gives \[  \int _ X\langle Bv,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2.  \] Set $T=D''$ from degree $(p,q-1)$ to $(p,q)$ and $S=D''$ to degree $(p,q+1)$ with maximal domains. For $q=n$ the latter space is zero and $S=0$. The preceding lemma supplies closedness, dense domains, $T^*=\delta ''$ and joint graph density; $ST=0$ follows from $(D'')^2=0$. Cauchy–Schwarz gives \[  |\langle g,v\rangle |^2 \leq M\bigl (\| T^*v\| ^2+\| Sv\| ^2\bigr ).  \] Since $g$ is globally $L^2$, both sides are continuous in the joint graph norm, so this holds on the full domains. Apply Hilbert-complex solvability from the dual energy estimate to obtain ( 6.26.6 ). Its minimum-norm solution is orthogonal to the closed kernel of $T$. The preceding maximal $D''$ operator has range in that kernel; the adjoint definition gives $\delta ''u=0$. When $q=1$ this equation is automatic. We justify the claimed local regularity. In local coordinates and smooth frames the principal symbol of $\Delta ''$ is $|\xi |_\omega ^2\operatorname {Id}/2$, as explicitly computed in equation 10.33.13 . For a smooth compactly supported coefficient vector $w$ in a fixed relatively compact coordinate ball, the same integration-by-parts calculation gives 8AF50F0EE8AA 6.26.7 \begin{equation}  \| w\| _{H^1}^2\leq C\bigl ( \| D''w\| ^2+\| \delta ''w\| ^2+\| w\| ^2\bigr ). \end{equation} Indeed its principal form is $\tfrac 12\int g^{ij}G_{AB}\partial _ jw_ A \overline{\partial _ iw_ B}\rho $, where $G$ is the positive coefficient metric and $\rho $ the volume density. It is uniformly positive on the entire matrix of first derivatives on this compact set. The remaining terms have absolute value at most $C\| w\| \| w\| _{H^1}$ and are absorbed by Young's inequality. This is a local use of the proved calculation; compactness of $X$ is not assumed. Now $D''u=g$ and $\delta ''u=0$ are locally $L^2$. Localize by a compactly supported chart cutoff and use the same matrix commutator approximation as above. The smooth approximants are bounded in $H^1$ by ( 6.26.7 ). Weak compactness of their derivatives identifies the weak limit as the distributional derivatives of the localized $u$, so $u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$. The equation $\Delta ''u=\delta ''g$ has smooth right-hand side. Its divergence-form principal coefficients are $\tfrac 12g^{ij}G_{AB}\rho $ and its remaining coefficients are smooth first- and zeroth-order matrices. Apply the full finite-vector theorem interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form on successively smaller balls, and then the local embedding in Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding , to obtain smoothness. No global Laplacian self-adjointness or harmonic decomposition is used. $\square$

title: 9.29 Discrete holomorphic jets and the Stein criterion
search_title: Discrete holomorphic jets and the Stein criterion
section: 9.29 Discrete holomorphic jets and the Stein criterion
text: Theorem 9.29.1 . 17CC905E00B7 Suppose $X$ has a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion and $\dim X=n\geq 1$. For every closed discrete subset $D=\{ a_ j\} \subset X$, every choice of nonnegative integers $\ell _ j$, and every prescribed holomorphic jet of order $\ell _ j$ at $a_ j$, there is $f\in \mathcal O(X)$ having all these jets simultaneously. The orders and coefficients may vary without a uniform bound. Proof. Shift the exhaustion so that $\rho \geq 0$, as justified for finite continuous exhaustions in section 9.26 . Use the complete Kähler form $\omega =\mathcal H(\mathrm e^\rho )$ from lemma 6.26.8 . The set $D$ is countable and meets every compact set in a finite set. Choose pairwise disjoint relatively compact coordinate balls $U_ j$ centered at $a_ j$, locally finite in $X$. One explicit choice starts with disjoint metric balls of radii less than1 and less than one quarter the distance to the other points of $D$, and places smaller coordinate balls inside. Local finiteness follows because centers of balls meeting a fixed compact set lie in its compact closed metric1-neighborhood, by lemma 9.28.1 . A finite discrete set is handled by the same choice with an arbitrary positive bound when the set of other points is empty. In each ball take coordinates $z_ j(a_ j)=0$, with $U_ j=\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $ and $r_ j<1$. Let $P_ j$ be the polynomial of degree at most $\ell _ j$ representing the prescribed jet, and take $\eta _ j\in C_ c^\infty (U_ j)$ with $0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1$, equal to one on $\{ |z_ j|\leq r_ j/2\} $. The locally finite smooth function $f_0=\sum _ j\eta _ jP_ j$ has these jets, and $g=\bar\partial f_0$ is smooth, closed and zero near every $a_ j$. Set $c_ j=n+\ell _ j$ and, off $D$, define the nonpositive function \[  P=\sum _ j c_ j\eta _ j\log |z_ j|^2,  \] with value $-\infty $ at $a_ j$. The summands extend by zero outside their coordinate balls. Choose $b_ j>0$ so large that $-1-b_ j<\log ((r_ j/2)^2)$. For $N\geq 1$ put \[  P_ N=\sum _ j c_ j\eta _ j \max \{ \log |z_ j|^2,-N-b_ j\} .  \] Then $P_ N$ is finite and continuous, and $P_ N\downarrow P$. There is a smooth nonnegative $C$ independent of $N$ such that FC59B92C1B6E 9.29.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H(P_ N)\geq -C\beta \quad \hbox{as currents}, \qquad \beta =\mathcal H(\rho ). \end{equation} Indeed $\log |z_ j|^2$ is PSH by plurisubharmonicity of logarithmic holomorphic norms , and its maximum with a constant is PSH by the line submean inequality. Where $\eta _ j=1$ this proves the lower bound. On the support of a derivative of $\eta _ j$, truncation is inactive for every $N\geq 1$, so the summand is the same smooth function there for all $N$. Its negative Hessian is bounded relative to $\beta $ on the compact support of these cutoff derivatives, with the factor $c_ j$ included. Choose a nonnegative smooth majorant equal to that bound on this derivative support and supported inside $U_ j$. The locally finite sum of these majorants is the required $C$. This local verification also proves the asserted distributional inequality across the maximum's joining surface. Let $K_ X=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*X$ with its metric from $\omega $. Its inverse has a smooth Hermitian curvature form $R=\mathrm i\Theta (K_ X^{-1})$. Choose continuous $a\geq 0$ with $R\geq -a\omega $, for example the pointwise operator norm of $R$. The function $F=|g|_\omega ^2\mathrm e^{-P}$, given value zero at $D$, is locally integrable: $g$ vanishes near the finitely many points of $D$ in any compact set, and elsewhere $P$ is smooth. Apply ( 6.26.9 ) with $A=2(a+1)\omega $ and this $C,F$. Thus \[  \Phi _ N=\chi (\rho )+P_ N,\qquad \mathcal H(\Phi _ N)\geq 2(a+1)\omega , \qquad M:=\int _ X|g|_\omega ^2\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P} \, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty .  \] These are continuous strictly PSH functions on the whole manifold, including the pole centers. Apply relative Richberg smoothing , with open set $X$ and $\lambda _ N=\min \{ 1/2,1/N\} $, to obtain smooth $v_ N$ such that 5140244168BF 9.29.3 \begin{equation}  \Phi _ N\leq v_ N\leq \Phi _ N+\lambda _ N, \qquad \mathcal H(v_ N)\geq (a+1)\omega . \end{equation} No monotonicity of $v_ N$ is asserted or needed. Identify scalar $(0,q)$-forms with $K_ X^{-1}$-valued $(n,q)$-forms by the map $v\mapsto (-1)^{nq}\sigma \wedge v\otimes \sigma ^{-1}$, where $\sigma $ is a nonvanishing local holomorphic top form. The map is independent of this frame and commutes with $\bar\partial $: the sign from differentiating past $\sigma $ changes $(-1)^{nq}$ to $(-1)^{n(q+1)}$. Its top-form/dual-frame factor has norm one. For $K_ X^{-1}$ with metric multiplied by $\mathrm e^{-v_ N}$ the curvature is $R+\mathcal H(v_ N)\geq \omega $. Its $(n,1)$ curvature operator is therefore at least the identity by proposition 10.33.6 . Both the ordinary squared norm and the inverse-curvature energy of $g$ for this metric are at most $M$, since $v_ N\geq \chi (\rho )+P$. Theorem 6.26.5 consequently gives scalar functions $u_ N$ such that 1650816EF3A8 9.29.4 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial u_ N=g,\qquad \int _ X|u_ N|^2\mathrm e^{-v_ N}\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M. \end{equation} Here is the weight-limit justification on all of $X$. For every fixed $k$ and $N\geq k$, $v_ N\leq \Phi _ k+\lambda _ k$. Thus ( 9.29.4 ) bounds the $u_ N$ for the fixed density $\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ k-\lambda _ k}$, in particular locally in unweighted $L^2$. Diagonal weak compactness on a compact exhaustion gives $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\bar\partial u=g$ distributionally. For fixed $k$, weak lower semicontinuity first gives on each compact $K$ \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ k-\lambda _ k} \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M.  \] The fixed densities increase as $k\to \infty $ to $\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P}$. Monotone convergence and then compact exhaustion give 8E331ACA3599 9.29.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P} \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M. \end{equation} This is the fixed-weight order of limits also used in theorem 6.25.10 ; the smoothing errors in ( 9.29.3 ) are globally controlled, so no varying-weight lower-semicontinuity step is hidden. Since $\bar\partial (f_0-u)=0$, the local statement holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions shows that $f=f_0-u$ is holomorphic on $X$. In particular $u$ is smooth and is holomorphic near each $a_ j$. Near that point the singular density in ( 9.29.5 ) is a smooth positive factor bounded above and below by positive constants times $|z_ j|^{-2(n+\ell _ j)}$ times Lebesgue measure. If the first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term of $u$ had degree $m\leq \ell _ j$, its squared spherical integral would be bounded below by a positive constant times $r^{2m}$ for small $r$. The radial integral would dominate $\int _0^{r_0}r^{2m-2\ell _ j-1}\, \mathrm dr=\infty $, contradicting ( 9.29.5 ). Thus $u$ vanishes to order at least $\ell _ j+1$ at $a_ j$, and $f$ has the prescribed jet. If $D$ is empty, the assertion holds with any constant function. $\square$ Corollary 9.29.6 . 476E1C34C3CF A second countable complex manifold with a smooth strictly PSH exhaustion is holomorphically convex. Its global holomorphic functions separate every pair of points, and at each point finitely many of them give holomorphic coordinates. In particular it is Stein, whether one uses local or global point separation in the defining axioms. Conversely, holomorphic convexity and local holomorphic separation give a smooth strictly PSH exhaustion. Such a Stein manifold therefore has the discrete jet interpolation property of the theorem. Proof. Prescribe distinct values at two points in theorem 9.29.1 to separate them. At one point prescribe the first jets of its $n$ local coordinate functions; the resulting global functions have identity Jacobian in that chart. the holomorphic inverse and submersion theorems gives the coordinate assertion. Let $K\subset X$ be compact. Its holomorphic hull is closed, being the intersection of the closed inequalities $|f(x)|\leq \sup _ K|f|$, $f\in \mathcal O(X)$. If this hull were noncompact, properness of the exhaustion would supply points $a_ j$ in it whose exhaustion values tend to infinity. title: Theorem 9.29.1
section: 9.29 Discrete holomorphic jets and the Stein criterion
text: Theorem 9.29.1 . 17CC905E00B7 Suppose $X$ has a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion and $\dim X=n\geq 1$. For every closed discrete subset $D=\{ a_ j\} \subset X$, every choice of nonnegative integers $\ell _ j$, and every prescribed holomorphic jet of order $\ell _ j$ at $a_ j$, there is $f\in \mathcal O(X)$ having all these jets simultaneously. The orders and coefficients may vary without a uniform bound. Proof. Shift the exhaustion so that $\rho \geq 0$, as justified for finite continuous exhaustions in section 9.26 . Use the complete Kähler form $\omega =\mathcal H(\mathrm e^\rho )$ from lemma 6.26.8 . The set $D$ is countable and meets every compact set in a finite set. Choose pairwise disjoint relatively compact coordinate balls $U_ j$ centered at $a_ j$, locally finite in $X$. One explicit choice starts with disjoint metric balls of radii less than1 and less than one quarter the distance to the other points of $D$, and places smaller coordinate balls inside. Local finiteness follows because centers of balls meeting a fixed compact set lie in its compact closed metric1-neighborhood, by lemma 9.28.1 . A finite discrete set is handled by the same choice with an arbitrary positive bound when the set of other points is empty. In each ball take coordinates $z_ j(a_ j)=0$, with $U_ j=\{ |z_ j|<r_ j\} $ and $r_ j<1$. Let $P_ j$ be the polynomial of degree at most $\ell _ j$ representing the prescribed jet, and take $\eta _ j\in C_ c^\infty (U_ j)$ with $0\leq \eta _ j\leq 1$, equal to one on $\{ |z_ j|\leq r_ j/2\} $. The locally finite smooth function $f_0=\sum _ j\eta _ jP_ j$ has these jets, and $g=\bar\partial f_0$ is smooth, closed and zero near every $a_ j$. Set $c_ j=n+\ell _ j$ and, off $D$, define the nonpositive function \[  P=\sum _ j c_ j\eta _ j\log |z_ j|^2,  \] with value $-\infty $ at $a_ j$. The summands extend by zero outside their coordinate balls. Choose $b_ j>0$ so large that $-1-b_ j<\log ((r_ j/2)^2)$. For $N\geq 1$ put \[  P_ N=\sum _ j c_ j\eta _ j \max \{ \log |z_ j|^2,-N-b_ j\} .  \] Then $P_ N$ is finite and continuous, and $P_ N\downarrow P$. There is a smooth nonnegative $C$ independent of $N$ such that FC59B92C1B6E 9.29.2 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H(P_ N)\geq -C\beta \quad \hbox{as currents}, \qquad \beta =\mathcal H(\rho ). \end{equation} Indeed $\log |z_ j|^2$ is PSH by plurisubharmonicity of logarithmic holomorphic norms , and its maximum with a constant is PSH by the line submean inequality. Where $\eta _ j=1$ this proves the lower bound. On the support of a derivative of $\eta _ j$, truncation is inactive for every $N\geq 1$, so the summand is the same smooth function there for all $N$. Its negative Hessian is bounded relative to $\beta $ on the compact support of these cutoff derivatives, with the factor $c_ j$ included. Choose a nonnegative smooth majorant equal to that bound on this derivative support and supported inside $U_ j$. The locally finite sum of these majorants is the required $C$. This local verification also proves the asserted distributional inequality across the maximum's joining surface. Let $K_ X=\Lambda ^{n,0}T^*X$ with its metric from $\omega $. Its inverse has a smooth Hermitian curvature form $R=\mathrm i\Theta (K_ X^{-1})$. Choose continuous $a\geq 0$ with $R\geq -a\omega $, for example the pointwise operator norm of $R$. The function $F=|g|_\omega ^2\mathrm e^{-P}$, given value zero at $D$, is locally integrable: $g$ vanishes near the finitely many points of $D$ in any compact set, and elsewhere $P$ is smooth. Apply ( 6.26.9 ) with $A=2(a+1)\omega $ and this $C,F$. Thus \[  \Phi _ N=\chi (\rho )+P_ N,\qquad \mathcal H(\Phi _ N)\geq 2(a+1)\omega , \qquad M:=\int _ X|g|_\omega ^2\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P} \, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty .  \] These are continuous strictly PSH functions on the whole manifold, including the pole centers. Apply relative Richberg smoothing , with open set $X$ and $\lambda _ N=\min \{ 1/2,1/N\} $, to obtain smooth $v_ N$ such that 5140244168BF 9.29.3 \begin{equation}  \Phi _ N\leq v_ N\leq \Phi _ N+\lambda _ N, \qquad \mathcal H(v_ N)\geq (a+1)\omega . \end{equation} No monotonicity of $v_ N$ is asserted or needed. Identify scalar $(0,q)$-forms with $K_ X^{-1}$-valued $(n,q)$-forms by the map $v\mapsto (-1)^{nq}\sigma \wedge v\otimes \sigma ^{-1}$, where $\sigma $ is a nonvanishing local holomorphic top form. The map is independent of this frame and commutes with $\bar\partial $: the sign from differentiating past $\sigma $ changes $(-1)^{nq}$ to $(-1)^{n(q+1)}$. Its top-form/dual-frame factor has norm one. For $K_ X^{-1}$ with metric multiplied by $\mathrm e^{-v_ N}$ the curvature is $R+\mathcal H(v_ N)\geq \omega $. Its $(n,1)$ curvature operator is therefore at least the identity by proposition 10.33.6 . Both the ordinary squared norm and the inverse-curvature energy of $g$ for this metric are at most $M$, since $v_ N\geq \chi (\rho )+P$. Theorem 6.26.5 consequently gives scalar functions $u_ N$ such that 1650816EF3A8 9.29.4 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial u_ N=g,\qquad \int _ X|u_ N|^2\mathrm e^{-v_ N}\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M. \end{equation} Here is the weight-limit justification on all of $X$. For every fixed $k$ and $N\geq k$, $v_ N\leq \Phi _ k+\lambda _ k$. Thus ( 9.29.4 ) bounds the $u_ N$ for the fixed density $\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ k-\lambda _ k}$, in particular locally in unweighted $L^2$. Diagonal weak compactness on a compact exhaustion gives $u\in L^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\bar\partial u=g$ distributionally. For fixed $k$, weak lower semicontinuity first gives on each compact $K$ \[  \int _ K|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\Phi _ k-\lambda _ k} \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M.  \] The fixed densities increase as $k\to \infty $ to $\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P}$. Monotone convergence and then compact exhaustion give 8E331ACA3599 9.29.5 \begin{equation}  \int _ X|u|^2\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )-P} \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M. \end{equation} This is the fixed-weight order of limits also used in theorem 6.25.10 ; the smoothing errors in ( 9.29.3 ) are globally controlled, so no varying-weight lower-semicontinuity step is hidden. Since $\bar\partial (f_0-u)=0$, the local statement holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions shows that $f=f_0-u$ is holomorphic on $X$. In particular $u$ is smooth and is holomorphic near each $a_ j$. Near that point the singular density in ( 9.29.5 ) is a smooth positive factor bounded above and below by positive constants times $|z_ j|^{-2(n+\ell _ j)}$ times Lebesgue measure. If the first nonzero homogeneous Taylor term of $u$ had degree $m\leq \ell _ j$, its squared spherical integral would be bounded below by a positive constant times $r^{2m}$ for small $r$. The radial integral would dominate $\int _0^{r_0}r^{2m-2\ell _ j-1}\, \mathrm dr=\infty $, contradicting ( 9.29.5 ). Thus $u$ vanishes to order at least $\ell _ j+1$ at $a_ j$, and $f$ has the prescribed jet. If $D$ is empty, the assertion holds with any constant function. $\square$

Lemma 6.33.7 . C9AA991622D8 Suppose $p\ge 1$, $D\Subset \Omega $ is open, and $v,w$ are continuous plurisubharmonic functions on a neighborhood of $\overline D$. If $v=w$ on a neighborhood of $\partial D$, then \[  \int _ D T\wedge (dd^ cv)^ p=\int _ D T\wedge (dd^ cw)^ p.  \] No smoothness of the boundary is required. Proof. Bounded-product symmetry and its defining recursion give \[  T\wedge (dd^ cv)^ p-T\wedge (dd^ cw)^ p =dd^ c\left((v-w)\sum _{j=0}^{p-1} T\wedge (dd^ cv)^ j\wedge (dd^ cw)^{p-1-j}ight).  \] For each summand the current after the weight has bidimension $(1,1)$; the recursion applies to $v$ and $w$ separately and is linear in their difference. The weighted current vanishes near $\partial D$. Restrict it to $D$ and extend it by zero; its support is a compact subset of $D$, so this extension introduces no boundary term. The same identity holds for this extension and for the difference measure restricted to $D$ and extended by zero. Pair that identity with a smooth compactly supported function equal to one near $\overline D$. The $dd^ c$ pairing is zero, because the derivatives of the test function vanish near the weighted current's support. On the left this pairing is exactly the difference of the two integrals over $D$: their measures agree near $\partial D$. This proves the claim. $\square$ Lemma 6.33.8 . 50567CE0F546 For $p\ge 1$, $s<\log r^2$ and $\overline{B(a,r)}\subset \Omega $, the bounded continuous plurisubharmonic function $u_ s(z)=\max \{ \log |z-a|^2,s\} $ satisfies 21D941444C0C 6.33.9  egin{equation}  \int _{B(a,r)}T\wedge (dd^ cu_ s)^ p=D_ T(a,r). \end{equation} Here $u_ s(a)=s$. This statement does not form a product of unbounded potentials at $a$. Proof. Again take $a=0$. Smooth $t\mapsto \max \{ t,s\} $ by convolution with an even nonnegative one-dimensional mollifier of integral one and support $[-\delta ,\delta ]$. The result $\chi _\delta $ is convex and nondecreasing, equals $s$ for $t\le s-\delta $, equals $t$ for $t\ge s+\delta $, and differs from $\max \{ t,s\} $ by at most $\delta $. Thus $\chi _\delta (\log |z|^2)$ extends smoothly and plurisubharmonically across zero, where it is constant, and converges uniformly to $u_ s$. The Kähler commutators and their adjoints give \[  [\Lambda ,\partial ]=\mathrm i ar\partial ^*,\quad [\Lambda , ar\partial ]=-\mathrm i\partial ^*,\quad [ ar\partial ^*,L]=\mathrm i\partial .  \] Since $\omega $ is closed, $[ ar\partial ,L]=[\partial ,L]=0$. Consequently \[  [\square ,L] =\mathrm i( ar\partial \partial +\partial  ar\partial )=0.  \] Taking formal adjoints gives $[\square ,\Lambda ]=0$. The square-zero identities give commutation of the respective complex Laplacians with $\partial , ar\partial $ and their adjoints; their equality gives commutation with $\square $ for all four operators. Finally $\Delta _ d$ is real, so ( 10.47.8 ) implies that $\square $ commutes with conjugation. The Green commutations follow from these differential identities. If an operator $A$, as well as its formal adjoint, preserves the harmonic spaces and commutes with $\square $, it preserves their orthogonal complements. Then $AGf$ is orthogonal to the target harmonic space and solves $\square AGf=A(f-\Pi f)$. This is the same equation and orthogonality condition as for $GAf$, since $A\Pi =\Pi A$. Conversely suppose that $\Pi \alpha =0$. Because $\alpha $ has pure type, $d\alpha =0$ implies separately $\partial \alpha = ar\partial \alpha =0$. This proves all equivalences. At either zero index $\Lambda G\alpha =0$ by type, so the same formula proves the endpoint claim. Both $G$ and $\Lambda $ commute with conjugation: the latter is the adjoint of multiplication by the real form $\omega $ for a real metric. Thus $ eta $ is real when $\alpha $ is real. There is no assertion of uniqueness for higher-degree potentials. $\square$ For real $(1,1)$-forms the exactness conclusion agrees with the compact Kähler $(1,1)$-current $dd^ c$ decomposition ; that theorem also supplies distributional potentials and the positive-current refinements. The formula above supplies the smooth all-bidegree extension of the argument. For smooth forms define \[  H^{p,q}_{\mathrm{BC}} = rac{\ker \partial \cap \ker  ar\partial \subset \mathcal A^{p,q}}{\partial  ar\partial \mathcal A^{p-1,q-1}},\qquad H^{p,q}_{\mathrm A} = rac{\ker (\partial  ar\partial :\mathcal A^{p,q} 	o \mathcal A^{p+1,q+1})}{\partial \mathcal A^{p-1,q}+ ar\partial \mathcal A^{p,q-1}}.  \] Let $H^{p,q}_{ ar\partial }$ have its usual smooth Dolbeault meaning. Corollary 10.47.11 . 34D74D92E956 The natural maps \[  H^{p,q}_{\mathrm{BC}}\longrightarrow H^{p,q}_{ ar\partial }\longrightarrow H^{p,q}_{\mathrm A}  \] are isomorphisms. All three spaces have unique representatives in $\mathcal H^{p,q}$, and all the displayed coboundary spaces are closed in the smooth topology. These assertions include $p=0$, $q=0$, $p=n$ and $q=n$. Proof. For a $d$-closed form, subtracting its harmonic projection and applying theorem 10.47.9 gives the Bott–Chern representative. Harmonic representatives for Dolbeault cohomology are given by theorem 10.46.6 and are $d$-closed here. For an Aeppli-closed form $\alpha $, the Green identity gives \[  \alpha =\Pi \alpha + ar\partial  ar\partial ^*G\alpha + ar\partial ^* ar\partial G\alpha .  \] Put $v= ar\partial G\alpha $. Its $\partial $ derivative is zero, since $\partial  ar\partial G\alpha =G\partial  ar\partial \alpha =0$. The Kähler commutator therefore gives C32800E862D8 10.47.12  egin{equation}  \alpha =\Pi \alpha + ar\partial ( ar\partial ^*G\alpha ) +\mathrm i\partial (\Lambda  ar\partial G\alpha ). \end{equation} A harmonic form in either coboundary space has zero norm by orthogonality, giving uniqueness. The natural maps preserve the harmonic representatives, and so are isomorphisms. The Bott–Chern coboundary space is $\ker \partial \cap \ker  ar\partial \cap \ker \Pi $, and the Aeppli coboundary space is $\ker (\partial  ar\partial )\cap \ker \Pi $, by the proved formulas. These are kernels of continuous smooth operators and are closed. Dolbeault closedness is part of the reused Hodge theorem. Out-of-range bundles and operators are zero, so every calculation remains valid at the four types of endpoint. $\square$ Write $H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C)$ for the quotient of smooth closed complex $k$-forms by smooth exact forms. Let $I^{p,q}\subset H^{p+q}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C)$ be the subspace represented by $d$-closed forms of type $(p,q)$. Theorem 10.47.13 . 8719651E2EA0 There are canonical isomorphisms A898F43A190B 10.47.14  egin{equation}  H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C) = igoplus _{p+q=k}I^{p,q},\qquad H^{p,q}_{\mathrm{BC}}\simeq I^{p,q} \simeq H^{p,q}_{ ar\partial }(X). \end{equation} These subspaces and isomorphisms depend only on the complex manifold, and complex conjugation gives $\overline{I^{p,q}}=I^{q,p}$. The wedge product respects the bigrading. If $b_ k=\dim _{\mathbb C}H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C)$ and $h^{p,q}=\dim _{\mathbb C}H^{p,q}_{ ar\partial }(X)$, then \[  b_ k=\sum _{p+q=k}h^{p,q},\qquad h^{p,q}=h^{q,p}, \qquad b_{2j+1}\  \hbox{is even}.  \] Complexification identifies real de Rham cohomology with the conjugation-fixed part of this decomposition. Proof. Smooth de Rham Hodge theory and lemma 10.47.7 identify de Rham cohomology with $\mathcal H^ k= igoplus \mathcal H^{p,q}$. Each pure harmonic form is $d$-closed; conversely a $d$-closed pure form has its unique de Rham harmonic representative of that same type, by the Green commutation and the de Rham Hodge decomposition. Thus the images are exactly $I^{p,q}$ and the sum is direct. For a pure closed form, $d$-exactness, Dolbeault exactness and Bott–Chern exactness agree by theorem 10.47.9 . Dolbeault surjectivity follows from its harmonic representatives. This proves every displayed isomorphism using the natural maps induced by representatives. Their definitions involve no metric, establishing the asserted independence. Conjugation exchanges types, preserves real $d$ and exactness, and therefore exchanges the displayed subspaces. The wedge of two closed pure forms is closed of the sum of their types. On the Bott–Chern quotient its independence of representatives also follows directly from $(\partial  ar\partial a)\wedge v=\partial  ar\partial (a\wedge v)$ when $v$ is closed. The dimension and symmetry formulas follow. In odd total degree every pair $(p,q),(q,p)$ has $p
e q$, so its contribution to $b_{2j+1}$ is twice an integer. Finally every complex closed form is the sum of its real and imaginary closed parts, and exactness splits into those same parts. This proves complexification of the real quotient and identifies its real image with the fixed vectors of conjugation. No integral-lattice assertion is used in these analytic cohomology statements. $\square$ Theorem 10.47.15 (Lefschetz decomposition and hard Lefschetz) . 9F95F07CA33F On harmonic forms, primitive means $\Lambda u=0$. There are orthogonal decompositions C16AD0CB2F69  egin{align}  \mathcal H^ k& = igoplus _{r=\max (0,k-n)}^{\lfloor k/2floor } L^ r\mathcal H^{k-2r}_{\mathrm{prim}}, 	ag{10.47.16}\  \mathcal H^{p,q}& = igoplus _{r=\max (0,p+q-n)}^{\min (p,q)} L^ r\mathcal H^{p-r,q-r}_{\mathrm{prim}}. \end{align} The pointwise primitive coefficients of a harmonic form are smooth and harmonic, and all the constants and norm formulas of lemma 10.47.1 hold with the global $L^2$ norm. Multiplication by the Kähler class gives isomorphisms 9D0CD285C6DD  egin{align}  [\omega ]^{n-k}:H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C) & \longrightarrow H^{2n-k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C), & & 0\leq k\leq n,	ag{10.47.17}\  [\omega ]^{n-p-q}:I^{p,q} & \longrightarrow I^{n-q,n-p},& & p+q\leq n. \end{align} For $k\leq n$ the primitive cohomology is exactly 7273117A9062 10.47.18  egin{equation}  P^ k_{[\omega ]}=\ker  igl ([\omega ]^{n-k+1}:H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}} 	o H^{2n-k+2}_{\mathrm{dR}} igr ); \end{equation} it is represented by $\mathcal H^ k_{\mathrm{prim}}$. Apply lemma 10.47.1 , retaining the bigrading. This proves both harmonic decompositions and the norm formulas. Alternatively the pointwise decomposition coefficients are precisely the rational polynomials ( 10.47.6 ). They are smooth, commute with the Laplacian, and hence are harmonic when the original form is. Thus the two decompositions agree. Multiplication by $\omega $ commutes with $d$, so defines multiplication by $[\omega ]$ on de Rham classes, independent of representatives. For example, replacing $\omega $ by $\omega +d\eta $ changes its action on a closed $u$ by $d(\eta \wedge u)$. Its harmonic representative is exactly $Lu$, because $L$ preserves harmonic forms. e 0$: indeed $r+s+1\leq n-(k-2r)=s+2r$. Images from different primitive degrees remain in distinct direct summands. Thus $L^{s+1}u=0$ if and only if $u=u_0$ is primitive. title: Lemma 10.47.1
section: 10.47 Hodge structure and Lefschetz decomposition
text: Lemma 10.47.1 . 99F7CD84D262 Let $V=\bigoplus _{k=0}^{2n}V^ k$ be a finite-dimensional graded Hermitian space with orthogonal degrees. Suppose that $L$ has degree two, $\Lambda =L^*$, and \[  [\Lambda ,L]|_{V^ k}=(n-k)I.  \] Set $P^ k=\ker \Lambda \cap V^ k$. Then $P^ k=0$ for $k>n$, and, for $u\in P^\ell $, the lowering formula holds for $1\leq j\leq n-\ell $ and the norm formula for $0\leq j\leq n-\ell $: 29B066DE4DF2 \begin{align}  \Lambda L^ j u& =j(n-\ell -j+1)L^{j-1}u, \tag{10.47.2}\\  \| L^ ju\| ^2& =\frac{j!(n-\ell )!}{(n-\ell -j)!}\| u\| ^2, \qquad L^{n-\ell +1}u=0. \tag{10.47.3} \end{align} Every $v\in V^ k$ has a unique orthogonal decomposition FCD784AF69AF 10.47.4 \begin{equation}  v=\sum _{r=\max (0,k-n)}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor }L^ ru_ r, \qquad u_ r\in P^{k-2r}. \end{equation} Each $u_ r$ is a polynomial in $L,\Lambda $ applied to $v$, with rational coefficients depending only on $n,k,r$. For $k\leq n$, $L^{n-k}:V^ k\to V^{2n-k}$ is an isomorphism. On the summand $L^ rP^{k-2r}$, writing $s=n-k$, its inverse and norm ratio are given by the following formulas, with the inverse acting on the image of that summand: A1C2A0FF7C70 10.47.5 \begin{equation}  (L^ s)^{-1}=\left(\frac{r!}{(r+s)!}\right)^2\Lambda ^ s, \qquad \| L^ s v\| ^2=\left(\frac{(r+s)!}{r!}\right)^2\| v\| ^2. \end{equation} These assertions apply pointwise to the complex exterior algebra of a Hermitian vector space. In its bigrading the summands are $L^ rP^{p-r,q-r}$, with $\max (0,p+q-n)\leq r\leq \min (p,q)$. Proof. Expanding a commutator of $\Lambda $ with $L^ j$ and applying the degree formula to $L^ a u$ gives \[  [\Lambda ,L^ j]u =\sum _{a=0}^{j-1}(n-\ell -2a)L^{j-1}u =j(n-\ell -j+1)L^{j-1}u.  \] For primitive $u$ this is ( 10.47.2 ). Taking its inner product with $L^{j-1}u$ proves the norm formula by induction. If $\ell >n$, the case $j=1$ gives $\| Lu\| ^2=(n-\ell )\| u\| ^2$, forcing $u=0$. For $\ell \leq n$ the norms are positive through $j=n-\ell $ and zero at $j=n-\ell +1$, proving termination. Here is a complete decomposition argument. In any nonzero graded subspace invariant under $L$ and $\Lambda $, choose a nonzero vector $u$ of its lowest nonzero degree. It is primitive. The chain $u,Lu,\ldots ,L^{n-\ell }u$ has nonzero, mutually orthogonal vectors and is invariant under both operators. Its orthogonal complement in the subspace is also invariant: this follows from $L^*=\Lambda $. It is graded since the chain is graded. Repeating on that complement terminates after finitely many steps and gives an orthogonal sum of such chains. If $V$ is bigraded and the degrees are orthogonal, with $L$ of type $(1,1)$ and $\Lambda $ of type $(-1,-1)$, choose the lowest-degree vector of pure type at each step; the complements still respect type. On each chain the kernel of $\Lambda $ is its first line, since all the lowering coefficients at the later vectors are positive. Thus the initial vectors of the chains of degree $\ell $ span $P^\ell $. In a chain of primitive degree $\ell $, the vector at degree $k$ is $L^ ru$, where $\ell =k-2r$ and $r\leq n-\ell $. These conditions give exactly the range in ( 10.47.4 ). The resulting summands are mutually orthogonal and account for all of $V^ k$. To see uniqueness independently of the chosen chains, put $T=L\Lambda $ on $V^ k$. On the displayed summand its eigenvalue is \[  t_ r=r(n-k+r+1).  \] These numbers are distinct: $t_{r+1}-t_ r=n-k+2r+2>0$ in the indicated range. Thus its component projection and primitive coefficient are 69B921CFAC64 10.47.6 \begin{equation}  Q_{k,r}=\prod _{a\ne r}\frac{T-t_ aI}{t_ r-t_ a},\qquad u_ r=\frac{(n-k+r)!}{r!(n-k+2r)!}\Lambda ^ rQ_{k,r}v, \end{equation} where the product runs over the same finite range and an empty product is $I$. All factorials are of nonnegative integers. The coefficient follows by applying the lowering formula $r$ times to $L^ ru_ r$. This also proves the claimed rational-polynomial expression. Each primitive chain has one vector in degree $k$ precisely when it has one in degree $2n-k$. Multiplication by $L^{n-k}$ takes the first to the second with nonzero coefficient. It is therefore an isomorphism. Applying ( 10.47.2 ) repeatedly, and then ( 10.47.3 ), gives both formulas in ( 10.47.5 ). For the exterior algebra, an $\omega $-unitary coframe gives $\omega =\mathrm i\sum \theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ j$. The creation/contraction calculation of the curvature operator on $(n,1)$-forms , with every curvature eigenvalue equal to one, gives $[L,\Lambda ]=(k-n)I$, or the commutator used here with the opposite order. The bigraded argument proves the last assertion. $\square$

text: Theorem 10.47.13 . 8719651E2EA0 There are canonical isomorphisms A898F43A190B 10.47.14 \begin{equation}  H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C) =\bigoplus _{p+q=k}I^{p,q},\qquad H^{p,q}_{\mathrm{BC}}\simeq I^{p,q} \simeq H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X). \end{equation} These subspaces and isomorphisms depend only on the complex manifold, and complex conjugation gives $\overline{I^{p,q}}=I^{q,p}$. If $b_ k=\dim _{\mathbb C}H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C)$ and $h^{p,q}=\dim _{\mathbb C}H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X)$, then \[  b_ k=\sum _{p+q=k}h^{p,q},\qquad h^{p,q}=h^{q,p}, \qquad b_{2j+1}\  \hbox{is even}.  \] Complexification identifies real de Rham cohomology with the conjugation-fixed part of this decomposition. Proof. Smooth de Rham Hodge theory and lemma 10.47.7 identify de Rham cohomology with $\mathcal H^ k=\bigoplus \mathcal H^{p,q}$. Each pure harmonic form is $d$-closed; conversely a $d$-closed pure form has its unique de Rham harmonic representative of that same type, by the Green commutation and the de Rham Hodge decomposition. Thus the images are exactly $I^{p,q}$ and the sum is direct. For a pure closed form, $d$-exactness, Dolbeault exactness and Bott–Chern exactness agree by theorem 10.47.9 . Dolbeault surjectivity follows from its harmonic representatives. This proves every displayed isomorphism using the natural maps induced by representatives. Their definitions involve no metric, establishing the asserted independence. Conjugation exchanges types, preserves real $d$ and exactness, and therefore exchanges the displayed subspaces. The wedge of two closed pure forms is closed of the sum of their types. On the Bott–Chern quotient its independence of representatives also follows directly from $(\partial \bar\partial a)\wedge v=\partial \bar\partial (a\wedge v)$ when $v$ is closed. The dimension and symmetry formulas follow. In odd total degree every pair $(p,q),(q,p)$ has $p\ne q$, so its contribution to $b_{2j+1}$ is twice an integer. Finally every complex closed form is the sum of its real and imaginary closed parts, and exactness splits into those same parts. This proves complexification of the real quotient and identifies its real image with the fixed vectors of conjugation. No integral-lattice assertion is used in these analytic cohomology statements. $\square$

section: 10.47 Hodge structure and Lefschetz decomposition
text: Theorem 10.47.15 (Lefschetz decomposition and hard Lefschetz) . 9F95F07CA33F On harmonic forms, primitive means $\Lambda u=0$. There are orthogonal decompositions C16AD0CB2F69 \begin{align}  \mathcal H^ k& =\bigoplus _{r=\max (0,k-n)}^{\lfloor k/2\rfloor } L^ r\mathcal H^{k-2r}_{\mathrm{prim}}, \tag{10.47.16}\\  \mathcal H^{p,q}& =\bigoplus _{r=\max (0,p+q-n)}^{\min (p,q)} L^ r\mathcal H^{p-r,q-r}_{\mathrm{prim}}. \end{align} The pointwise primitive coefficients of a harmonic form are smooth and harmonic, and all the constants and norm formulas of lemma 10.47.1 hold with the global $L^2$ norm. Multiplication by the Kähler class gives isomorphisms 9D0CD285C6DD \begin{align}  [\omega ]^{n-k}:H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C) & \longrightarrow H^{2n-k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,\mathbb C), & & 0\leq k\leq n,\tag{10.47.17}\\  [\omega ]^{n-p-q}:I^{p,q} & \longrightarrow I^{n-q,n-p},& & p+q\leq n. \end{align} For $k\leq n$ the primitive cohomology is exactly 7273117A9062 10.47.18 \begin{equation}  P^ k_{[\omega ]}=\ker \bigl ([\omega ]^{n-k+1}:H^ k_{\mathrm{dR}} \to H^{2n-k+2}_{\mathrm{dR}}\bigr ); \end{equation} it is represented by $\mathcal H^ k_{\mathrm{prim}}$. Consequently \[  h^{p,q}=h^{n-q,n-p}=h^{n-p,n-q},  \] and, with out-of-range numbers zero, \[  \begin{array}{lll} p+q\leq n:& h^{p,q}\geq h^{p-1,q-1},& b_{p+q}\geq b_{p+q-2},\\  p+q\geq n:& h^{p,q}\geq h^{p+1,q+1},& b_{p+q}\geq b_{p+q+2}. \end{array}  \] The decomposition into primitive cohomology depends on $[\omega ]$; the Hodge type decomposition in theorem 10.47.13 does not. Proof. The finite-dimensional graded space $\bigoplus \mathcal H^ k$ is invariant under $L,\Lambda $, by lemma 10.47.7 . Their adjoint relation and degree commutator restrict to it. Apply lemma 10.47.1 , retaining the bigrading. This proves both harmonic decompositions and the norm formulas. Alternatively the pointwise decomposition coefficients are precisely the rational polynomials ( 10.47.6 ). They are smooth, commute with the Laplacian, and hence are harmonic when the original form is. Thus the two decompositions agree. Multiplication by $\omega $ commutes with $d$, so defines multiplication by $[\omega ]$ on de Rham classes, independent of representatives. For example, replacing $\omega $ by $\omega +d\eta $ changes its action on a closed $u$ by $d(\eta \wedge u)$. Its harmonic representative is exactly $Lu$, because $L$ preserves harmonic forms. The finite linear-algebra isomorphisms therefore yield ( 10.47.17 ), including the pure-type maps. For a harmonic $k$-form write $u=\sum _ r L^ ru_ r$ and put $s=n-k$. The term $r=0$ is killed by $L^{s+1}$. For $r\geq 1$ its image $L^{r+s+1}u_ r$ is a nonzero multiple of a chain vector whenever $u_ r\ne 0$: indeed $r+s+1\leq n-(k-2r)=s+2r$. Images from different primitive degrees remain in distinct direct summands. Thus $L^{s+1}u=0$ if and only if $u=u_0$ is primitive. An exact harmonic form vanishes, so the same criterion on classes is exactly ( 10.47.18 ). This also proves that the resulting primitive decomposition on cohomology depends only on the class of $\omega $. The pure-type hard Lefschetz isomorphism gives $h^{p,q}=h^{n-q,n-p}$ for $p+q\leq n$. Applying it from the complementary degree gives the same equality above the middle degree. Conjugation symmetry then gives $h^{p,q}=h^{n-p,n-q}$. Each primitive chain shows that $L$ is injective below the middle degree and surjective above it: every chain starts at degree at most $n$ and terminates at the complementary degree. These assertions respect type and prove the inequalities. Below the middle degree, $h^{p,q}_{\mathrm{prim}}=h^{p,q}-h^{p-1,q-1}$ and $b_{k,\mathrm{prim}}=b_ k-b_{k-2}$; in all degrees the dimensions are the sums of their primitive dimensions over the displayed ranges. $\square$

text: Manifolds are Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. A constant sheaf is denoted by an underline. Cohomology of sheaves means the Godement cohomology already constructed. For the de Rham comparison write $\Psi _ q:H^ q_{\rm dR}(M,\mathbb R)\to H^ q(M,\underline{\mathbb R})$ for the successive positive resolution connecting maps in theorem 10.43.8 , corollary 10.43.11 . The same convention applies to complex coefficients. No singular-cohomology comparison is needed here. We use \[  dd^ c=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial , \qquad c_1(L,h)=-dd^ c\log |e|_ h^2 =\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta (L,h)  \] in a holomorphic frame $e$. Lemma 10.40.1 . E84E5EF6C697 For every sheaf $F$ of abelian groups, the natural map $\check H^1(X,F)\to H^1(X,F)$ is an isomorphism. Here the left side is the direct limit over open covers. For a short exact sheaf sequence $0\to F\to B\to Q\to 0$, a section $q\in Q(X)$ and local lifts $a_ i\in B(U_ i)$, the cocycle $a_ j-a_ i$ represents the connecting class $\partial q\in H^1(X,F)$ under this isomorphism. Proof. Use the Godement complex $C^\bullet F$ and the total-complex convention $\delta +(-1)^ a d_ G$ of theorem 10.43.16 , where $a$ is the Čech degree. Given a global degree-one cocycle $z$, sheaf exactness gives a cover and $b_ i\in C^0F(U_ i)$ with $d_ Gb_ i=z$. On overlaps $b_ i-b_ j$ lies in $\ker d_ G=F$. The total differential of $b=(b_ i)$ is $(-(b_ i-b_ j),z)$, so this Čech cocycle maps to $[z]$. This proves surjectivity; injectivity, including compatibility with refinements, is the cited theorem. For the last assertion choose a global Godement lift $A\in C^0B(X)$ of the augmentation of $q$; its existence follows from exactness of $\Gamma (X,C^0-)$. The global section $d_ GA$ comes from a unique $z\in C^1F(X)$ and represents $\partial q$. The differences $v_ i=a_ i-A$ lie in $C^0F(U_ i)$ and satisfy $d_ Gv_ i=-z$, while $\delta v=(a_ j-a_ i)$. Thus the total differential of $v$ is $((a_ j-a_ i),-z)$, proving the asserted sign. The same proof uses multiplicative notation for abelian multiplicative sheaves. $\square$ Theorem 10.40.2 . EA66BB854401 The tensor-product group $\operatorname {Pic}(X)$ of holomorphic line bundles on a complex manifold $X$ is naturally $H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X^*)$. With the frame convention 000537B2987D 10.40.3 \begin{equation}  e_ i=g_{ij}e_ j,\qquad g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}, \end{equation} the identification sends a line bundle to the class of $(g_{ij})$. The exponential sheaf sequence \[  0\longrightarrow \underline{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow \mathcal O_ X \xrightarrow {\  f\mapsto \exp (2\pi \mathrm i f)\  } \mathcal O_ X^*\longrightarrow 1  \] is exact. Its long exact sequence contains 4C4BC52B37E3 10.40.4 \begin{equation}  H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\longrightarrow H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X) \longrightarrow \operatorname {Pic}(X) \xrightarrow {\  c_1^{\mathbb Z}\  }H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}) \longrightarrow H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X), \end{equation} where $c_1^{\mathbb Z}$ is the connecting map. The group of smooth complex line bundles is likewise $H^1(X,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}^*)$, and its exponential connecting map is an isomorphism onto $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$; here $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ is the sheaf of smooth complex functions. Equivalently smooth Hermitian line bundles are classified by the same group, using smooth circle-valued transition functions. These smooth classification assertions hold on any real smooth manifold as well. Proof. Holomorphic frames give the cocycle in ( 10.40.3 ). Replacing $e_ i$ by $a_ i e_ i$ changes it to $a_ i g_{ij}a_ j^{-1}$, hence by a coboundary. Conversely a cocycle glues the trivial lines by identifying $z e_ i$ with $z g_{ij}e_ j$. The cocycle identity makes this an equivalence relation, and the trivializations give the local bundle charts. A change by a coboundary gives an isomorphism by the same frame change. Any bundle isomorphism has this local form. Passing to a common refinement treats different covers, and tensor products and duals multiply and invert cocycles. Apply lemma 10.40.1 . The proof works identically for smooth nonzero or circle-valued functions. A smooth line bundle has a smooth metric by the partition construction of smooth line-bundle metrics and curvature changes , whose partition formula uses only smooth transition functions. Dividing its local frames by their positive lengths makes its transitions circle-valued. Conversely the Euclidean metrics glue for circle-valued transitions. Rescaling a metric by the square of a positive smooth function gives a unitary isomorphism, so its choice does not change the classification. A nowhere zero holomorphic germ has a holomorphic logarithm after shrinking its domain: divide by its value at the center and use the convergent power series for $\log (1+w)$ on $|w|<1$. The exponential kernel consists exactly of locally constant integers. This proves sheaf exactness; it does not assert a logarithm on each whole overlap. The sheaf long exact sequence gives ( 10.40.4 ). The identical local argument gives the smooth complex exponential sequence. Its additive middle sheaf is a smooth-function module and is acyclic by proposition 10.43.10 ; its $H^1$ and $H^2$ vanish, so its connecting map is an isomorphism. Alternatively use $0\to \underline{\mathbb Z}\to \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} \to \mathcal T\to 1$, where $\mathcal T$ is the sheaf of smooth circle-valued functions. The inclusion of the holomorphic sequence in the smooth complex sequence, and the morphism from either to the circle sequence given by $f\mapsto \operatorname {Re}f$ and $g\mapsto g/|g|$, are the identity on $\underline{\mathbb Z}$. Naturality therefore identifies all the connecting classes of the same underlying line bundle. $\square$ Theorem 10.40.5 . F699EBC79AEB Let $L$ be a smooth Hermitian line bundle on a smooth manifold $M$, and let $D$ be a compatible connection, with curvature $\Theta (D)$. Its real coefficient class satisfies \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)_{\mathbb R} =\Psi _2\! \left(\left[\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta (D)\right]\right) \quad \hbox{in }H^2(M,\underline{\mathbb R}).  \] This is independent of the compatible connection. For a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth metric, it is the de Rham class of the canonical form $c_1(L,h)$ in the opening convention. Proof. In unit frames $u_ i=t_{ij}u_ j$ the connection is $d+A_ i$, where $A_ i$ is imaginary-valued and \[  A_ i-A_ j=t_{ij}^{-1}dt_{ij}.  \] Compatible connections exist: for a subordinate smooth partition $(\rho _ l)$ set $A_ i=\sum _ l\rho _ l t_{il}^{-1}dt_{il}$ on $U_ i$, extending each summand by zero from $U_ i\cap U_ l$. The supports of $\rho _ l$ make these extensions smooth and the sum locally finite. The cocycle identity gives exactly the displayed transformation law. Then $\Theta =dA_ i$ glues and is closed and imaginary-valued. The difference of two compatible connections is a global imaginary one-form, so their normalized curvatures differ by an exact real form. Write $\mathcal Z^ r_{\mathbb R}$ for the sheaf of closed smooth real $r$-forms. The logarithmic derivative gives a commutative diagram of exact sheaf sequences \[  \begin{array}{ccccccccc} 0& \to & \underline{\mathbb Z}& \to & \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} & \xrightarrow {\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\, \cdot )}& \mathcal T& \to & 1\\ & & \downarrow & & \Vert & & \downarrow \ell \\  0& \to & \underline{\mathbb R}& \to & \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} & \xrightarrow {d}& \mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R}& \to & 0, \end{array} \qquad \ell (t)=\frac{t^{-1}dt}{2\pi \mathrm i}.  \] Local logarithms and the real Poincaré lemma prove the exactness and that $\ell (t)$ is a closed real form. In the sequence $0\to \mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R}\to \mathcal A^1_{\mathbb R} \xrightarrow {d}\mathcal Z^2_{\mathbb R}\to 0$, put \[  b_ i=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }A_ i,\qquad \omega =db_ i=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta (D).  \] The crucial signs are \[  b_ j-b_ i=-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }t_{ij}^{-1}dt_{ij} =\ell (t_{ij}).  \] By lemma 10.40.1 , the connecting image of $\omega $ is $[\ell (t)]\in H^1(M,\mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R})$. Following by the connecting map of the lower row is exactly the de Rham resolution comparison: it is the succession of positive connecting maps in theorem 10.43.8 . Naturality of the displayed diagram identifies its value with the real image of the upper-row class $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)$. Thus no cover with simply connected intersections, or logarithms on whole overlaps, was assumed. In a holomorphic frame $e_ i$ write $h_ i=|e_ i|_ h^2$. The compatible connection with canonical $(0,1)$-part has form $\partial \log h_ i$; indeed metric compatibility determines its $(1,0)$-part by $dh_ i/h_ i$. In the unit frame $e_ i/\sqrt{h_ i}$ its form is $A_ i=\tfrac 12(\partial -\bar\partial )\log h_ i$. Hence \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }dA_ i =-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial \log h_ i =c_1(L,h).  \] This also proves the required normalization directly. An arbitrary complex connection differs from a compatible one by a global complex one-form; its normalized curvature has the same complex de Rham class, although its representative need not be real. $\square$ On $\mathbb P^1$ the canonical frames $X_0,X_1$ of $\mathcal O(1)$ satisfy $X_0=z^{-1}X_1$. Thus this proof uses $g_{01}=z^{-1}$, not its inverse. The Fubini–Study squared norm is $|X_0|^2=(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$, and \[  c_1(\mathcal O(1),h_{\rm FS}) =dd^ c\log (1+|z|^2),\qquad \int _{\mathbb P^1}c_1(\mathcal O(1),h_{\rm FS}) =\frac1\pi \int _{\mathbb C}\frac{dx\, dy}{(1+|z|^2)^2}=1.  \] The integral is $2\int _0^\infty r(1+r^2)^{-2}dr=1$. Consequently the connecting class and the canonical positive curvature have the same, explicitly positive, sign. This is the existing Fubini–Study computation of the Fubini–Study curvature computation , used as a sign check. Theorem 10.40.6 . 3A11E04C8D5D Let $X$ be any complex manifold and $\omega $ a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form. Suppose its de Rham class is the image of $a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. There are a holomorphic line bundle $L$ and a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ with \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)=a,\qquad c_1(L,h)=\omega .  \] Conversely every such curvature form has integral de Rham class. Proof. Choose a smooth Hermitian line bundle of class $a$ using theorem 10.40.2 , and a compatible connection $D_0$. Put $\omega _0=\mathrm i\Theta (D_0)/(2\pi )$. By theorem 10.40.5 , $\omega -\omega _0=d\beta $ for a global smooth real one-form $\beta $. The compatible connection $D=D_0-2\pi \mathrm i\beta $ has normalized curvature $\omega $. Its $(0,1)$-part squares to zero because $\omega ^{0,2}=0$. Here is the needed local rank-one integration, without a general bundle integrability theorem. In a smooth local frame write $D''=\bar\partial +A^{0,1}$. The curvature equation gives $\bar\partial A^{0,1}=0$, since the wedge square of a scalar one-form is zero. The smooth local Dolbeault lemma local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents gives, on a smaller coordinate neighborhood, $A^{0,1}=\bar\partial f$. The nonzero frame $e^{-f}e$ is annihilated by $D''$. Ratios between these frames are nonzero smooth functions annihilated by $\bar\partial $, hence are holomorphic. They define a holomorphic line bundle structure with canonical operator $D''$. Metric compatibility now makes $D$ its Chern connection, by the local calculation in the preceding theorem. Its curvature is therefore exactly $\omega $, and the underlying smooth class is still $a$. Naturality of the exponential sequences proves $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)=a$. The converse is the preceding theorem. $\square$ Proposition 10.40.7 . 95F15B630D64 Under the de Rham and Dolbeault comparisons of corollary 10.43.11 , the coefficient inclusion $\underline{\mathbb C}\to \mathcal O_ X$ induces $[\eta ]\mapsto [\eta ^{0,q}]$ from degree-$q$ complex de Rham cohomology to $H^ q(X,\mathcal O_ X)$. Proof. The projection of a degree-$q$ form to its $(0,q)$-component is a map from the de Rham resolution to the Dolbeault resolution, since $(d\eta )^{0,q+1} =\bar\partial \eta ^{0,q}$. On the augmented kernels it is precisely the coefficient inclusion. Naturality of that comparison proves the claimed map, including its sign. $\square$ Theorem 10.40.8 (Lefschetz $(1,1)$ theorem) . 7CEC8FD0F9CB Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. Write $a_{\mathbb C}$ for the complex de Rham image of $a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$, and use the canonical type subspaces of theorem 10.47.13 . Then \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(\operatorname {Pic}(X)) =\{ a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}): a_{\mathbb C}\in H^{1,1}(X)\} .  \] In particular the real Chern classes are exactly the integral real de Rham classes of type $(1,1)$, where integral means in the image of $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\to H^2_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb R)$. This includes every integral lift, rather than discarding classes whose real image is zero. Proof. By proposition 10.40.7 , the coefficient map $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb C})\to H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)$ sends a closed form to the Dolbeault class of its $(0,2)$-component. The Kähler Hodge theorem identifies this with projection to $H^{0,2}(X)$: choose the unique harmonic de Rham representative and split it by type. Each component is Dolbeault harmonic and represents the indicated Dolbeault class. Its $(0,2)$ class vanishes exactly when that component is zero. An integral class has real image, so complex conjugation exchanges its harmonic $(0,2)$ and $(2,0)$ components. Thus its image in $H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)$ is zero exactly when it is of type $(1,1)$. Exactness of ( 10.40.4 ) now proves the asserted equality with the full integral group. The real-image formulation follows from theorem 10.40.5 . $\square$ Corollary 10.40.9 . B92385CA0FAE Let $X$ be compact Kähler, $L$ a holomorphic line bundle, and $\theta $ a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form in its real Chern class. There is a smooth metric $h$ on this same $L$ with $c_1(L,h)=\theta $. In particular $L$ is positive if its real Chern class contains a Kähler form. Proof. Take a smooth metric $h_0$. The exact real $(1,1)$-form $\theta -c_1(L,h_0)$ equals $dd^ c\varphi $ for a smooth real $\varphi $ by the compact Kähler $(1,1)$-current $dd^ c$ decomposition . The canonical metric transformation formula gives $c_1(L,h_0e^{-\varphi })=\theta $. $\square$ Theorem 10.40.10 . 4B30A0968D23 For a compact complex manifold $X$, the following are equivalent: $X$ admits a holomorphic embedding as an algebraic submanifold of a finite-dimensional complex projective space; $X$ has a positive holomorphic line bundle; $X$ has a Kähler form whose de Rham class is integral; $X$ has a Kähler form with class in $I^2(X)_{\mathbb Q}=\bigcup _{m\geq 1}m^{-1}I^2(X)$, where $I^2(X)$ is the integral image in real de Rham cohomology. Proof. An embedding pulls back the positive Fubini–Study metric of $\mathcal O(1)$, proving (1)$\Rightarrow $(2). Its normalized curvature, or that of any positive line bundle, is an integral Kähler form by theorem 10.40.5 ; thus (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). Conversely (3)$\Rightarrow $(2) is theorem 10.40.6 . By theorem 10.39.5 , a positive line bundle has all sufficiently high powers very ample, giving a holomorphic embedding with closed complex submanifold image $Y$. The following finite homogeneous consequence of the already proved the Remmert–Stein extension theorem , Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules shows that this image is algebraic. Its inverse image in $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ is an analytic cone with every branch of dimension at least one. Remmert–Stein extends it across $0$ to an analytic cone $C$. Choose finite local holomorphic equations $f_ j=\sum _{k\geq 0}P_{jk}$ at $0$, with $P_{jk}$ homogeneous of degree $k$. Scaling on $C$ shows that every $P_{jk}$ vanishes on $C$. Conversely their simultaneous vanishing implies that of the $f_ j$ near $0$, and scaling then identifies their common zero set with $C$. The ideal of holomorphic germs generated by all $P_{jk}$ is finitely generated. Each generator is a finite combination of the $P_{jk}$, so a finite subcollection of these homogeneous polynomials generates the same germ ideal. Their global common zero set is still $C$: if they vanish at $z$, fix any other $P_{jk}$ and evaluate its germ relation at $tz$ for sufficiently small nonzero $t$. Homogeneity gives $P_{jk}(z)=0$. This holds for every $j,k$; the preceding paragraph then puts $z$ in $C$. Projectivizing the finite equations proves that $Y$ is algebraic. The empty case uses the equation $1$, and full projective space uses no equations. Thus (2)$\Rightarrow $(1). Finally (3) implies (4), and multiplying a form in (4) by its positive integer denominator gives (3). $\square$ Remark 10.40.11 . CECCCE9F65C5 Compact manifolds have finitely many components; all assertions apply componentwise. On a zero-dimensional compact component the degree-two groups, curvature forms and differentials vanish, and a finite set embeds in projective space. Positivity and the Kähler condition on the zero tangent space are vacuous. Embeddings of finitely many positive-dimensional components may be put into disjoint projective linear subspaces, and a common sufficiently high power works for all. The notation $I^2(X)_{\mathbb Q}$ explicitly means the rational span of the integral image. No identification with the image of all of $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Q})$, no singular integral lattice or integral Poincaré duality, and no ambient-dimension bound for the projective embedding is asserted here. Those conclusions require their respective additional comparison or projection theorem. In particular a positive real cohomology class is not declared integral.

text: Theorem 10.40.2 . EA66BB854401 The tensor-product group $\operatorname {Pic}(X)$ of holomorphic line bundles on a complex manifold $X$ is naturally $H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X^*)$. With the frame convention 000537B2987D 10.40.3 \begin{equation}  e_ i=g_{ij}e_ j,\qquad g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}, \end{equation} the identification sends a line bundle to the class of $(g_{ij})$. The exponential sheaf sequence \[  0\longrightarrow \underline{\mathbb Z}\longrightarrow \mathcal O_ X \xrightarrow {\  f\mapsto \exp (2\pi \mathrm i f)\  } \mathcal O_ X^*\longrightarrow 1  \] is exact. Its long exact sequence contains 4C4BC52B37E3 10.40.4 \begin{equation}  H^1(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\longrightarrow H^1(X,\mathcal O_ X) \longrightarrow \operatorname {Pic}(X) \xrightarrow {\  c_1^{\mathbb Z}\  }H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}) \longrightarrow H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X), \end{equation} where $c_1^{\mathbb Z}$ is the connecting map. The group of smooth complex line bundles is likewise $H^1(X,\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}^*)$, and its exponential connecting map is an isomorphism onto $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$; here $\mathcal A_{\mathbb C}$ is the sheaf of smooth complex functions. Equivalently smooth Hermitian line bundles are classified by the same group, using smooth circle-valued transition functions. These smooth classification assertions hold on any real smooth manifold as well. Proof. Holomorphic frames give the cocycle in ( 10.40.3 ). Replacing $e_ i$ by $a_ i e_ i$ changes it to $a_ i g_{ij}a_ j^{-1}$, hence by a coboundary. Conversely a cocycle glues the trivial lines by identifying $z e_ i$ with $z g_{ij}e_ j$. The cocycle identity makes this an equivalence relation, and the trivializations give the local bundle charts. A change by a coboundary gives an isomorphism by the same frame change. Any bundle isomorphism has this local form. Passing to a common refinement treats different covers, and tensor products and duals multiply and invert cocycles. Apply lemma 10.40.1 . The proof works identically for smooth nonzero or circle-valued functions. A smooth line bundle has a smooth metric by the partition construction of smooth line-bundle metrics and curvature changes , whose partition formula uses only smooth transition functions. Dividing its local frames by their positive lengths makes its transitions circle-valued. Conversely the Euclidean metrics glue for circle-valued transitions. Rescaling a metric by the square of a positive smooth function gives a unitary isomorphism, so its choice does not change the classification. A nowhere zero holomorphic germ has a holomorphic logarithm after shrinking its domain: divide by its value at the center and use the convergent power series for $\log (1+w)$ on $|w|<1$. The exponential kernel consists exactly of locally constant integers. This proves sheaf exactness; it does not assert a logarithm on each whole overlap. The sheaf long exact sequence gives ( 10.40.4 ). The identical local argument gives the smooth complex exponential sequence. Its additive middle sheaf is a smooth-function module and is acyclic by proposition 10.43.10 ; its $H^1$ and $H^2$ vanish, so its connecting map is an isomorphism. Alternatively use $0\to \underline{\mathbb Z}\to \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} \to \mathcal T\to 1$, where $\mathcal T$ is the sheaf of smooth circle-valued functions. The inclusion of the holomorphic sequence in the smooth complex sequence, and the morphism from either to the circle sequence given by $f\mapsto \operatorname {Re}f$ and $g\mapsto g/|g|$, are the identity on $\underline{\mathbb Z}$. Naturality therefore identifies all the connecting classes of the same underlying line bundle. $\square$
