title: Theorem 10.40.5
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Theorem 10.40.5 . F699EBC79AEB Let $L$ be a smooth Hermitian line bundle on a smooth manifold $M$, and let $D$ be a compatible connection, with curvature $\Theta (D)$. Its real coefficient class satisfies \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)_{\mathbb R} =\Psi _2\! \left(\left[\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta (D)\right]\right) \quad \hbox{in }H^2(M,\underline{\mathbb R}).  \] This is independent of the compatible connection. For a holomorphic line bundle with a smooth metric, it is the de Rham class of the canonical form $c_1(L,h)$ in the opening convention. Proof. In unit frames $u_ i=t_{ij}u_ j$ the connection is $d+A_ i$, where $A_ i$ is imaginary-valued and \[  A_ i-A_ j=t_{ij}^{-1}dt_{ij}.  \] Compatible connections exist: for a subordinate smooth partition $(\rho _ l)$ set $A_ i=\sum _ l\rho _ l t_{il}^{-1}dt_{il}$ on $U_ i$, extending each summand by zero from $U_ i\cap U_ l$. The supports of $\rho _ l$ make these extensions smooth and the sum locally finite. The cocycle identity gives exactly the displayed transformation law. Then $\Theta =dA_ i$ glues and is closed and imaginary-valued. The difference of two compatible connections is a global imaginary one-form, so their normalized curvatures differ by an exact real form. Write $\mathcal Z^ r_{\mathbb R}$ for the sheaf of closed smooth real $r$-forms. The logarithmic derivative gives a commutative diagram of exact sheaf sequences \[  \begin{array}{ccccccccc} 0& \to & \underline{\mathbb Z}& \to & \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} & \xrightarrow {\exp (2\pi \mathrm i\, \cdot )}& \mathcal T& \to & 1\\ & & \downarrow & & \Vert & & \downarrow \ell \\  0& \to & \underline{\mathbb R}& \to & \mathcal A_{\mathbb R} & \xrightarrow {d}& \mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R}& \to & 0, \end{array} \qquad \ell (t)=\frac{t^{-1}dt}{2\pi \mathrm i}.  \] Local logarithms and the real Poincaré lemma prove the exactness and that $\ell (t)$ is a closed real form. In the sequence $0\to \mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R}\to \mathcal A^1_{\mathbb R} \xrightarrow {d}\mathcal Z^2_{\mathbb R}\to 0$, put \[  b_ i=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }A_ i,\qquad \omega =db_ i=\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\Theta (D).  \] The crucial signs are \[  b_ j-b_ i=-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }t_{ij}^{-1}dt_{ij} =\ell (t_{ij}).  \] By lemma 10.40.1 , the connecting image of $\omega $ is $[\ell (t)]\in H^1(M,\mathcal Z^1_{\mathbb R})$. Following by the connecting map of the lower row is exactly the de Rham resolution comparison: it is the succession of positive connecting maps in theorem 10.43.8 . Naturality of the displayed diagram identifies its value with the real image of the upper-row class $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)$. Thus no cover with simply connected intersections, or logarithms on whole overlaps, was assumed. In a holomorphic frame $e_ i$ write $h_ i=|e_ i|_ h^2$. The compatible connection with canonical $(0,1)$-part has form $\partial \log h_ i$; indeed metric compatibility determines its $(1,0)$-part by $dh_ i/h_ i$. In the unit frame $e_ i/\sqrt{h_ i}$ its form is $A_ i=\tfrac 12(\partial -\bar\partial )\log h_ i$. Hence \[  \frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }dA_ i =-\frac{\mathrm i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial \log h_ i =c_1(L,h).  \] This also proves the required normalization directly. An arbitrary complex connection differs from a compatible one by a global complex one-form; its normalized curvature has the same complex de Rham class, although its representative need not be real. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.40.6
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Theorem 10.40.6 . 3A11E04C8D5D Let $X$ be any complex manifold and $\omega $ a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form. Suppose its de Rham class is the image of $a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$. There are a holomorphic line bundle $L$ and a smooth Hermitian metric $h$ with \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)=a,\qquad c_1(L,h)=\omega .  \] Conversely every such curvature form has integral de Rham class. Proof. Choose a smooth Hermitian line bundle of class $a$ using theorem 10.40.2 , and a compatible connection $D_0$. Put $\omega _0=\mathrm i\Theta (D_0)/(2\pi )$. By theorem 10.40.5 , $\omega -\omega _0=d\beta $ for a global smooth real one-form $\beta $. The compatible connection $D=D_0-2\pi \mathrm i\beta $ has normalized curvature $\omega $. Its $(0,1)$-part squares to zero because $\omega ^{0,2}=0$. Here is the needed local rank-one integration, without a general bundle integrability theorem. In a smooth local frame write $D''=\bar\partial +A^{0,1}$. The curvature equation gives $\bar\partial A^{0,1}=0$, since the wedge square of a scalar one-form is zero. The smooth local Dolbeault lemma local Dolbeault exactness for forms and currents gives, on a smaller coordinate neighborhood, $A^{0,1}=\bar\partial f$. The nonzero frame $e^{-f}e$ is annihilated by $D''$. Ratios between these frames are nonzero smooth functions annihilated by $\bar\partial $, hence are holomorphic. They define a holomorphic line bundle structure with canonical operator $D''$. Metric compatibility now makes $D$ its Chern connection, by the local calculation in the preceding theorem. Its curvature is therefore exactly $\omega $, and the underlying smooth class is still $a$. Naturality of the exponential sequences proves $c_1^{\mathbb Z}(L)=a$. The converse is the preceding theorem. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.40.7
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Proposition 10.40.7 . 95F15B630D64 Under the de Rham and Dolbeault comparisons of corollary 10.43.11 , the coefficient inclusion $\underline{\mathbb C}\to \mathcal O_ X$ induces $[\eta ]\mapsto [\eta ^{0,q}]$ from degree-$q$ complex de Rham cohomology to $H^ q(X,\mathcal O_ X)$. Proof. The projection of a degree-$q$ form to its $(0,q)$-component is a map from the de Rham resolution to the Dolbeault resolution, since $(d\eta )^{0,q+1} =\bar\partial \eta ^{0,q}$. On the augmented kernels it is precisely the coefficient inclusion. Naturality of that comparison proves the claimed map, including its sign. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.40.8 (Lefschetz (1,1) theorem)
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Theorem 10.40.8 (Lefschetz $(1,1)$ theorem) . 7CEC8FD0F9CB Let $X$ be a compact Kähler manifold. Write $a_{\mathbb C}$ for the complex de Rham image of $a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})$, and use the canonical type subspaces of theorem 10.47.13 . Then \[  c_1^{\mathbb Z}(\operatorname {Pic}(X)) =\{ a\in H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z}): a_{\mathbb C}\in H^{1,1}(X)\} .  \] In particular the real Chern classes are exactly the integral real de Rham classes of type $(1,1)$, where integral means in the image of $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Z})\to H^2_{\rm dR}(X,\mathbb R)$. This includes every integral lift, rather than discarding classes whose real image is zero. Proof. By proposition 10.40.7 , the coefficient map $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb C})\to H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)$ sends a closed form to the Dolbeault class of its $(0,2)$-component. The Kähler Hodge theorem identifies this with projection to $H^{0,2}(X)$: choose the unique harmonic de Rham representative and split it by type. Each component is Dolbeault harmonic and represents the indicated Dolbeault class. Its $(0,2)$ class vanishes exactly when that component is zero. An integral class has real image, so complex conjugation exchanges its harmonic $(0,2)$ and $(2,0)$ components. Thus its image in $H^2(X,\mathcal O_ X)$ is zero exactly when it is of type $(1,1)$. Exactness of ( 10.40.4 ) now proves the asserted equality with the full integral group. The real-image formulation follows from theorem 10.40.5 . $\square$

title: Corollary 10.40.9
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Corollary 10.40.9 . B92385CA0FAE Let $X$ be compact Kähler, $L$ a holomorphic line bundle, and $\theta $ a smooth closed real $(1,1)$-form in its real Chern class. There is a smooth metric $h$ on this same $L$ with $c_1(L,h)=\theta $. In particular $L$ is positive if its real Chern class contains a Kähler form. Proof. Take a smooth metric $h_0$. The exact real $(1,1)$-form $\theta -c_1(L,h_0)$ equals $dd^ c\varphi $ for a smooth real $\varphi $ by the compact Kähler $(1,1)$-current $dd^ c$ decomposition . The canonical metric transformation formula gives $c_1(L,h_0e^{-\varphi })=\theta $. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.40.10
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Theorem 10.40.10 . 4B30A0968D23 For a compact complex manifold $X$, the following are equivalent: $X$ admits a holomorphic embedding as an algebraic submanifold of a finite-dimensional complex projective space; $X$ has a positive holomorphic line bundle; $X$ has a Kähler form whose de Rham class is integral; $X$ has a Kähler form with class in $I^2(X)_{\mathbb Q}=\bigcup _{m\geq 1}m^{-1}I^2(X)$, where $I^2(X)$ is the integral image in real de Rham cohomology. Proof. An embedding pulls back the positive Fubini–Study metric of $\mathcal O(1)$, proving (1)$\Rightarrow $(2). Its normalized curvature, or that of any positive line bundle, is an integral Kähler form by theorem 10.40.5 ; thus (2)$\Rightarrow $(3). Conversely (3)$\Rightarrow $(2) is theorem 10.40.6 . By theorem 10.39.5 , a positive line bundle has all sufficiently high powers very ample, giving a holomorphic embedding with closed complex submanifold image $Y$. The following finite homogeneous consequence of the already proved the Remmert–Stein extension theorem , Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules shows that this image is algebraic. Its inverse image in $\mathbb C^{N+1}\setminus \{ 0\} $ is an analytic cone with every branch of dimension at least one. Remmert–Stein extends it across $0$ to an analytic cone $C$. Choose finite local holomorphic equations $f_ j=\sum _{k\geq 0}P_{jk}$ at $0$, with $P_{jk}$ homogeneous of degree $k$. Scaling on $C$ shows that every $P_{jk}$ vanishes on $C$. Conversely their simultaneous vanishing implies that of the $f_ j$ near $0$, and scaling then identifies their common zero set with $C$. The ideal of holomorphic germs generated by all $P_{jk}$ is finitely generated. Each generator is a finite combination of the $P_{jk}$, so a finite subcollection of these homogeneous polynomials generates the same germ ideal. Their global common zero set is still $C$: if they vanish at $z$, fix any other $P_{jk}$ and evaluate its germ relation at $tz$ for sufficiently small nonzero $t$. Homogeneity gives $P_{jk}(z)=0$. This holds for every $j,k$; the preceding paragraph then puts $z$ in $C$. Projectivizing the finite equations proves that $Y$ is algebraic. The empty case uses the equation $1$, and full projective space uses no equations. Thus (2)$\Rightarrow $(1). Finally (3) implies (4), and multiplying a form in (4) by its positive integer denominator gives (3). $\square$

title: Remark 10.40.11
section: 10.40 Line bundles and integral curvature
text: Remark 10.40.11 . CECCCE9F65C5 Compact manifolds have finitely many components; all assertions apply componentwise. On a zero-dimensional compact component the degree-two groups, curvature forms and differentials vanish, and a finite set embeds in projective space. Positivity and the Kähler condition on the zero tangent space are vacuous. Embeddings of finitely many positive-dimensional components may be put into disjoint projective linear subspaces, and a common sufficiently high power works for all. The notation $I^2(X)_{\mathbb Q}$ explicitly means the rational span of the integral image. No identification with the image of all of $H^2(X,\underline{\mathbb Q})$, no singular integral lattice or integral Poincaré duality, and no ambient-dimension bound for the projective embedding is asserted here. Those conclusions require their respective additional comparison or projection theorem. In particular a positive real cohomology class is not declared integral.

title: 7.29 Classical products with compact unbounded loci
search_title: Classical products with compact unbounded loci
section: 7.29 Classical products with compact unbounded loci
text: The unbounded locus $L(u)$ of a plurisubharmonic function is the closed set of points near which it is not locally bounded. It can be larger than $\{ u=-\infty \} $. We retain $d^ c=\frac{i}{4\pi }(\bar\partial -\partial )$. All products below are classical current products, defined by coefficient integrability and $dd^ c$, including any mass on pole sets. Lemma 7.29.1 . 438B9224299E Let $B=B(a,R)\Subset \mathbb C^ n$, put $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and $\omega =dd^ c\psi $, and let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Suppose the locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $f_0,\ldots ,f_ r$ are defined near $\overline B$, are nonpositive on $B$ and all equal $A\psi $ on a collar of $\partial B$, for some $A>0$. Write $M_ T=\int _ B T\wedge \omega ^ p$. Then 9135B1E39C61 \begin{align}  \int _ B dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r} & =A^ rM_ T & & (0\leq r\leq p), \tag{7.29.2}\\  \int _ B(-f_0)\, dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T \wedge \omega ^{p-r} & \leq \| \psi \| _{L^\infty (B)}A^{r+1}M_ T & & (0\leq r\leq p-1). \tag{7.29.3} \end{align} The constants do not involve bounds for the $f_ j$ inside $B$. Moreover, if $R_1$ is closed positive of bidimension $(1,1)$ near $\overline B$, $a_1$ is smooth, $b_1$ is $L^1$ for the coefficient variations of $R_1$, and $dd^ c(b_1R_1)$ has measure coefficients, then $a_1=b_1$ on a collar implies 90ED91EDE196 7.29.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ B a_1\, dd^ c(b_1R_1)=\int _ B b_1\, dd^ ca_1\wedge R_1, \end{equation} provided the left-hand measure has finite mass near $\overline B$. Proof. The bounded products, their locality, smooth-factor rules and symmetry are those of locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products , decreasing continuity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products . They have finite mass near $\overline B$ by the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate in the interior and their fixed smooth factors on the collar. Replace each $dd^ cf_ j$ in turn by $A\omega $: the difference is $dd^ c$ of $(f_ j-A\psi )$ times a closed product, compactly supported in $B$. Its integral against the remaining closed power of $\omega $ is zero, by testing with a compact cutoff equal to one near that support. This proves ( 7.29.2 ). For $r\leq p-1$, apply integration by parts with a common boundary collar to $f_0$ and the smooth function $A\psi $, with base current $dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r-1}$. Dividing the resulting identity by $A$ gives \[  \int _ B(-f_0)\, dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r} =\int _ B(-\psi )\, dd^ cf_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r \wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r-1}.  \] The mass identity with $r+1$ factors proves the bound. For the final assertion put $h=(b_1-a_1)|_ B$, which is $L^1(R_1)$ and has compact support in $B$; extend it by zero when needed. Since $R_1$ is closed, on $B$ one has $dd^ c(b_1R_1)=dd^ ca_1\wedge R_1+dd^ c(hR_1)$. Choose a compact cutoff $\chi $ equal to one near the support of $hR_1$. Distributional integration by parts gives \[  \int _ B a_1\, dd^ c(hR_1) =\int \chi a_1\, dd^ c(hR_1) =\int h\, dd^ c(\chi a_1)\wedge R_1 =\int _ B h\, dd^ ca_1\wedge R_1.  \] All integrals are finite: the smooth coefficients are bounded on $\overline B$, and $h\in L^1(R_1)$. Adding the smooth term proves ( 7.29.4 ). This extends the bounded common-collar argument using precisely the needed integrability. $\square$ Theorem 7.29.5 . 8FBB0E4DE397 Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold $X$. Suppose a finite family of plurisubharmonic functions has the following property: $X$ is covered by coordinate balls $B$ with compact closure in their charts, such that every function of the family is locally bounded on a neighborhood of $\partial B$. For $0\leq r\leq p$, their recursive products \[  P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) =dd^ c\bigl (u_1P_ T(u_2,\ldots ,u_ r)\bigr ),\qquad P_ T()=T,  \] are well defined closed positive currents. They are symmetric, additive and positively homogeneous in the potentials, unchanged by addition of constants, and local in the ordinary topology. For $0\leq r\leq p-1$, an additional function $u_0$ of the family is locally integrable for the coefficient variations of $P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r)$. If $u_{l,j}\downarrow u_ l$ are any decreasing plurisubharmonic approximations, then \begin{align*}  P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j})& \longrightarrow P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) & & (0\leq r\leq p),\\  u_{0,j}P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j}) & \longrightarrow u_0P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) & & (0\leq r\leq p-1) \end{align*} weakly. The limits need not be locally bounded in the interior of the balls. All listed potentials, including the limit of a weight, are subject to the common-boundary hypothesis. Proof. We prove the assertions simultaneously for arbitrary positive closed base currents and all their bidimensions. No assertion of integrability of an unbounded weight against a top-degree current is included. 1. A collar without cutting off interior singularities. Fix a ball $B$, a compact set $K\Subset B$ and the finitely many sequences involved. On a fixed annulus around $\partial B$, their limits are bounded below, and $u_ l\leq u_{l,j}\leq u_{l,1}$ gives bounds uniform in $j$. After subtracting constants, arrange that all these functions are at most $-1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Choose two concentric inner spheres, outside $K$ and all their unbounded loci in $B$, such that the closed annulus between and outside them lies where the limits are bounded below by $-M$. Let $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and take $A$ so large that $A\psi <-M-2$ on a neighborhood of the inner sphere. Leave each function unchanged inside that sphere, and on the outer annulus replace it by $\max \{ u,A\psi \} $. The formulas agree near the inner gluing sphere, so this is plurisubharmonic by maximum and boundary gluing of plurisubharmonic functions . Near $\partial B$ it is $A\psi $, since $u\leq -1$. The same choices work for every $j$, preserve inequalities and decreasing limits, and leave the functions unchanged near $K$. They are nonpositive on $B$. We henceforth use the modified functions and the same symbols. Each fixed modified function has smooth decreasing plurisubharmonic approximations with this same collar. Indeed, convolve the original function on a slightly larger ball and on the annulus use the smooth maximum $M_\varepsilon (u*\rho _\varepsilon ,A\psi )$ of smooth convex approximations of the maximum , with the decreasing regularization of the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . On the inner gluing annulus the two arguments have a gap greater than $2\varepsilon $ for small $\varepsilon $, so this equals $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ there. Near the outer sphere it equals $A\psi $. Thus it glues to the convolution in the interior. The convolution and smooth maximum both decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, so these smooth functions decrease to the modification. They remain nonpositive on $B$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon $: wherever the maximum is not an exact branch, both arguments are bounded away from zero; near the sphere the exact branch is $A\psi $. Their boundedness for fixed $\varepsilon $ follows from smoothness near $\overline B$. It suffices to prove the theorem for functions with this fixed collar, on $B$. On the collar all products are ordinary bounded products with factors $A\omega $, where $\omega =dd^ c\psi $. Consequently, whenever weak convergence is established in $B$, integrals over the whole ball converge as well if the currents in question have this fixed collar: split the integral with a compact cutoff equal to one away from the collar. The complementary integrals are fixed and finite. 2. Starting the induction. Suppose $p\geq 1$ and $u\leq 0$ has the fixed collar. Its bounded truncations $u_ N=\max \{ u,-N\} $ have the same collar for all large $N$. The $r=0$ case of ( 7.29.3 ) gives \[  \int _ B(-u_ N)T\wedge \omega ^ p \leq \| \psi \| _\infty A M_ T.  \] Monotone convergence, with the measure fixed, proves $u\in L^1(T\wedge \omega ^ p)$ and hence coefficient integrability. For $u_ j\downarrow u$, the normalized functions are nonpositive and $|u_ j|\leq |u|$; dominated convergence gives $u_ jT\to uT$. This is the weighted assertion for zero Hessian factors. The unweighted zero-factor assertion is $T\to T$. If $p=0$, only that unweighted assertion is required. 3. Constructing the next product and its unweighted limit. Assume the weighted assertions have been proved for fewer than $r$ Hessian factors, for all base currents, and let $1\leq r\leq p$. By induction the product with $r-1$ factors is closed positive, and the first potential is integrable for it. Therefore the displayed recursion defines $P_ T$ with $r$ factors. With this fixed base product, bounded truncations of the first potential converge in coefficient $L^1$. Applying $dd^ c$ shows that the new product is a weak limit of closed positive bounded products, hence closed positive. For simultaneous decreasing approximations, the weighted induction hypothesis with weight $u_{1,j}$ and factors $u_{2,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j}$, followed by $dd^ c$, proves the unweighted convergence for $r$ factors. Smooth decreasing approximations then show symmetry, because the smooth exterior products are symmetric. The recursion gives locality, linearity, invariance under constants and compatibility with multiplication of the base current by a smooth closed positive form; these follow exactly by coefficient integration and the smooth-factor Leibniz rule. In particular the construction agrees in overlapping charts and is independent of this local collar modification wherever that modification leaves the functions unchanged. For bounded simultaneous truncations, the mass identity ( 7.29.2 ) holds. Their just-proved unweighted convergence and the fixed collar pass that identity to the possibly unbounded limits. Thus $P_ T$ with $r$ factors has finite total trace mass on $B$, equal to $A^ rM_ T$ in the $\omega $ normalization. 4. Integrability of the next weight. Let $r\leq p-1$. Put $S=P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r)$ and $S_ N=P_ T(u_{1,N},\ldots ,u_{r,N})$, with simultaneous bounded truncations of all the functions, including $u_0$. We know $S_ N\to S$. The uniform bounded-collar estimate gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{0,N})S_ N\wedge \omega ^{p-r}\leq C, \qquad C=\| \psi \| _\infty A^{r+1}M_ T.  \] For fixed $m$ and $N\geq m$, one has $-u_{0,m}\leq -u_{0,N}$. For a nonnegative compact test cutoff $\chi \leq 1$, lower semicontinuity of $-u_{0,m}$ and weak convergence of the positive trace measures imply \[  \int _ B\chi (-u_{0,m})S\wedge \omega ^{p-r}\leq C.  \] The measure inequality used here follows from the bounded continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions in decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions , applied to the negative of the bounded lower semicontinuous test function. Let $m\to \infty $ by monotone convergence for the fixed measure $S\wedge \omega ^{p-r}$, then exhaust $B$ by such cutoffs. This proves integrability of $u_0$ and the same bound $C$. Coefficient domination in coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents gives all coefficient integrability. Applying this argument to each vector of functions shows that the weighted products for an arbitrary decreasing family have mass uniformly bounded by $C$. 5. An upper bound for every weighted weak limit. Continue with $r\leq p-1$ and put $S_ j=P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j})$. Their unweighted convergence is already known. Uniform weighted trace bounds and positive-current compactness give subsequential weak limits $W$ of $u_{0,j}S_ j$. For a nonnegative strongly positive test form $\alpha $, write $\mu _ j=S_ j\wedge \alpha $ and $\mu =S\wedge \alpha $. For fixed $l,m$ and all $j\geq l$, \[  \int u_{0,j}\, d\mu _ j \leq \int \max \{ u_{0,l},-m\} \, d\mu _ j.  \] The bounded upper semicontinuous function on the right has decreasing bounded continuous majorants on $B$, by decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions . Passing first to the weak limit in $j$, with a fixed compact cutoff near the test support, and then through those majorants gives $W(\alpha )\leq \int \max \{ u_{0,l},-m\} \, d\mu $. Let $m\to \infty $ and then $l\to \infty $ for the fixed measure, using the integrability from Step4. It follows that $u_0S-W$ is positive. On the common collar it is zero. 6. Reverse inequality for total masses. Set $\gamma =\omega ^{p-r}$ and $I=\int _ Bu_0S\wedge \gamma $, $I_ j=\int _ Bu_{0,j}S_ j\wedge \gamma $, all finite by Step4. We prove $I\leq I_ j$. Fix $j$ and choose smooth decreasing approximations $w_ l=u_{l,j}^{\varepsilon _ l}$ of Step1, for $0\leq l\leq r$. They satisfy $u_ l\leq w_ l$ and have the same collar. For $0\leq k\leq r$, define \[  J_ k=\int _ Bu_ k\, dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{k-1} \wedge dd^ cu_{k+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ r \wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Replacing $u_ k$ by its majorant $w_ k$ cannot decrease this integral. If $k<r$, use symmetry from Step3 and ( 7.29.4 ) to interchange the smooth weight $w_ k$ and the potential $u_{k+1}$. The base in that exchange is \[  R_ k=dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{k-1} \wedge dd^ cu_{k+2}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ r \wedge T\wedge \gamma ,  \] of bidimension $(1,1)$. Its product with $u_{k+1}$ is integrable by the weighted induction hypothesis for fewer factors, and its $dd^ c$ is the already-constructed product with $r$ factors. Thus the exchange satisfies every hypothesis of the lemma, and gives $J_ k\leq J_{k+1}$. Therefore \[  I=J_0\leq \cdots \leq J_ r \leq \int _ Bw_ r\, dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{r-1} \wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Let $\varepsilon _ r\downarrow 0$ first. The measure is fixed and smooth factors times $T$, and $u_{r,j}$ is integrable for it by the weighted zero-factor case with that base current, whose bidimension is $p-r\geq 1$. Dominated convergence applies. For $r\geq 2$, next let $\varepsilon _{r-1}\downarrow 0$, then the other parameters down to $\varepsilon _1\downarrow 0$, keeping $\varepsilon _0$ fixed. At the step for $\varepsilon _ k$, the smooth factors already fixed next to $T$ give a fixed positive closed base of bidimension $p-k$. There are $r-k\leq r-1$ remaining Hessian factors and fixed weight $u_{r,j}$. The weighted induction hypothesis applies, since $r-k\leq (p-k)-1$. Hence these sequential limits are justified without assuming the weighted assertion currently under proof. Every integral limit over $B$ is valid by the fixed-collar splitting from Step1. The resulting integral is \[  \int _ Bu_{r,j}\, dd^ cw_0\wedge dd^ cu_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_{r-1,j}\wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Interchange its weight with the smooth $w_0$ by the same $L^1$ collar exchange. This becomes $\int _ Bw_0S_ j\wedge \gamma $. Finally $w_0\downarrow u_{0,j}$, which is integrable for $S_ j$ by Step4; dominated convergence gives $I\leq I_ j$. Along a subsequence defining $W$, the fixed collar gives $I_ j\to \int _ BW\wedge \gamma $. The positive compactly supported current $u_0S-W$ therefore has trace mass $I-\lim I_ j\leq 0$. Its trace vanishes and coefficient domination implies $W=u_0S$. Every subsequence has this same further weak limit, so the whole weighted sequence converges. This completes the weighted induction, and consequently the construction through $r=p$. The original functions agree with their modifications near $K$; locality transfers every conclusion there. Compact sets in each covering ball and then a partition of unity give the conclusions on $X$. The coefficient recursion makes these local constructions agree on overlaps, so no choice of spheres or coordinates enters the result. $\square$ Lemma 7.29.6 . 7EADA0AAC4F2 Let $F\subset \mathbb C^ n$ be closed, let $0\leq s<n$, and suppose $\mathcal H^{2s+1}(F)=0$. Put $V=\{ 0\} ^ s\times \mathbb C^{n-s}$, and give $\mathrm U(n)$ the invariant probability measure of invariant probability on unitary homogeneous spaces . For almost every pair $(g,r)\in \mathrm U(n)\times (0,\infty )$, with Lebesgue measure in the second factor, \[  F\cap g\bigl (V\cap \{ |z|=r\} \bigr )=\varnothing .  \] Thus almost every coordinate system has this property for almost every positive radius. Proof. We first bound the probability that the first $s$ coordinates of a uniform unit vector have norm at most $t\leq 1/2$. For $s=0$ the bound is $1$. For $s>0$, write a unit vector in that band as \[  (w,\sqrt{1-|w|^2}\, \xi ),\qquad w\in \mathbb C^ s,\quad |w|\leq 1/2,\quad \xi \in S^{2(n-s)-1}.  \] This is a smooth parametrization of the band, and in finitely many coordinate charts of the compact sphere of $\xi $ its surface-volume density is bounded on $|w|\leq 1/2$. Its surface volume over $|w|\leq t$ is therefore at most $C_{n,s}t^{2s}$. The invariant probability on the unit sphere is its normalized surface measure: both are invariant and the probability is unique by invariant probability on unitary homogeneous spaces . The same estimate thus holds for $g^{-1}x/|x|$ when $g$ has the invariant distribution, for every fixed $x\ne 0$; invariance follows also directly by right translation of $g$. Fix $0<a<b<\infty $ and a ball $B(x,t)$ with $|x|\geq a$ and $0<t<a/2$. If $g(V\cap \{ |z|=r\} )$ meets this ball, then \[  |r-|x||<t,\qquad \operatorname {dist}(g^{-1}x,V)<t.  \] The first condition confines $r$ to an interval of length $2t$. The probability of the second is at most $C_{n,s}(t/a)^{2s}$, including the case $s=0$. Hence the product measure of pairs in $\mathrm U(n)\times [a,b]$ meeting this ball is at most $C_{n,s,a}t^{2s+1}$. These events are Borel, since distance from a fixed point to the continuously moving compact sphere is continuous. The compact set $F\cap \{ a\leq |z|\leq b\} $ has zero $\mathcal H^{2s+1}$ measure. Cover it by countably many balls with centers in that set, radii less than $a/2$, and arbitrarily small sum of the $(2s+1)$-st powers of their radii; this follows immediately by replacing the sets in a Hausdorff cover by balls. Any pair meeting $F$ at a point of norm $r\in [a,b]$ meets one of these balls. The preceding bound and countable subadditivity show that the measure of all such pairs is zero. The bad set is measurable: it is the projection of the closed subset \[  \{ (g,r,y):g\in \mathrm U(n),\  r\in [a,b],\  y\in V, \  |y|=r,\  gy\in F\}   \] of a compact product, and hence is compact. A countable exhaustion of $(0,\infty )$ by compact intervals proves the assertion for pairs; Fubini gives the final almost-every-coordinate-system formulation. Only finite smooth coordinate charts, Hausdorff covers and the exact invariant probability are used; no inverse-image dimension estimate or coarea formula is assumed. $\square$ Corollary 7.28.1 . 1BBBF8109419 Let $S$ be closed in a complex manifold and have locally zero one-dimensional Hausdorff measure in coordinates. For any positive closed current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ and any finite family of plurisubharmonic functions locally bounded on $X\setminus S$, all the conclusions of theorem 7.29.5 hold. In particular this applies if $S$ has Hausdorff dimension zero. Proof. Near $x$ choose a coordinate ball $\overline{B(x,R_2)}$ contained in the chart, and any $0<R_1<R_2$. The radial map $z\mapsto |z-x|$ is $1$-Lipschitz. Covering the compact set $S\cap \overline{B(x,R_2)}$ by sets of arbitrarily small sum of diameters shows that its radial image has length zero: the diameters do not increase, and the images can be covered by real intervals of those lengths. Choose $R\in (R_1,R_2)$ outside this image. Then $S\cap \partial B(x,R)=\varnothing $. Closedness and compactness give an annulus about that sphere disjoint from $S$, on which all the functions are locally bounded. The theorem applies on these covering balls. Hausdorff dimension zero implies zero one-dimensional measure directly from the definition. No slicing or coarea theorem is used. $\square$ The range for an unbounded weight is essential. In $\mathbb C$, the positive top-degree current $T=\delta _0$ and $u=\log |z|^2$ have compact unbounded locus but $u$ is not integrable for $T$. On the other hand, with base current $1$ the allowed one-factor classical product is $dd^ c\log |z|^2=\delta _0$ by the normalized Poincaré–Lelong formula ; its pole mass is retained.

title: Lemma 7.29.1
section: 7.29 Classical products with compact unbounded loci
text: Lemma 7.29.1 . 438B9224299E Let $B=B(a,R)\Subset \mathbb C^ n$, put $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and $\omega =dd^ c\psi $, and let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Suppose the locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $f_0,\ldots ,f_ r$ are defined near $\overline B$, are nonpositive on $B$ and all equal $A\psi $ on a collar of $\partial B$, for some $A>0$. Write $M_ T=\int _ B T\wedge \omega ^ p$. Then 9135B1E39C61 \begin{align}  \int _ B dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r} & =A^ rM_ T & & (0\leq r\leq p), \tag{7.29.2}\\  \int _ B(-f_0)\, dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T \wedge \omega ^{p-r} & \leq \| \psi \| _{L^\infty (B)}A^{r+1}M_ T & & (0\leq r\leq p-1). \tag{7.29.3} \end{align} The constants do not involve bounds for the $f_ j$ inside $B$. Moreover, if $R_1$ is closed positive of bidimension $(1,1)$ near $\overline B$, $a_1$ is smooth, $b_1$ is $L^1$ for the coefficient variations of $R_1$, and $dd^ c(b_1R_1)$ has measure coefficients, then $a_1=b_1$ on a collar implies 90ED91EDE196 7.29.4 \begin{equation}  \int _ B a_1\, dd^ c(b_1R_1)=\int _ B b_1\, dd^ ca_1\wedge R_1, \end{equation} provided the left-hand measure has finite mass near $\overline B$. Proof. The bounded products, their locality, smooth-factor rules and symmetry are those of locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products , decreasing continuity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products . They have finite mass near $\overline B$ by the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate in the interior and their fixed smooth factors on the collar. Replace each $dd^ cf_ j$ in turn by $A\omega $: the difference is $dd^ c$ of $(f_ j-A\psi )$ times a closed product, compactly supported in $B$. Its integral against the remaining closed power of $\omega $ is zero, by testing with a compact cutoff equal to one near that support. This proves ( 7.29.2 ). For $r\leq p-1$, apply integration by parts with a common boundary collar to $f_0$ and the smooth function $A\psi $, with base current $dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r-1}$. Dividing the resulting identity by $A$ gives \[  \int _ B(-f_0)\, dd^ cf_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r\wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r} =\int _ B(-\psi )\, dd^ cf_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cf_ r \wedge T\wedge \omega ^{p-r-1}.  \] The mass identity with $r+1$ factors proves the bound. For the final assertion put $h=(b_1-a_1)|_ B$, which is $L^1(R_1)$ and has compact support in $B$; extend it by zero when needed. Since $R_1$ is closed, on $B$ one has $dd^ c(b_1R_1)=dd^ ca_1\wedge R_1+dd^ c(hR_1)$. Choose a compact cutoff $\chi $ equal to one near the support of $hR_1$. Adding the smooth term proves ( 7.29.4 ). This extends the bounded common-collar argument using precisely the needed integrability. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.29.5
section: 7.29 Classical products with compact unbounded loci
text: Theorem 7.29.5 . 8FBB0E4DE397 Let $T$ be a closed positive current of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold $X$. Suppose a finite family of plurisubharmonic functions has the following property: $X$ is covered by coordinate balls $B$ with compact closure in their charts, such that every function of the family is locally bounded on a neighborhood of $\partial B$. For $0\leq r\leq p$, their recursive products \[  P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) =dd^ c\bigl (u_1P_ T(u_2,\ldots ,u_ r)\bigr ),\qquad P_ T()=T,  \] are well defined closed positive currents. They are symmetric, additive and positively homogeneous in the potentials, unchanged by addition of constants, and local in the ordinary topology. For $0\leq r\leq p-1$, an additional function $u_0$ of the family is locally integrable for the coefficient variations of $P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r)$. If $u_{l,j}\downarrow u_ l$ are any decreasing plurisubharmonic approximations, then \begin{align*}  P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j})& \longrightarrow P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) & & (0\leq r\leq p),\\  u_{0,j}P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j}) & \longrightarrow u_0P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r) & & (0\leq r\leq p-1) \end{align*} weakly. The limits need not be locally bounded in the interior of the balls. All listed potentials, including the limit of a weight, are subject to the common-boundary hypothesis. Proof. We prove the assertions simultaneously for arbitrary positive closed base currents and all their bidimensions. No assertion of integrability of an unbounded weight against a top-degree current is included. 1. A collar without cutting off interior singularities. Fix a ball $B$, a compact set $K\Subset B$ and the finitely many sequences involved. On a fixed annulus around $\partial B$, their limits are bounded below, and $u_ l\leq u_{l,j}\leq u_{l,1}$ gives bounds uniform in $j$. After subtracting constants, arrange that all these functions are at most $-1$ on a neighborhood of $\overline B$. Choose two concentric inner spheres, outside $K$ and all their unbounded loci in $B$, such that the closed annulus between and outside them lies where the limits are bounded below by $-M$. Let $\psi =|z-a|^2-R^2$ and take $A$ so large that $A\psi <-M-2$ on a neighborhood of the inner sphere. Leave each function unchanged inside that sphere, and on the outer annulus replace it by $\max \{ u,A\psi \} $. The formulas agree near the inner gluing sphere, so this is plurisubharmonic by maximum and boundary gluing of plurisubharmonic functions . Near $\partial B$ it is $A\psi $, since $u\leq -1$. The same choices work for every $j$, preserve inequalities and decreasing limits, and leave the functions unchanged near $K$. They are nonpositive on $B$. We henceforth use the modified functions and the same symbols. Each fixed modified function has smooth decreasing plurisubharmonic approximations with this same collar. Indeed, convolve the original function on a slightly larger ball and on the annulus use the smooth maximum $M_\varepsilon (u*\rho _\varepsilon ,A\psi )$ of smooth convex approximations of the maximum , with the decreasing regularization of the Levi criterion and decreasing convolution . On the inner gluing annulus the two arguments have a gap greater than $2\varepsilon $ for small $\varepsilon $, so this equals $u*\rho _\varepsilon $ there. Near the outer sphere it equals $A\psi $. Thus it glues to the convolution in the interior. The convolution and smooth maximum both decrease as $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$, so these smooth functions decrease to the modification. They remain nonpositive on $B$ for sufficiently small $\varepsilon $: wherever the maximum is not an exact branch, both arguments are bounded away from zero; near the sphere the exact branch is $A\psi $. Their boundedness for fixed $\varepsilon $ follows from smoothness near $\overline B$. It suffices to prove the theorem for functions with this fixed collar, on $B$. On the collar all products are ordinary bounded products with factors $A\omega $, where $\omega =dd^ c\psi $. Consequently, whenever weak convergence is established in $B$, integrals over the whole ball converge as well if the currents in question have this fixed collar: split the integral with a compact cutoff equal to one away from the collar. The complementary integrals are fixed and finite. 2. Starting the induction. Suppose $p\geq 1$ and $u\leq 0$ has the fixed collar. Its bounded truncations $u_ N=\max \{ u,-N\} $ have the same collar for all large $N$. The $r=0$ case of ( 7.29.3 ) gives \[  \int _ B(-u_ N)T\wedge \omega ^ p \leq \| \psi \| _\infty A M_ T.  \] Monotone convergence, with the measure fixed, proves $u\in L^1(T\wedge \omega ^ p)$ and hence coefficient integrability. For $u_ j\downarrow u$, the normalized functions are nonpositive and $|u_ j|\leq |u|$; dominated convergence gives $u_ jT\to uT$. This is the weighted assertion for zero Hessian factors. The unweighted zero-factor assertion is $T\to T$. If $p=0$, only that unweighted assertion is required. 3. Constructing the next product and its unweighted limit. Assume the weighted assertions have been proved for fewer than $r$ Hessian factors, for all base currents, and let $1\leq r\leq p$. By induction the product with $r-1$ factors is closed positive, and the first potential is integrable for it. Therefore the displayed recursion defines $P_ T$ with $r$ factors. With this fixed base product, bounded truncations of the first potential converge in coefficient $L^1$. Applying $dd^ c$ shows that the new product is a weak limit of closed positive bounded products, hence closed positive. For simultaneous decreasing approximations, the weighted induction hypothesis with weight $u_{1,j}$ and factors $u_{2,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j}$, followed by $dd^ c$, proves the unweighted convergence for $r$ factors. Smooth decreasing approximations then show symmetry, because the smooth exterior products are symmetric. The recursion gives locality, linearity, invariance under constants and compatibility with multiplication of the base current by a smooth closed positive form; these follow exactly by coefficient integration and the smooth-factor Leibniz rule. In particular the construction agrees in overlapping charts and is independent of this local collar modification wherever that modification leaves the functions unchanged. For bounded simultaneous truncations, the mass identity ( 7.29.2 ) holds. Their just-proved unweighted convergence and the fixed collar pass that identity to the possibly unbounded limits. Thus $P_ T$ with $r$ factors has finite total trace mass on $B$, equal to $A^ rM_ T$ in the $\omega $ normalization. 4. Integrability of the next weight. Let $r\leq p-1$. Put $S=P_ T(u_1,\ldots ,u_ r)$ and $S_ N=P_ T(u_{1,N},\ldots ,u_{r,N})$, with simultaneous bounded truncations of all the functions, including $u_0$. We know $S_ N\to S$. The uniform bounded-collar estimate gives \[  \int _ B(-u_{0,N})S_ N\wedge \omega ^{p-r}\leq C, \qquad C=\| \psi \| _\infty A^{r+1}M_ T.  \] For fixed $m$ and $N\geq m$, one has $-u_{0,m}\leq -u_{0,N}$. For a nonnegative compact test cutoff $\chi \leq 1$, lower semicontinuity of $-u_{0,m}$ and weak convergence of the positive trace measures imply \[  \int _ B\chi (-u_{0,m})S\wedge \omega ^{p-r}\leq C.  \] The measure inequality used here follows from the bounded continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions in decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions , applied to the negative of the bounded lower semicontinuous test function. Let $m\to \infty $ by monotone convergence for the fixed measure $S\wedge \omega ^{p-r}$, then exhaust $B$ by such cutoffs. This proves integrability of $u_0$ and the same bound $C$. Coefficient domination in coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents gives all coefficient integrability. Applying this argument to each vector of functions shows that the weighted products for an arbitrary decreasing family have mass uniformly bounded by $C$. 5. An upper bound for every weighted weak limit. Continue with $r\leq p-1$ and put $S_ j=P_ T(u_{1,j},\ldots ,u_{r,j})$. Their unweighted convergence is already known. Uniform weighted trace bounds and positive-current compactness give subsequential weak limits $W$ of $u_{0,j}S_ j$. For a nonnegative strongly positive test form $\alpha $, write $\mu _ j=S_ j\wedge \alpha $ and $\mu =S\wedge \alpha $. For fixed $l,m$ and all $j\geq l$, \[  \int u_{0,j}\, d\mu _ j \leq \int \max \{ u_{0,l},-m\} \, d\mu _ j.  \] The bounded upper semicontinuous function on the right has decreasing bounded continuous majorants on $B$, by decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions . Passing first to the weak limit in $j$, with a fixed compact cutoff near the test support, and then through those majorants gives $W(\alpha )\leq \int \max \{ u_{0,l},-m\} \, d\mu $. Let $m\to \infty $ and then $l\to \infty $ for the fixed measure, using the integrability from Step4. It follows that $u_0S-W$ is positive. On the common collar it is zero. 6. Reverse inequality for total masses. Set $\gamma =\omega ^{p-r}$ and $I=\int _ Bu_0S\wedge \gamma $, $I_ j=\int _ Bu_{0,j}S_ j\wedge \gamma $, all finite by Step4. We prove $I\leq I_ j$. Fix $j$ and choose smooth decreasing approximations $w_ l=u_{l,j}^{\varepsilon _ l}$ of Step1, for $0\leq l\leq r$. They satisfy $u_ l\leq w_ l$ and have the same collar. For $0\leq k\leq r$, define \[  J_ k=\int _ Bu_ k\, dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{k-1} \wedge dd^ cu_{k+1}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ r \wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Replacing $u_ k$ by its majorant $w_ k$ cannot decrease this integral. If $k<r$, use symmetry from Step3 and ( 7.29.4 ) to interchange the smooth weight $w_ k$ and the potential $u_{k+1}$. The base in that exchange is \[  R_ k=dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{k-1} \wedge dd^ cu_{k+2}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ r \wedge T\wedge \gamma ,  \] of bidimension $(1,1)$. Its product with $u_{k+1}$ is integrable by the weighted induction hypothesis for fewer factors, and its $dd^ c$ is the already-constructed product with $r$ factors. Thus the exchange satisfies every hypothesis of the lemma, and gives $J_ k\leq J_{k+1}$. Therefore \[  I=J_0\leq \cdots \leq J_ r \leq \int _ Bw_ r\, dd^ cw_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cw_{r-1} \wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Let $\varepsilon _ r\downarrow 0$ first. The measure is fixed and smooth factors times $T$, and $u_{r,j}$ is integrable for it by the weighted zero-factor case with that base current, whose bidimension is $p-r\geq 1$. Dominated convergence applies. For $r\geq 2$, next let $\varepsilon _{r-1}\downarrow 0$, then the other parameters down to $\varepsilon _1\downarrow 0$, keeping $\varepsilon _0$ fixed. At the step for $\varepsilon _ k$, the smooth factors already fixed next to $T$ give a fixed positive closed base of bidimension $p-k$. There are $r-k\leq r-1$ remaining Hessian factors and fixed weight $u_{r,j}$. The weighted induction hypothesis applies, since $r-k\leq (p-k)-1$. Hence these sequential limits are justified without assuming the weighted assertion currently under proof. Every integral limit over $B$ is valid by the fixed-collar splitting from Step1. The resulting integral is \[  \int _ Bu_{r,j}\, dd^ cw_0\wedge dd^ cu_{1,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_{r-1,j}\wedge T\wedge \gamma .  \] Interchange its weight with the smooth $w_0$ by the same $L^1$ collar exchange. This becomes $\int _ Bw_0S_ j\wedge \gamma $. Finally $w_0\downarrow u_{0,j}$, which is integrable for $S_ j$ by Step4; dominated convergence gives $I\leq I_ j$. Along a subsequence defining $W$, the fixed collar gives $I_ j\to \int _ BW\wedge \gamma $. The positive compactly supported current $u_0S-W$ therefore has trace mass $I-\lim I_ j\leq 0$. Its trace vanishes and coefficient domination implies $W=u_0S$. Every subsequence has this same further weak limit, so the whole weighted sequence converges. This completes the weighted induction, and consequently the construction through $r=p$. The original functions agree with their modifications near $K$; locality transfers every conclusion there. Compact sets in each covering ball and then a partition of unity give the conclusions on $X$. The coefficient recursion makes these local constructions agree on overlaps, so no choice of spheres or coordinates enters the result. $\square$

Any pair meeting $F$ at a point of norm $r\in [a,b]$ meets one of these balls. The preceding bound and countable subadditivity show that the measure of all such pairs is zero. The bad set is measurable: it is the projection of the closed subset \[  \{ (g,r,y):g\in \mathrm U(n),\  r\in [a,b],\  y\in V, \  |y|=r,\  gy\in F\}   \] of a compact product, and hence is compact. A countable exhaustion of $(0,\infty )$ by compact intervals proves the assertion for pairs; Fubini gives the final almost-every-coordinate-system formulation. Only finite smooth coordinate charts, Hausdorff covers and the exact invariant probability are used; no inverse-image dimension estimate or coarea formula is assumed. $\square$

All spaces are Hausdorff and complex. For continuous seminorms $p,q$ on $E,F$, respectively, put \[  \pi _{p,q}(t)=\inf _{t=\sum x_ j\otimes y_ j}\sum _ jp(x_ j)q(y_ j), \qquad \varepsilon _{p,q}(t)= \sup _{|\xi |\leq p,\, |\eta |\leq q}|(\xi \otimes \eta )(t)|.  \] The completions for these families are denoted $E\widehat\otimes _\pi F$ and $E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon F$. Dominated linear extension, already proved in section 2.12 , gives the crossnorm identity $\varepsilon _{p,q}(x\otimes y)=\pi _{p,q}(x\otimes y)=p(x)q(y)$ and $\varepsilon _{p,q}\leq \pi _{p,q}$. The continuous dual of the projective completion is precisely the jointly continuous bilinear forms. The ideal property follows by the same composition. A Banach nuclear series is uniformly approximated on the unit ball by its finite-rank heads, with tail operator norm at most $\sum _{j>N}|\lambda _ j|$. The heads have relatively compact bounded images; finite nets and completeness give a compact closure for the full image. In the factorization above a source neighborhood maps into a Banach unit ball, so its image in $F$ has compact closure as well. Every element of a completed projective tensor is a sum of simple tensors with summable products of norms: approximate it by algebraic tensors with geometrically small successive errors, then decompose each error with cost arbitrarily close to its projective norm. This proves surjectivity onto the nuclear operators and the asserted infimum/quotient norm. The kernel is closed since operator norm is bounded by projective norm. eq 0$, and zero otherwise. Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\| u\| ,\| v\| \leq (\sum _ j|\lambda _ j|)^{1/2}$ and the series for $v$ converges in norm. D02C4838DC99 If $A:E	o F$ is Banach nuclear, then for every Banach space $G$ \[  A\otimes \mathrm{Id}: E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon G \longrightarrow F\widehat\otimes _\pi G  \] is continuous with norm at most $\| A\| _

A46D09531259 The preceding definition is equivalent to admitting increasing Hilbertian defining seminorms with nuclear Hilbert-space links. Closed subspaces, closed-subspace quotients, countable products and countable inverse limits of nuclear Fréchet spaces are nuclear. A completed tensor product of two nuclear Fréchet spaces is nuclear. If one Fréchet factor is nuclear, its completed projective and injective tensor products with any Hausdorff locally convex space coincide topologically. Proof. Factor $E_{p_{j+1}}	o E_{p_ j}$ through a Hilbert space by the lemma. The Hilbertian seminorm $h_ j$ obtained from the first map, multiplied by the norm of the second, satisfies $p_ j\leq h_ j\leq C_ jp_{j+1}$. Zero links cause no exception. Put $q_ j=(\sum _{r\leq j}h_ r^2)^{1/2}$. These are increasing Hilbertian defining seminorms with $p_ j\leq q_ j\leq C'_ jp_{j+1}$. The map $E_{q_{j+2}}	o E_{q_ j}$ factors through the nuclear link $E_{p_{j+2}}	o E_{p_{j+1}}$, with bounded outer maps. Taking the even subsequence proves the Hilbertian criterion. The converse is immediate from the definition. Let $S\subset E$ be closed, use this Hilbertian family, and write $H_ j=E_{q_ j}$, $K_ j=\overline{S}^{\, H_ j}$. The completion of $S$ at $q_ j$ is $K_ j$, and the completion of $E/S$ at the quotient seminorm is $H_ j/K_ j$. The latter identity follows because the infimum over $S$ is the distance to $K_ j$. Its quotient link is, after identifying Hilbert quotients with orthogonal complements, a restriction followed by the projection onto $K_ j^\perp $. Both are nuclear by the ideal property. Orthogonal projections onto closed Hilbert subspaces follow by minimizing distance: the parallelogram identity makes a minimizing sequence Cauchy, and variation at its limit gives orthogonality. The subspace is Fréchet by closedness and the quotient is Fréchet by proposition 2.12.1 . For a countable product $\prod _ kE^ k$, choose Hilbertian nuclear families $q_ j^ k$ and use \[  P_ j(x)^2=\sum _{k\leq j}q_ j^ k(x_ k)^2.  \] Its Hilbert completion is the finite orthogonal sum of the corresponding completions. u \| B\| _
u $ for the projective tensor norms: the source functional is $\xi _ j\otimes \eta _ k$, and the target vector is $y_ j\otimes z_ k$. Apply this to defining links in the two Fréchet spaces. E8F18F08D2C8 For every complex manifold $X$ with a countable basis, $\mathcal O(X)$ with its compact-open topology is nuclear. Proof. They also show that an $L^2$-Cauchy sequence of holomorphic functions is locally uniformly Cauchy; its holomorphic limit agrees with its $L^2$ limit. Thus the Bergman spaces used below are complete. The completion at this seminorm is $A^2(D_ j)$. An algebraic tensor of $\pi _{ ar p_ j,q}$-size less than $r$ lifts to one of $\pi _{p_ j,q}$-size less than $r$: in a finite decomposition, choose each coefficient lift arbitrarily close to its quotient seminorm infimum. Continuous linear separation of the Hausdorff quotient gives a functional $\ell $ vanishing on $L$ but not on that vector. Its bilinear form $b$ on $E_2	imes F$ vanishes on $E_1	imes F$ and obeys $|b(x,y)|\leq C p_ j(x)q(y)$ for suitable seminorms. The descended functional on the projective completion therefore pulls back to $\ell $, contradicting its nonzero value on the kernel. This proves exactness and, with the already established closed embedding/open surjection, strictness. $\square$

text: Theorem 2.13.5 . 7434BE36F417 Let $0\to E_1\to E_2\overset {Q}{\to }E_3\to 0$ be a strict short exact sequence of Fréchet spaces: $E_1$ is identified with a closed subspace and $E_3$ with the quotient topology. The tensor products may use either topology. Proof. First the injective completion preserves a closed embedding. A continuous seminorm $p$ on $E_1$ has a continuous seminorm extension to $E_2$: choose $q$ on $E_2$ with $p\leq q$ on $E_1$, and set \[  \widetilde p(x)=\inf _{a\in E_1}\{ p(a)+q(x-a)\} .  \] This is a seminorm bounded by $q$ and equals $p$ on $E_1$. Dominated linear extension gives equality of the injective tensor seminorms on the subspace. Hence the completed inclusion is a topological embedding; its image is closed, since its complete Fréchet source is complete for the induced uniform topology. Next the projective completion preserves a Fréchet quotient surjection. Use increasing source seminorms $p_ j$ on $E_2$ and the quotient seminorms $\bar p_ j$ on $E_3$. An algebraic tensor of $\pi _{\bar p_ j,q}$-size less than $r$ lifts to one of $\pi _{p_ j,q}$-size less than $r$: in a finite decomposition, choose each coefficient lift arbitrarily close to its quotient seminorm infimum. Thus the closure of the image of every zero neighborhood in the completed source contains a zero neighborhood in the target. More precisely use any smaller radius and density of algebraic tensors in the completion. The successive-correction part of the proof of proposition 2.12.1 now proves surjectivity and openness: it needs just these neighborhoods in closures, not the preliminary Baire step that obtained them there. All completed spaces here are Fréchet. If $E_2$ is nuclear then so are $E_1,E_3$; if $F$ is nuclear it is already the common nuclear factor. Thus projective and injective completions coincide for all three terms. The first map consequently has closed image $L$ and the last is open and surjective. To prove equality of $L$ with the kernel, suppose a vector in the kernel were outside $L$. Continuous linear separation of the Hausdorff quotient gives a functional $\ell $ vanishing on $L$ but not on that vector. Its bilinear form $b$ on $E_2\times F$ vanishes on $E_1\times F$ and obeys $|b(x,y)|\leq C p_ j(x)q(y)$ for suitable seminorms. It descends to a bilinear form on $E_3\times F$ with bound $C\bar p_ j([x])q(y)$, by taking the infimum over $E_1$. The descended functional on the projective completion therefore pulls back to $\ell $, contradicting its nonzero value on the kernel. This proves exactness and, with the already established closed embedding/open surjection, strictness. $\square$

title: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison
section: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison
text: A paracompact space will mean a Hausdorff space every open cover of which has a locally finite open refinement. A family is locally finite if every point has a neighborhood meeting only finitely many members. For a sheaf $F$ and a subspace $S$, write $F|_ S=i^{-1}F$, where $i:S\to X$ is inclusion, and $F(S)=\Gamma (S,F|_ S)$. Thus a section on $S$ assigns an ambient germ to each point, locally represented by an actual section on an ambient open set. It remembers germs, not merely values of continuous functions at the points of $S$. Use the sheaf and inverse-image constructions of proposition 10.43.1 , proposition 10.43.2 .

title: 10.44.1 Closed refinements and neighborhood extension
section: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison

Lemma 10.44.2 . B28AAC964119 A paracompact space is regular and normal. Every open cover $(U_ i)$ has a locally finite open refinement $(V_ j)$ with $\overline{V_ j}\subset U_{ho (j)}$. Proof. Intersecting the defining refinement with $S$ proves the first assertion. In case(1), refine the cover together with $X\setminus S$ using lemma 10.44.2 , and retain the sets assigned to the given cover members. They cover $S$ and one can take $W=X$. These sets are locally finite near $S$, and $N\cap \overline{V_ j}\subset \overline{A_ j}^{\, P}$. Thus $W=N$ works. For case(3), work first in the product neighborhood. For every $s\in S$ choose a product $O_ s	imes P_ s$ about $(s,t_0)$ inside a prescribed cover member. Choose a locally finite open refinement $(A_ j)$ on $S$ with $\overline{A_ j}\subset O_{s(j)}$. The product sets $A_ j	imes P_{s(j)}$ are locally finite near the slice. Their closed bad parts, namely their closures minus the assigned cover members, miss the slice: at a slice point in such a closure, the first coordinate belongs to $O_{s(j)}$ and the second is $t_0\in P_{s(j)}$. Remove the union of these bad parts. This is a closed union near the slice by local finiteness, so its complement gives the required $W$. Take $(V_ j)$ and $W$ as in the definition, and restrict $W$ further to an open neighborhood of $S$ on which the family $(V_ j)$ is locally finite. On $W\cap \overline{V_ j}\cap \overline{V_ k}$ the sections $f_{ho (j)}$ and $f_{ho (k)}$ are both defined. Their unequal-germ locus is closed there, because the equality locus of two sections is open. These bad sets form a locally finite family: locally only finitely many pairs of closures meet. title: 10.44.5 Soft lifting, acyclicity and supported partitions
search_title: Soft lifting, acyclicity and supported partitions
section: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison
text: A sheaf $F$ of abelian groups is soft if $F(X)\to F(S)$ is onto for every closed $S\subset X$. On a paracompact space every flabby sheaf is soft: first extend a section to a neighborhood using theorem 10.44.4 , and then use flabbiness to extend to $X$. Restriction of a soft sheaf to a closed subspace is soft, because a closed subset of that subspace is closed in $X$ and restriction of germs composes. Proposition 10.44.6 . 8017BDB06160 On a paracompact space, $F$ is soft if and only if each point has a closed neighborhood $N$ such that $F|_ N$ is soft. In particular softness on an open neighborhood of every point suffices. No assertion that restriction to an arbitrary open subset preserves softness is needed. Proof. The forward implication is the closed-restriction observation. For the converse choose a locally finite closed refinement $(K_ i)$ of the open cover by interiors of such $N$, with its interiors still covering $X$, using lemma 10.44.2 . Each $F|_{K_ i}$ is soft. Given $f\in F(S)$ with $S$ closed, well-order the index set and extend it over successive closed sets $S\cup \bigcup _{j<i}K_ j$. At stage $i$, softness on $K_ i$ extends the already assigned section on its closed intersection with that set to all of $K_ i$; closed pasting attaches it. At a limit stage, the sections agree on their common pieces, and the family consisting of $S$ and the preceding $K_ j$ is locally finite and closed. Closed pasting therefore gives a section on their union. After all indices one has a global section extending $f$. If softness is known on open neighborhoods, take smaller closed neighborhoods inside them; closed restriction again gives the criterion. $\square$ Theorem 10.44.7 . 695AD5517AC4 Let $X$ be paracompact and $0\to A\xrightarrow {j}B\xrightarrow {p}Q\to 0$ an exact sequence. If $A$ is soft, then $B(S)\to Q(S)$ is onto for every closed $S$. If $A$ and $B$ are soft, then $Q$ is soft. Every soft sheaf is acyclic on $X$ and, after restriction, on every closed subspace. Proof. First lift $q\in Q(X)$. There is an open cover $(U_ i)$ on which it has local lifts $b_ i$. Choose a locally finite closed refinement $(K_ i)$ with $K_ i\subset U_{\rho (i)}$ and interiors covering $X$. Well-order these sets. Suppose a lift $b$ is already defined on $C=\bigcup _{j<i}K_ j$, which is closed. On $C\cap K_ i$, $b-b_{\rho (i)}$ is the image of a section of $A$. This uses left exactness of sections on the subspace and exactness of inverse image, as proved in proposition 10.43.1 , proposition 10.43.2 . Softness extends that section from the closed $C\cap K_ i$ to an $a\in A(X)$. Replace the lift on $K_ i$ by $b_{\rho (i)}+j(a)$ and paste it to $b$. At limit stages closed local finiteness and the closed-pasting argument apply. The final lift is global. On a closed $S$, its space is paracompact and $A|_ S$ is soft, so the identical construction proves the asserted lifting. If also $B$ is soft, lift a section of $Q(S)$ to $B(S)$, extend it to $B(X)$, and apply $p$. This proves softness of $Q$. For acyclicity, use the already constructed Godement resolution theorem 10.43.5 . Its terms $C^ qA$ are flabby, hence soft. Put $Z^0=A$ and $Z^{q+1}=\ker (C^{q+1}A\to C^{q+2}A)$. In $0\to Z^ q\to C^ qA\to Z^{q+1}\to 0$, the preceding quotient and lifting assertions inductively show that every $Z^ q$ is soft and the sequence is exact on global sections. Hence the unaugmented Godement section complex is exact in positive degree, proving $H^ q(X,A)=0$ for $q>0$. Apply the same theorem on a closed paracompact subspace to the soft restriction. This concerns ordinary cohomology of that subspace; no compact-support assertion is made. $\square$ Theorem 10.44.8 . 848B74D63948 If $F$ is soft on a paracompact space and $(U_ i)$ is any open cover, every $f\in F(X)$ can be written $f=\sum _ if_ i$ with $f_ i\in F(X)$, $\operatorname {Supp}f_ i\subset U_ i$, and the family of supports locally finite. Support here is the closed support of nonzero germs. Proof. Suppose first the cover is locally finite, and choose a shrinking $(W_ i)$, $K_ i=\overline{W_ i}\subset U_ i$, covering $X$. Well-order the indices. After choosing the previous sections put $C_ i=\bigcup _{j<i}K_ j$ and $r_ i=f-\sum _{j<i}f_ j$; the sum is defined because its supports lie in the locally finite family $(U_ j)$. Maintain $r_ i|_{C_ i}=0$. On the closed set \[  (C_ i\cup K_ i)\cup (X\setminus U_ i)  \] prescribe $r_ i$ on the first part and zero on the second. These germ sections agree: $K_ i\subset U_ i$ and $r_ i=0$ on $C_ i$. Closed pasting and softness extend the prescription to an $f_ i$ on $X$. Its germs vanish on $X\setminus U_ i$, so its closed germ support lies in $U_ i$. It vanishes on $C_ i$ and equals $r_ i$ on $K_ i$, maintaining the invariant. At limit stages the locally finite sum exists and has the same invariant. At the end it equals $f$ on the covering closed sets $K_ i$, hence everywhere. For a general cover take a locally finite refinement $(V_ j)$ with $V_ j\subset U_{\rho (j)}$. Apply the first case and group its sections by $\rho $: $f_ i=\sum _{\rho (j)=i}f'_ j$. Every grouped support is contained in the locally finite closed union of the corresponding supports, hence is a closed subset of $U_ i$. The grouped family of supports is locally finite, since any neighborhood meeting only finitely many original supports meets only finitely many groups. This proves the claim. $\square$ Corollary 10.44.9 . BE8990AF4756 Let $R$ be a soft sheaf of commutative unital rings on a paracompact space. Every open cover has a subordinate locally finite partition of $1$ by sections of $R$, with supports inside the prescribed open sets. Every sheaf of unital $R$-modules is soft and acyclic. Its positive-degree Čech cohomology vanishes for every open cover. Proof. Apply theorem 10.44.8 to $1\in R(X)$. For a section $s\in F(S)$ on a closed set, extend it to an open neighborhood $\Omega $ by theorem 10.44.4 . The prescription $1$ on $S$ and $0$ on $X\setminus \Omega $ is a section of $R$ on their disjoint closed union. Extend it by softness to $\psi \in R(X)$. Thus its germs equal1 on $S$ and vanish on $X\setminus \Omega $; in particular its support lies inside $\Omega $. The product $\psi s$ on $\Omega $, extended by zero, is a section on $X$: near every point outside $\Omega $ the section $\psi $ is identically zero. It extends the original germ section on $S$. Soft acyclicity follows from theorem 10.44.7 . The Čech contraction with the partition of1 is precisely lemma 10.43.14 ; no ordered positivity in $R$ is required. $\square$ For completeness the continuous-function example can be proved using only the normality established above. On a normal space, disjoint closed sets $A,B$ admit a continuous $h:X\to [0,1]$ with $h=0$ on $A$ and $h=1$ on $B$. Indeed choose open sets $O_ t$, for dyadic $0\le t\le 1$, with $A\subset O_0$, $O_1=X\setminus B$ and $\overline{O_ s}\subset O_ t$ for $s<t$. Start by shrinking around $A$ inside $X\setminus B$; insert the intermediate dyadics recursively using normality. Define $h(x)=\inf \{ t:x\in O_ t\} $, with the empty infimum equal1. The identities \[  \{ h<a\} =\bigcup _{t<a}O_ t,\qquad \{ h>a\} =\bigcup _{t>a}(X\setminus \overline{O_ t}) \quad (0<a<1)  \] prove continuity and the stated closed-set values. Given closed $S\subset \Omega $ open, normality twice and this construction produce a continuous $\chi :X\to [0,1]$ equal1 on a neighborhood of $S$ and with closed support contained in $\Omega $: choose $S\subset V\subset \overline V\subset W\subset \overline W\subset \Omega $, and separate $\overline V$ from $X\setminus W$. A germ section of continuous functions along $S$ extends first to $\Omega $; multiplying by $\chi $ and extending by zero gives a global section with exactly the same germs. Thus the real or complex continuous-function sheaf is soft. It need not be flabby: on $X=\mathbb R$, the continuous section $1/x$ on $(0,1)$ cannot extend across0. Smooth-function softness and its module acyclicity continue to reuse the existing smooth partition construction and proposition 10.43.10 .

At limit stages the locally finite sum exists and has the same invariant. At the end it equals $f$ on the covering closed sets $K_ i$, hence everywhere. For a general cover take a locally finite refinement $(V_ j)$ with $V_ j\subset U_{\rho (j)}$. Apply the first case and group its sections by $\rho $: $f_ i=\sum _{\rho (j)=i}f'_ j$. Every grouped support is contained in the locally finite closed union of the corresponding supports, hence is a closed subset of $U_ i$. The grouped family of supports is locally finite, since any neighborhood meeting only finitely many original supports meets only finitely many groups. This proves the claim. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.44.9
section: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison
text: Corollary 10.44.9 . BE8990AF4756 Let $R$ be a soft sheaf of commutative unital rings on a paracompact space. Every open cover has a subordinate locally finite partition of $1$ by sections of $R$, with supports inside the prescribed open sets. Every sheaf of unital $R$-modules is soft and acyclic. Its positive-degree Čech cohomology vanishes for every open cover. Proof. Apply theorem 10.44.8 to $1\in R(X)$. For a section $s\in F(S)$ on a closed set, extend it to an open neighborhood $\Omega $ by theorem 10.44.4 . The prescription $1$ on $S$ and $0$ on $X\setminus \Omega $ is a section of $R$ on their disjoint closed union. Extend it by softness to $\psi \in R(X)$. Thus its germs equal1 on $S$ and vanish on $X\setminus \Omega $; in particular its support lies inside $\Omega $. text: Use the full ordered-tuple Čech complex, including repetitions, and the refinement/prism and comparison maps already constructed in theorem 10.43.16 . Lemma 10.44.11 . D088E9B20989 Let $B\to Q$ be a surjective morphism of sheaves of abelian groups on a paracompact space. For every $q\ge 0$, open cover $\mathcal U$ and cochain $c\in \check C^ q(\mathcal U,Q)$, there is a refinement $\mathcal V\to \mathcal U$ on which the restricted cochain has a componentwise lift to $B$. Proof. First take a locally finite refinement of $\mathcal U$ and restrict $c$; it is enough to prove the result for that cover, again denoted $(U_ i)$. Take an open shrinking $(W_ i)$ with $\overline{W_ i}\subset U_ i$. At every $x$ choose a neighborhood $N_ x$ meeting only finitely many $U_ i$. There are only finitely many indices with $x\in U_ i$, and hence finitely many ordered $(q+1)$-tuples of such indices, including repetitions. Surjectivity of stalks gives a lift of each corresponding cochain component on some neighborhood of $x$. Shrink $N_ x$ to a common open $V_ x$ so that all these lifts are defined there, so that $V_ x\subset U_ i$ for each $U_ i\ni x$, and so that it avoids $\overline{W_ i}$ for every one of the finitely many nearby $U_ i$ not containing $x$. The latter is possible since $\overline{W_ i}\subset U_ i$. Sets not meeting the original $N_ x$ need no further avoidance. Finally choose $\rho (x)$ with $x\in W_{\rho (x)}$ and shrink $V_ x$ further inside this $W_{\rho (x)}$. If $V_{x_0}\cap \cdots \cap V_{x_ q}\ne \varnothing $, then $V_{x_0}$ meets $W_{\rho (x_ j)}$ for every $j$. By construction this implies $x_0\in U_{\rho (x_ j)}$ for every $j$. Consequently the component $c_{\rho (x_0)\ldots \rho (x_ q)}$ already has a lift on $V_{x_0}$, which restricts to the common intersection. Choose these lifts componentwise. This proves that the refinement $(V_ x)$ has the claimed property. $\square$ Theorem 10.44.12 . E83248AB1E9D For a sheaf of abelian groups $F$ on a paracompact space the canonical maps induce natural isomorphisms \[  \check H^ q(X,F)\simeq H^ q(X,F)\qquad (q\ge 0).  \] For every short exact sequence of sheaves the Čech direct-limit groups have a natural long exact sequence, and these isomorphisms commute with its connecting maps and the Godement connecting maps. No acyclic cover or good cover is assumed to exist. Proof. For $0\to A\to B\to Q\to 0$ let $\check C_ B^\bullet (\mathcal U,Q)$ be the image of $\check C^\bullet (\mathcal U,B)$ in $\check C^\bullet (\mathcal U,Q)$. This is a subcomplex and \[  0\to \check C^\bullet (\mathcal U,A) \to \check C^\bullet (\mathcal U,B) \to \check C_ B^\bullet (\mathcal U,Q)\to 0  \] is degreewise exact. Refinement preserves the liftable subcomplex. The prism homotopy for two refinement functions preserves it too: each component is a finite sum of restrictions of liftable components, which one lifts by the same sum of restricted lifts. Thus the cohomology groups $\check H_ B^ q(\mathcal U,Q)$ have well-defined refinement maps independent of the chosen function, and their long exact sequences are natural under refinement. The induced map \[  \varinjlim _{\mathcal U}\check H_ B^ q(\mathcal U,Q) \longrightarrow \check H^ q(X,Q)  \] is onto: a cocycle becomes a liftable cochain after lemma 10.44.11 , and remains a cocycle in the subcomplex. It is injective: if a liftable cocycle becomes a boundary after some refinement in the full $Q$-complex, refine again so that a chosen bounding $(q-1)$-cochain becomes liftable. It is then a boundary in the liftable complex. For $q=0$ there is no bounding cochain; a zero class is already the zero cochain after the indicated refinement. This proves the assertion in all degrees. Filtered direct limits of these long exact group sequences are exact by an elementary representative argument: represent an element at a cover; if its image is zero in the limit, pass to a common refinement where it is zero, and use exactness at that cover to find a preimage. The same argument proves equality of kernel and image at every position. This constructs the asserted Čech long exact sequence, using cohomology groups, without assuming that all cochain refinement functions define one canonical directed system of complexes. Covers may be taken as sets of open subsets. If an intermediate construction repeats an open set, retaining one copy gives refinement maps in both directions; the refinement homotopy makes their induced maps inverse. Hence this set-sized cofinal convention changes no group. We check compatibility with Godement connecting maps, not merely coefficient-map naturality. For a fixed cover use the double complexes $D_ F^{a,b}=\check C^ a(\mathcal U,C^ bF)$ and total differential $\delta +(-1)^ a d$, as before. By exactness of $\Gamma (U,C^ b-)$, proved in theorem 10.43.5 , the sequence of total complexes for $A,B,Q$ is degreewise exact. The sheaf augmentations give a morphism from the short exact sequence of Čech complexes above into this short exact sequence of total complexes; for its last term use the inclusion of liftable cochains followed by $Q\to C^0Q$. Therefore the cochain connecting maps commute by lemma 10.43.3 . The horizontal augmentations $\Gamma (X,C^\bullet F)\to \operatorname {Tot}D_ F$ give another morphism of short exact complexes, and are quasi-isomorphisms by lemma 10.43.14 , lemma 10.43.15 . Their natural cohomology identifications therefore also commute with connecting maps. Combining the two diagrams gives exactly the comparison already defined in theorem 10.43.16 , and proves the desired compatibility before and after passage to the limit. Finally embed any $F$ into $GF$ and put $Q=GF/F$. The flabby sheaf $GF$ has zero positive cohomology in both theories, by theorem 10.43.7 , lemma 10.43.14 . Both degree-zero groups are ordinary sections and the comparison is their identity. In degree one the two long exact sequences identify the groups with the same cokernel of $GF(X)\to Q(X)$; compatibility just proved identifies the comparisons. For $q\ge 2$ their connecting maps identify degree $q$ for $F$ with degree $q-1$ for $Q$. Induct simultaneously for all sheaves, using compatibility of these maps, to prove the isomorphism in every degree. Naturality follows from the constructed comparison and its refinement compatibility. These are ordinary section-cohomology groups; no comparison with singular cohomology or with a compact-support theory is being made. $\square$

title: 10.44.13 Alternating cochains and cover order
section: 10.44 Soft sheaves and paracompact comparison
text: Proposition 10.44.14 . 54F5489B5EF9 For every sheaf of abelian groups and every open cover, the inclusion of alternating Čech cochains into all ordered-tuple cochains is a cochain homotopy equivalence. Alternating means zero on repeated indices and multiplication by the permutation sign on reordering. Proof. Well-order the cover indices. Let $C_ q$ be the free abelian group on all ordered $(q+1)$-tuples, with omission boundary $\partial $, and let $A_ q$ be the subgroup spanned by strictly increasing tuples. The inclusion $i:A_\bullet \to C_\bullet $ is a chain map. Define $\pi :C_ q\to A_ q$ by sorting a tuple with its permutation sign, and by zero if an index repeats. It is a chain map: for distinct indices, reordering commutes with the signed omissions; when exactly one pair repeats, the only possibly surviving two omitted terms have opposite signed sorted values; with more repetitions every term vanishes. Also $\pi i=\mathrm{id}$. Here is an explicit integral homotopy for $P=i\pi $. Put $H_0=0$; $P$ is the identity on vertices. For a tuple $\sigma $ of degree $q\ge 1$, assume $H$ constructed in smaller degrees and put \[  e_\sigma =\sigma -P\sigma -H_{q-1}\partial \sigma , \qquad H_ q\sigma =\operatorname {cone}_{m(\sigma )}e_\sigma ,  \] where $m(\sigma )$ is its smallest index and the cone prefixes that index to every tuple in the chain. The induction identity and $\partial P=P\partial $ give $\partial e_\sigma =0$. For positive-degree chains the omission formula gives $\partial \operatorname {cone}_ m b=b-\operatorname {cone}_ m\partial b$. Thus $\partial H_ q\sigma =e_\sigma $, proving $\partial H+H\partial =\mathrm{id}-P$. Every tuple occurring in $H\sigma $ uses only indices already in $\sigma $. Dualize this construction to sheaf cochains: a tuple formula with integer coefficients is evaluated by restricting each of its finitely many terms to the common intersection of the original tuple. The last support property makes every such restriction defined. The restriction to increasing tuples is a retraction onto the alternating complex, and the dual $K$ of $H$ satisfies $\delta K+K\delta =\mathrm{id}-\mathrm{inclusion}\circ \mathrm{retraction}$. This proves the assertion for every cover and every abelian coefficient sheaf, without division by a factorial. $\square$ Corollary 10.44.15 . FC813BFC2984 Let $X$ be paracompact, $F$ a sheaf of abelian groups and $n\ge 0$ an integer. Suppose either there are arbitrarily fine open covers with every $n+2$ distinct members having empty common intersection, or there is one such cover acyclic for $F$ on all its nonempty finite intersections. Then $H^ q(X,F)=0$ for every $q>n$. Proof. The alternating cochain groups of any such cover vanish in degree $q>n$, since every tuple has either a repetition or an empty intersection. The proposition gives the same cohomology vanishing for its full complex. In the first case every direct-limit class restricts to zero on a sufficiently fine such cover; apply theorem 10.44.12 . In the second case apply the acyclic-cover comparison theorem 10.43.16 to that cover. $\square$
