section: 11.48 Hermitian torsion and the Bochner identity
text: Let $(X,\omega )$ be a smooth Hermitian manifold of complex dimension $n\geq 1$, and $(E,h)$ a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$. Use the Chern operators $D',D''$ and their formal adjoints $\delta ',\delta ''$, with $\mathrm dV=\omega ^ n/n!$ and inner products linear in the first entry. Set $L=\omega \wedge $, $\Lambda =L^*$, and \[  \Delta '=[D',\delta '],\quad \Delta ''=[D'',\delta ''],\quad D=D'+D'',\quad \delta =\delta '+\delta ''.  \] For operators of total degrees $a,b$ the bracket means $[P,Q]=PQ-(-1)^{ab}QP$. In particular, brackets between odd operators are anticommutators. A scalar form in a bracket denotes left exterior multiplication, tensored with $I_ E$. Define 494F31975749 11.48.2 \begin{equation}  a=\partial \omega \wedge ,\quad \bar a=\bar\partial \omega \wedge , \qquad \tau =[\Lambda ,a],\quad \bar\tau =[\Lambda ,\bar a]. \end{equation} These are order-zero operators; $\tau $ and $\bar\tau $ have types $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ respectively. A bar on $\tau $ designates this scalar conjugate operator on the exterior factor, and does not conjugate the bundle $E$. Superscript $*$ denotes the pointwise adjoint for order-zero operators and the formal adjoint for differential operators. We use the unscaled Chern curvature $\Theta $; for a line frame of squared norm $e^{-\phi }$, $\mathrm i\Theta =\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial \phi =2\pi dd^ c\phi $, where $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$. Theorem 11.48.3 . 9C30D850C771 In every bidegree and every bundle rank, 8C926C4A6B4A \begin{align}  [\delta '',L]& =\mathrm i(D'+\tau ),&  [\delta ',L]& =-\mathrm i(D''+\bar\tau ), \tag{11.48.4}\\  [\Lambda ,D'']& =-\mathrm i(\delta '+\tau ^*),&  [\Lambda ,D']& =\mathrm i(\delta ”+\bar\tau ^*). \tag{11.48.5} \end{align} Proof. We first prove the scalar identities, retaining the first jet of the metric. At a given point choose holomorphic coordinates in which $\omega (0)=\omega _0=\mathrm i\sum _ jdz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j$ and write $\gamma =\omega -\omega _0$, retaining its linear term. Put $L_0=\omega _0\wedge $ and $\Lambda _0=L_0^*$. On forms of each degree let $M$ be the smooth positive matrix defined by \[  \langle u,v\rangle _\omega \, \mathrm dV_\omega =\langle Mu,v\rangle _0\, \mathrm dV_0, \qquad \mathrm dV_0=\omega _0^ n/n!.  \] Its first variation is 34BA424819E3 11.48.6 \begin{equation}  M=I-[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]+O(|z|^2). \end{equation} Indeed, diagonalize $\gamma $ at a point with respect to $\omega _0$, with eigenvalues $\gamma _ j$, so the eigenvalues of $\omega $ are $1+\gamma _ j$. On the coefficient $dz_ I\wedge d\bar z_ J$ the metric-volume multiplier is \[  \frac{\prod _ j(1+\gamma _ j)}{\prod _{i\in I}(1+\gamma _ i)\prod _{j\in J}(1+\gamma _ j)} =1+\sum _ j\gamma _ j-\sum _{i\in I}\gamma _ i-\sum _{j\in J}\gamma _ j +O(|\gamma |^2).  \] The creation/contraction formula in the curvature operator on $(n,1)$-forms identifies its linear term with $-[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]$. This is an identity for the first derivative of the smooth matrix-valued function of the metric; it requires no smooth choice of diagonalizing frames. Its remainder and first derivatives vanish at zero. Write $\bar\delta _0$ for the flat scalar adjoint of $\bar\partial $. On the source and target form bundles, the exact adjoint formula is $\bar\partial ^*=M_{q-1}^{-1}\bar\delta _0M_ q$ for fixed $p$. Thus, as an operator on first jets at zero, FA92E1C99B83 11.48.7 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial ^* =\bar\delta _0-[\bar\delta _0,[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]] =\bar\delta _0+[\Lambda _0,C],\qquad C=[\bar\delta _0,\gamma ]. \end{equation} For the last equality use $[\bar\delta _0,\Lambda _0]=0$ and expand the three products. The flat scalar Kähler identities in the line-bundle Bochner–Kodaira identity give $[L_0,\bar\delta _0]=-\mathrm i\partial $. The operator $C$ has degree one. Since $[L_0,\gamma ]=0$, the graded Jacobi identity gives \[  [L_0,C]=[-\mathrm i\partial ,\gamma ] =-\mathrm i\partial \gamma \wedge , \qquad [C,L_0]=\mathrm i\partial \gamma \wedge .  \] Also $[L_0,\Lambda _0]$ acts on degree $k$ by $k-n$, so $[[L_0,\Lambda _0],C]=C$. Therefore \[  [L_0,[\Lambda _0,C]] =C-\mathrm i[\Lambda _0,\partial \gamma \wedge ].  \] Combining this with ( 11.48.7 ) and $L=L_0+\gamma $ gives, at zero, \[  [L,\bar\partial ^*] =-\mathrm i\partial +C-\mathrm i[\Lambda _0,\partial \gamma \wedge ]-C =-\mathrm i(\partial +\tau ).  \] Terms containing two factors of $\gamma $, with at most one derivative, vanish at zero. This accounts also for $[\gamma ,[\Lambda _0,C]]$ in this expansion. The point is arbitrary, proving the first scalar identity. Complex conjugation, for which $L,\Lambda $ and the metric-volume pairing are real, gives the second. Taking formal adjoints gives the last two. To pass to $E$, choose a holomorphic Chern-normal frame at the point. Its metric matrix is $H=I+O(|z|^2)$ and its connection matrix $H^{-1}\partial H$ vanishes there. This frame is obtained by the constant and holomorphic linear changes proved in theorem 10.33.2 ; that frame construction uses no derivative of the base metric. The bundle operators and their adjoints at the point are the componentwise scalar operators above, plus zeroth-order terms vanishing at that point. Their commutators with $L$ and $\Lambda $ consequently have exactly the same values. This proves all four identities in arbitrary rank. $\square$ For an explicit coefficient convention, in an $\omega $-unitary coframe write $a$ for the three-form $\partial \omega $ and use $\iota _ j,\bar\iota _ j$ for the contractions adjoint to multiplication by $\theta _ j,\bar\theta _ j$. Since $\Lambda =-\mathrm i\sum _ j\bar\iota _ j\iota _ j$, the operator in ( 11.48.2 ) is 863809BFB0AF 11.48.8 \begin{equation}  \tau =-\mathrm i\sum _ j\left( (\bar\iota _ j\iota _ ja)\wedge +(\iota _ ja)\wedge \bar\iota _ j -(\bar\iota _ ja)\wedge \iota _ j\right). \end{equation} To verify the signs, use $\iota _ j(a\wedge u)=(\iota _ ja)\wedge u-a\wedge \iota _ ju$ and apply $\bar\iota _ j$ once more. The remaining term $a\wedge \bar\iota _ j\iota _ ju$ cancels in the commutator. This also displays the order-zero and type assertions directly. Lemma 11.48.9 . A9F492A7F5C3 With the preceding conventions, CE861F2B34DA \begin{align}  [L,\tau ]& =3a,& [\Lambda ,\tau ]& =-2\mathrm i\bar\tau ^*, \tag{11.48.10}\\  [D',\bar\tau ^*]& =-[D',\delta '']=[\tau ,\delta ''], \tag{11.48.11}\\  -[D'',\bar\tau ^*]& =[\tau ,\delta '+\tau ^*]+T_\omega , \tag{11.48.12} \end{align} where the type-$(0,0)$ order-zero operator is DBCAF8FF0340 11.48.13 \begin{equation}  T_\omega = \left[\Lambda ,\left[\Lambda , \frac{\mathrm i}{2}\partial \bar\partial \omega \wedge \right]\right]-[a,a^*]. \end{equation} In particular $[a,a^*]=aa^*+a^*a$. Proof. The bracket $[L,a]$ is zero, and $a$ has degree three. Hence \[  [L,\tau ]=[[L,\Lambda ],a]=3a.  \] By ( 11.48.4 ), $\tau =-\mathrm i[\delta '',L]-D'$. Since $[D'',L]=\bar a$ and $[\Lambda ,\delta '']=[D'',L]^*=\bar a^*$, Jacobi gives \[  [\Lambda ,[\delta '',L]] =[[\Lambda ,\delta ''],L]+[\delta '',[\Lambda ,L]] =[\bar a^*,L]-\delta ''=\bar\tau ^*-\delta ''.  \] Here $[\delta '',[\Lambda ,L]]=-\delta ''$ follows by applying $[\Lambda ,L]=n-k$ in the input and output degrees. Substitute the contraction identity for $[\Lambda ,D']$ to obtain $[\Lambda ,\tau ]=-2\mathrm i\bar\tau ^*$. The Chern identities $(D')^2=(D'')^2=0$ were proved from $A=H^{-1}\partial H$ in equation 10.33.1 ; they do not use the Kähler condition. Expanding products therefore gives $[D',[\Lambda ,D']]=0$. The contraction identity yields $[D',\delta ''+\bar\tau ^*]=0$. Likewise $(\delta '')^2=0$ implies $[\delta '',[\delta '',L]]=0$, and the wedge identity yields $[D'+\tau ,\delta '']=0$. These two equalities prove ( 11.48.11 ). For the last identity put $c=\partial \bar\partial \omega \wedge $, of degree four, and $A=[D'',\Lambda ]=\mathrm i(\delta '+\tau ^*)$, of degree minus one. Since $[D',L]=a$ and $[\tau ,L]=-3a$, we have 93EA79ED3332 11.48.14 \begin{equation}  [\Lambda ,A]=\mathrm i[D'+\tau ,L]^*=-2\mathrm i a^*. \end{equation} The scalar evaluation Leibniz rule gives $[D'',a]=-c$. All required Jacobi steps can now be displayed with their signs: \begin{align*}  [D'',\tau ]& =-[\Lambda ,c]+[a,A],\\  [D'',[\Lambda ,\tau ]] & =[\tau ,A]-[\Lambda ,[\Lambda ,c]]+[\Lambda ,[a,A]],\\  [\Lambda ,[a,A]] & =[\tau ,A]+[a,[\Lambda ,A]] =[\tau ,A]-2\mathrm i[a,a^*]. \end{align*} It follows that \[  [D'',[\Lambda ,\tau ]] =-[\Lambda ,[\Lambda ,c]]+2[\tau ,A]-2\mathrm i[a,a^*] =2\mathrm i\bigl (T_\omega +[\tau ,\delta '+\tau ^*]\bigr ).  \] Finally $\bar\tau ^*=(\mathrm i/2)[\Lambda ,\tau ]$ by ( 11.48.10 ). Multiplying the last display by $\mathrm i/2$ proves ( 11.48.12 ). Each step is valid also at endpoint bidegrees, with the corresponding out-of-range operators zero. $\square$ Theorem 11.48.15 . E96E372480D4 Define \[  \Delta '_\tau =[D'+\tau ,\delta '+\tau ^*],\qquad \Delta _\tau =[D+\tau ,\delta +\tau ^*].  \] These are nonnegative formally self-adjoint second-order operators with the same principal parts as $\Delta '$ and $[D,\delta ]$ respectively. On every smooth bundle-valued bidegree, 2F5B471E480A \begin{align}  \Delta ''& =\Delta ' +[\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]+[D',\tau ^*]-[D'',\bar\tau ^*], \tag{11.48.16}\\  \Delta ''& =\Delta '_\tau +[\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]+T_\omega , \tag{11.48.17}\\  \Delta _\tau & =\Delta '_\tau +\Delta ”. \tag{11.48.18} \end{align} The operator $T_\omega $ is pointwise Hermitian and depends only on the first and second derivatives of the base metric, through $\partial \omega $ and $\partial \bar\partial \omega $ and their metric contractions. For every compactly supported smooth form $u$, 9CAE0D2A2536 11.48.19 \begin{equation}  \| D''u\| ^2+\| \delta ''u\| ^2 =\| (D'+\tau )u\| ^2+\| (\delta '+\tau ^*)u\| ^2 +\int _ X\langle ([\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]+T_\omega )u,u\rangle \, \mathrm dV. \end{equation} Proof. By the contraction identity, $\delta ''=-\mathrm i[\Lambda ,D']-\bar\tau ^*$. The Chern curvature relation $[D',D'']=\Theta \wedge $ and Jacobi give \[  [D'',[\Lambda ,D']] =[\Lambda ,\Theta ]+\mathrm i[D',\delta '+\tau ^*].  \] Multiply by $-\mathrm i$ and subtract $[D'',\bar\tau ^*]$ to obtain ( 11.48.16 ). Substitution of ( 11.48.12 ) combines its remaining three terms into \[  \Delta '+[D',\tau ^*]+[\tau ,\delta ']+[\tau ,\tau ^*]+T_\omega =\Delta '_\tau +T_\omega ,  \] proving ( 11.48.17 ). The mixed identity gives $[D'+\tau ,\delta '']=0$, and its formal adjoint is $[D'',\delta '+\tau ^*]=0$. Expanding $\Delta _\tau $ proves ( 11.48.18 ). For either odd operator $Q=D'+\tau $ or $Q=D+\tau $, the graded bracket $[Q,Q^*]=QQ^*+Q^*Q$ has quadratic form $\| Qu\| ^2+\| Q^*u\| ^2$ and is formally self-adjoint. Adding the order-zero $\tau $ does not change the second-order principal part. Integrating ( 11.48.17 ) now gives the energy identity. The pointwise curvature computation in proposition 10.33.6 uses only a unitary exterior coframe and the Chern curvature symmetry, so applies to the present Hermitian metric as well. In that coframe write $\mathrm i\Theta =\mathrm i\sum R_{j\bar k}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ k$. Write $\epsilon _ j,\bar\epsilon _ j$ for multiplication by $\theta _ j,\bar\theta _ j$. In a Chern-normal frame $R_{j\bar k}=-\partial _ j\partial _{\bar k}H$, so $R_{j\bar k}^*=R_{k\bar j}$, and that computation gives \[  [\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ] =\sum _{j,k}R_{j\bar k} (\epsilon _ j\iota _ k+\bar\epsilon _ k\bar\iota _ j-\delta _{jk}).  \] Taking its adjoint and exchanging $j,k$ proves it is Hermitian in every bidegree. The difference of the three formally self-adjoint operators $\Delta ''$, $\Delta '_\tau $ and this curvature operator is $T_\omega $. Since $T_\omega $ has order zero, formal self-adjointness implies pointwise Hermitian symmetry: testing its skew-adjoint part against arbitrary compactly supported coefficient vectors forces that smooth matrix to vanish at each point. The explicit formula ( 11.48.13 ) proves the claimed dependence on the base metric. $\square$ When $d\omega =0$, both torsion operators and $T_\omega $ vanish. The identities then give the Kähler formulas of theorem 10.33.2 . Corollary 11.48.20 . 222BB53B613A Suppose $X$ is compact and, in a fixed bidegree $(p,q)$, $[\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]+T_\omega $ is positive definite at every point. Then the smooth analytic Dolbeault group $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)$ vanishes. For $q\geq 1$ there is a constant $\lambda >0$ such that each smooth $D''$-closed $f$ in that bidegree has a unique smooth primitive $u$ of smallest $L^2$ norm, with \[  D''u=f,\qquad \delta ''u=0,\qquad \| u\| ^2\leq \lambda ^{-1}\| f\| ^2.  \] Here $\lambda $ can be any uniform positive lower bound for the displayed curvature-plus-torsion operator. For $q=0$, every $D''$-closed form in that bidegree is zero. Proof. Compactness of the unit sphere bundle gives such a $\lambda $. The energy identity gives $\lambda \| v\| ^2\leq \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2$. Harmonic forms are zero, so theorem 10.46.6 gives the cohomology conclusion. Its smooth Green operator $G$ satisfies $\Delta ''G=I$ in the selected degree. For closed $f$, the differential commutation in theorem 10.46.4 gives $D''Gf=0$. Hence $u=\delta ''Gf$ is a smooth primitive with $\delta ''u=0$. Writing $w=Gf$, the energy identity and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  \lambda \| w\| ^2\leq \langle f,w\rangle \leq \| f\| \| w\| ,\qquad \| u\| ^2=\langle f,Gf\rangle \leq \lambda ^{-1}\| f\| ^2.  \] It is orthogonal to every $D''$-closed form in its input degree, by integration by parts. All other primitives differ by such a form, so it is the unique smallest-norm primitive. If $q=0$, the adjoint term has zero target and the coercive estimate directly proves the last assertion. $\square$ Corollary 11.48.21 . 5029210C26BC Suppose that $X$ is compact, $\partial \bar\partial \omega =0$, and put $N=n\binom n2$. If in bidegree $(p,q)$ \[  [\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]\geq bI, \qquad b>2N\sup _ X|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2,  \] then the preceding vanishing and smooth solvability conclusions hold. The metric $\omega $ is allowed to have $\partial \omega \ne 0$. Proof. Here $T_\omega =-(aa^*+a^*a)$. A unitary exterior expansion of $\partial \omega $ has $N$ possible coefficients. Each exterior monomial has multiplication operator norm at most one on the full exterior algebra. The triangle and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities give $\| a\| _{\mathrm{op}}\leq \sqrt N|\partial \omega |_\omega $; the adjoint has the same full-algebra operator norm. Thus \[  \langle T_\omega v,v\rangle =-\| av\| ^2-\| a^*v\| ^2 \geq -2N|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2|v|^2.  \] The assumed strict bound gives the positive uniform constant $\lambda =b-2N\sup _ X|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2$. Apply corollary 11.48.20 . For $n=1$ the three-form is zero and $N=0$, with the same conclusion. $\square$

text: Theorem 11.48.3 . 9C30D850C771 In every bidegree and every bundle rank, 8C926C4A6B4A \begin{align}  [\delta '',L]& =\mathrm i(D'+\tau ),&  [\delta ',L]& =-\mathrm i(D''+\bar\tau ), \tag{11.48.4}\\  [\Lambda ,D'']& =-\mathrm i(\delta '+\tau ^*),&  [\Lambda ,D']& =\mathrm i(\delta ”+\bar\tau ^*). \tag{11.48.5} \end{align} Proof. We first prove the scalar identities, retaining the first jet of the metric. At a given point choose holomorphic coordinates in which $\omega (0)=\omega _0=\mathrm i\sum _ jdz_ j\wedge d\bar z_ j$ and write $\gamma =\omega -\omega _0$, retaining its linear term. Put $L_0=\omega _0\wedge $ and $\Lambda _0=L_0^*$. On forms of each degree let $M$ be the smooth positive matrix defined by \[  \langle u,v\rangle _\omega \, \mathrm dV_\omega =\langle Mu,v\rangle _0\, \mathrm dV_0, \qquad \mathrm dV_0=\omega _0^ n/n!.  \] Its first variation is 34BA424819E3 11.48.6 \begin{equation}  M=I-[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]+O(|z|^2). \end{equation} Indeed, diagonalize $\gamma $ at a point with respect to $\omega _0$, with eigenvalues $\gamma _ j$, so the eigenvalues of $\omega $ are $1+\gamma _ j$. On the coefficient $dz_ I\wedge d\bar z_ J$ the metric-volume multiplier is \[  \frac{\prod _ j(1+\gamma _ j)}{\prod _{i\in I}(1+\gamma _ i)\prod _{j\in J}(1+\gamma _ j)} =1+\sum _ j\gamma _ j-\sum _{i\in I}\gamma _ i-\sum _{j\in J}\gamma _ j +O(|\gamma |^2).  \] The creation/contraction formula in the curvature operator on $(n,1)$-forms identifies its linear term with $-[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]$. This is an identity for the first derivative of the smooth matrix-valued function of the metric; it requires no smooth choice of diagonalizing frames. Its remainder and first derivatives vanish at zero. Write $\bar\delta _0$ for the flat scalar adjoint of $\bar\partial $. On the source and target form bundles, the exact adjoint formula is $\bar\partial ^*=M_{q-1}^{-1}\bar\delta _0M_ q$ for fixed $p$. Thus, as an operator on first jets at zero, FA92E1C99B83 11.48.7 \begin{equation}  \bar\partial ^* =\bar\delta _0-[\bar\delta _0,[\gamma ,\Lambda _0]] =\bar\delta _0+[\Lambda _0,C],\qquad C=[\bar\delta _0,\gamma ]. \end{equation} For the last equality use $[\bar\delta _0,\Lambda _0]=0$ and expand the three products. The flat scalar Kähler identities in the line-bundle Bochner–Kodaira identity give $[L_0,\bar\delta _0]=-\mathrm i\partial $. The operator $C$ has degree one. Since $[L_0,\gamma ]=0$, the graded Jacobi identity gives \[  [L_0,C]=[-\mathrm i\partial ,\gamma ] =-\mathrm i\partial \gamma \wedge , \qquad [C,L_0]=\mathrm i\partial \gamma \wedge .  \] Also $[L_0,\Lambda _0]$ acts on degree $k$ by $k-n$, so $[[L_0,\Lambda _0],C]=C$. Therefore \[  [L_0,[\Lambda _0,C]] =C-\mathrm i[\Lambda _0,\partial \gamma \wedge ].  \] Combining this with ( 11.48.7 ) and $L=L_0+\gamma $ gives, at zero, \[  [L,\bar\partial ^*] =-\mathrm i\partial +C-\mathrm i[\Lambda _0,\partial \gamma \wedge ]-C =-\mathrm i(\partial +\tau ).  \] Terms containing two factors of $\gamma $, with at most one derivative, vanish at zero. This accounts also for $[\gamma ,[\Lambda _0,C]]$ in this expansion. The point is arbitrary, proving the first scalar identity. Complex conjugation, for which $L,\Lambda $ and the metric-volume pairing are real, gives the second. Taking formal adjoints gives the last two. To pass to $E$, choose a holomorphic Chern-normal frame at the point. Its metric matrix is $H=I+O(|z|^2)$ and its connection matrix $H^{-1}\partial H$ vanishes there. This frame is obtained by the constant and holomorphic linear changes proved in theorem 10.33.2 ; that frame construction uses no derivative of the base metric. The bundle operators and their adjoints at the point are the componentwise scalar operators above, plus zeroth-order terms vanishing at that point. Their commutators with $L$ and $\Lambda $ consequently have exactly the same values. This proves all four identities in arbitrary rank. $\square$

text: Corollary 11.48.20 . 222BB53B613A Suppose $X$ is compact and, in a fixed bidegree $(p,q)$, $[\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]+T_\omega $ is positive definite at every point. Then the smooth analytic Dolbeault group $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)$ vanishes. For $q\geq 1$ there is a constant $\lambda >0$ such that each smooth $D''$-closed $f$ in that bidegree has a unique smooth primitive $u$ of smallest $L^2$ norm, with \[  D''u=f,\qquad \delta ''u=0,\qquad \| u\| ^2\leq \lambda ^{-1}\| f\| ^2.  \] Here $\lambda $ can be any uniform positive lower bound for the displayed curvature-plus-torsion operator. For $q=0$, every $D''$-closed form in that bidegree is zero. Proof. Compactness of the unit sphere bundle gives such a $\lambda $. The energy identity gives $\lambda \| v\| ^2\leq \| D''v\| ^2+\| \delta ''v\| ^2$. Harmonic forms are zero, so theorem 10.46.6 gives the cohomology conclusion. Its smooth Green operator $G$ satisfies $\Delta ''G=I$ in the selected degree. For closed $f$, the differential commutation in theorem 10.46.4 gives $D''Gf=0$. Hence $u=\delta ''Gf$ is a smooth primitive with $\delta ''u=0$. Writing $w=Gf$, the energy identity and Cauchy–Schwarz give \[  \lambda \| w\| ^2\leq \langle f,w\rangle \leq \| f\| \| w\| ,\qquad \| u\| ^2=\langle f,Gf\rangle \leq \lambda ^{-1}\| f\| ^2.  \] It is orthogonal to every $D''$-closed form in its input degree, by integration by parts. All other primitives differ by such a form, so it is the unique smallest-norm primitive. If $q=0$, the adjoint term has zero target and the coercive estimate directly proves the last assertion. $\square$

text: Corollary 11.48.21 . 5029210C26BC Suppose that $X$ is compact, $\partial \bar\partial \omega =0$, and put $N=n\binom n2$. If in bidegree $(p,q)$ \[  [\mathrm i\Theta ,\Lambda ]\geq bI, \qquad b>2N\sup _ X|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2,  \] then the preceding vanishing and smooth solvability conclusions hold. The metric $\omega $ is allowed to have $\partial \omega \ne 0$. Proof. Here $T_\omega =-(aa^*+a^*a)$. A unitary exterior expansion of $\partial \omega $ has $N$ possible coefficients. Each exterior monomial has multiplication operator norm at most one on the full exterior algebra. The triangle and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities give $\| a\| _{\mathrm{op}}\leq \sqrt N|\partial \omega |_\omega $; the adjoint has the same full-algebra operator norm. Thus \[  \langle T_\omega v,v\rangle =-\| av\| ^2-\| a^*v\| ^2 \geq -2N|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2|v|^2.  \] The assumed strict bound gives the positive uniform constant $\lambda =b-2N\sup _ X|\partial \omega |_\omega ^2$. Apply corollary 11.48.20 . For $n=1$ the three-form is zero and $N=0$, with the same conclusion. $\square$

text: Use the conventions and maximal Dolbeault operators of section 6.26 . All manifolds are Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. In particular the curvature is unscaled, $\mathcal H(f)=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial f$, and all inverse energies use the semidefinite quotient convention. Here $m$-semipositivity means nonnegativity of the Nakano form on tensors of rank at most $m$, as in the strict version of proposition 10.33.6 . Lemma 6.27.1 . 13C546CE0C2F Let $\gamma \geq \omega $ be two Hermitian metrics and let $(E,h)$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle. In degree $(n,k)$, $0\leq k\leq n$, 0F966B814C47 6.27.2 \begin{equation}  |u|_\gamma ^2\, \mathrm dV_\gamma \leq |u|_\omega ^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega . \end{equation} Fix $1\leq q\leq n$ and suppose the curvature of $E$ is $m$-semipositive, where $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. If $B_\omega =[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]$ and similarly for $\gamma $, then these operators are semipositive on $(n,q)$ and 32414668D927 6.27.3 \begin{equation}  |g|_{B_\gamma ^{-1},\gamma }^2\, \mathrm dV_\gamma \leq |g|_{B_\omega ^{-1},\omega }^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega . \end{equation} No invertibility of either curvature operator is required. Proof. At the point under consideration choose coordinates and a fiber frame such that $\omega =\mathrm i\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, $\gamma =\mathrm i\sum _ j\gamma _ j\mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ j$, $\gamma _ j\geq 1$, and $h$ is the identity. Write $\Gamma =\prod _ j\gamma _ j$ and $\gamma _ J=\prod _{j\in J}\gamma _ j$, with empty product one. An $(n,k)$-form has coefficients $u_ J$ in the fixed holomorphic top form and increasing barred indices. Then \[  |u|_\gamma ^2=\Gamma ^{-1}\sum _ J\gamma _ J^{-1}|u_ J|^2, \qquad \mathrm dV_\gamma =\Gamma \, \mathrm dV_\omega .  \] This proves ( 6.27.2 ); at $k=0$ there is equality. The same calculation gives the pairing density. Write $\mathrm i\Theta (E)=\mathrm i\sum _{j,l}R_{j\bar l} \mathrm dz_ j\wedge \mathrm d\bar z_ l$ in this frame. Proposition 10.33.6 , applied to the coframe $\sqrt{\gamma _ j}\mathrm dz_ j$, gives A64C7F4820EA 6.27.4 \begin{equation}  \Gamma \langle B_\gamma v,v\rangle _\gamma =\sum _{|S|=q-1}\gamma _ S^{-1} \sum _{j,l}\gamma _ j^{-1}\gamma _ l^{-1} \langle R_{j\bar l}v_{jS},v_{lS}\rangle . \end{equation} For each $S$, the inner sum is nonnegative: the tensor $(\gamma _ j^{-1}v_{jS})_ j$ has zero rows for $j\in S$ and rank at most $\min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. The same rank test proves semipositivity of both operators. As $\gamma _ S\geq 1$, replacing $\gamma _ S^{-1}$ in this nonnegative sum by $\gamma _ S^{-2}$ gives a lower bound. Define $Dv$ by $(Dv)_ J=\gamma _ J^{-1}v_ J$. The resulting bound is exactly 129500DAFFAD 6.27.5 \begin{equation}  \Gamma \langle B_\gamma v,v\rangle _\gamma \geq \langle B_\omega Dv,Dv\rangle _\omega , \qquad \Gamma \langle g,v\rangle _\gamma =\langle g,Dv\rangle _\omega . \end{equation} If the inverse energy for $\omega $ is finite, its defining Cauchy–Schwarz inequality applied to $Dv$ implies \[  |\langle g,v\rangle _\gamma |^2 \leq \Gamma ^{-1}|g|_{B_\omega ^{-1},\omega }^2 \langle B_\gamma v,v\rangle _\gamma .  \] Taking the supremum over $v$ proves ( 6.27.3 ). This argument also handles zero denominators; when the original energy is infinite the claimed inequality is automatic. Only pointwise diagonalization is used; no smooth eigenframe is needed. $\square$ Theorem 6.27.6 . D64DD0A9DB51 Let $X$ admit a complete Kähler metric $\widehat\omega $, and let $\omega $ be any other Kähler metric. Let $(E,h)$ have $m$-semipositive curvature, with $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$ and $1\leq q\leq n$. If $g\in L^2_{n,q}(X,E;\omega ,h)$ is closed and \[  M=\int _ X|g|_{B_\omega ^{-1},\omega }^2\,  \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty ,  \] then a primitive $u$ exists with the estimate for the original metric 50E076EEA847 6.27.7 \begin{equation}  D''u=g,\qquad \int _ X|u|_\omega ^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M. \end{equation} Proof. For $\varepsilon >0$ put $\omega _\varepsilon =\omega +\varepsilon \widehat\omega $. It is complete: an $\omega _\varepsilon $-Cauchy sequence is $\widehat\omega $-Cauchy by the length lower bound $\sqrt\varepsilon $, and its limit also gives convergence for the smooth local $\omega _\varepsilon $ metric. The preceding lemma shows that $g$ is globally $L^2$ for $\omega _\varepsilon $ and its inverse energy is at most $M$. The curvature rank hypothesis is intrinsic and unchanged. Theorem 6.26.5 therefore gives \[  D''u_\varepsilon =g,\qquad \int _ X|u_\varepsilon |_{\omega _\varepsilon }^2 \, \mathrm dV_{\omega _\varepsilon }\leq M.  \] Choose $\varepsilon _ j\downarrow 0$. On each compact set, $\omega _{\varepsilon _ j}\leq C\omega $ for $\varepsilon _ j\leq 1$. The coefficient formula of the lemma, in degree $(n,q-1)$, then bounds the original norm density by $C^{q-1}$ times the varying one. Thus the $u_{\varepsilon _ j}$ are bounded locally in $L^2$. Diagonal weak compactness gives a local weak limit $u$ with $D''u=g$. For fixed $k$ and $j\geq k$, the norm-density comparison gives \[  \int _ K|u_{\varepsilon _ j}|_{\omega _{\varepsilon _ k}}^2 \, \mathrm dV_{\omega _{\varepsilon _ k}}\leq M  \] on any compact $K$. Its density is now fixed and equivalent to a coefficient $L^2$ norm, so weak lower semicontinuity gives the same bound for $u$. As $k\to \infty $, these fixed norm densities increase to the original $\omega $ density: monotonicity follows from ( 6.27.2 ) and the limit from its coefficient formula. Monotone convergence, followed by compact exhaustion, proves ( 6.27.7 ). In primitive degree $(n,0)$ the density is already metric-independent. $\square$ Lemma 6.27.8 . 94482D8B91F7 For a smooth Hermitian bundle and smooth Hermitian base metric, let $g$ be a smooth datum of type $(p,q)$, $1\leq q\leq n$, with a globally $L^2$ distributional primitive. Its minimum-norm primitive is smooth and coclosed, even if $g$ is not globally $L^2$. Proof. If the primitive has type $(p,q-1)$, $q\geq 1$, the solution set is $u_0+\ker T$, where $T$ is the maximal distributional $D''$ operator between the corresponding $L^2$ spaces. The kernel is closed and contains the range of the preceding maximal $D''$ operator. Hilbert projection gives a unique minimum orthogonal to that kernel, hence its formal codifferential is zero distributionally. This argument does not require $u_0$ to belong to $\operatorname {Dom}T$ when $g$ is not globally $L^2$; only the differences lie in the kernel. This is the affine argument of lemma 6.25.12 . The local matrix graph approximation, H1 estimate and elliptic bootstrap proved in theorem 6.26.5 use only the local equations $D''u=g$, $\delta ''u=0$. They therefore apply here in each relatively compact chart. When $q=1$ the codifferential is zero for degree reasons. No completeness or boundary regularity is needed for this local conclusion. $\square$ Theorem 6.27.9 . B68EDCF522DA Suppose $(X,\omega )$ is Kähler with a smooth PSH exhaustion and $(E,h)$ is $m$-semipositive. Fix $1\leq q\leq n$ with $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. Every locally $L^2$ closed $(n,q)$-form with finite original inverse energy $M$ has a primitive satisfying ( 6.27.7 ). If $g$ is smooth the primitive can be chosen smooth. Proof. Shift the exhaustion $\rho $ to be nonnegative, and take levels $c_ j\uparrow \infty $. The relatively compact open sets $X_ j=\{ \rho <c_ j\} $ have smooth PSH exhaustions $\rho _ j=\rho +(c_ j-\rho )^{-1}$: for a positive sublevel bound $A$, its closed sublevel lies in $\{ \rho \leq c_ j-1/A\} $, a compact subset of $X_ j$. Empty sublevels are omitted. By lemma 6.26.8 , each $X_ j$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Since $\overline X_ j$ is compact in $X$, the datum is globally $L^2$ there for the original smooth metrics. Apply theorem 6.27.6 on $X_ j$. It gives $u_ j$ with the original squared norm at most $M$. Weak diagonal limits on the increasing sublevels preserve the equation and the original norm bound, by restriction continuity, weak lower semicontinuity and monotone convergence. Finally use lemma 6.27.8 for smooth data. $\square$ Corollary 6.27.10 . 7B8770608F52 Let $(X,\omega )$ be weakly PSH-exhausted Kähler and let $(L,h)$ be a holomorphic line bundle. Let $\phi $ be smooth and real, and suppose $\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)+\mathcal H(\phi )$ has nonnegative $\omega $-eigenvalues $\lambda _1\leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ n$. For every locally $L^2$ closed $L$-valued $(n,q)$-form, $1\leq q\leq n$, such that the right side below is finite, there is a primitive with 8CA99039303D 6.27.11 \begin{equation}  D''u=g,\qquad \int _ X|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq \int _ X\frac{|g|_{\omega ,h}^2}{\lambda _1+\cdots +\lambda _ q} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV_\omega . \end{equation} Use the zero-denominator convention. Smooth data admit a smooth choice. Proof. Apply the preceding theorem to $h\mathrm e^{-\phi }$. Its curvature is the assumed semipositive form. The exact all-q eigenvalue action in proposition 10.33.6 bounds its inverse energy by the displayed integral. The weight need not itself be PSH. $\square$ Lemma 6.27.12 . D1744F9C1C65 For a positive continuous function $\lambda $ on $[0,\infty )$ and an integer $N\geq 1$, there is a smooth convex function $\chi $ such that 4E8BA81880DF 6.27.13 \begin{equation}  \chi ,\chi ',\chi ''\geq \lambda ,\qquad (1+\chi '+\chi '')^ N\mathrm e^{-\chi }\leq \lambda ^{-1} \quad \hbox{on }[0,\infty ). \end{equation} Proof. Replace $\lambda $ by a nondecreasing continuous majorant at least one; for example use the smooth step construction on its compact-interval suprema from ( 6.26.9 ). For each $p\geq 1$ choose strictly increasing integers $k_ p\geq p+1$ so large that \[  b_ p=\lambda (p+1)^{1/k_ p}/p\in [1/p,1/(p-1))\quad (p\geq 2).  \] For $p=1$ only $b_1\geq 1$ is needed. Set $a_0=\cdots =a_{k_1-1}=\mathrm e\lambda (2)$ and \[  a_ k=b_ p\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt{k}}\quad (k_ p\leq k<k_{p+1}), \qquad d_ k=a_0a_1\cdots a_ k, \qquad f(t)=\sum _{k\geq 0}d_ kt^ k.  \] The sequence $a_ k$ is nonincreasing, tends to zero, and satisfies $a_ k\geq 1/k$ for $k\geq 1$. At the first join use $b_1\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt{k_1}}\leq \mathrm e\lambda (2)$; at the later joins use $b_ p<1/(p-1)\leq b_{p-1}$. The geometric means $d_ k^{1/k}$ tend to zero, so the series is entire. Its positive coefficients and $(k+1)a_{k+1}\geq 1$ give $f''\geq f'\geq f$ on $t\geq 0$. For $0\leq t\leq 1$, $f(t)\geq a_0\geq \lambda (t)$. For $t\in [p,p+1]$, the term $k=k_ p$ gives \[  f(t)\geq d_ kp^ k\geq (a_ kp)^ k \geq (b_ pp)^{k_ p}=\lambda (p+1)\geq \lambda (t).  \] We check the derivative upper bound, including both parities of the series. For all $m$ there are constants $C,c>0$ independent of $m$ such that 0EC514D3F94F 6.27.14 \begin{equation}  \frac{d_{2m}}{d_ m^2}\leq C\mathrm e^{-c\sqrt m}. \end{equation} Indeed beyond finitely many indices the factors $a_ k$ are a nonincreasing block sequence $b_ p$ times $\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt k}$. Pair the block factors with indices $m+j$ and $j$; each ratio is at most one once $j\geq k_1$, and the finitely many other ratios have a fixed bound. The remaining exponent is \[  \sum _{j=m+1}^{2m}j^{-1/2}-\sum _{j=1}^ m j^{-1/2} \leq -(4-2\sqrt2)\sqrt m+2,  \] by comparison with the integrals of $t^{-1/2}$. This proves ( 6.27.14 ), absorbing small $m$ into $C$. Since $a_ k\leq a_0$ and is nonincreasing, \[  \frac{d_{2m+2}}{d_ m^2}\leq a_0^2 \frac{d_{2m}}{d_ m^2}, \qquad \frac{d_{2m+3}}{d_ md_{m+1}}\leq \frac{d_{2m+2}}{d_ m^2}.  \] Multiplication by any quadratic polynomial in $m$ leaves these ratios bounded. The coefficient of $t^{2m}$ in $f^2$ is at least $d_ m^2$, and its coefficient of $t^{2m+1}$ is at least $2d_ md_{m+1}$. Comparing with the coefficients $(k+1)(k+2)d_{k+2}$ of $f''$ therefore gives $f''\leq C_1f^2$. As $f\geq \lambda \geq 1$ and $f'\leq f''$, \[  \lambda (1+f'+f'')^ N\mathrm e^{-f} \leq (1+2C_1)^ N f^{2N+1}\mathrm e^{-f}\leq C_2<\infty .  \] Take $\chi =f+A$ with $A\geq \max \{ 0,\log C_2\} $. Its first two derivatives still dominate $\lambda $, as does $\chi $, and the last inequality proves ( 6.27.13 ). $\square$ Corollary 6.27.15 . E30B7AED0EB3 If $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion and a positive holomorphic line bundle $L$, then the smooth analytic groups $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)$ vanish when $p+q>n$. Proof. Choose its positive metric $h$ and put $\omega _0=\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)$, a Kähler form. Let $\rho \geq 0$ be a smooth PSH exhaustion. For a smooth closed datum $g$, choose a continuous $C\geq 1$ such that $\mathcal H(\rho )\leq C\omega _0$ and $\mathrm i\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho \leq C\omega _0$. For any increasing convex $\chi $, the forms \[  h_\chi =h\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )},\qquad \omega _\chi =\mathrm i\Theta (L,h_\chi ) =\omega _0+\mathcal H(\chi (\rho ))  \] satisfy $\omega _0\leq \omega _\chi \leq C(1+\chi '+\chi '')\omega _0$, where the derivatives are evaluated at $\rho $. Thus pointwise covector norms decrease, while volume increases by at most $C^ n(1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n$. Put $F=C^ n|g|_{\omega _0,h}^2$. Its integral over each compact exhaustion band is finite. Choose continuous $\lambda \geq 1$ so large on every band $[k,k+1]$ that $\int _ X F/\lambda (\rho )\, \mathrm dV_{\omega _0}<\infty $; the same compact-band step construction gives such a majorant. Apply lemma 6.27.12 with $N=n$. It gives \[  \int _ X|g|_{\omega _\chi ,h_\chi }^2\, \mathrm dV_{\omega _\chi } \leq \int _ X F(1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )} \, \mathrm dV_{\omega _0}<\infty .  \] Moreover $\chi ''\geq 1$ implies $\omega _\chi \geq \mathrm i\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho $, so $|\mathrm d\rho |_{\omega _\chi }^2\leq 2$. The exhaustion and corollary 6.26.3 make this metric complete. Since its unscaled curvature is exactly $\omega _\chi $, the all-bidegree formula in proposition 10.33.6 gives $B=(p+q-n)\operatorname {Id}$. Here $q\geq 1$ and this integer is positive. The complete Kähler theorem gives a primitive with finite norm for these modified metrics; its minimum-norm choice is smooth. This proves the analytic Dolbeault quotient assertion. $\square$

The kernel is closed and contains the range of the preceding maximal $D''$ operator. Hilbert projection gives a unique minimum orthogonal to that kernel, hence its formal codifferential is zero distributionally. This argument does not require $u_0$ to belong to $\operatorname {Dom}T$ when $g$ is not globally $L^2$; only the differences lie in the kernel. This is the affine argument of lemma 6.25.12 . The local matrix graph approximation, H1 estimate and elliptic bootstrap proved in theorem 6.26.5 use only the local equations $D''u=g$, $\delta ''u=0$. They therefore apply here in each relatively compact chart. When $q=1$ the codifferential is zero for degree reasons. No completeness or boundary regularity is needed for this local conclusion. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.27.9
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.27 Estimates for an original Kähler metric
text: Theorem 6.27.9 . B68EDCF522DA Suppose $(X,\omega )$ is Kähler with a smooth PSH exhaustion and $(E,h)$ is $m$-semipositive. Fix $1\leq q\leq n$ with $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. Every locally $L^2$ closed $(n,q)$-form with finite original inverse energy $M$ has a primitive satisfying ( 6.27.7 ). If $g$ is smooth the primitive can be chosen smooth. Proof. Shift the exhaustion $\rho $ to be nonnegative, and take levels $c_ j\uparrow \infty $. The relatively compact open sets $X_ j=\{ \rho <c_ j\} $ have smooth PSH exhaustions $\rho _ j=\rho +(c_ j-\rho )^{-1}$: for a positive sublevel bound $A$, its closed sublevel lies in $\{ \rho \leq c_ j-1/A\} $, a compact subset of $X_ j$. Empty sublevels are omitted. By lemma 6.26.8 , each $X_ j$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Since $\overline X_ j$ is compact in $X$, the datum is globally $L^2$ there for the original smooth metrics. Apply theorem 6.27.6 on $X_ j$. It gives $u_ j$ with the original squared norm at most $M$. Weak diagonal limits on the increasing sublevels preserve the equation and the original norm bound, by restriction continuity, weak lower semicontinuity and monotone convergence. Finally use lemma 6.27.8 for smooth data. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.27.10
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.27 Estimates for an original Kähler metric
text: Corollary 6.27.10 . 7B8770608F52 Let $(X,\omega )$ be weakly PSH-exhausted Kähler and let $(L,h)$ be a holomorphic line bundle. Let $\phi $ be smooth and real, and suppose $\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)+\mathcal H(\phi )$ has nonnegative $\omega $-eigenvalues $\lambda _1\leq \cdots \leq \lambda _ n$. For every locally $L^2$ closed $L$-valued $(n,q)$-form, $1\leq q\leq n$, such that the right side below is finite, there is a primitive with 8CA99039303D 6.27.11 \begin{equation}  D''u=g,\qquad \int _ X|u|_{\omega ,h}^2\mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq \int _ X\frac{|g|_{\omega ,h}^2}{\lambda _1+\cdots +\lambda _ q} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV_\omega . \end{equation} Use the zero-denominator convention. Smooth data admit a smooth choice. Proof. Apply the preceding theorem to $h\mathrm e^{-\phi }$. Its curvature is the assumed semipositive form. The exact all-q eigenvalue action in proposition 10.33.6 bounds its inverse energy by the displayed integral. The weight need not itself be PSH. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.27.12
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.27 Estimates for an original Kähler metric
text: Lemma 6.27.12 . D1744F9C1C65 For a positive continuous function $\lambda $ on $[0,\infty )$ and an integer $N\geq 1$, there is a smooth convex function $\chi $ such that 4E8BA81880DF 6.27.13 \begin{equation}  \chi ,\chi ',\chi ''\geq \lambda ,\qquad (1+\chi '+\chi '')^ N\mathrm e^{-\chi }\leq \lambda ^{-1} \quad \hbox{on }[0,\infty ). \end{equation} Proof. Replace $\lambda $ by a nondecreasing continuous majorant at least one; for example use the smooth step construction on its compact-interval suprema from ( 6.26.9 ). For each $p\geq 1$ choose strictly increasing integers $k_ p\geq p+1$ so large that \[  b_ p=\lambda (p+1)^{1/k_ p}/p\in [1/p,1/(p-1))\quad (p\geq 2).  \] For $p=1$ only $b_1\geq 1$ is needed. Set $a_0=\cdots =a_{k_1-1}=\mathrm e\lambda (2)$ and \[  a_ k=b_ p\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt{k}}\quad (k_ p\leq k<k_{p+1}), \qquad d_ k=a_0a_1\cdots a_ k, \qquad f(t)=\sum _{k\geq 0}d_ kt^ k.  \] The sequence $a_ k$ is nonincreasing, tends to zero, and satisfies $a_ k\geq 1/k$ for $k\geq 1$. At the first join use $b_1\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt{k_1}}\leq \mathrm e\lambda (2)$; at the later joins use $b_ p<1/(p-1)\leq b_{p-1}$. The geometric means $d_ k^{1/k}$ tend to zero, so the series is entire. Its positive coefficients and $(k+1)a_{k+1}\geq 1$ give $f''\geq f'\geq f$ on $t\geq 0$. For $0\leq t\leq 1$, $f(t)\geq a_0\geq \lambda (t)$. For $t\in [p,p+1]$, the term $k=k_ p$ gives \[  f(t)\geq d_ kp^ k\geq (a_ kp)^ k \geq (b_ pp)^{k_ p}=\lambda (p+1)\geq \lambda (t).  \] We check the derivative upper bound, including both parities of the series. For all $m$ there are constants $C,c>0$ independent of $m$ such that 0EC514D3F94F 6.27.14 \begin{equation}  \frac{d_{2m}}{d_ m^2}\leq C\mathrm e^{-c\sqrt m}. \end{equation} Indeed beyond finitely many indices the factors $a_ k$ are a nonincreasing block sequence $b_ p$ times $\mathrm e^{1/\sqrt k}$. Pair the block factors with indices $m+j$ and $j$; each ratio is at most one once $j\geq k_1$, and the finitely many other ratios have a fixed bound. The remaining exponent is \[  \sum _{j=m+1}^{2m}j^{-1/2}-\sum _{j=1}^ m j^{-1/2} \leq -(4-2\sqrt2)\sqrt m+2,  \] by comparison with the integrals of $t^{-1/2}$. This proves ( 6.27.14 ), absorbing small $m$ into $C$. Since $a_ k\leq a_0$ and is nonincreasing, \[  \frac{d_{2m+2}}{d_ m^2}\leq a_0^2 \frac{d_{2m}}{d_ m^2}, \qquad \frac{d_{2m+3}}{d_ md_{m+1}}\leq \frac{d_{2m+2}}{d_ m^2}.  \] Multiplication by any quadratic polynomial in $m$ leaves these ratios bounded. The coefficient of $t^{2m}$ in $f^2$ is at least $d_ m^2$, and its coefficient of $t^{2m+1}$ is at least $2d_ md_{m+1}$. Comparing with the coefficients $(k+1)(k+2)d_{k+2}$ of $f''$ therefore gives $f''\leq C_1f^2$. As $f\geq \lambda \geq 1$ and $f'\leq f''$, \[  \lambda (1+f'+f'')^ N\mathrm e^{-f} \leq (1+2C_1)^ N f^{2N+1}\mathrm e^{-f}\leq C_2<\infty .  \] Take $\chi =f+A$ with $A\geq \max \{ 0,\log C_2\} $. Its first two derivatives still dominate $\lambda $, as does $\chi $, and the last inequality proves ( 6.27.13 ). $\square$

title: Corollary 6.27.15
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.27 Estimates for an original Kähler metric
text: Corollary 6.27.15 . E30B7AED0EB3 If $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion and a positive holomorphic line bundle $L$, then the smooth analytic groups $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)$ vanish when $p+q>n$. Proof. Choose its positive metric $h$ and put $\omega _0=\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)$, a Kähler form. Let $\rho \geq 0$ be a smooth PSH exhaustion. For a smooth closed datum $g$, choose a continuous $C\geq 1$ such that $\mathcal H(\rho )\leq C\omega _0$ and $\mathrm i\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho \leq C\omega _0$. For any increasing convex $\chi $, the forms \[  h_\chi =h\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )},\qquad \omega _\chi =\mathrm i\Theta (L,h_\chi ) =\omega _0+\mathcal H(\chi (\rho ))  \] satisfy $\omega _0\leq \omega _\chi \leq C(1+\chi '+\chi '')\omega _0$, where the derivatives are evaluated at $\rho $. Thus pointwise covector norms decrease, while volume increases by at most $C^ n(1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n$. Put $F=C^ n|g|_{\omega _0,h}^2$. Its integral over each compact exhaustion band is finite. Choose continuous $\lambda \geq 1$ so large on every band $[k,k+1]$ that $\int _ X F/\lambda (\rho )\, \mathrm dV_{\omega _0}<\infty $; the same compact-band step construction gives such a majorant. Apply lemma 6.27.12 with $N=n$. It gives \[  \int _ X|g|_{\omega _\chi ,h_\chi }^2\, \mathrm dV_{\omega _\chi } \leq \int _ X F(1+\chi '+\chi '')^ n\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )} \, \mathrm dV_{\omega _0}<\infty .  \] Moreover $\chi ''\geq 1$ implies $\omega _\chi \geq \mathrm i\partial \rho \wedge \bar\partial \rho $, so $|\mathrm d\rho |_{\omega _\chi }^2\leq 2$. The exhaustion and corollary 6.26.3 make this metric complete. Since its unscaled curvature is exactly $\omega _\chi $, the all-bidegree formula in proposition 10.33.6 gives $B=(p+q-n)\operatorname {Id}$. Here $q\geq 1$ and this integer is positive. The complete Kähler theorem gives a primitive with finite norm for these modified metrics; its minimum-norm choice is smooth. This proves the analytic Dolbeault quotient assertion. $\square$

title: 9.30 Local separation without global separation
section: 9.30 Local separation without global separation
text: The holomorphic functions on a manifold locally separate points if each point has a neighborhood on which it is distinguished from every other point by some global holomorphic function. This condition alone does not imply separation of all pairs of points. Proposition 9.30.1 . 774E0C4C33DB There is a connected Hausdorff complex surface $X$ with a countable basis and a noninjective local biholomorphism $\pi :X\to \Delta ^2$, where $\Delta =\{ |z|<1\} $, such that pullback is an algebra isomorphism \[  \pi ^*:\mathcal O(\Delta ^2)\longrightarrow \mathcal O(X).  \] Two global holomorphic functions give local coordinates at every point of $X$, but its global holomorphic functions do not separate every pair of points. Moreover $X$ is not holomorphically convex. Proof. A Hartogs figure and its bridge. In coordinates $(z,w)$ put \[  H=\bigl (\Delta \times \{ 1/2<|w|<1\} \bigr ) \cup \bigl (\{ |z|<1/2\} \times \Delta \bigr ),  \] and set \[  Z=\{ |z-3/4|<1/8\} ,\qquad E=\{ |\operatorname {Re}w|<3/4,\  |\operatorname {Im}w|<1/8\} , \qquad B=Z\times E.  \] These are open subsets of $\Delta ^2$: on $Z$ we have $5/8<|z|<7/8$, and on $E$ we have $|w|<\sqrt{37}/8<1$. The sets $H$ and $B$ are connected. Their intersection has exactly two connected components \[  U_+=\{ (z,w)\in B:|w|>1/2,\  \operatorname {Re}w>0\} ,\qquad U_-=\{ (z,w)\in B:|w|>1/2,\  \operatorname {Re}w<0\} .  \] Indeed $\operatorname {Re}w$ cannot be zero in this intersection. For either sign, each horizontal section in $E\cap \{ |w|>1/2\} $ is an interval containing respectively $5/8$ or $-5/8$; horizontal segments followed by a vertical segment at that real part connect any two points on the same side. Thus both displayed components are nonempty, open and closed relative to $H\cap B$. Take separate copies of $H$ and $B$, and identify their points with the same coordinates precisely over $U_+$. Let $X$ be this quotient. Its quotient map is open: saturating an open set in either copy adds only its intersection with the open set $U_+$ in the other copy. Consequently the two copies embed as open subsets of $X$ and give complex charts, with identity transition on $U_+$. Their images meet, so $X$ is connected, and their countable bases give a countable basis for $X$. The coordinate map $\pi :X\to \Delta ^2$ is well defined, continuous and a local biholomorphism. We check Hausdorffness, which would fail if an inappropriate part of an overlap were glued. Points with distinct coordinate images are separated by inverse images of disjoint neighborhoods in $\Delta ^2$. Distinct points with the same image must be the two copies of a point of $U_-$. A sufficiently small common coordinate neighborhood lies in $U_-$; its two images in $X$ are disjoint open neighborhoods. This proves Hausdorffness. The space is also paracompact, as required in the complex-manifold convention. Here are explicit standard details. A locally compact Hausdorff space with a countable basis has a countable basis of relatively compact open sets. From that basis construct compact $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ exhausting the space, by adjoining finitely many relatively compact neighborhoods covering $K_ j$ and the first $j$ basis sets. Given any open cover, cover each compact layer $K_ j\setminus \operatorname {Int}K_{j-1}$ by finitely many open sets refining the cover and contained in $\operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}\setminus K_{j-2}$ (take negative-index sets empty). This is possible by local compactness and Hausdorff regularity: for a point and an open neighborhood, a compact neighborhood followed by finite separation from its closed complement gives an open neighborhood with closure inside it. The resulting layer refinement is locally finite. Thus the atlas just constructed is an atlas on a paracompact Hausdorff complex surface. All functions come from the bidisc. We first prove the needed filling of $H$ directly from the existing Cauchy calculus holomorphic power series and Cauchy bounds . For $h\in \mathcal O(H)$ and $1/2<R<1$ define, on $\Delta \times \{ |w|<R\} $, \[  F_ R(z,w)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int _{|\zeta |=R} \frac{h(z,\zeta )}{\zeta -w}\, d\zeta .  \] The compact contour lies in $H$ for every $z\in \Delta $. Differentiation under the integral locally in $(z,w)$ proves that $F_ R$ is holomorphic. For $|z|<1/2$ the function $h(z,\cdot )$ is holomorphic on $\Delta $, so Cauchy's formula gives $F_ R=h$ there. If $1/2<|w|<R$, both $z\mapsto F_ R(z,w)$ and $z\mapsto h(z,w)$ are holomorphic on $\Delta $ and agree on $\{ |z|<1/2\} $. The one-variable identity theorem gives equality for every $z$. For two choices of $R$, the functions $F_ R$ agree on their common connected domain, since they agree on its nonempty open subset with $|z|<1/2$. They therefore define $F\in \mathcal O(\Delta ^2)$ extending $h$. This extension is unique by the identity theorem. A holomorphic function $f$ on $X$ is a pair $h\in \mathcal O(H)$, $b\in \mathcal O(B)$ agreeing on $U_+$. Extend $h$ to $F$ as just proved. Then $b$ and $F|_ B$ agree on the nonempty open set $U_+$ and $B$ is connected, so the identity theorem gives $b=F|_ B$. Hence $f=F\circ \pi $. Conversely every such pullback is holomorphic, and its vanishing implies $F|_ H=0$, hence $F=0$. This proves the claimed algebra isomorphism. In particular the two components of $\pi $ are global holomorphic coordinate functions locally. However the two points over $(3/4,-5/8)\in U_-$ are distinct, and no global holomorphic function distinguishes them. A noncompact hull. Let $K$ be the copy in $H\subset X$ of $\{ z=3/4,\  |w|=7/8\} $. This is compact. For integers $j\geq 2$ let $x_ j$ be the point of the $B$ copy with coordinates \[  (z,w)=\left(3/4,\  i(1-1/j)/8\right).  \] For $f=F\circ \pi \in \mathcal O(X)$ the one-variable maximum principle in $w$ gives $|f(x_ j)|\leq \sup _ K|f|$. One may derive this bound directly from Cauchy: apply its estimate on the circle to $F(3/4,\cdot )^ m$, take the $m$-th root and let $m\to \infty $. Thus all $x_ j$ lie in the holomorphic hull of $K$. Their images tend to $(3/4,i/8)$, which belongs neither to $H$ nor to $B$ and hence is not in $\pi (X)$. If this hull were compact, its continuous image would be a compact, therefore closed, subset of $\Delta ^2$ containing these images and their limit. This is impossible. Thus $X$ is not holomorphically convex. $\square$

title: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text:
Hermitian products are linear in the first variable. For Hermitian spaces $T,E$, a Hermitian form $C$ on $T\otimes E$ is Griffiths semipositive if it is nonnegative on decomposable tensors. It is $m$-semipositive if it is nonnegative on tensors of rank at most $m$, and Nakano semipositive if it is nonnegative on all tensors. Strict versions test nonzero tensors. Tensor rank means the rank of $T^*\to E$. Write $g,h$ for the metrics and \[  C(u)=\sum _{j,k,\lambda ,\mu }c_{jk\lambda \mu } u_{j\lambda }\overline{u_{k\mu }},\qquad (\operatorname {tr}_ E C)_{j\bar k}=\sum _\lambda c_{jk\lambda \lambda }  \] in unitary bases. Unless explicitly zero, the spaces have positive dimension. All curvature forms below are unscaled: the normalized first Chern form of a line is $\mathrm i\Theta /(2\pi )$. Lemma 10.34.1 . 80CB7E919269 Let $q\geq 3$ be an integer and let $\sigma $ be uniformly distributed over the $r$-tuples of $q$th roots of unity. For $x'_\sigma =\sum _\lambda x_\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }$ and $y'_\sigma =\sum _\lambda y_\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }$, \[  \mathbb E\bigl (x'_\sigma \overline{y'_\sigma } \sigma _\alpha \overline{\sigma _\beta }\bigr ) =\begin{cases}  x_\alpha \overline{y_\beta },& \alpha \ne \beta ,\\  \sum _\lambda x_\lambda \overline{y_\lambda },& \alpha =\beta . \end{cases}  \] Proof. Expand the expression. Independence and $q^{-1}\sum _{\zeta ^ q=1}\zeta ^ a=0$ for $0<|a|\leq 2$ show that a term survives exactly when the multiset of the two positive phase indices equals that of the two negative ones. For $\alpha \ne \beta $ this forces the indicated single term; for $\alpha =\beta $ it forces equal indices from $x$ and $y$. The root sum follows by summing a finite geometric progression. The bound $q\geq 3$ is what excludes exponents $\pm 2$. $\square$ Theorem 10.34.2 . 69881B3187A9 If $C$ is Griffiths semipositive, then \[  C+(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h\quad \hbox{is Nakano semipositive}, \qquad m(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h-C \quad \hbox{is $m$-semipositive}  \] for every integer $m\geq 1$. If on decomposable tensors $C(\xi \otimes v)\geq \varepsilon |\xi |^2|v|^2$, then the two lower bounds are respectively E601DE45CB52 10.34.3 \begin{equation}  (r+1)\varepsilon |u|^2\quad \hbox{for all }u,\qquad (mr-1)\varepsilon |u|^2\quad \hbox{for }\operatorname {rank}u\leq m. \end{equation} Thus strict Griffiths positivity gives strict Nakano positivity in the first assertion, and strict $m$-positivity in the second unless $r=m=1$, when the second form is identically zero. Proof. Write $u=\sum _\lambda \xi _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda $, put $\widehat\xi _\sigma =\sum _\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }\xi _\lambda $ and $\widehat e_\sigma =\sum _\lambda \sigma _\lambda e_\lambda $. The preceding moment identity gives exactly 92B7B02AA2C7 10.34.4 \begin{equation}  \bigl (C+(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h\bigr )(u) =\mathbb E C(\widehat\xi _\sigma \otimes \widehat e_\sigma ) +\sum _\lambda C(\xi _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda ). \end{equation} Both terms are nonnegative. To verify the diagonal count, the expectation contains all off-diagonal coefficients of $C(u)$ and the whole trace term; it counts the coefficient with all fiber indices equal only once. The final sum supplies that missing copy. For the second assertion, let $u\ne 0$ have rank $k\leq m$, and let $F\subset E$ be the $k$-dimensional image of $T^*\to E$ defined by $u$. Restrict $C$ to $T\otimes F$. The form \[  D=(\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F)\otimes h_ F-C_ F  \] is Griffiths semipositive: in a unitary basis beginning with any given unit fiber vector, it is the sum of the other diagonal tests. This remains true for $k=1$, where $D=0$. Apply the first assertion to $D$ on $T\otimes F$ to get $D+(\operatorname {tr}_ F D)\otimes h_ F =k(\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F)\otimes h_ F-C_ F\geq 0$ on all tensors. Finally \[  m\operatorname {tr}_ E C-k\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F =(m-k)\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F +m\operatorname {tr}_{F^\perp }C_{F^\perp }\geq 0  \] as a form on $T$. Evaluate on $u\in T\otimes F$. For the quantitative statements apply these semipositive conclusions to $C-\varepsilon g\otimes h$. The trace of $g\otimes h$ is $rg$, so the two added scalar forms have coefficients $r+1$ and $mr-1$. If $C$ is strictly Griffiths positive, compactness of the two unit spheres supplies $\varepsilon >0$. This proves all strict claims and the exceptional rank-one case. $\square$ Example 10.34.5 . 3F9B151E377C The coefficient one in the trace-added inequality is optimal as a universal coefficient, even for strictly Griffiths-positive forms on $\mathbb C^2\otimes \mathbb C^2$. Proof. For $T=E=\mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 2$, set \[  C_0(u)=\sum _{j,\lambda }u_{j\lambda }\overline{u_{\lambda j}}.  \] Then $C_0(\xi \otimes v)=|\sum _ j\xi _ j\overline{v_ j}|^2\geq 0$, $\operatorname {tr}_ E C_0=g$, and $C_0(u)=-|u|^2$ for every nonzero skew-symmetric coefficient matrix. Put $C_\varepsilon =C_0+\varepsilon g\otimes h$, with $\varepsilon >0$. It is strictly Griffiths positive and its trace is $(1+n\varepsilon )g$. For every real $c<1$, the form $C_\varepsilon +c(\operatorname {tr}_ E C_\varepsilon )\otimes h$ has value \[  \bigl (c-1+(1+cn)\varepsilon \bigr )|u|^2  \] on such a matrix. Choosing $0<\varepsilon <(1-c)/(1+n|c|)$ makes it negative. Taking $n=2$ proves the assertion. In contrast $C_0+(\operatorname {tr}_ E C_0)\otimes h =\tfrac 12\sum _{j,\lambda }|u_{j\lambda }+u_{\lambda j}|^2$. The strict perturbation is essential to test a strict hypothesis. $\square$ Proposition 10.34.6 . E048AA8C1785 For induced Hermitian metrics, Chern curvature obeys \[  R_{E\otimes F}=R_ E\otimes I+I\otimes R_ F,\qquad R_{E^*}=-R_ E^{\mathsf T},\qquad R_{\det E}=\operatorname {tr}_ E R_ E.  \] Tensor products preserve $m$-semipositivity and strict $m$-positivity when both factors have the corresponding sign. On $E^{\otimes d}$, $d\geq 1$, a lower bound $\varepsilon $ for $E$ on rank-at-most-$m$ tensors gives the lower bound $d\varepsilon $. These assertions pass to any parallel holomorphic summand. In particular they apply to symmetric powers, exterior powers and the image of a fixed Young symmetrizer in a tensor power, whenever that image is nonzero. For Griffiths positivity take $m=1$; for Nakano positivity test all tensor ranks. Proof. The tensor connection is the sum of its two connection actions. Their squares give the first formula, since the mixed degree-one terms cancel. Differentiating the evaluation pairing gives the negative transpose formula. On the determinant the connection form is $\operatorname {tr}A$; its curvature is $d\operatorname {tr}A =\operatorname {tr}(dA+A\wedge A)$, since $\operatorname {tr}(A\wedge A)=0$ by exchanging the matrix indices. All these metric connections have the canonical $(0,1)$-parts. In a holomorphic frame, metric compatibility then forces the connection form to be $H^{-1}\partial H$, proving uniqueness and identifying them as Chern connections. This local calculation requires no Kähler metric on the base. For the tensor positivity claim write a tensor in $T\otimes E\otimes F$ in a unitary basis of $F$. The first curvature term is the sum of the curvature tests on its $T\otimes E$ slices. A contraction on the fiber factor cannot increase the rank of $T^*$ into that fiber, so each slice has rank at most the original tensor rank. The same argument, slicing by $E$, treats the second term. The sum of the squared slice norms is the original squared norm. This proves the quantitative bounds and, by induction, the tensor-power assertion. Permutations of equal tensor factors are parallel and commute with every transition $G^{\otimes d}$. A fixed linear combination $Y$ of them is therefore a parallel holomorphic map of constant rank: in each tensor frame it is the same fixed matrix. Its image $W$ is a holomorphic subbundle preserved by the connection. Metric compatibility also preserves $W^\perp $, so its induced connection has zero second fundamental form and its curvature is the restriction. This proves the summand assertion. The averaging and alternating maps give symmetric and exterior powers. More generally, for a Young diagram use the product of the sum over row permutations and the signed sum over column permutations; its image is all that is meant here by the corresponding Schur tensor bundle. No irreducibility or representation-classification assertion is needed. $\square$ Theorem 10.34.7 . FB187755A875 Let $E$ be a Hermitian holomorphic vector bundle of rank $r\geq 1$ on a complex manifold. Griffiths semipositivity implies Nakano semipositivity of $E\otimes \det E$, and $m$-semipositivity of $E^*\otimes (\det E)^ m$ for every integer $m\geq 1$. Strict Griffiths positivity gives the strict conclusions, except that the latter bundle is flat when $r=m=1$. More strongly, for every integer $k\geq 0$, \[  \operatorname {Sym}^ kE\otimes \det E \quad \hbox{is Nakano semipositive}.  \] It is Nakano positive when $E$ is Griffiths positive. A pointwise Griffiths lower bound $\varepsilon $ for $E$ gives the Nakano lower bound $(r+k)\varepsilon $ for this last bundle. Proof. The first assertion is theorem 10.34.2 applied to its curvature, using proposition 10.34.6 . The form $C=-R_{E^*}$ is Griffiths semipositive whenever $R_ E$ is: the negative-transpose formula, with the conjugate fiber coordinates, gives precisely the same decomposable tests. Its trace is $\operatorname {tr}R_ E$. Thus the curvature of $E^*\otimes (\det E)^ m$ is $m(\operatorname {tr}C)\otimes h-C$. The trace inequality gives the assertion and the lower bound $(mr-1)\varepsilon $. For $r=m=1$ the bundle with its induced metric is the canonically trivial $E^*\otimes E$ and has zero curvature. We prove the stronger symmetric assertion directly. At a point use unitary bases and identify a symmetric tensor $u\in \operatorname {Sym}^ kE$ with the homogeneous polynomial \[  p_ u(z)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ k}u_{i_1\cdots i_ k}z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_ k}.  \] Use the probability measure $d\gamma (z)=\pi ^{-r}e^{-|z|^2}dV(z)$ on $\mathbb C^ r$. Polar integration in each variable gives \[  \int z^\alpha \overline{z^\beta }\, d\gamma =\begin{cases} \alpha !,& \alpha =\beta ,\\ 0,& \alpha \ne \beta ,\end{cases} \qquad \langle u,v\rangle =\frac1{k!}\int p_ u\overline{p_ v}\, d\gamma .  \] For the second identity, a monomial with multi-index $\alpha $ has $k!/\alpha !$ equal tensor coefficients; the displayed moment computes its norm exactly. The degree-zero conventions are $0!=1$ and $p_ u=u$. Write $R_{j\bar k}e_\lambda =\sum _\mu c_{jk\lambda \mu }e_\mu $. Its symmetric action on polynomials is $\sum _{\lambda ,\mu }c_{jk\lambda \mu }z_\mu \partial _{z_\lambda }$. Gaussian integration by parts gives \[  \int \overline z_\lambda z_\mu p_{u_ j}\overline{p_{u_ k}}\, d\gamma =\int \bigl (\delta _{\lambda \mu }p_{u_ j} +z_\mu \partial _{z_\lambda }p_{u_ j}\bigr ) \overline{p_{u_ k}}\, d\gamma .  \] Indeed $\partial _{z_\lambda }e^{-|z|^2} =-\overline z_\lambda e^{-|z|^2}$; integrate over balls and let their radii tend to infinity. Polynomial times Gaussian boundary terms tend to zero, so every integral converges absolutely. For $u=\sum _ j t_ j\otimes u_ j$ the resulting identity is 36F0B3AD01F0 10.34.8 \begin{equation}  R_{\operatorname {Sym}^ kE\otimes \det E}(u) =\frac1{k!}\int R_ E\left( \Bigl (\sum _ j p_{u_ j}(z)t_ j\Bigr )\otimes \overline z\right) \, d\gamma (z). \end{equation} Each integrand is a decomposable curvature test and hence nonnegative. If $R_ E\geq \varepsilon $ on such tests, the right side is at least $\varepsilon \sum _ j\int |z|^2|p_{u_ j}|^2d\gamma /k!$. The monomial moment formula gives $\int |z|^2|p|^2d\gamma =(r+k)\int |p|^2d\gamma $ for homogeneous degree $k$. This proves the stated bound and strictness. All expressions on the left are intrinsic; the chosen coordinates only evaluate them. $\square$ Proposition 10.34.9 . A86F8BFD9ADD Let $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$ be a holomorphic exact sequence, with the induced subbundle and quotient metrics. If $E$ is $m$-semipositive, then $S\otimes (\det Q)^ m$ is $m$-semipositive. The implication is also strict. More precisely, writing $a=\operatorname {rank}Q$, a pointwise lower bound $\varepsilon \geq 0$ for $E$ on tensors of rank at most $m$ gives the bound $(1+ma)\varepsilon $ for this twist. Ranks one and zero of $S,Q$ are allowed with their usual conventions. Proof. If $S=0$, the assertion is vacuous, so assume its rank is positive. Use the smooth orthogonal splitting $E=S\oplus Q$. Its Chern connection has the block form \[  D_ E=\begin{pmatrix} D_ S

& -\beta ^*

\\ \beta 

& D_ Q

\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \beta =\sum _ j dz_ j B_ j\in \mathcal A^{1,0}(\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)).  \] Holomorphicity of $S$ makes the lower-left $(0,1)$-block zero; metric compatibility determines the opposite block. The diagonal connections have their canonical $(0,1)$-parts and preserve their induced metrics, so are the indicated Chern connections. Squaring gives, including the imaginary units, \begin{align*}  \mathrm i\Theta (S)& =\mathrm i\Theta (E)|_ S -\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ k^*B_ j,\\  \mathrm i\Theta (Q)& =\mathrm i\Theta (E)|_ Q +\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ jB_ k^*. \end{align*} For the first sign use $\beta ^*\wedge \beta =-\sum dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ k^*B_ j$. Let $C_ B$ be the form on $T\otimes S$ with coefficients $B_ k^*B_ j$. It is Nakano semipositive, since \[  C_ B(u)=\left|\sum _ j B_ ju_ j\right|^2,\qquad \operatorname {tr}_ Q(B_ jB_ k^*)=\operatorname {tr}_ S(B_ k^*B_ j).  \] Consequently the twist has curvature form \[  R_ E|_ S+m(\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q)\otimes h_ S +m(\operatorname {tr}_ S C_ B)\otimes h_ S-C_ B.  \] The last two terms together are $m$-semipositive by theorem 10.34.2 ; when $\operatorname {rank}S=1$ this uses its non-strict rank-one clause, not a false strict assertion. The first term has lower bound $\varepsilon $ on the tested tensors. Griffiths tests in an orthonormal basis of $Q$ give $\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q\geq a\varepsilon g$. This proves the displayed quantitative claim and strictness. If $Q=0$, its determinant is the flat trivial line and this is just $S=E$; if $S=0$ there are no nonzero tensors to test. $\square$ Example 10.34.10 . 722E8364B69C On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 1$, let $H$ be the quotient of the trivial $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ bundle by $\mathcal O(-1)$, with quotient metric. At $[1:0:\cdots :0]$ its curvature form is $C_0$ of example 10.34.5 . Its dual has Nakano form $-|\operatorname {tr}u|^2$. Moreover, under the induced metric, \[  T\mathbb P^ n\simeq H\otimes \mathcal O(1)\simeq H\otimes \det H, \qquad R_{T\mathbb P^ n}(u)=\tfrac 12\sum _{j,k}|u_{jk}+u_{kj}|^2.  \] Thus this tangent metric is Griffiths positive and Nakano semipositive, and is not Nakano positive for $n\geq 2$. For $n=1$ both $H$ and $T\mathbb P^1$ are Nakano positive. Proof. In the affine chart $[1:z]$, the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$. At $z=0$, its second fundamental maps satisfy $B_ j(1)=e_ j$. The quotient curvature formula in proposition 10.34.9 , applied to the flat ambient bundle, gives $R_{H,j\bar k}=B_ jB_ k^*$, hence $c_{jk\lambda \mu }=\delta _{k\lambda }\delta _{j\mu }$, the flip form $C_0$. The negative transpose gives the asserted dual trace square. Taking determinants of the tautological sequence identifies $\det H$ with $\mathcal O(1)$ after choosing a unit volume element in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$; its induced metrics agree. A tangent variation of a line $\ell $ defines the map $\ell \to \mathbb C^{n+1}/\ell $ given by differentiating a local generator modulo $\ell $. Rescaling the generator leaves this linear map unchanged. In graph coordinates it is the differential of $z$, so this is the holomorphic identification $T\mathbb P^ n=\operatorname {Hom}(\mathcal O(-1),H)$. Curvature addition now gives $C_0+g\otimes h$ and the displayed sum. On a decomposable tensor it is at least $|\xi |^2|v|^2$, whereas a nonzero skew-symmetric matrix gives zero for $n\geq 2$. Unitary transformations of the ambient vector space preserve all these metrics and are transitive on projective space, so the tests hold at every point. For $n=1$ the flip form is the scalar form $1$ and the tangent form is $2$, proving the endpoint assertion. $\square$ Corollary 10.34.11 . 670C664810C5 Let $X$ be compact of dimension $n\geq 1$, with positive-rank Hermitian holomorphic bundle $E$. All positivity assumptions in this corollary are strict at every point. Then: If $E$ is Griffiths positive, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,\operatorname {Sym}^ kE\otimes \det E)=0$ for $k\geq 0$ and $1\leq q\leq n$. This includes $E\otimes \det E$. For any nonzero degree-$d$ Schur tensor image $W\subset E^{\otimes d}$, $d\geq 1$, one also has $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,W\otimes \det W)=0$. If $E$ is Griffiths positive of rank $r\geq 2$, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E^*\otimes (\det E)^ m)=0$ whenever $q\geq 1$ and $m\geq \min (n-q+1,r)$. The same holds for $r=1,m>1$; no such assertion is made for $r=m=1$. In a holomorphic exact sequence $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$, put $s=\operatorname {rank}S$. If $E$ is $m$-positive, $m\geq \min (n-q+1,s)$, and a line bundle $L$ has a metric such that $L\otimes (\det Q)^{-m}$ is semipositive, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,S\otimes L)=0$ for $1\leq q\leq n$. For $s=0$ the group is zero without conditions. These analytic groups also have their sheaf-cohomology interpretation by corollary 10.43.11 . Proof. Each assumed positivity implies Griffiths positivity of $E$. Its determinant curvature $\mathrm i\operatorname {tr}\Theta (E)$ is a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form, so it itself supplies a Kähler metric on $X$; closedness follows locally from the determinant connection. The first two claims follow from theorem 10.34.7 , proposition 10.34.6 and the exact strict rank-$m$ vanishing range of corollary 10.33.14 . For the third, proposition 10.34.9 makes $S\otimes (\det Q)^ m$ strictly $m$-positive. Tensoring by the specified semipositive line adds a nonnegative scalar curvature form, so preserves that strict inequality. Apply the same rank-$m$ vanishing range to the rank-$s$ bundle $S\otimes L$. Compactness makes the pointwise strict bounds uniform on the relevant unit tensor bundles, exactly as in that canonical vanishing argument. No continuation theorem is used. $\square$ Corollary 10.34.12 . 10CC96C8D2BA Let $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$ be a holomorphic exact sequence on a compact $n$-dimensional complex manifold, and suppose $E$ is strictly $m$-positive everywhere, $m\geq 1$. Put $s=\operatorname {rank}S$. For $0\leq q<n$ and integers $l,m\geq \min (n-q,s)$, the map \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E\otimes (\det Q)^ l) \longrightarrow H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,Q\otimes (\det Q)^ l)  \] is onto. For $1\leq q\leq n$ it is an isomorphism if $l,m\geq \min (n-q+1,s)$. In degree $q=n$ it is always onto. If $S=0$ the map is an isomorphism in every degree and twist. Proof. The quotient curvature formula shows that $Q$ is Griffiths positive when its rank is nonzero: on a decomposable tensor the extra term is $|B(\xi )^*v|^2\geq 0$. Thus $\det Q$ is semipositive, also for $Q=0$. Let $a=\min (n-q,s)$ for surjectivity, with $s>0$ and $q<n$. Since $m\geq a$, the bundle $E$ is strictly $a$-positive. The preceding corollary with $L=(\det Q)^ l$ and exponent $a$ gives $H^{n,q+1}_{\bar\partial }(X,S\otimes (\det Q)^ l)=0$, because $l\geq a$ and $(\det Q)^{l-a}$ is semipositive. For the isomorphism condition use $a=\min (n-q+1,s)$; the same argument gives vanishing in both degrees $q$ and $q+1$, the latter automatic when $q=n$. The bundle sequence tensored with $K_ X\otimes (\det Q)^ l$ gives a short exact sequence of global smooth Dolbeault complexes: the surjectivity in each degree follows from a smooth bundle splitting. Its cohomology long exact sequence from lemma 10.43.3 proves the assertions. For $q=n$, its next degree is zero, so surjectivity is automatic. $\square$ Remark 10.34.13 . 7DF710595FC8 All pointwise semipositive assertions hold on arbitrary complex bases. The compact vanishing conclusions assume strict positivity everywhere; semipositivity with strictness at only one point requires an additional continuation argument and is not asserted. Nor does the projective tangent example rule out a different metric with stronger positivity. No preservation of Nakano positivity by arbitrary quotient bundles is used: the tensor summands above are parallel. On a zero-dimensional compact base every positive-degree Dolbeault group is zero; finite components are treated componentwise. A zero Schur/exterior image has zero cohomology, while a degree-zero tensor power is the flat trivial line. The symmetric determinant theorem includes degree zero explicitly; it then says that $\det E$ is positive. No unrestricted ample-vector-bundle positivity or promised later Griffiths/Le Potier theorem follows from these metric statements.

title: Lemma 10.34.1
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Lemma 10.34.1 . 80CB7E919269 Let $q\geq 3$ be an integer and let $\sigma $ be uniformly distributed over the $r$-tuples of $q$th roots of unity. For $x'_\sigma =\sum _\lambda x_\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }$ and $y'_\sigma =\sum _\lambda y_\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }$, \[  \mathbb E\bigl (x'_\sigma \overline{y'_\sigma } \sigma _\alpha \overline{\sigma _\beta }\bigr ) =\begin{cases}  x_\alpha \overline{y_\beta },& \alpha \ne \beta ,\\  \sum _\lambda x_\lambda \overline{y_\lambda },& \alpha =\beta . \end{cases}  \] Proof. Expand the expression. Independence and $q^{-1}\sum _{\zeta ^ q=1}\zeta ^ a=0$ for $0<|a|\leq 2$ show that a term survives exactly when the multiset of the two positive phase indices equals that of the two negative ones. For $\alpha \ne \beta $ this forces the indicated single term; for $\alpha =\beta $ it forces equal indices from $x$ and $y$. The root sum follows by summing a finite geometric progression. The bound $q\geq 3$ is what excludes exponents $\pm 2$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.34.2
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Theorem 10.34.2 . 69881B3187A9 If $C$ is Griffiths semipositive, then \[  C+(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h\quad \hbox{is Nakano semipositive}, \qquad m(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h-C \quad \hbox{is $m$-semipositive}  \] for every integer $m\geq 1$. If on decomposable tensors $C(\xi \otimes v)\geq \varepsilon |\xi |^2|v|^2$, then the two lower bounds are respectively E601DE45CB52 10.34.3 \begin{equation}  (r+1)\varepsilon |u|^2\quad \hbox{for all }u,\qquad (mr-1)\varepsilon |u|^2\quad \hbox{for }\operatorname {rank}u\leq m. \end{equation} Thus strict Griffiths positivity gives strict Nakano positivity in the first assertion, and strict $m$-positivity in the second unless $r=m=1$, when the second form is identically zero. Proof. Write $u=\sum _\lambda \xi _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda $, put $\widehat\xi _\sigma =\sum _\lambda \overline{\sigma _\lambda }\xi _\lambda $ and $\widehat e_\sigma =\sum _\lambda \sigma _\lambda e_\lambda $. The preceding moment identity gives exactly 92B7B02AA2C7 10.34.4 \begin{equation}  \bigl (C+(\operatorname {tr}_ E C)\otimes h\bigr )(u) =\mathbb E C(\widehat\xi _\sigma \otimes \widehat e_\sigma ) +\sum _\lambda C(\xi _\lambda \otimes e_\lambda ). \end{equation} Both terms are nonnegative. To verify the diagonal count, the expectation contains all off-diagonal coefficients of $C(u)$ and the whole trace term; it counts the coefficient with all fiber indices equal only once. The final sum supplies that missing copy. For the second assertion, let $u\ne 0$ have rank $k\leq m$, and let $F\subset E$ be the $k$-dimensional image of $T^*\to E$ defined by $u$. Restrict $C$ to $T\otimes F$. The form \[  D=(\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F)\otimes h_ F-C_ F  \] is Griffiths semipositive: in a unitary basis beginning with any given unit fiber vector, it is the sum of the other diagonal tests. This remains true for $k=1$, where $D=0$. Apply the first assertion to $D$ on $T\otimes F$ to get $D+(\operatorname {tr}_ F D)\otimes h_ F =k(\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F)\otimes h_ F-C_ F\geq 0$ on all tensors. Finally \[  m\operatorname {tr}_ E C-k\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F =(m-k)\operatorname {tr}_ F C_ F +m\operatorname {tr}_{F^\perp }C_{F^\perp }\geq 0  \] as a form on $T$. Evaluate on $u\in T\otimes F$. For the quantitative statements apply these semipositive conclusions to $C-\varepsilon g\otimes h$. The trace of $g\otimes h$ is $rg$, so the two added scalar forms have coefficients $r+1$ and $mr-1$. If $C$ is strictly Griffiths positive, compactness of the two unit spheres supplies $\varepsilon >0$. This proves all strict claims and the exceptional rank-one case. $\square$

The trace inequality gives the assertion and the lower bound $(mr-1)\varepsilon $. For $r=m=1$ the bundle with its induced metric is the canonically trivial $E^*\otimes E$ and has zero curvature. We prove the stronger symmetric assertion directly. At a point use unitary bases and identify a symmetric tensor $u\in \operatorname {Sym}^ kE$ with the homogeneous polynomial \[  p_ u(z)=\sum _{i_1,\ldots ,i_ k}u_{i_1\cdots i_ k}z_{i_1}\cdots z_{i_ k}.  \] Use the probability measure $d\gamma (z)=\pi ^{-r}e^{-|z|^2}dV(z)$ on $\mathbb C^ r$. Polar integration in each variable gives \[  \int z^\alpha \overline{z^\beta }\, d\gamma =\begin{cases} \alpha !,& \alpha =\beta ,\\ 0,& \alpha \ne \beta ,\end{cases} \qquad \langle u,v\rangle =\frac1{k!}\int p_ u\overline{p_ v}\, d\gamma .  \] For the second identity, a monomial with multi-index $\alpha $ has $k!/\alpha !$ equal tensor coefficients; the displayed moment computes its norm exactly. The degree-zero conventions are $0!=1$ and $p_ u=u$. Write $R_{j\bar k}e_\lambda =\sum _\mu c_{jk\lambda \mu }e_\mu $. Its symmetric action on polynomials is $\sum _{\lambda ,\mu }c_{jk\lambda \mu }z_\mu \partial _{z_\lambda }$. Gaussian integration by parts gives \[  \int \overline z_\lambda z_\mu p_{u_ j}\overline{p_{u_ k}}\, d\gamma =\int \bigl (\delta _{\lambda \mu }p_{u_ j} +z_\mu \partial _{z_\lambda }p_{u_ j}\bigr ) \overline{p_{u_ k}}\, d\gamma .  \] Indeed $\partial _{z_\lambda }e^{-|z|^2} =-\overline z_\lambda e^{-|z|^2}$; integrate over balls and let their radii tend to infinity. Polynomial times Gaussian boundary terms tend to zero, so every integral converges absolutely. For $u=\sum _ j t_ j\otimes u_ j$ the resulting identity is 36F0B3AD01F0 10.34.8 \begin{equation}  R_{\operatorname {Sym}^ kE\otimes \det E}(u) =\frac1{k!}\int R_ E\left( \Bigl (\sum _ j p_{u_ j}(z)t_ j\Bigr )\otimes \overline z\right) \, d\gamma (z). \end{equation} Each integrand is a decomposable curvature test and hence nonnegative. If $R_ E\geq \varepsilon $ on such tests, the right side is at least $\varepsilon \sum _ j\int |z|^2|p_{u_ j}|^2d\gamma /k!$. The monomial moment formula gives $\int |z|^2|p|^2d\gamma =(r+k)\int |p|^2d\gamma $ for homogeneous degree $k$. This proves the stated bound and strictness. All expressions on the left are intrinsic; the chosen coordinates only evaluate them. $\square$
