title: Proposition 10.34.9
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text:
Proposition 10.34.9 . A86F8BFD9ADD Let $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$ be a holomorphic exact sequence, with the induced subbundle and quotient metrics. If $E$ is $m$-semipositive, then $S\otimes (\det Q)^ m$ is $m$-semipositive. The implication is also strict. More precisely, writing $a=\operatorname {rank}Q$, a pointwise lower bound $\varepsilon \geq 0$ for $E$ on tensors of rank at most $m$ gives the bound $(1+ma)\varepsilon $ for this twist. Ranks one and zero of $S,Q$ are allowed with their usual conventions. Proof. If $S=0$, the assertion is vacuous, so assume its rank is positive. Use the smooth orthogonal splitting $E=S\oplus Q$. Its Chern connection has the block form \[  D_ E=\begin{pmatrix} D_ S

& -\beta ^*

\\ \beta 

& D_ Q

\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \beta =\sum _ j dz_ j B_ j\in \mathcal A^{1,0}(\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q)).  \] Holomorphicity of $S$ makes the lower-left $(0,1)$-block zero; metric compatibility determines the opposite block. The diagonal connections have their canonical $(0,1)$-parts and preserve their induced metrics, so are the indicated Chern connections. Squaring gives, including the imaginary units, \begin{align*}  \mathrm i\Theta (S)& =\mathrm i\Theta (E)|_ S -\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ k^*B_ j,\\  \mathrm i\Theta (Q)& =\mathrm i\Theta (E)|_ Q +\mathrm i\sum _{j,k}dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ jB_ k^*. \end{align*} For the first sign use $\beta ^*\wedge \beta =-\sum dz_ j\wedge d\overline z_ k B_ k^*B_ j$. Let $C_ B$ be the form on $T\otimes S$ with coefficients $B_ k^*B_ j$. It is Nakano semipositive, since \[  C_ B(u)=\left|\sum _ j B_ ju_ j\right|^2,\qquad \operatorname {tr}_ Q(B_ jB_ k^*)=\operatorname {tr}_ S(B_ k^*B_ j).  \] Consequently the twist has curvature form \[  R_ E|_ S+m(\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q)\otimes h_ S +m(\operatorname {tr}_ S C_ B)\otimes h_ S-C_ B.  \] The last two terms together are $m$-semipositive by theorem 10.34.2 ; when $\operatorname {rank}S=1$ this uses its non-strict rank-one clause, not a false strict assertion. The first term has lower bound $\varepsilon $ on the tested tensors. Griffiths tests in an orthonormal basis of $Q$ give $\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q\geq a\varepsilon g$. This proves the displayed quantitative claim and strictness. If $Q=0$, its determinant is the flat trivial line and this is just $S=E$; if $S=0$ there are no nonzero tensors to test. $\square$

title: Example 10.34.10
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Example 10.34.10 . 722E8364B69C On $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 1$, let $H$ be the quotient of the trivial $\mathbb C^{n+1}$ bundle by $\mathcal O(-1)$, with quotient metric. At $[1:0:\cdots :0]$ its curvature form is $C_0$ of example 10.34.5 . Its dual has Nakano form $-|\operatorname {tr}u|^2$. Moreover, under the induced metric, \[  T\mathbb P^ n\simeq H\otimes \mathcal O(1)\simeq H\otimes \det H, \qquad R_{T\mathbb P^ n}(u)=\tfrac 12\sum _{j,k}|u_{jk}+u_{kj}|^2.  \] Thus this tangent metric is Griffiths positive and Nakano semipositive, and is not Nakano positive for $n\geq 2$. For $n=1$ both $H$ and $T\mathbb P^1$ are Nakano positive. Proof. In the affine chart $[1:z]$, the tautological line is spanned by $(1,z)$. At $z=0$, its second fundamental maps satisfy $B_ j(1)=e_ j$. The quotient curvature formula in proposition 10.34.9 , applied to the flat ambient bundle, gives $R_{H,j\bar k}=B_ jB_ k^*$, hence $c_{jk\lambda \mu }=\delta _{k\lambda }\delta _{j\mu }$, the flip form $C_0$. The negative transpose gives the asserted dual trace square. Taking determinants of the tautological sequence identifies $\det H$ with $\mathcal O(1)$ after choosing a unit volume element in $\mathbb C^{n+1}$; its induced metrics agree. A tangent variation of a line $\ell $ defines the map $\ell \to \mathbb C^{n+1}/\ell $ given by differentiating a local generator modulo $\ell $. Rescaling the generator leaves this linear map unchanged. In graph coordinates it is the differential of $z$, so this is the holomorphic identification $T\mathbb P^ n=\operatorname {Hom}(\mathcal O(-1),H)$. Curvature addition now gives $C_0+g\otimes h$ and the displayed sum. On a decomposable tensor it is at least $|\xi |^2|v|^2$, whereas a nonzero skew-symmetric matrix gives zero for $n\geq 2$. Unitary transformations of the ambient vector space preserve all these metrics and are transitive on projective space, so the tests hold at every point. For $n=1$ the flip form is the scalar form $1$ and the tangent form is $2$, proving the endpoint assertion. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.34.11
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Corollary 10.34.11 . 670C664810C5 Let $X$ be compact of dimension $n\geq 1$, with positive-rank Hermitian holomorphic bundle $E$. All positivity assumptions in this corollary are strict at every point. Then: If $E$ is Griffiths positive, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,\operatorname {Sym}^ kE\otimes \det E)=0$ for $k\geq 0$ and $1\leq q\leq n$. This includes $E\otimes \det E$. For any nonzero degree-$d$ Schur tensor image $W\subset E^{\otimes d}$, $d\geq 1$, one also has $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,W\otimes \det W)=0$. If $E$ is Griffiths positive of rank $r\geq 2$, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E^*\otimes (\det E)^ m)=0$ whenever $q\geq 1$ and $m\geq \min (n-q+1,r)$. The same holds for $r=1,m>1$; no such assertion is made for $r=m=1$. In a holomorphic exact sequence $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$, put $s=\operatorname {rank}S$. If $E$ is $m$-positive, $m\geq \min (n-q+1,s)$, and a line bundle $L$ has a metric such that $L\otimes (\det Q)^{-m}$ is semipositive, then $H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,S\otimes L)=0$ for $1\leq q\leq n$. For $s=0$ the group is zero without conditions. These analytic groups also have their sheaf-cohomology interpretation by corollary 10.43.11 . Proof. Each assumed positivity implies Griffiths positivity of $E$. Its determinant curvature $\mathrm i\operatorname {tr}\Theta (E)$ is a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form, so it itself supplies a Kähler metric on $X$; closedness follows locally from the determinant connection. The first two claims follow from theorem 10.34.7 , proposition 10.34.6 and the exact strict rank-$m$ vanishing range of corollary 10.33.14 . For the third, proposition 10.34.9 makes $S\otimes (\det Q)^ m$ strictly $m$-positive. Tensoring by the specified semipositive line adds a nonnegative scalar curvature form, so preserves that strict inequality. Apply the same rank-$m$ vanishing range to the rank-$s$ bundle $S\otimes L$. Compactness makes the pointwise strict bounds uniform on the relevant unit tensor bundles, exactly as in that canonical vanishing argument. No continuation theorem is used. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.34.12
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Corollary 10.34.12 . 10CC96C8D2BA Let $0\to S\to E\to Q\to 0$ be a holomorphic exact sequence on a compact $n$-dimensional complex manifold, and suppose $E$ is strictly $m$-positive everywhere, $m\geq 1$. Put $s=\operatorname {rank}S$. For $0\leq q<n$ and integers $l,m\geq \min (n-q,s)$, the map \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E\otimes (\det Q)^ l) \longrightarrow H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,Q\otimes (\det Q)^ l)  \] is onto. For $1\leq q\leq n$ it is an isomorphism if $l,m\geq \min (n-q+1,s)$. In degree $q=n$ it is always onto. If $S=0$ the map is an isomorphism in every degree and twist. Proof. The quotient curvature formula shows that $Q$ is Griffiths positive when its rank is nonzero: on a decomposable tensor the extra term is $|B(\xi )^*v|^2\geq 0$. Thus $\det Q$ is semipositive, also for $Q=0$. Let $a=\min (n-q,s)$ for surjectivity, with $s>0$ and $q<n$. Since $m\geq a$, the bundle $E$ is strictly $a$-positive. The preceding corollary with $L=(\det Q)^ l$ and exponent $a$ gives $H^{n,q+1}_{\bar\partial }(X,S\otimes (\det Q)^ l)=0$, because $l\geq a$ and $(\det Q)^{l-a}$ is semipositive. For the isomorphism condition use $a=\min (n-q+1,s)$; the same argument gives vanishing in both degrees $q$ and $q+1$, the latter automatic when $q=n$. The bundle sequence tensored with $K_ X\otimes (\det Q)^ l$ gives a short exact sequence of global smooth Dolbeault complexes: the surjectivity in each degree follows from a smooth bundle splitting. Its cohomology long exact sequence from lemma 10.43.3 proves the assertions. For $q=n$, its next degree is zero, so surjectivity is automatic. $\square$

title: Remark 10.34.13
section: 10.34 Tensor curvature and determinant twists
text: Remark 10.34.13 . 7DF710595FC8 All pointwise semipositive assertions hold on arbitrary complex bases. The compact vanishing conclusions assume strict positivity everywhere; semipositivity with strictness at only one point requires an additional continuation argument and is not asserted. Nor does the projective tangent example rule out a different metric with stronger positivity. No preservation of Nakano positivity by arbitrary quotient bundles is used: the tensor summands above are parallel. On a zero-dimensional compact base every positive-degree Dolbeault group is zero; finite components are treated componentwise. A zero Schur/exterior image has zero cohomology, while a degree-zero tensor power is the flat trivial line. The symmetric determinant theorem includes degree zero explicitly; it then says that $\det E$ is positive. No unrestricted ample-vector-bundle positivity or promised later Griffiths/Le Potier theorem follows from these metric statements.

title: 7.30 Classical products under Hausdorff intersection conditions
search_title: Classical products under Hausdorff intersection conditions
section: 7.30 Classical products under Hausdorff intersection conditions
text: Write $\omega _0=dd^ c|z|^2$ in coordinates, with $dd^ c=\frac{i}{2\pi }\partial \bar\partial $. Trace mass and coefficient variation are equivalent on compact coordinate sets by coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents . The unbounded locus $L(u)$ is the complement of the open set where $u$ is locally bounded; it need not equal its pole set. Lemma 7.30.1 . 162A0666C4BB For a smooth real function $\chi $ and a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$, put $B_\chi (v)=dd^ c(\chi v)-\chi \, dd^ cv$. On relatively compact coordinate balls, this is a finite sum of Hessians of bounded plurisubharmonic functions with smooth bounded coefficients. The bounds depend only on a bound for $v$ and on $\chi $. If $v_ j\downarrow v$ with uniformly bounded limits there, the plurisubharmonic functions in this representation can be chosen decreasing with $j$. The representation holds also after wedging with any already defined closed positive base current. Proof. For nonnegative bounded plurisubharmonic $v$ and smooth nonnegative plurisubharmonic $\chi $, the identity is DBD412CA248A 7.30.2 \begin{equation}  B_\chi (v)=\tfrac 12dd^ c(v+\chi )^2-\tfrac 12dd^ cv^2 -\tfrac 12dd^ c\chi ^2-\chi \, dd^ cv. \end{equation} It follows by expanding the square, first for smooth functions and then distributionally for bounded functions. The squares are plurisubharmonic: in the smooth case their Hessians are the sum of a nonnegative multiple of the original Hessian and a nonnegative gradient form; decreasing regularization proves the assertion in general. They have uniform bounds and preserve decreasing limits. Add a constant to $v$ to make it nonnegative; the correction to $B_\chi (v)$ is a constant multiple of $dd^ c\chi $. Write a general smooth $\chi $ as $\chi ^+-\chi ^-$, with both functions smooth, nonnegative and plurisubharmonic on the ball, by adding a sufficiently large multiple of $|z|^2$ and a constant. Linearity in $\chi $ proves the assertion. The bounded recursive product and its smooth-factor rules in locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products justify the same identities against a base current. In particular, products of several such errors have bounded-current mass estimates by the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate , with no unbounded potential inserted into a bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality. $\square$ Proposition 7.30.3 . 1AC7DC75B159 Let $S,A_1,\ldots ,A_ q$ be closed in a coordinate open set $U$, and let $1\leq q\leq p\leq n$. Suppose E561BB270A1B 7.30.4 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H^{2p-2m+1}(S\cap A_{j_1}\cap \cdots \cap A_{j_ m})=0 \quad (1\leq j_1<\cdots <j_ m\leq q). \end{equation} For compact $L\subset \operatorname {int}K\Subset U$, there are neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $K\cap A_ j$ and a constant $C$ such that every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ supported in $S$ and all smooth plurisubharmonic $u_ j\leq 0$ near $K$ satisfy 1D4FB6D7DCBB \begin{align}  \| u_1dd^ cu_2\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T\| _ L & \leq C\| T\| _ K\prod _{j=1}^ q\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|, \tag{7.30.5}\\  \| dd^ cu_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T\| _ L & \leq C\| T\| _ K\prod _{j=1}^ q\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|. \tag{7.30.6} \end{align} The constant may depend on $S$, the $A_ j$, the compact sets and the dimensions; it is independent of the potentials and the mass of $T$. The same estimates hold for bounded plurisubharmonic potentials, using the bounded products. Proof. We prove the two estimates, denoted $a_ q,b_ q$, by induction on $q$. The assertion $b_0$ is trace domination and $a_0$ is unused. It suffices to work near each point of $L$ and use finitely many neighborhoods. All intermediate compact sets lie in $\operatorname {int}K$; the neighborhoods $V_ j$ will be shrunk finitely many times. Normalize the bounds outside $V_ j$ to at most one. For arbitrary bounds divide $u_ j$ by $\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|+\varepsilon $, and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ at the end. This also handles zero bounds. A bounded Hessian factor. Assume $a_{q-1},b_{q-1}$ are known. On a compact region where one Hessian potential, say $u_2$, has a uniform bound, the weighted estimate $a_ q$ follows from these two earlier estimates. To see this, cover that region by finitely many balls $B_0\Subset B_1$ where $u_2$ is bounded. The bounded collar construction gives a bounded plurisubharmonic $\widetilde u_2$ equal to $u_2$ near $B_0$ and to a fixed quadratic function on a collar of $\partial B_1$, with bounds depending only on the given bound and the balls. Choose $\zeta \geq 0$, equal to one on $B_0$, with compact support in $B_1$ and derivative support in that fixed quadratic collar. Then \[  dd^ c(\zeta \widetilde u_2) =\zeta \, dd^ c\widetilde u_2+F,  \] where $F$ is a fixed smooth form with controlled coefficients. Put $R=dd^ cu_3\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T$ and use a constant positive trace form $\tau $ of degree $(p-q+1,p-q+1)$. Integration by parts gives \[  \int u_1dd^ c(\zeta \widetilde u_2)\wedge R\wedge \tau =\int \zeta \widetilde u_2\, dd^ cu_1\wedge R\wedge \tau .  \] The right side is bounded by $b_{q-1}$ for $u_1,u_3,\ldots ,u_ q$. The term with $u_1F$ on the left is bounded by $a_{q-1}$ for the same family. Since $-u_1$ and $dd^ c\widetilde u_2\wedge R\wedge \tau $ are nonnegative, this bounds its inner-ball integral and proves the assertion. It also applies when other Hessian potentials are bounded replacements: assign the empty closed set to each such potential. All required intersection conditions for the remaining potentials are inherited. The outer support of $\zeta $ is $B_1$, and its inner value-one region contains the target; no reversed support radii occur. The projection cylinder. Translate the target point to zero; outside $S$ there is nothing to prove. Set $s=p-q$. If zero belongs to all $A_ j$, apply lemma 7.29.6 to $F=S\cap A_1\cap \cdots \cap A_ q$. Choose a sufficiently small vertical ball $B''\subset \mathbb C^{n-s}$ whose boundary at $z'=0$ misses $F$. Compactness and closedness give a base ball $B'\subset \mathbb C^ s$, a thin outer vertical corona and neighborhoods $W_ j$ of the $A_ j$ in the cylinder such that AC44B2B308D3 7.30.7 \begin{equation}  S\cap \overline W_1\cap \cdots \cap \overline W_ q \cap (\overline B'\times \text{outer vertical corona}) =\varnothing . \end{equation} For example, neighborhoods of sufficiently small common distance from the closed $A_ j$ have this property; otherwise a convergent sequence in the compact corona would lie in $F$ in the limit. Choose $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ supported in $W_ j$, equal to one near $A_ j$ in the closed cylinder and near zero. Their derivative supports in the cylinder are a positive distance from $A_ j$. If zero does not belong to some $A_ j$, first shrink the cylinder to be disjoint from that $A_ j$, and choose its $\chi _ j$ with small compact support in the interior, equal to one near zero; this gives the same compact support property without a projection argument. Take $\chi (z')\geq 0$ compactly supported in $B'$ and equal to one near zero. The form $\alpha _ s=\chi (z')(dd^ c|z'|^2)^ s$ is closed, since its $z'$ degree is already maximal. The whole product of localized factors with $T\wedge \alpha _ s$ has compact support in $B'\times B''$, by ( 7.30.7 ). This applies to its $dd^ c$ primitive as well. Consequently 41488626314D 7.30.8 \begin{equation}  \int dd^ c(\chi _1u_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q) \wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s=0. \end{equation} Proof of $b_ q$. Expand every localized Hessian as $\chi _ jdd^ cu_ j+B_{\chi _ j}(u_ j)$. The term with no error is nonnegative and equals the desired product near zero. For a term with $h\geq 1$ errors, restrict to their joint derivative support. Cover this compact set by finitely many balls on which the $h$ error potentials are uniformly bounded; shrink the $V_ j$ to avoid these neighborhoods. By lemma 7.30.1 , the errors become finite sums of $h$ bounded plurisubharmonic Hessians with smooth coefficients. The remaining $q-h$ Hessians form a positive closed base current. Its mass is bounded by $b_{q-h}$, and the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate controls the extra $h$ factors. This bounds every error term, including terms with several derivatives of different cutoffs. Equation ( 7.30.8 ) bounds the main term. Proof of $a_ q$. Let $h(z)=|z_{s+1}|^2$. Compactly supported distributional integration by parts gives \begin{align*} & \int \chi _1u_1\, dd^ c(\chi _2u_2)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q)\wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s\wedge dd^ ch\\ & =\int h\, dd^ c(\chi _1u_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q)\wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s. \end{align*} On the right, the main term is bounded by the just-proved $b_ q$; every error is bounded as in its proof. On the left, the term with no error is nonpositive and is the desired weighted product near zero. Every other term has a Hessian error with index at least two. The same local algebra expresses it with bounded Hessian potentials on its derivative support, leaving $u_1$ as the only weight. The bounded-factor argument above, using $a_{q-1},b_{q-1}$, bounds each of these terms. For $q=1$ there are no left errors. This proves the weighted bound against the positive form $\alpha _ s\wedge dd^ ch$ of degree $(p-q+1,p-q+1)$. To recover trace bounds in both arguments, use finitely many good coordinate systems whose constant positive test forms span all real forms of the required degree. The decomposable positive generators span by strong and weak positivity of differential forms , and unitary generators suffice by Gram–Schmidt. Good unitary systems have full invariant measure by the sphere-avoidance lemma. They are dense: a nonempty open set of the compact unitary group has positive invariant measure, since finitely many of its translates cover the group. Thus a finite spanning family can be perturbed to good systems while remaining spanning. The cylinders and cutoffs may differ; intersect their finitely many inner neighborhoods and the resulting $V_ j$. Trace domination then gives both norm estimates near zero. Finite covering proves the proposition. Decreasing local convolution and the bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity theorem extend it to bounded potentials. All convolutions and cutoff supports are taken in buffered compact sets inside $K$; convolution dominates the original negative function and therefore preserves its outside-$V_ j$ bound on the sets used in the estimates. $\square$ Theorem 7.28.1 . 1BBBF8109419 Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on a complex manifold, let $1\leq q\leq p$, and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ q$ be plurisubharmonic. Interpret the Hausdorff nullness locally in any coordinate chart. If \[  \mathcal H^{2p-2m+1} \bigl (L(u_{j_1})\cap \cdots \cap L(u_{j_ m})\cap \operatorname {supp}T\bigr )=0 \quad (1\leq j_1<\cdots <j_ m\leq q),  \] the coefficient product $u_1dd^ cu_2\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T$ is locally integrable and has locally finite variation. Its $dd^ c$ defines a closed positive classical product with $q$ Hessian factors. These products are symmetric, multilinear, local, and invariant under adding constants to the Hessian potentials. Both the weighted and unweighted products are continuous under simultaneous decreasing plurisubharmonic approximations to the $u_ j$. The approximants may also be unbounded. Their pole mass is retained. Proof. Everything is local in coordinates; put $A_ j=L(u_ j)$ and $S=\operatorname {supp}T$. Work with negative potentials on a compact coordinate neighborhood. The preceding estimates apply uniformly to their bounded truncations, decreasing smooth regularizations and all decreasing approximants, because these dominate the limits and have the same outside-$V_ j$ lower bound. Construction and integrability. Induct on the total number $q$ of potential slots, counting the weight as one slot. For $q=1$, the uniform weighted estimate and monotone convergence for the fixed trace of $T$ show $u_1\in L^1(T)$. Then $u_{1,j}T\to u_1T$ by dominated convergence, and $dd^ c(u_1T)$ is positive closed by bounded truncation. Suppose the theorem is proved with fewer than $q$ slots. Put $R=dd^ cu_2\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T$, already positive closed by induction. The analogous $R_ N$ for simultaneous bounded truncations converge to $R$. For fixed $m$ and $N\geq m$, \[  -\max \{ u_1,-m\} \leq -\max \{ u_1,-N\} .  \] The uniform weighted estimate bounds the latter weight against $R_ N$. For that fixed bounded lower semicontinuous weight, weak convergence and decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions give the limiting integral inequality. Then let $m\to \infty $ for the fixed limiting measure. This proves coefficient integrability and its uniform local bound. Define the new Hessian product by $dd^ c(u_1R)$. Bounded truncations of the first potential against this fixed $R$ converge in coefficient $L^1$, so positivity and closedness follow from the bounded recursion. A compact test cutoff and the weighted bound also control its trace mass. Thus every product used below is defined before its continuity is asserted. The same argument gives uniform weighted bounds for arbitrary decreasing families. The local induction for continuity. Induct additionally on the number $m$ of limit functions unbounded near the point under consideration. When $m=0$ the bounded Bedford–Taylor theorem applies. Before treating $m>0$, replace each function bounded near the point, and all its approximants, by a global maximum with a fixed plurisubharmonic quadratic function on the working coordinate neighborhood. Choose that quadratic below the common lower bound near the point and above the common upper bound outside a slightly larger ball. The new functions agree with the old ones near the point, are bounded on the entire working neighborhood and are equal to the fixed smooth quadratic on an outer corona. These modifications preserve decreasing limits. Only the other $m$ functions can now be unbounded anywhere used in the argument. Their unbounded loci still satisfy the hypotheses. Choose the modifications and cutoffs together. If a bounded slot is present, first fix a cylinder and make its quadratic modification in concentric balls compactly contained there; choose its cutoff with compact support and derivatives in that quadratic corona. This cutoff supplies the required compact support by itself. If every slot is unbounded, use the sphere-avoidance cylinder of the preceding proof. For any other bounded slot use the same construction. For the other functions derivatives are supported away from $A_ j$. Use the closed, positive test form \[  \alpha =\chi (z')(dd^ c|z'|^2)^{p-q}\wedge dd^ c|z_{p-q+1}|^2.  \] All localized primitives have compact support relative to $S$. Smooth approximants of a bounded modified function can be chosen equal to its fixed quadratic on that derivative support, using the same smooth-maximum construction as in theorem 7.29.5 . We record precisely how derivative remainders pass to the limit. If a remainder contains $B_{\chi _ j}$ for one of the $m$ unbounded slots, its support has a neighborhood where that slot is uniformly bounded. The local representation ( 7.30.2 ) expresses it as bounded plurisubharmonic Hessians with smooth coefficients. On each such neighborhood at most $m-1$ slots remain unbounded, so the induction at this same $q$ applies. If the derivative belongs to a slot bounded from the outset, the error is a fixed smooth form, and removing it leaves fewer than $q$ potential slots. The induction on $q$ applies. For several errors use a finite partition on their joint supports and the same representation for every bounded error slot. The transformed potentials decrease and have empty local unbounded locus, so all intersection hypotheses are inherited from the remaining original slots. This proves convergence of every remainder, also with any mixture of fixed limits and decreasing approximants, and with sequential smooth regularization parameters. Localized potentials $\chi _ j u_ j$ cause no additional product premise: near $A_ j$, $\chi _ j$ is constant, and elsewhere $u_ j$ is bounded. There they are finite differences of bounded plurisubharmonic functions by the same square decomposition. Their lower-slot products are therefore defined by expansion and are independent of the expansion by coefficient recursion and linearity. All lower-slot integration by parts below is legitimate for these closed signed currents as well. Every weighted weak limit has the right upper bound. Write $R_ j=dd^ cu_{2,j}\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_{q,j}\wedge T$, so $R_ j\to R$ by the already-proved theorem with $q-1$ slots. The positive currents $-u_{1,j}R_ j$ have uniformly bounded local mass. Choose any subsequential weighted limit $W$. Fixed upper semicontinuous truncations of the weight and their decreasing continuous majorants, followed by fixed-measure monotone limits, give $W\leq u_1R$, exactly by decreasing continuous majorants of upper semicontinuous functions . Thus $D=u_1R-W$ is positive. The reverse localized inequality. For a vector $v=(v_1,\ldots ,v_ q)$ define \[  J(v)=\int \chi _1v_1\, dd^ c(\chi _2v_2)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qv_ q)\wedge T\wedge \alpha .  \] Its main term is the expected weighted product times $\chi _1\cdots \chi _ q$; all other terms are the remainders just treated. Fix an approximant index $j$ and choose smooth plurisubharmonic majorants $w_ l\downarrow u_{l,j}$, with the fixed quadratic branch on bounded-slot derivative supports. Starting with $J(u)$, replace the weight $\chi _ lu_ l$ by $\chi _ lw_ l$ in turn, then interchange it with the next potential by integration by parts. The term in that replacement containing only $\chi _ i dd^ cv_ i$ is nonnegative, since $w_ l\geq u_ l$. Every other term contains a cutoff derivative. Hence after all $q$ replacements, 7103B94D137C 7.30.9 \begin{equation}  J(u)\leq J(w)+\sum _ l|E_ l(w,u)|, \end{equation} where each $E_ l$ is an integral with a derivative remainder and weight $w_ l-u_ l$; the other slots are fixed limits or the $w_ i$. The final all-smooth integral can be rotated back to weight slot one by ordinary integration by parts. For completeness, each interchange has smooth first factor $\chi _ lw_ l$ and second factor $\chi _{l+1}u_{l+1}$, against the closed signed current containing $q-2$ other localized Hessians and $T\wedge \alpha $. The second factor is coefficient-integrable by the already-proved theorem with $q-1$ slots and the local difference description above. Its $dd^ c$ is also a defined lower-slot current. The primitive has compact support by the cylinder construction. Distributional integration by parts, testing with a compact cutoff equal to one there, proves the interchange. Thus no unproved unbounded product identity is used in ( 7.30.9 ). Hold $w_1$ fixed and let the other smoothing parameters tend to zero. The $q-1$ localized Hessian factors in $J(w)$ converge by the unweighted theorem with $q-1$ slots, and the weight is smooth. Then let $w_1\downarrow u_{1,j}$: the signed lower-slot measure is fixed and its coefficient integrability follows from the main weighted bound and the remainder bounds, so dominated convergence applies. Consequently $J(w)\to J(u_{\bullet ,j})$. The remainder convergence proved above gives limits $e_{l,j}$ for $E_ l$ in the same order. As $j\to \infty $ they tend to zero: the two terms coming from $w_ l-u_ l$ have identical limit in every lower-$m$ or lower-$q$ remainder. Therefore \[  J(u)\leq \liminf _ j J(u_{\bullet ,j}).  \] Expand both sides into their main term and remainders. Along the subsequence defining $W$, all remainders converge to the same values. It follows that \[  \int \chi _1\cdots \chi _ q\, D\wedge \alpha \leq 0.  \] This is a nonnegative measure integral, and all cutoffs equal one near the target point. Use finitely many good unitary systems whose degree-$(p-q+1,p-q+1)$ forms span, as in the estimate proof. The trace of $D$ vanishes near that point, and coefficient domination gives $D=0$. Every subsequence has the same further limit, proving weighted convergence. Applying $dd^ c$ proves unweighted convergence with $q$ Hessian factors. Smooth approximation now gives symmetry; the coefficient recursion gives multilinearity, constants, locality and compatibility on overlaps. This completes both inductions. $\square$

title: Lemma 7.30.1
section: 7.30 Classical products under Hausdorff intersection conditions
text: Lemma 7.30.1 . 162A0666C4BB For a smooth real function $\chi $ and a locally bounded plurisubharmonic function $v$, put $B_\chi (v)=dd^ c(\chi v)-\chi \, dd^ cv$. On relatively compact coordinate balls, this is a finite sum of Hessians of bounded plurisubharmonic functions with smooth bounded coefficients. The bounds depend only on a bound for $v$ and on $\chi $. If $v_ j\downarrow v$ with uniformly bounded limits there, the plurisubharmonic functions in this representation can be chosen decreasing with $j$. The representation holds also after wedging with any already defined closed positive base current. Proof. For nonnegative bounded plurisubharmonic $v$ and smooth nonnegative plurisubharmonic $\chi $, the identity is DBD412CA248A 7.30.2 \begin{equation}  B_\chi (v)=\tfrac 12dd^ c(v+\chi )^2-\tfrac 12dd^ cv^2 -\tfrac 12dd^ c\chi ^2-\chi \, dd^ cv. \end{equation} It follows by expanding the square, first for smooth functions and then distributionally for bounded functions. The squares are plurisubharmonic: in the smooth case their Hessians are the sum of a nonnegative multiple of the original Hessian and a nonnegative gradient form; decreasing regularization proves the assertion in general. They have uniform bounds and preserve decreasing limits. Add a constant to $v$ to make it nonnegative; the correction to $B_\chi (v)$ is a constant multiple of $dd^ c\chi $. Write a general smooth $\chi $ as $\chi ^+-\chi ^-$, with both functions smooth, nonnegative and plurisubharmonic on the ball, by adding a sufficiently large multiple of $|z|^2$ and a constant. Linearity in $\chi $ proves the assertion. The bounded recursive product and its smooth-factor rules in locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products justify the same identities against a base current. In particular, products of several such errors have bounded-current mass estimates by the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate , with no unbounded potential inserted into a bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg inequality. $\square$

text: Proposition 7.30.3 . 1AC7DC75B159 Let $S,A_1,\ldots ,A_ q$ be closed in a coordinate open set $U$, and let $1\leq q\leq p\leq n$. Suppose E561BB270A1B 7.30.4 \begin{equation}  \mathcal H^{2p-2m+1}(S\cap A_{j_1}\cap \cdots \cap A_{j_ m})=0 \quad (1\leq j_1<\cdots <j_ m\leq q). \end{equation} For compact $L\subset \operatorname {int}K\Subset U$, there are neighborhoods $V_ j$ of $K\cap A_ j$ and a constant $C$ such that every closed positive current $T$ of bidimension $(p,p)$ supported in $S$ and all smooth plurisubharmonic $u_ j\leq 0$ near $K$ satisfy 1D4FB6D7DCBB \begin{align}  \| u_1dd^ cu_2\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T\| _ L & \leq C\| T\| _ K\prod _{j=1}^ q\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|, \tag{7.30.5}\\  \| dd^ cu_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T\| _ L & \leq C\| T\| _ K\prod _{j=1}^ q\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|. \tag{7.30.6} \end{align} The constant may depend on $S$, the $A_ j$, the compact sets and the dimensions; it is independent of the potentials and the mass of $T$. The same estimates hold for bounded plurisubharmonic potentials, using the bounded products. Proof. We prove the two estimates, denoted $a_ q,b_ q$, by induction on $q$. The assertion $b_0$ is trace domination and $a_0$ is unused. It suffices to work near each point of $L$ and use finitely many neighborhoods. All intermediate compact sets lie in $\operatorname {int}K$; the neighborhoods $V_ j$ will be shrunk finitely many times. Normalize the bounds outside $V_ j$ to at most one. For arbitrary bounds divide $u_ j$ by $\sup _{K\setminus V_ j}|u_ j|+\varepsilon $, and let $\varepsilon \downarrow 0$ at the end. This also handles zero bounds. A bounded Hessian factor. Assume $a_{q-1},b_{q-1}$ are known. On a compact region where one Hessian potential, say $u_2$, has a uniform bound, the weighted estimate $a_ q$ follows from these two earlier estimates. To see this, cover that region by finitely many balls $B_0\Subset B_1$ where $u_2$ is bounded. The bounded collar construction gives a bounded plurisubharmonic $\widetilde u_2$ equal to $u_2$ near $B_0$ and to a fixed quadratic function on a collar of $\partial B_1$, with bounds depending only on the given bound and the balls. Choose $\zeta \geq 0$, equal to one on $B_0$, with compact support in $B_1$ and derivative support in that fixed quadratic collar. Then \[  dd^ c(\zeta \widetilde u_2) =\zeta \, dd^ c\widetilde u_2+F,  \] where $F$ is a fixed smooth form with controlled coefficients. Put $R=dd^ cu_3\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q\wedge T$ and use a constant positive trace form $\tau $ of degree $(p-q+1,p-q+1)$. Integration by parts gives \[  \int u_1dd^ c(\zeta \widetilde u_2)\wedge R\wedge \tau =\int \zeta \widetilde u_2\, dd^ cu_1\wedge R\wedge \tau .  \] The right side is bounded by $b_{q-1}$ for $u_1,u_3,\ldots ,u_ q$. The term with $u_1F$ on the left is bounded by $a_{q-1}$ for the same family. Since $-u_1$ and $dd^ c\widetilde u_2\wedge R\wedge \tau $ are nonnegative, this bounds its inner-ball integral and proves the assertion. It also applies when other Hessian potentials are bounded replacements: assign the empty closed set to each such potential. All required intersection conditions for the remaining potentials are inherited. The outer support of $\zeta $ is $B_1$, and its inner value-one region contains the target; no reversed support radii occur. The projection cylinder. Translate the target point to zero; outside $S$ there is nothing to prove. Set $s=p-q$. If zero belongs to all $A_ j$, apply lemma 7.29.6 to $F=S\cap A_1\cap \cdots \cap A_ q$. Choose a sufficiently small vertical ball $B''\subset \mathbb C^{n-s}$ whose boundary at $z'=0$ misses $F$. Compactness and closedness give a base ball $B'\subset \mathbb C^ s$, a thin outer vertical corona and neighborhoods $W_ j$ of the $A_ j$ in the cylinder such that AC44B2B308D3 7.30.7 \begin{equation}  S\cap \overline W_1\cap \cdots \cap \overline W_ q \cap (\overline B'\times \text{outer vertical corona}) =\varnothing . \end{equation} For example, neighborhoods of sufficiently small common distance from the closed $A_ j$ have this property; otherwise a convergent sequence in the compact corona would lie in $F$ in the limit. Choose $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ supported in $W_ j$, equal to one near $A_ j$ in the closed cylinder and near zero. Their derivative supports in the cylinder are a positive distance from $A_ j$. If zero does not belong to some $A_ j$, first shrink the cylinder to be disjoint from that $A_ j$, and choose its $\chi _ j$ with small compact support in the interior, equal to one near zero; this gives the same compact support property without a projection argument. Take $\chi (z')\geq 0$ compactly supported in $B'$ and equal to one near zero. The form $\alpha _ s=\chi (z')(dd^ c|z'|^2)^ s$ is closed, since its $z'$ degree is already maximal. The whole product of localized factors with $T\wedge \alpha _ s$ has compact support in $B'\times B''$, by ( 7.30.7 ). This applies to its $dd^ c$ primitive as well. Consequently 41488626314D 7.30.8 \begin{equation}  \int dd^ c(\chi _1u_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q) \wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s=0. \end{equation} Proof of $b_ q$. Expand every localized Hessian as $\chi _ jdd^ cu_ j+B_{\chi _ j}(u_ j)$. The term with no error is nonnegative and equals the desired product near zero. For a term with $h\geq 1$ errors, restrict to their joint derivative support. Cover this compact set by finitely many balls on which the $h$ error potentials are uniformly bounded; shrink the $V_ j$ to avoid these neighborhoods. By lemma 7.30.1 , the errors become finite sums of $h$ bounded plurisubharmonic Hessians with smooth coefficients. The remaining $q-h$ Hessians form a positive closed base current. Its mass is bounded by $b_{q-h}$, and the bounded Chern–Levine–Nirenberg estimate controls the extra $h$ factors. This bounds every error term, including terms with several derivatives of different cutoffs. Equation ( 7.30.8 ) bounds the main term. Proof of $a_ q$. Let $h(z)=|z_{s+1}|^2$. Compactly supported distributional integration by parts gives \begin{align*} & \int \chi _1u_1\, dd^ c(\chi _2u_2)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q)\wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s\wedge dd^ ch\\ & =\int h\, dd^ c(\chi _1u_1)\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ c(\chi _ qu_ q)\wedge T\wedge \alpha _ s. \end{align*} On the right, the main term is bounded by the just-proved $b_ q$; every error is bounded as in its proof. On the left, the term with no error is nonpositive and is the desired weighted product near zero. Every other term has a Hessian error with index at least two. The same local algebra expresses it with bounded Hessian potentials on its derivative support, leaving $u_1$ as the only weight. The bounded-factor argument above, using $a_{q-1},b_{q-1}$, bounds each of these terms. For $q=1$ there are no left errors. This proves the weighted bound against the positive form $\alpha _ s\wedge dd^ ch$ of degree $(p-q+1,p-q+1)$. To recover trace bounds in both arguments, use finitely many good coordinate systems whose constant positive test forms span all real forms of the required degree. The decomposable positive generators span by strong and weak positivity of differential forms , and unitary generators suffice by Gram–Schmidt. Good unitary systems have full invariant measure by the sphere-avoidance lemma. They are dense: a nonempty open set of the compact unitary group has positive invariant measure, since finitely many of its translates cover the group. Thus a finite spanning family can be perturbed to good systems while remaining spanning. The cylinders and cutoffs may differ; intersect their finitely many inner neighborhoods and the resulting $V_ j$. Trace domination then gives both norm estimates near zero. Finite covering proves the proposition. Decreasing local convolution and the bounded Bedford–Taylor continuity theorem extend it to bounded potentials. All convolutions and cutoff supports are taken in buffered compact sets inside $K$; convolution dominates the original negative function and therefore preserves its outside-$V_ j$ bound on the sets used in the estimates. $\square$

section: 7.31 Collars relative to the support of the base current
text: Lemma 7.31.1 . FDDB630F0AA9 Suppose a neighborhood of a compact subset $K$ of a complex manifold carries a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic function $\rho $. Every plurisubharmonic function defined near $K$ is, on a fixed smaller neighborhood of $K$, the decreasing limit of smooth plurisubharmonic functions. Proof. We first localize the finite-cover proof of decreasing smooth regularization with a vanishing curvature error . For bounded $v$ on a slightly larger compact neighborhood and fixed $\eta >0$, that proof gives smooth $a_{\eta ,\delta }\downarrow v$ on a fixed open neighborhood $O$ of $K$, with $dd^ ca_{\eta ,\delta }\geq -\eta \, dd^ c\rho $. Here is why no compact-without-boundary assumption is needed for this use. Take finitely many nested charts $V_ i\Subset W_ i\Subset U_ i$ whose $V_ i$ cover a fixed larger compact neighborhood. The bounded coordinate-convolution comparison gives uniformly vanishing overlap errors. Add fixed small chart penalties, zero on $V_ i$ and negative near $\partial W_ i$, and take the smooth regularized maximum. Where a branch leaves $W_ i$ in $\overline O$, another branch has zero penalty and dominates it; the removal property of that maximum glues the formulas. All relevant boundaries intersecting $\overline O$ are compact. The curvature error is at most $\eta \, dd^ c\rho $ after choosing the penalties small enough. For the fixed cover and penalties the local convolutions and maximum decrease with $\delta $, and the zero-penalty branches give limit $v$ and the majorant inequality. These are exactly the local steps of the cited proof, on the fixed buffered compact neighborhood. Add a constant to $\rho $ so that $\rho \geq 0$ on that neighborhood. Put $v_ N=\max \{ u,-N\} $, choose $t_ N\downarrow 0$, and use the preceding construction with $\eta _ N=t_ N/2$. Choose its smoothing parameter so that \[  w_ N=a_{\eta _ N,\delta _ N}+t_ N\rho +2^{-N}  \] decreases strictly with $N$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, and $\| a_{\eta _ N,\delta _ N}-v_ N\| _{L^1}\leq 2^{-N}$ there. The choice is possible inductively: the pointwise limit of the candidate functions for index $N$ is $v_ N+t_ N\rho +2^{-N}$, below the previous smooth majorant by at least $2^{-N}$. Increasing open sets where the candidate lies below that previous function cover the compact set, so one sufficiently small parameter works everywhere. The $L^1$ condition is the bounded decreasing convergence for this fixed $v_ N$. Each $w_ N$ is smooth plurisubharmonic, since $dd^ cw_ N\geq (t_ N/2)dd^ c\rho $. Also $w_ N\geq u$, and $w_ N\to u$ in $L^1$, because $v_ N\downarrow u$ in $L^1$. The decreasing plurisubharmonic limit is therefore the canonical representative $u$ at every point, by decreasing nets of plurisubharmonic functions . Restriction to the interior of the fixed compact neighborhood proves the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 7.31.2 . F6EE68FA9FDA Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $X$. Suppose $X$ is covered by relatively compact open sets $D$, each carrying a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion, such that \[  \partial D\cap L(u_ j)\cap \operatorname {supp}T=\varnothing  \] for every member of a finite plurisubharmonic family. Then all conclusions of theorem 7.29.5 hold: products through $p$ Hessian factors, coefficient integrability of an additional weight through $p-1$ factors, and simultaneous decreasing continuity. In particular, for $p\geq 1$ a single such potential is coefficient-integrable for $T$. Proof. Fix a desired compact subset of one $D$. The closed set $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \bigcup _ jL(u_ j)\cap \overline D$ is compact and disjoint from $\partial D$. Choose a sublevel $\Omega =\{ \rho <c\} \Subset D$ of its strict exhaustion containing that set and the desired compact subset. Put $\psi =\rho -c$ and $\omega =dd^ c\psi >0$ near $\overline\Omega $. No regular-value choice is needed below: every integration by parts uses compact current differences rather than boundary integration. Take a smaller sublevel containing all these relative unbounded loci and the target compact set. Near $\operatorname {supp}T$ in the remaining closed collar, the limit functions are bounded below uniformly, and so are all their decreasing approximants. Subtract constants for a uniform negative upper bound. On an open neighborhood $U$ of $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \overline\Omega $, leave the functions unchanged in the inner sublevel and use $\max \{ u,A\psi \} $ in that collar neighborhood, choosing $A$ large enough that the formulas agree on the overlap. They are plurisubharmonic on $U$ and equal $A\psi $ near $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \partial \Omega $. The preceding regularization lemma supplies smooth decreasing plurisubharmonic majorants of each original function near $\overline\Omega $. Smooth-maximum gluing in the collar gives smooth decreasing majorants of its modification on the same $U$, equal exactly to $A\psi $ on a smaller relative collar. Uniform lower bounds give the inner branch gap, and the uniform negative upper bound gives the outer branch gap, just as in the coordinate collar construction. Every product on $U$ is supported in $\operatorname {supp}T$. It extends by zero to $\Omega $: each boundary point of $U$ inside $\Omega $ is outside the closed support of $T$, so all these currents already vanish near that point. This extension introduces no boundary derivative. We verify the exact hypotheses used in the proof of theorem 7.29.5 . Bounded products exist on $U$ by the canonical bounded theory and the just-described extensions. Their difference from the corresponding $A\psi $ product has compact support in $\Omega $. Hence testing $dd^ c$ against closed powers of $\omega $ proves the mass identity ( 7.29.2 ) on $\Omega $. The $L^1$ collar exchange uses only a compactly supported coefficient-integrable difference times a closed current, so its distributional proof also holds on $U$ with zero extension. Using the smooth function $A\psi $ gives the weighted identity ( 7.29.3 ), with $M_ T=\int _\Omega T\wedge \omega ^ p<\infty $. All constants are independent of interior truncation and approximant indices. Closedness and positivity of $\omega $, rather than constant coefficients, are all that those identities require. The complete induction of that theorem now applies with these data. Explicitly, the weighted identity first gives $uT\in L^1$ by fixed-measure monotone convergence. Weighted continuity with fewer Hessian factors gives the next unweighted product and its symmetry. The same bound with simultaneous bounded truncations then proves integrability of the next weight. Fixed USC truncations bound every weighted weak limit from above. Smooth majorants with the fixed relative collar, the $L^1$ exchange and the strictly lower-factor sequential limits give the reverse mass inequality. All its base currents remain supported in $\operatorname {supp}T$, and every degree inequality remains $r\leq p-1$ for an unbounded weight. Splitting integrals with a compact cutoff is valid because the relative collar currents are fixed and finite. Thus each step and each limit of that earlier proof has its required premise here; no global coordinate chart or unproved smoothing premise is added. Locality returns the original functions near the target set, and the covering by $D$ proves the theorem on $X$. $\square$ Corollary 7.31.3 . CF64F301AEAF Let $D\Subset X$ admit a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion. For $1\leq j\leq q\leq n-1$, let $u_ j$ be plurisubharmonic near $\overline D$, with $\partial D\cap L(u_ j)=\varnothing $. Every plurisubharmonic function $V$ defined near $\overline D$ is coefficient-integrable for $dd^ cu_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q$ locally in $D$. Proof. For a given compact target choose a strict exhaustion sublevel $\Omega \Subset D$ containing it and all the unbounded loci in $D$, as above, and write $\psi <0$ for its defining exhaustion level and $\omega =dd^ c\psi >0$. Modify the $u_ j$ outside the target to a common $A\psi $ collar. The preceding theorem defines the closed positive product $R$; it is $A^ q\omega ^ q$ on that collar. Choose $\Omega _\delta =\{ \psi <-\delta \} $ containing the target and the region where the factors differ from $A\psi $, and a nonnegative compact cutoff $\chi $ in $\Omega $ equal to $-\psi $ near $\overline{\Omega _\delta }$. By the regularization lemma, after subtracting a constant there are smooth nonpositive plurisubharmonic $V_ k\downarrow V$ near $\overline\Omega $. Distributional integration by parts gives \begin{align*}  \int _{\Omega _\delta }(-V_ k)R\wedge \omega ^{n-q} & =\int _\Omega \chi \, dd^ cV_ k\wedge R\wedge \omega ^{n-q-1}\\ & \quad -A^ q\int _{\Omega \setminus \Omega _\delta } V_ k\, \omega ^{n-1}\wedge dd^ c\chi . \end{align*} The first integral is uniformly bounded by the collar mass identity with base $dd^ cV_ k$ of bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$; it applies since $q\leq n-1$. Its bound is $\| \chi \| _\infty A^ q\int _\Omega dd^ cV_ k\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, uniformly finite by local weak convergence of these positive Hessian currents and a fixed outer trace cutoff. The second integral is uniformly bounded by the local $L^1$ convergence of $V_ k$ against smooth volume. Monotone convergence now uses the fixed trace measure of $R$. It proves $V\in L^1(R\wedge \omega ^{n-q})$ on the target, and coefficient domination finishes the proof. $\square$ Corollary 7.31.4 . EBA900FA96EF If $L(u)\cap \operatorname {supp}T$ is contained in an analytic set of dimension at most $p-1$, then $uT$ is coefficient-integrable and $dd^ c(uT)$ is a closed positive current for $p\geq 1$. For $T=1$, the mixed products of $q\leq n$ potentials exist and have the preceding decreasing continuity whenever $L(u_ j)\subset A_ j$ are analytic and every $m$-fold intersection of distinct $A_ j$ has codimension at least $m$. Proof. The analytic stratification and Hausdorff bounds of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension give exactly the zero measures in ( 7.30.4 ); apply theorem 7.28.1 . In the first assertion with $p=0$, the dimension condition instead forces $L(u)\cap \operatorname {supp}T=\varnothing $. Then $u$ is locally bounded on the support, so $uT$ is defined and its $dd^ c$ vanishes by degree. This is not a general integrability assertion for an unbounded weight against a top-degree measure. $\square$

Put $v_ N=\max \{ u,-N\} $, choose $t_ N\downarrow 0$, and use the preceding construction with $\eta _ N=t_ N/2$. Choose its smoothing parameter so that \[  w_ N=a_{\eta _ N,\delta _ N}+t_ N\rho +2^{-N}  \] decreases strictly with $N$ on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, and $\| a_{\eta _ N,\delta _ N}-v_ N\| _{L^1}\leq 2^{-N}$ there. The choice is possible inductively: the pointwise limit of the candidate functions for index $N$ is $v_ N+t_ N\rho +2^{-N}$, below the previous smooth majorant by at least $2^{-N}$. Increasing open sets where the candidate lies below that previous function cover the compact set, so one sufficiently small parameter works everywhere. The $L^1$ condition is the bounded decreasing convergence for this fixed $v_ N$. Each $w_ N$ is smooth plurisubharmonic, since $dd^ cw_ N\geq (t_ N/2)dd^ c\rho $. Also $w_ N\geq u$, and $w_ N\to u$ in $L^1$, because $v_ N\downarrow u$ in $L^1$. The decreasing plurisubharmonic limit is therefore the canonical representative $u$ at every point, by decreasing nets of plurisubharmonic functions . Restriction to the interior of the fixed compact neighborhood proves the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 7.31.2
section: 7.31 Collars relative to the support of the base current
text: Theorem 7.31.2 . F6EE68FA9FDA Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ on $X$. Suppose $X$ is covered by relatively compact open sets $D$, each carrying a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion, such that \[  \partial D\cap L(u_ j)\cap \operatorname {supp}T=\varnothing  \] for every member of a finite plurisubharmonic family. Then all conclusions of theorem 7.29.5 hold: products through $p$ Hessian factors, coefficient integrability of an additional weight through $p-1$ factors, and simultaneous decreasing continuity. In particular, for $p\geq 1$ a single such potential is coefficient-integrable for $T$. Proof. Fix a desired compact subset of one $D$. The closed set $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \bigcup _ jL(u_ j)\cap \overline D$ is compact and disjoint from $\partial D$. Choose a sublevel $\Omega =\{ \rho <c\} \Subset D$ of its strict exhaustion containing that set and the desired compact subset. Put $\psi =\rho -c$ and $\omega =dd^ c\psi >0$ near $\overline\Omega $. No regular-value choice is needed below: every integration by parts uses compact current differences rather than boundary integration. Take a smaller sublevel containing all these relative unbounded loci and the target compact set. Near $\operatorname {supp}T$ in the remaining closed collar, the limit functions are bounded below uniformly, and so are all their decreasing approximants. Subtract constants for a uniform negative upper bound. On an open neighborhood $U$ of $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \overline\Omega $, leave the functions unchanged in the inner sublevel and use $\max \{ u,A\psi \} $ in that collar neighborhood, choosing $A$ large enough that the formulas agree on the overlap. They are plurisubharmonic on $U$ and equal $A\psi $ near $\operatorname {supp}T\cap \partial \Omega $. The preceding regularization lemma supplies smooth decreasing plurisubharmonic majorants of each original function near $\overline\Omega $. Smooth-maximum gluing in the collar gives smooth decreasing majorants of its modification on the same $U$, equal exactly to $A\psi $ on a smaller relative collar. Uniform lower bounds give the inner branch gap, and the uniform negative upper bound gives the outer branch gap, just as in the coordinate collar construction. Every product on $U$ is supported in $\operatorname {supp}T$. It extends by zero to $\Omega $: each boundary point of $U$ inside $\Omega $ is outside the closed support of $T$, so all these currents already vanish near that point. This extension introduces no boundary derivative. We verify the exact hypotheses used in the proof of theorem 7.29.5 . Bounded products exist on $U$ by the canonical bounded theory and the just-described extensions. Their difference from the corresponding $A\psi $ product has compact support in $\Omega $. Hence testing $dd^ c$ against closed powers of $\omega $ proves the mass identity ( 7.29.2 ) on $\Omega $. The $L^1$ collar exchange uses only a compactly supported coefficient-integrable difference times a closed current, so its distributional proof also holds on $U$ with zero extension. Using the smooth function $A\psi $ gives the weighted identity ( 7.29.3 ), with $M_ T=\int _\Omega T\wedge \omega ^ p<\infty $. All constants are independent of interior truncation and approximant indices. Closedness and positivity of $\omega $, rather than constant coefficients, are all that those identities require. The complete induction of that theorem now applies with these data. Explicitly, the weighted identity first gives $uT\in L^1$ by fixed-measure monotone convergence. Weighted continuity with fewer Hessian factors gives the next unweighted product and its symmetry. The same bound with simultaneous bounded truncations then proves integrability of the next weight. Fixed USC truncations bound every weighted weak limit from above. Smooth majorants with the fixed relative collar, the $L^1$ exchange and the strictly lower-factor sequential limits give the reverse mass inequality. All its base currents remain supported in $\operatorname {supp}T$, and every degree inequality remains $r\leq p-1$ for an unbounded weight. Splitting integrals with a compact cutoff is valid because the relative collar currents are fixed and finite. Thus each step and each limit of that earlier proof has its required premise here; no global coordinate chart or unproved smoothing premise is added. Locality returns the original functions near the target set, and the covering by $D$ proves the theorem on $X$. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.31.3
section: 7.31 Collars relative to the support of the base current
text: Corollary 7.31.3 . CF64F301AEAF Let $D\Subset X$ admit a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion. For $1\leq j\leq q\leq n-1$, let $u_ j$ be plurisubharmonic near $\overline D$, with $\partial D\cap L(u_ j)=\varnothing $. Every plurisubharmonic function $V$ defined near $\overline D$ is coefficient-integrable for $dd^ cu_1\wedge \cdots \wedge dd^ cu_ q$ locally in $D$. Proof. For a given compact target choose a strict exhaustion sublevel $\Omega \Subset D$ containing it and all the unbounded loci in $D$, as above, and write $\psi <0$ for its defining exhaustion level and $\omega =dd^ c\psi >0$. Modify the $u_ j$ outside the target to a common $A\psi $ collar. The preceding theorem defines the closed positive product $R$; it is $A^ q\omega ^ q$ on that collar. Choose $\Omega _\delta =\{ \psi <-\delta \} $ containing the target and the region where the factors differ from $A\psi $, and a nonnegative compact cutoff $\chi $ in $\Omega $ equal to $-\psi $ near $\overline{\Omega _\delta }$. By the regularization lemma, after subtracting a constant there are smooth nonpositive plurisubharmonic $V_ k\downarrow V$ near $\overline\Omega $. Distributional integration by parts gives \begin{align*}  \int _{\Omega _\delta }(-V_ k)R\wedge \omega ^{n-q} & =\int _\Omega \chi \, dd^ cV_ k\wedge R\wedge \omega ^{n-q-1}\\ & \quad -A^ q\int _{\Omega \setminus \Omega _\delta } V_ k\, \omega ^{n-1}\wedge dd^ c\chi . \end{align*} The first integral is uniformly bounded by the collar mass identity with base $dd^ cV_ k$ of bidimension $(n-1,n-1)$; it applies since $q\leq n-1$. Its bound is $\| \chi \| _\infty A^ q\int _\Omega dd^ cV_ k\wedge \omega ^{n-1}$, uniformly finite by local weak convergence of these positive Hessian currents and a fixed outer trace cutoff. The second integral is uniformly bounded by the local $L^1$ convergence of $V_ k$ against smooth volume. Monotone convergence now uses the fixed trace measure of $R$. It proves $V\in L^1(R\wedge \omega ^{n-q})$ on the target, and coefficient domination finishes the proof. $\square$

title: Corollary 7.31.4
section: 7.31 Collars relative to the support of the base current
text: Corollary 7.31.4 . EBA900FA96EF If $L(u)\cap \operatorname {supp}T$ is contained in an analytic set of dimension at most $p-1$, then $uT$ is coefficient-integrable and $dd^ c(uT)$ is a closed positive current for $p\geq 1$. For $T=1$, the mixed products of $q\leq n$ potentials exist and have the preceding decreasing continuity whenever $L(u_ j)\subset A_ j$ are analytic and every $m$-fold intersection of distinct $A_ j$ has codimension at least $m$. Proof. The analytic stratification and Hausdorff bounds of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension give exactly the zero measures in ( 7.30.4 ); apply theorem 7.28.1 . In the first assertion with $p=0$, the dimension condition instead forces $L(u)\cap \operatorname {supp}T=\varnothing $. Then $u$ is locally bounded on the support, so $uT$ is defined and its $dd^ c$ vanishes by degree. This is not a general integrability assertion for an unbounded weight against a top-degree measure. $\square$

F0BF9030844C Let $M$ be a connected smooth manifold of positive real dimension and $F$ a smooth complex vector bundle. This symbol calculation holds in each coordinate patch. Apply the result to $2\square _ E$. $\square$

text: Lemma 2.16.5 . 0300AC2D4EAB Suppose $Pu=0$ near a point $x_0$, with $P$ of the scalar-principal form in lemma 2.16.1 , and $u$ smooth. text: Theorem 10.48.1 . D1E9C0156833 Let $(X,\omega )$ be compact and connected Hermitian, and let $E$ be a holomorphic Hermitian vector bundle. In a fixed bidegree $(p,q)$ suppose the Hermitian operator \[  C_\omega =[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda ]+T_\omega  \] is nonnegative everywhere and positive definite at one point. Then $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0$ for smooth analytic Dolbeault cohomology. Proof. For a smooth harmonic representative $h$, the energy identity in theorem 11.48.15 gives \[  0=\| (D'+\tau )h\| ^2+\| (\delta '+\tau ^*)h\| ^2 +\int _ X\langle C_\omega h,h\rangle .  \] Every term is nonnegative. Positivity at the chosen point, continuity and a smaller coordinate neighborhood give $C_\omega \geq \varepsilon I$ there for some $\varepsilon >0$. Its integral term forces $h=0$ in that neighborhood. By theorem 2.16.7 , $h=0$ everywhere. The smooth Hodge representation of theorem 10.46.6 proves the conclusion. $\square$ On a Kähler manifold $T_\omega =0$. Recall the curvature form on $T^{1,0}X\otimes E$, \[  \mathcal R_ E(\xi )=\sum _{j,k}\langle R_{j\bar k}\xi _ j,\xi _ k\rangle , \qquad \mathrm i\Theta (E)=\mathrm i\sum _{j,k} R_{j\bar k}\theta _ j\wedge \bar\theta _ k.  \] For an integer $m\geq 1$, the notation $\mathcal R_ E\geq _ m0$ means nonnegativity on tensors of rank at most $m$, and $>_ m0$ means strict positivity on their nonzero tensors. Negative versions are defined by reversing the signs. Corollary 10.48.2 . 4D525971142A Let $X$ be compact connected Kähler of dimension $n$, and let $E$ have rank $r$. If $\mathcal R_ E\geq _ m0$ everywhere and $\mathcal R_ E>_ m0$ at one point, then \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0 \quad \text{for }1\leq q\leq n,\quad m\geq \min (n-q+1,r).  \] If instead $\mathcal R_ E\leq _ m0$ everywhere and $\mathcal R_ E<_ m0$ at one point, then \[  H^{p,0}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0 \quad \text{for }0\leq p<n,\quad m\geq \min (p+1,r).  \] Thus the corresponding one-point Nakano semipositive and seminegative conclusions hold in these ranges. Proof. For $(n,q)$-forms the exact curvature formula in proposition 10.33.6 writes the quadratic form of $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda ]$ as $\sum _{|S|=q-1}\mathcal R_ E((u_{jS})_ j)$. Each tensor has rank at most $\min (n-q+1,r)$, and $\sum _{S,j}|u_{jS}|^2=q|u|^2$. Hence $B\geq 0$ everywhere. At the chosen point the compact set of unit tensors of rank at most $m$ has a positive minimum curvature $\varepsilon $; the rank condition is closed, so compactness applies. Thus $B\geq q\varepsilon I$ there. Apply theorem 10.48.1 . For the negative assertion put $a=n-p\geq 1$ and use $E^*$. In dual holomorphic frames its metric is $(H^{-1})^{\mathsf T}$, its Chern connection is $-A^{\mathsf T}$ and its curvature matrices are $R^{E^*}_{j\bar k}=-(R^ E_{j\bar k})^{\mathsf T}$. Indeed, differentiating the inverse metric gives the connection formula, and applying $\bar\partial $ gives the curvature formula. On $(a,n)$-forms the barred part of the all-degree curvature operator cancels its trace part. Writing $u=\sum _ Ju_ J\theta _ J\wedge \bar\theta _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \bar\theta _ n$ and alternating the coefficients in $jS$, its quadratic form is \[  \langle [\mathrm i\Theta (E^*),\Lambda ]u,u\rangle =\sum _{|S|=a-1}\sum _{j,k} \langle R^{E^*}_{j\bar k}u_{kS},u_{jS}\rangle =-\sum _{|S|=a-1}\mathcal R_ E((\bar u_{jS})_ j).  \] The coefficient conjugates in the last expression are vectors in $E$ under the unitary dual frame. Explicitly its summand is $-\sum _{j,k,\lambda ,\mu }(R^ E_{j\bar k})_{\lambda \mu } u_{kS,\lambda }\bar u_{jS,\mu }$, which is the claimed negative curvature form after setting $\xi _{j,\mu }=\bar u_{jS,\mu }$. Its tensor rank is at most $\min (n-a+1,r)=\min (p+1,r)$. Therefore this operator is nonnegative everywhere and at least $a\varepsilon I$ at the strict point, since $\sum _{S,j}|u_{jS}|^2=a|u|^2$. The preceding theorem gives $H^{n-p,n}_{\bar\partial }(X,E^*)=0$. Analytic Serre duality in theorem 10.46.7 then gives $H^{p,0}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0$. $\square$ Corollary 10.48.3 . 2CCDF84C1B3C Let $L$ be a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on a compact connected Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. If $\mathrm i\Theta (L)\geq 0$ everywhere and is positive definite at one point, then \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L) \simeq H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,K_ X\otimes L)=0 \quad (1\leq q\leq n).  \] If $\mathrm i\Theta (L)\leq 0$ everywhere and is negative definite at one point, then $H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0$ for $0\leq q\leq n-1$. Proof. The positive assertion is the preceding corollary with rank one. For the displayed complex isomorphism, a local section $\eta \otimes (\kappa \otimes e)$, where $\eta $ is a $(0,q)$-form and $\kappa $ a holomorphic canonical frame, is sent to $\eta \wedge \kappa \otimes e$. Its transition laws agree and it commutes with $\bar\partial $; hence it induces the stated cohomology isomorphism. In the negative case $L^*$ has the positive curvature just considered, so $H^{n,n-q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L^*)=0$ when $q\leq n-1$. Analytic Serre duality gives the conclusion. The same complex isomorphism holds for any holomorphic vector bundle in place of $L$, by applying the frame construction componentwise. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.48.1
section: 10.48 One-point curvature vanishing
text: Theorem 10.48.1 . D1E9C0156833 Let $(X,\omega )$ be compact and connected Hermitian, and let $E$ be a holomorphic Hermitian vector bundle. In a fixed bidegree $(p,q)$ suppose the Hermitian operator \[  C_\omega =[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda ]+T_\omega  \] is nonnegative everywhere and positive definite at one point. Then $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,E)=0$ for smooth analytic Dolbeault cohomology. Proof. For a smooth harmonic representative $h$, the energy identity in theorem 11.48.15 gives \[  0=\| (D'+\tau )h\| ^2+\| (\delta '+\tau ^*)h\| ^2 +\int _ X\langle C_\omega h,h\rangle .  \] Every term is nonnegative. Positivity at the chosen point, continuity and a smaller coordinate neighborhood give $C_\omega \geq \varepsilon I$ there for some $\varepsilon >0$. Its integral term forces $h=0$ in that neighborhood. By theorem 2.16.7 , $h=0$ everywhere. The smooth Hodge representation of theorem 10.46.6 proves the conclusion. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.48.3
section: 10.48 One-point curvature vanishing
text: Theorem 10.48.3 . 2CCDF84C1B3C Let $X$ be compact connected Kähler of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $(L,h)$ have semipositive curvature. Suppose that at one point the curvature has at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues, where $1\leq s\leq n$. Then \[  H^{n,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0\qquad (s\leq q\leq n).  \] Equivalently $H^ q(X,K_ X\otimes L)=0$ in this range, with the sheaf interpretation of corollary 10.43.11 . Dually, if the curvature of $L$ is seminegative and has at least $n-s+1$ negative eigenvalues at one point, then $H^{0,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=H^ q(X,L)=0$ for $0\leq q\leq n-s$. Proof. Use the compact bundle Dolbeault Hodge theorem 10.46.6 and let $u$ be a smooth harmonic representative. By ( 10.49.1 ), $B_\omega $ is semipositive on $(n,q)$ everywhere. At the specified point any $q$ indices include at least one of the positive eigenvalues, because the null space has dimension at most $s-1$. Thus $B_\omega $ is positive definite there, and on a neighborhood by continuity. The Kähler energy identity of theorem 10.33.2 gives \[  0=\| D'u\| ^2+\| \delta 'u\| ^2 +\int _ X\langle B_\omega u,u\rangle \, dV.  \] Every summand is nonnegative, so $\delta 'u=0$ and $u$ vanishes on that neighborhood. Here is a direct holomorphic argument for the remaining propagation. Let $*$ be the real Riemannian Hodge star extended complex linearly, acting on the exterior factor of bundle-valued forms. For a metric-compatible connection $D=D'+D''$, Stokes' formula Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners gives in real dimension $2n$ \[  D^*=-*D*,\qquad \delta '=-*D''*.  \] To check the sign, for a degree-$(k-1)$ form $a$ and degree-$k$ form $b$, use the metric wedge pairing $\{ a,b\} =\sum a_\lambda \wedge \overline{b_\mu } \langle e_\lambda ,e_\mu \rangle $. Their product is minus. Taking type components proves the second identity. The unitary exterior basis shows that $*$ has type change $(p,q)\mapsto (n-q,n-p)$. Consequently $*u$ is an $L$-valued $(n-q,0)$-form with $D''(*u)=0$, hence is holomorphic. It vanishes on a nonempty open set, so the holomorphic identity theorem on the connected manifold gives $*u=0$ and $u=0$. Thus every harmonic class is zero. No elliptic-system continuation theorem is needed for this argument. For the dual assertion apply the result to $L^{-1}$ and use the perfect analytic Serre pairing of theorem 10.46.7 between $H^{0,q}(X,L)$ and $H^{n,n-q}(X,L^{-1})$; the latter is zero when $n-q\geq s$. $\square$ Corollary 10.48.3 . 2CCDF84C1B3C Let $L$ be a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on a compact connected Kähler manifold of dimension $n$. title: 10.54 Filtered complexes and spectral sequences
section: 10.54 Filtered complexes and spectral sequences
text: All complexes in this section are cochain complexes of modules over a commutative ring. A decreasing filtration consists of subcomplexes $F^{p+1}K^\bullet \subset F^ pK^\bullet $, indexed by integers. It is exhaustive and separated if its union is $K^\bullet $ and its intersection is zero, degree by degree. For convergence we shall use the stronger, explicit condition of a degreewise finite filtration: for every $n$ there are integers $a_ n\le b_ n$ with \[  F^ pK^ n=K^ n\  (p\le a_ n),\qquad F^ pK^ n=0\  (p\ge b_ n).  \] The algebraic page construction itself does not require this condition.

title: 10.54.1 Pages, differentials and finite convergence
section: 10.54 Filtered complexes and spectral sequences
text: For $r\ge 0$ put \[  Z_ r^{p,n}=\{ x\in F^ pK^ n:dx\in F^{p+r}K^{n+1}\} .  \] Thus $Z_0^{p,n}=F^ pK^ n$. Define \[  E_0^{p,q}=F^ pK^{p+q}/F^{p+1}K^{p+q},\qquad E_ r^{p,q}= \frac{Z_ r^{p,p+q}}{Z_{r-1}^{p+1,p+q}+dZ_{r-1}^{p-r+1,p+q-1}}\quad (r\ge 1).  \] Both summands of the denominator lie in the numerator: their derivatives lie in $F^{p+r}$ or are zero, respectively. Theorem 10.54.2 . E83B7568FE4B The differential induced by $d$ on $E_0$ and, for $r\ge 1$, the rule \[  d_ r:E_ r^{p,q}\longrightarrow E_ r^{p+r,q-r+1}, \qquad [x]\longmapsto [dx],  \] are well defined and square to zero. There are natural isomorphisms \[  E_{r+1}^{p,q}\simeq \frac{\ker (d_ r:E_ r^{p,q}\to E_ r^{p+r,q-r+1})}{\operatorname {im}(d_ r:E_ r^{p-r,q+r-1}\to E_ r^{p,q})} \qquad (r\ge 0).  \] In particular $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(F^ pK/F^{p+1}K)$. Proof. For $r=0$ the subcomplex condition defines $d_0$ on the quotient. A quotient cocycle has a representative in $Z_1^{p,n}$, $n=p+q$, and its boundaries and zero representatives form $F^{p+1}K^ n+dF^ pK^{n-1}$. This is exactly the stated formula for $E_1$. For $r\ge 1$, $dx\in F^{p+r}$ and $d(dx)=0$, so it represents an element of the indicated target. Adding $a\in Z_{r-1}^{p+1,n}$ changes it by $da$, which is in the target's boundary denominator. Adding a boundary does not change it. Thus $d_ r$ is well defined, and $d_ r^2=0$. If $d_ r[x]=0$, write $dx=a+db$ with $a\in Z_{r-1}^{p+r+1,n+1}$ and $b\in Z_{r-1}^{p+1,n}$. Then $x-b\in Z_{r+1}^{p,n}$ and represents the same class. Conversely a representative in this latter group is a $d_ r$-cocycle. The incoming boundaries are represented by $dZ_ r^{p-r,n-1}$. Finally, if $x=a+db\in Z_{r+1}^{p,n}$ is in the old denominator, with $a\in Z_{r-1}^{p+1,n}$ and $b\in Z_{r-1}^{p-r+1,n-1}$, then $da=dx\in F^{p+r+1}$, so $a\in Z_ r^{p+1,n}$. Also $b\in F^{p-r}$ and $db\in F^ p$, so $b\in Z_ r^{p-r,n-1}$. This proves that the new kernel quotient by the incoming boundaries is exactly \[  Z_{r+1}^{p,n}/ \bigl (Z_ r^{p+1,n}+dZ_ r^{p-r,n-1}\bigr )=E_{r+1}^{p,q}.  \] Every identification uses representatives and commutes with filtered cochain maps, proving naturality. $\square$ For comparison with a formulation entirely inside the associated graded, write $\overline Z_ r^{p,n}$ for the image of $Z_ r^{p,n}$ in $F^ pK^ n/F^{p+1}K^ n$, and $\overline B_ r^{p,n}$ for the image of $F^ pK^ n\cap dF^{p-r+1}K^{n-1}$. The page formula gives $E_ r^{p,n-p}=\overline Z_ r^{p,n}/\overline B_ r^{p,n}$. For $r\ge 1$ the kernel of projection on the numerator is $Z_{r-1}^{p+1,n}$, and the other denominator summand projects to $\overline B_ r^{p,n}$; for $r=0$ the identity is immediate since $\overline B_0=0$. The $\overline Z_ r$ decrease, the $\overline B_ r$ increase, and every actual graded boundary is an actual graded cycle. Moreover $d$ gives the isomorphism \[  \overline Z_ r^{p,n}/\overline Z_{r+1}^{p,n} \simeq \overline B_{r+1}^{p+r,n+1}/\overline B_ r^{p+r,n+1}.  \] Surjectivity is exactly the definition of the boundary on the right. Changing a representative by an element of $F^{p+1}$ changes its derivative by a boundary in $\overline B_ r$. If its derivative is zero in that quotient, write $dx=db+dc$ with $b\in F^{p+1}K^ n$, $c\in F^ pK^ n$, $db\in F^{p+r}K^{n+1}$ and $dc\in F^{p+r+1}K^{n+1}$. Then $x-b\in Z_{r+1}^{p,n}$ and has the same graded class. Conversely such a representative maps to zero. This proves the kernel claim and the isomorphism, including $r=0$. Theorem 10.54.3 . 21231040599F Give cohomology its induced filtration \[  F^ pH^ n(K)=\operatorname {im}\bigl (H^ n(F^ pK)\to H^ n(K)\bigr ).  \] For any filtration its associated graded term is canonically B14FBC5EE8B8 10.54.4 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {gr}_ F^ pH^ n(K)= \frac{F^ pK^ n\cap \ker d}{(F^{p+1}K^ n\cap \ker d)+(F^ pK^ n\cap dK^{n-1})}. \end{equation} If the filtration is degreewise finite, each $E_ r^{p,q}$ stabilizes for sufficiently large $r$ to this term, with $n=p+q$. The induced filtration on $H^ n(K)$ is finite, exhaustive and separated. This is the convergence denoted $E_ r^{p,q}\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(K)$. Filtered cochain maps induce maps on all pages and on these filtered cohomology groups. If such a map between degreewise finitely filtered complexes induces an isomorphism at one page $r$ in every bidegree, it induces an isomorphism on total cohomology in every degree. Convergence identifies the associated graded groups; no canonical splitting of their extensions is asserted. Proof. The image defining $F^ pH^ n$ is $(F^ pK^ n\cap \ker d)/(F^ pK^ n\cap dK^{n-1})$. Taking its quotient by the next image gives equation 10.54.4 directly. For a fixed $p,n$ take $r$ so large that $p+r\ge b_{n+1}$ and $p-r+1\le a_{n-1}$. Then \[  Z_ r^{p,n}=F^ pK^ n\cap \ker d, \quad Z_{r-1}^{p+1,n}=F^{p+1}K^ n\cap \ker d, \quad dZ_{r-1}^{p-r+1,n-1}=F^ pK^ n\cap dK^{n-1}.  \] For the last equality, the potential primitive can now be any element of $K^{n-1}$, and the $Z$ condition says exactly that its derivative belongs to $F^ p$. The page formula proves the stabilization claimed. For $p\le a_ n$ every cohomology class has a cycle in $F^ pK^ n$; for $p\ge b_ n$ there are no such cycles. This proves finiteness, exhaustiveness and separation of the induced filtration. Page naturality was proved above and respects actual cycle and boundary representatives. An isomorphism on a page induces isomorphisms on its cohomology, hence on all later pages and, by the proved stabilization, on the graded cohomology groups. A map between finitely filtered modules that is an isomorphism on every graded term is an isomorphism: starting at the zero last filtration term, use induction on $0\to F^{p+1}\to F^ p\to \operatorname {gr}^ p\to 0$. For surjectivity lift the graded image and correct its error in $F^{p+1}$; for injectivity a zero image first has zero graded class and then is zero by the induction hypothesis. Apply this degree by degree to the cohomology map. $\square$ Call a convergent spectral sequence collapsed at page $R$ if $d_ r=0$ for every $r\ge R$. Then the page identifications above identify $E_ R$ with the stable page. For degreewise finite filtrations, if $R\ge 2$ and $E_ R^{p,q}=0$ except for one row $q=q_0$, then \[  H^ n(K)\simeq E_ R^{n-q_0,q_0}.  \] Indeed every later differential changes $q$ and is zero, and the finite filtration of each $H^ n$ has only that one nonzero graded term. If only one column $p=p_0$ survives, the same assertion holds already for $R\ge 1$, with $H^ n(K)\simeq E_ R^{p_0,n-p_0}$. These one-piece identifications are canonical; the assertion for several surviving terms is only the associated graded statement. The finite-filtration hypothesis cannot simply be replaced by exhaustiveness and separation on $K$. Over a field let $K^0=\bigoplus _{i\ge 0}ke_ i$, $K^1=\bigoplus _{i\ge 0}kf_ i$, $de_ i=f_ i-f_{i+1}$, and filter by tails with indices $i\ge \max \{ p,0\} $. The associated graded differential is the identity, so $E_1=0$. But $H^1(K)=k$: summing the coefficients of a finite $f$-combination kills all boundaries, and every finite combination with sum zero is a boundary by taking successive partial sums as its $e_ i$-coefficients. Every tail contains $f_ p$, whose class is the same generator. Thus $F^ pH^1=k$ for every $p$, which is not separated. A zero page has not recovered this cohomology. Even for finite filtrations, $\mathbb Z/4$ with middle subgroup $2\mathbb Z/4$ and $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$ with one middle factor have the same two graded groups; those groups alone do not choose the extension.

An isomorphism on a page induces isomorphisms on its cohomology, hence on all later pages and, by the proved stabilization, on the graded cohomology groups. A map between finitely filtered modules that is an isomorphism on every graded term is an isomorphism: starting at the zero last filtration term, use induction on $0\to F^{p+1}\to F^ p\to \operatorname {gr}^ p\to 0$. For surjectivity lift the graded image and correct its error in $F^{p+1}$; for injectivity a zero image first has zero graded class and then is zero by the induction hypothesis. Apply this degree by degree to the cohomology map. $\square$
