title: 10.54.5 Double complexes, edges and the five-term sequence
search_title: Double complexes, edges and the five-term sequence
section: 10.54 Filtered complexes and spectral sequences
text: A double complex has differentials $d_ h:K^{p,q}\to K^{p+1,q}$ and $d_ v:K^{p,q}\to K^{p,q+1}$ with $d_ h^2=d_ v^2=d_ hd_ v+d_ vd_ h=0$. Its algebraic total complex is \[  \operatorname {Tot}^ nK=\bigoplus _{p+q=n}K^{p,q},\qquad D=d_ h+d_ v.  \] If the original horizontal and vertical maps commute, replace the vertical map on $K^{p,q}$ by $(-1)^ p$ times that map. This gives the total convention $h+(-1)^ pv$ used in lemma 10.43.15 . Theorem 10.54.6 . C060D8E63B4F Suppose $K^{p,q}=0$ for $p<0$ or $q<0$. The column filtration $F^ a\operatorname {Tot}^ n=\bigoplus _{p\ge a}K^{p,n-p}$ gives \[  E_0^{p,q}=K^{p,q},\quad d_0=d_ v,\quad E_1^{p,q}=H^ q(K^{p,\bullet },d_ v),\quad d_1=[d_ h],\quad E_2^{p,q}=H^ p(E_1^{\bullet ,q},[d_ h]).  \] It converges to the associated graded of $H^{p+q}(\operatorname {Tot}K)$. Interchanging the indices gives the second, row-filtration spectral sequence, with first page $\widetilde E_1^{p,q}=H^ q(K^{\bullet ,p},d_ h)$ and differential induced by $d_ v$. Both induced filtrations are finite. A map of double complexes inducing an isomorphism on some page in all bidegrees induces an isomorphism on total cohomology. Proof. On each degree $n\ge 0$ there are just $n+1$ possible components, so either filtration is degreewise finite, with no completion or infinite-diagonal totalization involved. On the column-associated graded only the vertical differential remains. The page theorem gives $E_1$. A vertically closed $x\in K^{p,q}$ has $Dx=d_ hx$ in the next column, so the representative rule for $d_1$ gives the stated horizontal map. This gives $E_2$ as well. Apply theorem 10.54.3 . Exchanging the two indices proves the second statement; the same total differential is used because the two maps anticommute. The comparison assertion is that theorem applied to a filtration-preserving total map. $\square$ Theorem 10.54.7 . BD1FDFF09B89 For the column spectral sequence of a first-quadrant double complex, there are edge maps \[  H^ n(\operatorname {Tot}K)\longrightarrow E_ r^{0,n}\quad (r\ge 1), \qquad E_ r^{n,0}\longrightarrow H^ n(\operatorname {Tot}K) \quad (r\ge 2),  \] and a natural exact sequence \[  0\longrightarrow E_2^{1,0}\longrightarrow H^1(\operatorname {Tot}K) \longrightarrow E_2^{0,1}\xrightarrow {d_2}E_2^{2,0} \longrightarrow H^2(\operatorname {Tot}K).  \] Proof. For $r\ge 1$ no differential can enter $E_ r^{0,n}$, since its source has first coordinate $-r$. Hence $E_{r+1}^{0,n}=\ker d_ r\subset E_ r^{0,n}$. For $r\ge 2$ no differential leaves $E_ r^{n,0}$, since the target's second coordinate is $1-r<0$; thus its next term is a quotient. The finite cohomology filtration satisfies $F^0H^ n=H^ n$ and $F^{n+1}H^ n=0$. Its quotient onto $\operatorname {gr}^0H^ n=E_\infty ^{0,n}$ followed by these injections gives the first edge. The quotients to $E_\infty ^{n,0}=F^ nH^ n$, followed by inclusion, give the second. These two ranges are different; no bottom-edge assertion is made at $r=1$. The finite filtration of $H^1$ gives $0\to E_\infty ^{1,0}\to H^1\to E_\infty ^{0,1}\to 0$. Bidegrees show that $E_\infty ^{1,0}=E_2^{1,0}$, $E_\infty ^{0,1}=\ker (d_2:E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0})$, and $E_\infty ^{2,0}=\operatorname {coker}(d_2:E_2^{0,1}\to E_2^{2,0})$: after this $d_2$ no remaining differential reaches or leaves these positions. Insert these identities and the edge injection $E_\infty ^{2,0}=F^2H^2\hookrightarrow H^2$. The resulting sequence is exactly the displayed one, with exactness at every position. All maps are natural by their cycle and filtration constructions. $\square$ For every complex manifold take $K^{p,q}=\mathcal E^{p,q}(X)$, $d_ h=\partial $, $d_ v=\bar\partial $. The usual exterior-calculus identities give the anticommutation, and the total complex is the complex-valued smooth de Rham complex. Hence there is a natural spectral sequence \[  E_1^{p,q}=H_{\bar\partial }^{p,q}(X) \quad \Rightarrow \quad H_{\mathrm{dR}}^{p+q}(X,\mathbb C).  \] This existence and convergence do not require compactness or a Kähler metric. The Dolbeault and de Rham meanings are those of corollary 10.43.11 . No degeneration or Hodge splitting on a general complex manifold is asserted.

title: 10.55 Hypercohomology and direct-image spectral sequences
section: 10.55 Hypercohomology and direct-image spectral sequences
text: Let $L^\bullet $ be a bounded-below complex of sheaves of abelian groups, with differential $\delta $; say $L^ q=0$ for $q<q_0$. Use the exact functors and resolution from theorem 10.43.5 , writing $C^ pF=G^{p+1}F$. Form \[  K_ L^{p,q}=\Gamma (X,C^ pL^ q),\quad p\ge 0,\  q\ge q_0, \qquad d_ h=d_ G,\quad d_ v=(-1)^ pC^ p\delta .  \] Naturality gives $d_ hd_ v+d_ vd_ h=0$. Every total diagonal is finite. Define \[  \mathbb H^ n(X,L^\bullet )=H^ n(\operatorname {Tot}K_ L,D), \qquad D=d_ G+(-1)^ pC^ p\delta .  \] Complex morphisms give natural maps of these groups. Theorem 10.55.1 . C081C1E12790 For a sheaf in degree zero, this construction is its existing Godement cohomology. For a nonnegative complex, $\mathbb H^0(X,L)=\Gamma (X,\ker \delta ^0)$. Every degreewise short exact sequence of bounded-below sheaf complexes gives a natural long exact hypercohomology sequence. For the right shift $L\langle s\rangle ^ q=L^{q-s}$, with differential $(-1)^ s\delta $, one has \[  \mathbb H^ n(X,L\langle s\rangle ) \simeq \mathbb H^{n-s}(X,L).  \] Proof. A sheaf in degree zero leaves precisely its Godement section complex. In total degree zero of a nonnegative complex, the two components of the cocycle equation say $d_ Gx=0$ and $\delta x=0$; the first says $x$ is an actual section of $L^0$. There are no negative-degree boundaries. Exactness of every $\Gamma (X,C^ p-)$ and finiteness of each diagonal make a short exact sheaf-complex sequence a degreewise short exact sequence of total complexes. Apply lemma 10.43.3 , including its naturality. For shifts, multiply the component of Godement degree $p$ by $(-1)^{sp}$. This identifies the total complex of $K_{L\langle s\rangle }$ with the shifted total complex $(\operatorname {Tot}K_ L)\langle s\rangle $: on the horizontal map the multiplier changes by $(-1)^ s$, and on the vertical map the shift supplies the same factor. The shifted differential is $(-1)^ sD$, proving the cohomology assertion with its signs. $\square$ Theorem 10.55.2 . D461C5DFED48 There are natural convergent spectral sequences \[  E_2^{p,q}=H^ p(X,\mathcal H^ q(L)) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathbb H^{p+q}(X,L),  \] and \[  \widetilde E_1^{p,q}=H^ q(X,L^ p),\qquad \widetilde E_2^{p,q}=H^ p\bigl (H^ q(X,L^\bullet ),\delta \bigr ) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \mathbb H^{p+q}(X,L).  \] Both filtrations are degreewise finite. In the second first page the actual differential under these representative identifications is $(-1)^ qH^ q(\delta )$; this fixed-row sign does not change its cohomology groups. A quasi-isomorphism of bounded-below sheaf complexes induces isomorphisms on all hypercohomology groups. Here quasi-isomorphism means an actual complex morphism inducing isomorphisms of all cohomology sheaves; abstract graded isomorphism types alone are not asserted sufficient. Proof. Filter $K_ L$ first by Godement degree. Exactness of the functor $\Gamma (X,C^ p-)$ identifies vertical cohomology with $\Gamma (X,C^ p\mathcal H^ q(L))$. Indeed apply exactness to the kernel, image and quotient sequences defining each cohomology sheaf. The factor $(-1)^ p$ does not alter kernels or images. The next differential is $d_ G$, giving the first $E_2$ display. Filter instead by sheaf-complex degree. Horizontal cohomology is $H^ q(X,L^ p)$, and the induced other differential has exactly the factor $(-1)^ q$ from the original Godement degree. Multiplication of a whole row's differential by this unit preserves its kernel and image, giving the second $E_2$ display. For total degree $n$, Godement degree ranges from $0$ to $n-q_0$, and sheaf-complex degree from $q_0$ to $n$. Thus both filtrations have explicit finite bounds. The page and convergence proofs apply unchanged, or after translating the lower sheaf index to zero. There is no unbounded-total convergence assertion. For a quasi-isomorphism the first $E_2$ maps are isomorphisms, so theorem 10.54.3 proves the last claim by an actual filtered morphism. $\square$ Corollary 10.55.3 . D8E20B32F22B If $L^\bullet $ resolves $F$ in degree zero, its augmentation gives an isomorphism \[  H^ n(X,F)\longrightarrow \mathbb H^ n(X,L).  \] If every $L^ q$ is acyclic on $X$, inclusion of global sections by their Godement germs gives an isomorphism \[  H^ n(L^\bullet (X),\delta )\longrightarrow \mathbb H^ n(X,L).  \] More generally, if only $\mathcal H^{q_1}(L)$ is nonzero, the single-row identification gives \[  \mathbb H^ n(X,L)\simeq H^{n-q_1}(X,\mathcal H^{q_1}(L)).  \] Proof. The first augmentation is a quasi-isomorphism from $F[0]$, so the theorem applies. For the second, the germ inclusion is a cochain map: $d_ G\eta =0$ and on Godement degree zero the other differential is $\delta $. Its map to the second spectral sequence is the identity on the only nonzero first-page row, since all positive sheaf cohomology of the terms vanishes. Apply finite comparison, or the proved one-row collapse. In the final assertion the first $E_2$ has just the indicated row, so its finite filtration has a single graded piece in each total degree. $\square$ The augmentational normalization here can be compared explicitly with the successive positive connecting-map normalization of theorem 10.43.8 . Suppose $L$ is an acyclic resolution of $F$, and denote that earlier isomorphism by $\Psi _ n:H^ n(L(X))\to H^ n(X,F)$. If $j_ F$ and $j_ L$ are the two maps to hypercohomology in the corollary, then 9AECA85DAE24 10.55.4 \begin{equation}  j_ F^{-1}j_ L=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}\Psi _ n. \end{equation} To check this, take a closed $z\in L^ n(X)$. Exactness of the Godement degree functors gives finite zigzag lifts $a_ j\in \Gamma (X,C^ jL^{n-1-j})$, $0\le j<n$, with $\delta a_0=\eta z$ and $\delta a_ j=d_ Ga_{j-1}$ for $j>0$. The positive connecting construction represents $\Psi _ n[z]$ by $d_ Ga_{n-1}\in \Gamma (X,C^ nF)$. In the total complex, $Da_ j=d_ Ga_ j+(-1)^ j\delta a_ j$. The first relation replaces $[\eta z]$ by $-[d_ Ga_0]$; each subsequent replacement multiplies by $(-1)^ j$ for $j=0,\ldots ,n-2$. The product is $(-1)^{1+(n-2)(n-1)/2}=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}$. For $n=0$ both maps are the identity on the kernel sections. This proves the formula without silently changing either earlier connecting maps or the total differential.

title: 10.55.5 Higher direct images and Leray convergence
search_title: Higher direct images and Leray convergence
section: 10.55 Hypercohomology and direct-image spectral sequences
text: Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and $A$ a sheaf of abelian groups. Use the existing direct image $(f_*A)(V)=A(f^{-1}V)$. Direct image preserves flabby sheaves, because inverse images of inclusions of open sets are inclusions of open sets. Define \[  R^ qf_*A=\mathcal H^ q(f_*C_ X^\bullet A).  \] Left exactness gives $R^0f_*A=f_*A$. Theorem 10.55.6 . 2CFDCB1083B2 For every continuous map of topological spaces and every sheaf of abelian groups there is a natural spectral sequence \[  E_2^{p,q}=H^ p(Y,R^ qf_*A) \quad \Rightarrow \quad H^{p+q}(X,A),\qquad p,q\ge 0.  \] In each total degree convergence means the associated graded of a finite filtration. One has the stalk description \[  (R^ qf_*A)_ y=\varinjlim _{V\ni y}H^ q(f^{-1}V,A),  \] and every short exact sequence of coefficient sheaves gives the natural long exact sequence of higher-direct-image sheaves. If $R^ qf_*A=0$ for all $q>0$, the augmentation edge gives isomorphisms $H^ n(Y,f_*A)\to H^ n(X,A)$. This edge is the composite of inverse-image pullback and the coefficient map $f^{-1}f_*A\to A$. No identification of the displayed stalk with fiber cohomology is asserted without further hypotheses. Proof. Filtered direct limits of modules are exact by the representative argument: an image which is zero becomes zero at some later index, where exactness gives a preimage. The same argument shows that cohomology of a filtered limit of complexes is the limit of its cohomology: a limiting cocycle becomes a cocycle at some later index, and a limiting boundary has a primitive at a later index. Consequently stalkwise cohomology of $f_*C_ X^\bullet A$ is the displayed limit, by the definition of stalk and $\Gamma (V,f_*C_ X^\bullet A)=\Gamma (f^{-1}V,C_ X^\bullet A)$. Apply the sheaf-cohomology long exact sequence on $f^{-1}V$ and take these exact stalk limits to obtain the higher-image sequence; its maps are compatible with restriction and hence are sheaf maps. Put $L^\bullet =f_*C_ X^\bullet A$. Every term is flabby on $Y$, thus acyclic by theorem 10.43.7 . Hence corollary 10.55.3 identifies \[  \mathbb H^ n(Y,L)\simeq H^ n(L(Y)) =H^ n(C_ X^\bullet A(X))=H^ n(X,A).  \] The first hypercohomology spectral sequence for $L$ has the stated $E_2$, with finite first-quadrant convergence. All constructions are natural in $A$. Its bottom edge is the map induced by the inclusion $f_*A[0]\to L$: the spectral sequence of its source has just the bottom row, and naturality identifies its map to the stable bottom row and the final filtration inclusion with this edge. If all higher $R^ q$ vanish, this is also a quasi-isomorphism and the edge is an isomorphism. This proves the asserted edge statement within the given augmentational construction. $\square$ Here is a complete verification of the last edge identification, including the pullback construction. For a sheaf $B$ on $Y$ there is a natural map \[  \lambda _ B:f^{-1}G_ YB\longrightarrow G_ Xf^{-1}B.  \] For a section $u$ on an open set of $X$, its image is the arbitrary assignment whose value at $x$ is $e_{f(x)}^ B(u_ x)\in B_{f(x)}=(f^{-1}B)_ x$. The evaluation is well defined on the germ of an assignment, as in the Godement construction. This description commutes with restriction and coefficient maps, and \[  \lambda _ B f^{-1}\eta _ B=\eta _{f^{-1}B}.  \] Iterating gives $\lambda ^{(m)}:f^{-1}G_ Y^ mB\to G_ X^ mf^{-1}B$: take $\lambda ^{(1)}=\lambda _ B$ and compose $\lambda _{G_ Y^{m-1}B}$ with $G_ X\lambda ^{(m-1)}$. These iterates commute with every insertion of $\eta $. Indeed insertion in the first position is the displayed identity; insertion in a later position reduces, after the outer $G_ X$, to the preceding induction case by naturality of $\lambda $. Thus they commute with the alternating sums defining $d_ G$. Pulling back global sections and then applying these maps constructs the cochain map \[  \Gamma (Y,C_ Y^\bullet B)\longrightarrow \Gamma (X,C_ X^\bullet f^{-1}B)  \] and hence $f^*:H^ n(Y,B)\to H^ n(X,f^{-1}B)$. In degree zero it is ordinary section pullback. Since inverse image and the Godement section functors are exact, these cochain maps give morphisms of the short exact complexes for every short exact coefficient sequence; their cohomology maps commute with the connecting maps. We use the following elementary uniqueness argument. Natural maps from $H^ n(Y,B)$ to any coefficient functor with compatible connecting maps are determined by their degree-zero maps. To see this embed $B\to G_ YB$ and put $Q=G_ YB/B$. For $n=1$ the connecting map $H^0(Y,Q)\to H^1(Y,B)$ is onto, since $G_ YB$ is acyclic. For $n>1$ the map $H^{n-1}(Y,Q)\to H^ n(Y,B)$ is an isomorphism. Commutation with these maps and induction on $n$ prove uniqueness; no existence theorem for derived functors is being assumed. Apply this to the exact coefficient functor $B\mapsto f^{-1}B$. The augmented sheaf complex on $Y$ \[  B[0]\longrightarrow L_ B^\bullet :=f_*C_ X^\bullet f^{-1}B  \] uses the adjunction unit followed by Godement augmentation. All terms of $L_ B$ are flabby. Its hypercohomology therefore identifies with $H^ n(X,f^{-1}B)$ by the global-section inclusion already proved. The augmentation gives maps $e_ B^ n:H^ n(Y,B)\to H^ n(X,f^{-1}B)$. They commute with connecting maps: a short exact coefficient sequence gives short exact complexes $L_ B$, because $\Gamma (f^{-1}V,C_ X^ p f^{-1}-)$ is exact for every open $V$; both augmentations and the global-section inclusions are morphisms of these short exact complexes. Naturality of the cochain long exact sequence proves the assertion. In degree zero $e_ B^0$ is section pullback. The uniqueness argument thus gives $e_ B^ n=f^*$ in every degree. Finally take $B=f_*A$ and the counit $\epsilon :f^{-1}B\to A$. The composite \[  B[0]\longrightarrow f_*C_ X^\bullet f^{-1}B \xrightarrow {f_*C_ X^\bullet \epsilon } f_*C_ X^\bullet A  \] is the original augmentation: on a section of $A(f^{-1}V)$, taking its inverse-image germs and then evaluating them in $A$ returns the same section. The naturality of hypercohomology and of its global-section comparison therefore identifies its map with $H^ n(X,\epsilon )\circ f^*$. The preceding proof identified that augmentation map with the Leray bottom edge. This proves the claimed edge identification and, when all higher direct images vanish, the isomorphism induced by this precise composite.

title: Theorem 10.55.6
section: 10.55 Hypercohomology and direct-image spectral sequences
text: Theorem 10.55.6 . 2CFDCB1083B2 For every continuous map of topological spaces and every sheaf of abelian groups there is a natural spectral sequence \[  E_2^{p,q}=H^ p(Y,R^ qf_*A) \quad \Rightarrow \quad H^{p+q}(X,A),\qquad p,q\ge 0.  \] In each total degree convergence means the associated graded of a finite filtration. One has the stalk description \[  (R^ qf_*A)_ y=\varinjlim _{V\ni y}H^ q(f^{-1}V,A),  \] and every short exact sequence of coefficient sheaves gives the natural long exact sequence of higher-direct-image sheaves. If $R^ qf_*A=0$ for all $q>0$, the augmentation edge gives isomorphisms $H^ n(Y,f_*A)\to H^ n(X,A)$. This edge is the composite of inverse-image pullback and the coefficient map $f^{-1}f_*A\to A$. No identification of the displayed stalk with fiber cohomology is asserted without further hypotheses. Proof. Filtered direct limits of modules are exact by the representative argument: an image which is zero becomes zero at some later index, where exactness gives a preimage. The same argument shows that cohomology of a filtered limit of complexes is the limit of its cohomology: a limiting cocycle becomes a cocycle at some later index, and a limiting boundary has a primitive at a later index. Consequently stalkwise cohomology of $f_*C_ X^\bullet A$ is the displayed limit, by the definition of stalk and $\Gamma (V,f_*C_ X^\bullet A)=\Gamma (f^{-1}V,C_ X^\bullet A)$. Apply the sheaf-cohomology long exact sequence on $f^{-1}V$ and take these exact stalk limits to obtain the higher-image sequence; its maps are compatible with restriction and hence are sheaf maps. Put $L^\bullet =f_*C_ X^\bullet A$. Every term is flabby on $Y$, thus acyclic by theorem 10.43.7 . Hence corollary 10.55.3 identifies \[  \mathbb H^ n(Y,L)\simeq H^ n(L(Y)) =H^ n(C_ X^\bullet A(X))=H^ n(X,A).  \] The first hypercohomology spectral sequence for $L$ has the stated $E_2$, with finite first-quadrant convergence. All constructions are natural in $A$. Its bottom edge is the map induced by the inclusion $f_*A[0]\to L$: the spectral sequence of its source has just the bottom row, and naturality identifies its map to the stable bottom row and the final filtration inclusion with this edge. If all higher $R^ q$ vanish, this is also a quasi-isomorphism and the edge is an isomorphism. This proves the asserted edge statement within the given augmentational construction. $\square$

title: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates

section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Use the unscaled curvature, increasing barred multi-indices and metric volumes of section 6.26 . All bundle metrics in the first five statements are smooth. An inverse-curvature energy always has the semidefinite dual meaning; it does not presume an invertible curvature matrix. Lemma 6.28.1 . 2771F5EE97D1 For the Dolbeault Laplacian of a smooth Hermitian bundle and base metric, every distributional harmonic form with locally $L^2$ coefficients is smooth. Proof. The principal symbol of $P=D''\delta ''+\delta ''D''$ is a positive scalar quadratic form times the coefficient identity: the symbols of wedge and contraction satisfy their usual anticommutator identity. On a relatively compact real coordinate ball, multiplication by the smooth positive square root of the coefficient metric times the volume density identifies the $L^2$ pairing with the ordinary coefficient pairing. The conjugated operator still has this scalar principal symbol. It has divergence form $-\partial _ i(a^{ij}\partial _ j)$ plus smooth matrix terms of order at most one, with $a$ uniformly positive on a smaller ball. Choose a cutoff $\chi $ in that ball and set $v=\chi w$, extended by zero in the coordinate space. Since $Pw=0$, $Pv=[P,\chi ]w$ belongs to $H^{-1}$ and has norm bounded by a constant times the local $L^2$ norm of $w$. Extend the coefficients smoothly beyond the compact support, preserving uniform ellipticity there, and let $J_ t$ be ordinary convolution. The matrix first-order commutator calculation in graph-norm density by cutoffs and mollification gives \[  \| [a^{ij}\partial _ j,J_ t]v\| _2\leq C\| v\| _2.  \] Consequently $[P,J_ t]v$ is bounded in $H^{-1}$: write its principal part as $-\partial _ i[a^{ij}\partial _ j,J_ t]v$; its lower-order commutators have the same or better bound. Convolution is bounded on $H^{-1}$, so $PJ_ tv$ is uniformly bounded there. Integration by parts and uniform positivity give, for smooth forms $z$ supported in this fixed ball, \[  \| z\| _{H^1}^2\leq C\bigl (|\langle Pz,z\rangle |+\| z\| _2^2\bigr ).  \] Indeed the principal integral dominates the squared first derivatives, and each lower-order integral is bounded by $C\| z\| _2\| z\| _{H^1}$ and absorbed by Young's inequality. Apply this to $J_ tv$, using $H^{-1}$–$H^1$ duality, to obtain a uniform $H^1$ bound. Weak compactness and $J_ tv\to v$ in $L^2$ show that $v\in H^1$. Thus $w\in H^1_{\rm loc}$. The checked vector divergence-form interior theorem interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form , successively applied to $Pw=0$ on nested balls, now gives every Sobolev order and smoothness. This argument supplies the $H^1$ starting hypothesis of that theorem. $\square$ Theorem 6.28.2 . E15FB3F8A946 Let $(X,\omega )$ be complete Kähler, let $(E,h)$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic bundle, and let $1\leq q\leq n$. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$. Suppose $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]\geq 0$ in bidegree $(p,q)$. If $F$ is locally $L^2$, is closed distributionally, and has finite inverse energy $M=\int _ X|F|_{B^{-1}}^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega $, then 48191F980D4B 6.28.3 \begin{equation}  D''u=F,\qquad \| u\| _2^2\leq M \end{equation} for an $L^2$ form $u$ of type $(p,q-1)$. Global ordinary $L^2$ integrability of $F$ is not required. If $X$ merely possesses a complete Kähler metric and $\omega $ is any Kähler metric, the same conclusion holds in degree $(n,q)$ provided $E$ is $m$-semipositive with $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. The norm and inverse energy in this conclusion use the original $\omega $. Smooth data admit a smooth choice in either assertion. Proof. For compactly supported smooth $v$, curvature Cauchy–Schwarz and theorem 10.33.2 give \[  |\langle F,v\rangle |^2 \leq M\int _ X\langle Bv,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M\bigl (\| \delta ''v\| _2^2+\| D''v\| _2^2\bigr ).  \] Define $Av=(\delta ''v,D''v)$ in the direct sum of degrees $(p,q-1)$ and $(p,q+1)$. The displayed bound makes pairing with $F$ a well-defined bounded functional on $\operatorname {Ran}A$. Hilbert representation on its closure gives $(u,w)$ in that closure, with $\| u\| _2^2+\| w\| _2^2\leq M$, and \[  F=D''u+\delta ''w  \] distributionally. In top barred degree the second space is zero. Otherwise $w$ is an $L^2$ limit of forms $D''v_ j$, hence $D''w=0$ distributionally. Applying $D''$ to the last identity, using $D''F=0$, gives $D''\delta ''w=0$. Thus $w$ is distributionally harmonic and is smooth by lemma 6.28.1 . Take the complete gradient cutoffs of lemma 6.26.1 . Integrating the harmonic equation against $\chi _ R^2w$ and using $D''w=0$ gives \[  \| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2^2 \leq 2\| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2\,  \|  (\bar\partial \chi _ R\wedge )^*w\| _2.  \] All integrals here have compact support; no prior global derivative bound is assumed. It follows that $\| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2^2\leq C R^{-2}\| w\| _2^2$. Letting $R\to \infty $ on each compact set proves $\delta ''w=0$, and establishes ( 6.28.3 ). For the original-metric assertion put $\omega _\varepsilon =\omega +\varepsilon \widehat\omega $. These metrics are complete. The full coefficient inequalities of lemma 6.27.1 show semipositivity and bound the inverse energy by $M$ for each $\omega _\varepsilon $. The first assertion applies to the locally $L^2$ datum for each of these metrics. The fixed-comparison-density weak limit in the proof of theorem 6.27.6 now applies verbatim: first take local weak limits; test the norm with fixed $\omega _{\varepsilon _ k}$ for indices $j\geq k$; then let $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ and exhaust $X$. It gives the original norm bound. This argument uses no global ordinary norm of $F$. Finally lemma 6.27.8 gives a smooth minimum-norm primitive for smooth data. $\square$ Theorem 6.28.4 . FD2B7A8ED856 Let $(X,\omega )$ possess a complete Kähler metric. Let $G:E\to Q$ be a surjective holomorphic bundle map, with the induced quotient metric on $Q$. Put $r=\operatorname {rank}E$, $a=\operatorname {rank}Q$, $s=r-a$, and fix $0\leq k\leq n$. Set $m=\min (n-k,s)$. Suppose $E$ is $m$-semipositive and a Hermitian line bundle $L$ satisfies \[  \mathrm i\Theta (L)\geq (m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q), \qquad \epsilon >0.  \] Every closed $L^2$ form $f$ of type $(n,k)$ with values in $Q\otimes L$ has a closed lift $h$ with values in $E\otimes L$ such that 1FDBE18C9CE0 6.28.5 \begin{equation}  Gh=f,\qquad \| h\| _2^2\leq (1+m/\epsilon )\| f\| _2^2. \end{equation} Smooth data admit a smooth lift. When $m=0$, no curvature hypothesis is needed and the constant is one. Proof. If $Q=0$ take $h=0$. If $s=0$, the inverse of $G$ is holomorphic and isometric for the quotient metric. If $k=n$, the orthogonal lift $G^*f$ is automatically closed by degree and isometric. These cases give the stated $m=0$ clause. Assume henceforth $s\geq 1$, $k<n$, so $m\geq 1$. Let $S=\ker G$ and use the orthogonal splitting $E=S\oplus Q$. The complete connection and curvature calculation of proposition 10.34.9 writes the second fundamental form as $\beta =\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j B_ j$ and gives \[  R_ S=R_ E|_ S-C_\beta ,\qquad R_ Q=R_ E|_ Q+(B_ jB_ l^*)_{j\bar l},\qquad C_\beta (v)=\left|\sum _ jB_ jv_ j\right|^2.  \] Put $\alpha =\operatorname {tr}_ S C_\beta $. The rank-one tests contained in $m$-semipositivity give $\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q\geq 0$, hence $R_{\det Q}\geq \alpha $. Moreover $m\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta \geq _ m0$ by theorem 10.34.2 , including $s=m=1$. The curvature assumption therefore gives 8CCE15D3C2B6 6.28.6 \begin{equation}  R_{S\otimes L}\geq _ m(m+\epsilon )\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta \geq _ m(\epsilon /m)C_\beta . \end{equation} The last difference is $(1+\epsilon /m)(m\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta )$. In degree $(n,k+1)$ the coefficient tensors $(v_{jJ})_ j$ have rank at most $\min (n-k,s)=m$, by proposition 10.33.6 . If $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (S\otimes L),\Lambda _\omega ]$, then B33FBDD0925E 6.28.7 \begin{equation}  \langle Bv,v\rangle \geq (\epsilon /m) \sum _{|J|=k}\left|\sum _ j B_ jv_{jJ}\right|^2, \qquad |\beta ^*\wedge f|_{B^{-1}}^2\leq (m/\epsilon )|f|^2. \end{equation} Indeed the adjoint of $f\mapsto \beta ^*\wedge f$ is contraction with coefficients $\sum _ jB_ jv_{jJ}$, with the common top-form sign cancelled in its squared norm. Pairing with $f$ and applying finite-dimensional Cauchy–Schwarz proves the second inequality, also on a kernel of $B$. Write $j:S\to E$ for inclusion. The $(0,1)$ connection block gives $D''(G^*f)=-j(\beta ^*\wedge f)$. Thus $F=\beta ^*\wedge f$ is locally $L^2$ and closed distributionally: apply $(D'')^2=0$ and use that $j$ is holomorphic and injective. It need not be globally $L^2$. Its finite inverse energy is bounded by $(m/\epsilon )\| f\| _2^2$ by ( 6.28.7 ). The original-metric part of theorem 6.28.2 supplies $D''u=F$ with that squared norm bound. Set $h=G^*f+ju$. Then $Gh=f$, $D''h=0$, and orthogonality gives pointwise $|h|^2=|f|^2+|u|^2$. This proves ( 6.28.5 ). If $f$ is smooth, choose the smooth primitive supplied by the same theorem. $\square$ Corollary 6.28.8 . 2F176031B9F6 Under the bundle and curvature hypotheses of theorem 6.28.4 , if $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion, the induced map \[  H^ k(X,K_ X\otimes \mathcal O(E\otimes L))\longrightarrow H^ k(X,K_ X\otimes \mathcal O(Q\otimes L))  \] is surjective. Proof. Use the smooth bundle-valued Dolbeault resolution in corollary 10.43.11 and represent a class by a smooth closed $(n,k)$-form $f$. Shift the exhaustion $\rho $ to be nonnegative. The compact-band convex weight construction ( 6.26.9 ) gives increasing convex $\chi $ for which $f$ is $L^2$ after replacing the metric of $L$ by $h_ L\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )}$. Its added curvature is semipositive, so all lifting inequalities persist. A complete Kähler metric exists by lemma 6.26.8 . The preceding theorem gives a smooth closed lift, representing a preimage of the given class. This proves surjectivity, without any assertion that the entire next kernel-bundle cohomology group vanishes. $\square$ Theorem 6.28.9 . A32EC1620046 Let $G:E\to Q$ be surjective, now with an arbitrary smooth metric on $Q$, on a Kähler manifold possessing a complete Kähler metric. Keep $r,a,s,k,m$ as above and assume $E\geq _ m0$ and $\mathrm i\Theta (L)\geq (m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q)$. Put $H=GG^*$, $D=\det H$, and $H^{\rm adj}=\operatorname {adj}H$. For closed $(n,k)$ data satisfying \[  I=\int _ X\langle H^{\rm adj}f,f\rangle D^{-m-1-\epsilon }\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty  \] there is a closed lift with E2E00DB68AAD 6.28.10 \begin{equation}  Gh=f,\qquad \int _ X|h|^2D^{-m-\epsilon }\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq (1+m/\epsilon )I. \end{equation} Here all unmarked bundle norms use the original metrics. Proof. The case $a=0$ is trivial, with $D=1$; assume $a\geq 1$. Since $G$ is onto, $H$ is positive definite and $A=G^*H^{-1}$ satisfies $GA=I$. The map $AG$ is the orthogonal projection onto $(\ker G)^\perp $: it is self-adjoint and idempotent, has kernel $\ker G$, and is the identity on $\operatorname {Ran}G^*$. Thus $Av$ is the least-norm lift, and the quotient metric is \[  |v|_{Q'}^2=|Av|_ E^2=\langle H^{-1}v,v\rangle _ Q, \qquad \det h_{Q'}=D^{-1}\det h_ Q.  \] The cofactor identity $HH^{\rm adj}=DI$ gives $H^{-1}=D^{-1}H^{\rm adj}$. These expressions are frame-invariant: the endomorphism transforms by conjugacy and its determinant is a global positive scalar. The determinant metric identity gives \[  \mathrm i\Theta (\det Q')=\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q)+\mathcal H(\log D).  \] Replace $h_ L$ by $h_{L'}=h_ LD^{-m-\epsilon }$. Its curvature is $\mathrm i\Theta (L)+(m+\epsilon )\mathcal H(\log D)$, so it dominates $(m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q')$. Apply theorem 6.28.4 to $(Q',L')$. Its datum norm is exactly $I$ and its lift norm is the left side of ( 6.28.10 ). No inverse or fractional power is asserted at a singular matrix in this step. $\square$ Lemma 6.28.11 . 8746D0F80187 Let $(X,\omega )$ have a smooth PSH exhaustion $\rho \geq 0$, and let $\sigma $ be a holomorphic section of a smooth Hermitian bundle whose zero set $Y$ is nowhere dense. For each $c>0$, the open manifold $\{ \rho <c\} \setminus Y$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Alternatively, without an exhaustion, if $\omega $ is complete and the bundle curvature satisfies $R_ V\leq C\omega \otimes I$, $C\geq 0$, globally in the Griffiths sense, then $X\setminus Y$ has a complete Kähler metric. Proof. On the compact set $\{ \rho \leq c\} $ the bundle curvature is bounded. On its complement of $Y$, the Chern-normal-frame differentiation formula \[  \mathcal H(\log |\sigma |^2)(\xi ,\bar\xi ) =\frac{|D'_\xi \sigma |^2}{|\sigma |^2} -\frac{|\langle D'_\xi \sigma ,\sigma \rangle |^2}{|\sigma |^4} -\frac{\langle R_ V(\xi ,\bar\xi )\sigma ,\sigma \rangle }{|\sigma |^2}  \] shows $\mathcal H(\log |\sigma |^2)\geq -C\omega $ there: the first two terms are nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz. Subtract a constant to obtain $\tau =\log |\sigma |^2-A\leq -2$ and choose $a=1/(C+1)$. Set \[  r=-a\log (-\tau ),\qquad b=-\log (c-\rho ),\qquad \gamma =\omega +\mathcal H(r)+\mathcal H(b).  \] The chain rule gives \[  \mathcal H(r)\geq -\tfrac 12\omega + a^{-1}\mathrm i\partial r\wedge \bar\partial r, \qquad \mathcal H(b)\geq \mathrm i\partial b\wedge \bar\partial b.  \] Thus $\gamma $ is Kähler and the gradient of $F=-r+b$ is bounded for $\gamma $. The function $F$ is bounded below. Its closed sublevels are compact in the indicated open manifold: $r$ is bounded above and $b$ below, so a bound on their sum bounds $b$ above and $r$ below. It forces $\rho $ away from $c$ and $|\sigma |$ away from zero on the compact ambient sublevel. The bounded-gradient exhaustion criterion corollary 6.26.3 proves completeness. This construction uses only curvature bounds on this compact set. For the alternative assertion keep $\tau =\log |\sigma |^2$, now possibly unbounded above. Set $a=1/(2\pi (C+1))$ and choose $\chi '(t)=a(\arctan t+\pi /2)$, so $0<\chi '\leq 1/(2(C+1))$ and $\chi ''=a/(1+t^2)$. Then \[  \gamma =\omega +\mathcal H(\chi (\tau )) \geq \tfrac 12\omega + \mathrm i\partial (\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau ) \wedge \bar\partial (\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau ).  \] A $\gamma $-Cauchy sequence converges for the complete $\omega $. The bounded-gradient function $\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau $ has Cauchy values, so its limit cannot lie in $Y$, where it tends to $-\infty $. Local smooth metric equivalence at the limit proves $\gamma $ convergence and completeness. $\square$ Lemma 6.28.12 . 52E74CE23DF6 Let $Y$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset of a complex manifold. If $v$ is a locally $L^2$ bundle-valued form and $w$ is a locally $L^1$ form of the next barred degree, and $D''v=w$ distributionally off $Y$, then the equation holds everywhere. In particular a locally $L^2$ form closed off $Y$ is closed everywhere. Proof. First work near a regular point of $Y$, with coordinates in which $Y=\{ z_1=\cdots =z_ d=0\} $ and $d\geq 1$. Its regular part is contained in the coordinate hypersurface $z_1=0$. Take a cutoff $\lambda _ t$ which vanishes for $|z_1|\leq t$, equals one for $|z_1|\geq 2t$, and has derivative at most $C/t$. On a fixed compact polydisc, $\| \mathrm d\lambda _ t\| _2\leq C'$ because the transition tube has volume $O(t^2)$. Testing the equation away from $z_1=0$ with $\lambda _ t$ times a compact test form, the error is bounded by $C'\| v\| _{L^2(\{ |z_1|\leq 2t\} )}$ and tends to zero. The other terms, including the $L^1$ pairing with $w$, converge by dominated convergence. This proves removability near the regular locus. Smooth metrics and bundle coefficients change these compact estimates by fixed constants. Apply this argument successively to the finite singular-locus filtration of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . First it extends the equation through $Y_{\rm reg}$, leaving only $Y_{\rm sing}$; repeat with its regular part. Dimension drops strictly, so the process terminates. Analytic sets here have measure zero, by that corollary or measure-zero holomorphic zero sets ; hence choices of coefficients on $Y$ do not affect the form or the equation. $\square$ Theorem 6.28.13 . A729272B8D69 The conclusion of theorem 6.28.9 remains true for a generically surjective holomorphic $G:E\to Q$ if $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion. Its integral hypotheses and estimate are taken over $U=X\setminus Y$, where $Y$ is the rank-deficient analytic set. The datum is assumed locally $L^2$ and closed on $X$. Proof. For $a\geq 1$ take $\sigma =\bigwedge ^ aG\in \mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(\bigwedge ^ aE,\det Q))$. Then $Y=\{ \sigma =0\} $ is analytic and nowhere dense on each component by hypothesis. On $U$, the kernel is a holomorphic bundle: where $G=(G_0,G_1)$ has an invertible $a$-minor, its kernel frame is $w\mapsto (-G_0^{-1}G_1w,w)$. The adjugate matrix is defined polynomially even on $Y$. It is positive semidefinite there: diagonalize $H$ unitarily, when its adjugate eigenvalues are the products of all but one nonnegative eigenvalue. For $a=1$ the empty product gives $H^{\rm adj}=1$. Only on $U$ do we use $H^{-1}$ and negative powers of $D$. Choose $c_ j\uparrow \infty $. The preceding completeness lemma gives complete Kähler metrics on $U_ j=\{ \rho <c_ j\} \setminus Y$. The arbitrary-metric theorem, with the restricted original metric $\omega $, produces closed lifts $h_ j$ with uniform weighted norm at most $(1+m/\epsilon )I$. On every compact subset of $U$ this weight is fixed, smooth and positive, so diagonal weak limits give a closed lift $h$ on $U$. Fixed weighted weak lower semicontinuity on compact sets and exhaustion preserve the displayed integral bound. On a compact subset of $X$, the smooth $D$ is bounded above. Since $m+\epsilon >0$, $D^{-m-\epsilon }$ is bounded below on $U$ there. Consequently $h$ extends as an $L^2_{\rm loc}$ form across the null set $Y$. The preceding removal lemma gives $D''h=0$ on $X$. The identity $Gh=f$ holds almost everywhere and hence as distributions on $X$. The same estimates hold because $Y$ is null. This proof does not assert smoothness of a positive-degree lift across the rank locus. $\square$ Corollary 6.28.14 . CC5F6C2B80CC Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ possess a complete Kähler metric, let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$ be holomorphic, $r\geq 1$, and let $\phi $ be smooth PSH. Suppose $g$ is not identically zero on any component. Put $m=\min (n,r-1)$, $Z=\{ g=0\} $ and $\epsilon >0$. For holomorphic $f$ such that \[  I=\int _{\Omega \setminus Z}|f|^2|g|^{-2(m+1+\epsilon )} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty ,  \] there exist holomorphic $h_1,\ldots ,h_ r$ on $\Omega $ with 3CE759FE5C62 6.28.15 \begin{equation}  f=\sum _ jg_ jh_ j,\qquad \int _{\Omega \setminus Z}|h|^2|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV \leq (1+m/\epsilon )I. \end{equation} Here $\mathrm dV$ may be Lebesgue measure; the same constant occurs on both sides. Proof. The open manifold $U=\Omega \setminus Z$ possesses a complete Kähler metric even without a PSH exhaustion of $\Omega $. Indeed $\tau =\log |g|^2$ is smooth PSH on $U$. Choose $\chi '(t)=\arctan t+\pi /2>0$ and $\chi ''(t)=(1+t^2)^{-1}$. Then $\gamma =\widehat\omega +\mathcal H(\chi (\tau ))$ is Kähler, dominates the given complete metric, and dominates $\mathrm i\partial \operatorname {arsinh}\tau \wedge \bar\partial \operatorname {arsinh}\tau $. A $\gamma $-Cauchy sequence converges for $\widehat\omega $ to a point of $\Omega $. Its values of $\operatorname {arsinh}\tau $ are Cauchy by the gradient bound; thus its limit cannot lie in $Z$, where $\tau \to -\infty $. At a point of $U$ smooth local metric equivalence gives convergence for $\gamma $. This proves completeness. Apply theorem 6.28.9 on $U$ to the flat trivial bundles $E=\mathcal O^ r$, $Q=\mathcal O$, $G=g$, and $L$ with metric $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$, taking $k=0$ and the Euclidean original metric. Here $H=D=|g|^2$ and $H^{\rm adj}=1$. Identify functions with their multiples of the global holomorphic top form; its norm times metric volume is a common constant times Lebesgue measure, which cancels in the estimate. The lift is closed in degree $(n,0)$, so its coefficients are holomorphic on $U$ by holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions . The weight in the lift integral is bounded below on each compact set, since $|g|$ and $\phi $ are locally bounded above. Thus $h$ is locally $L^2$ across $Z$. Apply lemma 6.28.12 and the same holomorphy lemma to extend it holomorphically. The identity extends as well. When $r=1$, $m=0$, the argument is simply $h=f/g$ on $U$, followed by this same $L^2$ extension; no division by $m$ occurs. $\square$ Corollary 6.28.16 . C5757B16FD09 The same scalar conclusion holds for any PSH weight $\phi $ on a pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, with its usual upper-semicontinuous representative, provided $\phi \not\equiv -\infty $ on each component. Proof. Use the increasing relatively compact pseudoconvex exhaustion domains and radial regularizations from theorem 6.25.10 . They give $\Omega _ j\uparrow \Omega $ and smooth PSH $\phi _ j\downarrow \phi $ on every fixed $\Omega _ k$ for $j\geq k$, with $\phi _ j\geq \phi $. Each $\Omega _ j$ admits a complete Kähler metric by its smooth PSH exhaustion and lemma 6.26.8 . The preceding smooth-weight result gives holomorphic lifts $h_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with squared weighted norm at most $(1+m/\epsilon )I$. The input bound holds since $\mathrm e^{-\phi _ j}\leq \mathrm e^{-\phi }$. On a fixed compact subset, $|g|$ is bounded above and the $\phi _ j$ are bounded above by one fixed smooth approximant. The weighted bounds therefore give local ordinary $L^2$ bounds even across $Z$. Take a diagonal weak limit $h$, which is holomorphic distributionally and hence holomorphic. Multiplication by $g$ preserves local weak convergence, giving $g\cdot h=f$. On a fixed $\Omega _ k\setminus Z$, use the fixed weight $|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )}\mathrm e^{-\phi _ k}$, first on compact sets. For $j\geq k$ its integral is bounded by the corresponding $\phi _ j$ integral. Weak lower semicontinuity and exhaustion give the same bound for $h$. Now let $k\to \infty $ with the regularization indices fixed before each weak limit; monotone convergence of the weights gives ( 6.28.15 ) with $\phi $. Zero and infinite values of the weight are interpreted by this monotone limit. No smooth approximation on an arbitrary nonpseudoconvex complete Kähler open set is asserted here. $\square$

Convolution is bounded on $H^{-1}$, so $PJ_ tv$ is uniformly bounded there. Apply this to $J_ tv$, using $H^{-1}$–$H^1$ duality, to obtain a uniform $H^1$ bound. Weak compactness and $J_ tv\to v$ in $L^2$ show that $v\in H^1$. Thus $w\in H^1_{\rm loc}$. The checked vector divergence-form interior theorem interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form , successively applied to $Pw=0$ on nested balls, now gives every Sobolev order and smoothness. This argument supplies the $H^1$ starting hypothesis of that theorem. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.28.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Theorem 6.28.2 . E15FB3F8A946 Let $(X,\omega )$ be complete Kähler, let $(E,h)$ be a smooth Hermitian holomorphic bundle, and let $1\leq q\leq n$. Fix $0\leq p\leq n$. Suppose $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (E),\Lambda _\omega ]\geq 0$ in bidegree $(p,q)$. If $F$ is locally $L^2$, is closed distributionally, and has finite inverse energy $M=\int _ X|F|_{B^{-1}}^2\, \mathrm dV_\omega $, then 48191F980D4B 6.28.3 \begin{equation}  D''u=F,\qquad \| u\| _2^2\leq M \end{equation} for an $L^2$ form $u$ of type $(p,q-1)$. Global ordinary $L^2$ integrability of $F$ is not required. If $X$ merely possesses a complete Kähler metric and $\omega $ is any Kähler metric, the same conclusion holds in degree $(n,q)$ provided $E$ is $m$-semipositive with $m\geq \min (n-q+1,\operatorname {rank}E)$. The norm and inverse energy in this conclusion use the original $\omega $. Smooth data admit a smooth choice in either assertion. Proof. For compactly supported smooth $v$, curvature Cauchy–Schwarz and theorem 10.33.2 give \[  |\langle F,v\rangle |^2 \leq M\int _ X\langle Bv,v\rangle \, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq M\bigl (\| \delta ''v\| _2^2+\| D''v\| _2^2\bigr ).  \] Define $Av=(\delta ''v,D''v)$ in the direct sum of degrees $(p,q-1)$ and $(p,q+1)$. The displayed bound makes pairing with $F$ a well-defined bounded functional on $\operatorname {Ran}A$. Hilbert representation on its closure gives $(u,w)$ in that closure, with $\| u\| _2^2+\| w\| _2^2\leq M$, and \[  F=D''u+\delta ''w  \] distributionally. In top barred degree the second space is zero. Otherwise $w$ is an $L^2$ limit of forms $D''v_ j$, hence $D''w=0$ distributionally. Applying $D''$ to the last identity, using $D''F=0$, gives $D''\delta ''w=0$. Thus $w$ is distributionally harmonic and is smooth by lemma 6.28.1 . Take the complete gradient cutoffs of lemma 6.26.1 . Integrating the harmonic equation against $\chi _ R^2w$ and using $D''w=0$ gives \[  \| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2^2 \leq 2\| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2\,  \|  (\bar\partial \chi _ R\wedge )^*w\| _2.  \] All integrals here have compact support; no prior global derivative bound is assumed. It follows that $\| \chi _ R\delta ''w\| _2^2\leq C R^{-2}\| w\| _2^2$. Letting $R\to \infty $ on each compact set proves $\delta ''w=0$, and establishes ( 6.28.3 ). For the original-metric assertion put $\omega _\varepsilon =\omega +\varepsilon \widehat\omega $. These metrics are complete. The full coefficient inequalities of lemma 6.27.1 show semipositivity and bound the inverse energy by $M$ for each $\omega _\varepsilon $. The first assertion applies to the locally $L^2$ datum for each of these metrics. The fixed-comparison-density weak limit in the proof of theorem 6.27.6 now applies verbatim: first take local weak limits; test the norm with fixed $\omega _{\varepsilon _ k}$ for indices $j\geq k$; then let $\varepsilon _ k\downarrow 0$ and exhaust $X$. It gives the original norm bound. This argument uses no global ordinary norm of $F$. Finally lemma 6.27.8 gives a smooth minimum-norm primitive for smooth data. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.28.4
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Theorem 6.28.4 . FD2B7A8ED856 Let $(X,\omega )$ possess a complete Kähler metric. Let $G:E\to Q$ be a surjective holomorphic bundle map, with the induced quotient metric on $Q$. Put $r=\operatorname {rank}E$, $a=\operatorname {rank}Q$, $s=r-a$, and fix $0\leq k\leq n$. Set $m=\min (n-k,s)$. Suppose $E$ is $m$-semipositive and a Hermitian line bundle $L$ satisfies \[  \mathrm i\Theta (L)\geq (m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q), \qquad \epsilon >0.  \] Every closed $L^2$ form $f$ of type $(n,k)$ with values in $Q\otimes L$ has a closed lift $h$ with values in $E\otimes L$ such that 1FDBE18C9CE0 6.28.5 \begin{equation}  Gh=f,\qquad \| h\| _2^2\leq (1+m/\epsilon )\| f\| _2^2. \end{equation} Smooth data admit a smooth lift. When $m=0$, no curvature hypothesis is needed and the constant is one. Proof. If $Q=0$ take $h=0$. If $s=0$, the inverse of $G$ is holomorphic and isometric for the quotient metric. If $k=n$, the orthogonal lift $G^*f$ is automatically closed by degree and isometric. These cases give the stated $m=0$ clause. Assume henceforth $s\geq 1$, $k<n$, so $m\geq 1$. Let $S=\ker G$ and use the orthogonal splitting $E=S\oplus Q$. The complete connection and curvature calculation of proposition 10.34.9 writes the second fundamental form as $\beta =\sum _ j\mathrm dz_ j B_ j$ and gives \[  R_ S=R_ E|_ S-C_\beta ,\qquad R_ Q=R_ E|_ Q+(B_ jB_ l^*)_{j\bar l},\qquad C_\beta (v)=\left|\sum _ jB_ jv_ j\right|^2.  \] Put $\alpha =\operatorname {tr}_ S C_\beta $. The rank-one tests contained in $m$-semipositivity give $\operatorname {tr}_ Q R_ E|_ Q\geq 0$, hence $R_{\det Q}\geq \alpha $. Moreover $m\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta \geq _ m0$ by theorem 10.34.2 , including $s=m=1$. The curvature assumption therefore gives 8CCE15D3C2B6 6.28.6 \begin{equation}  R_{S\otimes L}\geq _ m(m+\epsilon )\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta \geq _ m(\epsilon /m)C_\beta . \end{equation} The last difference is $(1+\epsilon /m)(m\alpha \otimes I_ S-C_\beta )$. In degree $(n,k+1)$ the coefficient tensors $(v_{jJ})_ j$ have rank at most $\min (n-k,s)=m$, by proposition 10.33.6 . If $B=[\mathrm i\Theta (S\otimes L),\Lambda _\omega ]$, then B33FBDD0925E 6.28.7 \begin{equation}  \langle Bv,v\rangle \geq (\epsilon /m) \sum _{|J|=k}\left|\sum _ j B_ jv_{jJ}\right|^2, \qquad |\beta ^*\wedge f|_{B^{-1}}^2\leq (m/\epsilon )|f|^2. \end{equation} Indeed the adjoint of $f\mapsto \beta ^*\wedge f$ is contraction with coefficients $\sum _ jB_ jv_{jJ}$, with the common top-form sign cancelled in its squared norm. Pairing with $f$ and applying finite-dimensional Cauchy–Schwarz proves the second inequality, also on a kernel of $B$. Write $j:S\to E$ for inclusion. The $(0,1)$ connection block gives $D''(G^*f)=-j(\beta ^*\wedge f)$. Thus $F=\beta ^*\wedge f$ is locally $L^2$ and closed distributionally: apply $(D'')^2=0$ and use that $j$ is holomorphic and injective. It need not be globally $L^2$. Its finite inverse energy is bounded by $(m/\epsilon )\| f\| _2^2$ by ( 6.28.7 ). The original-metric part of theorem 6.28.2 supplies $D''u=F$ with that squared norm bound. Set $h=G^*f+ju$. Then $Gh=f$, $D''h=0$, and orthogonality gives pointwise $|h|^2=|f|^2+|u|^2$. This proves ( 6.28.5 ). If $f$ is smooth, choose the smooth primitive supplied by the same theorem. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.28.8
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Corollary 6.28.8 . 2F176031B9F6 Under the bundle and curvature hypotheses of theorem 6.28.4 , if $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion, the induced map \[  H^ k(X,K_ X\otimes \mathcal O(E\otimes L))\longrightarrow H^ k(X,K_ X\otimes \mathcal O(Q\otimes L))  \] is surjective. Proof. Use the smooth bundle-valued Dolbeault resolution in corollary 10.43.11 and represent a class by a smooth closed $(n,k)$-form $f$. Shift the exhaustion $\rho $ to be nonnegative. The compact-band convex weight construction ( 6.26.9 ) gives increasing convex $\chi $ for which $f$ is $L^2$ after replacing the metric of $L$ by $h_ L\mathrm e^{-\chi (\rho )}$. Its added curvature is semipositive, so all lifting inequalities persist. A complete Kähler metric exists by lemma 6.26.8 . The preceding theorem gives a smooth closed lift, representing a preimage of the given class. This proves surjectivity, without any assertion that the entire next kernel-bundle cohomology group vanishes. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.28.9
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Theorem 6.28.9 . A32EC1620046 Let $G:E\to Q$ be surjective, now with an arbitrary smooth metric on $Q$, on a Kähler manifold possessing a complete Kähler metric. Keep $r,a,s,k,m$ as above and assume $E\geq _ m0$ and $\mathrm i\Theta (L)\geq (m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q)$. Put $H=GG^*$, $D=\det H$, and $H^{\rm adj}=\operatorname {adj}H$. For closed $(n,k)$ data satisfying \[  I=\int _ X\langle H^{\rm adj}f,f\rangle D^{-m-1-\epsilon }\, \mathrm dV_\omega <\infty  \] there is a closed lift with E2E00DB68AAD 6.28.10 \begin{equation}  Gh=f,\qquad \int _ X|h|^2D^{-m-\epsilon }\, \mathrm dV_\omega \leq (1+m/\epsilon )I. \end{equation} Here all unmarked bundle norms use the original metrics. Proof. The case $a=0$ is trivial, with $D=1$; assume $a\geq 1$. Since $G$ is onto, $H$ is positive definite and $A=G^*H^{-1}$ satisfies $GA=I$. The map $AG$ is the orthogonal projection onto $(\ker G)^\perp $: it is self-adjoint and idempotent, has kernel $\ker G$, and is the identity on $\operatorname {Ran}G^*$. Thus $Av$ is the least-norm lift, and the quotient metric is \[  |v|_{Q'}^2=|Av|_ E^2=\langle H^{-1}v,v\rangle _ Q, \qquad \det h_{Q'}=D^{-1}\det h_ Q.  \] The cofactor identity $HH^{\rm adj}=DI$ gives $H^{-1}=D^{-1}H^{\rm adj}$. These expressions are frame-invariant: the endomorphism transforms by conjugacy and its determinant is a global positive scalar. The determinant metric identity gives \[  \mathrm i\Theta (\det Q')=\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q)+\mathcal H(\log D).  \] Replace $h_ L$ by $h_{L'}=h_ LD^{-m-\epsilon }$. Its curvature is $\mathrm i\Theta (L)+(m+\epsilon )\mathcal H(\log D)$, so it dominates $(m+\epsilon )\mathrm i\Theta (\det Q')$. Apply theorem 6.28.4 to $(Q',L')$. Its datum norm is exactly $I$ and its lift norm is the left side of ( 6.28.10 ). No inverse or fractional power is asserted at a singular matrix in this step. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.28.11
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Lemma 6.28.11 . 8746D0F80187 Let $(X,\omega )$ have a smooth PSH exhaustion $\rho \geq 0$, and let $\sigma $ be a holomorphic section of a smooth Hermitian bundle whose zero set $Y$ is nowhere dense. For each $c>0$, the open manifold $\{ \rho <c\} \setminus Y$ admits a complete Kähler metric. Alternatively, without an exhaustion, if $\omega $ is complete and the bundle curvature satisfies $R_ V\leq C\omega \otimes I$, $C\geq 0$, globally in the Griffiths sense, then $X\setminus Y$ has a complete Kähler metric. Proof. On the compact set $\{ \rho \leq c\} $ the bundle curvature is bounded. On its complement of $Y$, the Chern-normal-frame differentiation formula \[  \mathcal H(\log |\sigma |^2)(\xi ,\bar\xi ) =\frac{|D'_\xi \sigma |^2}{|\sigma |^2} -\frac{|\langle D'_\xi \sigma ,\sigma \rangle |^2}{|\sigma |^4} -\frac{\langle R_ V(\xi ,\bar\xi )\sigma ,\sigma \rangle }{|\sigma |^2}  \] shows $\mathcal H(\log |\sigma |^2)\geq -C\omega $ there: the first two terms are nonnegative by Cauchy–Schwarz. Subtract a constant to obtain $\tau =\log |\sigma |^2-A\leq -2$ and choose $a=1/(C+1)$. Set \[  r=-a\log (-\tau ),\qquad b=-\log (c-\rho ),\qquad \gamma =\omega +\mathcal H(r)+\mathcal H(b).  \] The chain rule gives \[  \mathcal H(r)\geq -\tfrac 12\omega + a^{-1}\mathrm i\partial r\wedge \bar\partial r, \qquad \mathcal H(b)\geq \mathrm i\partial b\wedge \bar\partial b.  \] Thus $\gamma $ is Kähler and the gradient of $F=-r+b$ is bounded for $\gamma $. The function $F$ is bounded below. Its closed sublevels are compact in the indicated open manifold: $r$ is bounded above and $b$ below, so a bound on their sum bounds $b$ above and $r$ below. It forces $\rho $ away from $c$ and $|\sigma |$ away from zero on the compact ambient sublevel. The bounded-gradient exhaustion criterion corollary 6.26.3 proves completeness. This construction uses only curvature bounds on this compact set. For the alternative assertion keep $\tau =\log |\sigma |^2$, now possibly unbounded above. Set $a=1/(2\pi (C+1))$ and choose $\chi '(t)=a(\arctan t+\pi /2)$, so $0<\chi '\leq 1/(2(C+1))$ and $\chi ''=a/(1+t^2)$. Then \[  \gamma =\omega +\mathcal H(\chi (\tau )) \geq \tfrac 12\omega + \mathrm i\partial (\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau ) \wedge \bar\partial (\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau ).  \] A $\gamma $-Cauchy sequence converges for the complete $\omega $. The bounded-gradient function $\sqrt a\operatorname {arsinh}\tau $ has Cauchy values, so its limit cannot lie in $Y$, where it tends to $-\infty $. Local smooth metric equivalence at the limit proves $\gamma $ convergence and completeness. $\square$

title: Lemma 6.28.12
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Lemma 6.28.12 . 52E74CE23DF6 Let $Y$ be a nowhere dense analytic subset of a complex manifold. If $v$ is a locally $L^2$ bundle-valued form and $w$ is a locally $L^1$ form of the next barred degree, and $D''v=w$ distributionally off $Y$, then the equation holds everywhere. In particular a locally $L^2$ form closed off $Y$ is closed everywhere. Proof. First work near a regular point of $Y$, with coordinates in which $Y=\{ z_1=\cdots =z_ d=0\} $ and $d\geq 1$. Its regular part is contained in the coordinate hypersurface $z_1=0$. Take a cutoff $\lambda _ t$ which vanishes for $|z_1|\leq t$, equals one for $|z_1|\geq 2t$, and has derivative at most $C/t$. On a fixed compact polydisc, $\| \mathrm d\lambda _ t\| _2\leq C'$ because the transition tube has volume $O(t^2)$. Testing the equation away from $z_1=0$ with $\lambda _ t$ times a compact test form, the error is bounded by $C'\| v\| _{L^2(\{ |z_1|\leq 2t\} )}$ and tends to zero. The other terms, including the $L^1$ pairing with $w$, converge by dominated convergence. This proves removability near the regular locus. Smooth metrics and bundle coefficients change these compact estimates by fixed constants. Apply this argument successively to the finite singular-locus filtration of analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . First it extends the equation through $Y_{\rm reg}$, leaving only $Y_{\rm sing}$; repeat with its regular part. Dimension drops strictly, so the process terminates. Analytic sets here have measure zero, by that corollary or measure-zero holomorphic zero sets ; hence choices of coefficients on $Y$ do not affect the form or the equation. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.28.13
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Theorem 6.28.13 . A729272B8D69 The conclusion of theorem 6.28.9 remains true for a generically surjective holomorphic $G:E\to Q$ if $X$ has a smooth PSH exhaustion. Its integral hypotheses and estimate are taken over $U=X\setminus Y$, where $Y$ is the rank-deficient analytic set. The datum is assumed locally $L^2$ and closed on $X$. Proof. For $a\geq 1$ take $\sigma =\bigwedge ^ aG\in \mathcal O(\operatorname {Hom}(\bigwedge ^ aE,\det Q))$. Then $Y=\{ \sigma =0\} $ is analytic and nowhere dense on each component by hypothesis. On $U$, the kernel is a holomorphic bundle: where $G=(G_0,G_1)$ has an invertible $a$-minor, its kernel frame is $w\mapsto (-G_0^{-1}G_1w,w)$. The adjugate matrix is defined polynomially even on $Y$. It is positive semidefinite there: diagonalize $H$ unitarily, when its adjugate eigenvalues are the products of all but one nonnegative eigenvalue. For $a=1$ the empty product gives $H^{\rm adj}=1$. Only on $U$ do we use $H^{-1}$ and negative powers of $D$. Choose $c_ j\uparrow \infty $. The preceding completeness lemma gives complete Kähler metrics on $U_ j=\{ \rho <c_ j\} \setminus Y$. The arbitrary-metric theorem, with the restricted original metric $\omega $, produces closed lifts $h_ j$ with uniform weighted norm at most $(1+m/\epsilon )I$. On every compact subset of $U$ this weight is fixed, smooth and positive, so diagonal weak limits give a closed lift $h$ on $U$. Fixed weighted weak lower semicontinuity on compact sets and exhaustion preserve the displayed integral bound. On a compact subset of $X$, the smooth $D$ is bounded above. Since $m+\epsilon >0$, $D^{-m-\epsilon }$ is bounded below on $U$ there. Consequently $h$ extends as an $L^2_{\rm loc}$ form across the null set $Y$. The preceding removal lemma gives $D''h=0$ on $X$. The identity $Gh=f$ holds almost everywhere and hence as distributions on $X$. The same estimates hold because $Y$ is null. This proof does not assert smoothness of a positive-degree lift across the rank locus. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.28.14
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Corollary 6.28.14 . CC5F6C2B80CC Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$ possess a complete Kähler metric, let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$ be holomorphic, $r\geq 1$, and let $\phi $ be smooth PSH. Suppose $g$ is not identically zero on any component. Put $m=\min (n,r-1)$, $Z=\{ g=0\} $ and $\epsilon >0$. For holomorphic $f$ such that \[  I=\int _{\Omega \setminus Z}|f|^2|g|^{-2(m+1+\epsilon )} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty ,  \] there exist holomorphic $h_1,\ldots ,h_ r$ on $\Omega $ with 3CE759FE5C62 6.28.15 \begin{equation}  f=\sum _ jg_ jh_ j,\qquad \int _{\Omega \setminus Z}|h|^2|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV \leq (1+m/\epsilon )I. \end{equation} Here $\mathrm dV$ may be Lebesgue measure; the same constant occurs on both sides. Proof. The open manifold $U=\Omega \setminus Z$ possesses a complete Kähler metric even without a PSH exhaustion of $\Omega $. Indeed $\tau =\log |g|^2$ is smooth PSH on $U$. Choose $\chi '(t)=\arctan t+\pi /2>0$ and $\chi ''(t)=(1+t^2)^{-1}$. Then $\gamma =\widehat\omega +\mathcal H(\chi (\tau ))$ is Kähler, dominates the given complete metric, and dominates $\mathrm i\partial \operatorname {arsinh}\tau \wedge \bar\partial \operatorname {arsinh}\tau $. A $\gamma $-Cauchy sequence converges for $\widehat\omega $ to a point of $\Omega $. Its values of $\operatorname {arsinh}\tau $ are Cauchy by the gradient bound; thus its limit cannot lie in $Z$, where $\tau \to -\infty $. At a point of $U$ smooth local metric equivalence gives convergence for $\gamma $. This proves completeness. Apply theorem 6.28.9 on $U$ to the flat trivial bundles $E=\mathcal O^ r$, $Q=\mathcal O$, $G=g$, and $L$ with metric $\mathrm e^{-\phi }$, taking $k=0$ and the Euclidean original metric. Here $H=D=|g|^2$ and $H^{\rm adj}=1$. Identify functions with their multiples of the global holomorphic top form; its norm times metric volume is a common constant times Lebesgue measure, which cancels in the estimate. The lift is closed in degree $(n,0)$, so its coefficients are holomorphic on $U$ by holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions . The weight in the lift integral is bounded below on each compact set, since $|g|$ and $\phi $ are locally bounded above. Thus $h$ is locally $L^2$ across $Z$. Apply lemma 6.28.12 and the same holomorphy lemma to extend it holomorphically. The identity extends as well. When $r=1$, $m=0$, the argument is simply $h=f/g$ on $U$, followed by this same $L^2$ extension; no division by $m$ occurs. $\square$

title: Corollary 6.28.16
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.28 Holomorphic lifting and division estimates
text: Corollary 6.28.16 . C5757B16FD09 The same scalar conclusion holds for any PSH weight $\phi $ on a pseudoconvex open set $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, with its usual upper-semicontinuous representative, provided $\phi \not\equiv -\infty $ on each component. Proof. Use the increasing relatively compact pseudoconvex exhaustion domains and radial regularizations from theorem 6.25.10 . They give $\Omega _ j\uparrow \Omega $ and smooth PSH $\phi _ j\downarrow \phi $ on every fixed $\Omega _ k$ for $j\geq k$, with $\phi _ j\geq \phi $. Each $\Omega _ j$ admits a complete Kähler metric by its smooth PSH exhaustion and lemma 6.26.8 . The preceding smooth-weight result gives holomorphic lifts $h_ j$ on $\Omega _ j$ with squared weighted norm at most $(1+m/\epsilon )I$. The input bound holds since $\mathrm e^{-\phi _ j}\leq \mathrm e^{-\phi }$. On a fixed compact subset, $|g|$ is bounded above and the $\phi _ j$ are bounded above by one fixed smooth approximant. The weighted bounds therefore give local ordinary $L^2$ bounds even across $Z$. Take a diagonal weak limit $h$, which is holomorphic distributionally and hence holomorphic. Multiplication by $g$ preserves local weak convergence, giving $g\cdot h=f$. On a fixed $\Omega _ k\setminus Z$, use the fixed weight $|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )}\mathrm e^{-\phi _ k}$, first on compact sets. For $j\geq k$ its integral is bounded by the corresponding $\phi _ j$ integral. Weak lower semicontinuity and exhaustion give the same bound for $h$. Now let $k\to \infty $ with the regularization indices fixed before each weak limit; monotone convergence of the weights gives ( 6.28.15 ) with $\phi $. Zero and infinite values of the weight are interpreted by this monotone limit. No smooth approximation on an arbitrary nonpseudoconvex complete Kähler open set is asserted here. $\square$

title: 9.41 Completed tensors, gluing and cohomology
section: 9.41 Completed tensors, gluing and cohomology
text: The functional-analytic spaces and maps are complex, Hausdorff and locally convex unless a quotient cohomology topology is explicitly allowed to be non-Hausdorff. We use the tensor seminorms and complete nuclear Fréchet theory of section 2.13 . In particular, completed tensoring a strict short exact sequence of Fréchet spaces is strictly exact when its middle space or the fixed other factor is nuclear. Nuclear Fréchet spaces have equal projective and injective completed tensor topologies; we write $\widehat\otimes $ in that case. The open mapping and cohomological openness assertions are those proved in proposition 2.12.1 , theorem 2.12.5 . Lemma 9.41.1 . 8B7B03395780 For complete Fréchet spaces the following hold. Product functionals separate points of $E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon F$. For $\xi \in E'$, contraction $c_\xi :E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon F\to F$ is continuous. If $j:F\to G$ is a continuous injection, then $\mathrm{Id}\widehat\otimes j$ is injective for the injective completed tensor topologies; $j(F)$ need not be closed. There is a natural topological isomorphism \[  E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon \prod _{a\geq 0}F_ a \simeq \prod _{a\geq 0} (E\widehat\otimes _\varepsilon F_ a).  \] If $E$ is nuclear this is also the completed projective tensor isomorphism. Finite direct sums are included. If $H$ is nuclear and $u:E\to G$ is any continuous map, 9AB3D9A1E143 9.41.2 \begin{equation}  \ker (\mathrm{Id}_ H\widehat\otimes u) =H\widehat\otimes \ker u \end{equation} as closed topological subspaces of $H\widehat\otimes E$. No closed-image hypothesis on $u$ is needed. Proof. On algebraic tensors, dominated functional extension gives 8C479FD0F455 9.41.3 \begin{equation}  \varepsilon _{p,q}(t) =\sup _{|\xi |\leq p}q(c_\xi t). \end{equation} The equality is just the seminorm norming formula $q(y)=\sup _{|\eta |\leq q}|\eta (y)|$ applied after contraction. It gives contraction continuity. Both this formula and the definition as a supremum of product tests remain valid on the completion: an algebraic Cauchy sequence converges uniformly over each indicated test family. Thus vanishing of all product tests implies that every completed injective seminorm vanishes, which implies the tensor is zero. If $(\mathrm{Id}\widehat\otimes j)t=0$, contraction gives $j(c_\xi t)=0$ for every $\xi $; injectivity of $j$ and the separation just proved give $t=0$. A defining seminorm on a product has the form $q(y)=\max _{a\in I}q_ a(y_ a)$ for finite $I$. Formula ( 9.41.3 ) gives exactly \[  \varepsilon _{p,q}(t) =\max _{a\in I}\varepsilon _{p,q_ a}(t_ a).  \] Hence the algebraic coordinate map is a topological embedding for the induced tensor topology. Its image is dense in the product of completions: approximate finitely many specified coordinates by algebraic tensors and insert each tensor vector into its single coordinate of $\prod F_ a$. section: 9.42 Coherent analytic applications and their analytic inputs
text: Here is the precise reduction from coherent analytic geometry to the preceding functional analysis. It retains arbitrary coherent sheaves and nonreduced analytic spaces in the analytic input category. For such a category, the required analytic section theorems are the following. Section spaces of coherent sheaves have Hausdorff Fréchet topologies, with continuous restrictions and the topological gluing property used in corollary 9.41.4 . Every coherent sheaf admits a countable cover by patches $U$ embedded in polydiscs $D$, with finite presentations whose sections give continuous exact sequences DDFEC4904A07 9.42.1 \begin{equation}  \mathcal O(D)^ r\longrightarrow \mathcal O(D)^ s \longrightarrow \mathcal F(U)\longrightarrow 0. \end{equation} Overlaps can be covered by countably many such patches. Analytic external products are right exact, and these presentations remain exact on sections after external product with a polydisc, and then after a presentation in the other variable. These are the local presentation, analytic external-product and Cartan section-exactness inputs. Countable covers used for cohomology have acyclic finite intersections and admit common countable acyclic refinements. The product rectangles needed below are acyclic for the external product. The canonical comparison with sheaf cohomology is the acyclic-cover theorem 10.43.16 . For the relative statement, $R^ q\pi _*$ is the sheafification of $U\mapsto H^ q(U\times Y,\mathcal S)$. For the relative statement, the global coherent Cartan vanishing theorem has been established on Stein spaces in the analytic category. The chosen finite intersections $V_ J$ are Stein, as are the products $X\times V_ J$ for Stein $X$. In particular their higher coherent cohomology vanishes, so $(X\times V_ b)$ is an acyclic cover for $\mathcal F\boxtimes \mathcal G$. A Stein basis of $X$ has these same properties for the sheafification argument. These inputs require their analytic proofs in the stated category. The following conclusions are conditional on these explicit inputs; the functional arguments supply the tensor, nonclosed gluing-image and completion steps in full. Proposition 9.42.2 . 7BF5CAEB536D Under the first two analytic inputs, all coherent section spaces are nuclear, and external products give natural topological isomorphisms \[  \mathcal F(X)\widehat\otimes \mathcal G(Y) \simeq (\mathcal F\boxtimes \mathcal G)(X\times Y).  \] Proof. In ( 9.42.1 ), the last map is a continuous surjection onto a Hausdorff Fréchet space. Its kernel is closed, and open mapping identifies its quotient topology with the stated topology of $\mathcal F(U)$. Nuclearity of $\mathcal O(D)^ s$ and closed quotient permanence give local nuclearity. Global sections are a closed gluing kernel in a countable product of these local nuclear spaces, hence nuclear. The tensor of the section presentation with $\mathcal O(D')$ is right exact: factor its first map through the closed kernel of its last surjection and apply strict tensor exactness to the resulting two short exact sequences. Their first two terms are identified by the polydisc case, so their quotient terms are canonically topologically isomorphic. Now present $\mathcal G$ on $V\subset D'$. For a sheaf $\mathcal S$ on $X\times Y$, suppose every $U_ I\times V_ J$ is acyclic. Use the Godement resolution $\mathcal I^\bullet $ of $\mathcal S$ and the triple array \[  \prod _{I,J}\mathcal I^ r(U_ I\times V_ J),\qquad D=\delta _ X+(-1)^ p\delta _ Y+(-1)^{p+q}d_{\mathcal I}.  \] For fixed $p,q$ its augmented $r$-column is exact by the assumed rectangle acyclicity. Applying finite comparison successively in these directions identifies the triple total with both $\operatorname {Tot}C$ and $\mathcal I^\bullet (X\times Y)$. Each total degree has finitely many triples, so these are the actual direct-sum totalizations covered by that lemma. This comparison is topological whenever the section spaces are Fréchet with continuous restrictions and sheaf cohomology carries its acyclic-Čech quotient topology. In the omission formula, the terms with an omission strictly to either side of the shared index $p$ give $A\delta _ X$ and $(-1)^ pA\delta _ Y$; the two terms at the shared index cancel between consecutive $p$. This proves $\delta A=AD$. The same map on Godement terms commutes with the resolution differential and is the identity on the augmented global section complex. The preceding comparisons therefore show that it induces the canonical cohomology isomorphism. Both its source and target are Fréchet complexes, so cohomological openness makes this isomorphism topological. The same argument with a common acyclic refinement shows independence of the chosen acyclic-cover quotient topology. Corollary 9.42.4 . FAB99B827E4B Under the analytic inputs above, suppose the cohomologies of $\mathcal F$ on $X$ and of $\mathcal G$ on $Y$ are Hausdorff in every degree for their acyclic-Čech topologies. Proof. For Stein $X$, the assumed global Stein coherent vanishing applies to $X$ and to every Stein rectangle $X\times V_ J$. Thus the product cover is acyclic for the external product. Hence corollary 9.41.4 makes the assignment \[  U\longmapsto \mathcal F(U)\widehat\otimes H^ q(Y,\mathcal G)  \] a sheaf, using symmetry of the tensor factors. Its comparison with $R^ q\pi _*$ is an isomorphism on the Stein basis by the first assertion and the stipulated sheafification description. It is therefore an isomorphism of sheaves and gives the stated formula on every open set. If $H^ q(Y,\mathcal G)$ is finite dimensional, its boundary space in the Čech cycle space is closed by corollary 2.12.2 . The one-degree version of the one-factor proposition applies even if other boundary images are not closed. Its finite-dimensional tensor factor is just a finite direct sum of $\mathcal F(U)$, already a sheaf. The same basis argument gives the final assertion. $\square$

All manifolds have no boundary. Hermitian products are linear in the first variable, and the curvature is unscaled: $\alpha =\mathrm i\Theta (L,h)=2\pi c_1(L,h)$ for a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle. For a Hermitian metric $\omega $ put $B_\omega =[\alpha ,\Lambda _\omega ]$. The pointwise exterior calculation of proposition 10.33.6 , valid also for Hermitian base metrics as checked in theorem 11.48.15 , says that if $\alpha =\mathrm i\sum _ j\gamma _ j	heta _ j\wedge \overline	heta _ j$ in a unitary coframe, then its eigenvalue on a $(p,q)$ coefficient with increasing index sets $I,J$ is 6BAE998D8301 10.49.1  egin{equation}  \sum _{i\in I}\gamma _ i+\sum _{j\in J}\gamma _ j-\sum _{j=1}^ n\gamma _ j =\sum _{j\in J}\gamma _ j-\sum _{i
otin I}\gamma _ i. \end{equation} This statement is pointwise and involves no derivatives of the metric. Lemma 10.49.2 . 1E60BABDFBAE The increasingly ordered eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix satisfy \[  |\lambda _ j(A)-\lambda _ j(B)|\leq \| A-B\| _{\mathrm{op}}.  \] If $\psi \in C^\infty (\mathbb R,\mathbb R)$, the matrix $\psi [A]$ defined by unitary diagonalization is a smooth function of $A$ on the real vector space of Hermitian matrices. It is equivariant under unitary conjugation. Consequently it defines a smooth self-adjoint endomorphism for every smooth self-adjoint bundle endomorphism. Proof. For completeness a unitary eigenbasis is obtained by maximizing the Rayleigh quotient on the unit sphere: variation in every real and imaginary direction makes a maximizer an eigenvector. Its orthogonal complement is invariant; induction gives a basis. For increasingly ordered eigenvalues, \[  \lambda _ j(A)=\min _{\dim W=j}\  \max _{v\in W,\  |v|=1}\langle Av,vangle .  \] The span of the first $j$ eigenvectors gives the upper bound. Every $j$-plane intersects the span of the last $n-j+1$ eigenvectors, giving the lower bound. Rayleigh quotients change by at most $\| A-B\| _{\mathrm{op}}$, proving the asserted inequality. Fix a bound $\| A\| <R$ and let $a=R+1$. Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff in $(-\pi ,\pi )$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$, and periodically extend its product with $\psi (at)$ to a smooth function $f$ of period $2\pi $. Its Fourier coefficients $b_ l$ have arbitrarily rapid polynomial decay, by repeated integration by parts. Here the Fourier inversion needed is elementary: the kernels \[  K_ N(t)= rac1N\left|\sum _{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ijt}ight|^2  \] are nonnegative, have integral one for normalized angular measure, and have supremum at most $1/(N\sin ^2(\delta /2))$ when $\delta \leq |t|\leq \pi $. Uniform continuity therefore gives $K_ N*f	o f$ uniformly. Expanding the finite square shows these are the Cesàro means of the Fourier series. Rapid coefficient decay makes that series absolutely uniformly convergent, so the means have the same limit. Thus $f(t)=\sum _ l b_ l e^{ilt}$. By diagonalization, 1DE3560759B1 10.49.3  egin{equation}  \psi [A]=\sum _{l\in \mathbb Z}b_ l e^{ilA/a} \qquad (\| A\| <R). \end{equation} We verify all matrix derivatives of this series. The convergent matrix exponential series, or differentiation of its product, gives the Duhamel identity \[  D_ Ae^{itA}[H]=\mathrm i\int _0^ t e^{i(t-u)A}H e^{iuA}\, du.  \] Indeed subtract the two exponentials for $A+H,A$ and differentiate $e^{i(t-u)(A+H)}e^{iuA}$; the residual after replacing $A+H$ by $A$ in the first factor is bounded by $t^2\| H\| ^2/2$. Iteration gives a sum over all orders of the derivative directions, integrated on the ordered simplex of volume $|t|^ k/k!$. Since $e^{iuA}$ is unitary, the $k!$ orders give \[  \| D_ A^ k e^{itA}[H_1,\ldots ,H_ k]\|  \leq |t|^ k\prod _
u \| H_
u \| .  \] The oriented integrals for $t<0$ give the same bound. For integers $p,q\geq 0$ the two-factor integral has the full normalization $\int _0^ t(t-u)^ p u^ qdu =t^{p+q+1}p!q!/(p+q+1)!$ for $t\geq 0$; substitution $u=tv$ and integration by parts prove it. Rapid decay of $b_ l$ now gives uniform convergence of every matrix derivative in ( 10.49.3 ), proving smoothness on $\| A\| <R$, hence everywhere. The definition by spectral subspaces gives unitary equivariance even at repeated eigenvalues. Smooth local unitary frames, obtained by Gram–Schmidt, and this equivariance prove the bundle assertion. No smooth eigenframe is used. $\square$ Theorem 10.48.3 . 2CCDF84C1B3C Let $X$ be compact connected Kähler of dimension $n\geq 1$, and let $(L,h)$ have semipositive curvature. Suppose that at one point the curvature has at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues, where $1\leq s\leq n$. Then \[  H^{n,q}_{ ar\partial }(X,L)=0\qquad (s\leq q\leq n).  \] Equivalently $H^ q(X,K_ X\otimes L)=0$ in this range, with the sheaf interpretation of corollary 10.43.11 . Use the compact bundle Dolbeault Hodge theorem 10.46.6 and let $u$ be a smooth harmonic representative. By ( 10.49.1 ), $B_\omega $ is semipositive on $(n,q)$ everywhere. At the specified point any $q$ indices include at least one of the positive eigenvalues, because the null space has dimension at most $s-1$. Thus $B_\omega $ is positive definite there, and on a neighborhood by continuity. The Kähler energy identity of theorem 10.33.2 gives \[  0=\| D'u\| ^2+\| \delta 'u\| ^2 +\int _ X\langle B_\omega u,uangle \, dV.  \] Every summand is nonnegative, so $\delta 'u=0$ and $u$ vanishes on that neighborhood. e 0$, for example the coordinate section $X_0$. C7B9CDDC2DB1 Let $X$ be a compact complex manifold of dimension $n$, $F$ a holomorphic vector bundle, and $(L,h)$ a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle. Let $s\geq 1$ be an integer. Suppose its curvature has at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues at every point. Then there is an integer $k_0\geq 0$ such that \[  H^ q(X,L^{\otimes k}\otimes F)=0 \qquad (q\geq s,\  k\geq k_0).  \] Here cohomology is sheaf cohomology of holomorphic sections, or its equal smooth Dolbeault quotient. title: Lemma 10.49.2
