text: Lemma 10.49.2 . 1E60BABDFBAE The increasingly ordered eigenvalues of a Hermitian matrix satisfy \[  |\lambda _ j(A)-\lambda _ j(B)|\leq \| A-B\| _{\mathrm{op}}.  \] If $\psi \in C^\infty (\mathbb R,\mathbb R)$, the matrix $\psi [A]$ defined by unitary diagonalization is a smooth function of $A$ on the real vector space of Hermitian matrices. It is equivariant under unitary conjugation. Consequently it defines a smooth self-adjoint endomorphism for every smooth self-adjoint bundle endomorphism. Proof. For completeness a unitary eigenbasis is obtained by maximizing the Rayleigh quotient on the unit sphere: variation in every real and imaginary direction makes a maximizer an eigenvector. Its orthogonal complement is invariant; induction gives a basis. For increasingly ordered eigenvalues, \[  \lambda _ j(A)=\min _{\dim W=j}\  \max _{v\in W,\  |v|=1}\langle Av,v\rangle .  \] The span of the first $j$ eigenvectors gives the upper bound. Every $j$-plane intersects the span of the last $n-j+1$ eigenvectors, giving the lower bound. Rayleigh quotients change by at most $\| A-B\| _{\mathrm{op}}$, proving the asserted inequality. Fix a bound $\| A\| <R$ and let $a=R+1$. Choose a smooth compactly supported cutoff in $(-\pi ,\pi )$ equal to one on $[-1,1]$, and periodically extend its product with $\psi (at)$ to a smooth function $f$ of period $2\pi $. Its Fourier coefficients $b_ l$ have arbitrarily rapid polynomial decay, by repeated integration by parts. Here the Fourier inversion needed is elementary: the kernels \[  K_ N(t)=\frac1N\left|\sum _{j=0}^{N-1}e^{ijt}\right|^2  \] are nonnegative, have integral one for normalized angular measure, and have supremum at most $1/(N\sin ^2(\delta /2))$ when $\delta \leq |t|\leq \pi $. Uniform continuity therefore gives $K_ N*f\to f$ uniformly. Expanding the finite square shows these are the Cesàro means of the Fourier series. Rapid coefficient decay makes that series absolutely uniformly convergent, so the means have the same limit. Thus $f(t)=\sum _ l b_ l e^{ilt}$. By diagonalization, 1DE3560759B1 10.49.3 \begin{equation}  \psi [A]=\sum _{l\in \mathbb Z}b_ l e^{ilA/a} \qquad (\| A\| <R). \end{equation} We verify all matrix derivatives of this series. The convergent matrix exponential series, or differentiation of its product, gives the Duhamel identity \[  D_ Ae^{itA}[H]=\mathrm i\int _0^ t e^{i(t-u)A}H e^{iuA}\, du.  \] Indeed subtract the two exponentials for $A+H,A$ and differentiate $e^{i(t-u)(A+H)}e^{iuA}$; the residual after replacing $A+H$ by $A$ in the first factor is bounded by $t^2\| H\| ^2/2$. Iteration gives a sum over all orders of the derivative directions, integrated on the ordered simplex of volume $|t|^ k/k!$. Since $e^{iuA}$ is unitary, the $k!$ orders give \[  \| D_ A^ k e^{itA}[H_1,\ldots ,H_ k]\|  \leq |t|^ k\prod _\nu \| H_\nu \| .  \] The oriented integrals for $t<0$ give the same bound. For integers $p,q\geq 0$ the two-factor integral has the full normalization $\int _0^ t(t-u)^ p u^ qdu =t^{p+q+1}p!q!/(p+q+1)!$ for $t\geq 0$; substitution $u=tv$ and integration by parts prove it. Rapid decay of $b_ l$ now gives uniform convergence of every matrix derivative in ( 10.49.3 ), proving smoothness on $\| A\| <R$, hence everywhere. The definition by spectral subspaces gives unitary equivariance even at repeated eigenvalues. Smooth local unitary frames, obtained by Gram–Schmidt, and this equivariance prove the bundle assertion. No smooth eigenframe is used. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.49.4 (Girbau vanishing)
section: 10.49 Partial curvature positivity and vanishing
text: Theorem 10.49.4 (Girbau vanishing) . 876EBA05B64C Let $X$ be compact Kähler of dimension $n\geq 1$ and $(L,h)$ a semipositive Hermitian holomorphic line bundle. If its curvature has at least $n-s+1$ positive eigenvalues at every point, where $1\leq s\leq n$, then \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)=0\qquad (p+q\geq n+s).  \] Proof. The empty case is immediate, so assume $X$ is nonempty. Fix a Kähler form $\omega $ and let $0\leq \gamma _1\leq \cdots \leq \gamma _ n$ be the curvature eigenvalues. They are continuous by lemma 10.49.2 . Compactness and the rank hypothesis give $\delta =\min _ X\gamma _ s>0$. For $\varepsilon >0$, the form $\omega _\varepsilon =\alpha +\varepsilon \omega $ is Kähler. Its curvature eigenvalues are \[  \lambda _{j,\varepsilon }=\frac{\gamma _ j}{\gamma _ j+\varepsilon }\in [0,1), \qquad \lambda _{j,\varepsilon }\geq 1-\varepsilon /\delta \quad (j\geq s).  \] The first equality follows by simultaneously diagonalizing at a point; the inequality is $1/(1+t)\geq 1-t$ for $t\geq 0$. For $p+q\geq n+s$ one has $q\geq s$, so any set of $q$ indices contains at least $q-s+1$ indices $j\geq s$. Formula ( 10.49.1 ) therefore gives \[  B_{\omega _\varepsilon }\geq \bigl (p+q-n-s+1-(q-s+1)\varepsilon /\delta \bigr )I.  \] Choose once and for all $\varepsilon =\delta /(2n)$. Since $p+q-n-s+1\geq 1$ and $q-s+1\leq n$, this is at least $\tfrac 12 I$ in every required bidegree simultaneously. Apply theorem 10.33.10 to this fixed Kähler metric. All such $q$ are positive. The conclusion is for the fixed Dolbeault complex, whose cohomology does not depend on the metric. $\square$

title: Example 10.49.5

text: Example 10.49.5 . 00E6A77FAC15 For every $n\geq 1$ there is a compact Kähler $n$-fold $X$ with a semipositive line bundle $L$ whose curvature is positive on a dense open set, but \[  H^{p,p}_{\bar\partial }(X,L)\ne 0\qquad (0\leq p\leq n-1).  \] For $n\geq 3$, the preceding Girbau theorem with $s=1$ therefore fails if its rank hypothesis is imposed only on a dense open subset. Proof. Write $\mathbb C^{n+1}=\mathbb Ce_0\oplus W$, put $a=[e_0]$ and $Y=\mathbb P(W)\simeq \mathbb P^{n-1}$, and let \[  X=\{ ([z_0:z'],[v])\in \mathbb P^ n\times Y:z'\in \mathbb Cv\} .  \] This is a closed complex submanifold: on the chart of $Y$ where $v_ i=1$, the map $(v,[b:t])\mapsto ([b:tv],[v])$ is a holomorphic trivialization with fiber $\mathbb P^1$. Its inverse reads $b=z_0$ and $t=z'_ i$ in homogeneous fiber coordinates. The equations $z'_ i v_ j-z'_ j v_ i=0$ show closedness. Thus $X$ is compact and the restriction of the product Fubini–Study form is Kähler. Near $a$ its charts are $z'_ i=t,z'_ j=tv_ j$, the usual point-blowup charts. Denote the two projections by $\pi _1,\pi _2$. The exceptional inclusion $j:Y\to X$, $v\mapsto (a,v)$, satisfies $\pi _1j=a$ and $\pi _2j=I_ Y$. Away from $j(Y)$, $\pi _1$ is a biholomorphism onto $\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ a\} $, with inverse $[z_0:z']\mapsto ([z_0:z'],[z'])$. Take $L=\pi _1^*\mathcal O(1)$ with the pullback Fubini–Study metric of the Fubini–Study curvature computation . Its curvature is semipositive everywhere and positive off $j(Y)$, a dense open set. Its restriction to $Y$ is the trivial bundle with fixed fiber $\mathcal O(1)_ a$. Choose a section $s$ of $\mathcal O(1)$ with $s(a)\ne 0$, for example the coordinate section $X_0$. For the Fubini–Study form $\eta $ on $Y$, the form \[  u_ p=\pi _2^*\eta ^ p\otimes \pi _1^*s  \] is $D''$-closed and restricts to $\eta ^ p\otimes s(a)$ on $Y$. The class of $\eta ^ p$ is nonzero. For $p=0$ this is immediate. For $1\leq p\leq n-1$, if $\eta ^ p=\bar\partial v$, then Stokes' formula Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners , applied to $v\wedge \eta ^{n-1-p}$, gives $\int _ Y\eta ^{n-1}=0$: its other exterior derivative has excessive holomorphic degree. This contradicts positivity of the volume form. Pullback commutes with $D''$ for these holomorphic maps, so an exact $u_ p$ would have exact restriction, a contradiction. Finally $p=q=n-1$ has $2p\geq n+1$ when $n\geq 3$, as required to contradict the dense-open version of $s=1$. $\square$

text: All de Rham groups in this section use smooth complex forms. Their coefficients are complex numbers; no integral or singular-cohomology comparison is assumed. Proposition 10.50.1 . DD72F1B19307 If a Hausdorff smooth manifold with a countable basis is the union of two open sets $U,V$, there is a natural long exact sequence \[  \cdots \longrightarrow H^{j-1}_{\rm dR}(U\cap V) \longrightarrow H^ j_{\rm dR}(X) \longrightarrow H^ j_{\rm dR}(U)\oplus H^ j_{\rm dR}(V) \longrightarrow H^ j_{\rm dR}(U\cap V)\longrightarrow \cdots .  \] The middle arrow is restriction, and the next arrow takes the difference of restrictions. Negative-degree groups are zero. Proof. The smooth partition construction in proposition 10.43.10 supplies $\rho _ U+\rho _ V=1$, with closed supports inside $U,V$ respectively. For a smooth form $\eta $ on $U\cap V$, extend $\rho _ V\eta $ by zero to $U$, and extend $-\rho _ U\eta $ by zero to $V$. These extensions are smooth: near each point outside the other open set the corresponding cutoff is identically zero. Their difference on the intersection is $\eta $. The restriction/difference sequence \[  0\longrightarrow \mathcal A^\bullet (X) \longrightarrow \mathcal A^\bullet (U)\oplus \mathcal A^\bullet (V) \longrightarrow \mathcal A^\bullet (U\cap V)\longrightarrow 0  \] is therefore exact in every degree. Its kernel assertion is smooth pasting, and its arrows commute with $d$. The cochain long exact sequence lemma 10.43.3 proves the claim. The cutoff lift need not commute with $d$; only the displayed complex arrows are required to do so. $\square$ Lemma 10.50.2 . 2E46F3014687 For the sphere $S^ m$, $m\geq 1$, \[  H^ j_{\rm dR}(S^ m)= \begin{cases} \mathbb C,& j=0\  \hbox{or}\  j=m,\\ 0,& \hbox{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] For $S^0$ the degree-zero group is $\mathbb C^2$ and all positive ones vanish. Proof. Cover $S^ m$ by the complements of its north and south poles. Each is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ m$ by stereographic projection, and hence has just the cohomology of a point by the de Rham homotopy formula . Their intersection retracts smoothly onto the equator $S^{m-1}$: write a point as $(\sqrt{1-h^2}\, \xi ,h)$ with $|h|<1$, and replace $h$ by $(1-t)h$, keeping $\xi $ fixed. The same homotopy formula identifies its de Rham cohomology with that of the equator. For $m=1$, the equator has two points. The degree-zero difference map from the two contractible opens has diagonal image $\mathbb C$ in $\mathbb C^2$, so its cokernel is $\mathbb C$ and gives $H^1(S^1)$ by proposition 10.50.1 . For $m\geq 2$ the intersection is connected. The degree-zero difference map is onto, giving $H^1(S^ m)=0$; in degrees $j\geq 2$ the same sequence identifies $H^ j(S^ m)$ with $H^{j-1}(S^{m-1})$. Induction proves all positive-degree assertions. In degree zero, closed functions are constant on each connected component, proving both the remaining assertion and the base case $S^0$. $\square$ Theorem 10.50.3 . 558E1268EEED Let $\omega =\omega _{\rm FS}$ be the normalized Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 0$. Then \[  H^*_{\rm dR}(\mathbb P^ n,\mathbb C) =\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1}),\qquad |t|=2,\quad t=[\omega ].  \] In particular each even group in degrees $0,2,\ldots ,2n$ is one-dimensional and every odd group is zero. The Dolbeault groups, and their sheaf interpretations, are \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n) \simeq H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,\Omega ^ p)= \begin{cases} \mathbb C,& 0\leq p=q\leq n,\\ 0,& p\ne q. \end{cases}  \] For $p=q$, the class of $\omega ^ p$ is a generator. Moreover $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega ^ n=1$, including the point case $n=0$. Proof. First compute the additive de Rham groups without any Hodge-theoretic assumption. For $n=0$ they are those of a point. For $n\geq 1$ let $p_0=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, let $U=\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ p_0\} $, and let $V$ be a small coordinate ball centered at $p_0$. The homotopy \[  [z_0:z']\longmapsto [(1-t)z_0:z'],\qquad z'\ne 0,  \] retracts $U$ smoothly onto the hyperplane $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The open set $V$ is contractible, and $U\cap V$ is a punctured $2n$-ball, smoothly retracting to $S^{2n-1}$ by radial projection. Apply the preceding two results and the de Rham homotopy formula . The degree-zero difference map is onto because the intersection is connected; induction gives $H^1(\mathbb P^ n)=0$. For $2\leq j\leq 2n-2$ the two adjacent intersection groups vanish, so $H^ j(\mathbb P^ n)=H^ j(\mathbb P^{n-1})$. At the top end, $H^{2n-1}(\mathbb P^ n)=0$ and the connecting map gives $H^{2n}(\mathbb P^ n)\simeq H^{2n-1}(S^{2n-1})=\mathbb C$. For $n=1$, only the already stated degree-one and top-degree steps are needed. Higher groups vanish by real dimension. This proves all the claimed additive groups. The existing curvature computation the Fubini–Study curvature computation proves that $\omega $ is a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form. Thus its top power has positive integral. For every $0\leq k\leq n$, the class $[\omega ^ k]$ is nonzero: if $\omega ^ k=d\eta $ for $k\geq 1$, Stokes applied to $\eta \wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ would make that positive integral zero. The degree-zero class is the constant function1. Each of the one-dimensional even groups therefore has the asserted generator, and multiplication of these powers gives the displayed ring. The relation $t^{n+1}=0$ follows by form degree and there are no others, since all the lower powers are nonzero. For the integral normalization, in the affine chart $\mathbb C^ n$ the Hessian matrix of $\log (1+|z|^2)$ has one eigenvalue $(1+|z|^2)^{-2}$ and $n-1$ eigenvalues $(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$. With $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$ this gives \[  \omega ^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-1}\, dV_{\mathbb R^{2n}}.  \] The omitted hyperplane has zero smooth volume, as follows in charts from its real codimension two and Fubini. Polar integration gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-1}dV =\frac{2\pi ^ n}{(n-1)!} \int _0^\infty \frac{r^{2n-1}}{(1+r^2)^{n+1}}\, dr =\frac{\pi ^ n}{n!}.  \] For the last integral use $s=r^2/(1+r^2)$, obtaining $\tfrac 12\int _0^1s^{n-1}ds=1/(2n)$. The polar sphere-area constant follows by applying polar integration to the product Gaussian integral $\int _{\mathbb C^ n}e^{-|z|^2}dV=\pi ^ n$; integration by parts gives its radial integral $(n-1)!/2$. This proves the normalization without an integral homology assertion. Finally $\mathbb P^ n$ is compact Kähler, so theorem 10.47.13 applies. The even one-dimensional group is already spanned by a closed pure $(k,k)$ form $\omega ^ k$, and every odd group is zero. Its direct Hodge sum therefore has no other type components. The natural pure-type Dolbeault identifications give the displayed groups, and the bundle resolution corollary 10.43.11 identifies them with $H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,\Omega ^ p)$. The point case is immediate. $\square$

text: Lemma 10.50.2 . 2E46F3014687 For the sphere $S^ m$, $m\geq 1$, \[  H^ j_{\rm dR}(S^ m)= \begin{cases} \mathbb C,& j=0\  \hbox{or}\  j=m,\\ 0,& \hbox{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] For $S^0$ the degree-zero group is $\mathbb C^2$ and all positive ones vanish. Proof. Cover $S^ m$ by the complements of its north and south poles. Each is diffeomorphic to $\mathbb R^ m$ by stereographic projection, and hence has just the cohomology of a point by the de Rham homotopy formula . Their intersection retracts smoothly onto the equator $S^{m-1}$: write a point as $(\sqrt{1-h^2}\, \xi ,h)$ with $|h|<1$, and replace $h$ by $(1-t)h$, keeping $\xi $ fixed. The same homotopy formula identifies its de Rham cohomology with that of the equator. For $m=1$, the equator has two points. The degree-zero difference map from the two contractible opens has diagonal image $\mathbb C$ in $\mathbb C^2$, so its cokernel is $\mathbb C$ and gives $H^1(S^1)$ by proposition 10.50.1 . For $m\geq 2$ the intersection is connected. The degree-zero difference map is onto, giving $H^1(S^ m)=0$; in degrees $j\geq 2$ the same sequence identifies $H^ j(S^ m)$ with $H^{j-1}(S^{m-1})$. Induction proves all positive-degree assertions. In degree zero, closed functions are constant on each connected component, proving both the remaining assertion and the base case $S^0$. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.50.3
section: 10.50 The cohomology of spheres and projective space
text: Theorem 10.50.3 . 558E1268EEED Let $\omega =\omega _{\rm FS}$ be the normalized Fubini–Study form on $\mathbb P^ n$, $n\geq 0$. Then \[  H^*_{\rm dR}(\mathbb P^ n,\mathbb C) =\mathbb C[t]/(t^{n+1}),\qquad |t|=2,\quad t=[\omega ].  \] In particular each even group in degrees $0,2,\ldots ,2n$ is one-dimensional and every odd group is zero. The Dolbeault groups, and their sheaf interpretations, are \[  H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial }(\mathbb P^ n) \simeq H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,\Omega ^ p)= \begin{cases} \mathbb C,& 0\leq p=q\leq n,\\ 0,& p\ne q. \end{cases}  \] For $p=q$, the class of $\omega ^ p$ is a generator. Moreover $\int _{\mathbb P^ n}\omega ^ n=1$, including the point case $n=0$. Proof. First compute the additive de Rham groups without any Hodge-theoretic assumption. For $n=0$ they are those of a point. For $n\geq 1$ let $p_0=[1:0:\cdots :0]$, let $U=\mathbb P^ n\setminus \{ p_0\} $, and let $V$ be a small coordinate ball centered at $p_0$. The homotopy \[  [z_0:z']\longmapsto [(1-t)z_0:z'],\qquad z'\ne 0,  \] retracts $U$ smoothly onto the hyperplane $\mathbb P^{n-1}$. The open set $V$ is contractible, and $U\cap V$ is a punctured $2n$-ball, smoothly retracting to $S^{2n-1}$ by radial projection. Apply the preceding two results and the de Rham homotopy formula . The degree-zero difference map is onto because the intersection is connected; induction gives $H^1(\mathbb P^ n)=0$. For $2\leq j\leq 2n-2$ the two adjacent intersection groups vanish, so $H^ j(\mathbb P^ n)=H^ j(\mathbb P^{n-1})$. At the top end, $H^{2n-1}(\mathbb P^ n)=0$ and the connecting map gives $H^{2n}(\mathbb P^ n)\simeq H^{2n-1}(S^{2n-1})=\mathbb C$. For $n=1$, only the already stated degree-one and top-degree steps are needed. Higher groups vanish by real dimension. This proves all the claimed additive groups. The existing curvature computation the Fubini–Study curvature computation proves that $\omega $ is a positive closed real $(1,1)$-form. Thus its top power has positive integral. For every $0\leq k\leq n$, the class $[\omega ^ k]$ is nonzero: if $\omega ^ k=d\eta $ for $k\geq 1$, Stokes applied to $\eta \wedge \omega ^{n-k}$ would make that positive integral zero. The degree-zero class is the constant function1. Each of the one-dimensional even groups therefore has the asserted generator, and multiplication of these powers gives the displayed ring. The relation $t^{n+1}=0$ follows by form degree and there are no others, since all the lower powers are nonzero. For the integral normalization, in the affine chart $\mathbb C^ n$ the Hessian matrix of $\log (1+|z|^2)$ has one eigenvalue $(1+|z|^2)^{-2}$ and $n-1$ eigenvalues $(1+|z|^2)^{-1}$. With $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$ this gives \[  \omega ^ n=\frac{n!}{\pi ^ n}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-1}\, dV_{\mathbb R^{2n}}.  \] The omitted hyperplane has zero smooth volume, as follows in charts from its real codimension two and Fubini. Polar integration gives \[  \int _{\mathbb R^{2n}}(1+|z|^2)^{-n-1}dV =\frac{2\pi ^ n}{(n-1)!} \int _0^\infty \frac{r^{2n-1}}{(1+r^2)^{n+1}}\, dr =\frac{\pi ^ n}{n!}.  \] For the last integral use $s=r^2/(1+r^2)$, obtaining $\tfrac 12\int _0^1s^{n-1}ds=1/(2n)$. The polar sphere-area constant follows by applying polar integration to the product Gaussian integral $\int _{\mathbb C^ n}e^{-|z|^2}dV=\pi ^ n$; integration by parts gives its radial integral $(n-1)!/2$. This proves the normalization without an integral homology assertion. Finally $\mathbb P^ n$ is compact Kähler, so theorem 10.47.13 applies. The even one-dimensional group is already spanned by a closed pure $(k,k)$ form $\omega ^ k$, and every odd group is zero. Its direct Hodge sum therefore has no other type components. The natural pure-type Dolbeault identifications give the displayed groups, and the bundle resolution corollary 10.43.11 identifies them with $H^ q(\mathbb P^ n,\Omega ^ p)$. The point case is immediate. $\square$

title: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces

section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Manifolds are Hausdorff, have a countable basis, and have no boundary unless a boundary is specified. A bordered surface below is a compact smooth real surface with smooth boundary. Cohomology of differential forms means smooth de Rham cohomology. We use $dd^ c=\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial /(2\pi )$. Theorem 10.77.1 . 5EC4372960F9 An oriented smooth Riemannian surface has, about each point, an orientation-preserving complex coordinate $w=u+\mathrm iv$ in which $g=\rho (du^2+dv^2)$, with $\rho >0$ smooth. Consequently every smooth almost complex structure on a real surface is integrable. On a fixed oriented surface its compatible complex structures correspond exactly to the conformal classes of oriented Riemannian metrics. More explicitly, if $z=x+\mathrm iy$ and $g=E\, dx^2+2F\, dx\, dy+G\, dy^2$, set $D=EG-F^2$. Then 7906738A51EC 10.77.2 \begin{equation}  g=\lambda |dz+\mu \, d\bar z|^2,\qquad \lambda =\frac{E+G+2\sqrt D}{4},\qquad \mu =\frac{E-G+2\mathrm iF}{E+G+2\sqrt D},\qquad |\mu |<1. \end{equation} The resulting coordinate satisfies $w_{\bar z}=\mu w_ z$ and has positive real Jacobian. Conversely every smooth $\mu $ with $|\mu |<1$ has such local coordinates. Proof. Choose positively oriented real coordinates centered at the point with $g(0)=I$, and write $a^{ij}(x)=\sqrt{\det g(x)}\, g^{ij}(x)$. On the unit disk, put $a_\epsilon (y)=a(\epsilon y)$. For small positive $\epsilon $ these matrices have a common positive lower bound and $\| a_\epsilon -I\| _{C^ k}\leq C_ k\epsilon $ for every fixed $k$. On $H^1_0(B_1;\mathbb R)$ solve 81982B590FB1 10.77.3 \begin{equation}  \int a_\epsilon ^{ij}\partial _ j v\, \partial _ i\eta =-\int (a_\epsilon ^{i1}-\delta _{i1})\partial _ i\eta . \end{equation} Here no boundary regularity theorem is necessary. For a compactly supported smooth function on the disk, extension by zero to a fixed square and the formula $v(x,y)=\int _{-2}^ x v_ x(t,y)\, dt$ give $\| v\| _2\leq C\| dv\| _2$. This passes to its $H^1$ completion. Thus the left side of ( 10.77.3 ) is a Hilbert inner product equivalent to the $H^1_0$ norm, and the right side has norm at most $C\epsilon $. The Hilbert representation theorem gives a unique real solution with $\| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\epsilon $. The proved divergence-form interior estimate interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form , applied on two smaller concentric disks, gives \[  \| v\| _{H^3(B_{1/2})} \leq C\bigl (\| v\| _{H^1(B_1)} +\| \partial _ i a_\epsilon ^{i1}\| _{H^1(B_1)}\bigr ) \leq C'\epsilon .  \] The constants are uniform: ellipticity and the finitely many coefficient norms in that difference-quotient proof are bounded uniformly here. The Fourier Sobolev estimate of Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding , localized by a cutoff, gives $\| dv\| _{C^0(B_{1/3})}\leq C\epsilon $. Higher interior estimates make $v$ smooth. Hence $u(y)=y_1+v(y)$ is harmonic for the rescaled metric and $du(0)\ne 0$. Rescaling back gives a real smooth harmonic function near the original point with nonzero differential there. The oriented real Hodge star on one-forms is characterized in an oriented orthonormal coframe by $*e^1=e^2$, $*e^2=-e^1$. Harmonicity is $d(*du)=0$. Shrink to a coordinate ball, and use the radial Poincaré homotopy formula to obtain a real function $v_0$ with $dv_0=*du$. If $J$ is positive rotation by $\pi /2$, this says $dv_0=-du\circ J$. Therefore $dw\circ J=\mathrm i\, dw$ for $w=u+\mathrm iv_0$. Moreover $du,dv_0$ are perpendicular of equal positive norm, so the Jacobian is positive and the real inverse function theorem applies. In these coordinates $g=|du|_ g^{-2}(du^2+dv_0^2)$. Transitions satisfy the ordinary Cauchy–Riemann equations and hence are holomorphic by the local Cauchy theorem. This constructs the asserted complex atlas. For a given smooth $J$, first choose any smooth positive metric $h$ and replace it by $h(v,w)+h(Jv,Jw)$. Its positive rotation is $J$ for the orientation defined by $J$. The construction therefore proves integrability, without using a theorem in higher complex dimension. Two inner products invariant under this rotation are positive scalar multiples: in a basis $(e,Je)$ both have equal diagonal entries and zero off-diagonal entry. This proves the conformal-class assertion. The same calculation shows uniqueness of the complex atlas for the given $J$. Expanding the right side of ( 10.77.2 ) gives its stated coefficients, and \[  |\mu |^2=\frac{E+G-2\sqrt D}{E+G+2\sqrt D}<1.  \] A positive conformal coordinate has $dw=c(dz+\mu d\bar z)$: these one-forms span the same complex $(1,0)$ cotangent line. Thus $c=w_ z\ne 0$ and $w_{\bar z}=\mu w_ z$; its Jacobian is $|c|^2(1-|\mu |^2)>0$. Conversely $|dz+\mu d\bar z|^2$ is a positive oriented smooth metric whenever $|\mu |<1$, so the preceding construction applies. $\square$ Corollary 10.77.4 . FB7A8CA804B1 On an almost complex surface, exact local complex coordinates give approximate complex coordinates to every finite order. If a smooth complex-valued local real coordinate $z$, centered at the point, satisfies $d''z=O(|z|^ s)$ for an integer $s\geq 3$, then, on a fixed sufficiently small neighborhood, \[  |z|^2,\qquad |z|^2+\log (|z|^2+\epsilon ^2)  \] are strictly subharmonic for every $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. The neighborhood is independent of $\epsilon $. Proof. Use the exact complex coordinate $w$ just constructed and put $r=|z|$. The coordinate change is a real diffeomorphism, so $r$ and $|w|$ are comparable. The hypothesis gives $z_{\bar w}=O(r^ s)$ and $z_{w\bar w}=O(r^{s-1})$; the latter follows by taking the Taylor polynomial of the smooth former function. Also $|z_ w|$ has a positive lower bound after shrinking. For $A=|z|^2$ direct differentiation gives \[  A_{w\bar w}=|z_ w|^2+O(r^ s),\qquad |A_ w|^2=|z_ w|^2r^2+O(r^{s+2}).  \] Consequently \[  (A+\log (A+\epsilon ^2))_{w\bar w} =A_{w\bar w} +\frac{\epsilon ^2|z_ w|^2}{(r^2+\epsilon ^2)^2} +O\! \left(\frac{r^ s}{r^2+\epsilon ^2} +\frac{r^{s+2}}{(r^2+\epsilon ^2)^2}\right).  \] For $r>0$ the error is bounded by $Cr^{s-2}$ independently of $\epsilon $; at $r=0$ the error terms are zero. The fixed positive lower bound for $A_{w\bar w}$ now proves both assertions. $\square$ Lemma 10.77.5 . 6E44892C19CA A connected compact Riemann surface with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. Proof. Choose any smooth Hermitian metric. Its fundamental form is closed because the real dimension is two. The analytic compact Kähler Hodge decomposition theorem 10.47.13 therefore gives $H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial }(X)=0$ from the vanishing of the complexified de Rham group. These are smooth analytic groups; no sheaf or integral comparison is needed. Choose a holomorphic coordinate $z$ about a point $p$ and a smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in its coordinate disk and equal to one near $p$. The form $\bar\partial (\chi /z)$ on $X\setminus \{ p\} $ extends to a smooth $(0,1)$-form on $X$, zero near $p$; it is closed. The just-proved cohomology vanishing, or its smooth Hodge realization, gives a smooth function $u$ with $\bar\partial u=\bar\partial (\chi /z)$. Thus $f=\chi /z-u$ is a meromorphic function with precisely one pole, a simple pole at $p$; it is holomorphic elsewhere. For $a\in \mathbb C$, the function $\log |f-a|^2$ is globally locally integrable. The canonical Poincaré–Lelong formula the normalized Poincaré–Lelong formula , applied also to the local quotient at the pole, gives \[  dd^ c\log |f-a|^2 =\sum _{f(x)=a}\operatorname {ord}_ x(f-a)\, \delta _ x-\delta _ p.  \] The sum is finite by isolatedness of zeros and compactness; a neighborhood of the pole contains no such zeros. Pairing this exact current with the constant function one gives total mass zero by Stokes. Hence every finite $a$ has exactly one preimage, of order one. Infinity has just the simple preimage $p$. The holomorphic map $f:X\to \mathbb P^1$ is therefore bijective and has nonzero local derivative everywhere, also in the coordinate $1/f$ at $p$. The local holomorphic inverse theorem gives a holomorphic inverse. $\square$ Lemma 10.77.6 . A2808AF4FEA1 Let $X$ be a connected noncompact oriented smooth surface with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$. There is an exhaustion by connected relatively compact open sets $\Omega _ j$, with smooth compact closures, $\overline\Omega _ j\subset \Omega _{j+1}$, such that no component of $X\setminus \overline\Omega _ j$ is relatively compact. Each $\partial \Omega _ j$ is one circle, and \[  H^1_{\rm dR}(\Omega _ j;\mathbb R)=0, \qquad H^1_{\rm dR}(Y_ j;\mathbb R)=0,  \] where $Y_ j$ is the oriented double of $\overline\Omega _ j$. Proof. We give the surface-topological details needed here, without using compact-support duality or classification of surfaces. Elementary neighborhoods and arcs. Every compact subset of a connected surface is contained in the interior of a connected compact bordered subsurface. Indeed, cover it by finitely many relatively compact coordinate disks, join their centers to a fixed center by finitely many coordinate paths, and cover those paths by finitely many more such disks with successive overlap. Choose their radii so that boundary circles meet transversely and avoid the finitely many earlier crossing points. This choice needs only the one-variable regular-value fact for the restriction of a radius function to an earlier boundary arc. For completeness, the critical values of a smooth function on a compact interval have measure zero: cover its critical set by finitely many intervals in the open set $|f'|<\delta $, merge overlapping intervals, and bound the total length of their images by $\delta $ times the total interval length. Let $\delta $ tend to zero, and use finitely many intervals for a circle. A regular level has finitely many intersections by compactness. Thus the disk union has finitely many corners and no triple corners. Round each corner outward inside a small coordinate box, disjoint from the others. In coordinates where the two crossing arcs are axes, replace their minimum defining function by $(s+t-\vartheta (s-t))/2$, where $\vartheta $ is a smooth convex regularization of $|\cdot |$, equal to it outside a small interval, with $|\vartheta '|\leq 1$. Its two partial derivatives sum to one, so its zero level is smooth. This gives the required neighborhood, still containing the original compact set in its interior. The boundary of a compact bordered surface has finitely many components, each a circle. One elementary verification of the last assertion is to flow a nonvanishing tangent vector field on a connected compact one-manifold: the orbit is open, hence is the whole component, and compactness forces a nonzero period; the component is a quotient of $\mathbb R$ by its period group. Each component of the complement of the bordered surface meets its boundary, by a path to an interior point, and one boundary circle has only one exterior side. There are therefore only finitely many such components. Adjoin the closures of all relatively compact ones. Their finite union is compact; the remaining boundary circles are unchanged and smooth. The resulting bordered surface is connected, and all its exterior components are not relatively compact. Starting with a countable relatively compact coordinate cover and repeating this construction with the previous bordered surface in the next interior proves the stated exhaustion. In a noncompact connected surface its bordered members have nonempty boundary. We will also use the following elementary arc constructions. A path in an open connected surface can be replaced by finitely many smooth coordinate arcs with transverse double crossings only. Each replacement inside a coordinate disk is a homotopy with fixed endpoints and preserves the integral of a closed form by its local primitive. To arrange this, subdivide into coordinate disks, move successive subarcs a small amount in their transverse coordinate, and choose regular values of the resulting one-variable restrictions to the finitely many earlier arcs. Avoid their finitely many crossing points as well. Transversality and compactness make all crossings finite. Erasing successive loops and rounding corners then gives an embedded arc, with prescribed transverse directions at its endpoints. The same procedure for a closed path gives finitely many embedded piecewise smooth circles after splitting at its finitely many crossings. Rounding a corner inside a coordinate disk does not change the integral of a closed form, because that form has a local primitive there. A connected noncompact surface with compact boundary has a proper embedded ray starting from any prescribed boundary point, transverse to the boundary there. Here proper means that the inverse image of every compact set is compact. To see this, exhaust it by the filled bordered neighborhoods just constructed, initially including a collar of its compact boundary. Begin an embedded arc to the first outer boundary. Given its endpoint, the component on the exterior side is not relatively compact. Join the endpoint, inside that component, to a point beyond the next exhaustion member; stop at the first exit from that member. Erase loops as above. This extension avoids the previous arc, which was inside the preceding member. The exterior component at the new endpoint is again not relatively compact, and is contained in the preceding exterior component. Continuing and rounding the locally finite joints produces an embedded ray whose successive tails lie outside every earlier compact member, proving properness. The same construction starts from an interior point. An embedded circle has a two-sided collar on an oriented surface: flow a smooth transverse normal field, and use compactness and the inverse function theorem to choose a uniform width. A proper embedded line likewise has a normal strip, parametrized by $(s,t)\in \mathbb R\times (-1,1)$, whose restriction to $\mathbb R\times [-1/2,1/2]$ is proper. To check the noncompact point in this assertion, exhaust the line by compact parameter intervals. Properness separates each such interval from sufficiently far tails, and compactness gives a positive tubular width on each remaining finite interval. Choose a positive smooth width below these locally finite bounds; the inverse function theorem and these separations make the normal flow injective. Shrink the width further on successive intervals so that their strips avoid each earlier ambient compact set once the line does. This proves the asserted properness. An embedded arc with endpoints on a smooth boundary has the identical construction with end half-strips. Every embedded circle has a compact side. Let $C\subset X$ be such a circle. Its complement has at most two components. Indeed, every component meets one of the two collar sides, by stopping a path to $C$ at its first contact with the collar; each collar side is connected. If the complement were connected, take a path in it joining the two outer sides of the collar, and complete it by an arc crossing the collar once. On the collar put $\beta =\chi (t)\, dt$, where $t$ is the normal coordinate, $\chi $ has support in the collar interior, and $\int \chi (t)\, dt=1$. Extend $\beta $ by zero. This is a smooth closed global form. On $X\setminus C$ it has a primitive: it is zero outside the collar, and on each half-collar take the integral of $\chi $ from its outer end. The joining path therefore has integral zero, whereas the crossing arc has integral one, up to orientation. This contradicts exactness of $\beta $ on $X$. Thus $C$ separates $X$ into two components. If the closures of both were noncompact, the proper-ray construction in each of these closed surfaces with boundary $C$, joined across its collar, would give a proper embedded line crossing $C$ just once. In its normal strip the form $\chi (t)\, dt$, with $\int \chi =1$ and support $|t|<1/2$, extends smoothly by zero and is closed on $X$. Properness ensures that no finite ambient point is an accumulation point of its support from unbounded $s$. Choose the strip thin enough that $C$ meets it only near the single crossing. Its integral on $C$ is $1$ or $-1$, again contradicting exactness. At least one closed side is consequently compact. It is a compact smooth surface $D$ with boundary $C$. Filled domains have zero first cohomology and one boundary. Let $W=\overline\Omega _ j$. If $C\subset \operatorname {int}W$ is an embedded circle, its compact side $D$ lies in $\operatorname {int}W$. Otherwise $D$ meets some exterior component of $W$: a point of $\partial W$ in $D$ is an interior point of $D$, since its boundary $C$ is disjoint from $\partial W$. Such an exterior component is connected and disjoint from $C$, so is wholly in the compact side, contradicting its failure to be relatively compact. Hence Stokes gives $\int _ C\alpha =0$ for every smooth closed one-form $\alpha $ on $\operatorname {int}W$. Splitting a general closed path into embedded circles by the finite arc construction proves that all its periods are zero. Path integration now supplies a smooth primitive: locally it differs by a constant from the radial Poincaré primitive. Thus $H^1_{\rm dR}(\operatorname {int}W;\mathbb R)=0$. If $W$ had two distinct boundary components, choose an embedded arc joining them and otherwise in the interior, meeting boundary collars only at its two ends. In its normal strip extend $\chi (t)\, dt$ by zero across the transverse sides; the longitudinal ends terminate on $\partial W$, so this is a smooth closed form on $W$. A sufficiently nearby interior parallel of the first boundary circle crosses this strip once, and has integral $1$ or $-1$. This contradicts the just proved exactness on $\operatorname {int}W$. The boundary is connected. The double. Glue two copies of $W$ with opposite orientations along their boundary, using the signed normal coordinate in a boundary collar. This gives a closed compact oriented smooth surface $Y$. It has open sets $A,B$ containing the two copies, respectively, each diffeomorphic to $\operatorname {int}W$ by compressing an attached collar. Their intersection is an annulus because the boundary is one circle. If $\alpha $ is a closed one-form on $Y$, write $\alpha =df_ A=df_ B$ on these two opens. Their primitives differ by a constant on the connected overlap. Adjusting that constant glues them to a global primitive. This proves $H^1_{\rm dR}(Y;\mathbb R)=0$. $\square$ Lemma 10.77.7 . 0FE8A815392E If $f:\Delta \to \mathbb C$ is injective and holomorphic, with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$, then for $0\leq r<1$ and $|z|\leq r$, BB0211131FFC 10.77.8 \begin{equation}  |f'(z)|\leq \left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right)^6,\qquad |f(z)|\leq r\left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right)^6. \end{equation} In particular these normalized functions form a locally bounded family. Proof. We include the coefficient estimate needed for compactness. First an injective holomorphic function has no zero derivative: if its local first nonconstant term had order $m>1$, the argument principle on a small circle, applied to a nearby regular value, would give $m$ preimages there. The argument principle here follows directly by integrating the logarithmic derivative after factoring its finitely many zeros. Write $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots $. Since $f(z)/z$ has no zeros on the disk, it has a holomorphic logarithm, normalized to be zero at zero: integrate its logarithmic derivative, whose periods are zero on the disk by Cauchy's theorem. Thus \[  h(z)=z\exp \bigl (\tfrac 12\log (f(z^2)/z^2)\bigr ) =z+\tfrac 12a_2z^3+\cdots  \] is an odd injective function. Indeed equality of two values implies equality of $f(z^2)$, hence the arguments are equal or opposite; oddness and the unique zero at zero handle the latter case. The exterior function \[  H(\zeta )=1/h(1/\zeta ) =\zeta +\sum _{k\geq 1}b_ k\zeta ^{-k},\qquad b_1=-a_2/2,  \] is injective for $|\zeta |>1$ and has no constant term. For $1<r<R$, change of variables and orthogonality of the exponential functions on circles give 66093CD4561E 10.77.9 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {area} H(\{ r<|\zeta |<R\} ) =\pi (R^2-r^2)+\pi \sum _{k\geq 1}k|b_ k|^2(r^{-2k}-R^{-2k}). \end{equation} The Laurent series and its derivative converge uniformly on each closed subannulus; integrating their squares and then exhausting the open annulus justifies the formula and its nonnegative series. For fixed $r$ and large $R$, the maximum principle on the annulus bounds its entire image by the disk of radius $R+|b_1|/R+O(R^{-2})$; this outer bound eventually exceeds the fixed maximum on $|\zeta |=r$. Therefore the area is at most $\pi R^2+2\pi |b_1|+o(1)$. Subtract $\pi R^2$ in ( 10.77.9 ), retain only its $k=1$ term, and let $R\to \infty $, then $r\downarrow 1$. This gives $|b_1|^2\leq 1+2|b_1|$, so $|a_2|\leq 2(1+\sqrt2)<5$. This deliberately nonsharp estimate requires no complement-area or boundary Jordan-curve theorem. For $a\in \Delta $, apply it to the normalized injective function \[  w\longmapsto \frac{f((a+w)/(1+\bar a w))-f(a)}{(1-|a|^2)f'(a)}.  \] Its second coefficient is $(1-|a|^2)f''(a)/(2f'(a))-\bar a$. Consequently \[  \left|\frac{f''(a)}{f'(a)}\right| \leq \frac{10+2|a|}{1-|a|^2} \leq \frac{12}{1-|a|^2}.  \] Integrating the radial derivative of $\log |f'|$ from zero to $z$ proves the first estimate in ( 10.77.8 ), because $\int _0^ r12(1-t^2)^{-1}dt=6\log ((1+r)/(1-r))$. Integration of $f'$ along the same radius proves the second. $\square$ Theorem 10.77.10 . F2BDA05453B5 Every connected noncompact Riemann surface $X$ with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$ admits an injective holomorphic map to $\mathbb C$. Every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of $\mathbb P^1$, $\mathbb C$, or the unit disk. Proof. First assume $X$ is noncompact with the stated de Rham vanishing, and take the exhaustion in lemma 10.77.6 . Its double $Y_ j$ admits a smooth positive metric agreeing with the given Hermitian metric on the first copy of $\overline\Omega _ j$. To construct it, use the metric already defined on both sides of $\partial \Omega _ j$ in $X$ to extend over a collar on the second copy; away from the seam interpolate with any positive metric by a smooth partition of unity. The signed collar defines the double's smooth structure, so this extension is smooth, including all derivatives at the seam. The orientation and theorem 10.77.1 give a complex structure on $Y_ j$ agreeing with the given one on the first copy. It has zero first de Rham cohomology and hence is biholomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. Send a point in the interior of the second copy to infinity by a Möbius map. Restriction then gives an injective holomorphic map $\Phi _ j:\Omega _ j\to \mathbb C$. Fix $a\in \Omega _1$ and a nonzero complex cotangent vector $\xi \in T_ a^{1,0*}X$. Composing with an affine map, uniquely normalize $\Phi _ j(a)=0$ and $d\Phi _ j(a)=\xi $. We check local boundedness on all of $X$, rather than only at $a$. In a fixed coordinate disk about $a$, its coordinate derivative at the center is fixed, so scaling lemma 10.77.7 gives uniform bounds on every smaller disk. Suppose bounds have already been obtained near a point $b$. Cauchy's formula bounds $\Phi _ j'(b)$ there, as well as $\Phi _ j(b)$. On any fixed coordinate disk centered at $b$, normalize by these two quantities. Its restriction is injective, so ( 10.77.8 ), rescaled to that disk, gives uniform bounds on its smaller concentric disks. Every point can be reached from $a$ by a finite chain of such overlapping coordinate disks: subdivide a path into disks and choose each next center in the preceding smaller disk. This propagates local boundedness. A compact subset needs finitely many of these neighborhoods, so the bounds are uniform on every compact set, for all sufficiently large $j$ for which these disks lie in $\Omega _ j$. Cauchy's derivative estimates give equicontinuity on smaller coordinate disks. The proved Arzelà–Ascoli theorem the Arzelà–Ascoli compactness theorem , followed by a diagonal subsequence over a countable relatively compact coordinate cover, gives a locally uniform limit $\Phi :X\to \mathbb C$. Cauchy's formula makes the limit holomorphic and makes all local derivatives converge. In particular $\Phi (a)=0$ and $d\Phi (a)=\xi \ne 0$. The limit is injective. Otherwise take distinct $x,y$ with $\Phi (x)=\Phi (y)$ and a small closed coordinate disk about $x$ not containing $y$, whose boundary contains no zero of $\Phi -\Phi (y)$. This is possible because $\Phi $ is nonconstant. The logarithmic-derivative integral on that boundary is a positive integer. Uniform convergence of both functions and first derivatives makes it the limit of the analogous integrals for $\Phi _ j-\Phi _ j(y)$. Those integrals are zero, since injectivity of $\Phi _ j$ excludes a zero in the disk. This contradiction proves injectivity. Its derivative never vanishes by the elementary local argument in lemma 10.77.7 ; thus it is a biholomorphism onto an open plane domain $D$. This proves the embedding assertion. On a simply connected smooth manifold every closed one-form has a global primitive by path integration. Its local primitives make the integral invariant under path homotopy: subdivide a continuous homotopy square into finitely many cells whose images lie in coordinate balls, and cancel the increments of those primitives along common edges. Thus the preceding hypothesis applies to a simply connected surface. In its compact case use lemma 10.77.5 . In its noncompact case the embedding just proved identifies $X$ with a simply connected plane domain $D$. If $D=\mathbb C$ we are done. If it is proper, the already proved the Riemann map constructed from a Green function maps it biholomorphically onto the unit disk. The compact sphere cannot be biholomorphic to either noncompact surface. Nor can $\mathbb C$ be biholomorphic to the disk: the map to the disk would be a bounded nonconstant entire function, contrary to Cauchy's derivative estimate on disks of arbitrarily large radius. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.77.1
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Theorem 10.77.1 . 5EC4372960F9 An oriented smooth Riemannian surface has, about each point, an orientation-preserving complex coordinate $w=u+\mathrm iv$ in which $g=\rho (du^2+dv^2)$, with $\rho >0$ smooth. Consequently every smooth almost complex structure on a real surface is integrable. On a fixed oriented surface its compatible complex structures correspond exactly to the conformal classes of oriented Riemannian metrics. More explicitly, if $z=x+\mathrm iy$ and $g=E\, dx^2+2F\, dx\, dy+G\, dy^2$, set $D=EG-F^2$. Then 7906738A51EC 10.77.2 \begin{equation}  g=\lambda |dz+\mu \, d\bar z|^2,\qquad \lambda =\frac{E+G+2\sqrt D}{4},\qquad \mu =\frac{E-G+2\mathrm iF}{E+G+2\sqrt D},\qquad |\mu |<1. \end{equation} The resulting coordinate satisfies $w_{\bar z}=\mu w_ z$ and has positive real Jacobian. Conversely every smooth $\mu $ with $|\mu |<1$ has such local coordinates. Proof. Choose positively oriented real coordinates centered at the point with $g(0)=I$, and write $a^{ij}(x)=\sqrt{\det g(x)}\, g^{ij}(x)$. On the unit disk, put $a_\epsilon (y)=a(\epsilon y)$. For small positive $\epsilon $ these matrices have a common positive lower bound and $\| a_\epsilon -I\| _{C^ k}\leq C_ k\epsilon $ for every fixed $k$. On $H^1_0(B_1;\mathbb R)$ solve 81982B590FB1 10.77.3 \begin{equation}  \int a_\epsilon ^{ij}\partial _ j v\, \partial _ i\eta =-\int (a_\epsilon ^{i1}-\delta _{i1})\partial _ i\eta . \end{equation} Here no boundary regularity theorem is necessary. For a compactly supported smooth function on the disk, extension by zero to a fixed square and the formula $v(x,y)=\int _{-2}^ x v_ x(t,y)\, dt$ give $\| v\| _2\leq C\| dv\| _2$. This passes to its $H^1$ completion. Thus the left side of ( 10.77.3 ) is a Hilbert inner product equivalent to the $H^1_0$ norm, and the right side has norm at most $C\epsilon $. The Hilbert representation theorem gives a unique real solution with $\| v\| _{H^1}\leq C\epsilon $. The proved divergence-form interior estimate interior regularity for elliptic systems in divergence form , applied on two smaller concentric disks, gives \[  \| v\| _{H^3(B_{1/2})} \leq C\bigl (\| v\| _{H^1(B_1)} +\| \partial _ i a_\epsilon ^{i1}\| _{H^1(B_1)}\bigr ) \leq C'\epsilon .  \] The constants are uniform: ellipticity and the finitely many coefficient norms in that difference-quotient proof are bounded uniformly here. The Fourier Sobolev estimate of Sobolev spaces, duality and local embedding , localized by a cutoff, gives $\| dv\| _{C^0(B_{1/3})}\leq C\epsilon $. Higher interior estimates make $v$ smooth. Hence $u(y)=y_1+v(y)$ is harmonic for the rescaled metric and $du(0)\ne 0$. Rescaling back gives a real smooth harmonic function near the original point with nonzero differential there. The oriented real Hodge star on one-forms is characterized in an oriented orthonormal coframe by $*e^1=e^2$, $*e^2=-e^1$. Harmonicity is $d(*du)=0$. Shrink to a coordinate ball, and use the radial Poincaré homotopy formula to obtain a real function $v_0$ with $dv_0=*du$. If $J$ is positive rotation by $\pi /2$, this says $dv_0=-du\circ J$. Therefore $dw\circ J=\mathrm i\, dw$ for $w=u+\mathrm iv_0$. Moreover $du,dv_0$ are perpendicular of equal positive norm, so the Jacobian is positive and the real inverse function theorem applies. In these coordinates $g=|du|_ g^{-2}(du^2+dv_0^2)$. Transitions satisfy the ordinary Cauchy–Riemann equations and hence are holomorphic by the local Cauchy theorem. This constructs the asserted complex atlas. For a given smooth $J$, first choose any smooth positive metric $h$ and replace it by $h(v,w)+h(Jv,Jw)$. Its positive rotation is $J$ for the orientation defined by $J$. The construction therefore proves integrability, without using a theorem in higher complex dimension. Two inner products invariant under this rotation are positive scalar multiples: in a basis $(e,Je)$ both have equal diagonal entries and zero off-diagonal entry. This proves the conformal-class assertion. The same calculation shows uniqueness of the complex atlas for the given $J$. Expanding the right side of ( 10.77.2 ) gives its stated coefficients, and \[  |\mu |^2=\frac{E+G-2\sqrt D}{E+G+2\sqrt D}<1.  \] A positive conformal coordinate has $dw=c(dz+\mu d\bar z)$: these one-forms span the same complex $(1,0)$ cotangent line. Thus $c=w_ z\ne 0$ and $w_{\bar z}=\mu w_ z$; its Jacobian is $|c|^2(1-|\mu |^2)>0$. Conversely $|dz+\mu d\bar z|^2$ is a positive oriented smooth metric whenever $|\mu |<1$, so the preceding construction applies. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.77.4
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Corollary 10.77.4 . FB7A8CA804B1 On an almost complex surface, exact local complex coordinates give approximate complex coordinates to every finite order. If a smooth complex-valued local real coordinate $z$, centered at the point, satisfies $d''z=O(|z|^ s)$ for an integer $s\geq 3$, then, on a fixed sufficiently small neighborhood, \[  |z|^2,\qquad |z|^2+\log (|z|^2+\epsilon ^2)  \] are strictly subharmonic for every $0<\epsilon \leq 1$. The neighborhood is independent of $\epsilon $. Proof. Use the exact complex coordinate $w$ just constructed and put $r=|z|$. The coordinate change is a real diffeomorphism, so $r$ and $|w|$ are comparable. The hypothesis gives $z_{\bar w}=O(r^ s)$ and $z_{w\bar w}=O(r^{s-1})$; the latter follows by taking the Taylor polynomial of the smooth former function. Also $|z_ w|$ has a positive lower bound after shrinking. For $A=|z|^2$ direct differentiation gives \[  A_{w\bar w}=|z_ w|^2+O(r^ s),\qquad |A_ w|^2=|z_ w|^2r^2+O(r^{s+2}).  \] Consequently \[  (A+\log (A+\epsilon ^2))_{w\bar w} =A_{w\bar w} +\frac{\epsilon ^2|z_ w|^2}{(r^2+\epsilon ^2)^2} +O\! \left(\frac{r^ s}{r^2+\epsilon ^2} +\frac{r^{s+2}}{(r^2+\epsilon ^2)^2}\right).  \] For $r>0$ the error is bounded by $Cr^{s-2}$ independently of $\epsilon $; at $r=0$ the error terms are zero. The fixed positive lower bound for $A_{w\bar w}$ now proves both assertions. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.77.5
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Lemma 10.77.5 . 6E44892C19CA A connected compact Riemann surface with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. Proof. Choose any smooth Hermitian metric. Its fundamental form is closed because the real dimension is two. The analytic compact Kähler Hodge decomposition theorem 10.47.13 therefore gives $H^{0,1}_{\bar\partial }(X)=0$ from the vanishing of the complexified de Rham group. These are smooth analytic groups; no sheaf or integral comparison is needed. Choose a holomorphic coordinate $z$ about a point $p$ and a smooth cutoff $\chi $ supported in its coordinate disk and equal to one near $p$. The form $\bar\partial (\chi /z)$ on $X\setminus \{ p\} $ extends to a smooth $(0,1)$-form on $X$, zero near $p$; it is closed. The just-proved cohomology vanishing, or its smooth Hodge realization, gives a smooth function $u$ with $\bar\partial u=\bar\partial (\chi /z)$. Thus $f=\chi /z-u$ is a meromorphic function with precisely one pole, a simple pole at $p$; it is holomorphic elsewhere. For $a\in \mathbb C$, the function $\log |f-a|^2$ is globally locally integrable. The canonical Poincaré–Lelong formula the normalized Poincaré–Lelong formula , applied also to the local quotient at the pole, gives \[  dd^ c\log |f-a|^2 =\sum _{f(x)=a}\operatorname {ord}_ x(f-a)\, \delta _ x-\delta _ p.  \] The sum is finite by isolatedness of zeros and compactness; a neighborhood of the pole contains no such zeros. Pairing this exact current with the constant function one gives total mass zero by Stokes. Hence every finite $a$ has exactly one preimage, of order one. Infinity has just the simple preimage $p$. The holomorphic map $f:X\to \mathbb P^1$ is therefore bijective and has nonzero local derivative everywhere, also in the coordinate $1/f$ at $p$. The local holomorphic inverse theorem gives a holomorphic inverse. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.77.6
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Lemma 10.77.6 . A2808AF4FEA1 Let $X$ be a connected noncompact oriented smooth surface with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$. There is an exhaustion by connected relatively compact open sets $\Omega _ j$, with smooth compact closures, $\overline\Omega _ j\subset \Omega _{j+1}$, such that no component of $X\setminus \overline\Omega _ j$ is relatively compact. Each $\partial \Omega _ j$ is one circle, and \[  H^1_{\rm dR}(\Omega _ j;\mathbb R)=0, \qquad H^1_{\rm dR}(Y_ j;\mathbb R)=0,  \] where $Y_ j$ is the oriented double of $\overline\Omega _ j$. Proof. We give the surface-topological details needed here, without using compact-support duality or classification of surfaces. Elementary neighborhoods and arcs. Every compact subset of a connected surface is contained in the interior of a connected compact bordered subsurface. Indeed, cover it by finitely many relatively compact coordinate disks, join their centers to a fixed center by finitely many coordinate paths, and cover those paths by finitely many more such disks with successive overlap. Choose their radii so that boundary circles meet transversely and avoid the finitely many earlier crossing points. This choice needs only the one-variable regular-value fact for the restriction of a radius function to an earlier boundary arc. For completeness, the critical values of a smooth function on a compact interval have measure zero: cover its critical set by finitely many intervals in the open set $|f'|<\delta $, merge overlapping intervals, and bound the total length of their images by $\delta $ times the total interval length. Let $\delta $ tend to zero, and use finitely many intervals for a circle. A regular level has finitely many intersections by compactness. Thus the disk union has finitely many corners and no triple corners. Round each corner outward inside a small coordinate box, disjoint from the others. In coordinates where the two crossing arcs are axes, replace their minimum defining function by $(s+t-\vartheta (s-t))/2$, where $\vartheta $ is a smooth convex regularization of $|\cdot |$, equal to it outside a small interval, with $|\vartheta '|\leq 1$. Its two partial derivatives sum to one, so its zero level is smooth. This gives the required neighborhood, still containing the original compact set in its interior. The boundary of a compact bordered surface has finitely many components, each a circle. One elementary verification of the last assertion is to flow a nonvanishing tangent vector field on a connected compact one-manifold: the orbit is open, hence is the whole component, and compactness forces a nonzero period; the component is a quotient of $\mathbb R$ by its period group. Each component of the complement of the bordered surface meets its boundary, by a path to an interior point, and one boundary circle has only one exterior side. There are therefore only finitely many such components. Adjoin the closures of all relatively compact ones. Their finite union is compact; the remaining boundary circles are unchanged and smooth. The resulting bordered surface is connected, and all its exterior components are not relatively compact. Starting with a countable relatively compact coordinate cover and repeating this construction with the previous bordered surface in the next interior proves the stated exhaustion. In a noncompact connected surface its bordered members have nonempty boundary. We will also use the following elementary arc constructions. A path in an open connected surface can be replaced by finitely many smooth coordinate arcs with transverse double crossings only. Each replacement inside a coordinate disk is a homotopy with fixed endpoints and preserves the integral of a closed form by its local primitive. To arrange this, subdivide into coordinate disks, move successive subarcs a small amount in their transverse coordinate, and choose regular values of the resulting one-variable restrictions to the finitely many earlier arcs. Avoid their finitely many crossing points as well. Transversality and compactness make all crossings finite. Erasing successive loops and rounding corners then gives an embedded arc, with prescribed transverse directions at its endpoints. The same procedure for a closed path gives finitely many embedded piecewise smooth circles after splitting at its finitely many crossings. Rounding a corner inside a coordinate disk does not change the integral of a closed form, because that form has a local primitive there. A connected noncompact surface with compact boundary has a proper embedded ray starting from any prescribed boundary point, transverse to the boundary there. Here proper means that the inverse image of every compact set is compact. To see this, exhaust it by the filled bordered neighborhoods just constructed, initially including a collar of its compact boundary. Begin an embedded arc to the first outer boundary. Given its endpoint, the component on the exterior side is not relatively compact. Join the endpoint, inside that component, to a point beyond the next exhaustion member; stop at the first exit from that member. Erase loops as above. This extension avoids the previous arc, which was inside the preceding member. The exterior component at the new endpoint is again not relatively compact, and is contained in the preceding exterior component. Continuing and rounding the locally finite joints produces an embedded ray whose successive tails lie outside every earlier compact member, proving properness. The same construction starts from an interior point. An embedded circle has a two-sided collar on an oriented surface: flow a smooth transverse normal field, and use compactness and the inverse function theorem to choose a uniform width. A proper embedded line likewise has a normal strip, parametrized by $(s,t)\in \mathbb R\times (-1,1)$, whose restriction to $\mathbb R\times [-1/2,1/2]$ is proper. To check the noncompact point in this assertion, exhaust the line by compact parameter intervals. Properness separates each such interval from sufficiently far tails, and compactness gives a positive tubular width on each remaining finite interval. Choose a positive smooth width below these locally finite bounds; the inverse function theorem and these separations make the normal flow injective. Shrink the width further on successive intervals so that their strips avoid each earlier ambient compact set once the line does. This proves the asserted properness. An embedded arc with endpoints on a smooth boundary has the identical construction with end half-strips. Every embedded circle has a compact side. Let $C\subset X$ be such a circle. Its complement has at most two components. Indeed, every component meets one of the two collar sides, by stopping a path to $C$ at its first contact with the collar; each collar side is connected. If the complement were connected, take a path in it joining the two outer sides of the collar, and complete it by an arc crossing the collar once. On the collar put $\beta =\chi (t)\, dt$, where $t$ is the normal coordinate, $\chi $ has support in the collar interior, and $\int \chi (t)\, dt=1$. Extend $\beta $ by zero. This is a smooth closed global form. On $X\setminus C$ it has a primitive: it is zero outside the collar, and on each half-collar take the integral of $\chi $ from its outer end. The joining path therefore has integral zero, whereas the crossing arc has integral one, up to orientation. This contradicts exactness of $\beta $ on $X$. Thus $C$ separates $X$ into two components. If the closures of both were noncompact, the proper-ray construction in each of these closed surfaces with boundary $C$, joined across its collar, would give a proper embedded line crossing $C$ just once. In its normal strip the form $\chi (t)\, dt$, with $\int \chi =1$ and support $|t|<1/2$, extends smoothly by zero and is closed on $X$. Properness ensures that no finite ambient point is an accumulation point of its support from unbounded $s$. Choose the strip thin enough that $C$ meets it only near the single crossing. Its integral on $C$ is $1$ or $-1$, again contradicting exactness. At least one closed side is consequently compact. It is a compact smooth surface $D$ with boundary $C$. Filled domains have zero first cohomology and one boundary. Let $W=\overline\Omega _ j$. If $C\subset \operatorname {int}W$ is an embedded circle, its compact side $D$ lies in $\operatorname {int}W$. Otherwise $D$ meets some exterior component of $W$: a point of $\partial W$ in $D$ is an interior point of $D$, since its boundary $C$ is disjoint from $\partial W$. Such an exterior component is connected and disjoint from $C$, so is wholly in the compact side, contradicting its failure to be relatively compact. Hence Stokes gives $\int _ C\alpha =0$ for every smooth closed one-form $\alpha $ on $\operatorname {int}W$. Splitting a general closed path into embedded circles by the finite arc construction proves that all its periods are zero. Path integration now supplies a smooth primitive: locally it differs by a constant from the radial Poincaré primitive. Thus $H^1_{\rm dR}(\operatorname {int}W;\mathbb R)=0$. If $W$ had two distinct boundary components, choose an embedded arc joining them and otherwise in the interior, meeting boundary collars only at its two ends. In its normal strip extend $\chi (t)\, dt$ by zero across the transverse sides; the longitudinal ends terminate on $\partial W$, so this is a smooth closed form on $W$. A sufficiently nearby interior parallel of the first boundary circle crosses this strip once, and has integral $1$ or $-1$. This contradicts the just proved exactness on $\operatorname {int}W$. The boundary is connected. The double. Glue two copies of $W$ with opposite orientations along their boundary, using the signed normal coordinate in a boundary collar. This gives a closed compact oriented smooth surface $Y$. It has open sets $A,B$ containing the two copies, respectively, each diffeomorphic to $\operatorname {int}W$ by compressing an attached collar. Their intersection is an annulus because the boundary is one circle. If $\alpha $ is a closed one-form on $Y$, write $\alpha =df_ A=df_ B$ on these two opens. Their primitives differ by a constant on the connected overlap. Adjusting that constant glues them to a global primitive. This proves $H^1_{\rm dR}(Y;\mathbb R)=0$. $\square$

title: Lemma 10.77.7
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Lemma 10.77.7 . 0FE8A815392E If $f:\Delta \to \mathbb C$ is injective and holomorphic, with $f(0)=0$ and $f'(0)=1$, then for $0\leq r<1$ and $|z|\leq r$, BB0211131FFC 10.77.8 \begin{equation}  |f'(z)|\leq \left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right)^6,\qquad |f(z)|\leq r\left(\frac{1+r}{1-r}\right)^6. \end{equation} In particular these normalized functions form a locally bounded family. Proof. We include the coefficient estimate needed for compactness. First an injective holomorphic function has no zero derivative: if its local first nonconstant term had order $m>1$, the argument principle on a small circle, applied to a nearby regular value, would give $m$ preimages there. The argument principle here follows directly by integrating the logarithmic derivative after factoring its finitely many zeros. Write $f(z)=z+a_2z^2+\cdots $. Since $f(z)/z$ has no zeros on the disk, it has a holomorphic logarithm, normalized to be zero at zero: integrate its logarithmic derivative, whose periods are zero on the disk by Cauchy's theorem. Thus \[  h(z)=z\exp \bigl (\tfrac 12\log (f(z^2)/z^2)\bigr ) =z+\tfrac 12a_2z^3+\cdots  \] is an odd injective function. Indeed equality of two values implies equality of $f(z^2)$, hence the arguments are equal or opposite; oddness and the unique zero at zero handle the latter case. The exterior function \[  H(\zeta )=1/h(1/\zeta ) =\zeta +\sum _{k\geq 1}b_ k\zeta ^{-k},\qquad b_1=-a_2/2,  \] is injective for $|\zeta |>1$ and has no constant term. For $1<r<R$, change of variables and orthogonality of the exponential functions on circles give 66093CD4561E 10.77.9 \begin{equation}  \operatorname {area} H(\{ r<|\zeta |<R\} ) =\pi (R^2-r^2)+\pi \sum _{k\geq 1}k|b_ k|^2(r^{-2k}-R^{-2k}). \end{equation} The Laurent series and its derivative converge uniformly on each closed subannulus; integrating their squares and then exhausting the open annulus justifies the formula and its nonnegative series. For fixed $r$ and large $R$, the maximum principle on the annulus bounds its entire image by the disk of radius $R+|b_1|/R+O(R^{-2})$; this outer bound eventually exceeds the fixed maximum on $|\zeta |=r$. Therefore the area is at most $\pi R^2+2\pi |b_1|+o(1)$. Subtract $\pi R^2$ in ( 10.77.9 ), retain only its $k=1$ term, and let $R\to \infty $, then $r\downarrow 1$. This gives $|b_1|^2\leq 1+2|b_1|$, so $|a_2|\leq 2(1+\sqrt2)<5$. This deliberately nonsharp estimate requires no complement-area or boundary Jordan-curve theorem. For $a\in \Delta $, apply it to the normalized injective function \[  w\longmapsto \frac{f((a+w)/(1+\bar a w))-f(a)}{(1-|a|^2)f'(a)}.  \] Its second coefficient is $(1-|a|^2)f''(a)/(2f'(a))-\bar a$. Consequently \[  \left|\frac{f''(a)}{f'(a)}\right| \leq \frac{10+2|a|}{1-|a|^2} \leq \frac{12}{1-|a|^2}.  \] Integrating the radial derivative of $\log |f'|$ from zero to $z$ proves the first estimate in ( 10.77.8 ), because $\int _0^ r12(1-t^2)^{-1}dt=6\log ((1+r)/(1-r))$. Integration of $f'$ along the same radius proves the second. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.77.10
section: 10.77 Complex coordinates and uniformization of surfaces
text: Theorem 10.77.10 . F2BDA05453B5 Every connected noncompact Riemann surface $X$ with $H^1_{\rm dR}(X;\mathbb R)=0$ admits an injective holomorphic map to $\mathbb C$. Every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of $\mathbb P^1$, $\mathbb C$, or the unit disk. Proof. First assume $X$ is noncompact with the stated de Rham vanishing, and take the exhaustion in lemma 10.77.6 . Its double $Y_ j$ admits a smooth positive metric agreeing with the given Hermitian metric on the first copy of $\overline\Omega _ j$. To construct it, use the metric already defined on both sides of $\partial \Omega _ j$ in $X$ to extend over a collar on the second copy; away from the seam interpolate with any positive metric by a smooth partition of unity. The signed collar defines the double's smooth structure, so this extension is smooth, including all derivatives at the seam. The orientation and theorem 10.77.1 give a complex structure on $Y_ j$ agreeing with the given one on the first copy. It has zero first de Rham cohomology and hence is biholomorphic to $\mathbb P^1$. Send a point in the interior of the second copy to infinity by a Möbius map. Restriction then gives an injective holomorphic map $\Phi _ j:\Omega _ j\to \mathbb C$. Fix $a\in \Omega _1$ and a nonzero complex cotangent vector $\xi \in T_ a^{1,0*}X$. Composing with an affine map, uniquely normalize $\Phi _ j(a)=0$ and $d\Phi _ j(a)=\xi $. We check local boundedness on all of $X$, rather than only at $a$. In a fixed coordinate disk about $a$, its coordinate derivative at the center is fixed, so scaling lemma 10.77.7 gives uniform bounds on every smaller disk. Suppose bounds have already been obtained near a point $b$. Cauchy's formula bounds $\Phi _ j'(b)$ there, as well as $\Phi _ j(b)$. On any fixed coordinate disk centered at $b$, normalize by these two quantities. Its restriction is injective, so ( 10.77.8 ), rescaled to that disk, gives uniform bounds on its smaller concentric disks. Every point can be reached from $a$ by a finite chain of such overlapping coordinate disks: subdivide a path into disks and choose each next center in the preceding smaller disk. This propagates local boundedness. A compact subset needs finitely many of these neighborhoods, so the bounds are uniform on every compact set, for all sufficiently large $j$ for which these disks lie in $\Omega _ j$. Cauchy's derivative estimates give equicontinuity on smaller coordinate disks. The proved Arzelà–Ascoli theorem the Arzelà–Ascoli compactness theorem , followed by a diagonal subsequence over a countable relatively compact coordinate cover, gives a locally uniform limit $\Phi :X\to \mathbb C$. Cauchy's formula makes the limit holomorphic and makes all local derivatives converge. In particular $\Phi (a)=0$ and $d\Phi (a)=\xi \ne 0$. The limit is injective. Otherwise take distinct $x,y$ with $\Phi (x)=\Phi (y)$ and a small closed coordinate disk about $x$ not containing $y$, whose boundary contains no zero of $\Phi -\Phi (y)$. This is possible because $\Phi $ is nonconstant. The logarithmic-derivative integral on that boundary is a positive integer. Uniform convergence of both functions and first derivatives makes it the limit of the analogous integrals for $\Phi _ j-\Phi _ j(y)$. Those integrals are zero, since injectivity of $\Phi _ j$ excludes a zero in the disk. This contradiction proves injectivity. Its derivative never vanishes by the elementary local argument in lemma 10.77.7 ; thus it is a biholomorphism onto an open plane domain $D$. This proves the embedding assertion. On a simply connected smooth manifold every closed one-form has a global primitive by path integration. Its local primitives make the integral invariant under path homotopy: subdivide a continuous homotopy square into finitely many cells whose images lie in coordinate balls, and cancel the increments of those primitives along common edges. Thus the preceding hypothesis applies to a simply connected surface. In its compact case use lemma 10.77.5 . In its noncompact case the embedding just proved identifies $X$ with a simply connected plane domain $D$. If $D=\mathbb C$ we are done. If it is proper, the already proved the Riemann map constructed from a Green function maps it biholomorphically onto the unit disk. The compact sphere cannot be biholomorphic to either noncompact surface. Nor can $\mathbb C$ be biholomorphic to the disk: the map to the disk would be a bounded nonconstant entire function, contrary to Cauchy's derivative estimate on disks of arbitrarily large radius. $\square$

title: 9.49 Convex functions near analytic subspaces
section: 9.49 Convex functions near analytic subspaces
text: Complex spaces here are Hausdorff with a countable basis. Smooth functions mean restrictions of smooth functions in local holomorphic embeddings; statements about functions depend only on the reduction. Fix an integer $q\geq 1$. A smooth function is strongly $q$-convex if locally it has an ambient extension whose Levi form has a positive subspace of codimension at most $q-1$. This condition is vacuous when the ambient dimension is less than $q$. An exhaustion has compact closed sublevels. A space is strongly $q$-complete if it has a smooth strongly $q$-convex exhaustion. In particular $q=1$ means a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion. Levi forms below use $\mathrm i\partial \bar\partial $; multiplying by $1/(2\pi )$ changes none of their signs. Lemma 9.49.1 . DD53C11960A9 Smooth partitions of unity subordinate to locally finite relatively compact embedding patches exist on a complex space. They can be chosen with nonnegative ambient extensions near every point. A smooth function on a closed analytic subspace has a global smooth extension. A complex space has a nonnegative smooth exhaustion. Strong $q$-convexity is independent of the embedding and is preserved by restriction to a complex submanifold or analytic subspace. If several Levi forms are positive on the same subspace of codimension at most $q-1$, every convex increasing combination has that property provided at least one positive coefficient is retained. Proof. Local compactness and a countable basis give compact sets $K_ j\subset \operatorname {int}K_{j+1}$ with union the space: take finite unions of closures from a countable relatively compact basis and enlarge successively. Cover each compact annulus by finitely many smaller embedding patches inside the prescribed cover. The resulting family is locally finite. Ordinary nonnegative ambient smooth bumps, positive on a smaller cover and supported in these patches, restrict to functions $b_ j$. Divide by the positive locally finite sum $\sum _ jb_ j$. Near a point all finitely many summands have ambient extensions, the denominator stays positive after shrinking, and each numerator may be chosen nonnegative, for example as a square. This proves the partition assertion and its local extension property. Patch local extensions of a smooth function on the analytic subspace using such a partition and the additional open set complementary to the subspace; their restrictions all equal the given function. Choose smooth $0\leq \chi _ j\leq 1$ equal to one near $K_ j$, supported in $\operatorname {int}K_{j+1}$. Then $r=\sum _ j(1-\chi _ j)$ is a locally finite smooth sum, is nonnegative, and satisfies $r\geq N$ off $K_{N+1}$, so is an exhaustion. Near a point choose $\lambda _0$ with $\theta _{\lambda _0}>0$ and use its embedding. Let $h=g_{\lambda _0}$ be the ambient ideal generators. Each of the finitely many other $g_\lambda $ can be written $A_\lambda h$ on $A$ after shrinking, since $h$ generates the ideal sheaf; the coefficient matrices lift holomorphically to the ambient patch. For $\lambda _0$ take $A_{\lambda _0}=I$. The nonnegative local extensions of the weights then give an extension \[  R_{\mathrm{ext}}=h^*Hh,\qquad H=\sum _\lambda \theta _\lambda A_\lambda ^*A_\lambda \geq \theta _{\lambda _0}I>0.  \] Thus $H$ is a smooth positive Hermitian matrix and is bounded above and below on a smaller compact patch. This proves the logarithmic comparison. Here is the required Levi bound, including its uniformity. At a fixed point a holomorphic linear change of frame makes $H=I$ and its holomorphic first derivatives zero: first take a constant square root, then cancel the first derivatives by a matrix affine in the coordinates. The line test proves the stated ambient plurisubharmonic extension. The identically zero ideal case has the same interpretation. These are intrinsic under changes of embeddings, so their local descriptions apply to spaces as well. Start with the irreducible components of $Y$; adjoin components of their singular sets and of finite intersections, and repeat. At most $d+1$ repetitions give a neighborhood meeting finitely many resulting components. The same argument works near every point, with its own finite $d$. It contains the singular set and all component intersections of its $k$-dimensional members in $Z_{k-1}$, and all smaller members are already there.
