The preceding conclusion applies with $K=\overline{X_ b}$ and gives an isomorphism $H^ k(X,\mathcal F)	o H^ k(X_ c,\mathcal F)$ for $k\geq q$, and density in degree $q-1$. Recursively include each previous compact closure and the next compact of an exhaustion of $U$ in $L$. This produces nested $V_
u \Subset V_{
u +1}$ of the form $X_ c$, for possibly different exhaustions, with union $U$. Restrictions $H^ k(V_{
u +1},\mathcal F)	o H^ k(V_
u ,\mathcal F)$ are isomorphisms for $k\geq q$: the two maps from $H^ k(X,\mathcal F)$ are isomorphisms and commute. In degree $q-1$ these restrictions are dense, because their images contain the dense image from $X$. Use again subfamilies of one countable relatively compact acyclic basis of $X$, this time with closures in $V_
u $. Their complexes have surjective coordinate transitions and inverse limit computing cohomology on $U$. Parts (1),(3) of the abstract theorem identify $H^ k(U,\mathcal F)$ with $H^ k(V_0,\mathcal F)$ for $k\geq q$. The restriction from $X$ is therefore an isomorphism, and it is topological by openness. For degree $q-1$, the complex on the full basis of $X$ projects degreewise surjectively onto that on $U$; all stage cohomology maps have dense image. Part (4) proves the asserted density on $U$. If $K=\varnothing $, shift the exhaustion to be nonnegative. Finite bumping from the empty sublevel $X_{-1}$ shows that every $H^ k(X_ c,\mathcal F)$ with $k\geq q$ is zero. The preceding limit isomorphism therefore proves full strongly $q$-complete vanishing. There is no degree-zero vanishing assertion. For generation take $q=1$ and $K=\varnothing $. The ideal $\mathcal I_ x$ of a point is coherent: locally it is generated by the ambient coordinate differences, acting on $\mathcal O_\Omega /\mathcal J$; off the point it is the whole structure sheaf. Its product $\mathcal I_ x\mathcal F$ is a coherent image of a finite local presentation. Its quotient is the skyscraper with finite stalk $\mathcal F_ x/\mathfrak m_ x\mathcal F_ x$. The vanishing already proved gives a surjection \[  \mathcal F(X)\longrightarrow \mathcal F_ x/\mathfrak m_ x\mathcal F_ x.  \] Lift a finite vector-space basis by global sections. title: Corollary 9.51.14
section: 9.51 Coherent sections and Stein vanishing
text: Corollary 9.51.14 . 19FC1BA2D71A Let $A\subset \Omega \subset \mathbb C^ N$ be any analytic patch, $\mathcal F$ coherent on $A$, and $U\subset A$ strongly $q$-convex. Then $H^ k(U,\mathcal F)=0$ for $k\geq q$. Moreover, for any coherent presentation $\mathcal O_ V^ r\to i_*\mathcal F\to 0$ on a strongly $1$-complete ambient $V$, the section map $\mathcal O(V)^ r\to \mathcal F(A\cap V)$ is an open surjection, and its quotient topology is the intrinsic one. Proof. The Euclidean compact-set upgrade already proved makes $U$ strongly $q$-complete. Apply the full coherent vanishing theorem, whose proof used sufficiently long resolutions only on smaller local patches available at every point. It places no resolution-length condition on $U$ or its given patch. For the second assertion the presentation kernel is coherent; its first cohomology on $V$ is zero by that theorem with $q=1$. Sheaf exactness gives section surjectivity. The section map is continuous between Fréchet spaces, so is open and has the asserted quotient topology. Thus the shorter local resolutions in a previously fixed distinguished patch are covered as well; the deliberately larger finite bound used in the foundational argument causes no loss of cases. $\square$

title: 10.56 Sheaf cohomology with prescribed supports
section: 10.56 Sheaf cohomology with prescribed supports
text: A family of supports on a space $X$ is a nonempty collection $\Phi $ of closed subsets, closed under finite unions and passage to closed subsets. In particular $\varnothing \in \Phi $. For a sheaf $F$ of abelian groups put \[  \Gamma _\Phi (X,F)=\{ s\in F(X):\operatorname {supp}s\in \Phi \} , \qquad \operatorname {supp}s=X\setminus \{ x:s_ x=0\} .  \] The zero-germ locus is open, so this support is closed. The support of a sum is contained in the union of the two supports, proving that $\Gamma _\Phi $ is an additive left-exact functor. For any subset $S\subset X$, the closed subsets contained in $S$ form a family, denoted $\Phi _ S$. All closed sets give ordinary global sections. The closed compact subsets form a family $c$ on any space: a closed subset of a compact space is compact, and finite unions are compact. On a Hausdorff space this is simply the family of all compact subsets. Closedness cannot be omitted in general: in the Sierpiński space with opens $\varnothing ,\{ 1\} ,\{ 0,1\} $ the compact subset $\{ 1\} $ is not closed. Use the exact Godement resolution of theorem 10.43.5 , with $C^ qF=G^{q+1}F$ and differential $d_ G$. Define \[  H^ q_\Phi (X,F)=H^ q\bigl (\Gamma _\Phi (X,C^\bullet F),d_ G\bigr ) \quad (q\ge 0),\qquad H^ q_\Phi (X,F)=0\quad (q<0).  \] Write $H^ q_ c$ for compact supports and $H^ q_ S$ for $\Phi _ S$. This latter group concerns supports in $S$; it is not the ordinary cohomology of the restricted sheaf on $S$. Theorem 10.56.1 . 391CCB0E8947 One has $H^0_\Phi (X,F)=\Gamma _\Phi (X,F)$. A short exact sequence of coefficient sheaves gives a natural long exact sequence of $H^ q_\Phi $. Inclusion of support families gives natural maps commuting with these sequences. Every flabby sheaf is $\Phi $-acyclic, for every family $\Phi $ on every space. More precisely, if $0\to A\to B\to Q\to 0$ has flabby kernel, every section of $Q$ lifts to a section of $B$ with support contained in the support of the given section. Proof. For a sheaf $E$, $GE(X)=\prod _{x\in X}E_ x$. An assignment with support in a closed $K$ is zero at every point outside $K$. Conversely an assignment zero there is a section zero on $X\setminus K$, so its support is contained in $K$. Given a surjection of sheaves, lift each nonzero coordinate and choose zero coordinates outside $K$. This proves that $\Gamma _\Phi (X,G-)$ is exact. Since $G$ itself is exact, every $\Gamma _\Phi (X,C^ q-)$ is exact. Thus a short exact coefficient sequence gives a degreewise short exact sequence of the defining complexes. Apply lemma 10.43.3 . Its representative construction proves naturality, including for inclusions of support families. The kernel in degree zero consists of actual sections of $F$; its support in $C^0F$ equals its support in $F$ because augmentation is injective on stalks. This proves $H^0$. For the asserted lift let $s\in Q(X)$, $K=\operatorname {supp}s$, and start with its zero lift on $X\setminus K$. Order extensions of this partial lift by extension. Gluing gives upper bounds for chains. If a maximal domain misses $x$, take a local lift $b_0$ near $x$. Its difference from the previous lift on the overlap is a section of $A$, by left exactness. Flabbiness extends that difference to the whole new neighborhood; correcting $b_0$ and gluing enlarges the domain. Hence the domain is $X$. The lift is zero on $X\setminus K$, so its support is contained in $K$. For flabby $A$, the kernels in its Godement resolution are flabby: the quotient of a flabby sheaf by a flabby subsheaf is flabby, by the ordinary lifting proof in theorem 10.43.7 . Each short kernel sequence is therefore exact after $\Gamma _\Phi $ by the just-proved support-preserving lift. This makes the supported Godement section complex exact in every positive degree. $\square$ Call a support family enlargable if for every $K\in \Phi $ there is $L\in \Phi $ with $K\subset \operatorname {int}L$. All paracompact spaces below are Hausdorff, as in section 10.44 . Theorem 10.56.2 . DE3B76CEB62B Let $X$ be paracompact and $\Phi $ enlargable. If $0\to A\to B\to Q\to 0$ has soft kernel, then $\Gamma _\Phi (X,B)\to \Gamma _\Phi (X,Q)$ is onto. Every soft sheaf on $X$ is $\Phi $-acyclic. Proof. Let $s$ have support $K\in \Phi $ and choose $L\in \Phi $ with $K\subset \operatorname {int}L$. By theorem 10.44.7 it has a global lift $b$. On the closed set $W=X\setminus \operatorname {int}L$ its image is zero, and exact inverse image and left exact sections give an $A$-section equal to $b|_ W$. Softness extends that section to $a\in A(X)$. Then $b-a$ is a lift of $s$ and its germ is zero at every point of $W$. Its support lies in $\operatorname {int}L$, hence is a closed subset of $L$ and belongs to $\Phi $. This argument allows enlargement from $K$ to $L$; it does not assert the exact-support property of the flabby case. Flabby sheaves are soft on a paracompact space, and quotients of soft sheaves by soft subsheaves are soft, by theorem 10.44.7 . Starting with a soft $A$, the kernel sequences of its Godement resolution therefore have soft kernels in every degree. The lifting just proved makes them exact after $\Gamma _\Phi $. This proves positive-degree acyclicity. $\square$ Theorem 10.56.3 . 7C0750CA5296 Let $0\to F\to L^0\to L^1\to \cdots $ be an exact augmented sheaf complex whose terms are $\Phi $-acyclic. Then successive positive connecting maps give natural isomorphisms \[  H^ q\bigl (\Gamma _\Phi (X,L^\bullet )\bigr )\simeq H^ q_\Phi (X,F).  \] They commute with augmented complex morphisms. In particular an identity-augmenting morphism between two such resolutions gives an isomorphism on supported section cohomology. Proof. Put $Z^0=F$ and $Z^ j=\ker (L^ j\to L^{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$. The exact sequences $0\to Z^{j-1}\to L^{j-1}\to Z^ j\to 0$ and the supported long exact sequence identify \[  \Gamma _\Phi Z^ q/d\Gamma _\Phi L^{q-1} \simeq H^1_\Phi (X,Z^{q-1}) \simeq \cdots \simeq H^ q_\Phi (X,F)\quad (q\ge 1).  \] The first step is a cokernel, and every subsequent step uses positive cohomological degree and acyclicity of the relevant $L^{j-1}$. The left side is the cohomology of the supported section complex, by left exactness of $\Gamma _\Phi $. For $q=0$ its kernel is simply $\Gamma _\Phi F$. Naturality of the connecting representatives proves the assertion about morphisms. This uses the same positive convention as theorem 10.43.8 . $\square$

title: 10.56.4 Compact supports and extension by zero
search_title: Compact supports and extension by zero
section: 10.56 Sheaf cohomology with prescribed supports
text: Lemma 10.56.5 . 899BD7174FB8 A locally compact Hausdorff space is regular. Every compact subset has an open neighborhood with compact closure, and such neighborhoods are cofinal among its open neighborhoods. Every compact subspace is strongly paracompact in the ambient space. Restriction of a flabby sheaf to a compact subspace is soft. In particular, a second-countable locally compact Hausdorff space is paracompact. Proof. For regularity choose a compact neighborhood $N$ of $x$ and an open set $O$ containing $x$. The compact Hausdorff space $N$ is paracompact (finite subcovers are locally finite), hence regular by lemma 10.44.2 . Inside $N$ choose a relative open neighborhood of $x$ whose relative closure lies in $O\cap \operatorname {int}_ X N$. That neighborhood is open in $X$, and its ambient closure is the same compact relative closure. This proves regularity and arbitrarily small relatively compact point neighborhoods. Finite unions give the assertion for compact subsets. For a compact $K$ and any ambient open cover, choose at each point an ambient open neighborhood with closure in a prescribed member; finitely many cover $K$. This is exactly the strong-paracompact refinement condition, with $W=X$. If $A$ is flabby, a section on a closed subset of $K$ extends to an ambient neighborhood by theorem 10.44.4 , since that subset is compact. Flabbiness extends it to $X$, then restrict to $K$. Thus $A|_ K$ is soft. For the final assertion choose countably many relatively compact basis members covering $X$. Repeatedly enlarge finite unions of their compact closures to relatively compact open sets, obtaining $V_ j$ with $\overline{V_ j}\subset V_{j+1}$ and $\bigcup V_ j=X$. Given any open cover, cover each compact annulus $\overline{V_ j}\setminus V_{j-1}$ by finitely many open sets subordinate to it, with closures contained also in $V_{j+1}\setminus \overline{V_{j-2}}$; take $V_ j=\varnothing $ for $j\le 0$. Regularity and compactness give these finite families. Together they cover $X$ and are locally finite: a neighborhood $V_ N$ misses every family with $j\ge N+2$. This is the required locally finite refinement. $\square$ Consequently compact supports are enlargable on a locally compact Hausdorff space. On a locally compact paracompact space soft sheaves are therefore compact-support acyclic. For an open $U\subset X$, let $F_ U$ denote the extension-by-zero subsheaf of $F$: on an open $V$ its sections are those sections of $F(V)$ whose germs vanish at every point of $V\setminus U$. Its stalk is $F_ x$ for $x\in U$ and zero otherwise. Thus $F\mapsto F_ U$ is exact, as can be checked on stalks. Proposition 10.56.6 . 984908A81943 On a paracompact space, extension by zero $A_ U$ of a soft sheaf $A$ is soft. For a closed subspace $Z$ of a locally compact paracompact space $X$, with $U=X\setminus Z$, there is a natural long exact sequence \[  \cdots \to H_ c^ q(U,F|_ U)\to H_ c^ q(X,F) \to H_ c^ q(Z,F|_ Z)\to H_ c^{q+1}(U,F|_ U)\to \cdots .  \] For any open cover $X=U\cup V$ there is the compact-support Mayer–Vietoris sequence \[  \cdots \to H_ c^ q(U\cap V,F)\to H_ c^ q(U,F)\oplus H_ c^ q(V,F) \to H_ c^ q(X,F)\to H_ c^{q+1}(U\cap V,F)\to \cdots .  \] Maps from an open subset are extension maps; arbitrary restriction from $X$ to an open subset need not preserve compact support. Proof. A section of $A_ U$ on a closed $S$ gives an $A$-section there whose germs vanish on $S\setminus U$. Paste it with the zero section on $X\setminus U$, using the closed-germ-pasting argument in section 10.44 . Softness of $A$ extends this section on $S\cup (X\setminus U)$ to $X$. Its germs vanish outside $U$, so the extension lies in $A_ U(X)$. This proves softness of $A_ U$. We first identify the groups needed in these sequences. A compactly supported section on $U$ extends by zero: its compact support is closed in the Hausdorff space $X$, and one glues on $U$ and the open complement of that support. Conversely a compactly supported section of $F_ U$ on $X$ has compact support contained in $U$. Hence these section groups agree. Apply this to the resolution $(C^\bullet F)_ U$ of $F_ U$. Its terms are soft on $X$ and compact-support acyclic. On $U$ the terms $C^ qF|_ U$ are flabby (the Godement construction commutes with open restriction), hence compact-support acyclic there. This does not require an arbitrary open subset of $X$ to be paracompact, or an arbitrary open restriction of a soft sheaf to be soft. The resolution comparison therefore gives \[  H_ c^ q(X,F_ U)\simeq H_ c^ q(U,F|_ U).  \] These identifications commute with the inclusion of open sets, by the same augmented-resolution maps. For the closed inclusion $i:Z\to X$, direct image is exact: its stalk at a point of $Z$ is the original stalk, and its stalk outside $Z$ is zero. It preserves flabby sheaves. A flabby resolution on $Z$ therefore pushes to a flabby resolution on $X$. Compact section groups agree under this pushforward, since compact subsets of $Z$ are exactly compact subsets of $X$ contained in $Z$. Thus $H_ c^ q(X,i_*F|_ Z)=H_ c^ q(Z,F|_ Z)$. The stalkwise exact sequence $0\to F_ U\to F\to i_*F|_ Z\to 0$ gives the first long exact sequence. No extension theorem for arbitrary sections across $Z$ is asserted: surjectivity of the sheaf map is a stalkwise assertion. Finally the sequence \[  0\to F_{U\cap V}\xrightarrow {s\mapsto (s,-s)}F_ U\oplus F_ V \xrightarrow {(a,b)\mapsto a+b}F\to 0  \] is exact on every stalk because $U\cup V=X$. The supported long exact sequence and the open identifications just proved give the displayed Mayer–Vietoris sequence with its stated signs. $\square$ Theorem 10.56.7 . 2E236442C324 Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and $F$ a sheaf. Then \[  H_ c^ q(X,F)\simeq \varinjlim _{U\Subset X} H^ q(\overline U,F_ U|_{\overline U}),  \] where $U\Subset X$ means open with compact closure. Transition maps are extension by zero, represented by the complexes in the proof. The closed subspace $\overline U$ is essential in this formula. Proof. The exact extension-by-zero functor and exact closed restriction make $(C^\bullet F)_ U|_{\overline U}$ a resolution of $F_ U|_{\overline U}$. Each $C^ qF$ is a module over the unital ring sheaf $C^ q\mathbb Z=G^{q+1}\underline{\mathbb Z}$, by iterating the pointwise product and module actions of $G$. Thus $(C^ qF)_ U|_{\overline U}$ is a module over $(C^ q\mathbb Z)|_{\overline U}$. This ring is soft by lemma 10.56.5 , since $C^ q\mathbb Z$ is flabby. The compact Hausdorff space $\overline U$ is paracompact, so corollary 10.44.9 makes these module terms acyclic for ordinary cohomology there. A section of $(C^ qF)_ U$ on $\overline U$ has closed support in that compact subspace and zero germs on $\overline U\setminus U$. Its support is consequently a compact subset of $U$. Restriction to $U$ followed by zero extension identifies it with a global $C^ qF$-section supported in $U$. Conversely any such section restricts to the prescribed sheaf on $\overline U$. The resolution comparison therefore identifies the displayed ordinary cohomology group with the cohomology of this global supported subcomplex. These subcomplexes increase under $U\subset V$, and their union is $\Gamma _ c(X,C^\bullet F)$, since every compact subset lies inside some relatively compact open set. Cohomology commutes with this directed union: a cycle is a cycle at one stage, and an equality to a boundary has its primitive at a later stage. This proves the isomorphism and defines its natural extension transition maps. No equality between $(C^ qF)_ U$ and $C^ q(F_ U)$ is used. $\square$

No extension theorem for arbitrary sections across $Z$ is asserted: surjectivity of the sheaf map is a stalkwise assertion. Finally the sequence \[  0\to F_{U\cap V}\xrightarrow {s\mapsto (s,-s)}F_ U\oplus F_ V \xrightarrow {(a,b)\mapsto a+b}F\to 0  \] is exact on every stalk because $U\cup V=X$. The supported long exact sequence and the open identifications just proved give the displayed Mayer–Vietoris sequence with its stated signs. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.56.7
section: 10.56 Sheaf cohomology with prescribed supports
text: Theorem 10.56.7 . 2E236442C324 Let $X$ be locally compact Hausdorff and $F$ a sheaf. Then \[  H_ c^ q(X,F)\simeq \varinjlim _{U\Subset X} H^ q(\overline U,F_ U|_{\overline U}),  \] where $U\Subset X$ means open with compact closure. Transition maps are extension by zero, represented by the complexes in the proof. The closed subspace $\overline U$ is essential in this formula. Proof. The exact extension-by-zero functor and exact closed restriction make $(C^\bullet F)_ U|_{\overline U}$ a resolution of $F_ U|_{\overline U}$. Each $C^ qF$ is a module over the unital ring sheaf $C^ q\mathbb Z=G^{q+1}\underline{\mathbb Z}$, by iterating the pointwise product and module actions of $G$. Thus $(C^ qF)_ U|_{\overline U}$ is a module over $(C^ q\mathbb Z)|_{\overline U}$. This ring is soft by lemma 10.56.5 , since $C^ q\mathbb Z$ is flabby. The compact Hausdorff space $\overline U$ is paracompact, so corollary 10.44.9 makes these module terms acyclic for ordinary cohomology there. A section of $(C^ qF)_ U$ on $\overline U$ has closed support in that compact subspace and zero germs on $\overline U\setminus U$. Its support is consequently a compact subset of $U$. Restriction to $U$ followed by zero extension identifies it with a global $C^ qF$-section supported in $U$. Conversely any such section restricts to the prescribed sheaf on $\overline U$. The resolution comparison therefore identifies the displayed ordinary cohomology group with the cohomology of this global supported subcomplex. These subcomplexes increase under $U\subset V$, and their union is $\Gamma _ c(X,C^\bullet F)$, since every compact subset lies inside some relatively compact open set. Cohomology commutes with this directed union: a cycle is a cycle at one stage, and an equality to a boundary has its primitive at a later stage. This proves the isomorphism and defines its natural extension transition maps. No equality between $(C^ qF)_ U$ and $C^ q(F_ U)$ is used. $\square$

title: 10.56.8 Compactly supported Čech cochains
section: 10.56 Sheaf cohomology with prescribed supports
text: Let $X$ be locally compact paracompact. Covers in this subsection are locally finite covers $\mathcal U=(U_ i)$ by relatively compact open sets. They are cofinal among open covers: choose relatively compact point neighborhoods subordinate to a given cover, then take a locally finite refinement, whose members still have compact closures. Common refinements of the same kind exist by the same argument. Use all ordered index tuples, including repetitions, as in theorem 10.43.16 . Let $C_ c^ a(\mathcal U,F)$ be the subgroup of cochains with only finitely many nonzero coefficient sections. It is a subcomplex. Indeed, for each nonzero tuple a nonzero coefficient of its coboundary can add only an index whose open set meets the tuple's intersection; all such indices meet the compact closure of one member of that tuple, hence are finite by local finiteness. There are only finitely many original tuples. Refinement maps preserve finite support: every refined index in a nonzero pulled-back tuple meets the compact union of the closures of the finitely many original active members, and only finitely many refined members do so. The refinement prisms have the same property. Thus the usual refinement homotopies define the groups \[  \check H_ c^ q(\mathcal U,F)=H^ q(C_ c^\bullet (\mathcal U,F)), \qquad \check H_ c^ q(X,F)=\varinjlim _{\mathcal U}\check H_ c^ q(\mathcal U,F).  \] Theorem 10.56.9 . C9EFB9BEE0D7 On a locally compact paracompact space there are natural fixed-cover comparison maps $\check H_ c^ q(\mathcal U,F)\to H_ c^ q(X,F)$, compatible with refinement. On direct limits they commute with the coefficient connecting maps and induce isomorphisms \[  \check H_ c^ q(X,F)\simeq H_ c^ q(X,F).  \] No good-cover or separability assumption is needed. Proof. Use the double complex $C_ c^ a(\mathcal U,C^ bF)$ with differential $D=\delta +(-1)^ a d_ G$. Its horizontal augmentation is $\Gamma _ c(X,C^ bF)$. The ring $C^ b\mathbb Z$ is flabby, hence soft on $X$, so it has a locally finite partition of $1$ subordinate to $\mathcal U$ by corollary 10.44.9 . Writing this partition as $(\rho _ i)$, the usual contraction is \[  (hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{a-1}}= \sum _ j\rho _ j c_{j i_0\ldots i_{a-1}}.  \] Products on an intersection extend by zero because $\operatorname {supp}\rho _ j\subset U_ j$. The identity $\delta h+h\delta =1$ follows by expanding the alternating sum and using $\sum \rho _ j=1$; it is the same identity as in lemma 10.43.14 . For a finite cochain the output has only tuples obtained by deleting the first index of an active tuple, so remains finite. In augmentation degree, a compactly supported section meets only finitely many $U_ i$, so its restrictions, and its partition components, are finite as well. Degree-zero cocycles glue to a global section supported in the compact union of the closures of their active members. Conversely a compactly supported global section restricts to finitely many nonzero members. Thus the horizontal augmented rows are exact. By lemma 10.43.15 , the horizontal augmentation identifies the cohomology of this finite-diagonal total complex with $H_ c^ q(X,F)$. The vertical sheaf augmentation from $C_ c^\bullet (\mathcal U,F)$ gives the fixed-cover comparison by this isomorphism. The construction commutes with refinement up to the same finite-support-preserving prism as above. We check the coefficient exact sequence rather than assuming cochain lifts on a fixed cover. For $0\to A\to B\to Q\to 0$, apply lemma 10.44.11 to a finite $Q$-cochain. Its pullback has a lift after a locally finite refinement. The refinement still consists of relatively compact sets. Choose the zero lift whenever the corresponding original coefficient is zero. Every potentially nonzero refined tuple then uses only members meeting the compact union of the original active closures, so there are only finitely many such tuples. The lift is a finite cochain. This also applies to a finite bounding cochain. Consequently the liftable-cochain argument of theorem 10.44.12 applies with finite cochains: a class is representable by a liftable cocycle after refinement, and a liftable class which bounds becomes a boundary of a liftable cochain after another refinement. Filtered limits are exact by the eventual-zero representative argument. This constructs the natural long exact sequence of $\check H_ c^ q(X,-)$. Compatibility with the supported Godement connecting maps follows from actual short exact total complexes: every $\Gamma (U_{i_0\ldots i_ a},C^ b-)$ is exact, and taking the algebraic direct sum over tuples, with finite support for each element, preserves exactness. The liftable finite-Čech complexes map to these totals by vertical augmentation, while the short exact supported Godement section complexes map by horizontal augmentation. Both commute with coefficient maps. The elementary long-exact-sequence naturality of lemma 10.43.3 in these two diagrams proves the asserted compatibility, with the unchanged total sign. In degree zero the comparison is the gluing isomorphism to $\Gamma _ c(X,F)$. For $C^0F$ its positive Čech groups on every cover vanish by the partition contraction above; its positive supported Godement groups vanish by flabbiness. Embed any $F$ in $C^0F$ and put $Q=C^0F/F$. In degree one, both long exact sequences give the cokernel of $\Gamma _ c C^0F\to \Gamma _ c Q$, and the comparison is the identity on that cokernel. In higher degrees the positive connecting isomorphisms shift to $Q$ and one lower degree. Induction, using the already checked connecting compatibility, proves that the canonical comparison is an isomorphism in every degree. $\square$

title: 10.57 Compact-supported forms, currents and compact duality

section: 10.57 Compact-supported forms, currents and compact duality
text: Corollary 10.57.1 . A9627E651E13 Let $M$ be a paracompact smooth real manifold without boundary. Its compactly supported de Rham complex computes $H_ c^ q(M,\mathbb R)$, and likewise with complex coefficients. If $M$ is oriented of dimension $d$, inclusion of forms into degree currents gives isomorphisms \[  H^ q(\mathcal A_ c^\bullet (M),d) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D_ c'{}^{\bullet }(M),d) \simeq H_ c^ q(M,\mathbb R).  \] A degree-$q$ current here acts on test forms of degree $d-q$; the corresponding dimension notation is therefore $\mathcal D'_{d-q}$. For a complex manifold $X$ and a holomorphic vector bundle $E$, one has, naturally and compatibly with inclusion of smooth forms in currents, \[  H^ q(\mathcal A_ c^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E) \simeq H_ c^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E)) \simeq H^ q(\mathcal D_ c'{}^{p,\bullet }(X,E),\bar\partial _ E).  \] Complex manifolds use their canonical orientation. No arbitrary metric connection is asserted to give a square-zero real de Rham complex. Proof. The complete local smooth/current de Rham and Dolbeault resolutions, including holomorphic bundle coefficients, are those of corollary 10.43.11 . Their terms are modules over the smooth function sheaf. That ring has subordinate smooth partitions and is soft by the checked cutoff construction; its module sheaves are soft by corollary 10.44.9 . Smooth manifolds are locally compact Hausdorff, so compact supports are enlargable. The terms are compact-support acyclic by theorem 10.56.2 . Apply theorem 10.56.3 . The inclusion of forms into currents is an identity-augmenting resolution morphism, with the exterior-current signs already fixed in those local resolutions, so it gives exactly the stated cohomology comparison. The orientation assumption is used to embed real forms by integration as currents acting on ordinary test forms. The smooth real de Rham resolution itself needs no orientation. $\square$ Corollary 10.57.2 . 12F3669A5BAA If $M$ is a compact oriented smooth manifold without boundary, the above identifications give a perfect pairing \[  H_ c^ q(M,\mathbb R)\times H^{d-q}(M,\mathbb R) \longrightarrow \mathbb R, \qquad ([u],[v])\longmapsto \int _ Mu\wedge v.  \] For a compact complex manifold and holomorphic bundle $E$, they give the perfect complex bilinear pairing \[  H_ c^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E))\times H^{n-q}(X,\Omega _ X^{n-p}\otimes \mathcal O(E^*)) \longrightarrow \mathbb C  \] represented by evaluation, wedge and integration. These assertions are for compact manifolds; no noncompact topological duality or closed-range statement follows from the support comparison alone. Proof. On a compact space every section has compact support, so the supported and ordinary Godement complexes coincide. The differential-resolution comparisons therefore reduce the statements to the already checked compact analytic pairings corollary 10.46.10 , theorem 10.46.7 . For the real scalar case take the trivial flat bundle. The real differential and its adjoint preserve real forms, so real harmonic representatives exist by taking real parts; the real Hodge star gives the positive norm-square pairing. Nondegeneracy and finite harmonic dimension give perfection over $\mathbb R$. In complex dimension $n$, use the dual holomorphic bundle and the complementary bidegree specified in the existing analytic theorem. No sheaf cup-product comparison or integral-homology duality is assumed in this reduction. $\square$

title: 20.5.1 Divisors on analytic cycles
section: 20.5 Divisors and logarithmic limits on analytic cycles
text:
We use $dd^ c= rac{i}{2\pi }\partial  ar\partial $ and therefore $dd^ c\log |f|^2=[\operatorname {Div}(f)]$ on a manifold. For a reduced pure-dimensional analytic subset $A$, $[A]$ denotes integration over $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$, with coefficient measures extended by zero on $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$, as in theorem 5.61.2 . An effective integral analytic $p$-cycle is a locally finite sum $\sum a_ j[A_ j]$, where the $A_ j$ are distinct irreducible $p$-dimensional analytic subsets and the $a_ j$ are positive integers. Lemma 20.5.2 . 551A781E3A1C Let $g_ j,g$ be holomorphic on a complex manifold, with $g_ j	o g$ locally uniformly. Suppose $g$ is not identically zero on any connected component. Then, locally for all sufficiently large $j$, $\log |g_ j|^2$ is integrable, and \[  \log |g_ j|^2\longrightarrow \log |g|^2 \quad \hbox{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}  \] with respect to smooth volume. In particular this holds for $g_ j=g-\varepsilon _ j$, $\varepsilon _ j	o 0$; no monotonicity is required. Proof. Work on a connected coordinate ball. The identity theorem shows that $g$ is not identically zero there. Choose a point $b$ with $g(b)
e 0$; then $g_ j(b)
e 0$ for all large $j$. By the distributional Hessian of a holomorphic logarithm , the logarithms are plurisubharmonic and integrable, and they are locally uniformly bounded above by local uniform boundedness of $g_ j$. Apply plurisubharmonic compactness and Hartogs' lemma to any subsequence. Its alternative of locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $ is excluded by convergence at $b$. It therefore has a further subsequence converging in local $L^1$. A further extraction converges almost everywhere: on each compact set choose summable $L^1$ errors and use the integrability of their sum, then diagonalize. Outside $\{ g=0\} $ the original sequence converges pointwise to $\log |g|^2$. That zero set is null by measure-zero holomorphic zero sets , so every $L^1$ cluster limit is $\log |g|^2$. If full convergence failed on a compact set, a subsequence with its $L^1$ distance bounded below would contradict this conclusion. Finite coordinate covers prove the assertion for any smooth volume. On a zero-dimensional manifold it is ordinary convergence at each of the finitely many points in a compact set. $\square$ Lemma 20.5.3 . 323D5DA3E240 Let $D$ be an irreducible hypersurface of a smooth complex manifold $M$ of dimension $r+1$, and let $F:M	o X$ be holomorphic, proper on $D$. Write $B=F(D)$. If $\dim B<r$, then $F_*[D]=0$. If $\dim B=r$, there is an integer $d\geq 1$ such that \[  F_*[D]=d[B].  \] Here $d$ is the number of sheets of $F|_ D$ over the complement of a proper analytic subset of $B$. No integrality assertion about an arbitrary weak limit of cycles is used. Proof. The image is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and has dimension at most $r$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . It is irreducible: a decomposition into two proper analytic subsets would pull back to such a decomposition of $D$. These assertions also give purity of $B$ by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . The current $[D]$ and its proper pushforward are well defined by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces , pushforward of currents proper on their support . If $\dim B<r$, the derivative of $F|_{D_{\mathrm{reg}}}$ has rank less than $r$ everywhere. Otherwise the constant rank theorem near a point of maximal rank would put an $r$-dimensional submanifold in $B$, contradicting its dimension. Every pulled-back $(r,r)$-form therefore vanishes on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$, proving the first assertion. For $r=0$, $D$ is one point and its pushforward is the unit point mass at its image, so the second assertion holds with $d=1$. Assume henceforth $r\geq 1$ and $\dim B=r$. We construct the entire critical exceptional set analytically, including at singular points of $D$. On a coordinate neighborhood in $M$, choose a reduced local equation $e$ of $D$ by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces . In target coordinates $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$, put C02C6380EF73 20.5.4  egin{equation}  Q=\left\{ e=0:\  de\wedge dF_{i_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge dF_{i_ r}=0 	ext{ for every }i_1<\cdots <i_ right\} . \end{equation} These equations include $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, where $de=0$, and on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ express exactly rank less than $r$. Multiplying $e$ by a unit changes its differential on $D$ by that unit; changing target coordinates takes invertible linear combinations of the displayed minors. Thus these local analytic sets agree and define a closed analytic subset $Q\subset D$. It is proper. If it were all of $D$, the image of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ would be $\mathcal H^{2r}$-null by dimension bounds for holomorphic images ; so would the image of $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, by its smaller dimension and analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Countably many charts suffice. This cannot cover the regular locus of the $r$-dimensional analytic set $B$. Hence $\dim Q\leq r-1$. The set \[  Z=B_{\mathrm{sing}}\cup F(Q)  \] is analytic, closed in $B$, and has dimension at most $r-1$; properness and the same image dimension bound justify this for $F(Q)$. The manifold $B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected by global irreducible analytic components . Removing its proper analytic subset $Z\cap B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ leaves it connected, by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements . Over $B\setminus Z$ every source point is regular with derivative rank $r$. The inverse function theorem on these two $r$-manifolds makes $F$ a local biholomorphism there. Every fiber is compact by properness and discrete by this local description, hence finite. For any such fiber take finitely many disjoint inverse neighborhoods. Properness supplies a smaller target neighborhood with its whole inverse image in their union: the image of their closed complement in $D$ is closed and misses the target point. Intersect the inverse neighborhood images as well. This is an evenly covered neighborhood. The sheet number is a positive locally constant integer and therefore a fixed $d\geq 1$ on the connected $B\setminus Z$. Holomorphic coordinate change preserves complex orientation, so integration over these sheets gives $F_*[D]=d[B]$ off $Z$. There is no unexamined current supported on $Z$ in this equality. Indeed $F^{-1}(Z)\cap D$ is a proper analytic subset of $D$. Its intersection with $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has smooth volume zero: locally it lies in a nontrivial holomorphic zero set, and the connectedness and density of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ exclude an open component. The integration defining $[D]$ assigns its singular locus zero coefficient mass as well. For a compact target set, properness puts its inverse image in a compact source set; there the coefficients of $F^*$ of a bounded test form are bounded by a constant times the induced volume on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Consequently every coefficient measure of $F_*[D]$ gives $Z$ zero mass. This follows first for positive trace tests from the integral formula and then for all coefficients by coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents . The same argument on $B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ shows that $[B]$ gives $Z$ zero mass. Their equality off $Z$ is therefore their equality everywhere. $\square$ Theorem 20.5.5 . F1C928146DBC Let $A$ be a reduced pure $p$-dimensional analytic subset of a complex manifold $X$, and let $f$ be holomorphic near $A$, not identically zero on any irreducible component of $A$. Then $\log |f|^2$ is coefficient-integrable for $[A]$. If $p\geq 1$ and $C_ k$ are the irreducible components of $A\cap \{ f=0\} $, there are positive integers $m_ k$ such that 14ADBD4BFF7F 20.5.6  egin{equation}  dd^ c igl (\log |f|^2[A] igr )=\sum _ k m_ k[C_ k]. \end{equation} The sum is locally finite. The same assertion applies linearly to effective integral analytic cycles whose components are not contained in $\{ f=0\} $. If $f_ j	o f$ locally uniformly holomorphically, the logarithms converge to $\log |f|^2$ in local coefficient $L^1([A])$, whenever the local logarithms are defined for large $j$. In particular 85DED4E0947F 20.5.7  egin{equation}  dd^ c igl (\log |f-\varepsilon |^2[A] igr ) \longrightarrow dd^ c igl (\log |f|^2[A] igr ) \quad (\varepsilon 	o 0). \end{equation} For $p=0$ the hypotheses force $f$ to be nonzero at every point of $A$; the Hessian current is zero and the local logarithm convergence is ordinary convergence against finitely many point masses. Proof. All assertions are local on $X$. Local finiteness of components reduces the proof to one irreducible component $A$; all sums below are finite over each compact target neighborhood. The identity principle on the connected $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$ shows that $f$ is nontrivial on every local branch: vanishing on one branch would force vanishing on a nonempty regular open subset of $A$, hence on $A$. In particular its zero set is pure of dimension $p-1$ when nonempty, by purity of a nontrivial holomorphic zero set . We may assume $p\geq 1$, the point-mass case being as stated. Take the proper bimeromorphic resolution $\pi :M	o A\subset X$ of the stated resolution-of-singularities input . The composition to $X$ is proper because $A$ is closed. Each component of $M$ has dimension $p$ and meets the isomorphism locus; the exceptional analytic set $E=\pi ^{-1}(A_{\mathrm{sing}})$ is proper on every such component by nowhere-dense inverse images under bimeromorphic maps . It has smooth volume zero by the holomorphic zero-set lemma. Off $E$ the map is a biholomorphism onto $A_{\mathrm{reg}}$. For a compact target set $K$, $\pi ^{-1}(K)$ is compact, and $\pi ^* eta ^ p$ is bounded by a smooth volume form times a constant there, where $ eta $ is any smooth positive ambient Hermitian form. Thus the pushforward of the integration current of $M$ has locally finite mass, equals $[A]$ off $A_{\mathrm{sing}}$, and gives that singular set zero mass because $E$ is null. Hence \[  \pi _*[M]=[A].  \] This also directly checks the coefficient convention at singularities. Put $g=f\circ \pi $. It is nontrivial on every component of $M$. By the distributional Hessian of a holomorphic logarithm , $\log |g|^2$ is locally integrable for smooth volume. The preceding compact pullback bound therefore proves \[  \int _ K|\log |f|^2|\, [A]\wedge  eta ^ p =\int _{\pi ^{-1}(K)}|\log |g|^2|\, \pi ^* eta ^ p<\infty .  \] The equality uses change of variables off the respective null sets; there is no product of an infinite value with a positive atom there. title: Lemma 20.5.2
section: 20.5 Divisors and logarithmic limits on analytic cycles
text: Lemma 20.5.2 . 551A781E3A1C Let $g_ j,g$ be holomorphic on a complex manifold, with $g_ j\to g$ locally uniformly. Suppose $g$ is not identically zero on any connected component. Then, locally for all sufficiently large $j$, $\log |g_ j|^2$ is integrable, and \[  \log |g_ j|^2\longrightarrow \log |g|^2 \quad \hbox{in }L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}  \] with respect to smooth volume. In particular this holds for $g_ j=g-\varepsilon _ j$, $\varepsilon _ j\to 0$; no monotonicity is required. Proof. Work on a connected coordinate ball. The identity theorem shows that $g$ is not identically zero there. Choose a point $b$ with $g(b)\ne 0$; then $g_ j(b)\ne 0$ for all large $j$. By the distributional Hessian of a holomorphic logarithm , the logarithms are plurisubharmonic and integrable, and they are locally uniformly bounded above by local uniform boundedness of $g_ j$. Apply plurisubharmonic compactness and Hartogs' lemma to any subsequence. Its alternative of locally uniform convergence to $-\infty $ is excluded by convergence at $b$. It therefore has a further subsequence converging in local $L^1$. A further extraction converges almost everywhere: on each compact set choose summable $L^1$ errors and use the integrability of their sum, then diagonalize. Outside $\{ g=0\} $ the original sequence converges pointwise to $\log |g|^2$. That zero set is null by measure-zero holomorphic zero sets , so every $L^1$ cluster limit is $\log |g|^2$. If full convergence failed on a compact set, a subsequence with its $L^1$ distance bounded below would contradict this conclusion. Finite coordinate covers prove the assertion for any smooth volume. On a zero-dimensional manifold it is ordinary convergence at each of the finitely many points in a compact set. $\square$

title: Lemma 20.5.3
section: 20.5 Divisors and logarithmic limits on analytic cycles
text: Lemma 20.5.3 . 323D5DA3E240 Let $D$ be an irreducible hypersurface of a smooth complex manifold $M$ of dimension $r+1$, and let $F:M\to X$ be holomorphic, proper on $D$. Write $B=F(D)$. If $\dim B<r$, then $F_*[D]=0$. If $\dim B=r$, there is an integer $d\geq 1$ such that \[  F_*[D]=d[B].  \] Here $d$ is the number of sheets of $F|_ D$ over the complement of a proper analytic subset of $B$. No integrality assertion about an arbitrary weak limit of cycles is used. Proof. The image is analytic by Remmert's proper mapping theorem and has dimension at most $r$ by dimension bounds for holomorphic images . It is irreducible: a decomposition into two proper analytic subsets would pull back to such a decomposition of $D$. These assertions also give purity of $B$ by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets . The current $[D]$ and its proper pushforward are well defined by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces , pushforward of currents proper on their support . If $\dim B<r$, the derivative of $F|_{D_{\mathrm{reg}}}$ has rank less than $r$ everywhere. Otherwise the constant rank theorem near a point of maximal rank would put an $r$-dimensional submanifold in $B$, contradicting its dimension. Every pulled-back $(r,r)$-form therefore vanishes on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$, proving the first assertion. For $r=0$, $D$ is one point and its pushforward is the unit point mass at its image, so the second assertion holds with $d=1$. Assume henceforth $r\geq 1$ and $\dim B=r$. We construct the entire critical exceptional set analytically, including at singular points of $D$. On a coordinate neighborhood in $M$, choose a reduced local equation $e$ of $D$ by local equations and currents of irreducible hypersurfaces . In target coordinates $F_1,\ldots ,F_ n$, put C02C6380EF73 20.5.4 \begin{equation}  Q=\left\{ e=0:\  de\wedge dF_{i_1}\wedge \cdots \wedge dF_{i_ r}=0 \text{ for every }i_1<\cdots <i_ r\right\} . \end{equation} These equations include $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, where $de=0$, and on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ express exactly rank less than $r$. Multiplying $e$ by a unit changes its differential on $D$ by that unit; changing target coordinates takes invertible linear combinations of the displayed minors. Thus these local analytic sets agree and define a closed analytic subset $Q\subset D$. It is proper. If it were all of $D$, the image of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ would be $\mathcal H^{2r}$-null by dimension bounds for holomorphic images ; so would the image of $D_{\mathrm{sing}}$, by its smaller dimension and analytic singular strata and Hausdorff dimension . Countably many charts suffice. This cannot cover the regular locus of the $r$-dimensional analytic set $B$. Hence $\dim Q\leq r-1$. The set \[  Z=B_{\mathrm{sing}}\cup F(Q)  \] is analytic, closed in $B$, and has dimension at most $r-1$; properness and the same image dimension bound justify this for $F(Q)$. The manifold $B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ is connected by global irreducible analytic components . Removing its proper analytic subset $Z\cap B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ leaves it connected, by bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements . Over $B\setminus Z$ every source point is regular with derivative rank $r$. The inverse function theorem on these two $r$-manifolds makes $F$ a local biholomorphism there. Every fiber is compact by properness and discrete by this local description, hence finite. For any such fiber take finitely many disjoint inverse neighborhoods. Properness supplies a smaller target neighborhood with its whole inverse image in their union: the image of their closed complement in $D$ is closed and misses the target point. Intersect the inverse neighborhood images as well. This is an evenly covered neighborhood. The sheet number is a positive locally constant integer and therefore a fixed $d\geq 1$ on the connected $B\setminus Z$. Holomorphic coordinate change preserves complex orientation, so integration over these sheets gives $F_*[D]=d[B]$ off $Z$. There is no unexamined current supported on $Z$ in this equality. Indeed $F^{-1}(Z)\cap D$ is a proper analytic subset of $D$. Its intersection with $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ has smooth volume zero: locally it lies in a nontrivial holomorphic zero set, and the connectedness and density of $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$ exclude an open component. The integration defining $[D]$ assigns its singular locus zero coefficient mass as well. For a compact target set, properness puts its inverse image in a compact source set; there the coefficients of $F^*$ of a bounded test form are bounded by a constant times the induced volume on $D_{\mathrm{reg}}$. Consequently every coefficient measure of $F_*[D]$ gives $Z$ zero mass. This follows first for positive trace tests from the integral formula and then for all coefficients by coefficient measures and compactness of positive currents . The same argument on $B_{\mathrm{reg}}$ shows that $[B]$ gives $Z$ zero mass. Their equality off $Z$ is therefore their equality everywhere. $\square$

Only finitely many $D$ meet the compact preimage of a compact target neighborhood, by local finiteness of analytic components. Apply lemma 20.5.3 to each of them. A component with lower-dimensional image contributes zero; every other contributes a positive integer sheet number times its image. Those images are irreducible analytic subsets of dimension $p-1$ in $A\cap \{ f=0\} $, so are its irreducible components. Every component $C_ k$ of that intersection receives a contribution. The resolution is surjective, since its proper image contains the dense regular locus. Therefore $\pi (\{ g=0\} )=\{ f=0\} \cap A$. Near a compact neighborhood of any point of $C_ k$, the finitely many images of the relevant $D$ cover that zero set. An irreducible local branch of $C_ k$ cannot be covered by finitely many analytic sets of smaller dimension, by purity and dimension of irreducible analytic sets and the local branch decomposition. At least one $D$ consequently has image of dimension $p-1$ containing an open subset of that branch, hence is the whole global component containing it. This proves $m_ k>0$; the formula gives explicitly \[  m_ k=\sum _{D:\, \pi (D)=C_ k}e_ D\deg (\pi |_ D)\in \mathbb Z_{>0}.  \] The current on the left defines these coefficients uniquely by restriction to regular points of $C_ k$ outside the other components, so the local formulas agree on overlaps and do not depend on the chosen resolution. text: Use the conventions and smooth bundle division interfaces of section 6.28 . Lemma 6.29.1 . E7FE74257DC3 Let $\phi $ be PSH on an open subset $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, not identically $-\infty $ on any component, and let $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ be a compact exhaustion. There are global smooth functions $\psi _ j\geq \phi +2^{-j}$ such that $\psi _ j$ is PSH near $K_ j$, $\psi _ j\leq \psi _{j-1}$ on $K_{j-1}$, and $\psi _ j\to \phi $ on every fixed compact set, decreasing there for all large $j$. No curvature sign is asserted outside a neighborhood of $K_ j$. Proof. First choose a smooth global majorant $b\geq \phi +1$: a locally finite relatively compact chart cover has finite upper bounds $M_ i$ for $\phi $ on the respective supports, and a subordinate smooth partition gives $b=\sum _ i\theta _ i(M_ i+1)$. Near each $K_ j$, the strictly PSH function $|z|^2$ allows lemma 7.31.1 to give smooth PSH $a_{j,l}\downarrow \phi $ on one fixed neighborhood. Choose a term and put $v_ j=a_{j,l}+2^{-j}$. If $\psi _{j-1}$ has been constructed, the pointwise limit of these candidates is at most $\psi _{j-1}-2^{-j}$ on $K_{j-1}$. The increasing open sets where a candidate is below $\psi _{j-1}$ cover that compact set, so one term works everywhere on it. Make the term fine enough also that $\int _{K_ j}(a_{j,l}-\phi )\, \mathrm dV\leq 2^{-j}$. Take a smooth cutoff equal to one near $K_ j$ and compactly supported in this fixed neighborhood; glue $v_ j$ to $b+2^{-j}$ by the ordinary cutoff combination. Both branches dominate $\phi +2^{-j}$, so the resulting global smooth $\psi _ j$ does too. It equals $v_ j$ near $K_ j$ and has the asserted order on $K_{j-1}$. On any fixed relatively compact open set it is eventually decreasing and PSH, and tends to $\phi $ in $L^1$ by the chosen error and $2^{-j}$ shift. The decreasing PSH limit is therefore the canonical representative $\phi $ at every point, as in the local regularization lemma. This proves the claim without globally preserving curvature. $\square$ Corollary 6.29.2 . E63E9389A415 Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb C^ n$, $n\geq 1$, possess a complete Kähler metric, let $g=(g_1,\ldots ,g_ r)$, $r\geq 1$, be holomorphic and not identically zero on any component, and set $m=\min (n,r-1)$, $Z=\{ g=0\} $. Let $\epsilon >0$ and let $\phi $ be PSH, not identically $-\infty $ on any component, with its usual upper-semicontinuous representative. For every holomorphic $f$ with \[  I=\int _{\Omega \setminus Z}|f|^2|g|^{-2(m+1+\epsilon )} \mathrm e^{-\phi }\, \mathrm dV<\infty ,  \] there are holomorphic $h_1,\ldots ,h_ r$ on $\Omega $ such that $f=\sum _ jg_ jh_ j$ and the exact estimate ( 6.28.15 ) holds with this $\phi $ and $I$. Proof. Keep $U=\Omega \setminus Z$ and its fixed complete Kähler metric $\gamma $ constructed in the smooth-weight proof. If $r=1$, take $h=f/g$ on $U$. Its requested norm equals the input norm, and the weight's local lower bounds give the same $L^2$ holomorphic extension across $Z$. Thus assume $m=\min (n,r-1)\geq 1$. Identify functions with their multiples of $\mathrm dz_1\wedge \cdots \wedge \mathrm dz_ n$, as in corollary 6.28.14 . Use the quotient sequence $0\to S\to \mathcal O^ r\to Q'\to 0$ on $U$, with $|v|_{Q'}^2=|v|^2/|g|^2$. Let $K_ j$ exhaust $U$ and choose the preceding majorants $\psi _ j$; write $\iota $ for the inclusion of $S$. Give $L_ j=\mathcal O$ the smooth metric $h_{L_ j}=|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )}\mathrm e^{-\psi _ j}$. Let $B_ j$ denote the curvature operator of $S\otimes L_ j$ in degree $(n,1)$ for $\gamma $. Flatness of $\mathcal O^ r$ gives $R_ S=-C_\beta $ and $R_{\det Q'}=\operatorname {tr}C_\beta =\mathcal H(\log |g|^2)$. Therefore \[  R_{S\otimes L_ j}=(m+\epsilon )\operatorname {tr}C_\beta \otimes I_ S -C_\beta +\mathcal H(\psi _ j)\otimes I_ S.  \] The rank-m trace inequality used in ( 6.28.6 ) applies to every tensor here, since $m=\min (n,\operatorname {rank}S)$. Its alternating coefficient formula gives \[  B_ j\geq (\epsilon /m)T_\beta + [\mathcal H(\psi _ j),\Lambda _\gamma ], \qquad T_\beta =(\beta ^*\wedge )(\beta ^*\wedge )^*.  \] Here the identity on $S$ in the second term is understood. Since $\psi _ j$ is PSH near $K_ j$, choose a nonnegative smooth function $a_ j$, zero on a neighborhood of $K_ j$, so that 95B04F2194E0 6.29.3 \begin{equation}  B_ j+a_ j^2\operatorname {Id}\geq (\epsilon /m)T_\beta \quad \hbox{on }U. \end{equation} To make this choice explicit, the operator norm of the negative part of $[\mathcal H(\psi _ j),\Lambda _\gamma ]$ is continuous and zero on that neighborhood. Choose a smooth majorant of its square root by a locally finite partition, and multiply by a smooth cutoff zero near $K_ j$ and one outside a slightly larger neighborhood where the negative part is still zero. This proves the stated inequality. Set $F=\beta ^*\wedge f$, a smooth closed $(n,1)$-form on $U$. All pairings in the next paragraph use the smooth $j$-th metrics and $\gamma $. For compactly supported smooth $v$, contraction duality, ( 6.29.3 ) and theorem 10.33.2 give \begin{align*}  |\langle F,v\rangle _ j|^2 & \leq M\int _ U\langle (B_ j+a_ j^2\operatorname {Id})v,v\rangle _ j\, \mathrm dV_\gamma \\ & \leq M\bigl (\| \delta ”_ jv\| _ j^2+\| D”v\| _ j^2+ \| a_ jv\| _ j^2\bigr ), \qquad M=(m/\epsilon )I. \end{align*} The input norm is at most $I$, because $\psi _ j\geq \phi $ and the top-degree metric density cancels as before. It produces $(u_ j,w_ j,z_ j)$ with total squared norm at most $M$, and the distributional equation FC57A5C2AE65 6.29.4 \begin{equation}  F=D''u_ j+\delta ''_ jw_ j+a_ jz_ j. \end{equation} The second component $w_ j$ is an $L^2$ limit of $D''v$ and is therefore closed. Choose $R$ with $\chi _ R=1$ on $K$, take the upper limit in $j$ in the last estimate, and then let $R\to \infty $. This proves $\delta ''_ jw_ j\to 0$ in ordinary $L^2(K)$. The same fixed lower weighted bounds give local ordinary $L^2$ boundedness of $u_ j$. A diagonal weak limit $u$ satisfies $D''u=F$ by ( 6.29.4 ): on each fixed compact the last term is eventually zero, and the middle term tends to zero as just proved. For fixed $k$ and $j\geq k$, the squared $\psi _ k$ norm on $K_ k$ is at most the squared $\psi _ j$ norm, hence at most $M$. Weak lower semicontinuity gives that bound for $u$ in this fixed norm. Then the densities $1_{K_ k}|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )}\mathrm e^{-\psi _ k}$ increase to $|g|^{-2(m+\epsilon )}\mathrm e^{-\phi }$ on $U$. Monotone convergence proves the exact singular-weight bound for $u$. Finally $h=G^*f+\iota u$ is closed, $Gh=f$, and the orthogonal norm identity gives ( 6.28.15 ), since the first summand has squared weighted norm $I$. Distributional holomorphy makes its coefficients holomorphic on $U$. The PSH weight is locally bounded above on $\Omega $, so the final weighted bound again gives $h\in L^2_{\rm loc}$ across $Z$. Apply lemma 6.28.12 , holomorphic distributions and minimal weighted solutions to extend $h$ holomorphically to all of $\Omega $. Each Hilbert representation above uses smooth global metrics. $\square$

text: Lemma 6.29.1 . E7FE74257DC3 Let $\phi $ be PSH on an open subset $U\subset \mathbb C^ n$, not identically $-\infty $ on any component, and let $K_ j\subset \operatorname {Int}K_{j+1}$ be a compact exhaustion. There are global smooth functions $\psi _ j\geq \phi +2^{-j}$ such that $\psi _ j$ is PSH near $K_ j$, $\psi _ j\leq \psi _{j-1}$ on $K_{j-1}$, and $\psi _ j\to \phi $ on every fixed compact set, decreasing there for all large $j$. No curvature sign is asserted outside a neighborhood of $K_ j$. Proof. First choose a smooth global majorant $b\geq \phi +1$: a locally finite relatively compact chart cover has finite upper bounds $M_ i$ for $\phi $ on the respective supports, and a subordinate smooth partition gives $b=\sum _ i\theta _ i(M_ i+1)$. Near each $K_ j$, the strictly PSH function $|z|^2$ allows lemma 7.31.1 to give smooth PSH $a_{j,l}\downarrow \phi $ on one fixed neighborhood. Choose a term and put $v_ j=a_{j,l}+2^{-j}$. If $\psi _{j-1}$ has been constructed, the pointwise limit of these candidates is at most $\psi _{j-1}-2^{-j}$ on $K_{j-1}$. The increasing open sets where a candidate is below $\psi _{j-1}$ cover that compact set, so one term works everywhere on it. Make the term fine enough also that $\int _{K_ j}(a_{j,l}-\phi )\, \mathrm dV\leq 2^{-j}$. Take a smooth cutoff equal to one near $K_ j$ and compactly supported in this fixed neighborhood; glue $v_ j$ to $b+2^{-j}$ by the ordinary cutoff combination. On any fixed relatively compact open set it is eventually decreasing and PSH, and tends to $\phi $ in $L^1$ by the chosen error and $2^{-j}$ shift. The decreasing PSH limit is therefore the canonical representative $\phi $ at every point, as in the local regularization lemma. This proves the claim without globally preserving curvature. $\square$

title: 10.58 Cup products and differential-resolution comparisons
section: 10.58 Cup products and differential-resolution comparisons
text: Let $R$ be a sheaf of commutative unital rings and $A,B$ sheaves of unital $R$-modules. Their tensor sheaf is the sheafification of $U\mapsto A(U)\otimes _{R(U)}B(U)$. It represents sheafwise balanced bilinear maps and has stalk $A_ x\otimes _{R_ x}B_ x$: a tensor is a finite sum of symbols with finitely many balancing relations, so both its representatives and any relation hold on one common neighborhood after shrinking. This proves the stalk assertion and the universal property directly from sheafification. In particular a tensor sequence is exact if the original sequence splits $R_ x$-linearly at every stalk; no flatness of an arbitrary module sheaf is presumed.

title: 10.58.1 An explicit Godement product
section: 10.58 Cup products and differential-resolution comparisons
text: Recall $GE(U)=\prod _{x\in U}E_ x$ and $C^ pE=G^{p+1}E$. Pointwise tensoring gives natural maps \[  \mu _ m:G^ mA\otimes _ R G^ mB\longrightarrow G^ m(A\otimes _ R B).  \] For $m=0$ this is the identity. Inductively, tensor the two assignments at each point and then apply $G\mu _ m$ to obtain $\mu _{m+1}$. These maps are associative, commute with coefficient maps, and carry two augmentations to the augmentation of the tensor. All these assertions hold pointwise for $m=1$ and then follow by induction. The $R$-action uses the canonical augmentation $R\to G^ mR$. Write $\eta _ E^{(r)}:E\to G^ rE$ for the iterated augmentation, with $\eta ^{(0)}=1$. For $f\in C^ pA$ and $g\in C^ qB$ define B28319B90BD6 10.58.2 \begin{equation}  f\smile g=\mu _{p+q+1}\bigl ( G^{p+1}\eta _ A^{(q)}(f),\,  \eta _{G^{q+1}B}^{(p)}(g)\bigr ). \end{equation} This is a bilinear sheaf map to $C^{p+q}(A\otimes _ RB)$. The first factor extends the front $p+1$ positions and the second extends the back $q+1$ positions, sharing their endpoint. Equivalently, in the nested assignment description it tensors the front value, continued by its germ to the final position, with the back value. Formula equation 10.58.2 makes that continuation precise without choosing global representatives of germs. Theorem 10.58.3 . 16CBD1C5A6C8 For nonempty closed support families $\Phi ,\Psi $ as in section 10.56 , this product induces natural $R(X)$-bilinear maps \[  H_\Phi ^ p(X,A)\times H_\Psi ^ q(X,B) \longrightarrow H_{\Phi \cap \Psi }^{p+q}(X,A\otimes _ RB).  \] They are associative, unital for the coefficient ring, and graded commutative under the tensor flip: $\beta \smile \alpha =(-1)^{pq}\tau (\alpha \smile \beta )$. Suppose $0\to B\to B'\to B''\to 0$ and its tensor sequence with $A$ are exact. Their supported connecting maps satisfy \[  \partial (\alpha \smile \beta '')=(-1)^ p\alpha \smile \partial \beta '', \qquad \partial (\beta ''\smile \alpha )=(\partial \beta '')\smile \alpha .  \] The coefficient and support maps in these formulas are the indicated tensor maps and the intersection family. Proof. Let $\delta _ i^ p=G^ i\eta _{G^{p+1-i}}$ be the Godement cofaces. Expansion of the front/back formula has the same cancellation as the alternating face rule: for a product of degrees $p,q$, the cofaces numbered $i\le p$ are $(\delta _ i^ pf)\smile g$, and those numbered $i\ge p+1$ are $f\smile \delta _{i-p}^ qg$. The two extra middle terms in $(d_ Gf)\smile g+(-1)^ pf\smile d_ Gg$ are $(\delta _{p+1}^ pf)\smile g$ and $f\smile \delta _0^ qg$. They are equal, since both insert the shared-endpoint augmentation, and their signs are opposite. These coface identities follow from naturality of $\eta $ and its compatibility with $\mu _ m$; alternatively each side omits the same position of a nested assignment. Hence 9E20CC3BE2A6 10.58.4 \begin{equation}  d_ G(f\smile g)=d_ Gf\smile g+(-1)^ pf\smile d_ Gg. \end{equation} Both parenthesizations of a triple product extend the three factors to the same front, middle and back blocks and apply the associative pointwise tensor map. They are thus equal already on cochains. The global unit is the augmented section $1$ and has the unit property by the same formula. Because cup is a bilinear sheaf map, its support is contained in the intersection of the two closed supports. A closed subset of that intersection belongs to both families. The Leibniz identity shows that cocycles multiply to cocycles and that changing a closed factor by a boundary changes the product by a boundary. This constructs the supported maps, with associativity, unit and naturality just proved. For the first connecting identity choose supported Godement cocycles $f,g''$ and a lift $g'$ of $g''$ in the $B'$ complex, with the same allowed support. Such a lift exists by exactness of supported Godement degree functors in theorem 10.56.1 . Then $d_ Gg'$ represents $\partial \beta ''$, while equation 10.58.4 makes the derivative of the product lift $f\smile g'$ equal to $(-1)^ pf\smile d_ Gg'$. This is precisely the defining connecting representative in the tensor sequence. If the lifted factor is on the left, the other factor is closed and the derivative is $d_ Gg'\smile f$, giving the second identity without an additional sign. It remains to prove graded commutativity. The map $B\to GB$ splits $R_ x$-linearly on each stalk by evaluation at $x$: evaluation retracts augmentation and respects the action of $R_ x$. Consequently tensoring $0\to B\to GB\to Q\to 0$ by $A$ remains exact. Since $GB$ is acyclic for every support family, each $\beta \in H_\Psi ^ q(X,B)$, $q\ge 1$, is $\partial \gamma $ for some $\gamma \in H_\Psi ^{q-1}(X,Q)$. Induct on $p+q$. The degree-zero assertion is the ordinary tensor flip of sections. When $q>0$, the two connecting identities and the induction hypothesis give \[  \beta \smile \alpha =\partial (\gamma \smile \alpha ) =(-1)^{p(q-1)}\tau \partial (\alpha \smile \gamma ) =(-1)^{pq}\tau (\alpha \smile \beta ).  \] If $q=0<p$, exchange the two factors and use the already proved case with a positive second degree. This completes the induction, including arbitrary supports and torsion coefficients. $\square$ Every bilinear coefficient morphism $A\otimes _ RB\to E$ now gives the corresponding contraction of cohomology classes by composition. In particular $H^\bullet (X,R)$ is a graded-commutative ring and $H_\Phi ^\bullet (X,A)$ is its graded module; two supported factors have support in the intersection family. These statements do not define a product of two arbitrary currents.

title: 10.58.5 Čech comparison and pullback
section: 10.58 Cup products and differential-resolution comparisons
text: Proposition 10.58.6 . 501BF07CE068 For any open cover, the ordered-tuple Čech cup product is \[  (c\smile e)_{i_0\ldots i_{a+a'}} =c_{i_0\ldots i_ a}\otimes e_{i_ a\ldots i_{a+a'}},  \] restricted to the common intersection. The canonical Čech-to- Godement comparison preserves this product. On locally compact paracompact spaces this also holds for compact-supported Čech cohomology and its mixed product with ordinary cohomology. Proof. The alternating coboundary has the Leibniz identity by the same front/back middle-term cancellation. In the comparison total complexes $T_ A^{a,b}=C^ a(\mathcal U,C^ bA)$, put \[  (c\odot e)_{i_0\ldots i_{a+a'}} =(-1)^{ba'}c_{i_0\ldots i_ a}\smile _ G e_{i_ a\ldots i_{a+a'}}.  \] Its total degree is $(a+b)+(a'+b')$. Expanding the two Leibniz identities shows that $D=\delta +(-1)^ a d_ G$ satisfies $D(c\odot e)=Dc\odot e+(-1)^{a+b}c\odot De$. Indeed the horizontal second term acquires $(a+b)+b(a'+1)\equiv a+ba'$, and the vertical first and second terms acquire $a+a'+ba'$ and $a+a'+ba'+b$, respectively, exactly the signs from differentiating the displayed formula. The horizontal augmentation from global Godement sections and the vertical augmentation from Čech cochains both preserve products: the former has $a=a'=0$, the latter $b=b'=0$, and $\mu $ respects augmentation. The horizontal augmentation is a cohomology isomorphism by theorem 10.43.16 ; therefore the comparison obtained by inverting it preserves products. For compact supports choose locally finite relatively compact covers as in theorem 10.56.9 . A product with one finite cochain is finite: all its additional indices meet the compact union of the active member closures, hence belong to a finite set. The total product thus also preserves the compact total subcomplex when either factor is compact. The two same augmentations, using the compact comparison for that factor and the ordinary comparison for the other, prove the assertion. Refinement compatibility then gives the direct-limit statement, including contraction by coefficient maps. $\square$ For $f:X\to Y$ and a support family $\Psi $ on $Y$, let $f^{-1}\Psi $ be the closed subsets of $X$ contained in $f^{-1}K$ for some $K\in \Psi $. This is again a nonempty support family. Proposition 10.58.7 . 6F68DD8223F3 The Godement pullback constructed in theorem 10.55.6 induces \[  f^*:H_\Psi ^ q(Y,A)\longrightarrow H_{f^{-1}\Psi }^ q(X,f^{-1}A).  \] It is functorial, preserves cup products and contractions, and commutes with coefficient connecting maps. The ordinary Čech pullback on inverse-image covers agrees with it under comparison. For proper maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces it preserves compact supports. For sheaves over a fixed commutative ring, define $A\boxtimes _ R B=\operatorname {pr}_1^{-1}A\otimes _ R \operatorname {pr}_2^{-1}B$. Its stalk is $A_ x\otimes _ RB_ y$. The external product $\alpha \times \beta = \operatorname {pr}_1^*\alpha \smile \operatorname {pr}_2^*\beta $ has support family $\Phi \times \Psi $, the closed subsets contained in some $K\times L$, $K\in \Phi ,L\in \Psi $. It obeys \[  (\alpha \times \beta )\smile (\alpha '\times \beta ') =(-1)^{q p'}(\alpha \smile \alpha ')\times (\beta \smile \beta '),  \] for degrees $p,q,p',q'$, with the canonical regrouping of tensor factors. text: Suppose $L,M,N$ are nonnegative sheaf complexes resolving $A,B,E$, with a bilinear pairing $L^ r\otimes M^ s\to N^{r+s}$ extending $A\otimes B\to E$ and satisfying the internal Leibniz rule $d(uv)=(du)v+(-1)^ ru(dv)$. Suppose their terms are respectively acyclic for $\Phi ,\Psi ,\Phi \cap \Psi $. Theorem 10.58.9 . 3E96DCA67FB2 There are augmentational comparison isomorphisms \[  \Theta _\Phi ^ n:H_\Phi ^ n(X,A) \longrightarrow H^ n(\Gamma _\Phi (X,L^\bullet ))  \] and likewise for $B,M$ and $E,N$, preserving the indicated pairings. If $\Psi _ n$ denotes the successive positive connecting-map comparison from the resolution section cohomology to sheaf cohomology, then 499EBF22C09F 10.58.10 \begin{equation}  (\Theta _\Phi ^ n)^{-1}=\epsilon _ n\Psi _ n, \qquad \epsilon _ n=(-1)^{n(n+1)/2}. \end{equation} Thus for the positive convention itself, \[  \Psi _{r+s}([u v])=(-1)^{rs}\Psi _ r[u]\smile \Psi _ s[v],  \] with the specified coefficient pairing. The positive convention is retained, rather than silently declared multiplicative. Proof. Form the finite-diagonal total complexes $\Gamma _\Phi (X,C^ aL^ r)$ with $D=d_ G+(-1)^ a d_ L$, and likewise for $M,N$. The maps from $\Gamma _\Phi C^\bullet A$ by resolution augmentation and from $\Gamma _\Phi L^\bullet $ by Godement germs are cochain maps, denoted $j_ A,j_ L$. The former is a cohomology isomorphism because $\Gamma _\Phi C^ a-$ is exact; the latter is one because the $L^ r$ are $\Phi $-acyclic. Apply the exact-augmented-row/ column proof of lemma 10.43.15 ; every total diagonal is finite and its proof works with these supported groups without alteration. Define $\Theta =j_ L^{-1}j_ A$. On elements of bidegrees $(a,r)$ and $(b,s)$ set \[  u\star v=(-1)^{rb}(u\smile _ G v),  \] followed by the internal coefficient pairing. The two Leibniz rules give $D(u\star v)=Du\star v+(-1)^{a+r}u\star Dv$. For example the internal first term has sign $a+b+rb$, and the internal second sign $a+b+rb+r$; the horizontal second has sign $a+rb$. These are exactly the signs obtained by differentiating the displayed product. Supports lie in the intersection family. Both $j_ A$ and $j_ L$ preserve pairings: their other bidegree is zero and the pairings respect augmentations. Inverting their cohomology isomorphisms proves multiplicativity of $\Theta $. The sign in equation 10.58.10 is also the finite zigzag calculation of equation 10.55.4 , now using the exact supported degree functors. Explicitly, for a closed supported $z\in L^ n(X)$ choose supported lifts $a_ j\in \Gamma _\Phi (X,C^ jL^{n-1-j})$ with $d_ La_0=\eta z$ and $d_ La_ j=d_ Ga_{j-1}$. The positive comparison is represented by $d_ Ga_{n-1}$. The relations $Da_ j=d_ Ga_ j+(-1)^ jd_ La_ j$ give $[\eta z]=\epsilon _ n[d_ Ga_{n-1}]$ in the total cohomology; for $n=0$ both maps are the kernel-section identity. This proves the formula with the existing normalization. Finally $\epsilon _{r+s}\epsilon _ r\epsilon _ s=(-1)^{rs}$, giving the last displayed relation. $\square$ Corollary 10.58.11 . 45A6B240A010 On a paracompact smooth manifold, ordinary de Rham comparison \[  \Theta :H^ q(X,\underline{\mathbb R})\longrightarrow H^ q_{\rm dR}(X)  \] preserves products. This remains true for compact supports and for the compact/ordinary mixed product, with wedge on representatives. It commutes with smooth pullback, including compact supports for proper maps. On a complex manifold let $E,F$ be holomorphic bundles. Write \[  \Theta _ p^ q:H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E)) \longrightarrow H_{\bar\partial }^{p,q}(X,E)  \] for the same augmentational comparison with the actual full-type $\bar\partial $ resolution. For $\alpha $ of type $(p,q)$ and $\beta $ of type $(r,s)$ on the analytic side, coefficient tensoring and holomorphic exterior product on the sheaf side satisfy 8E59D425DD0E 10.58.12 \begin{equation}  \Theta _{p+r}^{q+s}\bigl ((\Theta _ p^ q)^{-1}\alpha \smile (\Theta _ r^ s)^{-1}\beta \bigr ) =(-1)^{ps}[\alpha \wedge \beta ]. \end{equation} The formula holds for compact/mixed supports and after a holomorphic bundle contraction. The comparisons commute with holomorphic pullback. Proof. Use the local differential resolutions and supported acyclicity of corollary 10.57.1 , and their ordinary versions in corollary 10.43.11 . The real exterior complex is a differential graded algebra, so the preceding theorem applies directly with wedge. Its compact and ordinary terms have the required acyclicity. For full-type Dolbeault forms the actual formula is \[  \bar\partial (\alpha \wedge \beta ) =\bar\partial \alpha \wedge \beta +(-1)^{p+q}\alpha \wedge \bar\partial \beta .  \] The resolution degree is $q$, not $p+q$. Its chain pairing must therefore be $\alpha \circ \beta =(-1)^{ps}\alpha \wedge \beta $: the sign of the second differentiated term is then $ps+p+q=q+p(s+1)$, as required by the degree-$q$ Leibniz rule. This pairing is associative, since $ps+(p+r)t=rt+p(s+t)$, and at resolution degree zero it is the ordinary holomorphic coefficient wedge. Apply the theorem to this precise chain pairing to get equation 10.58.12 . The same proof works in holomorphic frames for bundle coefficients and their contractions. It multiplies smooth forms only; arbitrary current-current wedge products are not used. For naturality, use the explicit Godement pullback $\lambda $ on the two resolution total complexes and the usual smooth pullback of forms. They commute with $D$, products and both augmentations, since pullback commutes with exterior differentiation and wedge. Inverting the two augmentation isomorphisms proves the assertion. For Dolbeault use a holomorphic map, so the pulled-back coefficients and differentials have the specified types and $\bar\partial $ commutes with pullback. Properness ensures compact supports as proved above. No pullback of an arbitrary current by an arbitrary smooth map is asserted. $\square$ Proposition 10.58.13 . FF9CB82C72A2 For a locally finite cover of a smooth manifold with a subordinate smooth partition $(\rho _ i)$, a constant-sheaf Čech $n$-cocycle $c$ has the de Rham representative \[  \widetilde\Theta _ n(c)= \sum _{i_0,\ldots ,i_ n}c_{i_0\ldots i_ n}\rho _{i_ n} d\rho _{i_0}\wedge \cdots \wedge d\rho _{i_{n-1}}.  \] Each term extends by zero from its common intersection; the sum is locally finite by subordination and local finiteness of the cover. For $n=0$ this is the usual partition gluing. On cohomology its normalization is \[  \widetilde\Theta _ n=(-1)^ n\Theta _ n =(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}\Psi _ n^{-1}.  \] It too preserves products and smooth pullback. This is the partition normalization, distinct from the augmentational $\Theta $ fixed above. For finite cochains on relatively compact covers it preserves compact support as well. Proof. Let $h$ be partition contraction, inserting an index in the first position. In the differential resolution, a closed cochain $b$ with values in its kernel sheaf satisfies $\delta (hb)=b$; therefore $d(hb)$ is a cocycle in the next kernel sheaf. Its positive connecting image is $b$, because $hb$ is an actual local lift and its Čech coboundary is $b$. This uses precisely the connecting compatibility already proved in theorem 10.44.12 , not cochain surjectivity on an arbitrary fixed cover. Repeat this operation $n$ times and glue the final degree-zero cocycle by the partition. Each differential hits the newly inserted partition coefficient, since the kernel-valued cochain is $d$-closed. Moving that new $d\rho $ past the existing $t-1$ form differentials contributes $(-1)^{t-1}$ at stage $t$. Their product is $(-1)^{n(n-1)/2}$ and the resulting ordered expression is the displayed formula. Thus it equals that sign times $\Psi _ n^{-1}$. Combine with equation 10.58.10 to obtain $\widetilde\Theta _ n=(-1)^ n\Theta _ n$. The factor $(-1)^ n$ is multiplicative in total degree and commutes with pullback, proving the assertions independently of any good-cover construction. If $c$ is finite, every term is supported in the compact union of its active member closures, proving the compact assertion. $\square$
