text: For an oriented real $d$-manifold without boundary define $\operatorname {Tr}:H_ c^ d(X,\underline{\mathbb R})\to \mathbb R$ by integration after $\Theta $. For a complex $n$-manifold define $\operatorname {Tr}:H_ c^ n(X,\Omega _ X^ n)\to \mathbb C$ in the same way, integrating its compact $(n,n)$ representative. Compact Stokes makes these maps well defined, using the existing real Stokes theorem Stokes' formula on compact domains with corners and complex orientation. Corollary 10.59.1 . E68024FC9A71 Cup product followed by the real trace is represented by $\int _ Xu\wedge v$ for compact/ordinary complementary-degree de Rham representatives. For holomorphic bundles, exterior coefficient product and evaluation $E\otimes E^*\to \mathcal O_ X$ give \[  \operatorname {Tr}(a\smile b) =(-1)^{p(n-q)}\int _ Xu\wedge v,  \] where $u=\Theta _ p^ q a$ and $v=\Theta _{n-p}^{n-q}b$, and at least one factor is compact. On compact manifolds these pairings are perfect, by the exact compact duality of corollary 10.57.2 . On a noncompact manifold the displayed formulas define pairings; their nondegeneracy is not a consequence of the formulas alone. Proof. The real assertion is multiplicativity of $\Theta $ followed by its definition of trace. The complex assertion is equation 10.58.12 with $s=n-q$, followed by evaluation and integration. Compactness of one support makes all integrals legitimate. On a compact manifold, the analytic pairings in the cited compact-duality corollary transported in the cited corollary are perfect. Multiplication by the displayed sign does not change that fact. No period-lattice, singular cohomology or unproved noncompact Poincaré theorem is invoked. $\square$ Lemma 10.59.2 . 42254A734333 Let $E^\bullet $ be a complex of real or complex Fréchet spaces with continuous differentials. Suppose the ranges of $d^{k-1}$ and $d^ k$ are closed. Then restriction of functionals identifies \[  \frac{\{ T\in (E^ k)':T d^{k-1}=0\} }{\{ S d^ k:S\in (E^{k+1})'\} } \simeq \bigl (H^ k(E^\bullet )\bigr )',  \] where primes mean continuous linear duals and cohomology has its quotient topology. This is an algebraic isomorphism onto that continuous dual; no strong-dual topological isomorphism is claimed. The resulting pairing separates both cohomology factors. Proof. Put $Z=\ker d^ k$, $B=\operatorname {im}d^{k-1}$. The quotient $Z/B$ is Hausdorff Fréchet by proposition 2.12.1 , whose proof applies over either scalar field. A continuous functional on $Z/B$ is a continuous functional on $Z$ annihilating $B$. The dominated linear extension argument from Lamari's positivity criterion , in its generic seminorm form, extends it to $E^ k$. For complex functionals extend the real part and use $\ell (x)=a(x)-ia(ix)$. The extension annihilates $B$, so it belongs to the numerator. This proves surjectivity. If such a $T$ vanishes on $Z$, it factors algebraically through $d^ k(E^ k)$. This factor is continuous: the induced bijection $E^ k/Z\to d^ k(E^ k)$ is a homeomorphism by the closed-range Fréchet open-mapping theorem. Extend that continuous functional from the closed range to $E^{k+1}$ by the same dominated extension. Thus $T=S d^ k$, proving the kernel assertion. The reverse inclusion is immediate. Finally continuous functionals separate the Hausdorff locally convex space $Z/B$, and every nonzero dual functional is nonzero on some class, proving separation of both factors. $\square$ Corollary 10.59.3 . CFEFE5F704F2 Let $X$ be a Hausdorff second-countable oriented smooth $d$-manifold without boundary. If the two smooth de Rham maps into and out of degree $k$ have closed ranges in the topology of uniform coefficient derivatives on compact sets, then integration gives a nondegenerate pairing and a vector-space identification \[  H_ c^{d-k}(X,\mathbb R) \simeq \bigl (H^ k(X,\mathbb R)\bigr )',  \] with the ordinary group given its de Rham quotient topology. Likewise, on a second-countable complex manifold, suppose the smooth $\bar\partial _ E$ ranges into and out of bidegree $(p,q)$ are closed. Then the compact/ordinary integration pairing is nondegenerate and identifies \[  H_ c^{n-q}(X,\Omega _ X^{n-p}\otimes \mathcal O(E^*)) \simeq \bigl (H^ q(X,\Omega _ X^ p\otimes \mathcal O(E))\bigr )'.  \] The trace-cup realization has the sign already specified above. Closed range is an explicit hypothesis here; a noncompact manifold or a holomorphic bundle alone is not a proof of that hypothesis. Proof. The spaces of smooth forms are Fréchet by proposition 2.10.2 ; the same proof applies to bundle coefficients in a countable family of smooth frames, with the smooth frame-change matrices controlling seminorms on compact intersections. Their continuous duals are exactly compact-supported complementary currents by proposition 2.10.4 . The identical cutoff/finite-frame proof gives $E^*$ coefficients: a continuous functional has a bound by finitely many compact coefficient seminorms, and conversely a compact current extends to all smooth forms by a cutoff equal to one near its support. title: 10.60 Neighborhood continuity for a strongly paracompact subspace
search_title: Neighborhood continuity for a strongly paracompact subspace
section: 10.60 Neighborhood continuity for a strongly paracompact subspace
text: Theorem 10.60.1 . 26C06F3C11FF Let $S$ be strongly paracompact in $X$ in the precise sense of section 10.44 . For every sheaf $A$, restriction gives natural isomorphisms \[  \varinjlim _{\Omega \supset S}H^ q(\Omega ,A) \simeq H^ q(S,A|_ S),  \] over open neighborhoods $\Omega $. These are ordinary cohomology groups, distinct from groups with supports contained in $S$. Proof. A closed subspace $K$ of $S$ is strongly paracompact in $X$. Indeed add an ambient open set meeting $S$ in $S\setminus K$ to an ambient cover of $K$, apply the strong refinement of $S$, and retain members assigned to the original cover. They still cover $K$, are locally finite near it and obey the same closure condition. Consequently a flabby sheaf on $X$ restricts to a soft sheaf on $S$: sections on each such $K$ extend to an ambient neighborhood by theorem 10.44.4 , then to $X$ by flabbiness. The space $S$ is paracompact by lemma 10.44.3 , so that soft restriction is acyclic there. On open neighborhoods of $S$, a flabby sheaf remains flabby and acyclic. In degree zero the isomorphism is exactly the ambient germ-section extension theorem; injectivity follows because two sections with equal germs on $S$ agree on the open union of neighborhoods where those germs agree. Apply $0\to A\to GA\to Q\to 0$ on the open neighborhoods and, by exact inverse image, on $S$. Take their long exact sequences. Filtered direct limits are exact by the eventual-zero representative argument. The $GA$ terms vanish in positive degree on both sides by the preceding paragraph. Thus degree one is the corresponding cokernel of degree-zero maps, and higher degrees shift positively to $Q$. Induction over the degree, simultaneously for all sheaves, and naturality of the restriction maps prove the result. No proper-map or fiber-neighborhood assertion is inferred here. $\square$

title: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text:
Write $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$ for the subspaces of codimension $r$ in a complex vector space $V$ of dimension $d$, where $1\leq r\leq d$. Its compact topology is the existing topology of orthogonal projectors; it is independent of the auxiliary Hermitian inner product. Proposition 10.35.1 . C0EB2A25CDC8 The space $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$ is a compact connected complex manifold of dimension $r(d-r)$. Its tautological sequence is \[  0\longrightarrow S\longrightarrow \underline V\longrightarrow Q \longrightarrow 0,\qquad S_ a=a,\quad Q_ a=V/a.  \] There are natural holomorphic identifications \[  T\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)=\operatorname {Hom}(S,Q),\qquad H^0(\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V),Q)=V.  \] The Plücker map $j:\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)	o \mathbb P(\Lambda ^ rV^*)$ is a holomorphic embedding and $\det Q=j^*\mathcal O(1)$. Proof. For a decomposition $V=A\oplus W$, with $\dim W=r$, subspaces transverse to $W$ are graphs of matrices $Z:A	o W$. This set is open in the projector topology: invertibility of the projection onto $A$ is an open matrix condition. Its graph matrix and inverse depend continuously on the projector. On overlapping charts a graph basis is changed by an invertible block matrix, so the new graph matrix is obtained by matrix multiplication and inversion. These operations are holomorphic where the block is invertible. The charts therefore give the asserted complex structure and dimension. The graph vectors give a holomorphic frame of $S$; the images of a fixed basis of $W$ give a holomorphic frame of $Q$. Compactness is the closed bounded projector model. Connectedness follows from transitivity of the unitary group and its path connectedness: diagonalizing a unitary matrix gives the path obtained by replacing its eigenvalues $e^{i	heta _ l}$ by $e^{it	heta _ l}$. The finite-dimensional diagonalization follows by taking an eigenvector and its invariant orthogonal complement successively. A curve of graphs through $a$ has derivative a map $a	o V/a$. Changing the complement changes a lift by a map into $a$, so this identification is intrinsic. In graph charts it is holomorphic and fiberwise an isomorphism, proving the tangent-bundle identity. For Plücker, choose independent forms $\xi _1,\ldots ,\xi _ r$ annihilating $a$ and set $j(a)=[\xi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \xi _ r]$. Changing the basis multiplies the wedge by a nonzero scalar. Its contraction kernel is exactly $a$, proving injectivity. In the graph chart above take the rows of the quotient map $(v_ A,v_ W)\mapsto v_ W-Zv_ A$. Their wedge has its $W$ coordinate equal to one, and its coordinates with one $W$ index replaced by an $A$ index are the entries of $Z$, with fixed signs. Thus the map is holomorphic and these coordinate ratios recover every graph coordinate; its differential is injective. Compactness makes the continuous injection a homeomorphism onto its image. These same coordinate ratios give its local holomorphic inverse on that image, proving embedding. The pairing \[  ( ar v_1\wedge \cdots \wedge  ar v_ r, \xi _1\wedge \cdots \wedge \xi _ r) \longmapsto \det (\xi _ l(v_ k))  \] identifies $\det (V/a)$ with the dual of its annihilator wedge line. It is independent of the lifts $v_ k$ and varies holomorphically, proving the determinant assertion with the indicated dual-projective convention. It remains to prove the global-section assertion, rather than infer it from particular projective subspaces. For $\sigma \in H^0(Q)$ and $\xi \in V^*\setminus \{ 0\} $ consider $\xi (\sigma (a))$ for $a\subset \ker \xi $ of dimension $d-r$. The allowed $a$ form the compact connected Grassmannian $\operatorname {Gr}(d-r,\ker \xi )$, including its point cases. This scalar is holomorphic in $a$, hence constant by the local maximum principle on a compact connected complex manifold. Denote it $F(\xi )$. It is holomorphic in $\xi $: locally choose $v_0$ with $\xi (v_0)
e 0$, and map fixed independent vectors in $\ker \xi _0$ to $v-\xi (v)v_0/\xi (v_0)$. Any fixed $d-r$ of them remain independent near $\xi _0$ and give a holomorphic choice of $a\subset \ker \xi $. The empty choice handles $d=r$. Moreover $F(t\xi )=tF(\xi )$ for $t
e 0$. Continuity on the compact unit sphere gives $|F(\xi )|\leq C|\xi |$, so its singularity at zero is removable by the existing bounded holomorphic removal theorem bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements (or one-variable removal when $d=1$). Its Taylor expansion and homogeneity show $F(\xi )=\xi (v)$ for one $v\in V$. For every $a$ and every $\xi $ annihilating $a$, $\xi (\sigma (a))=\xi (v)$; hence $\sigma (a)=v mod a$. Conversely these constant-vector quotient sections are holomorphic. Their common kernel is $ igcap _ a a=0$, proving the claimed isomorphism. All assertions also cover $r=d$, when the Grassmannian is one point. $\square$ Lemma 10.35.2 . F9789093E482 Let $X$ be a countable-basis complex manifold and $E$ a holomorphic bundle. Let $B$ be a countable-basis complex manifold of dimension $b$, and let $A_ x:H^0(X,E)	o F_ x$ be surjective linear maps into a holomorphic bundle of rank $R\geq 1$ on $B$. Suppose evaluation of each section is holomorphic in $x\in B$, and the induced map of section spaces is continuous for compact convergence. If $p\geq b+R$, some $p$ sections span every $F_ x$ under these maps. The same $p$ sections can be required to do this for finitely or countably many such families satisfying their respective bounds. Proof. The space of holomorphic sections with compact convergence is Fréchet. Countably many coefficient suprema in compact local frames define its topology. A Cauchy sequence has locally uniform coefficient limits, holomorphic by the Cauchy formula. The limits agree on overlaps and form a global section. Thus its $p$-fold product is a complete metrizable vector space. Use the proved Baire nested-ball argument in proposition 2.10.3 . For a compact $K\subset B$, tuples failing to span at some point of $K$ form a closed set. In local frames failure is vanishing of all $R$-minors; the sum of their squared norms has positive minimum on $K$ precisely for a spanning tuple. Uniform convergence on $K$ proves the closed assertion. We prove this closed set has empty interior. By pointwise surjectivity and compactness choose finitely many sections $t_1,\ldots ,t_ N$ whose images span on a neighborhood $O$ of $K$. Perturb a given tuple by \[  s_ j+\sum _{l=1}^ N\lambda _{jl}t_ l,\qquad 1\leq j\leq p.  \] The map from $O	imes \mathbb C^{pN}$ to the $p$-fold fiber bundle of $F$ is a holomorphic submersion: its parameter derivative is onto. Concretely, invert a nonzero $R$-minor of the $t_ l$ evaluations; the corresponding $R$ parameters per column may be replaced by its fiber value, leaving the other parameters as coordinates. Rank-$k$ matrices in $\operatorname {Hom}(\mathbb C^ p,\mathbb C^ R)$ are smooth of complex codimension $(R-k)(p-k)$: after an invertible $k$-minor, the lower-right block is the product of the lower-left block, the inverse minor, and the upper-right block. This gives exactly $(R-k)(p-k)$ independent equations, also for $k=0$. Their inverse images under the displayed submersion therefore have dimension at most $b+pN-(p-R+1)\leq pN-1$ for $k<R$. Their parameter projections have Lebesgue measure zero. Here no Sard theorem is needed: on a compact coordinate box a smooth map from real dimension $a$ to $c>a$ is Lipschitz. Cover its domain by $O(\delta ^{-a})$ cubes of side $\delta $; the images fit in that many balls of radius $C\delta $, with total outer volume $O(\delta ^{c-a})	o 0$. Countably many boxes cover each stratum. Consequently arbitrarily small parameters avoid every bad rank on $O$. These finite-section perturbations tend to the given tuple in the section topology, proving density of good tuples on $K$. Take a countable compact exhaustion of each $B$. The resulting bad sets, for all specified families and all exhaustion members, are a countable union of closed sets with empty interior. Baire supplies a tuple outside their union, proving the lemma. $\square$ Theorem 10.35.3 . CD7786C05633 Let $E$ have rank $r\geq 1$ on a countable-basis complex $n$-manifold. If $E$ is globally generated, some subspace $V\subset H^0(X,E)$ with $\dim V\leq n+r$ generates it everywhere. If every first-jet map and every distinct-pair evaluation of global sections is onto, one may choose a single $V$ surjecting onto all of them with \[  \dim V\leq \max \{ nr+n+r,\, 2(n+r)\} .  \] These statements do not require compactness of $X$. Proof. Apply lemma 10.35.2 first to evaluation over $X$, of rank $r$ and base dimension $n$. For the second assertion the first-jet bundle has rank $r(n+1)$: in local coordinates/frame a first jet is a value and its $n$ first derivatives, whose transition matrix has holomorphic entries by the chain and frame-change rules. Its evaluation depends holomorphically on the base and continuously on sections by Cauchy's derivative formula. Apply the lemma simultaneously to that bundle over $X$, and to $\operatorname {pr}_1^*E\oplus \operatorname {pr}_2^*E$ over $X	imes X\setminus \Delta $, of rank $2r$ and dimension $2n$. Their required bounds are exactly the two numbers displayed. Taking the span of the selected tuple gives $V$; linear dependencies only reduce its dimension. Empty bases impose no condition. $\square$ Proposition 10.35.4 . 0CE84812A13F For any finite generating space $V\subset H^0(X,E)$ the map $\psi _ V(x)=\ker (V	o E_ x)$ is holomorphic to $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$, and $E=\psi _ V^*Q$ canonically. Every globally generated bundle has a smooth Griffiths semipositive metric whose dual is Nakano seminegative. A line bundle with a globally generated positive tensor power has a smooth semipositive metric. If every first jet of $E$ is generated, the metric can instead be chosen with Nakano negative dual, and is Griffiths positive. In particular an ample line bundle has a smooth positive metric. If $V$ also generates every first jet and every distinct pair, $\psi _ V$ is an injective immersion. It is an embedding when $X$ is compact (or when this map is proper). For a line bundle the converse holds: an injective immersive $\psi _ V$ makes all those evaluation maps onto. Proof. Write evaluation as a full-rank holomorphic matrix $B(x)$ in a local frame. Inverting an $r$-minor expresses its kernel as a graph holomorphically, proving the map assertion. Evaluation identifies $V/\ker B(x)$ with $E_ x$, giving the bundle isomorphism. Give $V$ an inner product and use its quotient metric on $E$. The checked subbundle/quotient curvature formula proposition 10.34.9 for a flat ambient bundle gives Griffiths nonnegativity of the quotient. Its dual is a holomorphic subbundle of the flat dual, whose Nakano curvature is the negative Gram form $-\left|\sum _ jB_ jv_ jight|^2$; hence is Nakano seminegative. These assertions use that exact formula, without assuming duality preserves Nakano positivity. For a line bundle a positive tensor power's quotient metric has the unique positive metric root; curvature divides by that tensor exponent, proving its metric claim. For the strict assertion choose a finite first-jet generating space by lemma 10.35.2 . At $x$, differentiation of evaluation on its kernel is a surjection \[  S_ x\longrightarrow T_ x^*X\otimes E_ x,\qquad s\longmapsto d_ xs.  \] Its dual $T_ xX\otimes E_ x^*	o S_ x^*$ is injective. It is, up to a sign, the second fundamental form of $E^*\subset \underline{V^*}$: differentiating the identically zero pairing of a local dual section with a local kernel section gives that identification. The flat subbundle curvature on a tensor $u$ is therefore exactly minus the squared norm of this dual map applied to $u$. It is strictly negative for $u
e 0$. Rank-one tests and the dual curvature transpose then give Griffiths positivity of $E$. For an ample line choose any very ample positive tensor power and take its metric root as above. Onto pair evaluations prevent equal kernels at distinct points: a common kernel would force the joint evaluation image to have dimension $r$, instead of $2r$. For $v\in T_ xX$, the derivative of the kernel map is, under $Q_ x=E_ x$, the map $s\mapsto -\partial _ v(Bs)$ for $s\in \ker B(x)$. This follows by differentiating $B(x(t))s(t)=0$ in graph coordinates. If $v
e 0$, first-jet surjectivity gives a section with value zero and nonzero derivative along $v$. The derivative of $\psi _ V$ is therefore injective. Compactness, or properness, makes an injective immersion a topological embedding; local holomorphic inverse charts then give the holomorphic embedding assertion. For rank one, $Q=\mathcal O(1)$ on the dual projective space. Linear homogeneous forms separate pairs there and generate every first jet: in an affine chart their ratios include the constant1 and all affine coordinates. Restriction along an injective immersion preserves pair separation and makes their derivative covectors span $T_ x^*X$. Pulling back these linear sections gives exactly the claimed surjections from $V$, proving the converse. $\square$ Example 10.35.5 . 75477746633A The line bundle $\det Q$ on $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$ is very ample in the first-jet/pair sense. The quotient $Q$ is not very ample for $2\leq r<d$; for $r=d$ it is very ample on the one-point base. Proof. Pullback of the preceding linear projective sections along the Plücker embedding generates all required jets and pairs of $\det Q$. For $Q$, the preceding global-section computation gives dimension $d$, whereas its first-jet fiber has dimension $r(1+r(d-r))$. For $d-r=k\geq 1$, their difference is $k(r^2-1)>0$ if $r\geq 2$, so evaluation cannot be onto. If $r=d$ the base is a point, the jet fiber equals $Q=V$, and there are no distinct pairs. $\square$ Example 10.35.6 . 384A806754ED On $X=\mathbb C$ the trivial line bundle and $V=\operatorname {span}\{ 1,e^ z,e^{\sqrt2z}\} $ generate every first jet and every distinct pair. The classifying map $z\mapsto [1:e^ z:e^{\sqrt2z}]$ is an injective immersion which is not a topological embedding. Proof. The first two sections already span each value/derivative jet. Equality of projective images gives a period $2\pi i k$ with both $k$ and $\sqrt2k$ integers, forcing $k=0$. Thus distinct evaluation rows are independent, proving the pair assertion; the derivative never vanishes. Pigeonhole subdivision of $[0,1)$ into $N$ equal intervals applied to the $N+1$ fractional parts of $0,\sqrt2,\ldots , N\sqrt2$ gives $1\leq k_ N\leq N$ with distance of $\sqrt2k_ N$ to an integer less than $1/N$. Such integers have an unbounded subsequence, since $\sqrt2$ is irrational. Along it the images of $2\pi i k_ N$ tend to $[1:1:1]$, the image of zero, while the parameters do not tend to zero. The inverse on the image is not continuous. The missing compactness/properness qualification is therefore necessary in the general embedding assertion. $\square$

section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text: Lemma 10.35.2 . F9789093E482 Let $X$ be a countable-basis complex manifold and $E$ a holomorphic bundle. Let $B$ be a countable-basis complex manifold of dimension $b$, and let $A_ x:H^0(X,E)\to F_ x$ be surjective linear maps into a holomorphic bundle of rank $R\geq 1$ on $B$. Suppose evaluation of each section is holomorphic in $x\in B$, and the induced map of section spaces is continuous for compact convergence. If $p\geq b+R$, some $p$ sections span every $F_ x$ under these maps. The same $p$ sections can be required to do this for finitely or countably many such families satisfying their respective bounds. Proof. The space of holomorphic sections with compact convergence is Fréchet. Countably many coefficient suprema in compact local frames define its topology. A Cauchy sequence has locally uniform coefficient limits, holomorphic by the Cauchy formula. The limits agree on overlaps and form a global section. Thus its $p$-fold product is a complete metrizable vector space. Use the proved Baire nested-ball argument in proposition 2.10.3 . For a compact $K\subset B$, tuples failing to span at some point of $K$ form a closed set. In local frames failure is vanishing of all $R$-minors; the sum of their squared norms has positive minimum on $K$ precisely for a spanning tuple. Uniform convergence on $K$ proves the closed assertion. We prove this closed set has empty interior. By pointwise surjectivity and compactness choose finitely many sections $t_1,\ldots ,t_ N$ whose images span on a neighborhood $O$ of $K$. Perturb a given tuple by \[  s_ j+\sum _{l=1}^ N\lambda _{jl}t_ l,\qquad 1\leq j\leq p.  \] The map from $O\times \mathbb C^{pN}$ to the $p$-fold fiber bundle of $F$ is a holomorphic submersion: its parameter derivative is onto. Concretely, invert a nonzero $R$-minor of the $t_ l$ evaluations; the corresponding $R$ parameters per column may be replaced by its fiber value, leaving the other parameters as coordinates. Rank-$k$ matrices in $\operatorname {Hom}(\mathbb C^ p,\mathbb C^ R)$ are smooth of complex codimension $(R-k)(p-k)$: after an invertible $k$-minor, the lower-right block is the product of the lower-left block, the inverse minor, and the upper-right block. This gives exactly $(R-k)(p-k)$ independent equations, also for $k=0$. Their inverse images under the displayed submersion therefore have dimension at most $b+pN-(p-R+1)\leq pN-1$ for $k<R$. Their parameter projections have Lebesgue measure zero. Here no Sard theorem is needed: on a compact coordinate box a smooth map from real dimension $a$ to $c>a$ is Lipschitz. Cover its domain by $O(\delta ^{-a})$ cubes of side $\delta $; the images fit in that many balls of radius $C\delta $, with total outer volume $O(\delta ^{c-a})\to 0$. Countably many boxes cover each stratum. Consequently arbitrarily small parameters avoid every bad rank on $O$. These finite-section perturbations tend to the given tuple in the section topology, proving density of good tuples on $K$. Take a countable compact exhaustion of each $B$. The resulting bad sets, for all specified families and all exhaustion members, are a countable union of closed sets with empty interior. Baire supplies a tuple outside their union, proving the lemma. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.35.3
section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text: Theorem 10.35.3 . CD7786C05633 Let $E$ have rank $r\geq 1$ on a countable-basis complex $n$-manifold. If $E$ is globally generated, some subspace $V\subset H^0(X,E)$ with $\dim V\leq n+r$ generates it everywhere. If every first-jet map and every distinct-pair evaluation of global sections is onto, one may choose a single $V$ surjecting onto all of them with \[  \dim V\leq \max \{ nr+n+r,\, 2(n+r)\} .  \] These statements do not require compactness of $X$. Proof. Apply lemma 10.35.2 first to evaluation over $X$, of rank $r$ and base dimension $n$. For the second assertion the first-jet bundle has rank $r(n+1)$: in local coordinates/frame a first jet is a value and its $n$ first derivatives, whose transition matrix has holomorphic entries by the chain and frame-change rules. Its evaluation depends holomorphically on the base and continuously on sections by Cauchy's derivative formula. Apply the lemma simultaneously to that bundle over $X$, and to $\operatorname {pr}_1^*E\oplus \operatorname {pr}_2^*E$ over $X\times X\setminus \Delta $, of rank $2r$ and dimension $2n$. Their required bounds are exactly the two numbers displayed. Taking the span of the selected tuple gives $V$; linear dependencies only reduce its dimension. Empty bases impose no condition. $\square$

title: Proposition 10.35.4
section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text: Proposition 10.35.4 . 0CE84812A13F For any finite generating space $V\subset H^0(X,E)$ the map $\psi _ V(x)=\ker (V\to E_ x)$ is holomorphic to $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$, and $E=\psi _ V^*Q$ canonically. Every globally generated bundle has a smooth Griffiths semipositive metric whose dual is Nakano seminegative. A line bundle with a globally generated positive tensor power has a smooth semipositive metric. If every first jet of $E$ is generated, the metric can instead be chosen with Nakano negative dual, and is Griffiths positive. In particular an ample line bundle has a smooth positive metric. If $V$ also generates every first jet and every distinct pair, $\psi _ V$ is an injective immersion. It is an embedding when $X$ is compact (or when this map is proper). For a line bundle the converse holds: an injective immersive $\psi _ V$ makes all those evaluation maps onto. Proof. Write evaluation as a full-rank holomorphic matrix $B(x)$ in a local frame. Inverting an $r$-minor expresses its kernel as a graph holomorphically, proving the map assertion. Evaluation identifies $V/\ker B(x)$ with $E_ x$, giving the bundle isomorphism. Give $V$ an inner product and use its quotient metric on $E$. The checked subbundle/quotient curvature formula proposition 10.34.9 for a flat ambient bundle gives Griffiths nonnegativity of the quotient. Its dual is a holomorphic subbundle of the flat dual, whose Nakano curvature is the negative Gram form $-\left|\sum _ jB_ jv_ j\right|^2$; hence is Nakano seminegative. These assertions use that exact formula, without assuming duality preserves Nakano positivity. For a line bundle a positive tensor power's quotient metric has the unique positive metric root; curvature divides by that tensor exponent, proving its metric claim. For the strict assertion choose a finite first-jet generating space by lemma 10.35.2 . At $x$, differentiation of evaluation on its kernel is a surjection \[  S_ x\longrightarrow T_ x^*X\otimes E_ x,\qquad s\longmapsto d_ xs.  \] Its dual $T_ xX\otimes E_ x^*\to S_ x^*$ is injective. It is, up to a sign, the second fundamental form of $E^*\subset \underline{V^*}$: differentiating the identically zero pairing of a local dual section with a local kernel section gives that identification. The flat subbundle curvature on a tensor $u$ is therefore exactly minus the squared norm of this dual map applied to $u$. It is strictly negative for $u\ne 0$. Rank-one tests and the dual curvature transpose then give Griffiths positivity of $E$. For an ample line choose any very ample positive tensor power and take its metric root as above. Onto pair evaluations prevent equal kernels at distinct points: a common kernel would force the joint evaluation image to have dimension $r$, instead of $2r$. For $v\in T_ xX$, the derivative of the kernel map is, under $Q_ x=E_ x$, the map $s\mapsto -\partial _ v(Bs)$ for $s\in \ker B(x)$. This follows by differentiating $B(x(t))s(t)=0$ in graph coordinates. If $v\ne 0$, first-jet surjectivity gives a section with value zero and nonzero derivative along $v$. The derivative of $\psi _ V$ is therefore injective. Compactness, or properness, makes an injective immersion a topological embedding; local holomorphic inverse charts then give the holomorphic embedding assertion. For rank one, $Q=\mathcal O(1)$ on the dual projective space. Linear homogeneous forms separate pairs there and generate every first jet: in an affine chart their ratios include the constant1 and all affine coordinates. Restriction along an injective immersion preserves pair separation and makes their derivative covectors span $T_ x^*X$. Pulling back these linear sections gives exactly the claimed surjections from $V$, proving the converse. $\square$

title: Example 10.35.5
section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text: Example 10.35.5 . 75477746633A The line bundle $\det Q$ on $\operatorname {Gr}_ r(V)$ is very ample in the first-jet/pair sense. The quotient $Q$ is not very ample for $2\leq r<d$; for $r=d$ it is very ample on the one-point base. Proof. Pullback of the preceding linear projective sections along the Plücker embedding generates all required jets and pairs of $\det Q$. For $Q$, the preceding global-section computation gives dimension $d$, whereas its first-jet fiber has dimension $r(1+r(d-r))$. For $d-r=k\geq 1$, their difference is $k(r^2-1)>0$ if $r\geq 2$, so evaluation cannot be onto. If $r=d$ the base is a point, the jet fiber equals $Q=V$, and there are no distinct pairs. $\square$

title: Example 10.35.6
section: 10.35 Grassmannians and finite generating spaces
text: Example 10.35.6 . 384A806754ED On $X=\mathbb C$ the trivial line bundle and $V=\operatorname {span}\{ 1,e^ z,e^{\sqrt2z}\} $ generate every first jet and every distinct pair. The classifying map $z\mapsto [1:e^ z:e^{\sqrt2z}]$ is an injective immersion which is not a topological embedding. Proof. The first two sections already span each value/derivative jet. Equality of projective images gives a period $2\pi i k$ with both $k$ and $\sqrt2k$ integers, forcing $k=0$. Thus distinct evaluation rows are independent, proving the pair assertion; the derivative never vanishes. Pigeonhole subdivision of $[0,1)$ into $N$ equal intervals applied to the $N+1$ fractional parts of $0,\sqrt2,\ldots , N\sqrt2$ gives $1\leq k_ N\leq N$ with distance of $\sqrt2k_ N$ to an integer less than $1/N$. Such integers have an unbounded subsequence, since $\sqrt2$ is irrational. Along it the images of $2\pi i k_ N$ tend to $[1:1:1]$, the image of zero, while the parameters do not tend to zero. The inverse on the image is not continuous. The missing compactness/properness qualification is therefore necessary in the general embedding assertion. $\square$

If $\Omega $ possesses a complete Kähler metric, it is pseudoconvex. Proof. Use the boundary-continuation definition of a domain of holomorphy in the Cartan–Thullen equivalences . Let $U$ be connected and open, meeting $\partial \Omega $, and let $V\subset U\cap \Omega $ be nonempty and open. Regular openness implies $U\setminus \overline\Omega 
e \varnothing $: otherwise the open $U$ would lie in $\operatorname {Int}\overline\Omega =\Omega $. Choose $a$ in this difference, so $d=\operatorname {dist}(a,\overline\Omega )>0$. For every $\epsilon >0$, \[  \int _\Omega |z-a|^{-2(n+\epsilon )}\, \mathrm dV \leq \int _{\{ |z-a|\geq d\} }|z-a|^{-2(n+\epsilon )}\, \mathrm dV <\infty ;  \] the radial tail is a constant times $\int _ d^\infty t^{-1-2\epsilon }dt$. title: Lemma 6.34.1
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.34 Weights and generalized Lelong masses
text: Lemma 6.34.1 . ECBFCBBB5EF1 Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$, and put $S=\operatorname {supp}T$. Suppose two continuous locally bounded plurisubharmonic functions $a,b$ agree on $S\cap D$ outside a compact set $K\subset D$, where $D$ is open and all measures under consideration have finite mass there. If their products agree on $S$ near $\partial D$, then \[  \int _ D T\wedge (dd^ ca)^ p=\int _ D T\wedge (dd^ cb)^ p.  \] It suffices that the differences and their coefficient primitives be compactly supported in $D$; no regular boundary is required. Proof. For $p=0$ both measures are $T$. For $p\geq 1$, bounded recursion and symmetry give \[  T\wedge (dd^ ca)^ p-T\wedge (dd^ cb)^ p =dd^ c\left((a-b)\sum _{j=0}^{p-1} T\wedge (dd^ ca)^ j\wedge (dd^ cb)^{p-1-j}\right).  \] Every current inside the sum is supported in $S$, so the primitive is compactly supported in $D$. Extend it by zero and test with a compact smooth function equal to one near that support. Its $dd^ c$ pairing is zero. The product measures agree elsewhere in $D$, which proves the equality. This is the support-relative form of lemma 6.33.7 ; all scalar multiplications and identities used here are the bounded recursion of locality and positivity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products , decreasing continuity of bounded Bedford–Taylor products . The same recursion shows relative locality: equality of potentials on $S$ in a relative neighborhood suffices for equality of the corresponding bounded products there. $\square$

title: Theorem 6.34.2
topic: Lelong numbers, multiplier ideals, and regularization
section: 6.34 Weights and generalized Lelong masses
text: Theorem 6.34.2 . 57F9C2832703 Let $T$ be closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$ and let $\varphi $ be semi-exhaustive on $S=\operatorname {supp}T$. For $s<r<R$ the finite number E50D452944E2 6.34.3 \begin{equation}  M_ T(\varphi ,r)=\int _{B_\varphi (r)}T\wedge (dd^ c\varphi _ s)^ p \end{equation} is independent of $s$. It is nonnegative, nondecreasing and left continuous in $r$, and \[  \nu (T,\varphi )=\lim _{r\to -\infty }M_ T(\varphi ,r)<\infty  \] exists. For $p=0$ these are $T(B_\varphi (r))$ and $T(P_\varphi )$. If a neighborhood of the compact low support sublevels admits a smooth strictly plurisubharmonic exhaustion as in theorem 7.31.2 , the classical measure $\sigma _\varphi =T\wedge (dd^ c\varphi )^ p$ is defined there, including its pole mass, and 268DE476A8A7 6.34.4 \begin{equation}  M_ T(\varphi ,r)=\sigma _\varphi (B_\varphi (r)),\qquad \nu (T,\varphi )=\sigma _\varphi (P_\varphi ). \end{equation} The truncation definition itself requires no such ambient exhaustion. Proof. Closed low sublevels on $S$ are compact. If $s,t<r$, the two potentials agree wherever $\varphi >\max \{ s,t\} $, and their bounded-product difference and its primitive are supported in $S\cap \{ \varphi \leq \max \{ s,t\} \} \Subset B_\varphi (r)$. The preceding lemma proves independence. Fixing a common truncation below two given levels gives monotonicity. Fixing one below an increasing sequence of levels gives left continuity by continuity from below of a fixed finite measure. A fixed larger level bounds the increasing masses from above, so their limit at $-\infty $ is finite. The measure case $p=0$ follows directly by continuity from above on the nested compact low support sublevels. Extended continuity makes $L(\varphi )=P_\varphi $. Under the stated exhaustion hypothesis, that unbounded locus on $S$ is compact and avoids a relative boundary. Thus theorem 7.31.2 defines the classical products and gives their convergence for $\varphi _ s\downarrow \varphi $. At every level carrying no $\sigma _\varphi $-mass, weak convergence and the compact support cutoff give ( 6.34.4 ). Only countably many levels can carry mass in any compact range. Approximation from below by other levels gives the open-sublevel formula at every $r$; approximation from above gives its closed-sublevel version. Finally the low sublevels decrease to $P_\varphi $ on $S$, giving the pole formula. This argument does not assert a classical unbounded product on an arbitrary non-Stein space. $\square$

E1AA7F10EA92 For $p\geq 1$ and every finite convex nondecreasing $\chi :\mathbb R\to \mathbb R$, 70CF1825304A 6.34.6 \begin{equation}  \int _{B_\varphi (r)}T\wedge \bigl (dd^ c(\chi \circ \varphi )\bigr )^ p =\chi '_-(r)^ p M_ T(\varphi ,r). \end{equation} On the left use the classical product when available, or the independent inner truncations $\chi \circ \varphi _ s$, $s<r$. In particular, with $N_\varphi =T\wedge (dd^ ce^\varphi )^ p$, 2B06A37CFD8E 6.34.7 \begin{equation}  M_ T(\varphi ,r)=e^{-pr}N_\varphi (B_\varphi (r)),\qquad M_ T(\varphi ,r+)=e^{-pr}N_\varphi (\{ \varphi \leq r\} ). \end{equation} Moreover $\nu (T,\lambda \varphi +c)=\lambda ^ p\nu (T,\varphi )$ for $\lambda >0$ and $c\in \mathbb R$. For $p=0$ use the direct measure definition, without a power of a possibly zero derivative. Proof. Convex nondecreasing composition preserves plurisubharmonicity: for smooth functions this follows from the positive chain-rule Hessian, and smoothing the convex function and the bounded continuous inner potential proves the assertion by local uniform convergence. The bounded-product uniform-continuity theorem uniform convergence of bounded Bedford–Taylor products justifies the same compositions and products in the following piecewise-linear constructions. All integrals with different inner cutoffs agree by the collar lemma. Put $a_\epsilon =\chi '_-(r-\epsilon )$. Extend $\chi $ linearly above $r-\epsilon $ with slope $a_\epsilon $; call the result $\chi ^-_\epsilon $. It is convex, agrees with $\chi $ below that level and is affine near $r$. Its mass over $B_\varphi (r)$ is $a_\epsilon ^ p M_ T(\varphi ,r)$ by relative collar equality with the affine potential. Conversely extend $\chi $ linearly below $r-\epsilon $ with that slope, leaving it unchanged above; call this $\chi ^+_\epsilon $. It has the same total mass as $\chi \circ \varphi $ over $B_\varphi (r)$ and has mass $a_\epsilon ^ pM_ T(\varphi ,r-\epsilon )$ in the smaller sublevel. These two inequalities, left continuity of the fixed composed measure and $a_\epsilon \to \chi '_-(r)$ prove ( 6.34.6 ). Take $\chi (t)=e^ t$ and then approach $r$ from above to obtain ( 6.34.7 ), including its closed endpoint. For an affine function, changing the sublevel variable gives the last assertion directly. $\square$

Proposition 6.35.1 . 9BBFC6858DCC Let $F:X	o Y$ be holomorphic and proper on $S=\operatorname {supp}T$, with $T$ closed positive of bidimension $(p,p)$. Throughout this section $X$ is a connected compact Riemann surface, $K_ X$ is its holomorphic cotangent line bundle, and $E$ denotes a holomorphic line bundle. Write $H^ q(E)=H^ q(X,\mathcal O(E))$ and $h^ q(E)=\dim _{\mathbb C}H^ q(E)$. These are the sheaf groups identified with smooth analytic Dolbeault cohomology by corollary 10.43.11 . The compact bundle Hodge theorem 10.46.6 makes $h^0,h^1$ finite; $H^ q(E)=0$ for $q\geq 2$ because the Dolbeault resolution has only degrees zero and one. A holomorphic function on $X$ is constant by the local maximum principle and compactness. Put $g=h^1(\mathcal O_ X)$. A divisor is a finite sum $D=\sum _ x m_ x[x]$ with $m_ x\in \mathbb Z$. The sheaf $E(D)$ consists of meromorphic sections $s$ of $E$ for which $\operatorname {ord}_ x(s)+m_ x\geq 0$ at every point. In a coordinate $z$ centered at $x$ and holomorphic frame $e$ of $E$, it has the free local generator $z^{-m_ x}e$. text: Lemma 10.78.7 . 378F4A64CA3C If $s$ is a nonzero meromorphic section of $E$, then 90C71A91CD02 10.78.8 \begin{equation}  dd^ c\log |s|_ h^2=[\operatorname {div}s]-c_1(E,h), \qquad \deg E=\sum _ x\operatorname {ord}_ x(s)\in \mathbb Z. \end{equation} In particular $\deg \mathcal O_ X(D)=\sum _ xm_ x$; degrees add under tensor product and change sign under dualization. A nonzero holomorphic section has an effective divisor, so $h^0(E)=0$ if $\deg E<0$, or if $\deg E=0$ and $E$ is nontrivial. In degree zero a nonzero holomorphic section trivializes $E$. Proof. In a local frame write $s=f e$ with $f$ meromorphic. The Poincaré–Lelong theorem the normalized Poincaré–Lelong formula , applied to the numerator and denominator of $f$, gives \[  dd^ c\log |s|_ h^2 =dd^ c\log |f|^2+dd^ c\log |e|_ h^2 =[\operatorname {div}s]-c_1(E,h).  \] The norm logarithm is a global locally integrable function, including its logarithmic zeros and poles. Stokes against the constant one gives the degree identity. The divisor bundle has the meromorphic section one with divisor $D$: in its local frame $z^{-m_ x}$ its coefficient is $z^{m_ x}$. Tensor products and duals either add the curvatures or add and negate these divisors. Finally an effective divisor has nonnegative degree; if that degree is zero it is empty, and the section is a holomorphic frame everywhere. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.78.9 (Riemann–Roch for a line bundle)
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Theorem 10.78.9 (Riemann–Roch for a line bundle) . 7F8CC797059F Every holomorphic line bundle $E$ on $X$ satisfies 8BE9F0A9B79D 10.78.10 \begin{equation}  h^0(E)-h^1(E)=\deg E+1-g,\qquad h^1(E)=h^0(K_ X\otimes E^*). \end{equation} The latter equality is induced by the perfect pairing \[  H^1(E)\times H^0(K_ X\otimes E^*)\longrightarrow \mathbb C, \qquad ([\alpha ],\beta )\longmapsto \int _ X\alpha \wedge \beta .  \] Proof. Set $\chi (E)=h^0(E)-h^1(E)$. Taking alternating dimensions in ( 10.78.3 ) gives \[  \chi (F(D))=\chi (F)+\sum _ xm_ x\qquad (D\geq 0).  \] For any divisor write $D=D_+-D_-$ with $D_\pm \geq 0$. Apply the effective case first to $(F,D_+)$ and then to $(F(D),D_-)$. The resulting identities have the same left-hand term $\chi (F(D_+))$, so subtraction gives \[  \chi (F(D))=\chi (F)+\sum _ xm_ x  \] for all integral divisors, including negative ones. Now take $E\cong \mathcal O_ X(D)$ as already proved. Since $h^0(\mathcal O_ X)=1$ and $h^1(\mathcal O_ X)=g$, the divisor-degree identity proves the first assertion. The second is precisely the analytic Serre pairing of theorem 10.46.7 with $n=1,p=0,q=1$, transported by the bundle Dolbeault/sheaf comparison. A smooth $E^*$-valued $(1,0)$-form killed by $\bar\partial $ is a holomorphic section of $K_ X\otimes E^*$, by its local holomorphic coefficients. Stokes makes the displayed integral independent of the representative of $[\alpha ]$, and the cited proved harmonic-star argument makes it perfect. This is complex bilinear duality, not an unsupported identification of the two spaces by a metric-linear map. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.78.11
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Corollary 10.78.11 . 43B79368A1B8 One has $h^0(K_ X)=g$, $h^1(K_ X)=1$, and 2681385859FF 10.78.12 \begin{equation}  \deg K_ X=2g-2. \end{equation} For every $a\in X$ and every integer $m$, 492C950FA104 10.78.13 \begin{equation}  h^0(K_ X(-m[a]))=h^1(\mathcal O_ X(m[a])) =h^0(\mathcal O_ X(m[a]))-m+g-1. \end{equation} If $\deg E>2g-2$, then $h^1(E)=0$ and $h^0(E)=\deg E+1-g$. In particular $h^0(\mathcal O_ X(m[a]))=m+1-g$ for every integer $m>2g-2$. Proof. Serre duality for $\mathcal O_ X$ gives $h^0(K_ X)=g$, and for $K_ X$ gives $h^1(K_ X)=h^0(\mathcal O_ X)=1$. Apply Riemann–Roch to $K_ X$. Apply it next to $\mathcal O_ X(m[a])$, whose dual is $\mathcal O_ X(-m[a])$ and whose degree is $m$. This proves ( 10.78.13 ) also for zero and negative $m$. If $\deg E>2g-2$, then $\deg (K_ X\otimes E^*)<0$, so its holomorphic sections vanish by lemma 10.78.7 . Serre and Riemann–Roch give the last assertions. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.78.14
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Corollary 10.78.14 . 5A3D6AC0AA3E For a fixed $a\in X$, the dimension increase \[  h^0(\mathcal O_ X(m[a]))-h^0(\mathcal O_ X((m-1)[a]))  \] is zero or one for $m\geq 1$. It is one exactly when there is a meromorphic function whose only pole is $a$ and whose pole order is exactly $m$. Exactly $g$ positive integers fail this property. For $g\geq 1$ all these gaps are at most $2g-1$; for $g=0$ there are no gaps. There is a nonconstant function with only a pole at $a$ of order at most $g+1$. Proof. Apply ( 10.78.2 ) to the inclusion $\mathcal O_ X((m-1)[a])\subset \mathcal O_ X(m[a])$. Its quotient has dimension one, and the first three terms of the section sequence give the increase bound and the exact-pole interpretation. For a large integer $M>2g-2$, telescoping the increases from $h^0(\mathcal O_ X)=1$ gives $M-g$ nongaps among $1,\ldots ,M$. If $g\geq 1$, consecutive dimensions are given by the polynomial formula for $m\geq 2g$, so all these increases are one; the same is true for every $m\geq 1$ when $g=0$. There are therefore precisely $g$ gaps in the stated range. Finally Riemann–Roch gives $h^0(\mathcal O_ X((g+1)[a]))\geq 2$, so a section independent of the constants is the required function. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.78.15
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Corollary 10.78.15 . F8C1FB7AE853 The additive sheaf $\mathcal M(E)$ of meromorphic sections satisfies \[  H^1(X,\mathcal M(E))=0.  \] Proof. Let $P(E)=\mathcal M(E)/\mathcal O(E)$. Local polar expansions identify it with the sheaf of locally finite assignments of principal parts in the abelian groups $A_ x=\mathcal M(E)_ x/\mathcal O(E)_ x$. To check surjectivity of this identification, realize any given principal part by its finite polar polynomial in a small frame disk; on the punctured disk its quotient class is zero and glues with zero. Locally finite families glue these representatives as quotient sections. Thus lemma 10.78.4 gives $H^1(X,P(E))=0$. Fix a point $a$ and choose a positive integer $m>2g-2-\deg E$. Then $H^1(E(m[a]))=0$ by corollary 10.78.11 . The boundary from $Q_{m[a]}(E)(X)$ onto $H^1(E)$ is therefore surjective. It factors through the boundary $P(E)(X)\to H^1(E)$ by naturality of the inclusions into $\mathcal M(E)$. The latter boundary is onto as well. The long exact sequence of $0\to \mathcal O(E)\to \mathcal M(E)\to P(E)\to 0$ now gives $H^1(X,\mathcal M(E))=0$. No commutation of sheaf cohomology with an increasing union of pole bounds has been assumed. $\square$

title: Corollary 10.78.16 (Riemann–Hurwitz)
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Corollary 10.78.16 (Riemann–Hurwitz) . 0DB2FC824E28 Let $f:X\to Y$ be a nonconstant holomorphic map between connected compact Riemann surfaces. For $x\in X$ let $e_ x$ be the order of $f-f(x)$ in local coordinates. There is a positive integer $d$ such that $\sum _{f(x)=y}e_ x=d$ for every $y\in Y$, and \[  K_ X\cong f^*K_ Y\otimes \mathcal O_ X\! \left( \sum _ x(e_ x-1)[x]\right),\qquad 2g_ X-2=d(2g_ Y-2)+\sum _ x(e_ x-1).  \] Only finitely many summands in the ramification divisor are nonzero. Proof. The map is open by its local nonconstant holomorphic power expansion and closed by compactness, so it is onto. Its fibers are finite, since their points are isolated. The usual local degree argument is short: around each point in a fiber choose a small coordinate disk whose boundary avoids that target value. All preimages of nearby values remain in their union, since otherwise compactness would give an additional point of the original fiber. In each disk the integral of the logarithmic derivative of the target coordinate expression minus the nearby value is a continuous integer and hence constant. Factoring its zeros identifies it with the sum of their orders. Thus the total fiber order is locally constant on connected $Y$, and is a fixed positive $d$. The derivative is a nonzero holomorphic section of $K_ X\otimes (f^*K_ Y)^*$. In local coordinates its coefficient is the derivative of $z^{e_ x}u(z)$, with $u(0)\ne 0$, so its zero order is exactly $e_ x-1$. These zeros are finite on compact $X$. The meromorphic-section bundle identification already proved gives the asserted isomorphism. For any line bundle $L$ on $Y$, take a meromorphic section with divisor $\sum m_ y[y]$. Its pullback has divisor $\sum _ y m_ y\sum _{f(x)=y}e_ x[x]$. The degree-divisor identity therefore gives $\deg f^*L=d\deg L$, without a separate topological covering-degree theorem. Taking degrees in the bundle isomorphism and using ( 10.78.12 ) finishes. $\square$

title: Theorem 10.78.17
section: 10.78 Divisors and Riemann–Roch on a compact curve
text: Theorem 10.78.17 . BE4F0C047320 Suppose $g\geq 1$ and let $u_1,\ldots ,u_ g$ be a basis of $H^0(X,K_ X)$. In a local coordinate $z$, write $u_ j=U_ j(z)\, dz$. With $N=g(g+1)/2$, the expression CB0D8959E769 10.78.18 \begin{equation}  W(u_1,\ldots ,u_ g) =\det \bigl (U_ j^{(k)}(z)\bigr )_{0\leq k\leq g-1,\, 1\leq j\leq g} (dz)^ N \end{equation} defines a nonzero holomorphic section of $K_ X^ N$. Its zero divisor does not depend on the basis. At each $a\in X$ there are exactly $g$ integers $1\leq s_1<\cdots <s_ g\leq 2g-1$ such that A7C22590729C 10.78.19 \begin{equation}  h^0(\mathcal O_ X(m[a]))=m+1-\# \{ j:s_ j\leq m\}  \qquad (m\geq 0). \end{equation} These are precisely the pole gaps. The multiplicity of $W$ at $a$ is \[  \mu _ a=\sum _{j=1}^ g s_ j-\frac{g(g+1)}2\geq 0, \qquad \sum _{a\in X}\mu _ a=g(g+1)(g-1).  \] The points with $\mu _ a>0$ are the Weierstrass points. There are at most $g(g+1)(g-1)$ such points. At every other point the gap sequence is $1,\ldots ,g$ and \[  h^0(\mathcal O_ X(m[a]))= \begin{cases} 1,& 0\leq m\leq g,\\ m+1-g,& m>g.\end{cases}  \] Proof. If $z=z(w)$, the coefficients in the $w$ coordinate are $V_ j(w)=U_ j(z(w))z'(w)$. Repeated differentiation gives \[  V_ j^{(k)}=(z')^{k+1}U_ j^{(k)}\circ z +\sum _{r<k}a_{kr}U_ j^{(r)}\circ z.  \] This follows by induction: differentiating the first term produces the next leading term and a lower derivative, and differentiating each remaining term keeps its derivative order at most $k$. The transformation matrix of the rows is triangular, with determinant $\prod _{k=0}^{g-1}(z')^{k+1}=(z')^ N$. This proves that ( 10.78.18 ) is a section of $K_ X^ N$. A constant basis change multiplies it by its nonzero determinant. At a fixed $a$, filter $H^0(K_ X)$ by order of vanishing at $a$. Each successive quotient has dimension at most one, by the first nonzero Taylor coefficient. Every nonzero section has zero divisor of degree $2g-2$, so its vanishing order is at most $2g-2$. Consequently the filtration terminates, and choosing one section at each strict decrease gives a basis with distinct leading orders: \[  \widetilde u_ j=(z^{s_ j-1}+O(z^{s_ j}))\, dz, \qquad 1\leq s_1<\cdots <s_ g\leq 2g-1.  \] Set $r_ j=s_ j-1$. Factoring $z^{r_ j}$ out of column $j$ and $z^{-k}$ out of row $k$ in its Wronskian gives, for $z\ne 0$, \[  W(\widetilde u_1,\ldots ,\widetilde u_ g) =z^{\sum r_ j-\sum _{k=0}^{g-1}k} \left(\det \bigl ((r_ j)_ k\bigr )_{k,j}+O(z)\right)(dz)^ N.  \] Here $(r)_0=1$ and $(r)_ k=r(r-1)\cdots (r-k+1)$; zero falling factorials are allowed. These are monic polynomials of degrees $k$, so elementary triangular row operations turn their determinant into the Vandermonde determinant $\prod _{i<j}(r_ j-r_ i)\ne 0$. The exponent is $\mu _ a=\sum s_ j-N$, which is nonnegative because $s_ j\geq j$. Thus the expression extends holomorphically at zero, is not identically zero, and has exactly that multiplicity. Distinct leading orders mean that a linear combination's lowest nonzero leading term cannot cancel. Hence $h^0(K_ X(-m[a]))=\# \{ j:s_ j>m\} $. Substitute this in ( 10.78.13 ) to obtain ( 10.78.19 ). Its consecutive differences give the exact gap interpretation. Also $\mu _ a=0$ exactly when every $s_ j=j$. This proves the stated dimensions at ordinary points. Finally $W$ is a nonzero section of $K_ X^ N$, so its finitely many zeros have total multiplicity $N\deg K_ X=g(g+1)(g-1)$ by the divisor-degree identity. Every positive multiplicity is an integer at least one, proving the bound on their number, including zero Weierstrass points for $g=1$. $\square$

text: Theorem 6.30.4 . D191522951EC Put $p=\min (n-1,r-1)$. For every real $t\geq p$, FE0312A8F3A0 6.30.5 \begin{equation}  \mathfrak a_+(t+1)=\mathfrak a\, \mathfrak a_+(t) =\mathfrak a_\infty (1)\mathfrak a_+(t). \end{equation} For every integer $k\geq 0$, 74FDC8170F34 6.30.6 \begin{equation}  \mathfrak a_\infty (k+p)\subset \mathfrak a_+(k+p) =\mathfrak a^ k\mathfrak a_+(p)\subset \mathfrak a^ k. \end{equation} Proof. The unit case is immediate. Suppose first $r\leq n$, so $p=r-1$. For $f\in \mathfrak a_+(t+1)$ choose a small ball and $\eta >0$ with $\int |f|^2|g|^{-2(t+1+\eta )}<\infty $. Use scalar division corollary 6.29.2 on that ball with $m=r-1$ and $\phi =(t-m)\log |g|^2$. Its coefficient $t-m$ is nonnegative, so this is PSH by plurisubharmonicity of logarithmic holomorphic norms , with zero understood when $t=m$. The ball is complete Kähler by lemma 6.26.8 , using its smooth PSH exhaustion $(R^2-|z|^2)^{-1}$. The data exponent is exactly $t+1+\eta $. Division gives $f=\sum g_ jh_ j$ with $\int |h|^2|g|^{-2(t+\eta )}<\infty $, so every $h_ j\in \mathfrak a_+(t)$. If $r>n$, use the preceding $n$-generator ideal $\mathfrak b$. text: Theorem 6.30.7 . D091ECF916A1 For every real $t\geq 0$, a germ $u$ belongs to $\mathfrak a_\infty (t)$ if and only if it satisfies a monic equation AFD88AFE39D9 6.30.8 \begin{equation}  u^ d+c_1u^{d-1}+\cdots +c_ d=0, \qquad c_ s\in \mathfrak a^{\lceil ts\rceil }\  (1\leq s\leq d). \end{equation} In particular $\mathfrak a_\infty (1)$ is the integral closure of $\mathfrak a$. There is always a rational $l\geq t$ such that $\mathfrak a_\infty (l)=\mathfrak a_\infty (t)$. Proof. If a monic equation holds, put $M=\max _ s|c_ s|^{1/s}$ at each point. The elementary root bound $|u|\leq 2M$ follows because $|u|>2M$ would give $\sum _ s|c_ s/u^ s|<\sum _{s\geq 1}2^{-s}=1$. Since $|g|\leq 1$, membership of each coefficient in the indicated ideal power gives $|c_ s|\leq C_ s|g|^{\lceil ts\rceil } \leq C_ s|g|^{ts}$. Hence $|u|\leq C|g|^ t$. For the converse, let $J=\mathfrak a_+(p)$. It is finitely generated by Noetherianity of convergent power-series modules and nonzero: for a nonzero $g_ j$, choose an integer $N>p$ and $0<\eta <N-p$; the integrand $|g_ j|^{2N}|g|^{-2(p+\eta )}$ is bounded near zero. Choose nonzero generators $v_1,\ldots ,v_ q$ of $J$. Their finitely many integrability margins give $\delta >0$ such that ACAC37891CB2 6.30.9 \begin{equation}  J=\mathfrak a_+(p+\eta )\qquad (0\leq \eta <\delta ). \end{equation} Indeed take $2\delta $ below all margins in the defining integrals; each generator then belongs to the right side, and the reverse inclusion follows from the stronger exponent. For any real $t\geq 0$ and any $\delta >0$ there are an integer $m\geq 1$ and $0\leq \eta <\delta $ with $N=mt+\eta $ an integer. For rational $t$ take a denominator and $\eta =0$. For irrational $t$, the pigeonhole principle applied to fractional parts $0,t,\ldots ,Lt$ gives $q_0\geq 1$ with the fractional part of $q_0t$ within $1/L$ of an integer. If it is $1-\beta $, take $m=q_0$ and $\eta =\beta $. If it is $\beta >0$, take $m=q_0\lfloor 1/\beta \rfloor $, whose fractional part lies in $(1-\beta ,1)$, and take $\eta =1-\lfloor 1/\beta \rfloor \beta $. Here $L$ is chosen with $1/L<\delta $; irrationality excludes equality at an integer. This proves the assertion. For $u\in \mathfrak a_\infty (t)$ choose such $m,\eta ,N$ and use ( 6.30.9 ), the product inclusion and ( 6.30.6 ) to get \[  u^ mJ\subset \mathfrak a_\infty (mt)\mathfrak a_+(p+\eta ) \subset \mathfrak a_+(p+N)=\mathfrak a^ N J.  \] Thus $u^ mv_ j=\sum _ l b_{jl}v_ l$ with $b_{jl}\in \mathfrak a^ N$. Multiplying $(u^ mI-B)v=0$ by its adjugate gives $\det (u^ mI-B)v=0$. Since $R$ is a domain and $v\ne 0$, its determinant is zero. The coefficient of $u^{m(q-s)}$ lies in $\mathfrak a^{Ns}\subset \mathfrak a^{\lceil mts\rceil }$. This is ( 6.30.8 ), with zero coefficients at degrees whose indices are not multiples of $m$. Finally choose finitely many generators of $\mathfrak a_\infty (t)$ by the same Noetherian theorem and equations of the proved type for them. If $t$ is rational use $l=t$. Otherwise the finitely many nonzero coefficient indices $s$ have $\lceil ts\rceil /s>t$. Choose rational $l\geq t$ below all these upper bounds. Then $\lceil ls\rceil =\lceil ts\rceil $ at every such index, and the same equations put all generators in $\mathfrak a_\infty (l)$. The reverse inclusion follows from $l\geq t$ and $|g|\leq 1$. If the index family is empty the corresponding generators are zero, and any rational $l\geq t$ suffices. $\square$

section: 10.51 Twisted differential forms on projective space
text: Let $V$ be a complex vector space of dimension $N=n+1$, and let $\mathbb P(V)$ parametrize its lines. The tautological line is $\mathcal O(-1)$ and $\mathcal O(k)=\mathcal O(-1)^{\otimes (-k)}$. Write $H^{p,q}(\mathcal O(k))=H^ q(\mathbb P(V),\Omega ^ p\otimes \mathcal O(k))$, with the smooth Dolbeault identification of corollary 10.43.11 . All duals below are complex linear duals, not Hermitian conjugate vector spaces. For $k\geq 0$ let \[  C^{p,k}(V^*)=\Lambda ^ pV^*\otimes \operatorname {Sym}^{k-p}V^*, \qquad Z^{p,k}(V^*)=\ker (\gamma :C^{p,k}\to C^{p-1,k}),  \] where negative symmetric or exterior degrees give zero spaces and $\gamma $ contracts polynomial forms with the Euler field $\xi =\sum _ jz_ j\partial _{z_ j}$. Exterior differentiation preserves total weight $k$, and the coordinate product rule gives 63641BE1C835 10.51.1 \begin{equation}  d\gamma +\gamma d=kI,\qquad \gamma ^2=d^2=0. \end{equation} Indeed the scalar polynomial degree contributes $k-p$ and the $p$ differential factors contribute $p$. This is the homogeneous polynomial specialization of the canonical radial homotopy formula the de Rham homotopy formula . For $k>0$ it proves exactness for $\gamma $ and the canonical splitting 796E28946350 10.51.2 \begin{equation}  C^{p,k}\longrightarrow Z^{p,k}\oplus Z^{p-1,k},\quad a\longmapsto (\gamma da/k,\gamma a),\qquad (b,c)\longmapsto b+dc/k. \end{equation} The two compositions are the identity by ( 10.51.1 ). In particular $P=\gamma d/k$ is a projection onto $Z^{p,k}$. For $k=0$ only $C^{0,0}=Z^{0,0}=\mathbb C$ is nonzero; this case is not asserted to be exact. Use the same notation with $V$ in place of $V^*$ for polynomial forms on $V^*$. Lemma 10.51.3 . CA86EAF3228C There is a canonical perfect bilinear pairing between $Z^{p,k}(V^*)$ and $Z^{p,k}(V)$, for every $k\geq 0$. For $0\leq p\leq n$ and $k>p$, these spaces are nonzero and CF26F1D71E2F 10.51.4 \begin{equation}  \dim Z^{p,k}(V^*) =\binom {k-1}{p}\binom {k+n-p}{n-p}. \end{equation} Moreover $Z^{p,p}=0$ for $p>0$. Proof. Pair exterior powers by evaluation determinants and pair homogeneous polynomials of the same degree by differential evaluation: \[  \langle f(z),g(w)\rangle =f(\partial _ w)g(w)|_{w=0}.  \] Equivalently the monomials $z^\alpha ,w^\beta $ have pairing $\alpha !\, \delta _{\alpha \beta }$. This is the canonical symmetric tensor pairing multiplied by the degree factorial, so is independent of the chosen dual coordinates and is nondegenerate. Multiplication by $z_ j$ is transpose to $\partial _{w_ j}$, while contraction on exterior powers is transpose to wedge multiplication. Thus $\gamma ^ t=d$ and $d^ t=\gamma $ on the dual complexes. Consequently $P^ t=P$ for the projections in ( 10.51.2 ). If $a\in Z^{p,k}(V^*)$ annihilates $Z^{p,k}(V)$, then for every $b\in C^{p,k}(V)$, \[  \langle a,b\rangle =\langle Pa,b\rangle =\langle a,Pb\rangle =0.  \] Nondegeneracy on $C^{p,k}$ gives $a=0$, and the same argument in the other factor proves perfection. The $k=0$ assertion is ordinary scalar evaluation (or the pairing of zero spaces). For $k>0$ the splitting gives $D_ p+D_{p-1}=\binom {n+1}{p}\binom {k-p+n}{n}$, where $D_ p=\dim Z^{p,k}$ and $D_{-1}=0$. The degree-zero term is $D_0=\binom {k+n}{n}$. Induction on $p<k$ gives ( 10.51.4 ): substituting the factorial expressions for $D_ p,D_{p-1}$ into this recurrence gives the common numerator $(n-p+1)(k-p)+p(k+n-p+1)=k(n+1)$. Nonzeroness is also explicit: in $p+1$ independent coordinates, \[  z_0^{k-p-1}\gamma (dz_0\wedge \cdots \wedge dz_ p)  \] is a nonzero horizontal form of weight $k$. Finally a constant $p$-form annihilated by contraction with every $z$ is zero for $p>0$, proving $Z^{p,p}=0$ directly. $\square$ Proposition 10.51.5 . 74AA0E1253DB Assume $n\geq 1$, $0\leq p\leq n$ and $k\in \mathbb Z$. Then \[  H^{p,0}(\mathcal O(k))= \begin{cases}  Z^{p,k}(V^*),& k>p,\\  \mathbb C,& (p,k)=(0,0),\\  0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The polynomial identification is canonical for the tautological linearization, and hence respects changes of basis of $V$. Proof. Let $\pi :V\setminus \{ 0\} \to \mathbb P(V)$ and let $\mu (z)=z$ be its nonzero tautological section of $\pi ^*\mathcal O(-1)$. From a holomorphic section $s$ of $\Omega ^ p\otimes \mathcal O(k)$ form the ordinary holomorphic $p$-form \[  \alpha _ z=(d\pi _ z)^*s(\pi (z))\otimes \mu (z)^ k.  \] The line factors cancel, including for negative powers. Since $\ker d\pi _ z=\mathbb Cz$, one has $\gamma \alpha =0$. The differential identity $d\pi _{tz}=t^{-1}d\pi _ z$ makes its coefficients homogeneous of degree $m=k-p$. Conversely every such horizontal form descends after multiplication by $\mu ^{-k}$: in a chart take the holomorphic representative with $z_ i=1$. Horizontalness removes vertical derivatives, and homogeneity gives exactly the transition factors of $\mathcal O(k)$. This construction is inverse to the pullback and is natural. We justify the homogeneous-function assertion at the puncture. If $m\geq 0$, each coefficient $f$ has $|f(z)|\leq C|z|^ m$, by bounding it on the unit sphere. The canonical bounded holomorphic removal theorem bounded holomorphic removal and connected complements extends it across zero. Its convergent Taylor series and homogeneity then leave only the degree-$m$ terms. Thus the lifted forms are exactly $Z^{p,k}$. If $m<0$, fix any nonzero $v$ and choose an independent $w$, possible because $N\geq 2$. The entire function $F(t)=f(v+tw)$ is bounded: for large $t$, it equals $t^ mf(w+v/t)$ and tends to zero. Cauchy's derivative estimate on arbitrarily large circles makes $F$ constant, and this limit makes it zero. Hence $f(v)=0$ for every $v$ and the section vanishes. For $m=0$ the Taylor polynomial is constant; when $p=k>0$ horizontalness makes that constant $p$-form zero by the preceding lemma. The scalar $p=k=0$ case gives exactly the constant sections. This proves all endpoints. $\square$ Theorem 10.51.6 . BEB304EB7449 Let $\dim V=n+1$ with $n\geq 1$, $0\leq p,q\leq n$ and $k\in \mathbb Z$. With canonical complex-linear identifications, \[  H^{p,q}(\mathcal O(k))\simeq \begin{cases}  Z^{p,k}(V^*),& q=0,\  k>p,\\  Z^{n-p,-k}(V),& q=n,\  k<p-n,\\  \mathbb C,& k=0,\  p=q,\\  0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] Each displayed group is nonzero. For $0\leq p\leq n$ and $k>p$, these spaces are nonzero and CF26F1D71E2F 10.51.4 \begin{equation}  \dim Z^{p,k}(V^*) =\binom {k-1}{p}\binom {k+n-p}{n-p}. \end{equation} Moreover $Z^{p,p}=0$ for $p>0$. text: Proposition 10.51.5 . 74AA0E1253DB Assume $n\geq 1$, $0\leq p\leq n$ and $k\in \mathbb Z$. Then \[  H^{p,0}(\mathcal O(k))= \begin{cases}  Z^{p,k}(V^*),& k>p,\\  \mathbb C,& (p,k)=(0,0),\\  0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}  \] The polynomial identification is canonical for the tautological linearization, and hence respects changes of basis of $V$. title: 10.61.1 A precise fiber comparison and finite-map theorem
search_title: A precise fiber comparison and finite-map theorem
section: 10.61 Fibers, closed maps and sheaf cohomological dimension
text: Lemma 10.61.2 . 2E03713CB092 If a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ is closed, the sets $f^{-1}V$, $V$ an open neighborhood of $y$, are cofinal among open neighborhoods of $f^{-1}(y)$. A proper map between locally compact Hausdorff spaces is closed, where proper means that inverse images of compact sets are compact. Every finite subspace of a Hausdorff space is strongly paracompact in the ambient space. Every compact subspace of a regular Hausdorff space has the same property. Proof. For an open $O\supset f^{-1}(y)$, the closed set $X\setminus O$ has closed image missing $y$. Set $V=Y\setminus f(X\setminus O)$. Then $y\in V$ and $f^{-1}V\subset O$. This also handles an empty fiber: taking $O=\varnothing $ gives a neighborhood with empty inverse image whenever $y$ is outside the closed image. Suppose now $f$ is proper as stated, and $C$ is closed in $X$. For each $y\in Y$ choose a compact neighborhood $K$ of $y$. The set $C\cap f^{-1}K$ is compact and its image is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff space $Y$. On $\operatorname {int}K$ this image agrees with $f(C)$. Thus $f(C)\cap \operatorname {int}K$ is closed in $\operatorname {int}K$. These open neighborhoods cover $Y$, so $f(C)$ is closed. This uses compactness rather than sequences. For a finite fiber set $S=\{ x_1,\ldots ,x_ m\} $ in a Hausdorff space, choose pairwise disjoint open neighborhoods $N_ i$ of its points by finitely many pairwise Hausdorff separations. Given an ambient open cover of $S$, choose $O_ i\subset N_ i$ containing $x_ i$ in a prescribed cover member $U_ i$. For $j\ne i$, $x_ j\notin \overline{O_ i}$ since $N_ j$ is an open neighborhood disjoint from $O_ i$. The finite closed union of the bad sets $\overline{O_ i}\setminus U_ i$ misses $S$. Its complement $W$ is a neighborhood of $S$ with $W\cap \overline{O_ i}\subset U_ i$. The finite family is locally finite, proving precisely the strong-paracompact definition of section 10.44 . For compact $S$ in a regular Hausdorff space, first choose point neighborhoods with ambient closures in the given cover members, then take a finite subcover; one can take $W=X$. $\square$ Theorem 10.61.3 . 73840D17A7B1 Let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous and closed, and suppose $S_ y=f^{-1}(y)$ is strongly paracompact in $X$. For every sheaf $A$ there are natural identifications \[  (R^ qf_*A)_ y\simeq H^ q(S_ y,A|_{S_ y}).  \] In particular the condition holds for proper maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces. It also holds, for arbitrary $Y$, whenever $X$ is Hausdorff, $f$ is closed and its fibers are finite. In this finite case \[  (f_*A)_ y\simeq \bigoplus _{x\in f^{-1}(y)}A_ x, \qquad R^ qf_*A=0\quad (q>0).  \] The direct-image functor is then exact, and the existing Leray edge $H^ k(Y,f_*A)\to H^ k(X,A)$ is an isomorphism. Its pullback/counit description is exactly the one already established. Proof. By the lemma the inverse-image neighborhoods form a cofinal system. The stalk limit therefore equals the limit over all open neighborhoods of $S_ y$. Apply ordinary continuity over neighborhoods from theorem 10.60.1 . In the proper locally compact Hausdorff case, closedness was just proved, fibers are compact and the ambient space is regular by lemma 10.56.5 . They are strongly paracompact by the lemma. A finite subspace of a Hausdorff space is discrete. On a finite discrete space the section functor is the finite product of stalk functors, which is exact. Its Godement section resolution consequently has no positive cohomology, and its degree-zero sections are the displayed finite direct sum. This proves both stalk assertions, including the empty sum. Stalkwise exactness of finite products shows that $f_*$ preserves short exact coefficient sequences. Finally use the exact vanishing-higher-image clause of theorem 10.55.6 ; no unrestricted proper finite-map assertion is needed. $\square$ The separation condition cannot be suppressed for an arbitrary topological proper map. For example take the finite poset of the three vertices and three edges of a triangle, with a vertex below its incident edges, and the topology of upper sets. The constant map to a point is proper with a finite fiber. The three principal vertex opens cover the space; their pairwise intersections are single edges and their triple intersection is empty. Sections on a principal open equal its least point's stalk, so those opens and their intersections are acyclic for every sheaf. For the constant $\mathbb Z$ sheaf the alternating Čech complex is that of the triangle: $\mathbb Z^3\to \mathbb Z^3$ in degrees zero and one, whose cokernel is $\mathbb Z$. The acyclic-cover comparison therefore gives $H^1=\mathbb Z$, rather than zero. Explicitly its differential is $(a,b,c)\mapsto (b-a,c-a,c-b)$, whose image is the kernel of the surjection $(r,s,t)\mapsto r-s+t$ onto $\mathbb Z$. The integral alternating comparison is proposition 10.44.14 . This is a counterexample outside the corrected hypotheses. Proposition 10.61.4 . 81E5880E3C4E Let $K$ be compact Hausdorff and $Y$ any space. For the projection $\pi :K\times Y\to Y$, \[  (R^ q\pi _*A)_ y\simeq H^ q(K,A|_{K\times \{ y\} }).  \] For a closed inclusion $i:S\hookrightarrow X$ on any space, $i_*$ is exact, $R^ qi_*=0$ for $q>0$, and $H^ q(S,A)=H^ q(X,i_*A)$. Proof. For an open $O$ containing $K\times \{ y\} $, each point $(x,y)$ has a product neighborhood $W_ x\times V_ x\subset O$. Finitely many $W_ x$ cover $K$, and the intersection $V$ of their $V_ x$ satisfies $K\times V\subset O$. Thus inverse-image neighborhoods are cofinal, directly by this finite tube argument. The slice is strongly paracompact by the product-slice case in lemma 10.44.3 , since a compact Hausdorff space is paracompact. Stalk limits and neighborhood continuity give the formula, without a separation assumption on $Y$. For a closed inclusion the stalk of $i_*A$ is $A_ x$ on $S$ and zero off $S$, so direct image is exact. It also preserves flabbiness. Pushing a flabby resolution forward therefore gives an exact flabby resolution, and its global section complex is exactly the original one on $S$. This proves the cohomology equality and higher-image vanishing on every open subset. This closed-inclusion argument does not require the finite-fiber Hausdorff theorem. $\square$

title: 10.61.5 Soft resolutions and local dimension
section: 10.61 Fibers, closed maps and sheaf cohomological dimension
text: Definition 10.61.6 . 849519FBA671 For a nonempty space define its sheaf cohomological dimension $\operatorname {cd}X$ as the least integer $n\ge 0$ such that $H^ q(X,A)=0$ for every sheaf of abelian groups and every $q>n$, or $+\infty $ if none exists. This is the cohomological definition at issue, not an unproved identification with covering dimension. All groups on the empty space are zero; bounds below can equivalently be read as their stated vanishing assertions there. Theorem 10.61.7 . 152F9B94113B For a paracompact Hausdorff space and an integer $n\ge 0$, the following conditions are equivalent: $H^ q(X,A)=0$ for all $q>n$ and all sheaves $A$; for every $A$, the $n$th cycle sheaf $Z^ n=\ker (C^ nA\to C^{n+1}A)$ is soft; every $A$ has a soft resolution of length $n$. More strongly, under the first condition the $n$th cycle sheaf of any soft resolution of $A$ is soft. For $n=0$ that cycle is identified with $A$ itself. Proof. Let $L^\bullet $ be a soft resolution with cycle $Z^ n$. For a closed $S\subset X$ put $U=X\setminus S$. Extension by zero is exact, and $(L^ j)_ U$ is soft by proposition 10.56.6 . For $n\ge 1$ the exact finite sequence \[  0\to A_ U\to (L^0)_ U\to \cdots \to (L^{n-1})_ U\to (Z^ n)_ U\to 0  \] and positive dimension shifting give $H^1(X,(Z^ n)_ U)\simeq H^{n+1}(X,A_ U)=0$. For $n=0$ this is simply the assumed vanishing of $H^1(X,A_ U)$. The stalkwise exact sequence \[  0\to (Z^ n)_ U\to Z^ n\to i_*(Z^ n|_ S)\to 0  \] and $H^1$ vanishing show that $Z^ n(X)\to Z^ n(S)$ is onto. This holds for every closed $S$, proving the stronger assertion. The Godement terms are flabby, hence soft on the paracompact space, so it implies condition(2). title: Definition 10.61.6
section: 10.61 Fibers, closed maps and sheaf cohomological dimension
text: Definition 10.61.6 . 849519FBA671 For a nonempty space define its sheaf cohomological dimension $\operatorname {cd}X$ as the least integer $n\ge 0$ such that $H^ q(X,A)=0$ for every sheaf of abelian groups and every $q>n$, or $+\infty $ if none exists. This is the cohomological definition at issue, not an unproved identification with covering dimension. All groups on the empty space are zero; bounds below can equivalently be read as their stated vanishing assertions there.

title: Theorem 10.61.7
section: 10.61 Fibers, closed maps and sheaf cohomological dimension
text: Theorem 10.61.7 . 152F9B94113B For a paracompact Hausdorff space and an integer $n\ge 0$, the following conditions are equivalent: $H^ q(X,A)=0$ for all $q>n$ and all sheaves $A$; for every $A$, the $n$th cycle sheaf $Z^ n=\ker (C^ nA\to C^{n+1}A)$ is soft; every $A$ has a soft resolution of length $n$. title: 10.62 Metric spaces, products and Euclidean bounds
