section: 10.62 Metric spaces, products and Euclidean bounds
text: Lemma 10.62.1 . D7F045ADC482 Every metrizable space is paracompact Hausdorff. Every subspace $S$ of a metrizable space $X$ is strongly paracompact in $X$. Proof. Replace a compatible metric by its minimum with $1$. Distance to a nonempty subset is then at most $1$; set distance to the empty set equal to $1$. These distance functions are continuous and $1$-Lipschitz. Well order an open cover $(U_\alpha )$ and put $f_\alpha (x)=d(x,X\setminus U_\alpha )$. For $n\ge 1$ define the closed sets \[  F_{\alpha n}=\{ f_\alpha \ge 2^{-n}\}  \cap \bigcap _{\beta <\alpha }\{ f_\beta \le 2^{-n-1}\} .  \] They lie in $U_\alpha $, and their union over $\alpha ,n$ is $X$: at a point choose its first cover member, then take $n$ large. For each fixed $n$ this is a discrete family of closed sets, meaning each point has a neighborhood meeting at most one member. Indeed, if there is a first $\alpha $ with $f_\alpha (x)>2^{-n-1}$, a small neighborhood misses every later member by this strict inequality; it misses every earlier member by the uniform gap from $2^{-n-1}$ to $2^{-n}$. If no such $\alpha $ exists, that same uniform gap gives a neighborhood missing every member. Hence the union of this family, and of any of its subfamilies, is closed. Omit empty $F_{\alpha n}$ and let $F_ n=\bigcup _\alpha F_{\alpha n}$. Define open neighborhoods \[  G_{\alpha n}=\left\{ x: d(x,F_{\alpha n})<\tfrac 13d(x,F_ n\setminus F_{\alpha n}),\quad d(x,F_{\alpha n})<\tfrac 13d(x,X\setminus U_\alpha )\right\} .  \] They contain $F_{\alpha n}$ and lie in $U_\alpha $. For fixed $n$ they are locally finite. At $x\in F_{\beta n}$, the closed union of the other $F_{\alpha n}$ has positive distance from $x$; sufficiently close to $x$, no other $G_{\alpha n}$ can satisfy its first inequality. At $x\notin F_ n$ put $a=d(x,F_ n)>0$ and choose $\beta $ with $d(x,F_{\beta n})<3a/2$. On $B(x,a/10)$ every $d(\cdot ,F_{\alpha n})\ge 9a/10$, while for $\alpha \ne \beta $ the distance to the other union is at most $8a/5$. Its one-third cannot exceed $9a/10$, so no such $G_{\alpha n}$ meets this ball. If $F_ n$ is empty there are no members to check. Set $W_ n=\bigcup _{j\le n,\alpha }G_{\alpha j}$ and $K_ n=\{ d(x,X\setminus W_ n)\ge 1/n\} $, with $K_0=\varnothing $. The $W_ n$ increase and cover $X$, the $K_ n$ are increasing closed subsets of $W_ n$, and their interiors cover $X$: once $x\in W_ N$, its positive distance from $X\setminus W_ N$ eventually exceeds $1/n$. The open sets $G_{\alpha n}\setminus K_{n-1}$ cover $X$, since the first level at which a point belongs to $W_ n$ cannot have been removed by $K_{n-1}$. They are locally finite: near a point in $\operatorname {int}K_ N$ all levels $n>N$ vanish, and the finitely many earlier levels are locally finite. This gives a locally finite refinement of the original cover, proving paracompactness. Every open neighborhood of a subspace $S$ is itself metrizable and therefore paracompact by what was just proved. Such neighborhoods form a fundamental system, so the neighborhood case of lemma 10.44.3 makes $S$ strongly paracompact in $X$. $\square$ Theorem 10.62.2 . 7857B1BE7A8D For a nonempty subspace $S$ of a metrizable space $X$, \[  \operatorname {cd}S\le \operatorname {cd}X.  \] For nonempty metrizable $X,Y$, one of them locally compact, \[  \operatorname {cd}(X\times Y)\le \operatorname {cd}X+\operatorname {cd}Y.  \] If a metrizable space is locally homeomorphic to subspaces of $\mathbb R^ n$, then its cohomological dimension is at most $n$. Proof. Only finite upper bounds need proof. Suppose $\operatorname {cd}X\le n$. First let $U\subset X$ be open. Each point of $U$ has a closed metric-ball neighborhood $N$ in $X$ contained in $U$; it is closed also in $U$. Its dimension is at most $n$ by closed-subspace monotonicity. Since $U$ is metrizable and paracompact, the closed- neighborhood locality theorem gives $\operatorname {cd}U\le n$. For any subspace inclusion $j:S\to X$ and sheaf $A$ on $S$, $j^{-1}j_*A=A$: intersections of ambient open neighborhoods with $S$ form its neighborhood basis, proving the identity on stalks. Strong-subspace continuity now gives \[  H^ q(S,A)=\varinjlim _{\Omega \supset S}H^ q(\Omega ,j_*A)=0 \qquad (q>n),  \] because every $\Omega $ is open in $X$ and has the proved dimension bound. This proves subspace monotonicity without assuming it in the open-neighborhood step. For the product first take a compact metric factor $K$, and a metric space $Y$, with dimensions bounded by $a,b$. By the compact-slice fiber formula, $R^ q\pi _*A=0$ for $q>a$ for every sheaf on $K\times Y$. The base bound gives $H^ p(Y,R^ q\pi _*A)=0$ for $p>b$. The actual first-quadrant Leray sequence of theorem 10.55.6 therefore has no terms of total degree greater than $a+b$ on its second page. Its finite cohomology filtration gives $H^\ell (K\times Y,A)=0$ for $\ell >a+b$. If $X$ is the locally compact factor, choose at each $x$ a compact closed neighborhood $K\subset X$. It has dimension at most $\operatorname {cd}X$. The sets $K\times Y$ are closed neighborhoods in the metrizable product. The compact-factor bound and closed- neighborhood locality prove the asserted inequality. Interchange the factors if $Y$ is locally compact. The interval $I=[0,1]$ has arbitrarily fine covers \[  U_{j,k}=I\cap ((j-1)/k,(j+1)/k),\qquad 0\le j\le k.  \] Only consecutive members can intersect, so there are no triple intersections of distinct members. These covers are cofinal: any open cover of a compact metric space has a positive Lebesgue number. For completeness, choose finitely many balls $B(x_ i,r_ i)$ covering the space, with $B(x_ i,2r_ i)$ in assigned cover members; then any nonempty set of diameter less than $\min r_ i$ lies in one such member. Choose $2/k$ smaller than this number. The proved cover-order corollary 10.44.15 gives $\operatorname {cd}I\le 1$. A point has dimension zero because its section functor is a stalk functor and exact. Repeatedly applying the compact product bound yields $\operatorname {cd}I^ n\le n$, including $n=0$. The usual coordinate homeomorphism $\mathbb R^ n\simeq (0,1)^ n\subset I^ n$ and metric-subspace monotonicity give the same bound for every subspace of $\mathbb R^ n$. Finally apply open-neighborhood locality on the given metrizable space to its neighborhoods homeomorphic to those subspaces. A homeomorphism preserves sheaf cohomology by its mutually inverse exact inverse-image maps, so the bound is transferred exactly. $\square$ Corollary 10.62.3 . BF9896E5CF4A Let $X$ be paracompact Hausdorff with $\operatorname {cd}X\le n$, and let $\Phi $ be enlargable in the precise sense of theorem 10.56.2 . Then \[  H^ q_\Phi (X,A)=0\qquad (q>n)  \] for every sheaf $A$. In particular this holds for compact supports when $X$ is also locally compact. A metrizable real manifold of dimension $d$ has the ordinary bound $d$, and its enlargable-support groups satisfy the same bound whenever the preceding hypotheses hold. Proof. The dimension criterion gives a soft resolution of length $n$. Its terms are $\Phi $-acyclic by the cited supported soft theorem. The actual supported resolution comparison theorem 10.56.3 computes the groups by a complex with zero terms above $n$. Local compactness makes the compact family enlargable. The manifold statement follows from the local subspace-of-$\mathbb R^ d$ theorem; it is a real dimension bound, not an assertion of coherent-sheaf vanishing above a complex dimension. $\square$
